title: 5 shows to watch this Easter weekend, starting with new Jon Hamm drama
content:
This month, Jon Hamm returns to what he does best (wear suits, talk business and look hot while doing it à la Don Draper) in the drama Your Friends and Neighbors — with one big twist.
It's not the only gem of a show out this April, though.
The new Michelle Williams series, Dying for Sex, will have you laughing unabashedly out loud, crying and feeling grateful for the privilege.
There's also a searing documentary looking at the perils of child influencing; a fresh Australian comedy about life as a first-gen, cringe-worthy teenager in the 2010s; and an adult cartoon starring and created by Ramy Youssef following a Muslim family trying to exist in the US post-9/11.
Let me tell you more about the best shows ready for streaming this Easter long weekend.
Your Friends and Neighbors — official trailer
There's just one little point of difference between Jon Hamm's iconic Mad Men character and the role he plays in his latest prestige drama series.
In a desperate attempt to maintain the creep of his lifestyle after losing his wife, house and job, hedge fund manager Andrew Cooper resorts to stealing from his rich neighbours.
It's easy, at first.
Coop knows where the rich people of the exclusive gated community keep their valuable items, and that they don't lock their doors or have alarm systems; he used to be one of them.
And no-one suspects the visibly wealthy, middle-aged white guy of larceny.
"Life boils down to a series of interconnected decisions," Coop declares as a matter of fact, upon breaking into his first home.
It's Jon Hamm, the burglar.  (Apple TV+)
But Coop uncovers more than the Patek Philippe watches and designer handbags he intends to pawn on his subsequent raids — the straight-laced people of Westmont Village, New York, are hiding dangerous secrets.
The premise is more than slightly absurd, but Hamm exists to embody a character like Coop, who suffers from an at-odds mix of high confidence and low self esteem, and frequently embarks on sharply written monologues.
The show has but one annoying quirk: every time Coop steals something, he assumes an infomercial narrator's voice and rattles off the product's specs and cost, supported by on-screen graphics.
But this is easily forgiven because Your Friends and Neighbors feels, in many ways, like Hamm's best role since Mad Men. Who cares that it bears more than a little resemblance to the part that made him a household name?
For fans of: Mad Men, Landman, Bling Ring
Dying for Sex — official trailer
The cancer is back and it's terminal.
But all Molly Kochan (Michelle Williams) can think about is sex, and how she and her meek husband Steve (Jay Duplass) haven't had it since she was first diagnosed with cancer three years ago.
Simultaneously struck by the realisation she's never had an orgasm with another person, and that she'll likely die never knowing what she's really into, Molly dumps him and logs onto the apps.
The unsolicited dick pics come thick and fast, but she revels in the attention, using the images of strangers' penises as a coping mechanism for her never-ending hospital appointments.
Molly's impending death hangs over this show, but Dying for Sex is as darkly comedic, hot and deeply horny as it is sad.
With the help of her chaos queen best friend Nikki Boyer (right), Molly Kochan (left) embarks on a sexual reawakening. (Supplied: Disney+)
Williams delivers a refreshingly raw performance as an unmoored woman desperate to embrace what she feels instead of being scared of it, and her narration of Molly's intrusive thoughts — along the lines of licking the sweat off a random man's neck in a lift — breaks the tension and electrifies this series.
The universe around Molly is impeccably crafted, too.
Guiding her through the Stage IV cancer diagnosis is best friend Nikki Boyer (comedy legend Jenny Slate), a chaos queen who doesn't hesitate to declare her undiagnosed ADHD to strangers and who fights everyone who deigns to come for her or Molly in the streets of New York.
The rest of the cast are just as distinct, with their own dramas, motivations — and ways of processing grief.
Unmistakably written and shot with the femme gaze in mind, Dying for Sex is based on the podcast of the same name, and inspired by things that actually happened to the real-life Molly Kochan.
The series' eight episodes are short, instantly moreish and somehow manage to walk the line between the absurd and a deep and meaningful exploration of desire and death, in all their complications.
For fans of: Fleabag, Joyride, Babygirl
Bad Influence: The Dark Side of Kidfluencing — official trailer
It's been a few months since the harrowing Devil in the Family docuseries revealed the extent of abuse inflicted by convicted former YouTuber Ruby Franke against her own children. Now, the similarly disturbing story of Piper Rockelle and her momager Tiffany Smith has been given the documentary treatment.
This series explores the allegations of cult-like manipulation, abuse and exploitation levelled at Smith by former members of The Squad, a YouTube collective formed in 2018 comprising aspiring child stars.
Fronted by Rockelle and controlled by Smith, The Squad racked up millions of followers and just as much money performing dances, challenges, frequently problematic pranks and creating "crush" content that crossed lines and fostered an audience overwhelmingly made up of older men.
Whether that last part was intentional or not is still in dispute.
But, in January 2022, 11 of The Squad's underage members alleged in a lawsuit they had been "frequently subjected to an emotionally, physically and sometimes sexually abusive environment" fostered by Smith.
The momager denies the allegations, and neither she nor the now-17-year-old Rockelle appear in Bad Influence.
This three-part series explores the rest of The Squad's perspectives of the ordeal, along with that of their parents.
And if one thing is made clear in Bad Influence — as in Devil in the Family — it's that the child influencers are not OK.
For fans of: Devil in the Family: The Fall of Ruby Franke, Dancing for the Devil: The 7m TikTok Cult
#1 Happy Family USA — official trailer
On September 10, 2001, things were looking up for the Muslim-American Hussein family.
Hussein (Ramy Youssef), the family's patriarch, had just brought on a new employee to help run his halal street food cart, while his wife Sharia (Salma Hindy) had just been freed from taking care of her parents.
Their eldest daughter, Mona (Alia Shawkat), had finally decided to come out to the family.
And Mona's younger brother Rumi (also Youssef) had just discovered cigarettes and become best friends with a talking lamb.
Then 9/11 happened.
Acutely aware that their New Jersey neighbours would look upon his family differently after the terror attacks, Hussein directs his family to blend in and change their values.
The first animated series from comedian, actor, writer and director Ramy Youssef (in collaboration with Pam Brady), #1 Happy Family USA is the story of the Hussein family's desperate attempt to escape Islamophobia by assimilating.
Inspired by Youssef's comedic material, the adult cartoon series is told in a mix of English and Arabic. Beyond that freshest of fresh premise, you can expect an eight-part series that's political, but not at the expense of its frequently dark humour.
For fans of: Bob's Burgers, Bojack Horseman, Tuca and Bertie
Urvi Went To An All Girls School — official trailer
It's 2010 and Naarm/Melbourne high school student Urvi only has two goals: become a famous actress like Nicole Kidman, and get Hot Ryan to break her hymen. (Hot Ryan is, of course, a forgettable douche.)
Urvi's parents, on the other hand, dream of a world in which their second-generation immigrant daughter loves trigonometry and aspires to become a doctor.
Naturally, Urvi lies to her parents about taking a make-up maths class so she can audition for the Grogan Girls and Boys combined school musical. Hot Ryan will of course be there, ready to finally notice her.
We've seen versions of teen, cringe-heavy stories featuring comics playing younger versions of themselves before, with the likes of PEN15, Fangirls and even Summer Heights High.
But this one is different.
It's distinctly Australian, speaks to creator and lead Urvi Majumdar's experience as a first-generation Indian-Australian immigrant, there's no Black or Brownface involved and it's been painstakingly honed since the first version of the show was published on YouTube a year ago.
Directed by Deadloch star Nina Oyama, this iteration of Urvi Went to an All Girls' School is part of the Fresh Blood initiative, which supports new Australian stories.
The finessed pilot episode will leave you laughing over painful straight teen culture, considering the intricacies of identity and reminiscing about how delightfully cringe we all were.
For fans of: PEN15, Content, Fangirls, White Fever

title: North of North is set in the Arctic but will make you feel warm and fuzzy
content:
A few years ago, Inuuk actors Anna Lambe and Maika Harper were doing a screen test in Germany, of all places, when they realised they had a shared dream.
"We were outside a pub chatting about how much we wanted a comedy for Indigenous people that's not trauma-centred, is funny and silly and complex," Lambe tells ABC Entertainment.
"[We thought] maybe eventually it'll come around — and maybe we'll be a part of it."
With North of North, everything they dreamed came true.
It's the first TV series of its size to be set and filmed in Nunavut — the biggest and most northern territory of Canada, which stretches across most of the country's Arctic region.
North of North — official trailer
The new coming-of-age comedy follows Inuk woman Siaja (Lambe) as she sets out to reinvent herself after a lifetime spent putting other people first.
Now 26 years old, she went from taking care of her mother Neevee (Harper) — who struggled with alcoholism in Siaja's childhood — to looking after her man-child husband Ting (Kelly William) alongside raising their six-year-old daughter Bun (Keira Cooper).
But life as a stay-at-home mum isn't for Siaja. So, she dumps Ting and starts looking for a job.
Reinventing herself in the small (fictional) town of Ice Cove is another challenge entirely: in a community where Inuit women are expected to devote their lives to raising children, Siaja's decision to work for the problematic and clueless white woman running the town community centre isn't popular.
Siaja's (left) new boss Helen (right) has good intentions, but couldn't be more exasperating. (Netflix)
Told in a mix of English and Inuktitut, North of North fuses a breadth of Inuit comedic styles — from the dry and witty to the broad and physical — creating characters that feel real and a world that's impossible to resist.
At the same time, the series doesn't shy away from the deeper issues that impact First Nations people: colonialism and its ongoing myriad impacts; tension between individualism and community; and intergenerational trauma and healing.
The contrast between light and dark makes both elements hit harder.
North of North's creators say the costumes on the show are representative of the fashion any visitor to the Arctic could expect to see. (Netflix)
Each of the series' eight episodes showcase different aspects of Inuit cultural identity, all while featuring vibrant costume design that draws inspiration from styles across the Arctic.
North of North also boasts a soundtrack including the likes of Caroline Polachek, Remi Wolf, Doja Cat and Alanis Morrisette, as well as Inuk covers of Dua Lipa's Levitating, from Riit, and Fleetwood Mac's Dreams, by Elisapie.
The result is a nuanced show that's surprising and heartbreaking at times, but also heartwarming, joyful and easy to watch.
Lambe describes it as "so unapologetically Inuk".
Stacey Aglok MacDonald and Alethea Arnaquq-Baril have been producing TV and movies in the Arctic for 20 years, and had the same dream of seeing their community represented.
They also knew from the outset that they wanted to use North of North as a way to help develop the television industry in Iqaluit, the Nunavut city where the show was shot.
So, they launched a mentorship program, which saw local trainees work in roles across departments throughout production, and hosted drama workshops for local actors, from which they cast some roles in the show — including Iqaluit's mayor, Solomon Awa.
North of North was set in the fake Nunavut town of Ice Cove, which is really Iqaluit. (Netflix)
The main cast is predominantly First Nations, with actors from other parts of Canada, Alaska and even New Zealand, and there were a number of Indigenous crew members.
Many Iqaluit residents also appear as extras throughout the series — the community feels as much like its own character in the show as the stunning Arctic landscapes.
"[The Iqaluit locals in the show] have all been getting so much love and shout-outs from within our community," Aglok MacDonald says.
"We even had a shot of a loose dog walking across the street and someone posted it on socials and they were like, 'Someone's dog made it to North of North!'"
Hacks stars Jean Smart and Hannah Einbinder talk comedy's power to platform women in Hollywood beyond their looks.
Lambe feels shooting in Iqaluit under the care of two Inuuk showrunners ensured that cultural safety and the production's impact on the community stayed front of mind.
"I think, in terms of Indigenous film and television, Indigenous representation [and] how to engage with [these] communities, it sets a new precedent," she says.
Aotearoa/New Zealand actor Jay Ryan, who plays an outsider in North of North visiting Ice Cove for research, agrees.
He recently starred in the Northern Territory-based Netflix show The Territory, which enjoyed a similar level of buzz for its representation of Indigenous people in Australia after its 2024 release — but thinks North of North reaches another level.
"Territory was great … it felt like a co-production with a lens on creating pathways for Indigenous crew members and cast, and that was a great stepping stone," he says.
"But North of North … was fully led by Indigenous creatives, cast, crew. I was the minority for once."
Jay Ryan (left) with Maika Harper (right), was on location in Nunavut for almost five months and says the few outsiders on the show were brought into the Iqaluit community "as family". (Netflix)
By all accounts, it would have been easier to film the majority of North of North somewhere like Toronto, and spend only a few weeks shooting in Iqaluit.
The show was the largest-scale project Aglok MacDonald or Arnaquq-Baril had attempted — and that Nunavut had ever seen.
The sets were built in Ontario, dismantled and then had to be either flown or shipped to Iqaluit, which cannot be reached by road from mainland Canada.
Some of the logistics had to be planned a year in advance, considering things such as when the ocean would freeze over.
Filming in -30°C weather was a standard day for the cast and crew on North of North. (Netflix)
Finding accommodation for a crew of 100 in a town of 8,000 also proved difficult: there are only so many hotels in Iqaluit, and when a big symposium was on at the same time as filming, the cast and crew had to leave Nunavut for a week.
And there was, of course, the frigid weather. Temperatures in Iqaluit are below freezing for an average of eight months a year.
In the show's first episode, two characters kiss outside. Ryan remembers it being -30°C at the time, and says the actors had to do the shot over 17 times.
But Ryan thinks the extreme cold fostered a sense of community among the cast and crew, saying there was a "real kind of school-camp mentality" at the hotel they stayed at — particularly on blizzard days, when they were forced inside.
And filming entirely on location makes North of North a Nunavut project through and through, so they wouldn't have it another way.
The Iqaluit community feels as much like its own character in North of North as the breathtaking Arctic landscapes depicted in the show. (Netflix)
There's no word yet on a second season but, with the first finally out in the world, Arnaquq-Baril has one wish.
"I hope [viewers] want to come north and are intrigued by our part of the world," she says.
"I think a lot of people don't know we exist or, if they do know anything about Inuit, they tend to think of us as historical figures — a culture that once was.
North of North is streaming now on Netflix.

title: Man saves penguin to impress a woman, ends up with a friend for life
content:
No-one does mild-mannered, gently acerbic cinema for the matinee crowd quite like the British, and the new Steve Coogan movie, The Penguin Lessons, is a no exception. Based on an unusual real-life story, it's a shamelessly corny heart-warmer, despite its outwardly grumpy protagonist and veneer of political engagement.
What: The life of a cynical English teacher in 1970s Argentina gets turned around after he rescues an orphaned penguin.
Starring: Steve Coogan, Jonathan Pryce, Vivian El Jaber, Alfonsina Carrocio, Björn Gustafsson
Director: Peter Cattaneo
When: In cinemas April 17
Likely to make you feel: Like adopting a penguin — or at least rescuing one
Coogan's on-screen partner — a Magellanic penguin by the name of Juan Salvador — may not be adept at a Michael Caine impersonation like Rob Brydon, but what he lacks in verbal wit he more than makes up for with an irresistible waddle and squawk. It's old-fashioned movie-animal charisma, the kind that's sure to melt all but the iciest of audiences.
The little guy up-ends the life of Coogan's Tom Michell, a middle-aged English teacher who's taken a position at a private boys' college in Buenos Aires in 1976. Argentina is in political turmoil, but the school — which caters to boys from rich families — is determined to stay out of the conflict, thanks to their expedient, rule-bound headmaster, Tim Buckle (the ever-wonderful Jonathan Pryce).
That suits Tom, whose youthful idealism has long since curdled into cynical indifference. To him, the appointment is an excuse for an extended holiday; so when the military stages a coup and the school is put on hiatus, he and the lovelorn Finnish science teacher, Tapio (Björn Gustafsson), take a trip to Punta del Este in Uruguay, hoping to find some local romance.
"People think penguins smell, they don't actually smell at all! They're quite interesting to watch and be alongside," Coogan told Australian Women's Weekly about working with Juan Salvador. (Supplied: Madman)
What Tom gets instead — after rescuing the lone surviving penguin from an oil slick, in a failed attempt to impress a woman — is an unwanted companion he can't seem to shake.
"Now, I've ended up with no sex and a penguin," he complains to a customs officer after he's pulled up at the border with his new avian chum — and waved through with the standard bribe.
Back at the college, this mismatched pair quickly settle into an endearing buddy comedy routine. Juan Salvador's hypnotic effect on the students, meanwhile — waddling around the classroom like a tiny field general — steers the movie into inspirational-teacher terrain.
Even Tom's old idealistic self begins to stir, especially around his working-class cleaner, Maria (a vibrant Vivian El Jaber), and her granddaughter, Sofia (Alfonsina Carrocio), a dissident whose kidnapping by the military forces Tom into a crisis of self.
"The key was to find the right balance, showing the tragic impact of the regime on two of our supporting characters, whilst keeping the story of Tom's redemption at the centre of the narrative," Director Peter Cattaneo told Variety. (Supplied: Madman/Lucia Faraig Ferrando)
As directed by The Full Monty's Peter Cattaneo, The Penguin Lessons is familiar comfort food: lovely performances, telegraphed beats and cheesy montages, with one of those jaunty scores that instructs the audience when to feel whimsical and when to be sad.
That said, it's hard not to be won over in the presence of Juan Salvador, who quietly becomes a confidante to his human companions, and who Cattaneo generously affords plenty of close-ups without making the mistake of attempting to anthropomorphise him.
The camera really loves this guy; I can't remember a penguin having this much soul on screen since the forlorn sentries that delivered Danny DeVito to his watery grave in Batman Returns. (OK, they may have been actors in penguin suits, but the point stands.)
"The penguin just listens, like very well-paid therapists often just listen,” Cattaneo told Variety. (Supplied: Madman)
Admittedly, Tom is the kind of role that Coogan could play in his sleep, and if the movie hardly tests the star's comic range, then it nestles neatly alongside his other feel-good, true-story outings — such as Philomena and Stan & Ollie (both, unsurprisingly, also penned by Jeff Pope).
Coogan does nice work shading the moral ambiguities of his character, although the movie is ultimately resistant to exploring the thornier aspects of its political backdrop — which is entirely its prerogative, as it goes, as a piece of entertainment.
Even so, things may have hit harder emotionally had the movie dared to be a little messier; as it stands, the story's suspiciously sanitised ending locks into place so neatly that you begin to wonder what's been left in the margins.
The best moment might be the actual footage of Juan Salvador, unspooling before the credits, taken by the real-life Tom Michell, whose book of the same name inspired the movie.
There were two main penguins used for most of the key scenes: life partners Richard and Baba. (Supplied: Andrea Resmini/Madman)
It's a bittersweet passage: as the penguin darts back and forth across a swimming pool to the delight of the assembled students, you can't help but be reminded of a creature taken from its natural habitat and forced to live among humans — and to serve, at least in the film's retelling, as a catalyst for their petty dramas.
Of course, as The Penguin Lessons takes pains to explain, Juan Salvador likely would have perished if left on the beach on his own, so his time at the boys' college represented an extended lease on life.
But who's to ever know what he thought of it all?

title: Aussie star Cate Blanchett 'serious' about giving up acting
content:
Oscar-winning Australian star Cate Blanchett has said she is "serious" about giving up acting.
In an interview with Radio Times in London, the 55-year-old Lord Of The Rings actor said she wanted to focus on life away from the world of stage and screen.
"My family roll their eyes every time I say it, but I mean it," Blanchett said.
The Melbourne-born actor was promoting her latest major film, Black Bag, in which she stars opposite Michael Fassbender, released in March.
Black Bag is the latest spy drama to grace our screens. But could our obsession with espionage reflect a deeper anxiety?
The movie, directed by Steven Soderbergh, is a thriller about married spies who live and work together at the Secret Intelligence Service in London.
Should she decide to retire from the profession, her latest film would top a long list of achievements.
Born in 1969, Blanchett's professional acting career began on the Australian stage.
She performed with the Sydney Theatre Company in Caryl Churchill’s Top Girls and Timothy Daly’s Kafka Dances.
In 1993, she starred opposite Geoffrey Rush in David Mamet’s Oleanna, as a student who accuses her teacher of sexual harassment.
Her breakthrough role came in 1999, however, with her Bafta-winning role as Elizabeth I in Shekar Kapur's Elizabeth.
She went on to international success and to win two Oscars — best actress for Blue Jasmine in 2014 and best supporting actress for The Aviator in 2005 — and two best actress awards at the Venice Film Festival — for I'm Not There in 2007 and Tár in 2022.
Cate Blanchett is at the 95th Academy Awards in Hollywood, Los Angeles, in 2023.  (AP: Invision/Jordan Strauss)
Blanchett spoke about her latest project during the interview and suggested that, despite her success, she considers herself to be something of an outsider in Hollywood.
"It's been a long time to remotely get comfortable with the idea of being photographed," Blanchett told the Radio Times.
"I've always felt like I'm on the periphery of things, so I'm always surprised when I belong anywhere.
"I go with curiosity into whatever environment that I’'m in, not expecting to be accepted or welcomed," she added, "I've spent a lifetime getting comfortable with the feeling of being uncomfortable.”

title: In 2013, an Aussie journalist was arrested in Egypt. His story is now a movie
content:
In February 2015, Australian journalist Peter Greste was released after spending 400 days in prison in Egypt on terrorism charges.
Greste had travelled to Egypt as a journalist for Arabic news network Al Jazeera at the end of 2013, in the wake of the Arab Spring, a series of anti-government protests and uprisings in the Middle East.
He expected to be in Egypt only a few weeks, covering for another journalist. But in December, he and his colleagues Mohamed Fadel Fahmy and Baher Mohamed were arrested, accused of spreading false information and aiding a terrorist group, the Muslim Brotherhood, who had been removed from office earlier that year.
Greste stands in a metal cage during his trial in a court in Cairo on March 24, 2014. (Reuters)
Six months later, Greste was convicted and sentenced to seven years' jail.
It was a story that galvanised journalists across the world: Ahead of the trial, journalists in 30 countries taped their mouths shut in protest.
On the 10th anniversary of Greste's release, The Correspondent — starring Richard Roxburgh (ABC TV's Rake; Prosper) as the imprisoned journalist — is in cinemas.
Screenwriter Peter Duncan suggested Roxburgh play Greste. Director Kriv Stenders thought he had the "humility, empathy and gravitas to pull it off, to make it complex and human, funny and emotional".  (Supplied: Maslow/John Platt)
The movie is based on Greste's 2017 memoir, The First Casualty, which charts his experience in prison in Egypt, while reflecting on the threats to press freedom following the 9/11 attacks and the subsequent War on Terror.
First watching the movie in a private screening, Greste was struck by the way director Kriv Stenders (Red Dog), screenwriter Peter Duncan (ABC TV's Operation Buffalo) and Roxburgh captured not only the details of his confinement and "Kafkaesque" trial, but his loss of agency and control.
"That was a pretty freaky watch," he says. "They nailed it in ways I really didn't anticipate."
The movie follows Roxburgh as Greste from his arrest in a hotel room in Cairo — where he had been listening to triple j on his computer — through a series of Egyptian prisons, to his trial, and eventual release.
The song playing on Greste's computer at the time of his arrest was Let Her Go, by Jagwar Ma. He is pictured with Roxburgh and Stenders at the Sydney premiere. (Supplied: Maslow)
Much of it is shot in close-up, the camera trained on Roxburgh's face, reflecting the claustrophobia of Greste's experience.
"It was important that the audience felt like they were Peter going into this completely surreal, unfolding nightmare," Roxburgh says.
While Greste was at first anxious about making The Correspondent, he quickly came to trust the filmmakers with his story.
"They showed the kind of empathy and curiosity that made me feel quite safe," he says.
The Correspondent trailer
He became a collaborator on the movie, including lending the art department the Akubra hat he was wearing when he was arrested.
The hat sits between Greste and Roxburgh as they talk to ABC Entertainment. "This hat's been with me through most of my career," Greste says, gesturing to it. "I'd like to think that when you put it on, Rox, it kind of inhabited something."
"I didn't have to do anything; just let the hat do the work," Roxburgh quips.
Stenders came on board after talking with producer Carmel Travers. When she asked if he knew anything about Greste's story, he answered with a laugh: "I've known Peter since I was a child."
While they'd only met once or twice as kids, their families are still friends today — living in Brisbane as part of the Latvian migrant community, their fathers having come to Australia as refugees.
"I knew [Greste's] story well. It was a big story amongst our family," Stenders says.
But Stenders wanted to focus the film on the book and the script, which had Greste's tick of approval.
"It's about telling that story as truthfully and as authentically as possible," Stenders says. "I felt like I had the permission to go tell the story with the kind of verisimilitude that it needed."
WATCH: Richard Roxburgh and Peter Greste talk about The Correspondent (ABC News Breakfast)
That verisimilitude — the appearance of being real — is remarkable, considering The Correspondent was shot in Sydney.
Much of the cast is made up of Middle Eastern Australian actors, including Julian Maroun as Fahmy and Rahel Romahn as Mohamed.
"Sydney's got one of the deepest, widest, richest Middle Eastern diasporas in the world," Stenders says. "It's amazing the amount of talent that's out there, and I was [spoiled] for choice.
"[I wanted to] make the film feel really authentic and not feel like we'd shot in Australia and used anglicised Middle Eastern actors, or God forbid, non-Middle Eastern actors."
Locations for the movie included the colonial Parramatta Gaol; Manly Barracks; Callan Park, a disused mental health facility; and the Coal Loader, a 1920s transfer depot for coal, where Stenders had previously shot NCIS Sydney.
"We knew that we could pull the film off because we had these locations," Stenders says. "And because of this first-person, point-of-view style we shot the film in, we didn't have to build Egypt.
"We just had to build what Peter saw, which unlocked the whole film for me."
For Roxburgh, some of the emotional truth of the movie came from the conditions on set, shooting over Sydney summer.
"Happily, it was a really horrible working environment," he says with a smile. "That was really helpful. It was smelly and hot [and] we were underground for a lot of it."
The movie was also shot on 50-millimetre lenses, giving it a sense of intimacy and immediacy. (Supplied: Maslow/John Platt)
To try to replicate the look and feel of the light in Egypt, director of photography Geoffrey Hall shot on lenses without a final resin coating on them.
"They flare really beautifully," Stenders explains. "Once we found those lenses, we went, 'Wow, that throws you somewhere that isn't Australia. That's going to cover up a lot of sins, but it's also going to give us this feeling that we're in the Middle East.'"
In The Correspondent, as Greste comes to terms with the restrictions of his new life in prison, he flashes back to a haunting memory of the murder of his producer Kate Peyton (played by Yael Stone) in Somalia in 2005.
For Stenders, the dual plot lines in Somalia and Egypt "point to the price journalists pay: Sometimes they pay for it with their lives. Sometimes they have to pay for it with their conscience." (Supplied: Maslow)
She is just one of the 1,963 journalists and media workers killed in the line of duty since 2001, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.
More journalists and media workers were killed last year — at least 124 — than have been killed since the organisation began collecting data in 1992, with nearly two-thirds of them Palestinians killed in the Israel-Gaza war.
These statistics — alongside other attacks on journalism, like the Trump administration banning the Associated Press from the White House — make The Correspondent feel urgent in 2025.
"It's not new for journalism to be curtailed and for journalists to be imprisoned," Roxburgh says. "What I guess is new is the amount of times now that journalists are deliberately targeted.
"I thought it was an important message to start to talk more about. If we can make a film — make art — that provokes conversations around that, great."
Roxburgh recalls feeling "gobsmacked" when he first heard about Greste's imprisonment in 2013. (Supplied: Maslow)
Stenders adds: "If the film just makes people stop for a second and think about [censorship and press freedoms], then it's done its job, because complacency is a killer."
For Greste, the ongoing relevance of his story feels almost eerie.
"The War on Terror created a kind of rhetoric around national security that allowed governments to come after uncomfortable journalism," he explains.
"I felt as we moved further away from 9/11, the more we'd leave that rhetoric behind … and journalism would recover its position. I never really expected that it would feel more relevant now, than it did back then, 10 years ago, when I walked out of prison.
"That's both gratifying for the film, but also really troubling for me."
Greste greets supporters at Brisbane Airport after arriving home from Egypt in 2015. (AAP: Dave Hunt)
Greste sees parallels between the challenges facing journalism and the arts, both in terms of changing business models and in terms of their social license.
"The attacks that we're seeing on journalism I think are reflected in the arts community," he says.
"The attacks on both of these institutions in the culture wars, the attacks from government of these institutions, all of it's part of the same narrative."
As attacks on journalists in places like Gaza and Ukraine have increased over the past couple of years, there have also been attempts to stymie artists' political expression in Australia, as in the cases of Khaled Sabsabi, Jayson Gillham, Kellee Green at the Queensland Music Awards and the cast of The Seagull at Sydney Theatre Company.
"I feel strongly that one of the great roles of art is to be a place of provocation," Roxburgh says.
"Artists have to be free to think and to discuss and to talk and to have opinions, otherwise we may as well be doing other stuff."
The Correspondent is in cinemas from April 17.

title: Napoleon Dynamite and Mad Max are indi success stories. Can it still happen?
content:
Western cinema is littered with rags-to-riches stories of independent films making millions, but in an age of streaming where box offices are bypassed altogether, are windfalls becoming a thing of the past?
George Miller's Mad Max of 1979, for example, was made with a budget of $350,000 and went on to make nearly $100 million in box office gross earnings.
In the United States, Jared Hess's Napoleon Dynamite of 2004 cost about $400,000 and grossed more than $46 million.
South Australian filmmaker John deCaux has recently received funding from a US company to make a feature horror film called Drop Bear.
He said the market for independent films had changed, but pointed to Adelaide's Michael and Danny Philippou's 2023 debut feature, Talk to Me, as a recent example of success.
Film studio logos are as well-known as our favourite movie actors, but are they finally losing their prominence due to the rise of streaming?
It was made for about $5 million and became the highest-grossing horror film for American independent entertainment company, A24, earning $140 million in global box office sales.
"The Napoleon Dynamites are super rare and are exceptions to the rule but traditionally, for most filmmakers, it's about learning a craft and doing it over and over, and building up to those bigger projects.
"We found our way of making money through a beekeeping series on YouTube, and through YouTube revenue."
Danny and Michael Philippou debuted their first feature film at the Adelaide Film Festival in 2022. (Supplied)
The Philippous too had been creating short films and clips for their YouTube channel RackaRacka for about a decade prior to securing backing for their first feature, which is now getting a second life on Netflix — currently ranked in the global top 10 most watched chart.
deCaux said there had been two major shifts in filmmaking over the past 20-odd years.
First was the shift in medium from film to digital, making cameras more affordable and bypassing the need to buy, develop and edit on film.
Then there was the emergence of online streaming services in the mid-1990s that evolved with technology into more user-friendly platforms, like YouTube in 2005 and Netflix in 2007.
Ratings data shows young people are turning away from traditional television in droves in favour of online streaming platforms and social media. But an expert says free-to-air television still has a role.
But streaming's convenience reduced attendance numbers in cinemas, prompting major Hollywood studios to take less risks on new ideas and spend big money on safer bets like superhero franchises.
Conversely, streaming platforms opened up new channels for low and mid-budget films that might not have been made or distributed otherwise.
South Australian Film Corporation chief executive Kate Croser said "the era of breakout indie films certainly isn't over, it's just evolving".
"The more popular the film is on the [streaming] platform, the more views it gets, and the more buzz it generates, the more likely the streamer is to want to work with the filmmaker again and may even directly commission their next project," she said.
"Streaming can amplify success, in many ways … it can mean massive global exposure, sometimes more than a limited theatrical release could, and it can also allow films to have two rounds of critical and audience success."
Kate Croser says streaming has created new opportunities. (ABC Radio Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)
Beyond negotiating acquisition contracts, however, independents creating a film for streaming platforms alone cannot benefit from the box office sales of the past.
Ms Croser said acquisition agreements with streaming services and the rates paid were often commercial in confidence, but they could be boosted by star power or large existing audiences.
"Typically, the streamer either pays the filmmaker a flat fee to win the rights to the film outright, or the filmmaker will licence the film to the streamer for a set period of time, either exclusively or non-exclusively, after which they may licence it elsewhere," she said.
"Revenue sharing arrangements can be a possibility, more commonly on smaller platforms [based on subscriber views or engagement time]."
1979's Mad Max made nearly $100 million in gross box office sales off a budget of $350,000. (Supplied)
But she said there were other benefits, such as low and mid-budget films not needing to sell as much to break even and return a profit, and streamers being able to commission directly from filmmakers and finance their production.
"Depending on the platform, this can open up much bigger budgets and global audiences than might otherwise be available," Ms Croser said.
She added the lack of a programming schedule and the need for a "huge catalogue of content" for varied demographics made it an "especially fertile ground for genre films or those with a specific or niche interest audience".
Regardless of how a project would be distributed, Ms Croser added that international film festivals remained "critical launch pads" that contributed to whether an independent film, or TV series, was a critical and/or commercial success.
SA animated feature Lesbian Space Princess premiered at the Berlinale in Germany. (Supplied: We Made A Thing Studios)
She said SA's Run Rabbit Run was acquired by Netflix off the back of its world premiere at Sundance Film Festival in 2023 and "smashed the streamer's ratings in its first week of release" with 6 million views.
Stan series Thou Shalt Not Steal premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and SXSW Sydney and became one of Australia's biggest critical hits last year.
And SA's animated feature, Lesbian Space Princess, has recently been acquired for worldwide distribution after winning best feature after its premiere at the Berlinale in Germany.
"Cinemas aren't the only kingmakers anymore," Ms Croser said.
"It's a mix including streaming, festivals, smart distribution and a rise in audience-generated buzz."

title: Why is Oscar-winner Viola Davis in a straight-to-streaming action flick?
content:
There are movies you'd expect to see critically revered EGOT winner Viola Davis star in, and there are those you wouldn't.
G20 is the latter.
What: Action thriller in which a Black woman US president becomes the number one target of terrorists who take over the annual G20 summit.
Directed by: Patricia Riggen
Starring: Viola Davis, Marsai Martin, Anthony Anderson, Antony Starr
Where: Streaming now on Prime Video
Likely to make you feel: Exhausted from the suspension of disbelief required to finish this movie
In the political action thriller, the 59-year-old plays Danielle Sutton, a Black woman president of the United States whose administration is flailing at home and abroad.
Sutton worked twice as hard to reach the presidency so she could make a difference. But now that she's in office, all people care about is what she's wearing. All Sutton wants is for them to listen to what she has to say.
At the same time, her daughter Serena (Marsai Martin) has a tendency to slip her Secret Service detail and sneak out of the White House, prompting political pundits to question how Sutton could possibly keep her country safe when she can't even keep track of her daughter.
Things take a drastic turn for the worse at the eponymous G20 summit in Cape Town, where the majority of this movie is set (the film's director said South Africa offered tax incentives).
Sutton brings her rebellious daughter with her to the annual meeting so that she and her doting husband (Martin's former Black-ish co-star, Anthony Anderson) might keep her safe and under control.
Except the summit is overtaken by terrorists, and Sutton is their number one target.
With help hours away and no other world leader possibly capable of stepping up, the US president must save everyone.
Luckily, Sutton saw combat in the US military 20 years ago and still has the muscles to prove it.
G20 — official trailer
Davis is best known for her dramatic work, such as her Oscar-winning role in Fences, that often tackles big themes: from the power and powerlessness of Black women and the way we hold this at the same time, to what it is to be a woman in charge in the 2020s.
But she has delved into the world of action and thriller movies before, including Suicide Squad, Widows and The Woman King.
So, in that respect, leading a film like this isn't totally out of left field.
Except G20 is a slow and forgettable straight-to-streaming action movie that feels like a satire but isn't.
G20 has a formulaic plot and requires near total suspension of disbelief — at one point, Davis maneuvers a helicopter that's about to fall off a skyscraper. (Prime Video: Ilze Kitshoff)
It's doused in a confusing combination of dated, surface-level feminist rhetoric and pro-US government and military sentiment.
Even Davis can't save a character like Sutton, whose defining characteristics are that she's a mother and wife above all, who refuses to wear "medieval torture devices", AKA high heels.
Sutton's sullen daughter isn't any better, though it is refreshing to see former child star Martin take on a more serious role after years in the comedy scene.
Serena's transformation from unruly teen to devoted daughter who helps save the day is entirely predictable. (Prime Video: Ilze Kitshoff)
It's not a good sign when you're forced to admit a white man is the most exciting character in a Black-led film trying very hard to be feminist. But the film's racist and anti-big-government villain — brought to life by The Boys' Antony Starr — is the only one who will make you feel something in G20 beyond mild disappointment.
And that's only because his diabolical one-liners offer a perverse comedic relief. (At one point, he threatens to thumb someone's eyes out; at another, he declares he doesn't "speak Asian".)
"I remember Viola saying, 'I want a popcorn movie! I want to watch it with my daughter and have fun,'" director Patricia Riggen told a virtual press conference ahead of the film's release.
Riggen, whose credits include Dopesick and The 33, thinks the most important thing people will get from the film is "two hours of straight fun in which they won't think about anything else, but just be clapping and cheering and feeling and laughing".
"And the other thing, and that's a more subconscious thing, is how cool it is to have a woman in the presidency? That's something I personally am very proud of."
"[I've] heard from people that ... there's a moment in which you actually side with the villain [played by Antony Starr]," director Patricia Riggen said.  (Prime Video: Ilze Kitshoff)
Davis agreed, saying the effect of G20 is "exactly" what was intended and that she hopes "girls and women" will walk away from the film and "feel like they're capable".
This begs the question: are we talking about the same film?
Women's empowerment doesn't feel like the biggest takeaway from G20. The fact that the concept of a Black woman president of the United States remains a fantasy does.
It doesn't even feel like the second-biggest takeaway, which is probably that even if we were to see a Black woman president of the United States in our lifetime, she would apparently have to be an overwhelmingly patriotic ex-soldier capable of single-handedly defeating armed terrorists if she were to have any chance at earning the respect of her peers.
How fun and inspiring.
G20 is streaming now on Prime Video.

title: Why China's hit against Hollywood should have Trump worried
content:
Welcome to ICYMI, where we recap the pop culture and entertainment news you might have missed over the past week.
If you have a stonks-minded person in your life, you may have noticed them melting down for the past week over US President Donald Trump's wild tariff frenzy.
US markets plunge again as optimism over President Donald Trump's tariffs "pause" is overshadowed by his escalating trade war with China.
After promising to heavily increase taxes on imports from basically every country in the world, Trump then created further chaos by enacting a 90-day pause on the most extreme tariffs for every country — except China.
In retaliation to eye-watering tariffs on Chinese goods, Beijing's National Film Administration released a statement claiming the tariffs further soured domestic demand for US cinema in China.
"We will follow market rules, respect the audience's choices, and moderately reduce the number of American films imported," the NFA said on its website.
But Trump seems less than concerned.
"I think I've heard of worse things," he said when asked about the issue at a US cabinet meeting on Thursday, eliciting chuckles from his surrounding secretaries.
And… he might not be far off.
It's true that, since the turn of the millennium, Hollywood has seen China as a potential area for profit, as the second-largest film market in the world.
2019's Avengers: Endgame pulled in nearly $US1 billion in the Chinese market alone, and they're really into the Fast and Furious, with the seventh and eighth instalments of the franchise each clocking a cool $US500 million in the Chinese box office.
But the popularity of domestic films has exploded post-COVID, with locally produced animation Ne Zha 2 raking in $US3.3 billion this year, toppling Pixar's Inside Out 2 to become the highest-grossing animated film of all time.
NeZha 2 International Trailer
Aside from the financial loss, there is some concern over the US losing its "soft power" influence in China.
Chen Hong, executive director of the Asia-Pacific Studies Centre at East China Normal University, told The Global Times that American films had long been a key tool for spreading their values and establishing a polished image of itself around the globe.
"[But these policies have] led audiences to question the authenticity of US cultural narratives, fuelling a preference for homegrown content that reflects China's cultural confidence," Chen said.
Trump's blasé attitude towards the NFA's announcement could also have something to do with his general disdain for Hollywood, as many prominent figures backed democratic rival Kamala Harris in the 2024 US election.
In January, Trump announced long-time supporters Jon Voight, Mel Gibson and Sylvester Stallone as "special ambassadors" to Hollywood.
"They will serve as Special Envoys to me for the purpose of bringing Hollywood, which has lost much business over the last four years to Foreign Countries, BACK—BIGGER, BETTER, AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!," Trump said on Truth Social at the time.
About four years on from her most-recent album, Solar Power, Aotearoa/New Zealand singer-songwriter Lorde has joined TikTok and teased a tantalising snippet of upcoming track 'WWT' (What Was That).
The clip sees the angsty 28-year-old walk-running through New York's Washington Square Park wearing an untucked white shirt, grungy jeans with a thick, heavily accessorised chain (is this the next level up from the carabiner?) and over-ear headphones, while she vaguely sings along to the lyrics.
"Since I was 17 / I gave you everything / Now we wake from a dream / Well baby, what was that? / What was that?"
We only have 15 seconds to go off, but it's already clear 'WWT' is a significant departure from Lorde's last studio album.
This isn't the sort of song you have to sit with to truly appreciate: it goes hard.
Could the Grammy-Award-winning artist's next record be a return to her Melodrama era, with added Charli XCX influences (who could forget the collab of 2024, 'Let's Work it Out on the Remix')?
Whatever the Lorde giveth, we shall taketh.
The world's biggest artists return to Coachella this weekend, and you can catch their sets from home. (Supplied)
Coachella (the couch sitter's version) is back for another year, with the festival's 24th edition once again live-streamed for all of us unable to make it to Indio, California.
Saturday 12 April
Featuring: Lady Gaga, Missy Elliott, Parcels, LISA, Mustard, Lola Young, The Prodigy, Djo, SPEED, Kneecap and more.
AEST: 9am-6pm
ACST: 8.30am-5.30pm
AWST: 7am-4pm
Sunday 13 April
Featuring: Travis Scott, Green Day, Charli XCX, Jimmy Eat World, Misfits, Beth Gibbons, Clairo, The Dare and more.
AEST: 9am-7pm
ACST: 8.30am-6.30pm
AWST: 7am-5pm
Monday 14 April
Featuring: Post Malone, Megan Thee Stallion, Shaboozey, JENNIE, Zedd, XG, Arca, Amyl and the Sniffers and more.
AEST: 9am-4.30pm
ACST: 8.30am-4pm
AWST: 7am-2.30pm
Headlined by Lady Gaga, Green Day, Travis Scott and Post Malone, the three-day festival — held twice, this weekend and next — also features performances from the likes of Missy Elliott, Charli XCX, the Misfits, Megan thee Stallion, Lisa, Kraftwerk, The Prodigy and many, many more.
Australian acts include Amyl and the Sniffers, five-piece band Parcels, Sydney hardcore group SPEED, techno DJ HAAi and Glass Beams.
The stream kicks off on Saturday at 9am AEST (Friday 4PM PDT), and there are two ways to watch: Coachella's Youtube channel, which boasts six-concurrent streams, as well as the Coachella Livestream app on iOS and Android. Additionally, DJ sets from the electronic Quasar Stage will also be live-streamed as vertical videos via Youtube Shorts.
Each day's stream will be broadcast again in full after it ends, meaning you have two chances to catch each performance. There's also next weekend.
With each day's stream beginning a few hours into the festival, you can't watch every single artist's set at home, but more than 70 acts will be shown — including all of the above names, with the full list of live-streamed acts underneath each stage's Youtube videos.
Two acts you definitely won't catch are Brazilian artist Anitta and alt-pop artist FKA Twigs, with both dropping off the line-up in recent weeks.
There are also questions as to whether Weezer, a last-minute addition, will play their set slated for 4pm Sunday AEST.
Earlier this week, writer Jillian Shriner — the wife of Weezer bassist Scott Shriner — was shot by the LAPD and charged with attempted murder after allegedly turning a pistol on officers as they followed a hit-and-run suspect to Shriner's neighbour's yard. Sources tell Variety the band will perform "as of now".
The prestigious Cannes Film Festival has just announced their 2025 line up, with projects from Wes Anderson, Ari Aster and Richard Linklater among the 19 films vying for the coveted Palme d'Or.
Anderson's The Phoenician Scheme has been pegged as an espionage black comedy; Aster's Eddington is a pandemic-set Western starring Joaquin Phoenix, Pedro Pascal and Emma Stone; and Linklater's Nouvelle Vague is a French-language tribute to director Jean-Luc Godard and the French New Wave.
Behind the blood and guts, The Substance carried a viscously important message about how society treats women as they age. Its breakthrough at the Oscars is a landmark moment for women in horror.
Among the other nominations for the top prize, six films are directed by women, including a new title from Julia Ducournau — whose win for Titane in 2021 made her only the second female filmmaker to ever receive the top honour. Her new film, Alpha, set in 1980s New York, follows an 11-year-old with a parent who has AIDS.
Last year's festival premiered Academy Award best-picture winner Anora, as well as Oscar contenders like Emilia Pérez and The Substance.
The Un Certain Regard category — which recognises the first or second films of promising filmmakers — includes directorial debuts from actors Scarlett Johansson and Babygirl's Harris Dickinson. Johansson will premiere Eleanor the Great, a drama starring Thelma's June Squibb, while Dickinson's Urchin follows a homeless person in London trying to turn his life around.
Spike Lee's English-language remake of Japanese filmmaker Akira Kurosawa's Highest 2 Lowest will also premiere out of competition, after being belatedly announced by Lee himself over Instagram.
The 78th Cannes Film Festival runs May 13 to 24, with Robert De Niro set to receive an honorary Palme d'Or for lifetime achievement.
Britpop legends Pulp will release their first album in 24 years this June (Tom Jackson)
Legendary British band Pulp have announced they will release their first new album in 24 years. The band's eighth album will be called More and released on Friday June 6. It is dedicated to the band's bassist Steve Mackey, who died in 2023.
Pulp's last album was 2001's We Love Life, produced by the great Scott Walker and released the year before the band split for the first time in 2002.
A reunion in 2011 saw them make only their second visit to Australia (gee those shows were good), but the band broke up again in 2013. They reactivated in 2022 for a string of dates in the UK and US, and it was during those tours that they got the itch to start creating new music for the first time in decades.
"This seemed to open the floodgates: we came up with the rest of the songs on this album during the first half of 2024. A couple are revivals of ideas from last century," frontman Jarvis Cocker said.
Pulp formed in 1978 but didn't find success until the mid-1990s, when they became one of the leading lights in the dominant Britpop movement. Songs like 'Common People', 'Do You Remember The First Time?', 'Disco 2000' and 'Party Hard' remain indie anthems of the era.
Today, the band released 'Spike Island', the first single from the new album. Watch the video, in which Cocker uses AI to animate old photos of the band from the 90s, below.
Pulp - Spike Island
We might have to wait a little while to see snippets of other Cannes-premiering films, but Wes Anderson has already blessed us with a trailer for his upcoming project. A gift for fans of symmetry and Michael Cera.

title: This post-apocalyptic film uses real footage from the world right now
content:
When the pandemic racked the globe in 2020 and many of us feared it was the literal end of the world, London filmmaker Asif Kapadia (Amy, Senna, Diego Maradona) recruited the journalists he trusted most to help him piece together what on earth was going on.
What: A hybrid documentary about the end of the world that's happening now.
Directed by: Asif Kapadia
Starring: Samantha Morton in the speculative fiction elements, with journalists including Carole Cadwalladr as documentary talking heads
When: Streaming on DocPlay now
Likely to make you feel: Despairing but determined
Not just regarding the disaster of COVID-19, but also the proliferation of misinformation exploding during that time.
"I remember thinking, 'Can everyone see what I can see?'"
Kapadia had become increasingly unnerved in 2016 when the twin shock waves of Brexit and Donald Trump's election win dealt an enormous blow to progressive politics.
"Lots of politicians were coming on TV and the radio and being quite overtly racist, and the journalists interviewing them were letting it slide," he says.
"It's everything that's happening here in the UK, in the US, India, Turkey, China, Hong Kong, Brazil, Gaza, all over the place. Every day you wake up, you read the news, and you go, 'My God, what have they done?'"
One of the people Kapadia trusted was investigative reporter Carole Cadwalladr: "She was the first journalist that I read saying that it was Facebook that was somehow helping to manipulate us, and I thought, 'I'm not crazy.'"
Wanting to explore further how our social-media addiction was exacerbating overlapping crises, Kapadia reached out to Cadwalladr and other journalists connecting the dots. It was the beginning of what would become his hybrid documentary-fiction film, 2073.
It posits a near-future world in which "the event" 37 years before has precipitated the collapse of everything. The climate is almost unliveable. Those who can, cluster in ivory towers far above the horror below. An Ivanka-Trump-like figure rules over America with an authoritarian grip as drones surveil all those who scrabble in the ruins. Armoured cops act as judge, jury and executioner.
Kapadia says Samantha Morton's character represents "all the stuff going on in my head ... all of this stuff bombarding us, and all you're trying to do is survive". (Supplied: Madman)
The Serpent Queen star, Samantha Morton, is our window on this dark mirror world, a survivor fighting the system who says, "It's too late for me. It may not be too late for you."
But here's the thing: the shocking scenes of armoured police brutalising protesters, of bomber drones and devastating fires and floods, aren't fiction. They're actual documentary footage spliced into the sci-fi story.
Thanks to the global success of Amy — Kapadia's 2015 Oscar-winning documentary about the tragic loss of singer-songwriter Amy Winehouse, stitched entirely from archival material — many people see him as a straight-up documentarian.
But Kapadia's debut feature, 2001's BAFTA-winning The Warrior, was a feudal epic riffing on Indian mythology. Before that, his film-school short, Indian Tales, set in contemporary Hackney, also delved into the fantastical.
"My drama background is where the idea of turning the news into a narrative came from," Kapadia says.
He was also inspired by French filmmaker Chris Marker's 1962 science-fiction short, La Jetée. Set in a destroyed Paris post-WWIII, it follows a time traveller as he attempts to avert nuclear war. Remarkably, it's predominantly told via still photography.
"I thought if Chris could use stills to do time travel in the 60s, then I could use archive footage in a film set in the future, but obviously it's yesterday, it's now, it's tomorrow," Kapadia says.
Kapadia says he wants 2073 to galvanise, rather than paralyse its audience. (Supplied)
He says 2073's Blade-Runner-like scenario reflects our current-day slide towards technology-fuelled fascism.
"It's this gradual creep of laws, with protest banned and immigrants and disabled people framed as bad, but we won't tax those tech billionaires as AI replaces doctors in our health systems," he says.
"Journalists are being cut week by week. Who sponsors culture?"
Morton's character represents Kapadia's (and our) inner monologue as disaster after disaster is beamed into our living rooms.
"Her voice is all of the stuff going on in my head, trying to struggle through every day with all of this stuff bombarding us, and all you're trying to do is survive," he says.
But the last thing the filmmaker wants is to paralyse. Instead, 2073, five years in the making, is a rabble-rousing rallying cry.
The fearless journalists Kapadia spoke to for 2073 gave him great hope for the future. Cadwalladr says the feeling is mutual.
"That's the magic of the film because I've been trying to tell these stories journalistically and it's really complex and hard for people to grasp," she says.
"But by injecting this emotional story into it, with Samantha Morton, it's a gateway to a whole different level of understanding. You feel it personally."
Cadwalladr says the film crystallises what's at stake.
In 2073, the climate is almost unliveable and armoured cops act as judge, jury and executioner. (Supplied: Madman)
"Even for the doomsters amongst us, of which I very much count myself, it's the rate of acceleration happening in the US that nobody really predicted that's very worrying."
With more than 70 per cent of the world living under authoritarian rule, the film underlines how the increasing reach of digital technology, including AI, is bound up in the grip of autocratic leaders and their billionaire backers. There's everything from facial recognition scanning to bot farms swaying elections, all while the planet heats up uncontrollably.
"Every year, computer power is doubling," Cadwalladr says. "It's like the pandemic, doubling every day, and we don't know where that ends — it feels very scary."
But much like Kapadia, she refuses to lose hope.
Kapadia agrees it's not too late to stop "the event".
"I'm an eternal optimist and I grew up in a family that's very mouthy," he says.
"Don't just sit there saying, 'Well, what's the point?' The moral of 2073 is do whatever is in your power now."
2073 screens on DocPlay from April 10.

title: Cillian Murphy has used his fame to tell a very Irish tragic tale
content:
If Hollywood works the way it does in the popular imagination, then Cillian Murphy presumably could have cashed in his Oscar-winning performance in Oppenheimer for any number of leading-man offers: the dreamy, conflicted man of science presiding over an apocalyptic thriller; a brooding hit-man dispensing existential bon mots over bone-crunching beat-downs; a galaxy-eyed supervillain in the next multi-million dollar Marvel movie that nobody in particular cares about.
What: In 1985, an Irish coal merchant discovers a dark secret at a convent whose sisters wield power over the town.
Starring: Cillian Murphy, Emily Watson, Eileen Walsh, Zara Devlin
Director: Tim Mielants
When: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Quietly moved
Instead, he's done what any self-respecting Irishman with limited interest in stardom might do, and returned to his homeland — and to his old collaborators — for a sombre, knitwear-clad drama about a family man wrestling with the dark secrets preying on a small town. (Proving his dedication, Murphy actually pitched the project to co-producer Matt Damon while on the set of Christopher Nolan's blockbuster.)
In Small Things Like These — which is based on Claire Keegan's acclaimed, prize-winning 2020 novel — Murphy is all gloomy grey beanies and dirty fingernails as Bill Furlong, a hardworking coal merchant and well-loved father of five girls in the quiet, drizzly Irish town of New Ross.
It's Christmas 1985, although aside from the sound of 'Come On Eileen' squeaking from a pub jukebox, the sleepy port town might as well exist out of time.
"[Author Claire Keegan] is so precise in what she chooses to say ... and that's perfect for [director Tim Mielant]'s way of working," Eileen Walsh (pictured) told Radio Times. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Bill himself is a man adrift, increasingly unmoored from a clockwork life and otherwise loving family. It's an impression that Murphy's boyishness, even in middle age, lends itself to perfectly; he's a man with one foot in childhood, haunted by memories to his life as a lonely, bullied child back in the 1950s, when he lived with his single mother.
The flashbacks are beginning to worry his wife, Eileen (Eileen Walsh), who fears her husband is on the verge of a breakdown, and Bill's episodes are only exacerbated after he stumbles upon Sarah (Zara Devlin), a young woman five months pregnant and locked, shivering and distressed, in a freezing shed.
"[These women] were just taken out of society, sometimes for just being too attractive," Murphy told CBC. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Bill delivers Sarah to the local convent, where the sisters' veneer of compassion can barely disguise their sinister motives. When he meets the mother superior (Emily Watson), by turns warm and secretive, it's apparent that something untoward is afoot.
Despite a title that sounds suspiciously similar to (and most likely inspired) this classic tweet, Small Things Like These is anything but twee contemporary fiction.
Keegan, the writer behind 2022's sleeper hit The Quiet Girl, drew her tale from the notorious Magdalene Laundries scandal in Ireland, in which asylums set up for "fallen women" were exposed to have engaged in decades of abuse.
"It's the most unholy, un-Christian thing that she [Sister Mary] presides over," Emily Watson told Deadline. (Supplied: Roadshow)
There's menace rippling under the movie's slow-burn exterior. As in the real-life events, the members of the convent wield enormous influence over the good Catholic townsfolk, and at one point even threaten the education of Bill's kids — to every effect, they're mafia with a habit.
The knowledge that the Catholic Church was up to no good is hardly breaking news, but the movie nonetheless has a quiet power and grace, telling a story of corruption and control that remains resonant.
Deftly written by Irish playwright Enda Walsh — whose stage play (and later, film) Disco Pigs gave Murphy his early career breakout — and directed with unfussy modesty by Tim Mielants (Peaky Blinders), the film is empathic and clear-eyed, in spite of material that could easily have lent itself to cliché.
"It's a book written by a woman about a man ... but it's actually a story about women, really," Murphy told Radio Times. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Murphy is the essential element here; he holds the movie together through sheer force of presence, even as it sometimes threatens to tread familiar terrain.
His performance is a study in compassion and survival, in the ways one's own traumatic experience might lead to empathy instead of cyclical abuse. Here's a man raised by a single mother, and a foster mother, a man who has possibly been abused himself, who has taken his own pain and transformed it into something almost maternal.
It's all there in Murphy's silence; he's one of the rare modern actors capable of conveying emotional depth while speaking very little, of suggesting decades of repressed trauma with a look. Of course, those expressively opaque eyes, popping like street lamps against the Irish winter, don't go astray, either.
As he did in Oppenheimer, Murphy suggests worlds of conflict beyond the word. In repose, his stillness says so much.
