title: A Minecraft Movie's viral moment sheds light on shift in film industry
content:
A Minecraft Movie hit cinemas last week, and it predictably took over the box office, the world and the internet.
The film — based on the highest-selling video game of all time, Minecraft — delivered a global opening weekend of $US301 million ($493 million), unseating 2023's The Super Mario Bros. Movie as the biggest video game adaptation opening ever.
The movie centres around a washed-up gamer, a real estate agent, and two kids who find themselves sucked into The Overworld of Minecraft, where they join forces with a man trapped there years previously.
Before this weekend, box office returns were lagging 13 per cent compared with last year.
Thanks to A Minecraft Movie, that gap is down to 5 per cent.
In a tale as old as time for both kids' movies and video game adaptations, critics haven't exactly been as kind to A Minecraft Movie as audiences have.
Review aggregators Metacritic and Rotten Tomatoes have it sitting at 47 and 48 per cent, respectively, meaning less than half of official critical reviews are positive.
The mammoth box office returns and soaring audience ratings of 87 per cent on Rotten Tomatoes suggest critic scores do not really matter on films made to capitalise on what is popular with kids.
Meg Herrmann says production companies are still working out how to create viral content. (
               ABC News: Christopher Gillette
            )
University of Queensland PhD candidate Meg Herrmann said producers were trying to find ways to bridge the gap as younger generations flocked to short-form media platforms.
"So, what we see is a few different changes that are moving away from some of the conventions that have existed in film and television for a while, where filmmakers are aware that they need to have a presence on social media platforms where people are engaging and creating their own [interpretations]," she said.
Despite big recent examples such as Disney film Encanto and Netflix show Wednesday, Ms Herrmann said the industry's manufacturing of viral moments was still in its infancy.
"It's helpful to look at what's going on in the music industry to sort of get a sense of where the film industry is trying to go, because the music industry has already sort of monetised that practice in a more formalised way," she said.
A Minecraft Movie is filled with moments that could translate to short-form video, mainly in the form of songs performed by star Jack Black.
The Super Mario Bros. Movie also featured a massive musical number by Black, with his character Bowser going viral with Peaches and Black performing the tune at the 2023 Game Awards.
But this time, it was something slightly more quirky and organic that popped off on social media: the chicken jockey.
Videos posted on social media show audiences sitting respectfully, watching the movie, before a small square-headed zombie drops onto the back of a chicken in a boxing ring, and all hell breaks loose.
A Minecraft Movie star Jack Black has history with viral moments in movies. (AP: Scott A. Garfitt)
Black's character, Steve, declares "chicken jockey!" and the crowd goes ballistic, throwing popcorn around, taking off their shirts and generally screaming loudly in the theatre.
Audience members getting into the trend stood up to film the furore before heading online and posting to their social media accounts, prompting others who might see the videos to take part.
Ms Herrmann said it was an example of the kind of "clippable moment" film producers were looking for, even if they had not necessarily planned this one.
The traditional entertainment model is changing fast, with younger audiences moving away from pay TV and traditional media.
"There are these quite clear moments starting to be embedded, all these clippable moments that really function as prompts or invitations for viewers to remix, edit, parody, replicate, or otherwise create additional paratexts and completely saturate the internet," she said.
She said there were no guarantees that a planned viral moment would come off, but that production companies were packing them in, in the hope some of them got picked up.
author: Ned Hammond

title: The new Minecraft movie is a Jack Black musical
content:
Minecraft is the biggest video game of the 21st century — so of course the entertainment industry found a way to break more money out of its blocks.
Like the Super Mario film before it, simply mentioning the concept of A Minecraft Movie is likely to bring on eye rolls from fans and detractors alike.
And it's this very attitude that the new film from director Jared Hess — best known for cult comedy Napoleon Dynamite — has leaned into.
At many points, A Minecraft Movie feels like a parody of its own image: it's making fun of itself before you get the chance to.
The result is a goofy, CGI-heavy adventure with plenty of familiar faces from both the game's world and our own (think Jennifer Coolidge dating a villager).
The Minecraft movie is one of several fresh family flicks to choose from these school holidays, with picks like Dog Man and a new Looney Tunes also paired well with a popcorn.
A Minecraft Movie | Official Trailer
A blend of live-action and CGI, A Minecraft Movie sees regular people stumble into the sandbox game.
Our humble humans must find their way back to their own world and, along the way, prevent the hell-like Nether's army of piglins from taking over the luscious, bright Overworld.
Shot in New Zealand, the film features plenty of friends from across the ditch, with Rachel House voicing the evil piglin overlord Malgosha, and Jemaine Clement also starring.
The movie is also essentially a musical, with Jack Black lending his talents to multiple performances, and Kiwi pop icon Benee behind the film's pivotal song.
Minecraft's key NPCs — such as zombies, piglins and villagers — have been transformed from the game's low-res block figures to hyper-realistic CGI, with creepy, unsettling results.
While we do see a chicken jockey in the new Minecraft movie, the simplistic block creations of the original game are nowhere to be found. (Warner Bros.)
For an adaptation of a world-building game that's all about imagination, the film feels like a missed opportunity to portray a sense of wonder, or to think outside the box.
While there are of course some references to Minecraft, characters largely stay in the same locations and interact with the same array of creations. Paired with the film's endless Marvel-style quips, it doesn't take us anywhere particularly compelling in emotion, style or plot.
But Jack Black shines as the game's default player, Steve, a role that would be unimaginable without him, bringing his much-needed signature charm and energy to an otherwise lacklustre script.
While A Minecraft Movie is unlikely to become one of the great movies of our time, it is still an enjoyable watch — with butt jokes, chase scenes and call-backs to the game still likely to delight young fans.
Age range: Rated PG for mild fantasy violence and coarse language, with some scenes that may scare young children — those zombies aren't for the faint-hearted.
Dog Man | Official Trailer
Chances are, if you already have a Dog Man obsessed kiddo in your life, you're seeing this film whether you like it or not.
Captain Underpants author Dav Pilkey continues to delight primary school children everywhere with this spin-off series following the madcap adventures of a part-dog, part-human cop with a nose for chasing bad guys.
The first film adaptation of the wildly popular novels sees the titular squirrel-obsessed crime fighter up against his nemesis, Petey, aka the "world's most evilest cat", voiced by none other than Pete Davidson.
The movie is endless gags and thwarted plans — everything from the "Butt Sniffer 2000" to Ricky Gervais as a snarky psychic fish. And with critics commending the "relentless pace" and "very, very silly" energy, it's perfect fodder for its young target audience, and a fun ride for their adult chaperones too.
Age range: Rated G for very mild themes, animated violence and coarse language.
Disney’s Snow White | Official Trailer | In Theaters March 21
To say Disney's live-action remake of their 1937 animation Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs has received mixed reviews would be an understatement.
Critics have called the film everything from "toe-curlingly terrible" to "show-stopping", with the ABC's review arguing it faced a "no-win situation" from its very outset.
"Stick too close to the original and it becomes a pointless retread; deviate from the classic text and risk incurring the wrath of everyone with an axe to grind," Luke Goodsell wrote.
Almost 90 years after their first imagining of Snow White, Disney decided to take another bite of the apple. But what does each era's "fairest of them all" reflect about attitudes towards women?
Comments by leads Gal Gadot and Rachel Zegler — which angered both sides of the political divide — hasn't helped the film's reputation. Meanwhile, sensitivities around the original film's portrayal of people with dwarfism saw Doc, Grumpy, Dopey and co turned into bizarre little CGI men in this rendition.
But kids are unlikely to be too worried about any of these socio-cultural implications and can instead channel their focus into this extravagant retelling of the classic Brothers Grimm fairytale.
Along with its original tunes, 2025's Snow White boasts several new tracks from La La Land songwriters Benj Pasek and Justin Paul, with its lead, Rachel Zegler, flexing her impressive vocal abilities and Broadway performance skills.
The film's mammoth budget is evident throughout, with intricately colourful sets, costumes and exciting chase scenes bringing the story to life in spectacular style.
Age range: Rated PG for mild fantasy themes and violence. Children and Media Australia (ACCM), the peak body representing children as media users, recommends this one for children aged 6 and over, with parental guidance for those under 8.
Looney Tunes Movie | The Day The Earth Blew Up | Teaser Trailer
Like Snow White, Looney Tunes is a 1930s animation classic, yet its latest revamp exists in a whole other universe to Disney's.
The Day the Earth Blew Up has gone back to the days of hand-drawn animation and is somehow the first fully animated Looney Tunes feature ever released in cinemas.
It sees Daffy Duck and Porky Pig back in action as they attempt to stop a mind-controlling alien from taking over the world, after discovering said creature has infiltrated the bubble gum at their factory, zombifying anyone who chews their fresh new flavour.
Despite the absence of Bugs Bunny, it's received glowing reviews from critics, who praised the film's "gloriously stupid" plot and the endless gags, which will please adults and kids alike.
In classic Looney Tunes style, they do not hold back on the slapstick violence; think hammers to the head, electrocutions and Daffy's whole body exploding (classic).
If you're after some cartoonish nostalgia and over the modern sanitisation, this might just be the pick for you.
Age range: Rated PG for Mild crude humour, science fiction themes and animated violence, the ACCM recommends this for kids 8 and up, with parental guidance suggested for kids under 9.
Flow | Official Trailer
While it's one of the only picks to have a 'G' parental rating, it's hard to say if Flow really belongs in this list of kids' movies.
The captivating Latvian animation was an Oscars stand-out this year, taking home two Academy Awards and seeing its directors become national heroes in the small North-Eastern-European nation.
Told from a cat's point of view and entirely dialogue free, Flow has been heralded "epic", with a "sense of wonder [and] imagination" that excels beyond the tropes of the big studios.
Set in a world without humans, Flow's animal protagonists — which also include a lemur, a labrador and a capybara — learn to survive after being washed away by a flash flood.
While it may be slightly too slow for bouncing-off-the-walls-type young ones, Flow's foray into the world of animals has made it popular with parents, kids and pets alike.
Age range: Rated G with the caveat that some scenes may scare very young children. The ACCM recommends this one for children over 6, with parental guidance suggested for kids under 7.

title: White Lotus composer ditches series, dishes on creator Mike White
content:
Welcome to ICYMI, where we recap the pop culture and entertainment news you might have missed over the past week.
The man behind the "ooh-loo-loo-loo"-heavy theme song that made The White Lotus intro one to watch has quit the show days before the hit social satire's season three finale.
Cristóbal Tapia de Veer's Emmy-Award-winning White Lotus scores were fan favourites in seasons one and two.
But in an explosive interview with The New York Times, the composer said show creator Mike White never liked his work and had to be convinced to use his season one theme.
I can hear God when the beat drops at 1:01 of #whitelotus S2 theme song  pic.twitter.com/47wbY7oXN7
Season three, he said, was "for sure" his last on the show.
"Maybe I was being unprofessional and, for sure, Mike feels that I was always unprofessional to him because I didn't give him what he wanted. But what I gave him did this, you know — did those Emmys, people going crazy," he told the paper.
And De Veer, as it turns out, was just as upset over The White Lotus season three theme treatment as the rest of the internet — albeit for different reasons.
The current season's score appeared to have scrapped the ululation that made it so popular; the intro credits run for 1:45 and the all-important "ooh-loo-loo-loo's" don't come in until 2:08.
De Veer says this was another point of tension between him and White: "I told [the producer] that it would be great to, at some point, give them the longer version with the 'ooh-loo-loo-loos', because people will explode if they realise that it was going there anyway.
"But then, Mike cut that — he wasn't happy about that. At that point, we already had our last fight forever, I think."
Two weeks ago, De Veer went ahead and uploaded the full score to his YouTube account.
The White Lotus Season 3 Soundtrack — Enlightenment UNCUT ENDING (Main Title Theme)
Occult (and comedy and cinema) lovers rejoice this week as Australian comedian Cassie Workman officially announced her upcoming docuseries, Cassie Workman is Witchy AF.
That alone is worth celebrating, but there's more! The eclectic show has the backing of legendary director Lilly Wachowski who, along with her sister Lana, directed and wrote The Matrix films.
Workman and Wachowski are both trans women, so it was apt that the show announcement was made on International Day of Trans Visibility AND exactly 26 years since The Matrix was released.
The series is described as an "adult comedic documentary" and set in a fictional occult store owned by Workman, who will take the audience through "a world of ritual magic, identity, demons, tarot, love, death and possible salvation".
"It's been an honour to work with the incredible Lilly Wachowski, and an amazing production team, to make this weird and wonderful show," Workman said on Instagram.
Workman has been a mainstay in Australian comedy since she won Melbourne International Comedy Festival's RAW Comedy competition in 2009. She's written for shows like Shaun Micallef's Mad As Hell and Aaron Chen Tonight. Most recently, she toured her show Aberdeen — a tribute to her "idol" Kurt Cobain — internationally.
Witchy AF marks Wachowski's return to TV following her stint as a showrunner on comedy-drama Work in Progress, which lasted for two seasons from 2019-2021.
The British Academy of Film and Television Arts awards — better known as the BAFTAs — have released their 2025 nominations, with Netflix's darkly comic stalker series, Baby Reindeer, picking up a sweep of nominations.
Richard Gadd's semi-autobiographical program, for which he was sued for defamation, landed him a Best Actor nomination, along with seven other nods.
Nava Mau, who plays Gadd's girlfriend in the show, is the first out trans actor to be nominated for a BAFTA, going up against co-star Jessica Gunning for Best Supporting Actress.
Trailing Baby Reindeer with six nominations each are Toby Jones docudrama Mr Bates vs The Post Office, Gary Oldman thriller Slow Horses, and Rivals, a soapy comedy starring David Tennant set in the 1980s.
Nicola Coughlan posted about "ringing my mum and getting to tell her forehead the news". (Instagram: @nicolacoughlan)
Irish sweetheart Nicola Coughlan is also up for an award, and was in tears at the news of her first-ever BAFTA nomination, taking to Instagram to express a big "holy moly" at the news, feeling "overwhelmed and excited and emotional".
The Derry Girls and Bridgerton actor is in the running for Best Female Performance in a Comedy for Big Mood, a sitcom about mental health and friendship.
Between the announcement of four incoming Beatles biopics and confirmation that Spiderman: Beyond The Spiderverse finally has a release date, it might have seemed like there was a lot of movie news this week. And you would be correct!
It's all because of CinemaCon, the yearly convention where many of the major and minor studios come to hock the films that will be filling our cinemas in the next few years.
Here are just some of the announcements made over the convention:
However, it didn't take long for fans to notice that the majority of the films announced for 2026 are remakes, reboots or sequels.
And while it appears we are in an era of filmmaking that is pretty much just repeating the past 40 years, it's not all dire.
Challengers director Luca Guadagnino showed off his new thriller After The Hunt, a new original Wes Anderson joint is imminent and Yorgos Lanthimos teased his next project with muse Emma Stone.
Aussie filmmakers Danny and Michael Philippou, AKA The RackaRacka brothers, have returned.
You might remember when they scared the wits out of us with their 2023 screamer, Talk To Me, and now they're offering Bring Her Back — a supernatural horror that seems to share some themes with their debut film.

title: Tom Cruise pays tribute to 'dear friend' Val Kilmer
content:
Tom Cruise paid tribute to late Top Gun co-star Val Kilmer by leading movie theatre owners in a moment of silence at the CinemaCon event on Thursday.
The moment stood in stark contrast to the otherwise action-packed presentation of Paramount Pictures' upcoming movies.
"I'd like to honour a dear friend of mine, Val Kilmer," said Cruise, at the start of his hotly anticipated appearance at the annual industry summit in Las Vegas.
Since they met on the set of Top Gun in 1986, Tom Cruise and Val Kilmer have shared a close friendship.
"I really can't tell you how much I admired his work, how much I thought of him as a human being, and how grateful and honoured I was when he joined Top Gun and then came back for Top Gun: Maverick," he said.
Kilmer, one of the biggest Hollywood actors of the 90s, shot to fame playing the cocky, square-jawed and mostly silent fighter pilot in training Tom 'Iceman' Kazansky in the original 1986 Top Gun.
Kilmer died of pneumonia aged 65, his family announced this week.
He battled throat cancer after being diagnosed in 2014, and made his final on-screen appearance in the long-awaited sequel Top Gun: Maverick.
Kilmer's real-life health issues were written into the character, giving him a physically diminished appearance and a raspy voice.
Top Gun star Val Kilmer dies aged 65. (ABC News: Andrea Jonson)
"Thank you, Val. I wish you well on your next journey," Cruise said to the silent room.
Cruise was there to build hype for Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning, the eighth instalment of the franchise set to hit theatres May 23.
He introduced a trailer for the new release, which shows Cruise playing Ethan Hunt as he clings to the wheels of a small biplane as it soars down a narrow canyon and barrel rolls through the skies.
The trailer contained extensive flashbacks to famous scenes from earlier in the eight-film blockbuster franchise, such as Cruise dangling between lasers and climbing the Burj Khalifa tower in Dubai.
"I need you to trust me one last time," says Cruise's character, in what Paramount is marketing as supposedly the final movie of the franchise.

title: Head South is a love letter to New Zealand's post-punk scene
content:
Filmmaker Jonathan Ogilvie can pinpoint the moment where, as a teenager, his world extended far beyond the confines of 1970s Ōtautahi/Christchurch — it's recreated early on in Head South, his semi-autobiographical coming-of-age movie set in the city's nascent post-punk scene.
What: A charming but dark coming-of-age story set in 1979 Christchurch's post-punk scene.
Starring: Ed Oxenbould, Stella Bennett/Benee, Márton Csókás, Roxie Mohebbi
Writer-director: Jonathan Ogilvie (The Tender Hook, Lone Wolf)
When: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Ready to pick up a guitar
Ogilvie's stand-in, the shaggy-haired, meek Angus, is in a record store — still in his school blazer — when he hears the frenetic drums and simple yet searing bass lines of the Public Image Ltd song, 'Public Image', for the first time.
Even before frontman John Lydon's angsty vocals come in, something's clicked: Angus turns to the camera, his eyes alight, and the film itself stretches out from a 4:3 box into wide-screen.
Stella Bennett (aka Benee) performs Head South's titular song on the soundtrack. (Dougal Holmes/Supplied)
Neither Ed Oxenbould, who plays Angus, or Stella Bennett — better known as Kiwi pop star Benee — were super familiar with 1970s post-punk prior to starring in Head South, both being born in the 2000s. But they had their own version of 'Public Image', as many watching will.
"That scene's so sick," says Bennett. "For me, it was James Blake — he opened the door for me to the sad boys of the alt world, like Yung Lean. That was the coolest world, and [I just saw] how experimental and broad music can be."
Controversial frontman Johnny Rotten has been replaced with some younger blood, and Steve Jones says playing in the band has never been better.
"My parents are big Beatles fans and played them a lot when I was a kid," says Oxenbould. "I remember hearing 'Across The Universe' and being like, 'Oh my God, I didn't know songs could do that."
Set in 1979, Head South is a love letter to New Zealand's burgeoning post-punk scene, which two years later would birth Flying Nun Records — the internationally renowned independent label founded in Christchurch by Roger Shepherd, though most acts were found south in Dunedin.
The roster included The Chills, Headless Chickens, and Straitjacket Fits — all acts Ogilvie made music videos for a decade before his feature film debut in 2008 with Sydney noir The Tender Hook, starring Hugo Weaving and Rose Byrne.
Straightjacket Fits - She Speeds (Official Video)
The Head South soundtrack is a who's who of the era, albeit with Ogilvie sneaking in a song by F.Y.C, his own band formed in 1981 with two bass guitars — lead guitar was deemed "too phallic" at the time.
"That's my only concession to anachronism," Ogilvie laughs.
"In a way, this is an origin story for Flying Nun. When Roger came and saw it as we were mixing, he went 'Oh my God, you've got that world perfect. Exactly how I remember it with all those odd characters."
As with so many of the era, Angus's mission after hearing 'Public Image' is immediately clear: He must start a band.
Sure, he has no friends and no musical knowledge, but he has a name, Daleks, and soon looks the part too, modelling himself off of the snarling lead singer of a band (Demos Murphy). The surfer locks are gone, his trousers are stapled into stovepipes and he raids his dad's (Márton Csókás) closet for his pointy wedding shoes.
The writer-director of Head South discusses re-creating 1979 Christchurch and its post-punk scene with The Screen Show host Jason Di Rosso.
Along the way, he's taken by both the older, worldly Holly (Roxie Mohebbi) and Kirsten, a dry-witted teen and potential band member (Bennett). But for Ogilvie, post-punk was never just about girls, a look, or a sound: It was purpose, community and a release from stifling middle-class suburban life.
"It's like a portal into this underground world," says Ogilvie. "It sounds like The Hobbit, doesn't it? But not like The Hobbit! A cultural underworld with denizens, some of them are older and more worldly. Some of them have got access to drugs. As a young person, you're moving into that world naively, but it's fascinating.
From the opening credits, Head South is a time machine. While shot digitally, it's rendered with a 16mm film filter, complete with the splices, scratches and hops that come with the era's DIY music videos and films.
Malcolm (Demos Murphy), the lead singer of local band The Cursed, both encourages and mocks Angus's enthusiasm — and uses it to his own advantage. (Supplied)
Its opening credits — names and titles scratched in as if with a key — set Toy Love's angsty 'Squeeze' against Laurence Aberhart's black-and-white photos of 1970s Christchurch's art-deco houses and graffitied sheds.
It fills in a world beyond the (tight) frames of the film, given Head South was shot in Christchurch, which was a challenge since many of the era's sites were damaged in Christchurch's deadly 2011 earthquakes. Visible damage or construction sites were routinely just a few millimetres off-camera, and some CGI work was required, via Peter Jackson's Park Road Post studio, to recreate pubs like Noah's Hotel.
Kirsten, played by Stella Bennett/Benee, is a bored pharmacy worker who sells Angus KY lubricant as hair gel before befriending him. (Supplied)
"The wisdom was, 'Oh, you can't possibly make this film in Christchurch, there's nothing left.' But that was nonsense. They just wanted to make it in Auckland", says Ogilvie.
"We never set foot in Auckland, which I'm delighted to say because I'm a mainlander, I'm going to have loyalty to that."
What proved easier was finding era-appropriate props and settings, be it an orange 1970s Flymo lawnmower, homely wooden interiors, or the slight time-delay to punk fashion, with trends a few months or years behind London or New York.
"New Zealanders tend to be collectors," Ogilvie says. "Creating that world was surprisingly easy."
Made on a tight budget of $NZ3.8m ($3.4m), the film doesn't just reflect the aesthetics of the era but the ethos of DIY authenticity too. It's part of why Ogilvie was eager to work with Bennett for her major acting debut, after having cast Marlon Williams in his 2021 feature, Lone Wolf.
In early scenes, Angus hangs nervously outside the independent Middle Earth Records, but is ragged on for his hair by rocker Malcolm. (Supplied)
"I saw Benee's videos and I thought, 'Yes, she's ready to do some acting," he says. "She just brings a natural spirit to it. I'm keen on working with musicians. I think they bring something less actorly in terms of energy. It's a naturalism, a natural rhythm."
"I didn't even know how a scene was shot," says Bennett. "I didn't even know that you do it so many times, from different angles!"
While there's huge appeal in Head South as a nostalgia play, this is a deeply personal story for Ogilvie — one that oscillates between joyous coming-of-age tropes and a darker, eerier edge that unnerves throughout, only coalescing after the film's ending.
Angus's dad  Gordon is played by New Zealand actor Márton Csókás, who won a Best Supporting Actor AACTA Award in 2007 for Romulus, My Father. (Supplied)
"Everything that happens in the film happened, and most of it happened to me," says Ogilvie, who is fond of calling Head South "almost true" in interviews.
This isn't a rose-tinted depiction of the past. Several of the older characters take advantage of Angus's naivety, and there's a quiet, rising tension throughout — largely in scenes featuring Angus's family and father, who struggles to stay present after his wife left them unannounced, with frozen meals to last a fortnight.
Head South's rollicking music often clears from scenes between Angus and his dad, the house quiet. Early on, the two watch rolling footage of the Erebus disaster — New Zealand's worst aviation disaster in history.
Holly (Roxie Mohebbi) quickly grabs Angus's attention as a cool Londoner now living in Chirstchurch for mysterious reasons. (Supplied)
"For me, that was very much part of growing up in Ōtautahi/Christchurch," says Ogilvie. "Some people describe it as Southern Gothic — in terms of what happens in the South Island, a slight dread underneath everything. There's a certain darkness underpinning it, which people relate to, not just in New Zealand."
With the film a hit when it opened Rotterdam Film Festival last year, Ogilvie hopes that Head South, like Flying Nun before it, helps prove that antipodean art isn't inferior.
"All of our musical influences were coming out of London," says Ogilvie of the post-punk scene. "But the irony of that was that, when I lived there, I realised the music and art we were making in Ōtautahi/Christchurch was equal to, if not better than what I was hearing on the other side of the world."
"I'm calling for a cultural coup d'etat, where we need to take pride in our own stories."
Head South is in limited cinemas now.

title: What we learnt about Val Kilmer's illness from his documentary
content:
The death of Val Kilmer — the brooding actor most well-known for his turns as Batman and as Jim Morrison in The Doors — was confirmed on Tuesday, local time, by his daughter Mercedes Kilmer.
The 65-year-old actor died from pneumonia following a decade of health problems including a 2014 throat cancer diagnosis that required two tracheotomies. The stress on his throat from the cancer and treatment left Kilmer with a diminished speaking ability.
In 2021, filmmakers Leo Scott and Ting Poo released Val, a documentary compiled from more than 800 hours of footage Kilmer had taken over his life, detailing his rise to fame as well as his struggles with sickness.
Here's what we learnt.
In his later years, Kilmer frequently wore neck scarves to cover his tracheotomy in public. (Supplied: Prime Video)
The documentary is written by Kilmer but narrated by his son, Jack, who is also an actor.
Opening on Kilmer at the start of his acting career, it quickly veers to an older version deeply enthralled in scrapbooking.
"I was recently diagnosed with throat cancer, though I healed quickly from the cancer. The extensive radiation and chemotherapy that followed treatment has left my voice impaired," he says through his son.
"I am still recovering and it is still difficult to talk and be understood."
Jack Kilmer narrates the film from words written by his father. (Supplied: Prime Video)
Kilmer sometimes talks straight to the camera, pressing on his throat to speak in a rasp that will shock those used to his robust movie star cadence. He speaks about his need to share the visual archive that he's accumulated over 60 years.
"I have lived my life and it's sort of all in these boxes, but what is part of the profound sadness is that I know it's incomplete. As much as I filmed and as hard as I've tried, there's nothing I can do to make any of it understood," Kilmer says.
"I know that that's not true but it's how I feel."
Late in his career, just before his illness, Kilmer starred in a stage production about author Mark Twain. In debt from his recent divorce, he sold 6,000 acres (2,428 hectares) of land he owned in New Mexico — and intended to turn into an artist's community — to fund the production.
But after several successful performances of the show, Kilmer began to feel ill.
"I was getting ready to put on Citizen Twain in Nashville when I lost my voice. I postponed the show for what I thought would be a month or two. My voice didn't get better, it got worse, and one day I started coughing up blood and was rushed to the hospital," he says.
Actor Val Kilmer, star of Top Gun and Tombstone, has died aged 65.
While in hospital, he began to paint again — a hobby he'd picked in his youth. When he got out, he threw himself into making art, founding a studio "big enough" for his ideas.
"That studio has become a sacred space where artists gather and collaborate and help the next generation of artists in our community grow," he says.
The film cuts to archive interview footage of Kilmer, young and effervescent as he is asked by an interviewer: "If heaven exists, what would you like to hear God say at the pearly gates?"
"Well, I had this dream once," Kilmer begins, clear and measured.
"Where this happened and she opened what would be her arms, that feeling, and enveloped me and said, 'I love you.'"
At times, Kilmer is incredibly frank about how cancer has changed his life. It's possible to see the tracheotomy band around his neck and the artificial hole that allows him to speak. Midway through the film, he addresses his concept of the afterlife.
"I see this hole in my throat and I wonder whether people wonder if I had any fear of dying," he says.
The scene quickly moves on to Kilmer meeting his child, Mercedes, who he proclaims in the title card as "My genius daughter".
Mercedes Kilmer excitedly talks to her father on video call moments before they meet. (Supplied: Prime Video)
Confirming that their meeting is imminent, Kilmer is so excited he does a small dance. The film reveals that they live next to each other, before the action cuts to grainy home videos of Kilmer and his then-wife, actor Joanne Whalley, celebrating their baby daughter.
At points in the film, Kilmer reckons with the shift in his career post cancer, saying he has no doubt that his "illness shut down professional opportunities".
He appears at a 2019 fan screening in Texas of his 1993 film Tombstone, the full crowd beaming at the movie star as he struggles to thank them for coming out.
Val Kilmer and his Top Gun co-star Barry Tubb at the Val Kilmer Weekend screenings in Texas in 2019. (Getty: Gary Miller)
"Sometimes, I feel so low and I have the blues really, really hard about having to fly around the country," he says.
Later on, Kilmer rasps to camera that he is on his way to Arizona because his mother, Gladys, had died and "Right now she doesn't have anyone to cremate her."
Arriving in the family home, surrounded by cactus and desert, Kilmer immediately starts shooting his loved ones with silly string ("It glows in the dark!" he joyfully informs them) as they're donning their funeral blacks.
"I wrote something nice last night all about her style, her hairdo, her jewellery, they always popped," he says about his mother, before the action cuts to Kilmer quietly sobbing.
"I miss my mama but I had a vision that she was so happy with her youngest son."
VAL - Official Trailer | Prime Video
Kilmer speaks frequently of his faith and how it intersects with his life.
"I've studied all the major religions, I've always been interested in religion. Often when I talk to someone, I end up talking about their faith. I'll ask them…" Kilmer starts but then struggles to breathe, before fainting over a nearby sofa, only to reveal that it was a joke played on his worried son.
"That's not funny," Jack says off camera.
"I can't help it," Kilmer says, smiling wide at the perfectly executed prank.
"I'm a bastard and I love you. It's very, very funny."
Val is streaming on Prime Video now.

title: 'I'm still your wingman': The 39-year friendship of Tom Cruise and Val Kilmer
content:
It was a scene that brought tears to Tom Cruise's eyes.
The moment two close friends — once bitter fictional rivals — reunited on-screen.
"I just want to say that was pretty emotional," Cruise reflected on Jimmy Kimmel Live.
Cruise first met Val Kilmer in 1986 on the set of high-octane blockbuster Top Gun.
Decades later, in 2022, the pair reunited for the sequel, Top Gun: Maverick.
Val Kilmer and Tom Cruise shared a powerful scene in Top Gun: Maverick. (Supplied: Paramount)
In one of the film's most memorable scenes, Captain Pete "Maverick" Mitchell, played by Cruise, meets with Kilmer's character, Admiral Tom "Iceman" Kazansky.
He's asking for advice on how to handle Rooster, the wild son of his former wingman, Goose.
"The only reason I'm here, is you," Cruise's character Maverick says in the scene, tears in his eyes.
It was a powerful moment — a moving reflection of the pair's almost 40-year friendship off-screen.
Val Kilmer and Tom Cruise share a brief scene in Top Gun: Maverick.
It also touched on Kilmer's real-life health struggles.
The character of Iceman, like Kilmer, had throat cancer and typed words on a screen to communicate.
Artificial voice technology was also used in post-production to allow Kilmer to speak during his brief cameo.
Actor Val Kilmer, star of Top Gun and Tombstone, has died aged 65.
For Cruise, and countless viewers, the scene packed an emotional punch.
"I've known Val for decades. He's such a powerful actor that he instantly became that character again," he told Jimmy Kimmel.
It was the last glimpse the world would get of Kilmer on the silver screen.
On April 1, aged 65, he died in Los Angeles of pneumonia.
And the curtain closed on a decades-long friendship between Kilmer and Cruise.
Tom Cruise tells Jimmy Kimmel about the emotional scene he shared with Val Kilmer.
Cruise and Kilmer weren't always close friends.
In fact, their relationship had a frosty start.
However, Kilmer said this wasn't personal but stemmed from his fascination with method acting.
Even when the cameras were off, he'd act hostile towards his co-stars.
"I would purposely play up the rivalry between Tom's character and mine off-screen as well," he said in the 2021 documentary Val.
"And what ended up happening is the actors, in true method fashion, split into two distinct camps.
Val Kilmer and Tom Cruise on the set of Top Gun in 1986. (Getty: Paramount Pictures)
In his memoir I'm Your Huckleberry, Kilmer wrote that Cruise also refrained from "revelry" during the filming of Top Gun.
He said this was because Cruise was "laser-focused" on becoming "the greatest action hero in the history of film".
"He was up nights learning lines; he spent every waking hour perfecting his stunts," Kilmer wrote.
"His dedication was admirable. Of course, even more admirable is the fact that he achieved his goal."
Tom Cruise portraying Pete "Maverick" Mitchell in Top Gun: Maverick.
Kilmer also shared in his memoir about a "small prank" he played on Cruise during filming.
"I gave him an extremely expensive bottle of champagne but placed it in the middle of a giant field and made him follow scavenger-hunt-style clues to find it," he said.
"I hid behind a bleacher and watched him lug the giant crate to his motorcycle. He never did thank me for the Iceman-style bit. I thought it would break the ice, but I guess the ice was just right."
Val Kilmer was Iceman in Top Gun. (Getty Images: CBS)
In an interview via email with the LA Times in 2022, Kilmer said the duo had remained friends since.
"We talked quite a bit about what was best for the story [of Top Gun: Maverick] and I think they got it right at the end," Kilmer wrote of Cruise.
"Tom and I get along really well. We giggled like little kids in school between takes.
"I consider him a real friend."
That same year, Kilmer posted a still from the Top Gun sequel with the caption: "36 years later… I'm still your wingman."
Speaking to the LA Times, Top Gun: Maverick director Joseph Kosinski said the two actors often reflected on their shared history.
"When we weren't shooting, they were sharing funny stories with [producer] Jerry [Bruckheimer] about making the original film," he said.
Tom Cruise in Top Gun: Maverick. (Supplied: Paramount)
He said the sequel was a genuine reflection of the duo's relationship.
"I think there is a lot of Maverick in Tom, and Iceman in Val, so what you are seeing on-screen is an authentic friendship that has lasted over 36 years," he said.
"After one of the takes … I noticed that both Tom and Val had tears in their eyes. It felt like a genuine moment between two old friends."

title: Why the AI-generated 'Studio Ghibli' trend is so controversial
content:
Legendary animator and founder of Studio Ghibli, Hayao Miyazaki, has captivated audiences around the world with his whimsical storytelling that explores the human experience and celebrates the natural world.
His films take several years to make and are famously hand-drawn, with each intricate frame meticulously crafted.
Now, OpenAI's new image-generation tool allows users to render images in Mr Miyazaki's signature style in a matter of seconds.
The new tool has become immensely popular with thousands of people sharing AI-generated memes and personal portraits in Studio Ghibli's style on social media.
This trend has raised broader discussions about the ethical concerns of AI-generated art, copyright issues and the future livelihoods of animators and artists.
OpenAI unveiled its new image-generation tool for ChatGPT last week, which allows users to transform images into different styles, including the Studio Ghibli style.
Users simply upload an image onto the platform and request it to be rendered in the style of Studio Ghibli, and within seconds, it will do so.
Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, took to X on Tuesday to announce that the new tool will be rolled out to all free users, enabling people to generate up to three images a day.
The demand for AI-generated Ghibli-style art caused such a surge in users that OpenAI's servers were reportedly "melting", prompting Mr Altman to implement rate limits temporarily.
Many users have taken to X to share examples of AI-generated Ghibli-style internet memes.
OpenAI has largely encouraged "Ghiblification", with Mr Altman even changing his profile picture on X into a Ghibli-style portrait.
While many users have created personal portraits and memes with the tool, some have used it to generate unsettling and violent images, including depictions of the World Trade Center towers falling on September 11 and the murder of George Floyd.
The White House's official X account also posted an AI-generated image of an ICE agent detaining a tearful Virginia Basora-Gonzalez for allegedly dealing fentanyl, sparking outrage for its insensitivity.
Mr Miyazaki once called artificial intelligence in animation "utterly disgusting" and "an insult to life itself".
He even said he would "never wish to incorporate this technology into [his] work at all".
Today, nearly a decade later, the internet is awash with AI-generated images replicating his style.
Hayao Miyazaki is behind Oscar-winning movies Spirited Away and The Boy and the Heron. (Reuters: Kevork Djansezian)
Mr Miyazaki has consistently stayed true to traditional hand-drawn techniques that give Studio Ghibli its distinctive expressive animations and attention to detail.
The beloved Japanese animation production company is behind Oscar-winning movies Spirited Away and The Boy and the Heron.
As the trend gained momentum, Mr Miyazaki's past comments on AI animation resurfaced, sparking renewed discussions about the ethics of AI-generated art.
Deborah Szapiro, an academic specialising in design, animation and interaction, expressed concerns about OpenAI's exploitation of Mr Miyazaki's work.
"It's not replicating or mimicking it, it's stealing it," Ms Szapiro told the ABC.
"And in actual fact, none of it actually retains the soul of any artwork because what's happening with it is that it's kind of like the world's biggest photocopier, whilst it's stealing."
Ms Szapiro notes that OpenAI is exploiting Miyazaki's world, though it can never truly capture the essence of his work, as it fails to grasp the fundamental human element that is essential to art.
"They do not understand art, they understand profit, so it can't possibly capture the soul of Miyazaki's artwork," she said.
"Almost anyone under 35 in the Western world has grown up with Ghibli films and that comfort and safeness and the beauty of Miyazaki's world is being exploited in this case."
Deborah Szapiro notes that OpenAI is exploiting the "comfort and safeness and the beauty of Miyazaki's world". (Facebook: Studio Ghibli)
OpenAI, which is already facing copyright lawsuits over its flagship chatbot, has stated that it has implemented safeguards.
"We added a refusal which triggers when a user attempts to generate an image in the style of a living artist," OpenAI said in a technical paper.
While Miyazaki, 84, is a living artist, OpenAI permits the replication of broader studio styles like the Ghibli style.
OpenAI defended the trend, noting that users have shared "truly delightful and inspired original fan creations".
John McGhee, a professor of 3D Visualisation within the Faculty of Arts, Design, and Architecture at UNSW, voiced concerns about the widespread, uncontrolled proliferation of Ghibli-style content on the internet.
"If it's not being curated in any way, it's not representative of the brand of the original artist who generated them," Professor McGhee told the ABC.
He argues this could harm the integrity of the brand.
Academy Award-winner Hayao Miyazaki returns to Studio Ghibli with The Boy and the Heron.
He also pointed out the cultural and philosophical differences between traditional artists like Miyazaki and AI-generated content.
Miyazaki's work often addresses themes like environmentalism and human impact, while AI companies consume significant power and contribute to environmental costs.
"A lot of the content of the films that he makes have got, like, an environmental kind of component to them, and about human waste, and then in contrast to that, you've got Sam Altman tweeted that it was melting the GPUs," he said.
Professor McGhee raised an important question: Is OpenAI's model trained on Studio Ghibli's work without permission?
"The algorithm has to be trained on something … I suspect there will be legal implications because it's taking someone else's artwork, and it hasn't asked permission to do that," Professor McGhee said.
One intellectual property lawyer, who spoke to the ABC but did not want to be named in this piece, said there had not yet been a specific case that had really tested these boundaries.
They said that in the US, OpenAI could argue that it taught its AI using other people's artworks but that other influences were also included, thus transforming the original artwork — a so-called "fair use" argument.
Australia's "fair dealing" laws are more restrictive and would usually allow content to be reused in news reports, or academic or other research.
The situation could also be complicated by any agreements OpenAI might have with image libraries, or if a creator like Studio Ghibli posted content on a platform such as Facebook, which then had a license to pass the material on to someone else.
In the age of the internet, they said, it was very easy to lose control of your copyright license.
While Mr Miyazaki is yet to release a statement, it's not hard to imagine what he would make of this new trend.

title: Val Kilmer's most notable roles
content:
Actor Val Kilmer, star of Top Gun and Tombstone, has died aged 65.
He died from pneumonia, The New York Times reported, attributing Kilmer's daughter Mercedes Kilmer.
In a career spanning decades, Kilmer took on supporting and leading roles spanning from Batman to Doc Holliday.
Kilmer started his career on the stage in New York when he co-wrote and starred in the aptly named play How It All Began.
His commitment to the stage saw him turn down a role in director Francis Ford Coppola's film The Outsiders in 1983, but he would end up on the big screen anyway when he took the lead role as rock star Nick Rivers in the spy spoof Top Secret! in 1984.
The actor was best known for his roles in Top Gun, Tombstone, and Batman Forever but also earnt a reputation as a temperamental star.
He threw himself into the role, performing all his character's songs and releasing a companion album.
It was the start of a run of supporting roles for Kilmer, who appeared in 1986 action flick Top Gun as Iceman, the rival of Tom Cruise's Maverick.
In 1988, he appeared alongside Joanne Whalley and Warwick Davis in fantasy adventure movie Willow as the irreverent mercenary Madmartigan.
After meeting on the set, Kilmer and Whalley married in 1988 and had two children, before divorcing in 1995.
Val Kilmer and wife Joanne Whalley met on the set of Willow in 1988, and appeared together in Kill Me Again in 1989.  (Getty: Paul Harris)
Kilmer reached stardom in 1991 when he took on the role of Jim Morrison in Oliver Stone's biographical film The Doors.
The film released to middling reviews, but critics were unanimous in their praise for Kilmer's portrayal of the troubled rock star.
Film critic Roger Ebert gave the film 2.5 stars out of 4, but wrote that Kilmer's performance was "the best thing in the movie — and since nearly every scene centres on Morrison, that is not small praise."
1993's western Tombstone saw Kilmer relish in the swagger of Wild West gunfighter and dentist Doc Holliday in a performance nominated for Most Desirable Male at the MTV Music Awards.
Two of his most notable roles came in 1995, with the releases of Batman Forever and Heat.
Val Kilmer and Nicole Kidman on the set of Batman Forever in 1995.  (Getty: Warner Bros. Pictures)
Batman Forever saw Kilmer taking over the role of the caped crusader from Michael Keaton, the sort of change that always sparks a whirl of discourse.
In a movie given generally lukewarm reviews, Kilmer's performance was praised by critics, including Peter Travers of Rolling Stone who wrote that Kilmer had a "deftly understated […] comic edge".
Michael Mann's crime thriller Heat released the same year, and featured Al Pacino and Robert De Niro as a cop and criminal on a collision course.
Kilmer played De Niro's right hand man in the film, which became a cult classic and is considered the gold standard for action sequences.
Val Kilmer appeared opposite Tom Cruise in action flick Top Gun in 1986. (Getty: Paramount Pictures)
He worked solidly in Hollywood over the next two decades.
Kilmer was diagnosed with throat cancer in 2014 and later recovered, daughter Mercedes Kilmer said.
Val, a 2021 documentary about his life, showed him needing a breathing tube.
Kilmer reprised his Iceman character for a cameo in Top Gun's 2022 follow-up Top Gun: Maverick, in what would become his final film appearance before his death.

title: Top Gun star Val Kilmer dies, aged 65
content:
Actor Val Kilmer, star of Top Gun and Tombstone, has died aged 65.
He died from pneumonia,The New York Times reported, attributing Kilmer's daughter Mercedes Kilmer.
He was also known for donning the batsuit in Batman Forever, following Michael Keaton.
Kilmer was diagnosed with throat cancer in 2014 and later recovered, Ms Kilmer said.
Val, a 2021 documentary about his life, showed him needing a breathing tube.
Val Kilmer seen here in 2014.

  (AP: Mark Humphrey)
After losing his voice, a cameo in Top Gun: Maverick was made possible with the aid of AI technology.
Kilmer's breakthrough role came with the 1986 classic Top Gun, and his role as Tom "Iceman" Kazansky.
But it almost didn't happen.
Kilmer was courted by director Tony Scott but initially baulked.
"I didn't want the part. I didn't care about the film. The story didn't interest me," he wrote in his memoir.
He agreed after being promised that his role would improve from the initial script.
Film critic Giles Hardie reflects on Val Kilmer's legacy.
However, it was his portrayal of rock star Jim Morrison in 1991's The Doors that earned him MTV's Movie Award for Best Male Performance.
Actor Josh Brolin was among the first to pay tribute to the star, saying he was a "challenging, brave, uber-creative firecracker".
Kilmer was one of Hollywood's most prominent leading men in the 1990s before numerous spats with directors and co-stars and a series of flops dented his career.
The youngest actor ever accepted to the Juilliard School at the time he attended, experienced the ups and downs of fame more dramatically than most.
In his later life, Kilmer gained a reputation as temperamental, intense, perfectionistic and sometimes egotistical.
Kilmer garnered a perfectionist reputation at times.  (Getty Images: Jason LaVeris/FilmMagic)
"I have behaved poorly. I have behaved bravely. I have behaved bizarrely to some," he said in his 2021 documentary.
"I deny none of this and have no regrets because I have lost and found parts of myself that I never knew existed.
"And I am blessed."
He made his film debut starring in the 1984 spy spoof Top Secret! before appearing in the goofy 1985 comedy Real Genius.
Kilmer starred in director Ron Howard's 1988 fantasy Willow and married his British co-star Joanne Whalley, with whom he had two children before divorcing.
He also dated Cher for a period.
Kilmer dated popstar Cher for a period of time.  (Getty Images: Walter McBride/Corbis)
One of his most challenging roles came in director Oliver Stone's The Doors in which he played Jim Morrison, the charismatic and ultimately doomed lead singer of the influential rock band The Doors.
To try to persuade Stone to cast him, Kilmer put together an eight-minute video of himself singing and looking like Morrison at various points in his life. Kilmer's own singing voice is used in the film.
The Doors ushered in the highest-profile years of his career.
Kilmer's portrayal of Morrison was critically acclaimed.
In the 1993 Western Tombstone, he played Old West gunfighter Doc Holliday.
The actor — who took part in the Method branch of Suzuki arts training — threw himself into parts.
When he played Doc Holliday, he filled his bed with ice for the final scene to mimic the feeling of dying from tuberculosis.
To play Morrison, he wore leather pants all the time, asked castmates and crew to only refer to him as Jim Morrison and blasted The Doors for a year.
He had two commercial successes in 1995, co-starring with Al Pacino and Robert De Niro in the crime drama Heat and Batman Forever.
Kilmer was panned by critics during his time in the batsuit.  (Getty Images: Warner Bros)
The instalment in the franchise was received tepidly by critics, and Kilmer was upstaged by co-stars Tommy Lee Jones and Jim Carrey.
Kilmer pulled out of the next Batman movie.
Director Joel Schumacher called Kilmer "the most psychologically troubled human being I've ever worked with."
Kilmer talked about his experience in the suit during his documentary.
"It was a struggle for me to get a performance past the suit, and it was frustrating until I realised that my role in the film was just to show up and stand where I was told to," he said.
From Iceman to Batman, these are the notable roles Val Kilmer starred in throughout his decades-long career.
His next projects were the film version of the 1960s TV series The Saint — fussily putting on wigs, accents and glasses — and The Island of Dr. Moreau with Marlon Brando, which became one of the decade's most infamously cursed productions.
John Frankenheimer, the director who finished The Island of Dr. Moreau, said there were two things he would never do: ″Climb Mount Everest and work with Val Kilmer again.″
Other artists came to his defence, like DJ Caruso, who directed Kilmer in The Salton Sea and said the actor simply liked to talk out scenes and enjoyed having a director's attention.
″Val needs to immerse himself in a character. I think what happened with directors like Frankenheimer and Schumacher is that Val would ask a lot of questions, and a guy like Schumacher would say, 'You're Batman! Just go do it,'″ Caruso told The New York Times in 2002.
The Saint director Phillip Noyce also called the reputation "unjustified".
"The real Val Kilmer is a lamb. And he is the hardest-working actor I've ever seen."
ABC/AP/Reuters

title: Controversies around Snow White tell us more about women's role in society
content:
In 1934, Walt Disney gave his most trusted employees 50c to buy dinner and asked them to meet him in the studio's sound stage after work. When they arrived, they found a single spotlight: Walt stepped into it and spent the next three hours acting out the story of Snow White.
He pranced around and pitched his voice up as the princess, before lowering it into a wicked laugh for the evil queen. The animators were enraptured, proving Disney's long-held belief that fairytales could captivate an adult audience.
Snow White was not an original story, but when Disney released Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs three years after Walt's one-man show, it became the definitive version of the fairytale. And in each new twist on the story since, Snow White has become the heroine of her era — or at least, the girl each era wants to create.
Snow White was Disney's first feature film, and animation was still an emerging form in the 30s. Ham Luske, the animator Walt hand-picked to design Snow White, originally suggested she should be a gangly, awkward teenager with a comic charm and cartoon proportions like Mickey Mouse. Other animators made Snow White prettier and gave her a sunny disposition that would become the template for beautiful, bird-befriending princesses across the Disney brand.
The Ink and Paint Department of Disney was the only place where women were allowed to work at the time of Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. (Photo by PhotoQuest/Getty Images)
Urban legend says that Snow White got her rosy glow from the women of Disney's Ink and Paint Department, who supposedly applied their own cosmetics to the princess's cheeks. Real cosmetics were tested, but the actual process most likely involved a red dye, painstakingly applied to every single frame.
But the all-female staff of Ink and Paint did reflect the reality of life for women in the 30s that Snow White belied. Mostly under 25, they had to work to make ends meet, pulling double shifts and sleeping beneath their desks to finish the film on time. They were siloed away in a building known as "The Nunnery" and were paid significantly less than their male colleagues.
Snow White, on the other hand, cooked and cleaned and whistled while she worked, for the Queen and the Dwarfs. She was the homemaker that the conservative male animators wanted to idealise, while relying on the underpaid labour of working women to make their animated dreams come true.
Because of the cultural dominance of Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, most Snow White films since have been radical new takes on the story, each reflecting changing attitudes about what makes the "fairest of them all".
1997's Snow White: A Tale of Terror is a dark medieval horror, where Snow White antagonises her stepmother in bouts of teenaged petulance, but has little narrative agency and suffers for her naivety.
In Mirror, Mirror, Julia Roberts plays the Evil Queen, who is ruling the land after the king left to fight great evil and never returned.  (IMDB)
In 2007's campus comedy Sydney White, a tomboyish Amanda Bynes tops her college's hot list without ever meaning to, showcasing an effortless "not like other girls" beauty that eats bacon and plays video games (while still, crucially, being conventionally attractive).
In the wake of Disney's 2010 Alice in Wonderland remake and the era of girlboss 'Lean In' feminism, 2012 produced two competing Snow White films: fluffy fairytale Mirror Mirror and gritty fantasy Snow White and the Huntsman. Despite their wildly different visual styles, both Mirror Mirror and Huntsman rewrite Snow White as the Queen's prisoner — rather than a scullery maid — who escapes captivity and ventures out to save her people by overthrowing her usurper stepmother.
Both films stress Snow White's kind personality over her outer beauty, and show Snow White rescuing herself. Huntsman has Snow White leading soldiers into battle, while Mirror Mirror has Snow White declaring that she's "read so many stories where the prince saves the princess in the end. I think it's time we changed that ending".
Universal Pictures: Snow White and the Hunstman — trailer
But it's also telling that in both films, the Huntsman, the Prince and the Seven Dwarfs are all given as much screen time as Snow White. Both films make Snow White's core motivation a need to live up to her missing father's expectations. Snow White could be taken seriously — and could even rescue herself — but she has to share the story with men.
After 88 years, Disney is now taking another bite at the apple with a live-action remake simply titled Disney's Snow White.
Before filming even started, a tea-cup-sized storm began over star Rachel Zegler's comment that the film had "taken [Snow White's] narrative and turned it into something that's a lot stronger". The brave culture warriors defending the original presumably haven't watched it recently: with its focus on gags and the more cartoony dwarfs, Snow White's narrative arc isn't exactly 'strong'.
Rachel Zegler copped criticism when she described the original 1937 Snow White film as "extremely dated when it comes to the ideas of women being in roles of power" to Entertainment Weekly.  (Supplied: Disney)
It's more likely some detractors' real issue was the casting of Zegler, a Latina actress, as the princess traditionally named after the whiteness of her skin. The film offers a new explanation for the name — Snow White was born during a blizzard — and Zegler is by far the best part of the film, giving Snow White the same determined optimism that she brought to Maria in West Side Story.
Since 2012, film trends have now moved beyond sword-wielding maidens reclaiming their kingdoms and into respectability politics. This new Snow White rejects the violence the Evil Queen uses to rule and instead brings the kingdom together through a combination of kindness, good vibes and remembering people's names.
"Fairest of them all" now means Snow White is a just and honest ruler with the best interests of her people at heart, reflecting the 2020s dream of democratic leaders governing by consent (in a hereditary monarchy).
There is a disappointing irony to the fact that Zegler has been blamed for the film's failure for tweeting "and always remember: free Palestine" alongside the trailer. This has been positioned by anonymous "Disney insiders" as the reason the film has been box office poison, with poor reviews and audience fatigue wilfully ignored by executives looking for a scapegoat. It seems Zegler can call for peace in character, but not on social media.
Despite her plans to save herself, Snow White still can't resist the poisoned apple.  (Supplied: Disney)
The shadow of a princess in need of rescue still hangs over the film: Snow White dreams of being "someone no-one needs to save", but reverence to the original film still calls for her to eat the poisoned apple and be saved by true love's kiss.
The film doesn't end there, though, and Snow White emerges as a new kind of heroine: no longer a damsel in distress, or a damsel taking up a sword to rescue herself, but someone who questions why a sword is needed in the first place.
But for all the reimaginings of the story, one thing remains unchanged: no matter how the film defines "fairest", Snow White has always been beautiful outside as well as in. Perhaps the next radical step for the character is a Snow White who genuinely isn't defined by beauty.

title: Here's who will play The Beatles in the four movies about the band
content:
Music and film tragics have had one burning question over the past 14 months: who will play The Beatles?
It's already considered one of the more ambitious film projects of recent times, and now director Sam Mendes has revealed who will play the legendary British band in a forthcoming series of four separate biopics.
At a speech at CinemaCon in Las Vegas on Monday night, local time, Mendes was joined on stage by the four actors who will play The Beatles.
Paul Mescal will play Paul McCartney, Harris Dickinson will be John Lennon, Joseph Quinn is George Harrison, and Barry Keoghan takes on the role of Ringo Starr.
Sam Mendes, Joseph Quinn, Barry Keoghan, Harris Dickinson and Paul Mescal at CinemaCon 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada (Eric Charbonneau/Sony Pictures via Getty Images)
On stage, the four men reportedly recited a line each from The Beatles' 1967 song 'Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band' before giving a Beatles-esque bow to the crowd of movie theatre industry representatives assembled.
Announced last year, each of the four films will focus on a specific member of the group. At the time, Mendes hinted that he was "excited to challenge the notion of what constitutes a trip to the movies".
In his speech this week, Mendes confirmed all films would come out concurrently, with a theatrical release date set for April 2028, calling it "the first binge-able theatrical experience". Principal photography on the films alone is expected to take an entire year.
From 1979's Birth of The Beatles to 1994's Backbeat, there have been plenty of attempts to tell the story of The Beatles on film over the years. Mendes's series, however, will be the first to have rights to the band's extensive catalogue of music.

title: Nicole Kidman is once again a domestic goddess with a secret in new film
content:
There's no doubt that Nicole Kidman is one of the hardest-working actors in Hollywood. In the past year alone, she has starred in age-gap rom-com A Family Affair, melodramatic crime soap serial The Perfect Couple, and erotic workplace drama Babygirl about a woman on the cusp of obliteration. Treading similar themes is her latest turn as Nancy Vandergroot in director Mimi Cave's underwhelming film, Holland.
What: A familiar suburban psychological thriller centred on a woman's quest to uncover the reasons behind her husband's frequent work trips.
Directed by: Mimi Cave
Starring: Nicole Kidman, Matthew Macfadyen, Gael García Bernal
Where: Streaming now on Prime Video
Likely to make you feel: Mildly diverted, mostly bored
There's a feeling of déjà vu watching Kidman reprise the role of a well-coiffed domestic goddess who begins to see past the idyll of her cushioned middle-class existence in the kitschy mid-western town of Holland. Nancy Vandergroot very much feels like a composite of Kidman's past roles.
There's a touch of the Stepford Wives in the way Nancy dutifully juggles her job as home economics teacher alongside maintaining the household for her optometrist husband Fred (Matthew Macfayden) and son Harry (Jude Hill). There's a hint of Babygirl's Romy in the traumatic childhood that's never touched upon and how dissatisfied Nancy is in her passionless marriage to Fred — there's a masturbating scene here too, though nowhere near as pointed as in Babygirl. There's a tinge of Big Little Lies' Celeste in the way Nancy is prone to maintaining appearances even as she grows increasingly suspicious that Fred is up to no good.
"All the scenes were really juicy and really interesting," Macfadyen told The Movie Report. (Supplied: Amazon Prime)
Aiding her on her journey to find out what Fred is doing when he embarks on frequent out-of-town work trips is her work-husband-turned-lover Dave (Gael García Bernal). The two fumble through several high-risk reconnaissance expeditions where exactly what you'd expect to happen happens.
The best-laid break-in plans are foiled by unexpected returns. The suspect is tailed at perilously close distances. Disguises are employed. No-one ever picks up their phones (Nokia, because it's the year 2000) when you most need them to. Injuries that are life-threatening decidedly aren't.
"There's a big subversion of what the story is to begin with, and it happens very fast," Gael Garcia Bernal (right) told The Movie Report. (Supplied: Amazon Prime)
If this trope-filled, derivative mess of a film was at least a fun romp, its faults could perhaps be overlooked. As it is, Holland is neither camp nor wry enough to descend into a full-blown farce, nor serious enough to be an actual propulsive crime mystery thriller like The Perfect Couple, which offset its soapiness with a genuinely unpredictable whodunnit.
Surreal, dreamlike sequences that Nancy finds herself almost trapped within every other night seem to suggest something sinister is taking place in the town on a more overarching level — ala The Stepford Wives, Don't Worry Darling or even WandaVision. But this strong suggestion — like many such instances in the film — never materialises into anything.
And even before Nancy starts to realise something is very wrong with her life, the artifice of domesticity that she so meticulously maintains comes to assume a sheen of abject horror. In a scene that's almost de rigueur for the genre, Nancy splatters tomato sauce all over herself, uncannily conjuring the look and feel of blood.
"It's that sort of American dream ... a promise of security and safety ... tied up in a pretty bow, but realising ... we couldn't be further from that," director Mimi Cave told Interview Magazine. (Supplied: Amazon Prime)
Holland is a predictably stylised film without much substance. Which is not to say it is without any redeeming qualities.
The real-life setting of Holland, Michigan is one of the more memorable quirks the film has going for it. A place founded by Dutch settlers that continues to feel like it's been transplanted straight out of the Netherlands, the white-picket-fence town contains every cultural emblem you'd stereotypically associate with the Dutch — windmills, tulips, clogs, bitterballen, traditional 'klederdracht' outfits.
The simulated otherworldly nature of this town, no doubt at odds with the carapace of Americana that surrounds it, exacerbates the eeriness of the film. As does the frightening colonial overtones of the town, whose sole resident of colour seems to be Dave (not that this is delved into much).
"I loved the colours and I loved how [director Mimi Cave] created this world," Kidman told The Movie Report. (Supplied: Amazon Prime)
With such a star-studded cast, it's a shame Holland never reaches for anything more than mild diversion. Having perfected this role, Kidman is eminently watchable as the conflicted Nancy. As is quickly becoming his archetype, Macfadyen inhabits the slippery, morally ambiguous Fred whose benign charm casts a hazy film over his motivations. Bernal's evolution from devoted colleague to slightly crazed lover is plausible, particularly due to the strong chemistry he and Kidman share.
The bones are there for something more compelling, but Holland can never decide what exactly it wants to be.

title: Filmmaker George Miller says he has another Mad Max movie in him
content:
George Miller, the Academy Award-winning polymath filmmaker, is leaning towards me intently.
I am telling him that in the 11 years that I presented News Breakfast on ABC TV, I don't once remember dreaming. My overnight life of epic, cinematic dreams ended the moment I became an early-morning broadcaster, but then returned the very night I stopped.
George's eyes widen: this celebrated director of action movies — considered one of the greatest of his time — is deeply taken with the life of the unconscious.
A post shared by ABC Arts (@abc_arts)
He believes in the creative power of wakeful dreaming and that fugitive space between sleep and consciousness; it's been fertile ground for almost every one of his movies.
"That's fascinating," he says: "Tell me all about that."
Turns out George Miller is the only person in my life who is happy to hear about my dreams.
George and I spent almost four days together for the premiere episode of the new season of Creative Types with Virginia Trioli, and our conversations stretched deep into the boundless role of the unconscious, the history of cinema and the intricate mechanics of movie-making.
"What I've found is that everyone essentially goes through the same thing," George says of making a film.
"It's essentially an interplay between the intuition and the intellect.
"A film is made on the run. You're making intuitive decisions, micro decisions, at every moment, at every turn."
Anya-Taylor Joy, George Miller and Chris Hemsworth on set of Furiosa A Mad Max Saga (Warner Bros. Pictures: Jason Boland)
There's an energy and focus he brings to his filmmaking that was there in his first career, too, as an emergency room doctor. It was by taking to the road to do locum work — with his partner, the late Byron Kennedy — that he financed his first film, the iconic Mad Max.
And yes, he says he has another Mad Max film left in him.
"Once you've visited that world … you can't help. I've become a habitual storyteller. There are many, many stories in my head and not enough time to tell them.
"And it's sort of Darwinian: what happens is some stories insist on themselves and they won't let you go and you keep thinking about them and you start putting them together in your mind."
George lives a rich, internal life driven by the stories that he dreams up and the long history of cinema he holds in his head. Daydreaming, he says, is crucial to his process.
"I remember as a kid, people saying, 'Oh, George is a bit of a daydreamer.' And I thought, 'Oh gee, there's something wrong with that.' But then I'm very grateful that I was: you're making up little stories in your head. It's more than just stories or narratives but playing in your mind."
He is probably the most thoughtful and deep-thinking director I have ever met — a kind of philosopher of film, a scholar of narrative. And he is without question the most easygoing and affable.
On hot and dusty days filming Creative Types on location, George was unfussed, agreeable and interested in everything. (Supplied)
Delayed from Melbourne, I almost missed the connecting flight that would take George, the ABC crew and me to Broken Hill and on to Silverton, the famous location of Mad Max II and Fury Road, where we planned to film with him.
As I raced to the gate in panic, I saw the last of the passengers boarding, but there was George Miller, relaxed on the terminal's plastic chairs and in a happy chat with our director of photography, Aaron Smith.
George turned to me beaming and strolled with me to the gate. He was not carrying a thing apart from his phone.
"He's really a pirate who has a very noble and completely renegade ship that he's just sailing wherever he wants it to be," the star of Three Thousand Years of Longing, Tilda Swinton, tells me of his work.
Actors who work with him fall in love with him and wait to be asked back. Tilda says she'd work with Miller again "in a heartbeat." Chris Hemsworth tells me he rang his agent from the foyer of the cinema in which he saw Fury Road and begged him to secure a part in the next Mad Max.
Tilda Swinton and Idris Elba, stars of Three Thousand Years Of Longing, with Miller at Cannes film festival. Swinton would happily work with the director again. (Getty: Pascal Le Segretain)
Charlize Theron, who had a very difficult time working with her Fury Road co-star, Tom Hardy, relied on Miller to get through the conflict in the desert, and later became a dear friend of the director and Margaret Sixel, his wife and editor.
George Miller is a curious mixture of restless and calm. When he wasn't shooting with us, out in the boundless landscape of his dystopian vision, he was remotely working on projects back home in Sydney.
His view forever pushes forward.
"Every filmmaker will tell you once the film is done, there's no point in looking at it again," he says. "You know it. I could play every frame in my head, and you can do nothing about it. We are verbs, not nouns … and we have to be because everything's changing."
Watch Creative Types with Virginia Trioli: George Miller on April 1 at 8.30pm on ABC TV, or stream the whole series now on ABC iview.
