title: Tracie was looking for her dad on Facebook but found something better
content:
When filmmaker Tracie Laymon was growing up in Houston, Texas, she used to perch in her bedroom closet, writing. "I called it my office," she chuckles.
A queer person, Laymon jokes, "I eventually came out of that closet."
That creative space, and a finely honed sense of humour, were the best ways to process her father's often angry, unpredictable behaviour, and tendency to disappear for long periods.
"My mum and I, we'd be going through so much awful stuff, and we would just laugh at the absurdity of how bad it was," Laymon says.
"When I tried to talk to him about things that were important to me, it was not a welcoming space."
Laymon tried to connect to him through their mutual love of cinema.
"I thought if I wrote a movie about the things that mattered to me, then maybe he'd see it and we could talk," she recalls.
"That drove me for a long time, until I realised that's not the healthiest of motivations."
"There are moments where Barbie [Ferreira, pictured] goes through three or four emotions in a couple of seconds," Laymon says. (Supplied: Roadside Attractions)
Eventually, they became estranged. But after a long time of no contact, Laymon sent him a friend request on Facebook.
He accepted.
Only, it wasn't her father. It was another man with the same name.
"It was kind of a shock at first because, in the moment where I thought it was him, he had access to my heart," Laymon says. "That felt good. I needed that, so I decided to stay friends with him."
While the perils of connecting with strangers online are well known, the other Bob became the source of paternal positivity in Laymon's life she had always yearned for.
"I got a little bullied when I shaved my head during the pandemic," she recalls as we sit in a cosy corner of a quiet Melbourne wine bar. "And then I got a comment from Bob Laymon saying, 'I think it looks great.'
"[The movie] really impacted me and it brought up a lot of stuff that I've put deep down," Ferreira told Pop Culture Planet. (Supplied: Roadside Attractions)
"I got a happy birthday from him every single year when my dad never said it.
"I was in a beautiful state of shock."
This remarkably wholesome bond is fictionalised in Bob Trevino Likes It, Laymon's adorably bittersweet debut feature.
Euphoria star Barbie Ferreira stands in for the filmmaker. "I did imagine myself when I was writing it, but when it came time to cast the lead, I was looking for someone with vulnerability, a sense of humour, kindness and a hopeful, determined optimism," Laymon says.
"I thought if I wrote a movie about the things that mattered to me, then maybe [my dad] would see it and we could talk," Laymon says.  (Getty Images: Amanda Edwards)
Ferreira fit the bill. Renamed Lily Trevino, we first meet her as she's just found out via an errant text message that her boyfriend's cheating. Later, in a therapy session, Lily says, "Despite what my father says, I'm pretty sure it was not all my fault."
John Leguizamo (Romeo + Juliet) plays Lily's newly acquired Facebook dad, with French Stewart (3rd Rock from the Sun) as her irascible biological father.
Lily goes on an emotional rollercoaster. You can see a cascade of feels flicker across her face.
"There are moments where Barbie goes through three or four emotions in a couple of seconds," Laymon says. "It's an acting masterclass."
Laymon says it wasn't too weird, directing someone playing a version of herself. "We built trust together and really made it a safe space," she says. "I always had her back, and she always had mine. The truth was in the collaboration."
"I've had a lot of moments of loneliness ... so it was easy to tap into that and then just make him [Bob Trevino] like a regular guy," John Leguizamo (pictured) told The Mary Sue. (Supplied: Roadside Attractions)
The film won both the Grand Jury and the Audience Award at the 2024 SXSW film festival in Austin, Texas. It's where Laymon went to film school, interning for director Richard Linklater of the Before trilogy fame, shooting award-winning music videos to get by.
"I didn't have a lot of money and was struggling, but I figured that I could get bands to pay if I could convince them they wanted to do a narrative video," Laymon recalls. "My biological dad never came to any of my screenings."
Now based in Los Angeles, Laymon's family moved from Houston to Moscow when she was 14. It was the mid-90s and it was a culture shock.
"I found myself freezing, walking to Red Square and watching the changing of the guard while reading Catcher in the Rye," Laymon recalls.
She attended an international school. "My friends were from Nepal, Germany and Namibia, and those different points of view have really impacted my storytelling," she says. "I learned to appreciate belonging in a new space, because I realised over time that when I was a child, I didn't really feel like I belonged."
"It was such a small cast and crew, we were all really invested in this film," Ferreira told Film Independent. (Supplied: Roadside Attractions)
This yearning informs Bob Trevino Likes It. As does a horrific car accident after Laymon returned to America at 17, necessitating a painful, prolonged recovery.
Lauren 'Lolo' Spencer — The Sex Lives of College Girls star and proud disability advocate — plays Lily's best mate and live-in care client Daphne.
"Because I had a physical disability as a teenager, it was very important to me that character be authentically cast."
Laymon's father died in November 2022. She's processing that in new writing.
"We did have a peaceful end, thankfully, but I think without this healing period of my life where I learned healthy boundaries, I couldn't have had that," Laymon says.
"He didn't get to see the film, but it's strange. In a weird way, I feel like he's with me at the screenings."
And she'll never forget the kindness of the other Bob.
"He had no idea of the power of his words. It was just so beautiful, and now I try to be kind to everybody because it takes two seconds to reach out to someone who might really need it."

title: SA's last drive-in repaired over scorching summer in time for tourist season
content:
When contractor Dan Measey found out on Christmas eve he had won the public tender to rebuild Coober Pedy's drive-in cinema he knew he had a David and Goliath task ahead of him.
That is, he would be David, and working at the height of an outback summer would be his Goliath.
"The biggest enemy for us was the temperature and wind," Mr Measey said.
"We had a few days there where we were nudging 45, 46 [degrees Celsius].
"We're lifting sheet metal and long, steel members up into the air.
"Some late evening work and early morning work to try and avoid the heat and wind was really key because some of those things pretty much stopped the job."
The Coober Pedy Drive-in was repaired during hot and windy conditions this summer. (Facebook: Coober Pedy Drive-in)
The screen was pulled down last October but repairs would not take place until January.
They took about four weeks and were finally completed mid-February — Coober Pedy's hottest time of the year.
Several working bees with local volunteers also contributed to getting the venue running again.
While assessing the site Mr Measey also found much of the timber structure supporting the screen had rotted away over time.
Crews adding the finishing touches to the new screen.  (Facebook: Coober Pedy Drive-in)
Coober Pedy is in South Australia's outback, about a nine-hour drive north of Adelaide.
Its drive-in cinema is the last in the state after Adelaide's closed in November 2021.
Mr Measey has lived in Coober Pedy on and off, and is also the chair of a community group called Coober Pedy Together.
He said the drive-in had been "a big part of Coober Pedy's history" since it opened in 1965.
"Obviously back then no TV, no video, no DVD, no streaming," he said.
"The drive-in was open sometimes five, six, seven times a week.
"I remember my mother telling me, back in the 1970s her and Dad, when they first met, used to go there."
The first drive-in screen in Coober Pedy was built in 1964 and opened in 1965. (Supplied: Bill McDougall, Coober Pedy Drive-in)
The venue was forced to close when the screen was damaged by a storm on November 16, 2023.
Coober Pedy Drive-in committee chair Chantelle Bamford said the repairs took so long to happen because they were waiting on insurance to confirm if they could cover the costs.
Coober Pedy Drive-in chair Chantelle Bamford with her son, Tyrone, in front of the repaired screen. (Supplied: Chantelle Bamford)
In the end the insurance company covered the entire $150,000 required.
"They [the contractors] did such a good job, and they did it so quickly."
The asset is owned by the local council but run entirely by a committee of volunteers, and all the money made at the drive-in goes back into running the venue.
Ms Bamford said the drive-in was a major tourist attraction for Coober Pedy with some visiting the town just to have a drive-in experience.
She said the location made the drive-in unique.
The Coober Pedy Drive-in reopens in March for its 2025 season. (Facebook: Coober Pedy Drive-in)
"When you're looking towards the screen it faces town so you get to see the lights of town, the hills … it's a completely different backdrop to anywhere else," she said.
The first movie of this year's season was shown on March 1 ahead of the official reopening for the drive-in this Saturday, March 22.
author: Viki Ntafillis

title: Netflix spent $500m on this film yet couldn't afford a decent wig
content:
When it comes to its line-up of exclusive blockbusters, Netflix has never been one to spare any expense — even if it means hitting subscribers with another price hike.
Netflix's latest big-ticket release arrives in the form of The Electric State, a $US320 million adaptation of Simon Stålenhag's dystopic graphic novel, which sits among the most expensive movies ever made.
What: In an alternate sci-fi vision of the 90s where robots have been outlawed, a teenage girl goes searching for her brother with a smuggler and a team of misfit machines.
Starring: Millie Bobby Brown, Chris Pratt, Ke Huy Quan, Stanley Tucci, Giancarlo Esposito
Directed by: The Russo Brothers
Where: Streaming now on Netflix
Likely to make you feel: Negatively charged
Its directors, Joe and Anthony Russo, are no strangers to titanic Hollywood productions. Avengers: Infinity War and Endgame had a combined price tag of a billion dollars and demonstrated the brothers' unparalleled talent for finding a clear path through an impenetrable thicket of plot lines, acting schedules, CGI punch-ons and merchandising deals.
The Electric State has no shortage of other Avengers alumni. Chris Pratt (Guardians of the Galaxy) stars as another Han Solo rip-off, whose robot sidekick is voiced by Anthony Mackie (Captain America: Brave New World). Writers Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely, editor Jeffrey Ford and composer Alan Silvestri also collaborated with the Russos on Endgame.
Anthony and Joseph Russo worked on episodes of cult comedy shows Arrested Development and Community, but they're best known for directing Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame. (Supplied: Netflix)
But even when re-assembled with the talents behind their record-breaking superhero hits and equipped with a blank cheque, the film suffocates within the brothers' narrow creative limits.
Stålenhag's enigmatic approach to world building is immediately jettisoned via an opening info-dump montage: an alternate timeline of the 90s has seen animatronics revolt against their human masters, resulting in all-out war. The machines are on the precipice of winning — until tech CEO Ethan Skate (Stanley Tucci) invents an army of humanoid drones (controlled via neural interface) that turn the tide.
The Electric State kicks off several years after the war, where the surviving robots have been contained within a walled-off chunk of New Mexico termed the 'Exclusion Zone', and Skate's technology has enjoyed widespread adoption in the form of 'Neurocasters': chunky helmets that silo brainwaves into remote work and VR leisure simultaneously, leaving its users drooling and slack-jawed underneath.
The movie is strongest when it leans into the famous imagery from Stålenhag's graphic novel, particularly the disintegrating machines left to rust away after the war. (Supplied: Netflix)
Millie Bobby Brown plays Michelle, a rebellious teenager whose family died in a car accident during the war. At home, her foster dad lords over her primarily in drone form; at school, she resists the mandatory use of Neurocasters.
When the mind of her genius brother Christopher (Woody Norman; C'mon C'mon) suddenly resurfaces as the robot mascot from their favourite cartoon, she embarks on a road trip to the Exclusion Zone — picking up Pratt's roguish smuggler Keats along the way — to uncover the truth behind his apparent death.
The sooner movies abandon Gen X nostalgia, the better. The Electric State isn't a sci-fi adventure so much as it is a saccharine skip down memory lane; tributes are lovingly paid to a bygone American era of strip malls and twinkies, littered with twee covers of rock anthems.
Nowhere is the film's consumerist zeal more grating than in the prominence of real-life peanut butter mascot Mr Peanut, who's first glimpsed negotiating a peace treaty with Bill Clinton — an absurd sight gag that grows less funny the more screen time he's afforded. Voiced by Woody Harrelson, he's the leader of a group of animatronics who've made a new home within the Zone, and inexplicably becomes a driving voice of reason and compassion within the film.
Mr Peanut was killed off during a Superbowl commercial in 2020. Now he's the face of the revolution, for some reason.
There are other characters that exist within the Russos' new film, but none of them manage to crawl out from the shadow cast by this civil rights figurehead wrought from a walking, talking, and ghoulishly rendered advertising meme.
Besides, what else is there to say about Chris Pratt's reluctant manchild hero, except that he's clearly too old to still be doing this shtick? Ke Huy Quan (Everything Everywhere All At Once), on the other hand, has been criminally underutilised in his post-Oscars career — and is stuck playing a mysterious scientist working for Skate, with a screen time of mere minutes. Both are straddled with the least-convincing wigs $US320 million can buy.
The Electric State briefly switches on when it recreates Stålenhag's famous imagery, particularly that of hulking mechanical colossi rusting away in misty fields, or the parasitic headsets lodged to people's faces. The more disquieting implications of its world, as well as the despairing, melancholic tone of the Swedish artist's work, are understandably elided in this family-friendly blockbuster, yet raises questions of why the graphic novel was adapted in the first place.
The enormous budget seemingly doesn't extend to the wig department in Electric State. (Supplied: Netflix)
From their beginnings in experimental film to their pitch-perfect genre parodies in Community, it's apparent the Russo brothers have some affection for the medium. Yet their output over the past decade suggests a far greater passion for distilling cinema into content. Their films have increasingly challenged how flat and colourless an action blockbuster can be, and how hard the backs of CGI artists can be broken.
They bill themselves as independent filmmakers, only to use their extraordinary capital, goodwill and creative largesse to cook up different flavours of generic, straight-to-streaming slop.
The Electric State not only suggests that robots can have a soul — it convincingly argues that its filmmakers are still searching for one.

author: Jamie Tram

title: Cate Blanchett and Michael Fassbender play married sexy spies in Black Bag
content:
Stop me if you've heard this one before: a dashing secret agent discovers their glamorous partner may be the leak in a classified operation, and faces the unenviable task of flushing them out — or worse, taking their life.
What: A British intelligence agent suspects his wife might be involved in a threat to global security. Will he have to eliminate her?
Director: Steven Soderbergh
Starring: Michael Fassbender, Cate Blanchett, Naomi Harris, Marisa Abela, Tom Burke, Regé-Jean Page, Pierce Brosnan
When: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Hot and bothered
It's one of spy movies' most enduring hooks, and with good reason: who among us can't relate to the suspicion that can take root between partners, colleagues, or classmates, and the full-blown mania that follows?
Hot on the ectoplasmic heels of their ghost story Presence, director Steven Soderbergh and screenwriter David Koepp's latest collaboration stars Michael Fassbender as George Woodhouse, a steely British intelligence operative who finds himself in just such a classic pickle.
Cornered by a shady informant, he gets a tip that his work colleague and wife of many years, Kathryn St. Jean — an ice-cool Cate Blanchett — might be involved in a high-level security breach that could lead to global apocalypse.
"I'm fascinated by female spies," Blanchett tells the SMH. "I think there's a whole series of things women can achieve in espionage because they are underestimated." (Supplied: Universal)
It's a dilemma, to say the least, for the tightly coiled Woodhouse, a cipher who trades in double-think and speaks in the clipped tones of a man who might have stepped from the pages of a John Le Carré novel. He can't abide liars, and even surveilled his own secret agent father, ruining the old man's life and career in the name of truth and justice. But he's also fiercely dedicated to his wife, to the point where he'd do anything for her — including tracking her every move across the globe.
"I watch her," Woodhouse says at one point, more sexual voyeur than secret agent, "and I assume she watches me."
Few actors wear a turtleneck and black-rimmed glasses better than Fassbender, who looks as though he'd be equally at home in a 1960s espionage caper or at a Stereolab listening party.
"The opportunity to work with Steven Soderbergh again… I jumped at it," Fassbender told Men's Health. (Supplied: Universal)
He and a slinky, purring Blanchett make a formidable couple. Their erotic frisson is off the charts: when they throw a dinner party at their designer London terrace — and Woodhouse laces the drinks with truth serum — it's as much for the perverse thrill of the parlour game as it is to ostensibly set a trap.
In this thrillingly messy conversation, Woodhouse grills his romantically entangled colleagues — an MI6 therapist (Naomie Harris) and a cocky field operative (Bridgerton's Regé-Jean Page); a young hacker (Marisa Abela) and a jaded older spook (Furiosa's Tom Burke) — over cocktails and clandestine glances, generational hang-ups and sadomasochistic subterfuge.
When someone puts a dinner knife through their partner's hand, we get the distinct impression that the fate of the free world might hinge upon the whim of a jealous lover.
"[Soderbergh] is a real master," Fassbender (r) tells Today (US). "That's why you get this incredible bunch of actors together." (Also pictured: Rege-Jean Page and Naomi Harris) (Supplied: Universal)
Just who is playing who, especially when everyone is a professional liar? Is St. Jean spying on her husband? And might the security breach go all the way to intelligence top brass Arthur Stieglitz — played by former James Bond himself, Pierce Brosnan — a man who enjoys snacking on a cruel Japanese dish involving a live fish?
Award-winning director Steven Soderbergh talks about his unusual upbringing, falling in love with film and finally getting to work with Lucy Liu.
With few exceptions, the best spy movies understand that intrigue only gets you so far until you need to offer the audience something kinetic for their investment — a car chase, a daringly staged heist, hell, even a brisk stroll along the sidewalk can help break up the monotony of an overly tangled plot.
Based on its exhilarating and somewhat misleading trailer, Black Bag appears to be going down that route, but be warned: this is a movie steeped in conversations and endless meetings, where even an extended polygraph examination fails to quicken the pulse. (Its subjects are too calm and collected to fall for a lie detector, for one thing.)
From a certain perspective, it's all a little dull, especially when the plot — which is gussied up with tech gibberish — boils down to a good-versus-evil nuclear threat no more imaginative than a routine Fast and the Furious instalment.
"It’s a very, very specific take on people who are in the intelligence business but also have complex personal, emotional lives," Soderbergh tells The Playlist. (Supplied: Universal)
Still, Soderbergh is a slippery filmmaker with style to spare, as evidenced by a delicious tracking shot that follows Woodhouse into a dimly lit London nightclub, or the way he mines the movie's slick, sickly world of country-club fashion, cool surfaces and blown-out lighting for psychic menace.
There's a simmering tension to it all, rendered ever more anxious by the fact that it never quite comes to a boil.
Black Bag might end up being a stylish sliver of a movie, as spare and elusive as its protagonists. But there's at least one great joke to take away: the men and women charged with protecting the security of the world should probably all be in therapy.

title: First national Indian film festival goes beyond Bollywood
content:
Flashmobs, colourful lenghas and Bollywood songs are common features in Indian cinema.
However, Australia's first national Indian film festival is pulling away from this stereotype, screening films in multiple languages and genres.
The National Indian Film Festival of Australia (NIFFA) has wrapped up its first array of programs across the country, with plans to return annually.
The festival was held across 18 days, over February and early March, and aims to bring South Asian films to screens down under.
NIFFA director and Indian-Australian filmmaker Anupam Sharma hoped the festival would expose Australian audiences to the diversity of South Asian cinema.
Maa Oori Ramayanam is one of the documentaries that debuted at NIFFA, by Indian-Australian producer Pradeep Maduri.
Set in the Seethampalli village in Telangana, Mr Maduri depicts the collective efforts of performing an ancient Indian story, the Ramayana.
Maa Oori Ramayanam delves into the lives of villagers who have an unwavering devotion to a traditional theatre practice. (Supplied: NIFFA)
Mr Maduri's work centres around sharing stories from rural India across the globe.
Mr Sharma said NIFFA aimed to "empower Australians, particularly of Indian and South Asian origin, to tell their story themselves without … supervision of any other culture".
"Once you are telling cultural stories from a culturally authentic space, the stereotypes will wash away … So, I hope the more stories we tell, the more Australian film agencies [will] support diverse Australian storytellers."
The festival aims to allows creatives the opportunities to tell powerful stories. (Supplied: NIFFA)
While Australia's film industry is recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, South Asian cinema has experienced a pocket of growth.
Mr Sharma said the Indian diaspora in Australia contributed more to box office sales than the average cinema-goer.
"They are punching way above their weight, some might say even eight [or] nine times."
Indian film releases, like Pushpa: The Rule — Part 2, brought in millions of dollars at the Australian box office.
Screen Australia figures show India produced more than 1,300 films locally in 2022, compared to 24 in Australia.
In 2023, the majority of films released in Australia came from Asia, at 44 per cent, followed by 23 per cent by the US.
In November 2023, the federal government announced the Australia-India Audio-visual Co-production Agreement, which provides filmmakers with access to shared funding and resources.
"This is such an overdue tool for us to narrate our shared stories with investment from India," Mr Sharma said.
"The moment I structure a co-production I have got benefits from Australia and benefits from India. Those are the financial benefits, on top of them I have the creative benefits."
This year's Indian film festival screened at local cinemas across the country, including Dendy's Cinema in Newtown.
Cinema attendees said diverse films acted as "gateways to other cultures" and were "really important to understand the communities we live in, in Australia".
One patron told the ABC that having an Indian film festival in Australia "was quite exciting and gave people a unique opportunity [to see] what Indian cinema is all about".
Festival patrons tell ABC News they were "excited" to see Indian films hit the Australian mainstream. (Supplied: NIFFA)
Mr Sharma noted there was "interest in non-Indians to see Indian cinema and not Bollywood".
"All the mainstreamed films get screened throughout the year … but it is films which have never been screened in a theatre that catches the attraction," he said.
NIFFA's program this year included 36 Australian premieres and three world premieres.
With plans for NIFFA to return in 2026, featuring films in Punjabi, the festival is also going regional.
Dendy's Cinema in Newtown is one of multiple cinemas across Australia that has taken part in NIFFA. (ABC News: Thorsten Joses)
Filmmakers believe there is demand for South Asian cinema in smaller towns as well, particularly as migrant populations are growing in regional Australia.
"Dubbo Film Society and Dubbo Indian Society have signed up, and now NIFFA will have a regional arm, called NIFFA Regional," Mr Sharma said.
"When we talk about diversity in cinema, we're not asking for a favour, we are not asking for a handout. All we want is for our streets to be accurately represented on our screens."
author: Nandini Dhir

title: Shakespeare enters the virtual world in new doco Grand Theft Hamlet
content:
Despite releasing 12 years and three console generations ago, the seedy metropolis of Grand Theft Auto V (GTA V) remains an unsurpassed feat of virtual simulation.
What: A doco about the staging of a Hamlet production in the virtual world of Grand Theft Auto Online.
Directed by: Pinny Grylls, Sam Crane
Starring: Sam Crane, Mark Oosterveen
Where: Streaming on Mubi
Likely to make you feel: Inspired
Its 80-square-kilometre map is flush with sports cars, heavy artillery and trigger-happy cops that tempt players to enact their grandest Hollywood crime fantasies. But in its sheer fidelity to real-life Los Angeles, the open world of Los Santos caters to other comparatively mundane pleasures.
It's easy to spend hours admiring the city's famous architectural hotspots, snapping golden-hour selfies, or cycling across the surrounding wilderness; when playing with friends in GTA Online, the city's interactive casinos, night clubs and dive bars redress the game as a decadent hangout simulator.
In the new doco Grand Theft Hamlet, the seemingly boundless possibilities of Los Santos are stretched to their limits when two out-of-work actors attempt to stage a live production of Shakespeare within the game itself.
"The game is very chaotic but it is ultimately a beautiful world," Sam Crane told Hammer To Nail. "In order for the audience to appreciate that beauty we needed to find this way to get a bit more contemplative with the shot making." (Supplied: MUBI)
Though the outside world is never once glimpsed — the film is comprised solely of gameplay footage recorded from the perspective of its subjects — the backdrop of England's third COVID lockdown is palpable.
Productions across the country have shuttered, and alternate avenues for work are scarce. Even the joys of escaping into video games have grown tired for thespians Sam Crane (whose career spans Assassin's Creed: Syndicate and the lead role in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child) and Mark Oosterveen (The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare), who nonetheless find they're unable to tear themselves away.
Rehearsals for the play can become shootouts in the blink of an eye. (Supplied: MUBI)
Following a night spent grinding at slot machines and half-heartedly gunning down civilians, the two friends stumble upon an open-air auditorium. Mark instinctively rattles off a Macbeth soliloquy on stage, and they begin pondering the possibilities of live theatre within the ultra-violent sandbox of GTA Online (where players earn points for killing other active users). The idea of orchestrating a production of Hamlet quickly materialises.
Logistical concerns aside, their chaotic choice of venue feels appropriate in its own way — few of The Bard's tales sport a higher body count than the tragedy that befalls the Prince of Denmark. As Sam neatly summarises: "People are violent in Shakespeare. It's f***ing brutal."
As filmmaker Sam Crane says, the violence in Shakespeare — not unlike in GTA — is "f***ing brutal". (Supplied: MUBI)
Grand Theft Hamlet is frequently hilarious in capturing the unpredictable human interactions that arise within online multiplayer games. When approaching other users to advertise their casting call, Sam and Mark are shot, pulverised, and burnt to a crisp. Rehearsals escalate into shoot-outs on a dime. Outside of Baz Luhrmann's cinema, you're unlikely to see Shakespeare recited with quite so many rifles and suggestive outfits.
On the other hand, there's a touching sincerity in many of the interactions shared with those who express interest in the production. The online players include 'DJPhil', a literary agent using her nephew's GTA account, who's always wanted to act in Hamlet; 'Turkomas', the Shakespeare nerd with a self-described "face for radio and a voice for mime"; 'ParTebMosMir', an enigmatic passer-by who, when encouraged, performs a moving recitation from the Quran while dressed as an alien.
GTA user ParTebMosMir performing a moving recitation from the Quran while dressed as an alien. (Supplied: MUBI)
Both the play and the broader film are enormously creative in how they repurpose the game's mechanics to tell their own story. The freedom of physical movement in GTA is largely restricted to running, shooting and driving, while faces don't evolve beyond lips that move in real-time when speaking into a microphone. There's an inherent, charming jank to the game's limited suite of expressions, yet it can feel surprisingly alive to behold — a stand-out monologue sees one player carefully pace the stage with a knife in hand, embellishing her monologue with a stabbing motion and custom emotes.
The show's production design is certainly unique in its Michael Bay maximalism, with Hamlet's city of Elsinore reinterpreted through Los Santos's corporate high-rises and luxury vehicles (all painstakingly bought with in-game currency). One scene even takes place atop a moving blimp, and features the inherent comedy of watching the performers trying not to fall off.
Could this be "poor Yorick's" final resting place in GTA? Alas, you'll have to watch the movie to find out. (Supplied: MUBI)
Not unlike last month's Sing Sing, Grand Theft Hamlet can feel a little too conventional and streamlined in its approach to theatre making. Neither Sam nor his co-director and wife, doco filmmaker Pinny Grylls, spend much time lingering on the artifice of its world, when so much of the online-gaming experience can be steeped in a quiet, uncanny ennui between the explosive interruptions.
At times, it's hard not wonder how much of the on-screen footage has been re-enacted or exists purely for the sake of the documentary, such as an argument between Sam and Pinny (which reveals just how much he's been neglecting offline), or the first time Sam tries out Hamlet's iconic speech. There's a cinematic slickness to the film which, ironically, takes away from the authentically inhuman qualities of its world.
Still, the sheer novelty and emotional gravitas of Grand Theft Hamlet shines through. Grylls and Crane remind us not just of the rich, untapped potential of video games (at a time when the industry predominantly caters to violent escapism), but also of the sheer necessity of art, even in the face of seemingly insurmountable barriers.

title: David Wenham still gets stopped in the street over this iconic character
content:
Australian actor David Wenham was in Brisbane late last year and had just left the Queensland Gallery of Modern Art when a holler interrupted his thoughts.
"I turned around to see where it was coming from and a bus had pulled up behind me, door open, and the driver's asking me if I needed any assistance with my bus fare."
What: A big-hearted follow-up to cult classic Gettin' Square
Directed by: Jonathan Teplitzky
Starring: David Wenham, Arlo Green, David Field, Gary Sweet
When: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: like getting your thongs on and causing trouble
It's been more than 20 years since Wenham played hapless, bus-fare-deficient crim Johnny Francis "Spit" Spiteri in Gettin' Square, but it's still the film that folks stop him in the street about most. And it wasn't even a box office hit at the time.
"The release was botched at the cinema," Wenham says of Jonathan Teplitzky's cracking heist caper. "It found a subsequent life of its own through VHS and then DVD, which was extraordinary. It just developed this pretty incredible sort of cult following."
So much so that Teplitzky and Gettin' Square screenwriter Chris Nyst have been discussing crafting a sequel over the years. But it was Wenham's close friend and fellow filmmaker Robert Connolly who convinced him to step back into Johnny's thongs.
"We were talking about Johnny, thinking up all the bizarre little situations he could be involved in, so I rang Chris and talked about it with him," Wenham says. "Very soon after arrived the first draft of Spit, which he had been working on for quite some time.
Wenham's never quite shaken the strangely lovable character of Johnny since first playing him in 2003. (Supplied: Transmission Films)
"When I read it, it was on."
And Nyst already knows Johnny's underbelly world inside out.
"He's an extremely successful and revered criminal lawyer who's represented some incredibly colourful characters," Wenham says. "[Nyst's] ability to really put that on the page is pretty neat."
Released in 2003, Gettin' Square starred Sam Worthington as Barry, a prison inmate alongside Johnny, who sets his heart on going straight after they are both released. The two wind up working in the same restaurant kitchen.
Spit sees Wenham's Johnny return to Australia, with no sign of Barry, after fleeing the cops at the end of the original film.
"He comes with the same wardrobe and mullet, albeit a little less hirsute and not as greasy now, because he hasn't been on the gear for more than 20 years," Wenham says.
"As soon as I put those thongs on, bizarrely, I could just feel Johnny instantly again."
Johnny's thongs and mullet are more simple nods to Australian cliches: they're intrinsic to his identity. (Supplied: Transmission Films)
Wenham first had another crack at playing Johnny when he happened to be in London at the same time as Teplitzky, Nyst and makeup artist Tess Natoli.
"I pitched the idea of going to an op-shop and buying clothes Johnny would wear, and Tess said she could do a dodgy little trial run," Wenham explains.
Fully made-up, Wenham took to the streets as Johnny.
"We started on the tube escalators, filmed him coming out of Scotland Yard, then we went into the Portrait Gallery and got thrown out of it," he says. "None of that's in the movie and never was going to be, but once I'm in [character] we can throw him in any situation."
Of course, trouble's never far behind Johnny. Spit begins with him returning to Australia on a fake passport. Arrested in the airport, he's sent to a detention camp predominantly populated by refugees, including Jihad Kalif (Iranian New Zealand actor Arlo Green).
Always a good soul, if a misguided one, Johnny helps Jihad and his fellow detainees learn very colloquial Aussie English.
When Johnny finds himself locked up, again, in a detention centre, he meets (from left to right) Hayyan (Sami Afuni), Baktash (Ayik Chut) and Jihad Kalif (Arlo Green). (Supplied: Transmission Films)
"It was a little stroke of genius of Chris's to have a very touchy issue portrayed in a comedic way that's also very touching," Wenham says. "The majority of actors who portrayed the detainees were either refugees themselves or offspring of refugees and it was amazing working with them."
Sadly for Johnny, his old nemeses — David Field's bent cop Arne Deviers and Gary Sweet's gangster Charles "Chicka" Martin — are still looking for him, knowing that he can tilt an ongoing investigation against them.
Speaking on a dreary London morning, Teplitzky says they had no idea how iconic Wenham's character would become for Australians who largely missed the film in cinema.
"Gettin' Square's not really about Johnny," he says. "He's like the icing on the cake that brings a lot of the fun and silliness."
Telling honest stories about Australian history and culture is "what defines us", says Wenham (left), pictured with Jonathan Teplitzky (centre) and Chris Nyst. (Supplied: Transmission Films)
Johnny may be off the gear, but nostalgia's a powerful drug.
"When you think about the things that really bring you pleasure, so often, they're from the past," Teplitzky says.
"If you ask six of your friends what bit they love most from Gettin' Square, they would all tell a slightly different story. We wanted to tap into that energy, rather than follow in exactly the same footsteps. It's a great credit to David that you can take an audience anywhere with this character because they trust him."
Johnny is an everyman and that's why people identify with him so much, Teplitzky says.
"There was a lot more mileage to go slightly deeper with him as an anti-authority guy, the mythological version of what Australians would like to be."
The refugee angle, with the detention centre filmed in a COVID-19 isolation centre built on the Gold Coast, allowed Nyst and Teplitzky to burst the bubble around that myth.
Johnny's willingness to take people as they come, without fear or judgement, is something many of us could learn from. (Supplied: Transmission Films)
"In many ways, mateship is this cornerstone of Australian culture," the director says.
"I grew up hearing this eternal phrase about how Australia is the most tolerant country in the world. And as you get older, you realise what nonsense that is. If our culture is based on mateship and tolerance towards all people, then you can't go locking people up in the way that we have done historically."
Spit has a jab at this hypocrisy without ever feeling didactic.
"The first thing we wanted to do is try and make a really funny film and give cinema audiences a laugh," Teplitzky says. "Johnny is completely unjudgemental [sic]. If you do right by him, he'll do right by you, and vice versa. It doesn't matter where you come from. And that should be our cornerstone."
As far as Wenham is concerned, telling Australian stories truthfully is vitally important.
"It's what defines us. It's our history. Without stories, we're nothing."

title: Charles thought he'd end up in jail. Now he's directing Guy Pearce
content:
Growing up in Melbourne's outer suburbs with family members in and out of prison, Charles Williams credits film with changing his life.
What: Australian thriller about the prisons we build for ourselves and each other.
Director: Charles Williams
Starring: Guy Pearce, Cosmo Jarvis, Vincent Miller, Toby Wallace, Chloe Hayden
When: In cinemas now
Likey to make you feel: Tense and apprehensive
As a teenager, he often drove an hour-and-a-half to the Astor Theatre in St Kilda to catch a double feature.
"I'd go like four times a week, and I'd see two doubles on Sundays, driving home at midnight in Mum's shitty car … half asleep, dreaming about the movie," says the director.
"I'd just be washed in this incredible experience of seeing something that just infected me completely, that I couldn't put into words."
Two decades later, Williams has won the Short Film Palme d'Or at Cannes Film Festival for All These Creatures, and has just debuted his first feature.
INSIDE Official Trailer
Inside — starring Guy Pearce, Cosmo Jarvis and teen newcomer Vincent Miller — is the result of years of research into Victoria's corrections system and William's own life experiences.
The result is a tightly packed, thought-provoking crime thriller featuring characters less concerned with busting out of prison than they are with breaking free of themselves.
In Inside, we meet 18-year-old Mel as he's transferred from a juvenile detention centre to an adult prison.
Vincent Miller was just 15 years old when he took on the role, responding to an open-call with a taped audition that Williams called "magnetic".
Vincent Miller landed his first lead role in Inside at just 15. (Bonsai Films)
Miller travelled from his home in the NSW Northern Rivers region to spend months shooting in Victorian correction centres, completing his Year 10 schoolwork remotely.
While he admits spending days at a time in real prisons "did feel a bit weird", learning from the likes of Guy Pearce meant he "didn't really want to go back to normal life, I just missed [the film] so much".
Miller's character is taken in by Mark Shepard (Cosmo Jarvis), a man despised across the country for the horrific crime he committed at age 13, and Warren Murfett (Pearce), a soon-to-be-paroled inmate with debts to pay.
Miller's Mel is taken in by adult criminals in the film, including Jarvis's character Mark Shepard. (Bonsai Films)
"I learnt a lot of things about these environments that not a lot of other people my age would know," Vincent, who's now 17, says.
"I think that definitely made me a lot more independent and mature."
Much of Inside, like All These Creatures before it, centres on a feeling of inevitability. It asks: If all my family before me is violent, or an addict, or in prison, why would I turn out any different?
Williams didn't want to become like the adults he grew up around, but he wasn't sure if he'd be able to avoid it.
"I don't think they wanted to end up that way [either], and yet they did," he says.
"Growing up, I felt guilty for stuff I hadn't done … [wondering], 'Am I just gonna wake up one day and be this other person, and then justify it all … blaming everyone else?'"
Williams says he and Guy Pearce spoke for a year in the lead-up to the film, mostly about their family backgrounds. (Bonsai Films)
There's a sense that Mel in the film could be Williams, in another life, on another path.
The director says, if anything, he put a little too much of himself into Inside.
"I showed the film to my partner … she was in tears watching the movie, and her first comment to me was: 'Don't do that to yourself again.'"
But for Williams, working on the project also helped him process his experiences, something he hoped his cast took away from the project, too.
Most of the background actors in Inside are former prisoners and current guards. (Bonsai Films)
He spent four years researching, visiting prisons and interviewing officers and inmates, many of whom also starred in the film, and who were encouraged to participate and speak up during production.
"[I told the former inmates]: 'I want you guys involved, I want you to feel that the years you wasted in this f***ing place, like you got something out of it, you got to contribute something.'
"And I think they [did get] a lot of out of it, particularly [acting alongside] the officers and realising that not everyone's against them."
Released after the Queensland election, when "adult crime, adult time" was a key campaign promise, along with a similar recent move to lower the age of criminal responsibility in the NT, Williams maintains the film is not a political statement.
"No-one goes into a movie like this and goes: 'You know what, before I got here, I thought kids should be locked up. And now I don't.'
"I just don't think that's what art is for. I think that's what propaganda is for."
However, Inside does raise questions around the culpability, rehabilitation and intergenerational trauma of young, violent offenders.
The characters in Inside look for ways to overcome their guilt and trauma. (Bonsai Films)
Williams points to statistics around acquired brain injuries, which affect 40 per cent of the prison population in Victoria, compared to 2 per cent of the wider population.
"If someone's 10 years old, even if they had a great upbringing, are they really completely culpable for their behaviour when we know their brains haven't developed yet?
"[What if] they have a learning disability from their upbringing, and they're six years old mentally, [or they] have a traumatic brain injury … so they can barely make decisions properly?"
He also approached the issue of Indigenous incarceration rates with real-world examples in mind.
"I took the exact percentage of Indigenous people incarcerated in Victoria, which is 10.8 per cent, and then I cast exactly 11 per cent of the cast Indigenous, and the same with Sudanese and other CALD communities."
Inside was shot in real prisons, its cast and crew undergoing security scans and eating lunch in the facility. (Bonsai Films)
Prison setting aside, the themes of trying to control our own habits and actions, no matter "how small or big", is relevant to just about everyone.
He hopes people leave Inside with the same feeling he swam in on those long drives home from the cinema as a teenager.
"You weren't like: 'Now I know it's bad to be mean. Now I know racism is bad.' It was never that.
"You just felt less lonely and more connected to the human experience, almost in the world of the character … [those] movies were the ones that really made such a difference to my life."
Inside is in cinemas now.

title: A son reckons with his dad's mortality in this shockingly funny doc
content:
Lars Hammar was a beloved French high school teacher for 40 years in the small Swedish town of Köping.
Alongside raising two children with his wife Tiina, he nursed a lifelong obsession with the life and culture of France. When he retired at the age of 66, he was full of hope and anticipation for the life he was about the embark on outside the strictures of a full-time job.
What: A son's gradual acceptance of his ageing father's mortality
Director: Filip Hammar and Fredrik Wikingsson
Starring: Lars Hammar, Filip Hammar, Fredrik Wikingsson
When and where: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Frustrated and incredibly moved
Fast forward 14 years and the reality is quite different. Belaboured by a host of health problems, Lars is living for the sake of living, his former zest for life extinguished by the physical and emotional tolls of ageing.
Increasingly disheartened by his father's malaise, Lars' son Filip decides to take his father on a road trip to the French coastal town of Beaulieu-sur-Mer where they used to holiday — the site of his happiest memories. Filip ropes in his best friend Fredrik Wikingsson (the film's co-director) and buys a dinky orange Renault 4, the exact same car his father used to drive their family around in.
"Just to see my dad smile again, those moments were incredible," Filip Hammar told ABC News Breakfast. (Supplied: Universal Pictures)
A reluctant Lars is cajoled into going, but the three hit a snag early in the trip when Lars suffers a fall in his hotel room. Undeterred, Filip and Fredrik continue their road trip while Lars heals, and he flies to join them in Beaulieu-sur-Mer.
The quest to reacquaint Lars with everything that excited him about life resumes, with varying results.
For non-Swedish viewers, it's important to spell out that Filip and Fredrik are a popular TV duo who have been gracing Swedish television screens for decades.
This explains the superior production values of a film seemingly put together by two friends with no media experience.
Though well-intentioned, Filip's actions can be hard to watch. Exceedingly bullish and insensitive as he chides his father to do things, it's clear Filip has never lived with someone who has a mental illness, let alone one exacerbated by the physical challenges of ageing.
In turn, we see Lars carrying the heavy burden of someone else's lofty expectations of him.
The Renault 4 the trio drove for their journey had to have liquid lead poured into the fuel. (Supplied: Universal Pictures)
Filip's inability to grapple with his father's mortality waxes and wanes across the course of the film, culminating in a particularly heartbreaking scene towards the end when Filip encourages his father to recreate his famed ratatouille, with disastrous consequences.
The film morphs into Filip's gradual journey of acceptance as he contends with the inevitabilities of ageing and mortality.
But there's much to love about the film as well. Fredrik is a useful foil to Filip's insistence that his father can resurrect his former glory by retracing the footsteps of his life, and Lars genuinely does seem to come alive during their trip — a joy to watch.
The film is also exceedingly funny, despite itself, particularly in Lars' mordant humour and the hijinks that ensue in the "the most overtaken car in Europe".
Footage of present-day Lars gingerly reorienting himself with places of his youth is overlaid with audio diaries that show him in his younger years — a gregarious, often sunburnt life-of-the-party who wore many hats: avid storyteller, guitarist, chef.
Filip Hammar (L) told ABC News Breakfast the message of the film "is something as basic as: enjoy hanging out with your loved ones, and don't try to make them something they aren't anymore".  (Supplied: Universal Pictures)
The distance between the two imbues the film with an inescapable melancholy. But the quieter, more emotional beats of the film are rarely left to be, often drowned out by Christian Olsson's overbearing score that, at times, seems emblematic of Filip's smothering of his father.
The close friendship Filip and Fredrik share and the bond Filip has with his father are nevertheless powerful ripostes against the stifling cloak of toxic masculinity.
These men are open with their feelings for one another, prone to outbursts of emotion and professions of love. It's a beautiful thing to observe in a film that, apart from Filip's mother, features predominantly men.
How 'The Last Journey' became Sweden's most-watched documentary (ABC News Breakfast)
Some of the issues documentary purists may have with The Last Journey lie in its construction. Close-up shots of Filip, Fredrik and Lars in their bright orange Renault from Köping to Beaulieu-sur-Mer are interspersed with cinematography drawing on the stunning vistas that surround them — rendering it much more like a feature film than a documentary.
The autumnal transcendence of north-western Europe is so beautifully evoked, the film almost feels like a tourism ad at times.
In the outlandish lengths they go to in a bid to jog Lars' memory and reconjure that same sense of joy, Filip and Fredrik are also provoking a reaction from Lars using completely fabricated set pieces, further blurring the line between fact and fiction and relegating him to an inert actor in his own life.
"[Lars is] a hilarious character, but also very kind and good, and we wanted the film to feel as joyous as he is, and his whole life has been," co-director Fredrik Wikingsson told ABC News Breakfast about his best friend's dad.  (Supplied: Universal Pictures)
That this film was entered by Sweden as its International Feature Submission in the Oscars further muddles matters, though its emotional resonance means it's also the highest grossing documentary ever released in the country.
Anyone with ageing parents will no doubt find much affinity with the circumstances depicted in The Last Journey, but its greatest achievement arguably lies in its ability to elevate the life of an ordinary person — who lives in what Filip calls the "most boring town in Sweden" — into something worthy of adulation and preservation.
An incredibly moving moment towards the end is an absolute tear-jerker — it's less about a linear path to recovery, and more an acknowledgement of someone who's had a sizeable impact on the great many people who have crossed his path.

title: Tired of dark projects, this First Nations director made a joyful animation
content:
Having children changed the way Chantelle Murray tells stories.
The trailblazing writer, director and performer grew up in the Kimberley's Djarindjin community, a few hours north of Broome.
She's worked alongside the likes of Taika Waititi and Baz Luhrman, and is behind a string of short films exploring the brutal experiences of First Nations communities, including the Stolen Generations.
"All my previous stuff has been quite heavy, and becoming a mum, it changes you as a person," Murray explains.
Her debut animated feature, The Lost Tiger — about a plucky young tiger who sets off on an adventure to find his people — was released in cinemas last week.
The Lost Tiger | Trailer
While she says it does still have "all of those undertones of generational trauma", with themes around stolen land and resources, it's ultimately a lively, light family adventure.
"I just wanted to bring out some happiness for myself and for my children, because that's how I'm able to function in life."
Adopted as a baby by a family of kangaroos, Teo (voiced by Heartbreak High's Thomas Weatherall) doesn't know who he is or where he's from.
Commonly referred to as a Tasmanian tiger, Murray explains the thylacine was actually found Australia wide, with the last of its species confined to Tasmania.
She says the extinct carnivore appears in "cave paintings all through Arnhem Land, all through the Kimberleys".
"I really wanted to explore what that's like, for one animal to feel like it's the only one left … and how isolating that must feel."
Teo searches for his people and reconnects with his Nana in The Lost Tiger. (Like a Photon Creative)
Teo soon sets off on an epic quest to find his homeland and his tribe, alongside wannabe adventurer and oddball sidekick Plato (voiced by Our Flag Means Death's Rhys Darby).
But in hot pursuit of the unlikely duo is Celeste Barber's Quinella Quoll, who wishes to strip Teo's home island of its natural resources and add them to her collection. Murray says to keep an eye out for hidden details — like Quinella's numberplate being the postcode of the British Museum.
The Lost Tiger is Chantelle Murray's debut feature. (Supplied)
Teo's adoptive kangaroo family are also on the chase, with his dad Red (Jimi Bani) and mum Kara (Nakkiah Lui) worried sick.
For Murray, Teo's story of finding his country was partly inspired by her late father, a white man who fell in love with her Indigenous and Malaysian mum and community, back when having interracial relationships and mixed-race children was "such a frowned-upon thing".
Murray says her dad was always searching for where he belonged.
"His only place he ever found in the world was getting to know my people.
"I think it's not just an Aboriginal thing of someone finding their home. It's a universal [experience] for every person trying to find their place in the world and where they belong, finding their tribe."
Murray's upbringing in Broome and the Kimberley is evident throughout the film: red dirt, towering cliffs and shimmering turquoise ocean colour Teo's world.
The beauty of Broome and the Kimberley is captured throughout The Lost Tiger. (Like a Photon Creative)
As a 14-year-old, the director's first job was at the iconic Sun Pictures deckchair cinema — which is now showing The Lost Tiger. She can't make it along, but her mum will travel into town for a screening.
Strong women appear in all their forms throughout the film — Teo's kangaroo mum in the movie is jacked: "Obviously, [she's] what I aspire to look like," Murray jokes.
Teo's mum (right) is quite literally a strong woman. (Like a Photon Creative)
Murray says she was inspired by her own experiences of being raised by her nana, who "held down the community", and her primary school teacher mum, who "always took in children in need".
"It's a reflection of my life and the women around me."
Having family around has always been important for Murray, but was particularly vital throughout the recent Voice to Parliament debate and result.
"When the vote came out, I was heartbroken, because I've got children that are Aboriginal," she says.
"I called up my mum, and I was like: 'How do we navigate this?'"
Chantelle looks to her mum for guidance and support. (Instagram: @chantellejmurray)
She tears up as she remembers her mum's response, who said the only way to cope was to remember that "all we can control is [ourselves] and the people around us and choose to be kind".
"Mum's not the person who's at the front of the rallies," Murray says.
Chantelle's own contribution is through storytelling, and she added a similar line in the film.
"You can't prevent bad things from happening, but you can trust that you will be strong enough to endure them," Teo and the young audience is told.
"All you can control is how you respond."
The Lost Tiger is in cinemas now.

title: The biggest moments from the 2025 Oscars ceremony
content:
The final major event of award season, the 2025 Oscars, had it all.
Shock wins, lengthy acceptance speeches, show-stopping performances and plenty of political statements filled the 3-hour ceremony.
Here are the key moments from the 2025 Oscars.
The 25-year-old star of Anora, Mikey Maddison, has shocked viewers by winning Best Actress at the 97th Academy Awards.
Madison scored an upset over Demi Moore, who had been favoured to claim the gong for her role in The Substance.
"I grew up in Los Angeles, but Hollywood always felt so far away from me," Madison said on stage.
"To be here standing in this room today is really incredible."
She said she wanted to "thank and honour the sex worker community".
"I will continue to be an ally."
The film also won Best Picture following an unpredictable Oscars race.
Conclave and The Brutalist were initially thought to be frontrunners for Best Picture.
Ariana Grande looks ethereal while opening the show with a rendition of Somewhere Over the Rainbow.  (Reuters: Carlos Barria )
In one of the moments audiences had been excited for weeks, Wicked stars Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo took to the stage to sing a medley of songs from the Wizard of Oz universe.
Looking ethereal in a red and sparkly gown with rainbow lights flooding her face, Grande began the medley with a rendition of Somewhere Over the Rainbow.
Cynthia Erivo then entered stage right, crooning the song Home, originally sung by Diana Ross in the 1978 musical The Wiz.
And the singers joined each other for Defying Gravity, with the emotion of the moment obvious for each star.
Now that Wicked part two has finished production, the pair may have sung the iconic song together for the last time.
The audience gave a standing ovation.
The song followed an opening montage of films such as Lala Land which were shot in Los Angeles — a homage to the city which endured wildfires earlier this year.
The pair sang in front of a backdrop of the city throughout the performance.
Sean Baker wins the Oscar for Best Film Editing at the 97th Oscars.  (Reuters: Carlos Barria)
It was a historic night for several winners but no-one had a night as eventful as Anora's Sean Baker.
Baker has won the most personal awards for one film ever.
Baker, who directed, wrote and edited the film took home the Oscars for Best Director, Best Original Screenplay, Best Editing and Best Picture.
Walt Disney also won four Oscars in 1953, but that was for four different films.
Mikey Madison also took home Best Actress for her role in Anora.
In Baker's third speech of the night, for Best Director, the filmmaker encouraged people to keep going to movie theatres and supporting cinema.
After winning Best Picture, Baker thanked the academy for recognising a "truly independent film" which cost $US6 million ($9.64) to make.
Zoe Saldana also took home the Supporting Actress honour, making her the first actress with Dominican heritage to win the category.
Zoe Saldana emotionally accepts her Oscar for Best Supporting Actress.  (Reuters: Carlos Barria)
"I am a proud child of immigrant parents with dreams and dignity and hard-working hands," she said.
"I am the first American of Dominican origin to accept an Academy award, and I know I will not be the last. I hold the fact that I am getting an award for a role where I got to sing and speak in Spanish."
Paul Tazewell became the first black man to win Best Costume Design.
And, in big news for Latvia, Flow won the Best Animated Feature award, giving the small European country its first Oscar.
This is Adrien Brody's second Oscar win.  (Reuters: Carlos Barria)
Best Actor winner Adrien Brody gave a heartfelt but pretty long speech.
The actor had a long list of people to thank and was determined to get through it.
He spent a large majority of the speech talking about having the "privilege of perspective".
"Acting is a very fragile profession. It looks very glamorous, and in certain moments it is, but the one thing that I have gained, having the privilege to come back here, is to have some perspective," he said.
When the orchestra began to play Brody off, he demanded it stop and said he would finish quickly.
"I'm wrapping up, please, please, please, I will wrap up. Please turn the music off. I've done this before. It's not my first rodeo. Thank you."
He then went on.
"I pray for a healthier and happier and more inclusive world, and I believe if the past can teach us anything, it is a reminder: Do not let hate go unchecked."
He was played out once again and hastily wrapped up after saying: "OK, I'll get out of here."
Shirin Sohani and Hossein Molayemi with their Oscars after a difficult journey to the Dolby Theatre. 

  (Reuters: Carlos Barria )
Iranian filmmakers Hossein Molayemi and Shirin Sohani, the duo behind the Oscar-winning animated short In the Shadow of the Cypress, almost didn't make it to the ceremony.
In their acceptance speech, they said they stepped off a plane to LA three hours before the ceremony began, having had great difficulty securing visas to the United States.
"It's a miracle, and speaking in front of this expectant audience is very hard for us," Molayemi said.
"Yes, if we preserve and remain faithful, miracles will happen."
The film is about a captain living a remote life by the sea with his daughter while struggling with post-traumatic stress disorder.
In the weeks leading up to the ceremony, Variety reported that the filmmakers also saw promised government aid rescinded, leaving them with limited options regarding international travel.
Molayemi told Variety that they had always faced great difficulty travelling overseas but it had become worse since Donald Trump returned to the White House.
Clément Ducol and Camille sing together during their acceptance speech.  (Reuters: Carlos Barria )
French composer duo Clément Ducol and Camille took home the Best Original Song award for their track, El Mal, which appears in Emilia Perez.
"We are so grateful," Camille said in her acceptance speech.
"We wrote El Mal as a song to denounce corruption, and we hope it speaks to the role music and art can play and continue to play as a force of good and progress in the world."
Camille and Ducol, who are married, finished their speech by singing in harmony "Emilia Perez" repeatedly.
The camera panned to some viewers in the crowd looking a little puzzled, clapping, or laughing.
Members of the Los Angeles Fire Department join Conan O'Brien on stage.  (Reuters: Carlos Barria)
Following on from other award ceremonies this season, the Oscars ceremony included a section paying homage to firefighters who fought the LA wildfires.
Host and comedian Conan O'Brien brought numerous members of the Los Angeles and Pasadena fire departments on stage.
"Please welcome members of the fire service who bravely responded to and battled the Palisades and Eaton wildfires. On behalf of everyone in greater Los Angeles, thank you for all that you do," O'Brien said.
"Now I know you're going to find this hard to believe, but there are some jokes even I'm not brave enough to tell. So on behalf of myself, would you please read what's in the prompter. And remember, everyone in this audience has to laugh. These are heroes!"
LAFD Captain Erik Scott read the first joke, which took aim at box office bomb Joker: Folie à Deux.
"Our hearts go out to all of those who lost their homes," he said.
"And I'm talking about the producers of Joker 2."
Pasadena Fire Department Captain Jodi Slicker said: "It's great to be back with Conan. Usually when he calls, he's stuck in a tree."
Basel Adra, Rachel Szor, Hamdan Ballal and Yuval Abraham won the Oscar for Best Documentary Feature Film for No Other Land.  (Reuters: Carlos Barria)
A film showing the alliance that develops between a Palestinian activist and an Israeli journalist amid their people's conflict on the occupied West Bank won the Oscar for Documentary Feature Film.
Accepting the award for No Other Land at Hollywood's Dolby Theatre were Palestinian Basel Adra, and journalist Yuval Abraham.
The film shows Adra resisting the forced displacement of his people by the Israeli army in the West Bank community of Masafer Yatta and Israeli soldiers tearing down homes and evicting residents to create a military training zone.
Adra said: "No Other Land reflects the harsh reality that we have been enduring for decades and still resist as we call on the world to take serious actions to stop the injustice and to stop the ethnic cleansing of the Palestinian people."
Abraham said they made the film because together their voices were stronger combined.
"We see each other, the atrocious destruction of Gaza and its people which must end, the Israeli hostages brutally taken in the crime of October 7 which must be freed.
"When I look at Basel I see my brother but we are unequal. We live in a regime where I am free under civilian law and Basel is under military law that destroys his life and he cannot control.
"There is a different path. A political solution without ethnic supremacy, with national rights for both of our people. And I have to say as I'm here, the foreign policy in this country is helping to block this path.
"And why? Can't you see that we are intertwined? That my people can be truly safe if Basel's people are truly free and safe. There is another way. It's not too late for life, for the living."
