title: Initially panned, this 25-year-old film became a 'beloved' cult classic
content:
Made by community for community, But I'm a Cheerleader has become one of the most iconic queer films of all time.
It could have gone terribly wrong — media executives could have become overly involved, toning down the project until it was palatable for mainstream audiences and the male gaze.
And yet, this campy, irreverent film set in a conversion camp was somehow greenlit in 1999, and enjoyed a cinematic release in Australia by 2000, premiering at the Mardi Gras Film Festival.
25 years on, But I'm a Cheerleader remains a beloved re-watch for queers both in Australia and globally.
But I’m a Cheerleader: Director’s Cut Official Trailer
To explore its cross-generational impact, we spoke with Alice Maio Mackay — a 20-year-old trans filmmaker from Kaurna/Adelaide, who's behind a string of horror flicks, including T Blockers — and Kate Jinx, an "older millennial", programmer at the Melbourne International Film Festival, and the co-host of the See Also podcast, which featured an episode on the modern classic.
But I'm a Cheerleader follows the life of preppy blonde teen Megan, played by honorary queer Natasha Lyonne, who is sent to a conversion camp to make her "normal" after her friends and family accuse her of being a lesbian.
The cult comedy, which also stars the actually gay Clea Duvall, has been heralded as a "sea change" for queer cinema in the 21st century, and is widely regarded as ahead of its time.
The film's impressive cast includes Cathy Moriarty, Michelle Williams, Bud Court, New Zealand's Melanie Lynskey and even a young RuPaul out of drag. (Lionsgate)
Many other LGBTQA+ films of the era told soul-crushing stories of repressed sexuality and the AIDS crisis, or featured straight actors "playing gay" for a mainstream audience.
Instead, But I'm a Cheerleader poked fun at heteronormativity and gender roles, taking dark themes of homophobia, social isolation and conversion therapy and turning them into a candy-coloured romantic romp.
For Jinx, who watched the film as a 20-year-old from Sydney's Western suburbs, the film was "hugely influential".
"A lot of what I was watching and dealing with were quite sad portrayals [of queer life]," she says.
"The tragic lesbian is such a thing, and I felt like everything was so loaded, but this film had so much life and energy and lightness and a great soundtrack … it really blew me away."
Since But I'm a Cheerleader and Heavenly Creatures, Melanie Lynskey has become known for Yellowjackets and countless other roles. (Lionsgate)
She had a friend who worked at their local cinema, who would let Jinx and her housemate enjoy back-to-back viewings.
"We would watch the film and then wait 15 minutes, and then it would start again."
For Maio Mackay, who first watched the film as a 12-year-old exploring the tantalising world of SBS content, it's But I'm a Cheerleader's expert handling of light and shade that makes it so special.
Cathy Moriarty's Mary Brown ran True Directions with her "straight" son, Rock, played by Eddie Cibrian. (Lionsgate)
True Directions is a 1950s-style world, where girls vacuum and wear plastic pink dresses, and boys play with toy guns among phallic blue trees. RuPaul, who's an "ex-gay" camp counsellor, preaches about masculinity while wearing a "Straight is Great" T-shirt.
As Maio Mackay says, it's "not a grounded film".
"It's very satirical and colourful and campy and it's not like the real world.
"But at the same time, there's some sad and pretty shitty stuff that happens … we see these characters go through it but [because] it is such a vibrant world, it's still a fun watch."
Jinx agrees the film is rooted in truth; director Jamie Babbit's mother even ran a rehabilitation centre called New Directions, albeit for drug addiction.
"Even though it comes off as this pastel-coloured confection, there's so much honesty in there too," Jinx says.
At its time of release, But I'm a Cheerleader was widely panned by reviewers, many of whom were straight men who misunderstood the film's humour, or who were scandalised by its focus on queer love and belonging.
But there was backlash from the LGBTQA+ community too, especially from the generation who'd lived through the AIDS crisis and didn't think it appropriate to laugh at topics such as homophobia.
But I'm a Cheerleader, a silly, irreverent film about conversion therapy, also has plenty of heart. (Lionsgate)
Over time, attitudes have changed, as has our understanding of gender and sexuality.
There's a character in the film who's implied to be a transgender man, however this isn't overtly explored, and they're mostly just the butt of the joke.
"It's not the greatest representation of all time," Maio Mackay says.
"But it's a product of its time and it still meant a lot to see a character like that when I was younger, when there weren't a lot — there still isn't a lot — of that kind of thing in the media."
The film's tender portrayal of female love and desire has also kept it relevant to modern teens, including a sex scene the director had to fight for.
And Clea Duvall's soft butch character, Graham, clearly intended for the queer female gaze, has captured the imagination of a whole new generation.
TikTok today is full of horny Graham edits, with Gen Zs expressing their love for the film through sexualised montages of her character, as well as more generalised tributes and cosplays, all backed by a soundtrack of modern pop hits.
While many members of But I'm a Cheerleader's cast have gone on to have mammoth careers in the two and a half decades since the film's release, it's a project they're still frequently asked about; Natasha Lyonne and Melanie Lynskey recently reunited for Variety's Actors on Actors series.
The film was adapted into a stage musical in 2005, premiering at the New York Musical Theatre Festival, with a 2022 London production of the same script winning WhatsOnStage's Best Off-West End Production.
It's unclear if pop superstar Chappell Roan's cheerleading bop Hot To Go! was inspired by the film, but she is evidently a fan.
MUNA and Phoebe Bridgers's gay anthem, Silk Chiffon, made a more direct homage in its music video, with band members playfully re-enacting scenes and characters.
MUNA - Silk Chiffon (feat. Phoebe Bridgers) (Official Video)
On an individual level, But I'm a Cheerleader has had a personal impact on many in the queer community, including trans actor Elliot Page, who credited it with changing his life.
Page brought up the film while receiving an award at Outfest film festival: "We don't talk enough about how important representation is and … how many lives it saves."
For Jinx, the film has been "such a touchstone" in her life.
"It was the kind of film I wanted to show everyone … it's those sorts of films that make you want to go into film curation and programming because it's all about connecting with people and creating dialogues."
For Maio Mackey, the way the movie blends queerness with comedy influenced her own style of twisting the transgender experience through horror.
"A lot of people my age and a lot of people I work with really love the film and the story and how it's told.
"For any film made 25 years ago … I think that's pretty special."
But I'm a Cheerleader is now streaming on SBS OnDemand and Prime Video.
author: Rachel Rasker

title: Actor Gene Hackman's home was full of life. Then it fell silent
content:
There was a time when the New Mexico home of actor Gene Hackman and his wife Betsy Arakawa was a hive of activity.
The "massive and cosy" house set amid the pine trees on a hilltop north of Santa Fe had been completely remodelled by the couple in 1990.
Gene Hackman’s crib in Santa Fe. I love that he lived in style. pic.twitter.com/DmTLtW4ZJF
Hackman, according to the architects involved, called constantly, checking in every few days.
Arakawa buzzed around the site, taking photos and calling Hackman to update him.
"We had to call him and send sketches constantly," architect Stephen Samuelson told Architectural Digest at the time.
Once it was finished, the home became a "haven", its open floor plan allowing music to fill the rooms for hours.
Both he and Arakawa became fixtures of the Santa Fe community, investing in several businesses and being seen regularly around town up until a few years ago.
In one restaurant downtown, a mural painted by Hackman still adorns the dining room wall.
In the end, it was two weeks of silence from the couple that ultimately sounded the alarm.
Santa Fe County deputies outside the house of Gene Hackman and Betsy Arakawa where the couple were found dead. (AP: Roberto E Rosales)
Gene Hackman decided he wanted to be an actor when he was 10 years old.
Born to a working-class family at the height of the Great Depression, Hackman spent his early years moving around the mid-western United States following his father's job as he nursed his passion for cinema.
He was just 13 years old when his father walked out on his family.
Gene Hackman circa 1965. (Getty Images: Michael Ochs Archives)
Hackman later recalled playing in his friend's front yard when his father's car drove past for the last time, Eugene waving out the window.
"'OK, it's all yours,' that wave was saying," Hackman said.
Hackman credited that wave for his decision to strike out on his own, choosing to lie to the US Marine Corps about his age to enlist.
He worked in China, Hawaii and Japan as a radio operator before he was discharged in 1952 and moved to New York at age 22.
While he began his pursuit of acting there, he only found casual work — including as a shop assistant, door-to-door salesman, furniture-mover and doorman at a Times Square Hotel.
Gene Hackman on a private visit to Havana, Cuba, in 2000. (Reuters: STR New)
Hackman later told David Letterman it was a run-in with his old marine drill instructor, who had coincidentally walked past him on the job, that forced him to leave New York for the west coast.
"He never looked at me but muttered, 'Hackman, you're a sorry son of a bitch,'" he said.
The comment — which Hackman later put down to his deep dislike of rejection — sent him to California with his new wife Faye Maltese to double down on his efforts to become an actor.
A Vanity Fair piece covered Gene Hackman, Robert Duvall and Dustin Hoffman about their rise to stardom in the 60s. (Supplied: Vanity Fair)
At 26 he was five years older than the average student at the Pasadena Playhouse, California's main theatre acting school, and he had an uphill battle when he and fellow classmate Dustin Hoffman were voted "the least likely to succeed" by their class alumni.
However, Hackman took it as a challenge and went on to feature in television and Broadway shows, as well as films over the next 20 years of his career.
His break-out role was in Bonnie and Clyde, and he would go on to feature in about 80 movies, including cultural touchstones Mississippi Burning and The French Connection.
In his Oscars speech for best actor in 1972 for his work in The French Connection, Hackman reflected the everyman persona he was later known for.
"My first ever acting scene ever was in New York, and the gentlemen sitting in front of us when we were doing that scene was my acting teacher, and I just have to mention his name: George Morrison," he said.
"I want to thank him."
His entire speech was just over a minute long.
Betsy Machiko Arakawa was 28 years younger than Hackman when they met.
She was born in Honolulu, Hawaii, and it was her love of piano that would define most of her early life.
Betsy Arakawa at 11 years old. (Supplied: Honolulu-Star Bulletin via Newspapers.com)
Arakawa played in front of thousands of students at the Honolulu International Center Concert Hall at just 11 years old, and later worked with the Honolulu Symphony Orchestra as a pianist.
Betsy Arakawa in 1981.  (Supplied: Honolulu Star-Advertiser via Newspapers.com)
According to the New York Times, Arakawa was also a cheerleader for a professional soccer team, a production assistant on a television game show, and a part-time assistant at a Los Angeles fitness centre before she met Hackman.
Not much is known about their first meeting in the mid-80s, but Hackman was still married to his first wife, Maltese.
While entertainment reporters would later describe the marriage as "crumbling", it wasn't until sometime later Hackman and Maltese officially divorced.
"By the way, I did not leave my real-life wife for a younger woman," he reportedly told People Magazine.
Gene Hackman and Betsy Arakawa at a celebrity golf event in 1991.  (Getty Images: Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection )
"We just drifted apart."
Arakawa and Hackman were married in 1991 and went on to have an incredibly private life, with the pair often only attending award shows.
Arakawa also no longer performed as a pianist.
Hackman did not often comment on his relationship with his wife, but did call her his rock.
Arakawa was a loving step-mother to Hackman's three children he shared with his ex-wife.
The call to the police was made by a maintenance worker at 1:43pm, local time, on February 26.
The front door of 1425 Old Sunset Trail was ajar.
All other doors were locked and there was no sign of forced entry, according to a search warrant affidavit.
The two workers, who had discovered the open door, said they rarely saw Hackman and Arakawa when doing routine maintenance on the property but usually kept in contact with the couple via text and phone calls.
A-lister celebrities are paying tribute to actor Gene Hackman following his 'suspicious' death.
They had last had contact with Arakawa two weeks earlier.
Inside, police found Arakawa body on the floor of a bathroom to the left of the front door.
A space heater was found near her head, which the police officer on scene suspected "could have fallen in the event [she] abruptly fell to the ground".
An orange prescription bottle was found open "with pills scattered around" on the bathroom counter-top.
A German shepherd dog was found dead in an adjoining "closet" to the bathroom. Two other dogs, one inside and one outside, were found alive.
As police moved through the home, they found another body in the mud-room near the kitchen.
"Deputy Thomas indicated he observed a pair of sunglasses located near the deceased, left of his body," the affidavit said.
A reporter outside the entrance to the gated community where Gene Hackman and Betsy Arakawa were found dead. (Reuters: Andrew Hay)
"Based on Deputy Thomas' training and experience, he suspected male individual has suddenly fallen."
Both bodies showed obvious signs of decomposition, with the report noting "mummification" in Arakawa's hands and feet.
Perhaps best known for his portrayal of tough and vulgar New York cop Jimmy "Popeye" Doyle in1971's The French Connection, he mined personal pain to give intense, edgy performances.
While Hackman's children initially said they suspected a possible carbon monoxide leak, police and the New Mexico Gas Company have since confirmed there was no sign of any issue with the pipes.
There was "no immediate signs or indications of blunt force trauma".
"[Detective Roy Arndt] believes the circumstances surrounding the death … to be suspicious enough in nature to require a thorough search and investigation," the affidavit said.
They cited the two surviving dogs running loose, the moved space heater, the pill bottle, and the two bodies being in separate parts of the house as reasons for their investigation.
The search warrant indicates officers would be looking for camera, narcotics, flammable substances, fingerprints, DNA, phones and blunt or sharp force weapons, among other items.
As Hollywood mourns, Hackman was remembered by Dustin Hoffman.
"We used to play congas together on the roof [of Pasadena Playhouse], trying to be like our hero Marlon Brando," he said.
"Gene was like Brando … he was that good.
While the couple valued their privacy, another friend Barbara Lenihan gave a small insight into their relationship.
After Hackman retired from acting in 2004, he began writing historical and Western novels.
Long-time friend Lenihan told the New York Times Arakawa was a quiet hand during the process.
Betsy Arakawa and Gene Hackman at the Golden Globes in 2003.  (AP: Mark J Terrill)
Gene would hand write his books with pen and paper, she said, and Betsy would type them up on a computer for him.
"She was very involved with what he did," she said.
"She made it very possible for him to do it."
author: Brianna Morris-Grant, Hannah Murphy

title: See youth detention through a Black man's eyes in Oscar-nominated film
content:
Formally audacious and emotionally bracing, RaMell Ross's adaptation of Colson Whitehead's Pulitzer-Prize-winning novel pushes the very limits of perspective in cinema.
What: Nominated for Best Picture and Best Adapted Screenplay at this year's Oscars, a tale of two teenagers at reform school in 1960s Florida — as told through their eyes.
Director: RaMell Ross
Starring: Ethan Herisse, Brandon Wilson, Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor, Daveed Diggs, Fred Hechinger
When: Streaming on Amazon Prime from February 27
Likely to make you feel: Floored
In a medium so often praised for allowing audiences to see the world through the eyes of another, it challenges that notion of empathy. How much do we ever really see, even if it's right before us?
Whitehead's 2019 novel is a searing first-person account of a notorious youth penal institution in 1960s Florida. Retaining this perspective, Nickel Boys is filmed entirely from the point of view of its protagonists, removing any pretence of the camera's 'objectivity' and suggesting the characters as the authors of their own story.
It's a bold — and potentially suffocating — conceit, forcing the viewer into a subjective point of view inseparable from that of the characters. There's no third-person distance. None of dramatic cinema's comforting remove.
"It required an unlearning of everything I knew about acting, and the learning of a new language," Ethan Herisse told The Hollywood Reporter about RaMell Ross's filmmaking style. (Supplied: Prime Video)
The effect is both immediate and disorientating. In a certain sense, it's not unlike the first-person perspective prevalent across so much online video content, XR and games — a clever gambit that reactivates history through an acutely current lens.
Like slipping on a virtual-reality headset, Nickel Boys opens on the perspective of the young Elwood Curtis (Ethan Cole), eyes tilted to the sky as he lays in the backyard he shares with his Nana (Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor) in Tallahassee, Florida. Poetic glimpses of an early-60s childhood — a jungle gym, a tooth getting pulled, MLK beaming from storefront TVs — bleed into teenage impressions — a sweetheart in a photo booth, the space race on the news, racial segregation in the South.
"What she [Aunjanue Ellis Taylor, pictured] does in this movie is truly, truly incredible," Brandon Wilson told IndieWire. (Supplied: Prime Video)
A gifted student, the now-17-year-old Elwood (Ethan Herisse) is en route to begin a scholarship at a technical school when he hitches a ride in a stolen car and gets implicated as an accessory — a promising life cut short in a moment of racial profiling.
He's shipped off to Nickel Academy, a segregated reform school where the white kids play sports and their Black counterparts — when they're not being brutally beaten by teachers — are forced to perform convict labour or compete in boxing tournaments for money.
It's here that Elwood befriends Turner (Brandon Wilson), a Texan teen who's the cynical opposite to his idealistic world view.
"The fix has always been in, the game's rigged," Turner tells him.
"It's not like the old days," Elwood replies. "We can change things."
"Even looking into the lens, that just starts to all fade into natural movements," Brandon Wilson told IndieWire of the POV filming style. (Supplied: Prime Video)
Elwood's point of view is so immersive — so inescapable — that it takes a moment to register when the film suddenly switches to Turner's perspective, and what might have come off as a stylistic gimmick begins to reveal a more complicated, slippery hand.
At the same time, Ross splices in archival news footage, vintage home movies and excerpts from the 1958 Hollywood race drama The Defiant Ones — with Sidney Poitier chained in a prison truck — that recalls the evocative collage of his breakthrough Oscar-nominated documentary, Hale County This Morning, This Evening (2018).
When Elwood is sent to get a whipping from the teachers, the film cuts away from explicit violence to a series of black-and-white images depicting students of the historical Dozier School for Boys — the infamous real-life Florida reform school upon which Whitehead based the Nickel Academy.
"While you're encountering this image, you know that it's from a specific person's consciousness ... And with that, it's a type of personal truth that I think one fundamentally connects to," director RaMell Ross told NPR. (Supplied: Prime Video)
The moment sparks an ambitious time leap to 2018, where the much older Elwood (now played by Daveed Diggs) clicks though a series of grisly images on his desktop, playing amateur detective in the historical archive.
In these future sequences, spread across the 70s, 80s and 2010s, the camera is mounted behind the back of Elwood's head, and moves as he does.
It's an unusual, disembodied point of view, suggesting, perhaps, that something spectral is shadowing Elwood — an effect that's eerily reminiscent of Steven Soderbergh's recent Presence, a ghost story about very different trauma.
If Nickel Boys is a film haunted by the phantoms of the past, then its stylistic accomplishment is less in reanimating history than making it live and breathe in the present — to interrogate ideas about the gaze, and what we as an audience bring to the table.
Just as the film invites us to experience and to empathise with the lives of Elwood and Turner, it challenges our ability to ever truly experience the life of another person.
Either way, by the time Nickel Boys reaches its transcendent, almost cosmic finale — which finally teases a release from our myopic worldview — it's impossible not to be moved by its emotional punch. Don't miss it.

title: Oscar tips from a film critic and a mathematician
content:
It's now a time-honoured tradition on the eve of the Academy Awards that we ask a film critic and mathematician to pull out their crystal balls and tea leaves and tell us who they think will take home the big Oscars.
While the first showdown was a draw, last year our resident mathematician took home the chocolates by correctly guessing nine winners out of 10, two better than our critic.
Returning as carryover champ is Ben Zauzmer, an American maths whiz who penned the book Oscarmetrics: The Math Behind The Biggest Night in Hollywood, and whose computations are sought out every year by The Hollywood Reporter.
Zauzmer analyses other award ceremonies, past Oscar-winner trends and other factors to build up a mathematical profile of each Academy Award category.
And the new challenger is Melbourne-based critic Sonia Nair, whose writing has been published by The Age, The Guardian, Time Out Melbourne, Kill Your Darlings and The Big Issue, among others.
May the best expert win, and you can see for yourself who is correct on Monday, March 3 from 11am AEDT.
Anora is the hot favourite to win the best film Oscar. (Supplied: IMDB)
The critic says: Anora
The Best Picture chances of Conclave, the suitably compelling Succession meets Mean Girls set in the Vatican, seemed to receive a late boost with wins at the SAG (Screen Actors Guild) Awards and the BAFTAs, but I still believe this award will go to the critics' indie darling Anora after it swept top gongs at the Critics' Choice, DGA (Directors Guild of America), and PGA (Producers Guild of America) awards.
The mathematician says: Anora
At first, The Brutalist looked like the film to beat. And more recently, thanks to BAFTA and SAG wins, Conclave is coming on strong. But in between, Anora had a massive weekend with Critics Choice, DGA, and PGA honours, and that's good enough to be a weak frontrunner.
Director Sean Baker has won plenty of awards already for directing Anora, including the Palme d'Or at Cannes. (Reuters: Stephane Mahe)
The critic says: Sean Baker (Anora)
Sean Baker and Brady Corbet (The Brutalist) are neck and neck for this one, but due to his wins at the DGA and PGA, which are typically reliable predictors of success, I'm calling it for Baker.
The mathematician says: Sean Baker (Anora)
This one is extremely close with Brady Corbet, but it's hard to go against the DGA given their outstanding track record in this category.
Timothée Chalamet's performance as Bob Dylan has him in the running for best actor. (Supplied: Disney)
The critic says: Timothée Chalamet (A Complete Unknown)
Adrien Brody (The Brutalist) is decidedly the favourite for this, but I'm going out on a limb and saying the award will go to Timothée Chalamet, whose Oscar campaign's zany pageantry and recent acceptance speech on wanting to "be one of the greats" after winning the SAG Award for Male Actor in a Leading Role have charmed me. And as Luke Goodsell observed in 2023, Oscar voters love leading actors playing music legends. If Chalamet were to win this, he'd break Brody’s own record of being the youngest person to win Best Actor after the latter won in 2002 at the age of 29 (one month shy of 30) for his role in The Pianist.
The mathematician says: Adrien Brody (The Brutalist)
Timothée Chalamet made this a race at the last second by winning an SAG Award on Sunday night. But Brody had too big a lead to be knocked out of the leading spot going into Oscar Sunday.
Demi Moore has won rave reviews for her turn in The Substance. (Supplied: Working Title Films)
The critic says: Demi Moore (The Substance)
Anyone who saw Moore play a woman so embattled by her insecurities that she fails to get ready for a long-awaited date in The Substance can't deny her acting chops, but Mikey Madison, who did a superb job in Anora, did win this award at the BAFTAs, posing a last-minute threat to Demi's sweep at precursor ceremonies. However, with this accolade functioning as a sort of lifetime achievement award for an actress who has never been nominated for an Oscar before, I believe it's in the bag for Moore.
The mathematician says: Demi Moore (The Substance)
This is the closest of the four acting races, with both Mikey Madison (Anora) and Fernanda Torres (I'm Still Here) lined up as solid picks as well. But my model prefers Moore thanks in part to her Golden Globe, Critics Choice, and SAG victories.
Kieran Culkin (left, pictured with Jesse Eisenberg) is a scenestealer in A Real Pain. (Supplied: 20th Century Studios)
The critic says: Kieran Culkin (A Real Pain)
This seems like almost the easiest category to pick as Kieran Culkin has won nearly all the awards in this category. I'm looking forward to the memes contrasting his lackadaisical acting style with Succession co-star and fellow Best Supporting Actor nominee Jeremy Strong's incredibly rigorous one.
The mathematician says: Kieran Culkin (A Real Pain)
Best not to overthink this one if filling out an Oscar pool. He has swept through the major awards and shows no signs of slowing down at the Oscars.
Zoe Saldaña plays Rita, a lawyer in the Academy Award-nominated film Emilia Pérez. (Supplied: Pathé Distribution)
The critic says: Zoe Saldaña (Emilia Pérez)
I detest Emilia Pérez with a passion, but although I believe it has lost its chance at winning most of its 13 nominations, it won't go home with nothing (which explains one of my later picks too). Zoe Saldaña is arguably the best part of a horrendous thing — I thought that was Karla Sofía Gascón before tweetgate — and she, like Kieran Culkin, has swept nearly all the awards in this category.
The mathematician says: Zoe Saldaña (Emilia Pérez)
It's possible that the broader controversies surrounding the film could drag her down, but despite it all she keeps racking up award season victories.
The critic says: Anora
The mathematician says: Anora
The critic says: Conclave
The mathematician says: Conclave
The Wild Robot was a hit with all ages, and is the top pick to win best animated feature at the Oscars. (Supplied: Universal)
The critic says: The Wild Robot
The mathematician says: The Wild Robot
The critic says: Emilia Pérez
The mathematician says: Emilia Pérez

title: Deaths of 'one of the greats' Gene Hackman and his wife 'suspicious', police say
content:
Celebrities are paying tribute to actor Gene Hackman following the "suspicious" death of him and his wife in New Mexico.
A-list stars, including Viola Davis, Tom Hanks and Morgan Freeman paid tribute to the Hollywood actor who won two Oscars in his 60-year career.
Actor Gene Hackman, winner of Best Supporting Actor at academy awards in March 1993. (AP Photo: File)
"You were one of the greats," Davis said on social media.
Hanks, known for his roles Forrest Gump and Cast Away, said, "There has never been a 'Gene Hackman Type'. There has only been Gene Hackman."
Freeman said one of his career highlights was working with the "incredibly gifted" actor, known for his roles in Unforgiven, The French Connection and The Poseidon.
The academy award-winning actor Gene Hackman, his wife and their dog were found dead in different rooms of their home, in an incident police have called "suspicious".
Gene Hackman at the Golden Globe Awards with his wife in 2003.   (Getty: Kevin Winter)
The bodies of the Hollywood giant, 95, and his classical pianist wife Betsy Arakawa, 63, along with their pet dog, were discovered by a maintenance worker in New Mexico on Wednesday.
A search warrant said the deaths were "suspicious enough in nature to require a thorough search and investigation", according to AFP.
It also said the maintenance worker had found the home's front door ajar, although there were no signs of forced entry.
Actor Gene Hackman with wife Betsy Arakawa in June 1993. (AP Photo: File)
Police said the couple "had been deceased for quite a while", although authorities were still trying to determine the last time anybody had contact with them.
Police initially reported there were no signs of foul play, but new information has revealed there was an open prescription bottle and pills scattered on a countertop near Arakawa in the couple's Santa Fe home.
The house belonging to actor Gene Hackman and his wife Betsy Arakawa in Santa Fe County.  (AP: Roberto E Rosales)
Hackman was found dead in a mudroom, while Arakawa was found in a bathroom next to a space heater, detectives said.
A German shepherd was found dead in the bathroom, and two other healthy dogs were at the house.
A detective wrote in a warrant that there were no obvious signs of a gas leak, but he noted that people exposed to gas leaks or carbon monoxide might not show signs of poisoning.
Detectives were awaiting autopsy reports and toxicology test results.
Hackman, his wife Betsy Arakawa and one of their three dogs were found dead by a maintenance worker who had arrived to do routine work at their Santa Fe home on Wednesday.
The Fire Department also wrote that they found no signs of a carbon monoxide leak or poisoning.
It remains unclear whether police were responding to a report or if they were making a welfare check, local media said.
Hollywood director Francis Ford Coppola has said he is mourning the "great artist" but is celebrating his "magnificent work".
"The loss of a great artist, always cause for both mourning and celebration: Gene Hackman a great actor, inspiring and magnificent in his work and complexity," Coppola wrote in a post on Instagram.
"I mourn his loss, and celebrate his existence and contribution."
Hackman was an intense character actor who won Academy Awards for the violent 1971 drug saga The French Connection and the 1992 western Unforgiven.
The former marine appeared in more than 80 films, as well as on television and the stage during a lengthy career that started in the early 1960s.
Living outside Santa Fe, New Mexico, he was married twice and had three children.
Hackman married Arakawa in 1991.

title: ​​'No-one could play this role but me': Pamela Anderson in The Last Showgirl
content:
In 2022, streaming service Hulu released the series Pam & Tommy, a fictionalised account of the sex tape scandal that derailed Pamela Anderson's acting career in the late 1990s.
Made without her consent, the series dredged up some of the darkest moments of her life.
Now, the former Baywatch star is telling her side of the story and, she shares, things are looking up.
Jason Di Rosso interviews the makers of the movies and TV you need to see.
She's released a memoir — Love, Pamela — to accompany a Netflix documentary, Pamela: A Love Story, detailing how she's reinvented herself as an activist, campaigning for issues such as animal rights and Julian Assange.
And she's just made her Broadway debut, playing Roxie Hart in Chicago, the stirrings of a career resurgence the internet has come to dub the 'Pam-aissance'.
Living in Canada now her children are grown, anything seems possible.
"I'm sure I'm not finished," she says in her documentary.
Nonetheless, Anderson's next move surprised many, including the star herself: She landed her first lead role in a feature film since the 1996 action flick, Barb Wire.
In The Last Showgirl, Anderson plays Shelly Gardner, a 57-year-old dancer in Las Vegas revue Le Razzle Dazzle, which has been axed after a three-decade run.
Anderson, pictured while shooting The Last Showgirl, says she could empathise with the character of Shelly. (Supplied: Madman Films)
The performance earned Anderson her first Golden Globe and Screen Actors Guild (SAG) award nominations.
Directed by Gia Coppola (Palo Alto), the film features an ensemble cast, including Jamie Lee Curtis as Shelly's best friend Annette, Kiernan Shipka and Brenda Song as showgirls and Dave Bautista as a gruff stage manager.
Coppola, who always envisioned Anderson as Shelly, sent the script to Anderson's son Brandon after the star's agent knocked it back.
Her persistence paid off. When Anderson finally read the script, she jumped at the chance to play the dancer.
"When I read it, I thought, 'This is what I've been waiting my whole life for. This is the reason I've even had this life'; I couldn't play her this way if I hadn't had the experiences I had," Anderson tells ABC Radio National's The Screen Show.
Le Razzle Dazzle is based on Jubilee!, a famous Las Vegas showgirl revue which ended its three-decade run in 2016.
At its peak, the spectacular show featured more than 100 performers decked out in elaborate bejewelled costumes designed by the legendary Bob Mackie and Pete Menefee, which appear in the film.
In The Last Showgirl, the glory days when showgirls performed to a full house in every casino and hotel on the Las Vegas Strip are long gone.
Shipka plays Jodie in the film, a 19-year-old dancer who treats Anderson's character Shelly as a maternal figure. (Supplied: Madman Films)
Audiences have dwindled and Le Razzle Dazzle's days are numbered.
Replacing it is a risqué neo-burlesque show Shelly disparagingly calls "the dirty circus".
Shelly sees Le Razzle Dazzle as part of an artistic tradition that has its roots in Parisian Lido culture, a reference to the famous Paris venue synonymous with cabaret before its closure in 2022.
Her daughter Hannah (Billie Lourd) dismisses Le Razzle Dazzle as a "stupid nudie show" but Shelly corrects her: it's "a spectacle with dancing nudes", she says.
The distinction matters to Shelly, who remembers a time when Las Vegas showgirls were treated like movie stars.
"We were ambassadors for style and grace," she tells her friends. "The costumes — it makes you feel like you're stepping out of the pages of Vogue magazine."
Curtis, pictured on The Last Showgirl set, earned a SAG award nomination for her role as retired dancer Annette. (Supplied: Madman Films)
Shelly has dedicated her life to Le Razzle Dazzle with little to show for it but a dwindling pay cheque, a failed marriage and a strained relationship with her daughter, and its closure leads to a personal reckoning for the veteran dancer.
Anderson felt Shelly's story was deeply relatable for any woman who had found herself at a crossroads in middle age.
"It's a movie about second chances; it's about reinvention," she says.
Viewers don't see the showgirls on stage until The Last Showgirl's dying minutes.

  (Supplied: Madman Films)
"I felt like there was a lot of room to collaborate with Gia on creating this vulnerable character."
Anderson wanted to tell a story about the grit behind the city's glitz and glamour.
"I thought, here's an opportunity to meet the women that hold up the rhinestones; the working-class people … that make Las Vegas sparkle — these are the interesting stories," she says.
The Last Showgirl was shot on location in Las Vegas for $2 million in just 18 days.
"It was really important to me to make an intimate movie, to stay small," Coppola says.
"A lot of the crew is either family or close friends."
"I longed to tell my version of how I see Las Vegas," Coppola says. (Supplied: Madman Films)
Fortunately for Coppola — the granddaughter of Francis Ford Coppola and niece of Sophia Coppola — filmmaking is the family business.
Her mother, Jacqui Getty, was the film's costume designer.
Her cousins Robert Schwartzman and Matthew Shire were producers on the film, while Jason Schwartzman, another cousin, plays a casting director in Shelly's pivotal audition scene.
The screenplay is based on a play written by Shire's wife, writer Kate Gersten, after seeing the Jubilee! show in Las Vegas before it closed.
Jubilee! dancers famously had to navigate 1700 stairs each performance between the stage and the basement-level dressing rooms. (Supplied: Madman Films)
"She's very much part of the theatre world," Coppola says of Gersten, whose writing credits include TV series The Good Place and Mozart in the Jungle.
Much of the film's action takes place backstage, in the dressing room and the theatre's narrow corridors and stairwells.
"That's what I loved about the script — it felt really authentic to what backstage life is like," Coppola says.
Anderson agrees. She says playing Roxie on Broadway was like a "warm-up" for her role in The Last Showgirl.
In her next flex, Anderson will host a plant-based cooking show, Pamela's Cooking With Love. (Supplied: Madman Films)
"I got to experience what it's like to be surrounded by these people that have been in the show for 20 years and have this muscle memory … to be able to talk about what they're going to have for dinner and then hear their cue and then get off stage and continue the conversation where they left off."
While films such as Paul Verhoeven's 1995 film Showgirls have played up the rivalry between performers, Anderson wanted to portray the intimacy and sisterhood she witnessed backstage.
"It's easy to play the cattiness [but] I think the vulnerability and the hopefulness … and the inspiration is more interesting to watch."

title: Cast and creators of Iranian film banned from leaving the country
content:
Filmmaker Mohammad Rasoulof knew his life in Iran would be placed in (further) jeopardy when he made The Seed of the Sacred Fig — he was already awaiting a sentence from the Islamic Revolutionary Court and had spent multiple stints in prison and under house arrest for opposing the Ayatollah regime.
What: A gripping domestic thriller that invokes the tyranny of the repressive Iranian regime.
Directed by: Mohammad Rasoulof
Starring: Soheila Golestani, Missagh Zareh, Mahsa Rostami, Setareh Maleki
When: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Absorbed and disturbed
When asked from his new home in Germany, where he lives in exile, why it was so important this film be made, Rasoulof simply answers: "I think freedom is really important."
The pulsating, Oscar-nominated domestic thriller is set in Tehran amid the Woman, Life, Freedom uprising — which catalysed following the police-custody death of Kurdish-Iranian woman Mahsa Amini, after she was apprehended for not wearing her hijab properly.
Against this backdrop, we witness the unravelling of a family of four. Conservative matriarch Najmeh (a masterful Soheila Golestani, an activist herself) parrots government propaganda and is intent on the family maintaining a certain image after her husband Iman (Missagh Zareh) is promoted to judicial investigator.
"The limitations and the repression began from the inception of the script. When you make a film this way, it automatically reflects the circumstances that surround it," Rasoulof explains. (Pictured: Setareh Maleki as Sana) (Supplied: Sharmill Films)
Despite having a father who's initially, at least, an unwilling foot soldier of the repressive Iranian regime, Iman's daughters, Rezvan (Mahsa Rostami) and Sana (Setareh Maleki), sympathise with the protesters as they experience the unfolding of the movement in real-time, mediated through their phones and social media. (Funnily enough, this is exactly how Rasoulof experienced the protests while serving prison time in 2022 for signing a petition critical of the government.)
The far-reaching ramifications of what's happening on the streets infiltrate their home, turning parents and daughters against one another as Najmeh covertly begins to second-guess everything she's ever believed about the regime. Things come to a head when Iman's gun goes missing, his suspicions and paranoia turning in terrifying ways onto his wife and two daughters.
The conditions in which The Seed of the Sacred Fig was made were impossibly prohibitive.
Rasoulof had to direct the film secretively from afar and, when the shoot was completed, his looming eight-year sentence — for public statements he'd made and continued involvement in films and documentaries deemed crimes "against the country's security" — was handed down.
Rasoulof had only two hours to decide between imprisonment and leaving Iran. Having been in prison numerous times before, it wasn't incarceration that scared him, but the prospect of never finishing The Seed of the Sacred Fig.
"From dealing with people who work for the Iranian government ... I could always see someone suffocating within the person who'd made the decisions," Rasoulof says. (Pictured l-r: Reza Akhlaghirad as Ghaderi and Missagh Zareh as Iman) (Supplied: Sharmill Films)
Abandoning all his possessions and discarding all trackable electronic devices, he embarked on a 28-day treacherous journey to Europe via the mountainous land border that Iran shares with Turkey. His passport had been confiscated by the Iranian regime, but he was able to find shelter in Germany because he'd lived there before and was identifiable via his fingerprints.
All key members of the film are being investigated by intelligence.
This suppression and censorship experienced by the cast and crew seeped into the very raison d'être of the film.
"The limitations and the repression began from the inception of the script. When you make a film this way, it automatically reflects the circumstances that surround it," Rasoulof explains.
"What matters is that filmmakers operating under these circumstances are able to turn the limitations they face into a new way of storytelling."
"I've come to know this young generation of Iranian men and women who have decided to live the life they want to live," Rasoulof says. (Pictured: Setareh Maleki as Sana) (Supplied: Sharmill Films)
Rasoulof was guided by three principles: have a very small cast and crew; work with limited equipment, similar to what you'd see on student films; and direct remotely. That this culminated in a film as ambitious and searing in its critique of the Iranian regime is a marvel.
Having previously been arrested for making his 2010 film about Iran's reformist Green Movement — a film he never finished — and many times since, Rasoulof says the cast and crew had to be ready to change course at a moment's notice.
"You have to be highly adaptable on set, in the sense that you may have to completely forego and abandon something you prepared in detail and thought very much about and immediately find a different way of proceeding in the moment" he says.
"The fact that I directed remotely not only affected me, but the entire cast and crew. What we had to do is try and remedy this physical distance, which we did thanks to their creativity."
Some of the most striking scenes in the film are lifted wholesale from Woman, Life, Freedom protests, with the real-life footage enhancing the film's verisimilitude and further blurring the lines between fact and fiction.
The National News: Iranian women cut hair in protest against death of Mahsa Amini
The veracity and beating heart of these protests could never have been replicated in a staged scene, notwithstanding the impossibility of filming such a scene in Iran.
"I asked myself: 'Even in a utopian scene where I'd be able to reconstruct these scenes, would I ever manage to achieve the same impact as the truth?'
"I told myself: 'You have to free yourself from all expectations and allow the form of the film to be borne of the circumstances you're living and shooting in.'"
Although Iman's increasingly extreme actions act as a metaphor for the totalitarian Iranian regime, there are no clear-cut good or bad characters in The Seed of the Sacred Fig.
Iman confides in Najmeh at the outset about his moral reservations in effectively acting as a rubber stamp for death warrants, while Najmeh — even as she clings to the way of life that's been afforded to her through Iman's position — comes to endanger herself in her pursuit of the truth.
"The fact that I directed remotely not only affected me, but the entire cast and crew," Rasoulof says. (Pictured: Missagh Zareh as Iman and and Soheila Golestaniin as Najmeh) (Supplied: Sharmill Films)
Rasoulof observed this moral complexity in his time in prison, and was moved to explore what impels people to abandon their humanity.
"From dealing with people who work for the Iranian government — in the judiciary, in the security apparatus, interrogators, judges, prosecutors — I could always see someone suffocating within the person who'd made the decisions. The humanity that was being drowned due to career choices, really."
For all the liberties granted by living in Germany, Rasoulof suffers from the dislocation of not living and working in his home country. Like Rasoulof, Rostami and Maleki escaped Iran, while Golestani faces a travel ban.
"I can't make the films that I want to make because I want to make films in Iran, films that have to do with the culture I know best among all the cultures in the world," he says.
Like Rasoulof (centre), Setareh Maleki (left) and Mahsa Rostami (right) escaped Iran. (Getty: Stephane Cardinale)
But thanks to technology, Rasoulof says exile has taken on new forms and he's able to remain in daily contact with his friends, family and collaborators.
Buoyed by the work of his colleagues Jafar Panahi (The White Balloon, Taxi), Maryam Moghaddam and Behtash Sanaeeha (My Favourite Cake), among countless others who have been deemed dissidents by the state, he remains hopeful about the future of Iranian filmmaking and, on a broader level, the future of Iran.
"In exactly the same way whereby the repression of the regime grows stronger and harsher every day, so does the courage and the need to find new ways to make films and achieve artistic freedom," he says.
"I've come to know this young generation of Iranian men and women who have decided to live the life they want to live. So I know great changes await us."

title: What we know about Michelle Trachtenberg's death
content:
Actor Michelle Trachtenberg, who is known for her roles in Gossip Girl and Buffy the Vampire Slayer, has died at 39.
The New York Medical Examiner is investigating her death — here's what we know.
Trachtenberg was found "unresponsive" in her luxury apartment in New York.
Police responded to a 911 call shortly after 8am local time, where officers found her, according to an NYPD statement.
Paramedics pronounced her dead at the scene.
Her public relations team confirmed her death in a statement released Wednesday.
"It is with great sadness to confirm that Michelle Trachtenberg has passed away," they wrote.
"The family requests privacy for their loss. There are no further details at this time."
Trachtenberg pictured in Los Angeles in 2010. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)
The cause of Trachtenberg's death is not known.
No foul play is suspected, and the New York Medical Examiner is investigating her death.
US outlet ABC has reported Trachtenberg recently underwent a liver transplant and may have been experiencing complications, citing anonymous police sources.
The Australian ABC has not been able to verify the report and the actor never publicly shared any health conditions.
Trachtenberg was an actor best known for her roles in teen dramas during the 2000s.
She got her start in Hollywood when she was three years old, appearing in commercials.
She rose to prominence with a recurring role in the Nickelodeon series The Adventures of Pete & Pete in 1994.
At 10 years of age, she landed her first title role in the 1996 movie Harriet the Spy.
She had roles in several Nickelodeon productions, leading up to her being cast in the cult classic EuroTrip in 2004.
Trachtenberg played Dawn Summers in the supernatural drama Buffy the Vampire Slayer in 2000 and Georgina Sparks on the CW television series Gossip Girl in 2007.
Some of her other roles include television films Killing Kennedy, Sister Cities, and the science-fiction film The Scribbler.
She also appeared in music videos from emo-rock band Fall Out Boy for their song This Ain't a Scene, It's an Arms Race, and the Joaquin Phoenix-directed music video for Tired of Being Sorry by Ringside.
ABC/Reuters

title: These treasures were stolen 130 years ago. This film charts their journey home
content:
The first sign that things are askew is the talking sculpture.
"It was so dark in this foreign place that I lost myself in these dreams," a centuries-old effigy murmurs over a pitch-black screen.
What: A documentary about the politics of repatriating artwork that's far stranger than its subject implies.
Director: Mati Diop
Starring: A talking sculpture and a bunch of university debaters
When and where: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Haunted
Its voice (Makenzy Orcel) is at once guttural, sonorous, translucent: an artless whisper layered above a bass that seems to vibrate from the earth itself.
It speaks as if roused from a trance, still caught in the crosshairs between slumber and reality. "[I was] cut off from the land of my birth," it laments. "Uprooted. Ripped out. The spoils of massive plundering."
The sculpture is one of 26 artefacts returning to their homeland in present-day Benin after decades in a Parisian museum.
These artefacts are "royal treasures", an early title card in Mati Diop's documentary Dahomey informs us, that were pilfered from the kingdom of Dahomey by French colonisers in an 1892 invasion. They are works of wood and bronze — emblems of military brawn and intricate depictions of historical rulers.
"For them," the text reads, "130 years of captivity are coming to an end."
"The spectator has a big role in the film," Mati Diop told Screen Daily. "[The film] allows audiences to enter into the complexities of colonial history and reflection and responsibility." (Supplied: Rialto)
This is the first and last piece of context in a documentary that begins in observation but frequently slopes towards something far richer, far eerier. Last year, it became one of the shortest films to win the top prize at the Berlinale — though its gaunt, 68-minute run time belies its glut of ethical quandaries and its commitment to utter ambiguity.
Diop wields a keen ear for the narcotising rhythms of labour. We spend much of the film's opening stretch in the cloistered corridors of Paris's Musée du Quai Branly, where the artefacts are readied for their repatriation.
"I represent something and someone elusive, as a mixed-race artist who makes hybrid films," director Mati Diop told Screen Daily. "I'm from a cinema family but I'm … not a [nepo baby]." (Supplied: Rialto)
The sequence is mostly wordless. Punctuating the silence is the beep of a forklift, the hum of machinery.
In one astoundingly claustrophobic shot from the perspective of an artefact, we're strapped into a shipping container and plunged into total darkness. A lid is secured, drills whirr, wheels knock against one another.
The effect is curiously perverse. Diop anthropomorphises these treasures, imagining their distress and disorientation.
In a way, Dahomey feels like an extension of Diop's widely lauded 2019 film, Atlantics — her debut fiction feature where a ring of vengeful wraiths in Dakar plague the unscrupulous employer who terrorised them in life.
Dahomey is similarly haunting. In recurring soliloquies, the speaking effigy ponders its place in a motherland that it no longer recognises. "Everything is so strange," it says. "Far removed from the country I saw in my dreams."
These doubts, it turns out, are mirrored by disputes raging in the real world.
The room becomes increasingly heated. Are the sculptures merely a meaningless political gesture? (Supplied: Rialto)
The artefacts are airlifted back to Benin, where they're met with fervent celebration — and yet a murky undercurrent eddies just beneath the spectacle.
Dahomey's second half mostly comprises an organised debate among students at the University of Abomey-Calavi, who interrogate the value of restitution.
The objects are so sacred, says one participant, that she burst into tears on viewing them — but not all are so convinced. "It's an insult," another student avers. "Out of 7,000 works, they bring back 26."
The room grows increasingly heated; the afternoon dissolves into an endless stream of declarations and rebuttals. Are the sculptures a lodestone of national identity or a meaningless political gesture? Are they totems of spiritual significance or are they works of art? Is this all just image laundering for the French government?
"The return to the native land was something I felt very close to," Diop told POV Magazine. "Wondering … if they're going to be recognised there." (Supplied: Rialto)
Diop, of course, resists the prosaic guarantee of a resolution. These questions are hard enough; an answer seems nigh on impossible.
By the film's conclusion, the artefacts are safely housed in a Beninese institution — though perhaps they've merely been transposed from one airless atrium into another.
In the absence of clarity, Diop instead opts for a spectral poeticism. By nightfall, venturing outside the museum, she finds a phantom city.
Gauzy curtains billow in the breeze as if shrouding a spirit. A lone figure paces a darkened shoreline, illuminated only by the glimmering pinprick of a cigarette. Shots of dense vegetation distort and meld into one another, always haloed by an amber glow, always scored by a quivering glissando.
These images feel mesmeric and possessed: perched on the cliff between this world and the next, between the ghosts of the past and the discord of the present.

title: An evil toy monkey plagues generations of men in this comedy horror
content:
It's a surprise when blood-soaked man-of-the-moment Adam Scott, decked out in a pilot's uniform, erupts onto the screen — feverishly trying to offload an eerie wind-up toy monkey onto a pawn shop owner.
What: Final Destination if a cursed family heirloom toy monkey was involved
Directed by: Osgood Perkins (Longlegs)
Starring: Theo James, Adam Scott, Elijah Wood, Christian Convery, Tatiana Maslany
Where: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Tickled and grossed out
After a failed attempt by Captain Petey Shelburn to banish the monkey forever, we cut to his twin sons, Hal and Bill (played by Christian Convery in an impressive double turn), who thoroughly hate each other. For all the neuroses harboured by on-screen twins, rarely has a dynamic been depicted where one mercilessly bullies the other, aided by a gang of evil high school girls.
Their enmity gives way to shared curiosity, momentarily at least, when they discover a toy monkey among their missing father's possessions — wrapped in a box emblazoned with the words 'organ grinder monkey — like life'. Which turns out to be accurate.
"These two brothers have the same experiences but… evolve so differently and in such a lonely way," Perkins told ScifiNow. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Once the key at the back of the monkey is turned, he bares his teeth in a sickly grin, his gruesome drumsticks descending onto his drums in a sickening thudding sequence, signalling that someone will die. Exactly who and how isn't known until, well, it happens.
Director Osgood Perkins is the son of horror icon Anthony Perkins, who was forever defined thereafter by what Osgood calls the 'curse' of playing Norman Bates in Alfred Hitchcock's seminal 1960 film, Psycho. Surrounded by uncanny instances of death from a young age himself (including one that's gestured to obliquely in the film), the younger Perkins revels in freshly inventive and gruesome ways to kill off his characters in The Monkey.
The randomness and sheer incredulity of the violence is where this adaptation of a Stephen King short story is most like horror franchises such as Final Destination. But unlike the invisible strings of fate acting as the puppet master, it's an evil monkey — one that's been plaguing the Shelburn men for generations.
"The monkey is a totem for the fact that everybody dies, and there's nothing you can do about it," Perkins told Dazed. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Much has been made of the monkey's symbolism for intergenerational trauma, but if I could employ the monkey as a metaphor for the patriarchy instead, it's almost as though the violence of the monkey ripples outwards to hurt everyone except the Shelburn men, even as this violence comes at a great personal cost to them.
After nearly everyone close to the twins dies in newly sickening ways, we journey into the future, where a disillusioned adult Hal (a suitably nerdy Theo James, changing things up from his star turn as an arsehole in White Lotus) works a dead-end job. He's a single father who's forbidden himself from seeing his son Petey (a forlorn Colin O'Brien) more than once a year, owing to fear of the curse that hasn't left his mind, despite leaving his family alone for 25 years.
No-one was allowed to see Nicolas Cage's face as Longlegs before the film was released. Is it really terrifying or just marketing bluster?
Mayhem ensues when Hal discovers the monkey is very much back, this time graduating to massacring an entire town.
Tracking down his estranged brother — the suitably goth and deranged Bill (who James also plays) — Hal reckons with the cursed monkey perhaps one last time, as his son discovers the true reason behind his father's abandonment.
The rules aren't exactly clear in this adaptation of Stephen King's 1980 short film. Sometimes, no-one's there to turn the key in the back of the monkey, but people still die. It can magically teleport anywhere, but only when it decides it wants to. It's established the monkey listens to no-one — if you turn the key, you won't die, but neither will the subject of your ire.
Theo James told SciFiNow that the film is also about "male toxicity and regression", saying that "fear leads to anger, controlling, violence". (Supplied: Roadshow)
Unlike Perkins' decidedly different Longlegs, The Monkey is more a comedy than it is a horror film. In fact, it's very much not a horror film — you're unlikely to have nightmares plaguing your sleeping hours, but you will find much humour in the minutely drawn characters, even if they don't grace the screen for very long. Perkins himself plays the twins' swinger stepdad Uncle Chip, and Tess Degenstein is a gloriously chipper real estate agent.
A deeply unserious film, The Monkey is an entertaining romp through one man's conceptions of the myriad blood-curdling ways in which we can die. To outline any of them would rob the film of the main thing it's got going for it — a sense of suspense and the wonder of discovery.
The film's pacing does sag towards the end when it attempts to introduce ancillary characters superfluous to the plot. You never get attached enough to any character to care if they live or die.
So there's no greater meaning to be derived from The Monkey, beyond the fact that we all die — some in more heinous fashion than others.

title: Why an Oscar-nominated documentary was kept top-secret for a year
content:
A studio in Sydney's inner city appears unassuming from the outside, but for over a year it has been the hub of a top-secret documentary project, for fear of Russian interference.
Sydney-based production company Songbird Studios is behind the Oscar-nominated documentary Porcelain War which follows three Ukrainian artists who take up arms to defend their country and their culture.
The secure facility was built in Paddington and fitted with an air-gapped server protected by firewalls — all in a bid to address safety concerns and hacking threats.
The Sydney-based production studio sent a dozen cameras to Ukraine. (Supplied: Picturehouse, 2024)
The film's production started about a year after Russia invaded Ukraine.
In the documentary, footage shows streets of buildings ravaged in the throes of war.
It also highlights the juxtaposition of fragile, porcelain figurines being handed to Ukrainian soldiers preparing for battle.
These animal figurines were designed and painted by Anya Stasenko.
Anya Stasenko delicately finishes a porcelain snail. (Supplied: Picturehouse, 2024)
Instead of fleeing the city of Kharkiv amid the threat of warfare, Ms Stasenko and her husband Slava Leontyev decided to stay.
She wanted to create a peaceful world, while the reality she faced was anything but.
"Everyday there was shelling attacks and other terrible situations around me, and I started to understand my way was to keep making my figurines."
Ms Stasenko and Mr Leontyev decided to stay in their Ukrainian city despite the war. (Supplied: Picturehouse, 2024)
Mr Leontyev became a member of the Ukrainian special forces.
"When I was on the [frontline], fighting villains, I felt life or death of these people in my hands, and I was focused on this when Anya painted figurines," he said.
Before Ms Stasenko and Mr Leontyev started filming their lives, they had no experience behind the camera.
The production studio sent a dozen cameras to Ukraine and the documentary's director taught the couple and a third artist the principles of filmmaking online over Zoom.
"We were scared that we might be hacked, or the footage might be compromised somehow, and we had a huge responsibility to the artists and the other film participants living in Ukraine who were trusting us with this footage," Camilla Mazzaferro, the documentary's producer said.
The documentary's producer Camilla Mazzaferro said the team based in Sydney worked tirelessly on the film. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)
For Mr Leontyev, he only saw an upside to taking part in the documentary.
"It was already very dangerous because Russia was shelling districts of apartment houses.
Those on the ground sent about 550 hours of raw footage to Sydney, and much of the material was sensitive.
The film is now nominated for an Oscar. (Supplied: Picturehouse, 2024)
"Everybody [on] the film team worked in complete secret for over a year," Ms Mazzaferro said.
"We had a team of 10 translators, many of whom had escaped the war themselves and it was incredible, we had this little resistance effort here in Sydney."
Their efforts paid off. Porcelain War has already won more than 50 awards including the Sundance US Grand Jury Prize for documentary.
It is also nominated for Best Documentary at arguably the most prestigious night in Hollywood, the Academy Awards, which are coming up on Monday, March 3 (AEDT).
The makers of the porcelain figurines hope the film will send a poignant message. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)
Mr Leontyev and Ms Stasenko will be in LA for the ceremony alongside Ms Mazzaferro, who cannot believe how successful their film has been.
"We knew how special it was, and we knew how special the artists were, but this has definitely exceeded all of our wildest dreams," Ms Mazzaferro said.
Once award season has wrapped up, the Ukrainians will return to their homeland where they face an uncertain future. Their hope is that the film will send a poignant message.
"Resistance is possible. It is possible for everyday people in any situation, even in [such] dark times, regular people are able to defend independence, to preserve humanity and even develop culture," Mr Leontyev said.
Porcelain War is now streaming on DocPlay in Australia and New Zealand.
author: Victoria Bourne

title: Amazon takes control of James Bond franchise
content:
A James Bond shake-up has "stirred" the film industry after Amazon announced it has taken control of the spy franchise.
The long-serving British-American heirs, Michael G Wilson and Barbara Broccoli, said they would be stepping back after they struck a deal to hand over creative control to the tech giant.
Barbara Broccoli (left) and Michael G Wilson have reportedly clashed with Amazon over the direction of the franchise. (AP: Photo/Chris Pizzello)
"With my 007 career spanning nearly 60 incredible years, I am stepping back from producing the James Bond films to focus on art and charitable projects," Wilson said in a statement.
The Broccoli dynasty agreed on a new joint venture to co-own James Bond intellectual property rights and give Amazon the power to move forward without their approval with the creative reins.
Financial terms were not disclosed, with the deal set to close sometime this year.
Broccoli and Wilson have reportedly clashed with Amazon over the direction of the franchise, leading to a stand-off which froze development.
No script, director or star has been announced for the next film, an unusually long break that has spaced films two or three years apart.
It has been four years since the release of No Time to Die — the last Bond movie — starring Daniel Craig in 2021.
Amazon bought MGM — an American production company — in 2022 for $US6.1 billion ($9.5 billion), giving it the right to distribute all the 007 films.
Billionaire Jeff Bezos, who founded Amazon, posted on X to ask his followers who the next James Bond should be.
Amazon aims to move beyond the franchise of the James Bonds movies.
James Bond had been a family business since Albert "Cubby" Broccoli secured the rights to make the films based off Ian Fleming's novels.
The producer kicked off a run of 25 films, beginning with 1962's Dr. No. The franchise has since made $US7.6 billion at the box office.
Actor Sean Connery, who died in 2020, is remembered as the first British agent 007 in 1962. (Supplied: IMDb)
In 1995, the Broccoli family handed over control to his daughter, Barbara, and stepson, Michael.
In recent years, the 64-year-old daughter of Broccoli has largely taken the lead as Wilson, 83, has aged into retirement.
"My life has been dedicated to maintaining and building upon the extraordinary legacy that was handed to Michael and me by our father, producer Cubby Broccoli," she said in a statement.
"With the conclusion of No Time to Die and Michael retiring from the films, I feel it is time to focus on my other projects."
The future of James Bond in the hands of Amazon has prompted doubts from fans, including co-director of Marvel films, Joe Russo.
The director, who is known for his work on Avengers: Endgame, pleaded with the company on socials.
"Don't dilute that [James Bond franchise] with a plethora of streaming spin-offs," he said on X.
"It is one of our last, great theatrical events."
Head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios Mike Hopkins said the company was honoured to usher the legendary franchise into the next phase.
"We are grateful to the late Albert R. Broccoli and Harry Saltzman for bringing James Bond to movie theatres around the world," he said.
ABC/AP

title: The Last Showgirl is fiction, but it shows a very real Pamela Anderson
content:
Who is Pamela Anderson? That might seem like a strange question to pose about someone who's been a pop culture fixture for the better part of four decades but, if anything, the blonde bombshell's ubiquity has rendered her an enigma, a star for whom fame is her greatest performance.
Sure, everyone can picture the slow-motion sequence of her striding across a Santa Monica beach in that iconic red swimsuit, or vaguely recall the rock-babe celebrity scandal of it all, but what do we really know of the woman, and the work that goes into the construction of such a talismanic American image?
Gia Coppola's The Last Showgirl, in which Anderson plays a Vegas dancer staring down the end of an era, serves as a reckoning with our image of a star who has recently — in her 2023 memoir and documentary — taken back control of her narrative.
What: The dancers in an old-school Las Vegas revue face an uncertain future as their show comes to a close.
Director: Gia Coppola
Starring: Pamela Anderson, Kiernan Shipka, Brenda Song, Dave Bautista, Billie Lourd, Jason Schwartzman
When: In cinemas February 20
Likely to make you feel: The grind behind the glamour
The former Baywatch star plays Shelly Gardner, a 57-year-old dancer in the revue Le Razzle Dazzle, which — not unlike Anderson — got its start in the 80s but has become something of a relic in the Disney-fied Vegas of the Sphere and other massive spectacles.
Among the troupe of dancers, Shelly acts as a den mother to her younger colleagues, Jodie (Kiernan Shipka) and Mary-Anne (Brenda Song), a chosen family that Coppola captures with hand-held camera in a series of tender backstage vignettes.
Their producer — played by a wonderfully warm Dave Bautista — has worked to protect the show but, faced with dwindling attendance, Le Razzle Dazzle will soon be cancelled to make way for a kind of erotic Cirque du Soleil that Shelly dismisses as "a dirty circus".
The Last Showgirl features original costumes from Jubilee!, a Las Vegas showgirl revue, which closed in 2016. (Supplied: Madman Films)
The Last Showgirl bears witness to lives on the margins of big entertainment, where the lure of fame can vanish at the whim of commerce. "Las Vegas used to treat us like movie stars," says Shelly, who's gone from being feted on international tours to living in a dilapidated mid-century house that she's transformed into a chintzy Graceland.
It's not like there are many options for an ageing showgirl, as evidenced by a former dancer played by Jamie Lee Curtis, chewing the scenery as a cocktail waitress in an industrial layer of spray tan.
Coppola, making her third feature after Palo Alto (2013) and the largely ignored Mainstream (2020), is sensitively attuned to the experience of these women, finding beauty and grace among their struggle and anxiety.
Jamie Lee Curtis plays Shelly's best friend Annette in The Last Showgirl, which was shot in 18 days in Las Vegas. (Supplied: Madman Films)
She shares her famous aunt's sense of space and detail — though, where Sofia has become ever more precise and distilled, Gia is loose and expressive, letting her camera float like a headpiece plume in the Nevada breeze.
Her Vegas is an oblique tapestry of cold dawns and empty parking lots, of razed building sites, tiny apartments and slot machine floors where 'Dance Hall Days' echoes into infinity.
The filmmaker's gauzy lyricism — half the movie feels comprised of Anderson twirling against diffuse sunlight — won't be to everyone's taste, but Coppola's style is an essential part of The Last Showgirl's substance. It suggests a town buried in the psychic layers of history, a purgatory for souls doomed to wander its garish present. L'appel du vide!
The Last Showgirl is a film about "second chances", Anderson told ABC Radio National's The Screen Show. (Supplied: Madman Films)
Less successful are elements of Kate Gestren's screenplay, such as a subplot involving Shelly's estranged daughter (Billie Lourd), a college student who arrives to pour scorn on her mother and fulfil the obligatory hint of redemption.
It's the one off-key note in an otherwise tough, clear-eyed study in the precarious nature of glamour. What happens, the movie wonders, to a life dedicated to an art form that no longer holds currency — be it dancing in Vegas or posing for Playboy — where a performer's livelihood is their ageing body?
The Last Showgirl director and lead actor discuss their creative collaboration on ABC Radio National's The Screen Show.
The weight of Anderson's own career hangs over a moment in which Shelly auditions for the brutally expedient — though no less misogynist — producer of the new burlesque circus, played by an almost unrecognisable Jason Schwartzman. It's here that the star's famously feathery voice finally breaks, and a lifetime of objectification explodes in a scream.
That no-one respects Shelly's artistry might be read as an analogy for Anderson's life, where the art of playing the fizzy, pin-up ideal is rarely ever given its due credit — something that's plagued almost every screen blonde, from Marilyn right up to the present.
Shelly not only understands the appeal of a show that gives its audience "breasts and rhinestones and joy', as she exclaims at one point, but also its power and sense of belonging — a spotlight that amounts to being seen.
In showing the labour, talent and personal sacrifice that goes into the image, The Last Showgirl gets at something about Anderson to which we've never really been exposed — the actor, and the artist, behind the icon.
"This is the beginning of my career," she told Us Weekly of her performance. A star is reborn.
The Last Showgirl trailer
The Last Showgirl is in cinemas now.

title: Chinese movie becomes highest-grossing animated film in the world
content:
Chinese fans are hailing the success of the animation film Ne Zha 2, calling it "China's answer to Hollywood's superhero hegemony".
"Hollywood spent a century exporting superheroes. Now, we have our Ne Zha," read a top-liked comment on Chinese social platform Weibo.
Ne Zha 2 became the highest-grossing animated film globally on Tuesday, after amassing a total box office of 12.3 billion yuan ($2.66 billion) — surpassing Pixar's Inside Out 2, according to data from ticketing platform Maoyan.
But in contrast to Hollywood films, which typically rely on a more global distribution strategy, over 99 per cent of Ne Zha 2's box office income has come from mainland China.
The film attracted massive crowds after it was released during the Lunar New Year holiday, with companies sending busloads of staff to see the film in a show of nationalism.
Videos of employees lining up to board yellow buses bearing banners with the words "Boosting Box Office for Ne Zha 2. Go, go, go! Achieving the top selling global film" were posted on X earlier this week.
Directed by Yang Yu, also known as "Jiaozi" — who helmed the first film in 2019 — Ne Zha 2 continues the story of Ne Zha, a mythical figure grappling with his demonic heritage while striving to protect his loved ones.
On Chinese social media, netizens hailed the film as a "historic moment of cultural confidence".
Videos with hashtags like 'RiseOfChineseAnimation' amassed 10 billion views on Douyin, the domestic version of TikTok used in China.
In Australia, limited screenings of the film have also drawn dedicated fans who say they are eager to see a blockbuster film that blends Chinese mythology and cutting-edge animation production.
Sheng Ruonan says she is an "experienced" anime fan.  (Supplied: Sheng Ruonan)
"Whether it's the portrayal of mythical creatures, dragons, immortals, or the intricate costumes and landscapes, all of it breathes classical Chinese aesthetics," said Melbourne anime fan Sheng Ruonan.
"This artistic approach enhances cultural confidence and a sense of identity."
But in contrast to the overwhelming praise online, Ms Sheng also took issue with some aspects of the film.
The 28-year-old said she didn't like the film's "preachiness" and "patriarchal tone".
"It constantly tries to convey grand and vague lessons in a comedy intended for all ages."
Viewers in China flocked to see the film when it was released during the Lunar New Year holiday.  (Supplied: Wang Ning)
Comments similar to Ms Sheng's have also gained traction on social media.
Another criticism was the trailer, which briefly showed a female character's skirt being stepped on.
Filmgoers complained about the "male-gazing humour", arguing the focus should instead be on the characters' strength.
Kenny Ng, an associate professor from the School of Film and Television at Hong Kong Baptist University, said the use of 5G and new visual technologies significantly lifted the animation quality.
"The promotion of the film in the Chinese cultural market and on social media also played a crucial role in its success," Dr Ng said.
Xingyu Chen, a 25-year-old from China's eastern Jiangsu province, has watched the film twice.
"I feel that the movie's marketing is really well done because I keep seeing related social media content," Ms Chen said.
"I'm not someone who usually enjoys watching animation films, but this time I was really drawn to the movie's intellectual property because it's a Chinese production, and it feels very passionate."
Blind box toys like these figurines sold out within two weeks of the film's release. (Supplied: Weibo)
Ms Chen has also bought collectible Ne Zha 2 toys, which sold out everywhere within two weeks of the film's release in China.
The filmmakers are also collaborating with China's biggest internet game company Tencent to create a Ne Zha 2 game.
Timmy Chih-Ting Chen, an assistant professor in cultural studies at Hong Kong Metropolitan University, said the impact of Ne Zha 2 would go beyond the screen, as it disseminated the "uniqueness of Chinese culture" around the world.
Film fans at a screening of the hit film in China. (Supplied)
During the 1950s to 1970s, animation evolved into an educational and propaganda tool in China, with iconic works like Havoc in Heaven (1965) becoming cultural staples.
Following the economic reforms of the 1980s, Chinese animation began integrating modern technology with traditional narratives.
By 2022, China's animation industry comprised over 6,800 enterprises nationwide and supported a workforce of approximately 340,000 people, according to statistics from the China Audio-Video and Digital Publishing Association.
The promotional poster of Big Fish & Begonia (2016). (Supplied: Weibo)
While this film is a stand-out, Mr Chen said other Chinese animated films like Fantastic Tales, also based on Chinese mythology, and Art College have also garnered international praise.
"Liu Jian's Art College was a surprise highlight, being selected for the main competition at the Berlin Film Festival," he said.
Films like Big Fish & Begonia (2016) and the first Ne Zha film (2019) also highlighted China's growing presence on the global animation stage.
ABC/Reuters
