title: Barry Keoghan is a drug-addled dad trying his best in this transcendent film
content:
Twelve-year-old Bailey (Nykiya Adams) leads a precarious existence, punctuated by insecure housing, careless drug use by her parents, friends caught up in gang-related crime and no formal education.
What: A fantastical bildungsroman set amid self-perpetuating cycles of disadvantage
Directed by: Andrea Arnold
Starring: Nykiya Adams, Barry Keoghan, Franz Rogowski
Where: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Humoured by Keoghan's antics, moved and perhaps weepy
Set in the rundown north Kent of director Andrea Arnold's childhood, Bailey squats in an abandoned apartment with her half-brother Hunter (Jason Buda) and their single father Bug (Barry Keoghan), a drug-addled, emotionally immature man barely past the precipice of puberty that his children are manoeuvring.
Bailey's delicately constructed veneer of normalcy comes crashing down when Bug announces his impending marriage to Kayleigh, a woman he has known for three months who has a young daughter of her own. Battling through her own gender expression and the onset of her first period, Bailey struggles to make sense of all the change in her life, until she finds a salve in the titular Bird (Franz Rogowski) — a mystical outsider she chances upon after spending a night in a paddock.
"I think any character that you sign on, there's a bit of them in you," Barry Keoghan told Forbes. (Supplied: The Reset Collective)
Bug is an affectionate yet neglectful father, parenting Bailey in the ways he knows best — constantly yelling at her to do things she doesn't want to do and scooting around town with her reluctantly clinging to his back. It's testament to Keoghan's ability to oscillate between paternal concern and general uselessness that sees Bug come across as well-meaning, if not misguided.
But you soon realise how relatively lucky Bailey is when she visits her biological mother. Trapped in a relationship with a violent man and living in a house teeming with drug-abusing visitors, Bailey's mother and younger half-sisters are in imminent danger.
Adams is superb in an understated performance as the disdainful Bailey, resigned to being let down by those who should be taking care of her, yet equipped with a wellspring of kindness and responsibility for those she loves — an orbit that grows to encompass Bird.
"We [actors] bring our life to the table ... our background story ... If you ask me, 'How did you become Bird?' I mean, it took me 38 years," Franz Rogowski told Indiewire. (Supplied: The Reset Collective)
Rogowski inhabits Bird in a beautifully transcendent performance. Simple, childlike and, like Bailey, gender nonconforming, his unguarded openness beguiles her, despite her trenchant mistrust of people. Ascending an elevator every day to visit Bird on the rooftop of an old, abandoned building, every night she falls asleep to him perched aloft looking over her, almost like a guardian angel.
Arnold is less concerned with the material realities of Bailey's life — we almost never see her eat, for one, and the rhythms of her existence unfold entirely outside of the usual strictures of a teenage girl's life. The director is more preoccupied with the ephemera of a life on the margins.
Director Andrea Arnold also grew up in a rundown area of north Kent. (Supplied: The Reset Collective)
The camerawork in Bird often mimics the discombobulation of Bailey's youth — it's jerky, haphazard and at her eye level, showcasing the world in its terrifying breadth and tumult. Bailey's life is mediated through her phone, footage of which she plays on a projector that splays images across the graffiti-covered walls of her squat.
For a film focused on heavy themes, Bird never feels superfluous in its depiction of its darker material. For every shot of unwashed dishes, unkempt bathrooms you might expect to find in a nightclub rather than a home, and the bone-chilling immediacy of family violence, there's an adulation afforded to nature, birds and their restorative properties. Arnold shows the interconnectedness of a small tight-knit community where everyone knows everyone, the simple joys of whizzing through town on an electric scooter.
"Everyone that sits and is watching Bug is like, 'I know that character, that's a bit of my dad, that's a bit of my brother,'" Barry Keoghan told Forbes. (Supplied: The Reset Collective)
Surreal, fantastical imagery characteristic of Arnold's polyphonic filmmaking style combine with a humour that ungirds the realism (there's a throwaway line made by Keoghan that may or may not be referencing a notorious dance scene in Saltburn).
A soundtrack of a bygone era, spotlighting hits of the 90s and early 2000s, adds to this feeling of levity. You'll never see a more spirited rendition of 'Yellow' by a group of men intent on making Bug's get-rich-quick drug toad sweat hallucinogens (yes, you read that right).
Blur's 'The Universal' is the unofficial soundtrack of the film, popping up often as Bug rehearses renditions — replete with killer dance moves — leading up to his wedding.
"She [director Andrea Arnold] creates a world in which you can just allow yourself to respond to whatever she creates," Franz Rogowski told Indiewire. (Supplied: The Reset Collective)
Damon Albarn's hopeful refrains of "It really, really, really could happen / When the days they seem to fall through you / Well, just let them go" feel indicative of the expansive possibilities of Bailey's everyday life, enhanced by the newfound presence of Bird.
The mystery of who Bird is adds an undercurrent of urgency to a film that occasionally unfolds at a lackadaisical pace, with one too many portentous shots of soaring birds. As Bird embarks on a mission to find his biological parents who used to live on a local estate, Bailey hatches a plan to save her half-sisters from the wrath of her stepfather. The two endeavours culminate in surprising revelations.
Arnold has spun a magical yet unflinching story centred on the people left behind by self-perpetuating cycles of drug abuse, poverty and neglect. But at its heart, Bird is about the joys to be found in constellations of families — whether they are the ones we don't choose to be born into, or the ones we make for ourselves.

title: Two other women willing to testify in Blake Lively, Justin Baldoni lawsuit
content:
Two other actresses on the set of It Ends With Us are prepared to come forward and testify about being made "uncomfortable" by actor Justin Baldoni, an amended legal complaint from Blake Lively has revealed.
Warning: This story contains graphic allegations of sexual misconduct
The actress has filed an amended complaint in her lawsuit against Justin Baldoni for sexual harassment and a retaliatory smear campaign.
The amended complaint, which does not name the two women, said that two actresses raised their concerns with Lively and the production company over Baldoni's "unwelcome" behaviour during filming.
Baldoni has denied all allegations and filed a counter-lawsuit against Lively, her husband Ryan Reynolds and her PR firm in addition to a defamation suit against the New York Times for its reporting of the allegations.
The lawsuit is expected to be heard in court in March next year.
Here’s the latest on the complex and public legal feud between the film’s stars.
The amended legal complaint alleges Baldoni was made aware of concerns over his behaviour by several actresses on set and acknowledged their concerns.
Here's a basic breakdown of what's going on between actors Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni.
"The experiences of Lively and others were documented at the time they occurred starting in May of 2023," the document read.
"Importantly, and contrary to the entire narrative the defendants have invented, Mr. Baldoni acknowledged the complaints in writing at the time.
"He knew that women other than Ms. Lively also were uncomfortable and had complained about his behaviour."
The amended complaint said that on May 26, 2023, Ms Lively reported her concerns regarding unwelcome and inappropriate behaviour by Mr Baldoni and Mr Heath, the chief executive officer of Wayfarer and producer of the film, to Sony employee Ange Gianetti, the film's representative for its distributor Sony Pictures Entertainment.
Three days later, another female cast member reported her own concerns regarding  Baldoni's “unwelcome behaviour” to both Ms Gianetti and one of the film's producers.
"Notwithstanding that female cast member's considerable reservations, she nonetheless spoke up and conveyed her feelings that the work on the film was suffering as a result of Mr Baldoni's behaviour," it said.
Ms Gianetti shared those concerns with Wayfarer.
The complaint said that Baldoni wrote to the cast member and said changes would be made on set but this did not happen.
Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds attend the 'It Ends With Us' premiere in New York City, US, August 6, 2024.  (Reuters: Caitlin Ochs)
On June 8, the same female cast member told Lively her growing concerns about set conditions and that she found it difficult to work with Baldoni.
The text messages are not included in the complaint to protect the anonymity of the other female witnesses.
But, it said that Lively responded by saying" "I know I find it really hard to speak to him. I try cover it with busyness but not sure that covers what's going on."
Later, it is alleged that another female cast member confided to Lively that she too felt uncomfortable on set.
"All of this occurred, and was documented in writing, almost one year before the editing of the Film began," the complaint said.
Lively also added two new causes to her lawsuit, alleging that Baldoni's attorney, Bryan Freedman, made defamatory comments about Lively in the media, retaliating against her for "speaking up and bringing legal claims against Mr Baldoni."
The complaint also reveals more detail about some of the "invasive" comments Baldoni is accused of making to Lively.
The comments were made in response to Lively's objection to additional graphic content added into the script without Lively's consent.
"When Ms Lively objected to these additions, Mr Baldoni insisted he had added them because he was making the Film "through the female gaze."
"Although he agreed to remove the scenes, he made a last-ditch attempt to keep one in which the couple orgasm together on their wedding night, which he said was important to him because he and his partner climax simultaneously during intercourse."
It Ends With Us stars Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni. (Supplied: Sony Pictures/Nicole Rivelli)
It is alleged Baldoni then intrusively asked Lively whether "she and her husband climax simultaneously during intercourse, which Ms Lively found invasive and refused to discuss".
There are also allegations that in the wake of the public legal feud, others who have publicly support Lively have been subjected to harassment and threats.
“One fact witness known to publicly support Ms Lively recently received a written threat indicating that the witness's family would be sexually assaulted and killed unless the witness agreed to ‘make a statement and give the truth.’”
The complaint said that “this type of climate was the predictable, if not inevitable, result of the retaliatory campaign launched by the Baldoni-Wayfarer parties, both before and after the litigation began.”
The complaint also names Steve Sarowitz who was the executive producer of the film and the co-founder of Wayfarer Studio and said that he once compared his battle against her and her husband Ryan Reynolds to the war between Israel and Hamas.
The suit claims that Mr Sorowitz told an employee of Wayfarer that if Lively and Reynolds "ever cross the line, I will go after them."
"I will protect the studio like Israel protected itself from Hamas. There were 39,000 dead bodies. There will be two dead bodies when I’m done. Minimum,” he allegedly said, per the complaint.
"Not dead but 'you're dead to me' so that kind of dead."
He said he would "spend a lot of money to make sure the studio is protected."
A federal judge has warned the lawyers of Blake lively to tone down media battle between the former It Ends with Us co-stars.
In a statement to the New York Times, Baldoni’s lawyer Bryan Freedman said: “Her underwhelming and amended complaint is filled with unsubstantial hearsay and unmanned persons who are clearly no longer willing to come forward.”
Lively’s lawyers Esra Hudson and Mike Gottlieb said in a statement that the amended complaint “includes significant contemporaneous evidence” and that Lively was “not alone” in raising concerns.
Lively and Baldoni have been engaged in a heated legal saga since she came forward with allegations against him in December.
The New York Times and other US  media outlets reported on her civil rights complaint in a story shortly after.
Baldoni has sued The Times for libel, claiming that the newspaper relied on Lively's "unverified and self-serving narrative."
The newspaper has said that the story was "meticulously and responsibly reported," and that the newspaper planned to "vigorously defend" against the lawsuit.
Two weeks ago, the federal judge presiding over the federal case warned Lively and Baldoni’s lawyers to obey court rules about public statements to ensure a fair trial.
Judge Lewis Liman suggested he could make the trial scheduled for March 9, 2026 start sooner if lawyers were able to stop making fiery public comments that could contaminate a potential jury pool.

title: All these Oscar-nominated movies are now streaming
content:
With the film world in the golden grip of awards season, film recommendations are flying around thick and fast.
It can be hard to know what to watch, and how. Some of the films generating awards buzz are still in cinemas; others finished their runs months ago. Some films, like Nickel Boys, didn't get a cinema release at all (it's coming to Prime on Feb 27).
While many of the biggest films can be bought or rented online, they also carry a big price tag. But you don't have to fork out to see high-quality films — these Oscar-nominated flicks are available on streaming for no additional charge.
What: An ageing movie star trades her body for a younger specimen — with dire consequences.Award nominations: 5Directed by: Coralie FargeatStarring: Demi Moore, Margaret Qualley, Dennis QuaidWhere to watch: StanLikely to make you feel: Nauseous
Would you take a miracle drug that guaranteed eternal youth? That granted pore-less skin and supple limbs?
What if it wasn't so eternal after all? What if it came with a raft of unknown — and grotesque — side effects? What if your flesh rotted and bruised, peeled off like mandarin skin? Would you keep taking it? Would you?
Sue (Margaret Qualley) quickly usurps her counterpart’s life. (Supplied: Madman)
The Substance is not a film for the faint of heart, and has divided audiences. The Academy recognised this bold picture, handing out five nominations for:
The film's hair and makeup has already been recognised at the Critics Choice Awards and the BAFTAs. Director Coralie Fargeat took home Best Original Screenplay at the Cannes Film Festival and the Critics Choice Awards.
But the nominations are perhaps most thrilling for Moore — "the film's beating heart, and its sinew bone and tendon" — who won the Best Actress gong at the Critics Choice awards, and made headlines for her emotional speech when she was awarded the Golden Globe for her performance.
The Substance - official trailer
What: The second chapter in Denis Villeneuve's adaptation of Frank Herbert's classic sci-fi novel.Award nominations: 5Directed by: Denis VilleneuveStarring: Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya, Florence Pugh, Austin Butler, Rebecca Ferguson, Javier Bardem, Dave Bautista, Josh Brolin, Christopher Walken, Léa Seydoux, Anya Taylor-JoyWhere to watch: NetflixLikely to make you feel: Ready to ride a sandworm
Dune: Part One made $US407.7 million in the global box office and won five Oscars in 2022, including for Best Sound and Best Achievement in Visual Effects. So the arrival of its sequel was hotly anticipated.
Picking up right where its stately predecessor left off, Part Two finds the spice-rich desert planet Arrakis in the grip of the invading villainous warlords who wiped out their rivals, the noble House Atreides.
From riding sandworms to creating an entire new planet, Australian cinematographer Greig Fraser shares how he created the look of Dune: Part Two.
Atreides' boy prince — and possible cosmic Messiah — Paul (Timothée Chalamet) has been provided sanctuary by the planet's besieged local population, the Fremen, along with his pregnant mother, Lady Jessica.
Paul is determined to reject his lineage and lead the indigenous people to a rebellion and exact revenge for the death of his father. But Jessica is set on seeing her son fulfil his Messianic destiny.
Dune Part Two is colossal in scope, and in a class — or at least a budget — of its own, and the Academy agrees, nominating it for:
Dune: Part Two trailer
What: Another Wallace & Gromit adventure featuring automated gnomes and an old villain.Award nominations: 1Directed by: Nick Park and Merlin CrossinghamStarring: Ben Whitehead, Peter Kay, Lauren Patel, Reece ShearsmithWhere to watch: NetflixLikely to make you feel: Utterly delighted (and like you want to eat cheese)
Wallace & Gromit are back!
Wallace once again finds himself in financial distress. "Maybe I'm just making too many gadgets," he ponders as an automated hand pours milk onto Gromit's head, missing the cereal bowl below.
Naturally, his solution to their predicament comes in the form of a new invention: an automated "smart gnome" named Norbot.
Enter Feathers McGraw — "one of fiction's most terrifying villains" — who's been spending his time in prison plotting revenge ever since 1993's The Wrong Trousers. He manages to tap into Norbot's system and take control.
It's hard not to love the claymation shenanigans of this silly pair, and the Academy agrees, nominating it for:
Wallace and Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl - official trailer
What: A documentary set in the West Bank, following attempts to evict residents.Award nominations: 1Directed by: A collective of Palestinian and Israeli journalistsStarring: Basel Adra, Yuval Abraham, Hamdan BallalWhere to watch: Docplay from February 24
"I see it like a responsibility to be [with my people] with my camera or with my body," says Basel Adra, a journalist and activist from the West Bank.
He's one of the two co-directors of No Other Land, alongside Israeli journalist Yuval Abraham. Together they have been documenting the lives of residents in Masafer Yatta, in the southern region of the West Bank, where residents have been evicted over decades after Israel designated the area a firing zone.
Basel Adra first picked up a camera as a teenager to record demolitions in a neighbouring village.  (Supplied: Hi Gloss Entertainment)
The film premiered at the Berlin Film Festival in 2024, winning Best Documentary and an audience award, and has since taken home a clutch of other awards at smaller ceremonies.
The filmmakers have been unable to find a distributor in the US — despite being distributed in 24 other countries — but it had a one-week run in New York City that allowed it to qualify for an Academy Award.
Luckily, as No Other Land is one of the films shortlisted for:
No Other Land - official trailer
What: A robot washes up on a desolate island and finds herself caring for a baby gosling.Award nominations: 3Directed by: Chris SandersStarring the voices of: Lupita Nyong'o, Pedro Pascal, Kit Connor, Bill Nighy, Stephanie Hsu, Mark Hamill, Catherine O'Hara, Matt Berry and Ving RhamesWhere to watch: BingeLikely to make you feel: In need of a good hug
The Wild Robot is a simple story about android Roz, short for ROZZUM unit 7134, who is waylaid from her mission of aiding humans with day-to-day tasks after a storm strands her on an island.
Writer-director Chris Sanders was inspired by classic Disney animated and Studio Ghibli movies. (Supplied: Universal)
This is a lush fable about a robot unexpectedly grappling with motherhood amid a broader evolutionary struggle. Its simple story is enlivened by expressive CGI animation and grand ideas that explore the process of adaptation on both intimate and cosmic scales, coalescing into a plea for new, unconventional forms of coexistence in the face of extinction.
It is also, at its core, a shameless tear-jerker.
The film missed out on the four Golden Globes it was nominated for, but has been picking up plenty of other awards, including Best Animated Feature Film at the Critics Choice Awards.
The Academy was obviously moved by this simple story, nominating it for:
The Wild Robot trailer
What: A buddy road trip comedy interwoven with a delicate rumination on how intergenerational trauma trickles down.Award nominations: 2Directed by: Jesse EisenbergStarring: Jesse Eisenberg, Kieran Culkin, Will Sharpe, Jennifer GreyWhere to watch: Disney+ from February 26Likely to make you feel: Confused but delighted that you're laughing and crying at the same time.
A Real Pain follows two radically different cousins, David and Benji — played by Jesse Eisenberg and Kieren Culkin — as they embark on a Polish Holocaust tour to honour their recently deceased grandmother and reconcile their fractured relationship.
Eisenberg has made a career out of putting his neuroticism to film, whether it be as a misguided youth in Adventureland or Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network, but the anxiety in A Real Pain comes from its modern characters attempting to reconcile their daily problems with the atrocities in their ancestors' history.
Halfway through A Real Pain, I realised why Majdanek concentration camp in the Polish town of Lublin sounded so familiar.
But don't let the Holocaust talk trick you into thinking A Real Pain is a drama; it's firmly in the comedy genre.
Its solemn setting is enlivened by Culkin's endearingly madcap performance, with Eisenberg mining David's exasperated realisation that he'll never be as charming as his cousin for big laughs.
Culkin's turn as Benji has seen him sweep nearly every major award this season, including a Critics Choice and Golden Globe Award for Best Supporting Actor.
Eisenberg received an AACTA International Award for Best Screenplay and the Waldo Salt Screenwriting Award at Sundance Film Festival, and the film also won Best Comedy at the Critics Choice Awards.
For the big race, A Real Pain has been nominated for:
The official trailer for A Real Pain.
What: A bleakly funny psychodrama about an actor with a rare genetic disorder who undergoes a miraculous face surgery.Award nominations: 1Directed by: Aaron SchimbergStarring: Sebastian Stan, Renate Reinsve, Adam PearsonWhere to watch: Binge/FoxtelLikely to make you feel: Compelled
Right off the back of playing Donald Trump in The Apprentice (also nominated for an Oscar, and streaming on Stan from March 3), Sebastian Stan commits to a different transformation altogether in A Different Man.
He plays Edward, an actor living with neurofibromatosis: a rare genetic disorder that manifests as a spread of benign tumours on his face.
An estimated one in 3,000 people in Australia have Neurofibromatosis, according to the Royal Children's Hospital, but the large benign tumours seen here are very rare. (Supplied: Kismet)
Frustrated by his thwarted ambitions and unrequited love for his neighbour, he starts a brutal experimental treatment to alleviate his condition, faking his own death and starting a new life.
But then, another actor with the same condition shows up (played by breakout star Adam Pearson, who lives with neurofibromatosis in real life), and gets everything Edward has been yearning for.
Stan won the Golden Globe for his dual performance efforts, as well as the Silver Bear at the Berlinale for Best Leading Performance.
But it's the visual transformation that the Academy has recognised, designed by The Penguin's make-up maestro Michael Marino, nominating the film for:
A Different Man trailer
What: A sequel to the Apes trilogy, where a new leader sets about crushing his enemies and wiping out the remnants of humanity.Award nominations: 1Directed by: Wes BallStarring: Owen Teague, Freya Allan, Kevin Duran, Peter Macon, William H. MacyWhere to watch: Disney+Likely to make you feel: Like a barrel of monkeys
Civilisation has crumbled, culture has been lost and humans have been reduced to feral, slow-witted creatures who can no longer form intelligible words. What better place to film it all than Australia?
Shot at Disney Studios in Sydney and on location in the wilds of New South Wales, Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes is a sequel to the 2011–2017 simian trilogy, set many generations after the reign of the legendary chimpan-A, Caesar.
Noa, voiced by Owen Teague, is the new chimp hero in Kingdom of the Planet of The Apes. (Supplied: 20th Century Studios)
While the film had mixed critical reaction, there are no questions about the level of skill on display here in the exquisite visual effects, executed by Wētā FX from Aotearoa/New Zealand, who have offices in Melbourne.
In fact, VFX artists the Corridor Crew told Screenrant that the effects used in the film "are pushing us forward into the next level".
"Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes sets the bar so goddamn high that none of the other movies can really fairly compare," said Wren Weichman.
So they're big favourites when it comes to the Academy Award race for:
Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes Trailer
The 97th Academy Awards take place on March 3, 2025, at 11am AEDT.
author: Katherine Smyrk, Jamie Tram, Luke Goodsell, Michael Sun, Velvet Winter

title: William Tell shot an apple off his son's head for one tragic reason
content:
What do you know about William Tell? Unless you grew up in Switzerland, your grasp of the mountainous European country's crossbow-wielding folk hero might only extend to him shooting an apple off his son's head.
But how on earth did this less-than-ideal family get-together occur?
What: Action epic spinning a tall Swiss story into a TIFF hit
Directed by: BAFTA-winning Nick Hamm
Starring: Bad Sisters star Claes Bang alongside Golshifteh Farahani, Emily Beecham, Connor Swindells, Ben Kingsley and more
When: In cinemas from February 20
Likely to make you feel: Up for some swashbuckling
The good news is Claes Bang, the strapping Danish star of Palme-d'Or-winning film The Square, is here with a fun refresher. Heading up an expansively starry cast in William Tell, he takes the title role of this rousing action adventure from The Hole director Nick Hamm.
"It's a bit Braveheart," Bang offers. "Everybody knows about the apple, but it's essentially a story about aggressors from somewhere else trying to take over your land and the little man standing up for himself."
Loosely inspired by the 1804 play by German writer Friedrich Schiller, the scene is set five centuries earlier. Switzerland was occupied by bad neighbour Austria, ruled by the House of Habsburg's bolshie King Albrecht (Ben Kingsley). Not a very nice guy, his lackey, Governor Gessler (SAS Rogue Heroes star Connor Swindells), is even worse.
Opening the film with a wicked flourish before we flash back, it's the wicked Gessler who forces Tell to make the call. Shoot the apple at risk of killing his son, Walter (Tobias Jowett), or watch everyone he loves die. This dilemma is all the more awful because, in this version, Tell swore off violence following his Crusading days, after he stepped in to save Muslim woman Suna (Golshifteh Farahani) during an attack in Jerusalem, and they fell in love.
"Golshifteh [Farahani] and I have this really great scene ... debating whether to go into battle or not, and we knew from that that the cornerstone of the story is reluctance," Claes Bang says. (Supplied: Rialto)
Having depicted a fair few meanies himself — including Dracula; the treacherous Fjölnir the Brotherless in Robert Eggers' Viking drama The Northman; and the insidious JP in Apple TV+ show Bad Sisters — Bang jumped at the chance to play a good guy.
"That was part of the attraction," Bang says, cracking a mischievous grin. "I was afraid I was starting to get myself boxed into this little corner of only ever playing really nasty ones."
Not that William Tell is a pacifist, exactly. His people are in the midst of a war they didn't ask for and terrible decisions must be made if his country folk want to remain free from brutality.
Bang says the weight on his character's shoulders was made all the heavier with conflicts raging around the globe.
"We felt a responsibility to say something meaningful," Bang says.
"I was really allowed to play around with the part, [director] Nick [Hamm] gave me free rein. I had an amazing time," Connor Swindells told Hey U Guys about playing villain Governor Gessler. (Supplied: IMDB)
"Will we never learn anything? Will we just keep going with these conflicts, where someone else is trying to take over land that is not theirs? In that sense, I do feel that what we've made is an anti-war movie."
Hamm's screenplay delivers a fast-paced film, but Bang is impressed that it also considers the consequences.
"It's a very physical movie that has all of this action, but it becomes more philosophical," he says. "A lot of people will die, and we will lose our best friends."
When we talk, Bang's in Aotearoa/New Zealand, filming The Wrecking Crew with Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista, so he's no stranger to action movies. But even he didn't immediately grasp that's what William Tell is.
Having depicted a fair few bad apples, Bang jumped at the chance to play a good guy. (Supplied: Getty)
In fact, it was Bang's wife, artist Lis Kasper Bang, who pointed out the obvious.
"I was so taken with the existential aspect that it wasn't until she read the script and said, 'Wow, this is such a massive action movie', that I realised what I was in for."
This included learning how to handle a crossbow, "Though I never fired a real-life bolt, because that would be massively dangerous", Bang chuckles. "But I had to come across as someone who knows what he's doing, handling it, so we did a lot of training."
A small army of stunt folks handled much of the biffo, but Bang did roll with the punches in sequences, including a storm-lashed boat battle in which he fights side-by-side Princess Bertha, played by Willow star Ellie Bamber.
"It turned out so good, man," Bang enthuses. "Bamber was amazing and that's the brilliance of Nick's writing, that he's written a story in which the women are as important to how this plays out as the men."
He adds, "Golshifteh and I have this really great scene, early on, when we're in our bedroom, debating whether to go into battle or not, and we knew from that that the cornerstone of the story is reluctance."
If being typecast as bad to the bone is a career risk, playing characters causing a ruckus in the art world might also be a thing for Bang to watch out for. He's now done so in The Square, The Last Vermeer and The Burnt Orange Heresy.
Pointing this out elicits more chuckles.
"Will we never learn anything? Will we just keep going with these conflicts, where someone else is trying to take over land that is not theirs?" Claes Bang says of William Tell being an anti-war film. (Supplied: Rialto)
"I'm a lover of art and enjoy going to museums and all that, but it's purely coincidental," he says of the run.
"But the funny thing is, I just did a movie in Paris about the Danish architect [Johan Otto von Spreckelsen] who designed the Grande Arche de la Défense."
In his research for the role, Bang read up on Spreckelsen's desire for the new monument to be dedicated to humanity, rather than a military victory, as used to be the case.
In this way, the role loops us back to Tell's hope.
"It's about allowing a place for people to meet in peace."

title: Harrison Ford is a Trump-coded president in the new Captain America
content:
When Iron Man started filming in 2007, it did not have a completed script. New pages were written on set; dialogue was routinely improvised. Actor Jeff Bridges likened the experience to shooting a "$200 million student film".
What: Captain America investigates a global conspiracy that engulfs the White House. Mind control, esoteric space deities and a Red Hulk are involved.
Directed by: Julius Onah
Starring: Anthony Mackie, Harrison Ford, Giancarlo Esposito
Where: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Like taking a break from the MCU for good
From the very beginning, the cultural juggernaut of the Marvel Cinematic Universe has been making it up as it goes. The well-publicised rewrites, delays, title changes and last-minute reshoots of Captain America: Brave New World are nothing new.
What's changed is the insurmountable fatigue that's sunk in post-Endgame — the fourth chapter of the Avengers saga and the culmination of a web of interconnected Marvel films, where we last saw Captain America.
Brave New World is saddled with dense, interconnected lore from as far back as 17 years ago. Its conspiracy thriller plot is reconstituted wholesale from prior entries. Even at a slimmed-down run time of 2 hours, it feels galaxies away from the breezy charms of a Phase 1 instalment.
At least the multiverse isn't anywhere to be found.
A quick recap, for those who aren't fluent in MCU history: way back in 2011, Captain America: The First Avenger introduced audiences to Steve Rogers (Chris Evans), a scrawny kid from 1940s Brooklyn who's injected with a 'super-soldier serum' and becomes the titular Nazi-fighting hero.
Rogers is frozen under the Arctic and defrosted in time to join the Avengers, where he becomes its leader. Despite being a flesh-and-blood symbol of his country, he's regularly tousled with its government; the last film, Civil War, saw him in hiding after America pushed to regulate superheroes across the world.
"I'm proud of who Sam Wilson has become in this universe, and watching him grow — from a guy who just went to take a jog to Captain America — is honestly the American Dream," Anthony Mackie told Deadline.
Rogers retired after the events of Endgame and handed his shield to his crime-fighting partner, Sam Wilson (Anthony Mackie), aka Falcon: the ex-airman with a deadly wingsuit introduced in 2014's The Winter Soldier, and the first Black American superhero in mainstream comics.
Notably — aside from packing some serious military gear — he declines to take any strength-enhancing serum himself.
In the 2021 Disney+ series, The Falcon and The Winter Soldier, the government briefly introduced its own Captain America, which ended in disaster — and Wilson stepped up to take the mantle himself.
Like many Marvel films, Captain America: Brave New World coalesces around a powerful resource. This time it's adamantium: the indestructible super-metal of Wolverine fame, described as even more desirable than Wakanda's coveted vibranium (which now coats Wilson's own suit with its shimmering, purple energy).
"This is meant to be two hours where you get to escape from everything else. So … I really wanted this story to have heart, and that's really what I leaned into with this cast and crew," director Julius Onah told Deadline. (Pictured: Takehiro Hira, Anthony Mackie and Harrison Ford)  (Supplied: Disney)
And there happens to be a gargantuan cosmic deity (called a Celestial) made almost entirely of the substance, suspended in deep freeze over the Indian Ocean (after the events of 2021's Eternals film).
Global leaders are locked in diplomatic negotiations over slicing up the Celestial pie, including the new president of the United States, recurring antagonist Thaddeus Ross (a snarling Harrison Ford replacing the late William Hurt).
Wilson has been trying to make amends with his new president; Ross wants his country's mascot on his side — and, having previously disbanded the Avengers with the Sokovia Accords, is now keen on restoring the superhero A-Team.
But shadowy forces converge around an attempt on the president's life made by Wilson's close friend, former super-soldier Isaiah Bradley (Carl Lumbly, introduced in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier).
Danny Ramirez fights alongside Captain America as Falcon-in-training. (Supplied: Disney)
A hawkish, increasingly unstable Ross once again turns on Captain America, forcing Wilson on the run to piece together the truth before the adamantium race reaches boiling point.
Somewhat hilarious is that this fictional setting has seen world leaders and government agencies infiltrated by Nazis and shape-shifting aliens, yet a failed political assassination doesn't immediately register as a red (false) flag.
Rather than seizing upon a new Captain America as a fresh slate, Brave New World is designed as a greatest-hits playlist to remind audiences of how much they enjoyed previous films, featuring dispassionate rehashes of international conspiracies, mind-controlled minions and resource wars.
It's less of a problem that the action scenes are inherited directly from Winter Soldier and Civil War — those sequels offer some of Marvel's best set pieces — but none of the hand-to-hand brawls, aerial dogfights and cataclysmic superhuman showdowns offer the memorable choreography of those entries.
"When I've seen the Marvel movies ... I've watched some really wonderful actors have a really good time and I thought, 'Hey, why not give me a piece of that?'" Harrison Ford told the Wall Street Journal. (Supplied: Disney)
In an inexplicable unforced error, many of the film's biggest character moments and twists require an intimate knowledge of 2008's forgettable monster mash, The Incredible Hulk, to truly land.
New additions include a mercenary played by Giancarlo Esposito (doing yet another spin on Gus Fring), and Shira Haas's Ruth Bat-Seraph, an Israeli former Black Widow known in the comics as Sabra. Danny Ramirez reprises his role as Joaquin Torres, an irritating, Gen Z Miami bro in training as the new Falcon. All are of virtually no consequence to the plot, largely functioning as potential teases of things to come.
At some point, as the trailers have eagerly advertised, we get to watch Harrison Ford's Trump-coded president transform into Red Hulk. In a film that oscillates between government black sites, supermax prisons and the remains of a nation-sized alien, it's a development that inspires little more than a shrug.
"I want little Black kids to look up and say, 'Wow, Captain America is Black'. But I want little white, Asian and Latino kids to look up and say, 'Wow, Captain America is Black'," Anthony Mackie told Atlanta News First. (Supplied: Disney)
Brave New World is exasperatingly risk-averse in addressing the only compelling question of its story: what does it mean for a Black man to take up the mantle of Captain America, particularly at a time when DEI has been twisted into an anti-minority rallying cry?
The script broadly gestures towards the expectations he must fill — Ross curtly reminds him that he's not Steve Rogers — and only directly acknowledges the colour of Sam's skin in a single, hammy monologue about having to be a flawless role model in a way his predecessor didn't.
Steve Rogers' appeal lay in his symbolic strength: he was a whitebread, goody two-shoes trying to reconcile old-fashioned heroism with modern-day morality. Sam Wilson feels more grounded as a jaded ex-soldier and counsellor, with Mackie hinting at a bruised interior, but it's unclear what compels him to stand as an emblem for his own country.
Like Captain Marvel before him, the new Captain America feels like a representational milestone more than a thought-out character in his own right. At a certain point, you can't fix these problems in post.

title: An animated film by these SA creators is taking Berlin by storm
content:
Lesbian Space Princess was always going to be the title of Leela Varghese and Emma Hough Hobbs' first film.
Emma was in the shower when the title — and nothing else — suddenly came to her.
"I ran out, dripping, and I was like: 'Babe, I got it'!"
Leela says she initially took the proclamation as a joke, noting her girlfriend literally "had a towel on her head", but the couple soon turned a "very camp, ridiculous and very literal title" into an adult animation with laughs, thrills and "a lot of heart and meaning".
Now, the pair's debut has been selected for the coveted Berlin International Film Festival, the only Australian feature film to make the cut in a program that includes the premiere of Parasite director Bong Joon-ho's hotly anticipated Mickey 17.
Leela (left) and Emma (right) on their first day of production for Lesbian Space Princess. (Supplied)
Lesbian Space Princess, produced by Adelaide's We Made A Thing Studios, is also thought to be the first full-length animated feature made in the state, with an impressive cast including Richard Roxburgh (Rake), Kween Kong (RuPaul's Drag Race Down Under), Shabana Azeez (Birdeater), Gemma Chua-Tran (Heartbreak High) and Madeleine Sami (Deadloch) to boot.
We caught up with the Kaurna/Adelaide pair to hear more about making a full-length animated feature on a shoestring budget, in a male-dominated industry, as a queer couple.
Lesbian Space Princess is, quite literally, about an introverted lesbian space princess, who goes on an "inter gay-lactic quest" to save her bounty hunter ex-girlfriend from the Straight White Maliens (voiced by the Aunty Donna boys, of course).
Along the way, she realises she might not need her ex so much after all.
Leela and Emma hired a huge cohort of Australian actors and comedians for the film, including Aunty Donna's Mark Bonanno, Broden Kelly and Zachary Ruane. (Supplied)
Leela, who's 33, says the film is about "self-love and trying to figure out who we are, and be OK with who we are, separate of relationships and other people".
"At one point [it was] more centred around the bounty hunter as the main character," she explains.
But they realised it was a story they'd seen before, particularly from male creators.
"We were like, 'Let's be true to who we are' … so we tried to capture a character that was sad and anxious and struggled with getting girls [laughs]."
The bounty hunter of Lesbian Space Princess was originally going to be its protagonist. (We Made A Thing Studios)
Lesbian Space Princess blends Emma's background as an animator with Leela's experience in comedy, two areas in which they felt women were under-represented.
"[Animation] is very much a boys club," Emma, who's 27, says.
She points to the allegations of inappropriate workplace behaviour around Justin Roiland, a voice-actor on Adventure Time and the creator of Rick & Morty.
"He's an executive producer on like, every animated TV project, [whereas there's] hardly any women."
Equal parts hilarious, heartbreaking and daring, the popularity of this cartoon about a chemically unbalanced horse has endured for a decade.
Leela feels the same about comedy and adds that, tonally, they wanted to move away from the crass male humour we've come to associate with adult animation — think Family Guy, South Park — and create something unique.
"We're so used to thinking adult animation has to be a certain way, because of the voices that have made it," Leela says.
"Our movie still has crudeness and swearing but, somehow, everything I ever make always ends up feeling so wholesome as well."
They went out of their way to hire female animators for the project, which Emma says was an "awkward" process.
"I had to ask guys that worked in these big studios. I was like: 'We can't have you, sorry. But [what women] have you worked with recently?'"
Emma Hough Hobbs, Gemma Chua-Tran and Leela Varghese debuted Lesbian Space Princess at Adelaide Film Festival. (Instagram: @adlfilmfest / @fenj_)
By doing some "crazy maths", they figured they could finish the film within budget by having Emma animate alongside two full-time animators and two part-time background artists.
For context, about 200 people are listed as animators on Inside Out 2.
"We called it our own little Suicide Squad," Leela says.
"So many people thought that this film was going to crash and fail and burn because it was such an experiment."
Leela and Emma had never had a fight as a couple… until this movie came along.
"I wish I could sell some fantasy fairytale that it was like a fun, amazing ride, but it was very, very hard," Leela says.
Leela and Emma spent years working in a tiny team to bring Lesbian Space Princess to life. (Supplied)
The pair met through being "lesbians in the film industry" and had only been together a year when they started on the project.
While co-writing was a breeze, co-directing the film as self-confessed "stubborn control freaks", balancing budget and time constraints with wanting to make the best film possible, was a different story.
"It is hard not to resent the movie a little bit sometimes, being the thing that's causing all the drama," Leela jokes.
Now entering their fifth year as a couple, they've made it through, and have even adopted a small, yet extremely energetic kitten, affectionately named Ayo Edebiri after the culturally Irish actor and comedian.
Lesbian Space Princess will enjoy its world premiere today at the Berlin International Film Festival, also known as Berlinale — one of the "big five" festivals in the film industry.
Lesbian Space Princess's Berlinale premiere will open doors for the film's future success. (We Made A Thing Studios)
The film has already had a ton of wins: the South Australian Film Corporation's New Voices grant, which is what made the project possible; the Adelaide Film Festival's Audience Award; and, most recently, Queer Screen's Completion Fund.
At Berlinale, the film will go up against other international offerings for the Panorama Audience Award and will be in the running for the prestigious Teddy Award for LGBTQIA+ films, purported to be the oldest and most important queer film award in the world.
Previous Teddy Award winners include Paris Is Burning, Hedwig and the Angry Inch, and the Australian feature 52 Tuesdays.
"[Berlin] unlocks a lot of doors and legitimises you as a filmmaker, so it's absolutely insane," Leela says.
"When the email came through it was like: 'Holy shit' … yeah, it's trippy."

title: Anora's Mikey Madison trumps Demi Moore for best actress at BAFTAs
content:
Conclave hive, rise up.
After an awards season spent standing mostly on the sidelines, papal drama Conclave has won best film at the 2025 BAFTA awards.
The high-stakes story also nabbed the outstanding British film award, which was accepted by the film's director, Edward Berger.
"We live in a time of a crisis of democracy," Berger said as he accepted the award. "Institutions that used to bring us together are tearing us apart. It's hard to keep faith in these situations, but that's why we make films like these.
"To quote Leonard Cohen, there's a crack in everything, that's how the light gets in."
Director Edward Berger and the Conclave cast accept the award for best film at the 2025 BAFTA awards. (Getty: Stuart Wilson)
Conclave tied for the most awards of the night, also picking up BAFTAs for Best Editing and Best Adapted Screenplay.
Post-WWII epic The Brutalist won four awards, including best leading actor for Adrien Brody, best direction for Brady Corbet, best cinematography and best original score.
As well as being an opportunity to celebrate British filmmaking, the BAFTAs are the last major awards ceremony before the Oscars, so they also provide valuable insight into who might take home a statue or two in just a few weeks.
Scroll down for the full list of BAFTA 2025 winners.
Back for his second hosting gig in a row, Dr Who legend David Tennant (sporting some fiery red hair) bounded on stage singing The Proclaimers, after being slung some encouragement from the "gods of BAFTAs" (Helen Mirren, Jim Broadbent and Brian Cox.)
Like any good awards ceremony host, he got in some jabs towards the Best Picture nominees early.
"You're fresh faced, wide-eyed like you've all had a couple shots of the Substance," Tennant said.
"I've been there, I was the Doctor and then I turned into Ncuti Gatwa."
UK actor David Tennant hosted the BAFTA awards for the second year in a row. (Getty: Tristan Fewings)
In front of A Complete Unknown star Timothee Chalamet and his date Kylie Jenner, Tennant confidently called the Bob Dylan biopic "Mamma Mia for middle-aged dads".
He wrapped up with a warning for winners to, "Please keep your speeches the opposite of your films: nice and short". This was a knowing nod to the fact that not a single best film nominee is less than two hours long (thank goodness The Brutalist at least has an intermission).
Perhaps the biggest surprise from the evening was Mikey Madison finally taking home an acting award for her fierce and aching performance as the titular character in Anora.
The 25-year-old was an early frontrunner in the best actress category, but has been pipped at almost every ceremony this season by Demi Moore in The Substance.
While Madison has featured in films like Scream 5, Anora is largely considered her breakout role. (Getty: Stuart Wilson)
Madison looked as shocked as anyone as she ascended to the BAFTAs stage to collect her award.
Our brightest film buffs weigh in on their favourite films to hit the Australian big screen this year.
"I probably should have listened to my publicist and wrote something," she laughed.
She began her speech with a shout-out to her mum: "She has driven me to hundreds of auditions, taped so many, she is my favourite scene partner — I love you, Mummy."
In Anora, Madison plays a young sex worker and dancer in New York that endures a stressful recovery mission after her impulsive marriage to the young son of a Russian oligarch goes awry.
She ended her speech with a call to action for greater understanding of the lives of sex workers.
It was Anora's night to shine: as well as nabbing best casting, it was the only film honoured with a musical performance.
Beloved British boy band Take That were on hand to perform 'Greatest Day', which is heavily featured in the opening scenes of Anora.
It's been a rollercoaster trajectory for Kneecap, the incendiary quasi-true story about the rise of the real-life Irish hip hop trio.
Controversial Irish rap group Kneecap tell their origin story, in their own language, in a riotous new biopic.
After exploding onto screens with its rollicking tale of music, rebellion and Irish language, it won the NEXT award at Sundance last year. The comedy drama then collected a laundry list of nominations — including falling on the Oscars long list — but didn't pick up nearly as many wins.
Nominated for six awards at this year's BAFTAs, Kneecap only managed to take home one, for Outstanding British Debut, but writer and director Rich Peppiatt made the most of his stage time.
"Kneecap is more than a film, it's a movement about how everyone should have their language respected, their culture respected and their homeland respected," he said.
"This award is for anyone out there fighting that fight."
Anora's surprise Best Picture win at the Critics Choice awards and Madison's best actress BAFTA win has definitely put the film back in the conversation for a number of Academy Awards.
It's most likely going to be a race between Madison and The Substance's Demi Moore for Best Actress at the Oscars, with the latter picking up pretty much every award in the season so far.
Conclave and The Brutalist are still neck and neck, with both picking up the same number of awards at the BAFTAs. However, with Corbet winning the BAFTA and Golden Globe for Best Direction, as well as Adrien Brody sweeping nearly every Best Actor award, it's safe to say The Brutalist will be called out at least once on Oscars night.
Like we saw with the Critics Choice awards, former frontrunner Emilia Pérez continues to lose steam from its flashbang outing at the Globes in January, where it won Best Drama.
Taking home BAFTAs for Best Film Not in the English Language and Best Supporting Actress for Zoe Saldaña is nothing to sniff at, but chances for Oscars beyond those seem to have been dampened by the controversy surrounding lead Karla Sofía Gascón.
If there's one lock for Oscars night, it's Best Supporting Actor for Kieran Culkin in A Real Pain. Culkin won the BAFTA in this category and at pretty much every awards stop this season, all but sealing his name in the Academy Award envelope.
More surprising was seeing A Real Pain writer Jesse Eisenberg pick up the BAFTA for Best Original Screenplay. This category has kind of been shared around this season, with Conclave nabbing it at the Golden Globes and The Substance taking the Critics Choice gong. Eisenberg's win at the BAFTAs means his name could still be in the mix come Oscars night.
On top of accepting the BAFTA for best original screenplay, A Real Pain's Jesse Eisenberg also accepted Kieran Culkin's BAFTA on his behalf. (Getty: Tristan Fewings)

title: From The Muppets to Wayne's World — SNL changed comedy over 50 years
content:
For the past half-century, US sketch show Saturday Night Live has defied the odds, delivering weekly live shows and lifting up some of the most famous comedy creators in history.
This Sunday, the show will celebrate its 50th anniversary with a big blow-out party set to feature former "Not Ready For Primetime Players" from across the decades.
It's almost impossible to honour a full five decades of one show, and each devoted viewer will have their own favourite moments. But, as massive comedy nerds, we thought we'd look back at the sketches that have stayed with us as fans, and the moments that influenced comedy and culture worldwide.
Before anyone says "won't someone think of the musical guests?" Yes, the 50 years of SNL has been littered with groundbreaking performances, from Sinead O'Connor ripping up a picture of Pope John Paul II (and receiving a lifetime ban), or Ashlee Simpson tanking her own career.
But for today, it's all about the comedy.
I was somewhat surprised to discover childhood fave The Muppets were once foul-mouthed characters on Saturday Night Live.
After creating a series of delightful fuzzy characters for Sesame Street, Jim Henson was determined not to be pigeonholed as just a children's entertainer. So he came up with something a little more… grown-up.
The Land of Gorch was a series of sketches across the very first season of SNL, in 1975. It followed the lives of a Muppet royal family in a faraway land but, in keeping with the late-night vibes, they were foul-mouthed and made frequent references to drugs and alcohol.
The segment was a notorious flop. As well as audience skepticism about puppet humour, Writers Guild of America rules meant only SNL staff writers could contribute to scripts. This meant Henson wasn't able to execute his vision, and also bred resentment among the staff who didn't want to "write for felt".
The Land of Gorch didn't live past the first season, but it provided inspiration and momentum for The Muppet Show, which was picked up in 1976 and introduced the world to Miss Piggy and Kermit.
— Katherine Smyrk
Beloved actor and comedian Eddie Murphy is often credited with saving SNL during a rough ratings patch that followed the brief departure of creator Lorne Michaels in the early 1980s (he returned in 1985).
Getting his start on the program at just 19 years old, Murphy's highlights include the light-fingered Mr Robinson — his twist on the beloved children’s TV host Mr Rogers — and his mockumentary-style video sketch Mr White, where he dressed up in whiteface and playfully explored white privilege.
But he's perhaps most remembered for impersonating comedy legend James Brown.
James Brown's Celebrity Hot Tub Party - SNL
Season 9, in 1983, featured a sketch called Celebrity Hot Tub Party, where Murphy gives his all in an energetic impression of the iconic 60s musician and dancer, stripping right down to his golden speedos.
Murphy's recurring impression of the singer was so uncanny that Brown even suggested he should play him in a biopic.
— Rachel Rasker
In my family, the first Wayne's World movie is a sacred text. We couldn't tell you any lines from an actual sacred text like The Bible, but we can recite Wayne's gun rack quote like scripture. Ahem…
"A gun rack. I don't even own a gun, let alone many guns that would necessitate an entire rack. What am I gonna do with a gun rack?" Amen.
Like the Blues Brothers before it, the origins of Garth and Wayne go all the way back to Studio 8H, when they debuted on SNL's 14th season in 1989. The bones of the movie are there: two hip SoCal stoner types have a lo-fi public access show. In their debut sketch they interview a local business owner who turns out to be Garth's dad. Party on.
Every Wayne’s World Ever: Part 1 - SNL
The idea of extrapolating an entire low-budget comedy film from a series of six-minute sketches feels like a relic of a bygone era, but Lorne Michaels and co did it twice with a 50/50 hit rate. Not bad. Most excellent.
— James Brennan
One of the great things about SNL is looking back at the many, many, MANY stars that got their first leg-up in studio 8H.
And one of those rising stars (for better or worse) was Adam Sandler, who was an official featured player in his early 20s. While his impressions were nothing to write home about, he really excelled behind the weekend update desk, first as the dramatic Opera Man and then with his iconic 1994 performance of 'The Chanukah Song'.
Weekend Update: Adam Sandler on Hanukkah - SNL
I was born a year after Sandler first performed this on SNL, so my first introduction to it was through my Dad's crackly car speakers as Sandler rattled off the names of people who I did not know who also happened to be Jewish. But the tune and Sandler's playful delivery had me so hooked I still frequently revisit the song to this day (I know most of the name-checked people now, not to brag).
Sure, he might have created some of the worst comedy films around but, thanks to SNL, we can always revisit a brighter time when Adam Sandler was young, upcoming and, yeah, I'm gonna say it, hot.
— Velvet Winter
Even with a revered acting career that spans more than seven decades, Christopher Walken has said on many occasions that no performance of his has followed him around more than the SNL Cowbell sketch.
On Late Night with Conan O'Brien in 2020 he recalled being at a restaurant in Singapore when a couple called out to him "I think my salad needs more cowbell!"
The sketch, written by Will Ferrell, sees Walken play fictional 70s music producer Bruce Dickinson, who has been called upon to record hit song '(Don't Fear) The Reaper' by (real) rock band Blue Oyster Cult. Ferrell plays Gene, the band's overzealous cowbell player (also fictional), who disrupts the recording several times.
But what truly makes the sketch is Walken's brilliant delivery of iconic lines, such as the immortal "I've got a fever. And the only prescription is more cowbell!" Ferrell really steers things off the rails, causing the cast (most notably Jimmy Fallon) to break character and laugh several times.
You can watch this sketch over and over and it'll never stop being funny. And it will never stop haunting poor Christopher Walken.
Gotta have more cowbell, baby!
— Christian Harimanow
Impersonating political figures of the day is very standard and important fare for any comedy show worth their salt, and SNL has embraced it wholeheartedly over the years.
Will Ferrell's impersonation of George W Bush in 2000 had the former US President convinced he had actually said the word "strategery" while debating with Al Gore.
We've had Fred Armisen as Barack Obama and Larry David as Bernie Sanders. Maya Rudolph perfectly embodied Kamala Harris, with Andy Samberg at her side as a simpering Doug.
Tina Fey's impersonation of Alaskan senator and 2008 vice-presidential candidate Sarah Palin won the actor and comedian a Primetime Emmy (Amy Poehler as an enraged Hillary Clinton is also worthy imo).
Saturday Night Live: Sarah Palin and Hillary Address the Nation - SNL
Kate McKinnon — who was also the first out lesbian in the SNL cast — is a particular master at transforming herself. The MVP of the Barbie film is not only an effortless Elizabeth Warren, she has also morphed into former attorney-general Jeff Sessions and, most hysterically, Rudy Giuliani.
A special shout-out must go to Melissa McCarthy as Trump's former White House press secretary, Sean Spicer, and Sarah Saltman as former congressman and alleged statutory rapist Matt Gaetz — both of these jump-scares still haunt my dreams.
— Katherine Smyrk
From Dick in a Box to Jizz In My Pants and I'm On A Boat, the music of comedy troupe The Lonely Island (SNL cast member Andy Samberg and writers Jorma Taccone and Akiva Schaffer) was on the lips of every young person in the late 2000s/early 2010s.
But beyond giving teens grotty things to yell out in class, did you know that The Lonely Island changed the internet forever with their second digital short?
Back in 2005, The Lonely Island boys wrote and performed a skit called Lazy Sunday, which featured Samberg and SNL cast mate Chris Parnell rapping about their perfect Sabbath day, including cupcakes and catching a screening of The Chronicles of Narnia.
Lazy Sunday
The sketch just happened to debut on broadcast TV the same week a brand new video-sharing website was launched: YouTube, maybe you've heard of it?
SNL fans jumped on the clip, uploading multiple unofficial versions that clocked a cumulative 5 million views in just a few days, making it one of the very first examples of a viral video.
So, next time you're enjoying a Vine or cute cat compilation. throw some thanks to the three boys and multiple internet pirates that made it possible.
— Velvet Winter
On Saturday Night Live, there are three constants: a celebrity host, a musical guest and Weekend Update. The latter is extremely fertile ground for oddball freaks to look down the barrel of the camera and flourish. Enter Stefon, created by Bill Hader and then writing partner John Mulaney.
Stefon is the type of character that could only really find its footing in the pressure cooker environment of a weekly live sketch show. Having originally appeared in a failed sketch alongside Ben Affleck in 2008, the weirdo "club kid" was then plonked on Update two years later as a way to fill time.
Stefon segments go as follows: Weekend Update host Seth Meyers brings him out to introduce "family-friendly" events for tourists in New York. Stefon then describes completely absurd and hedonistic watering holes that would probably make tourists either cry or puke.
Weekend Update: Stefon on Halloween's Hottest Tips - SNL
But there's a meta element in every Stefon sketch that takes the segment from good to classic. Between dress rehearsal and air, then staff writer Mulaney would swap out lines with new jokes that Hader hadn't seen. Hader has described himself as a "light touch" when it comes to breaking live on air, and Mulaney knew exactly how to push his buttons in the best ways possible.
— James Brennan
Kristen Wiig is among SNL's all-time best physical comedians, with an elasticity that lets her scrunch her face and body to suit any impersonation or original oddball. Her Liza Minnelli — a broad brushstroke that's all jittery energy, slurred words and absurd poses, but clearly made with love for Liza — is a perfect show of her talents.
In this sketch, Liza and a friend are off to a Broadway production of Cats — but first, Liza has to turn off a lamp at her apartment. Cue the jazz drums, as Wiig slinks around trying various dance moves to turn it off while offering nonsensical one-liners punctuated by sharp horns and jazz hands.
Liza Minnelli Tries to Turn Off a Lamp - SNL
Host Jonah Hill plays a perfect straight man to Wiig, suggesting Minnelli's absurd behaviour is part and parcel of being her friend. He's never irritated as he repeatedly, across the four minutes, suggests she simply find the switch.
Warning: Once you watch this, there's a high chance that "Will a Fosse neck do it?" will enter your regular lexicon.
– Jared Richards
Every now and then, a new player lands on the show and immediately enriches it with a fresh brand of unhinged comedy. The most recent example of this is Sarah Sherman, who was performing under the moniker Sarah Squirm before landing SNL.
As her stage name would suggest, this lady is the ruler of gross-out humour. Her on-air sketches have included sentient, singing meatballs that grow out of her skin, an impromptu infomercial for the "Glamgina" make-up kit at a gynaecology check-up, and a business meeting where she reveals she has replaced her eyes with plastic googly ones.
Much like Hader's Stefon, Sherman shines brightest when she's brought to the Weekend Update desk to unleash chaos on the unsuspecting host. Her first Update feature had her laying verbal traps for Colin Jost in an attempt to "gotcha" him with unflattering headlines. These poked fun at his Hamptons home, his famous wife and overall "white Harvard guy" vibe.
Weekend Update: Sarah Sherman Roasts Colin Jost - SNL
This angle has pretty much become a staple of Colin Jost's stint as Weekend Update host, with writers and other cast members expanding the premise to hilarious heights.
— James Brennan

title: Forget The Notebook, try these unconventional Valentine's Day films
content:
It's that time of February again, isn't it? The shops are full of paper hearts and teddy bears and bright pink representations of romantic love.
Valentine's Day is arguably the rom-com "holiday", where meet-cutes, mixed messages and 11th-hour declarations loom large.
But love doesn't always have to come in sickly sweet wrapping. It can be silly, platonic, angry, sexy, fun.
In light of that, here are five unconventional Valentine's Day flicks to dive into.
What: The third film in the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise, which is (surprisingly) getting better with each edition.
Directed by: Jeff Fowler
Starring: Ben Schwartz, Jim Carrey, Idris Elba, Keanu Reeves
Where: In cinemas now (with the original film on Netflix)
Likely to make you feel: Like all love is valid! Even if it's the villain/henchman type
When film reviewing site Letterboxd revealed that Sonic the Hedgehog was one of its most rewatched Valentine's day films, many were surprised.
Letterboxd’s Top 10 Most Obsessively Rewatched Films on Valentine’s Day 2024. (Supplied: Instagram)
Not me. Firstly, the first Sonic film was released on Valentine's Day 2020, which led the franchise's rabid fanbase to forever deem it a film made for the holiday.
But dig deeper than the kid-friendly action and you'll find a love story for the ages — between antagonist Dr Ivo "Eggman" Robotnik and his devoted assistant, Agent Stone.
Officially, their relationship is that of villain and henchman, but there's a devotion from Stone that knows no bounds (that is, unfortunately, not reciprocated by Robotnik most of the time). And I'm not the only one who's picked up on it.
The pair's tumultuous relationship really shines in the franchise's latest outing and, no spoilers, but a third-act confession might even bring a tear of joy to your eye.
So this Valentine's Day, why not grab your evil henchman/best friend and line up Sonic the Hedgehog 3.*
*This blurb also doubles as a Valentine's present for my partner, a massive fan of the Sonic games. You win, I admit it, I like the little blue hedgehog, too.
— Velvet Winter
What: The art-house Adam Sandler rom-com
Directed by: Paul Thomas Anderson
Starring: Adam Sandler, Emily Watson
Where: Buy or rent from YouTube or Prime
Likely to make you feel: The perfection of imperfect love
It was hard in 2002 to imagine Adam Sandler leading a Paul Thomas Anderson film, especially as it came fresh off the back of the director's critical darling, Magnolia. But Punch-drunk Love works precisely because Sandler is allowed to be himself, just the art-house film version.
The Happy Gilmore star plays Barry Egan, a business owner with social anxiety who falls in love with his sister's co-worker, Lena. Oh, and he's also trying to amass more frequent flyer points than he could ever use by buying obscene amounts of pudding. Of course.
It was a box office flop when it came out but the film has become a cult favourite over the years. It's now remembered for its gorgeous visual tone, an anxiety-inducing score, Sandler's revelatory dramatic turn, as well as an underrated powerhouse performance by the late Phillip Seymour Hoffman.
As for its V-Day bona fides? This six-and-a-half-minute sequence set to Shelley Duvall's He Needs Me is all you need to know. It's everything.
— Christian Harimanow
Punch Drunk Love — He Needs Me Scene
What: Neo-noir erotic crime thriller about two lesbians trying to make a new life for themselves
Directed and written by: Lana and Lilly Wachowski
Starring: Jennifer Tilly, Gina Gershon, Joe Pantoliano
Where: Streaming on Stan
Likely to make you feel: …excited
A sexy lesbian heist thriller that was the feature film debut of The Matrix's Wachowski sisters — need I say more? Probably not, but I will, because Bound is a must-see film, and a perfect V-day flick.
Our story centres on two dark-haired sapphics, Violet (Jennifer Tilly) and Corky (Gina Gershon).
Violet (Jennifer Tilly) — hysterically described on Wikipedia as a "gun moll" — is the sultry lipstick lesbian of your dreams, who also happens to be dating Caesar, a money launderer for the Mafia. Corky (Gina Gershon) is a stunning soft butch ex-con, complete with wife-beater and sharp-eyed pout, who happens to be hired as a plumber and painter in the apartment next door to Violet and her crim boyfriend.
The fact that Violet and Corky hook up is not a spoiler, nor is the fact that Violet begs for her new lover's help to escape her violent boyfriend and start a new life for herself. But for that, they need money, and so devise a dangerous plan to steal from right under the Mafia's nose.
The film is dark and moody and violent, while also being deeply erotic and pretty camp. While there may be more bloodshed than your average romantic watch, Bound is a perfect film to watch with a lover, lights down low.
— Katherine Smyrk
HD Retro Trailers: Bound (1996) ORIGINAL TRAILER
What: Besties and high school outcasts Romy and Michele attend their 10-year reunion and turn the tables on the popular girls
Directed by: David Mirkin
Starring: Mira Sorvino, Lisa Kudrow, Janeane Garofalo
Where: Streaming on Disney+
Likely to make you feel: amused, nostalgic, warm and fuzzy
This female-forward buddy comedy is a Valentine to the 90s, BFFs, and everyone who was a loner in high school.
Mira Sorvino and Lisa Kudrow play Romy and Michele, grown-up high school besties-turned-roommates living in LA. They love watching Pretty Woman, designing cute outfits and going clubbing every night.
How many of these classics from the year 2000 have you seen?
Faced with the prospect of attending their 10-year high school reunion in Tucson, Romy and Michele come up with a plan to impress the 'A' group of cheerleaders who ruled the school: black power suits and a backstory that birthed the iconic line, "I invented Post-its".
Everything comes to a head in the silly and satisfying final act — a high school reunion where the 'A' group's mediocrity is exposed, outcasts triumph, and female friendship prevails. Moody Gen X indie movie queen Janeane Garofalo, Alan Cumming and Justin Theroux fill out the cast.
At a brisk 90 minutes, keep the Galentine's vibes going afterwards with a Golden Girls marathon. And don't forget to tell your bestie how much you love her.
— Beverley Wang
Romy and Michele's high school reunion trailer
What: An action movie about a woman hell-bent on revenge.
Directed: Quentin Tarantino.
Starring: Uma Thurman, Daryl Hannah, Lucy Liu.
Where: Streaming on Stan, Netflix and SBS on Demand.
Likely to make you feel: Catharsis
The first time I watched Kill Bill on Valentine's Day, I was in my early 20s and reeling from the break-up of my five-year relationship. It was the kind of catastrophic heartbreak that feels like a knife being thrown straight into your chest.
But I wasn't just sad. I was furious. So furious I invited my friends over to project a spectre of hyper-violence by Quentin Tarantino on a grimy share-house wall.
Former assassin the Bride (Uma Thurman) is hell-bent on revenge after she is shot in the head by the father of her unborn child. From the moment she wakes up from a coma, four years later, it's almost two hours of blind fury (she's got nothing to lose), where she murders people in a mesmerising, kinda balletic way, including many, many with a katana.
Plus, you have the power of a villainous Daryl Hannah and Lucy Liu, and the strange, captivating unspoken language of professional assassins (see also: John Wick, another perfect Valentine's Day watch when you're single).
Kill Bill: it's the Valentine's Day pick of single women who never learned how to process their anger. (I promise I'm less angry now.)
— Hannah Story
Kill Bill: Volume 1 trailer
What: Two high school best friends try to have the night of their lives before moving away for college.
Created by: Seth Rogen, Evan Goldberg
Starring: Jonah Hill, Michael Cera, Christopher Mintz-Plasse, Emma Stone, Seth Rogen, Bill Hader
Where: Streaming on Netflix, Prime Video
Likely to make you feel: Happy, silly, grossed-out, wanting to call your high school bestie
Star-crossed lovers. Unrequited passion. A tragic separation, taken from each other too soon.
I am, of course, talking about Seth and Evan from Superbad.
Jonah Hill and Michael Cera's 2007 portrayal of co-dependent teen besties about to be torn apart when they go off to college has to be one of the most iconic movie relationships of all time.
Forget romance — find yourself someone who'll run from the police through an underage house party, cradling you in his arms.
The pair unconvincingly mask their deep affections for each other with crass jokes, homophobia, sexism and other general attempts to be perceived as cool.
There's even a fan theory that Hill's character, Seth, is actually bisexual, with his intense jealousy of the character McLovin (real name irrelevant) and childhood obsession with drawing dicks on everything.
Whatever kind of love these two share, the film's final scene is undeniable proof of their chemistry.
As the two separate to wander the mall with the girls they've been obsessing over all movie, they glance back at each other, a longing look in their eyes, as Curtis Mayfield softly croons his 1976 classic 'P.S. I Love You' in the background. Truly a poignant, romantic, Valentine's Day classic.
— Rachel Rasker
