title: Get ready to cry a lot during the new Bridget Jones film
content:
I've tried to block out the last attempt to defrost Bridget Jones.
What: A widowed Bridget Jones navigates life, love, parenting and friendship
Director: Michael Morris
Starring: Renée Zellweger, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Leo Woodall, Hugh Grant
When and where: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Nostalgic, giggly and a bit weepy
While I'm a mega-fan of the original film, and have been known to dabble in its sequel, 2016's Bridget Jones's Baby is an iteration I'd rather forget.
So it's probably an understatement to say I was apprehensive heading in to Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy, in cinemas now.
Having not even seen the trailer, I assumed this revamp would be terrible. But I'm big enough to admit when I'm wrong.
The last film felt like a desperate attempt to cling to the over-the-top silliness of the original with a markedly older cast.
This new film is still fun and silly — it's the same old klutzy Bridget who's always saying the wrong thing — but it doesn't feel forced. It keeps all that's great about the early days while acknowledging that everyone has grown up.
Just like in the original, there's a scene where our hapless heroine chases her love interest through London's snow. Except this time, she's not in her underwear — she's in a sensible silk blouse after her child's concert.
Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy — official trailer
Mad About the Boy begins as Bridget (Renée Zellweger) heads once again to a dreaded dinner of 'smug married couples'.
Except this time around, the event is a memorial for her late husband, Mark Darcy (Colin Firth), who died a few years earlier. That doesn't stop the married men at the table grilling her about finding love as a 'single middle-aged woman', of course.
From blue soup to fireman pole mishaps, Bridget Jones's Diary portrayed women as flawed, daggy and real.
An aging Daniel Cleaver (Hugh Grant) is still trying to shag every 20-something with legs, although he does later refer to this pastime as a "tad tragic". He also puts his charm to good use as Bridget's kids' favourite babysitter.
Bridget's friends are all back too: Shazzer (Sally Phillips) has a podcast (of course); Jude (Shirley Henderson) is a CEO, but still calls Bridget crying about boy troubles; and Tom (James Callis) is still living off his one-hit wonder, which luckily went viral again after featuring in a video of a dog doing maths.
There are plenty of contemporary jokes — some of which are repeated and painfully obvious spon-con for the likes of Netflix and Tinder — while others poke fun at generation gaps or modern celebrities. But, thankfully, the iPad of the last movie is nowhere in sight, and Bridget's trademark red diary is back.
In Mad About the Boy, Bridget is coping with the loss of a husband and navigating life as a single parent, which adds another layer to her usual chaos. Of course she wears her pyjamas to school drop-off: she's been through a lot.
But rather than just playing her fumbles for laughs, this film is a surprisingly moving exploration of what it's like to manage your own grief while trying to support your children through that same loss.
Bridget does her best to remember Mark Darcy while keeping life moving for her children. (Supplied: Universal Studios)
Darcy's death isn't brushed over or treated as an afterthought, and Bridget carries it everywhere.
Colin Firth pops up frequently as the husband of Bridget's memory, singing songs from Oliver as part of his children's bedtime routine.
Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy is a reintroduction to the character we've loved for decades — and a fitting goodbye.
On her first date since his death, Bridget takes a moment to herself in the bathroom, gasping for air.
And try not to cry at her young family's tributes to their father's memory towards the end of the film.
Bridget's grief is in many ways the through line of the story, as she learns to "live at the same time as those you've lost" taking her dad's advice to not just survive, but to live.
Among all this grief and growing up there are still, of course, two hot new love interests.
Bridget first swoons for Roxster (Leo Woodall), a much younger stud who saves her from an attempt to climb a tree in Hampstead Heath.
Bridget falls for the charming and cute Roxster in the new film. (Supplied: Universal Studios)
He has her head over heels, with everyone in the audience kicking their feet too, as Woodall displays the same cheeky, boyish charm and heart-melting smile he put to use in The White Lotus season two.
There's even a scene where he dives into a pool to save a small dog, coming out dripping wet in a white shirt and kissing Bridget in front of all her friends. It's all very sexy Pride and Prejudice.
Then there's Mr Wallaka (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a science teacher at Bridget's children's school, who's adorably neurotic about enforcing school rules.
Mr Wallaker is the sweetly sensible science teacher of Bridget's son. (Supplied: Universal Studios)
Sensible and sweet, Bridget's son Billy already sees him as a father figure and a mentor, while Bridget attracts Mr Wallaka's attention by spilling a bagful of her young daughter's syphilis leaflets in front of him (you had to be there).
While in many ways there's a similar dynamic to the early films — Roxster is the vivacious young hunk reminiscent of Daniel Cleaver, Mr Wallaka has the awkward seriousness of Mark Darcy — the new leads still feel fresh, and their playful flirting will leave you blushing.
After all, the film isn't particularly about these new guys anyway. It's about Bridget.
There's never a point where she needs a partner, or where a lover swoops in and saves the day (except, maybe, when she needs a little help with her dress zip).
The final scene has Bridget hosting a New Years Eve party, far from the gherkins at her parents' house in the first film.
She marks the occasion by dancing with her friends and children, celebrating the community she's built over the two decades we've known her.
Bridget has filled a whole lounge room with people who love her, just as she is.
Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy is in cinemas now.

title: Forget Emilia Pérez and check out this unhinged French musical instead
content:
Hold onto your rainbow lanyards, Mardi Gras is set to glitter-bomb Sydney with its celebration of Australia's LGBTQIA+ community.
There will, of course, be the iconic Pride parade — now a much more boisterous affair compared to its brutal origins — as well as countless parties and events set to push people to their absolute partying limits.
But what's a quiet queer to do?
The Mardi Gras Film Festival, put on by Queer Screen, is the perfect way to celebrate the glory of queer history, identity and expression, all while sitting down.
The program is bursting with funny, inspiring and passionate films — here are five picks from film critic Jamie Tram.
If you're itching for an unhinged French musical, skip right past Emilia Pérez and make a beeline for Queens of Drama.
Taking place in a bedazzled version of mid-2000s France, the film follows the rise, flop and post-ironic reappraisal of rival lesbian musicians Mimi Madamour and Billie Kohler. As young adults, they meet-cute behind the scenes of a reality TV contest, moments before Billie spectacularly crashes out with her feminist punk act. Conversely, the hosts find potential in Mimi's angelic voice and set about sculpting her into a pop princess across the season.
The two budding musicians fall madly in and out of love, the ferocious currents of their closeted relationship harmonising with the trajectory of their careers. Both draw divine inspiration from each other, even if that spark leads to a chart-topping break-up hit. Queens' musical numbers are endlessly delightful and unapologetically histrionic, spanning sugary bops to punk anthems about motorbike sex.
It's a work of pure sensory overload; director Alexis Langlois' brand of over-saturated, adrenalised camp perfectly syncs up with the onslaught of a voracious music industry and its surrounding ecosystem of tabloid rags, internet fandoms and trash TV.
Catch it before it becomes a cult classic.
Queens of Drama - clip
Based on Kim Hye-jin's international bestseller, this gracefully understated drama excavates the growing rift between a widow and her adult lesbian daughter.
When she fails to secure a housing deposit, part-time lecturer Green retreats into a familiar cost-of-living nightmare: moving back in with her passive-aggressive mum. Few words are ever exchanged between them; South Korean director Lee Mi-rang (in her debut feature) pointedly focuses on everything the disapproving mother does to avoid confrontation.
The influence of Japanese filmmaker Yasujirō Ozu (Tokyo Story) is recognisable not just in the patient, stripped-back style, but the carefully observed family dynamics on display — particularly in Green's blithely inconsiderate manner to their shared predicament. For one thing, she fails to give notice that her long-term girlfriend, Je-hee, will also be staying as an indefinite house guest.
As the situation deteriorates, Green's mother throws herself into her work at a care home — "Resting only makes me feel sore," she insists. She finds herself latching onto a childless dementia patient whose needs are being curtailed by a cost-cutting administration, wondering if she's staring into the abyss of her own future.
Lee deftly uncovers not just each characters' shortcomings, but the broader forces that feed into intergenerational conflict — and ultimately points the way towards reconciliation.
Concerning My Daughter - official trailer
Darknoon, a popular online role-playing game (RPG), is closing its servers come the impending winter solstice. For Pablo and his young sister Apolline, who've shared countless hours slashing through its vibrant high-fantasy realm, it might as well be the apocalypse.
Eat the Night largely unfolds offline in Le Havre, France, where Pablo runs an independent drug-dealing operation. It's risky work that sees him hustling on hostile territory, poaching clients and making himself scarce around local gang members.
Directors Caroline Poggi and Jonathan Vinel (Jessica Forever) zero in on the compulsive grind of work, digital reality and crime, fuelled by soaring highs and violent conquest. As the days to Darknoon's demise ticks down, Pablo's enterprise finds itself at risk when he recklessly provokes a rival organisation.
The film couches its escalating drug war in the relationship that strikes up between Pablo and Night, a supermarket worker he recruits to assist with production and distribution. It's a thrillingly romantic take on Bonnie and Clyde, swapping out a Ford V8 for a green Kawasaki hurtling down the highway with giddy abandon.
Hazy urban night scapes and a gentle score from electronic musician ssaliva surround this crime thriller with a melancholy, dreamlike aura — but sooner or later, it all comes crashing down to earth.
Eat the Night - official trailer
In cinema, nothing seems to inspire yearning quite like the European countryside. The gay teenage romance of Young Hearts blossoms among the verdant fields, dilapidated estates and dusty gravel roads of rural Belgium — boundless spaces of discovery and play for its love-struck leads.
14-year-old Elias has a dorky dad and suffers older bullies at school, but the real trouble begins when an athletic city boy, Alex, moves in across the road. Fearless and frank, his new neighbour makes a splash in his friendship group at school, and they begin bonding on the cycling commute home.
Complicating their fledgling relationship is Elias's own girlfriend, who — to everyone's surprise — he's remained chaste with. The attentive direction from Anthony Schatteman (in his feature debut) evokes the skewed perspective of early adolescence, where friends still gossip about seating arrangements and delight in underage drinking on weekends.
Enormous generosity is bestowed upon each character as they attempt to sketch out the world around them. Elias doesn't have anyone in his life who's queer; his own feelings for Alex, however overwhelming, are also entirely foreign to him.
The teenage ensemble offer remarkably nuanced performances across the board, imbuing Young Hearts with plenty of soul.
Young Hearts - official trailer
Not quite documentary and not quite fiction, this Sundance-winning film from director Jules Rosskam forms a candid, partly confessional meditation on trans-masculine desire.
The film opens with a sensuous tracking shot down the corridor of a gay bathhouse, casting furtive glances into open rooms, before diverting into a sterile, near-colourless archive. The ceiling leaks and the lights flicker, but it's home to a treasure trove of queer history — and the place where Ahmad, an Iranian American trans man, seeks to understand his own sexuality.
With its surreal synthesis of narrative, archival footage and contemporary interviews, Desire Lines places itself in conversation with the work of Chase Joynt (Framing Agnes). Rosskam unearths stories and documents (particularly of pioneer Lou Sullivan) from a probing, deeply personal perspective, linked by fictional detours into saunas and theatres that seek to reinterpret and relive a difficult history.
A series of talking heads also recur throughout the film, featuring trans men reflecting on their own experiences of sex with cisgender men. Fetishes, kink, AIDS, dating apps and transphobia are all explicated in detail, situating the film as its own valuable chronicle of our present moment. Entrenched feelings of shame echo across past and present, narrative and documentary; through history, we can liberate ourselves.
Desire Lines - official trailer
Mardi Gras Film Festival is in Sydney cinemas from 13 — 27 Feb, and on demand Australia-wide from 28 Feb — 10 Mar.

title: Hollywood action star wows fans ahead of Victorian shoot for new movie
content:
A regional Victorian highway will be shut down next week to accommodate filming for a movie featuring Hollywood actor Liam Neeson.
Neeson, 72, is down under to film The Mongoose, which will be his third movie filmed in Victoria in four years.
The veteran actor, best known for his work in films such as Schindlers List and Taken, posed for media at the Bacchus Marsh Aerodrome on Wednesday.
Neeson said the setting, which had been transformed to look like America's south west, was an attractive place to act.
Liam Neeson has featured in films such as Schindler's List, Star Wars, and Love Actually. (Supplied: Code Entertainment/Shivhans/EMA productions)
The film's producers Al Corley and Bart Roseblatt said crews were planning to shut down parts of the Calder Freeway near Castlemaine to film Neeson in a high-speed car chase next week.
"In order to shoot a chase movie you have to shoot on a highway, so we've shut down a freeway up there for one day.
"We only actually need one and a half kilometres, so we'll only be shooting in a certain area, so we'll try not to inconvenience anybody."
The state government said the movie was set to inject more than $19 million into the Victorian economy with an estimated $2 million being spent in regional communities.
Neeson's previous Victorian-based productions include Ice Road 2: Road to the Sky and Blacklight.
Producers praised the work of the Australian crew on The Mongoose. (Supplied)
Code Entertainment said Victorian crews were second to none.
"It's a long hard shoot. You're here with flies and it's 36 degrees [today] and 25 the other [days]," Mr Corley said.
"The Australian crews are not only technically savvy, but they rate right up with the Hollywood crews.
"They also have this sort of hearty go get 'em attitude, and that's really important when shooting a film."
But the Victorian weather has proved challenging so far.
"Today we have four helicopters flying around … and when we got here this morning it was fogged in and by 10 we were able to fly," Mr Rosenblatt said.
"Last week we had a set-up in the quarry and out of the blue with no warning, the night before a flash flood and storm came through and 50-kilometre winds, and it blew the entire set away.
"So we keep adapting … If you don't like the weather here [in Victoria] just wait five minutes."
Crews will film until February next year and the movie will be released on Amazon at the end of 2026.

title: Watch a ghost story from the ghost's perspective in new Lucy Liu film
content:
Horror has always been one of cinema's most formally inventive genres, a playground for filmmakers to pioneer everything from creepy first-person perspectives to found footage freak-outs and desktop-bound thrillers.
What: A supernatural entity watches over a family in the house that it's haunting.
Director: Steven Soderbergh
Starring: Lucy Liu, Chris Sullivan, Callina Liang, Eddy Maday, West Mulholland, Julia Fox
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: Spooked.
Even measured against that storied history, Steven Soderbergh's Presence might be the first horror film — at least in wide release — that's convincingly told from the point of view of a ghost.
Sure, there have been attempts to approximate the supernatural perspective — think 2017's A Ghost Story, featuring Casey Affleck literally covered in a sheet, or any number of movies that turn out to be the reverie of a character who was dead all along. (For spoiler reasons, let's leave them unnamed.)
But Soderbergh's new film differs in the way it conveys that perspective, summoning something that feels authentically inhuman, a spectre-vision that might plausibly be a transmission from the next dimension.
Shooting with a Sony DSLR still camera switched to video mode, Soderbergh conjures the impression of a spirit hovering between planes. The camera roams in long takes with an eerie staccato rhythm, as though every second frame were missing, the actors' dialogue rendered slightly out of sync as a result. The effect is both disconcerting and exhilarating, like watching CCTV footage from beyond.
"I would catch glimpses of the [monitor during filming] and ... I was like, 'OK, wow. This is really going to be something different but it was exciting," Callina Liang told Hey U Guys. (Photo by Peter Andrews)
Presence opens with the entity already inside the empty, 100-year-old property where events unfold, watching on as a real-estate broker (Brat muse Julia Fox) arrives to prep the house for inspection. (If you've ever clicked through a 360-degree view of a property listing, the imagery is uncanny.)
Moments later, middle-aged couple Rebekah (Lucy Liu) and Chris (Chris Sullivan) arrive with their teenage children Tyler (Eddy Maday) and Chloe (Callina Liang). Mum, who's very much in charge of the family, insists on snapping up the house and moving in; there's an intimation that she might be involved with something vaguely illegal, a situation that's seeding tension in the marriage.
Award-winning director Steven Soderbergh talks about his unusual upbringing, falling in love with film and finally getting to work with Lucy Liu.
More concerning is the sullen, anxiety-riven Chloe, who's become withdrawn after the recent drug-overdose death of her best friend, Nadia. Skittish and moody, she's the opposite of her obnoxious, swim-team jock brother, who wants her to get over it and not embarrass him in front of his new cool-guy friend, Ryan (West Mulholland).
When objects start to move around the house of their own volition, it's Chloe, the sensitive one, who picks up on the presence. School books float across the room and neatly rearrange themselves. Light bulbs glitch and pop. She's convinced it's the work of Nadia, still tethered to the mortal coil. But might it be something more sinister, an ancient poltergeist that's long resided on the premises?
That all of this unfolds through the eyes of the ghost itself gives the movie its sustained, unsettling tension, which isn't so much terror as it is dread — you're never quite sure what's happening, because the perspective is so unmoored from what we traditionally deem reality.
"Steven is willing to try different genres and ways of filming," Lucy Liu told NBC. "It takes courage because when you are somebody who is well-established and has a huge following of people, you don't want to disappoint them." (Photo by Peter Andrews)
At times it threatens to become one of those old YouTube videos where nothing much happens as the audience braces itself for the inevitable jump scare — but the frights never quite arrive, just a steady accumulation of discomfort.
"It's suffering," a visiting psychic (Natalie Woolams-Torres) tells the family of their spooky cohabitant. Whatever it is, it's not operating on human time.
If Presence seems like unusual terrain for Soderbergh, an indie wunderkind who went on to reshape American studio movies with Erin Brockovich, Magic Mike and the Ocean's Eleven series, the movie is more personal than you might imagine. Soderbergh's mother was a parapsychologist, and he's said that Presence was inspired by the fact that his own home is said to be haunted.
"When I read [the script], within the first five pages, you can really tell no film has ever been made like this before," Callina Liang told Women's Wear Daily. "And I was very intrigued." (Supplied: Rialto Pictures )
It's a bold swing from a director whose experiments with form are periodically reinvigorated by toying with technology — see, for example, his digital experiments Bubble and The Girlfriend Experience, or the psychological thriller Unsane, shot on an iPhone.
Yet even at a fleet 84 minutes, the movie can't quite sustain its supernatural bravado, and elements of a more conventional plot — the work of veteran screenwriter David Koepp, whose credits range from Jurassic Park to Soderbergh's Kimi — eventually come to the fore.
That said, the movie is hardly diminished by its conventional narrative punch. Soderbergh and Koepp keep the movie tense and twisty right through to its disquieting final image, landing an ending as chilling as it is emotional. You might even emerge a little haunted yourself.

title: Aussie director's film about neo-Nazis in the 80s is shockingly timely
content:
Like Michael Mann (Heat) and Paul Schrader (First Reformed), the work of director Justin Kurzel can largely be characterised as variations on the same, recurring theme. Drawing upon true crime, national myths and Shakespeare, his films have continually fed into an ongoing interrogation of disturbed, white men and their path to radicalisation.
What: An FBI crime thriller centred on a real-life neo-Nazi terrorist organisation
Director: Justin Kerzel
Starring: Jude Law, Nicholas Hoult, Tye Sheridan, Jurnee Smollett
When and where: On Prime Video now
Likely to make you feel: Grimly excited
It's a challenging creative trajectory to pull off; at what point does iteration become stagnation — or worse, self-parody?
Kurzel's last film, Nitram, hewed dangerously close to the latter. Despite purposefully omitting Martin Bryant's name and the Port Arthur massacre from the proceedings, it nonetheless elevated its infamous subject with its bellowing, portentous miserabilism. Artfully shot and forcefully acted, it played to the taste of global film festival juries without offering a shred of psychological insight.
Thankfully, The Order marks a return to form for one of Australia's foremost filmmakers, who flexes a fine-tuned genre sensibility in this explosive cat-and-mouse game between a raggedy FBI agent and a neo-Nazi terrorist in the 1980s.
Jude Law magnificently radiates 'divorced dad' energy as Terry Husk, a bureau operative with a fierce moustache who relocates to Idaho in search of some inner peace.
"The one person who deals with this kind of male, violent terrain brilliantly, unpacks it with such clarity and humanity, is Justin Kurzel," Jude Law told IndieWire about his production company Riff Raff approaching the director for The Order. (Supplied: Amazon Prime)
As the kind of cop who goes deer hunting in his downtime, it doesn't take long for him to sniff out the oncoming race war brewing in the Northwest, signposted by the numerous Aryan Nation flyers plastered around town.
While the old guard of the Nation favour a more discreet, long-term strategy to overthrowing the government — "In 10 years, we'll have members in congress," its leader assures — a younger cohort of followers have broken off to ignite the revolution with violent zeal.
The new organisation, calling themselves The Order, have started hitting up local banks in a streak of armed heists, amassing millions of dollars before Husk manages to catch on.
Director Justin Kurzel told Deadline: "I was really intrigued by this, are people following Bob Matthews... because they believe in this sort of hate speech? Or are they following him because he's the only one that's listening to them?" (Supplied: Amazon Prime)
Familiar hallmarks of cops-and-robbers cinema are intriguingly re-contextualised by the film's focus on white nationalism; it goes without saying that the film's resurgence of Nazis amid a wave of economic grievance feels depressingly timely.
In this genre, there's usually more fun to be had identifying with the charismatic crooks and their pursuit of big-time scores, rather than the grizzled lawmen who believe that the sanctity of insured megabanks is worth shedding blood for. Law enforcement tends to be depicted as serving a rigged justice system that will crack down on small-time thieves while protecting the ill-gotten gains of the rich and powerful; who wouldn't want to turn those tables?
The Order's founder, Bob Matthews (portrayed by Nicholas Hoult with an assured intensity), persuasively exploits those real inequities to recruit followers for his cause; his latest convert isn't even a white man, but a discontented Mexican American keen to overthrow a government who, in his eyes, has privileged other racial minorities over hard-working Americans.
"It's important to dismantle these situations so that we hopefully learn from them and understand rather than point fingers or say, 'This is wrong, this is right. He's good, he's bad'," Law told IndieWire. (Supplied: Amazon Prime)
Hoult's recent villainous roles, however entertaining, have threatened to wear out his arrogant, twitchy energy; here, he portrays Matthews as an uncanny rendition of traditional American masculinity, pushed to the edge with an unmistakeable chill. It's an engrossing about-face from his last Kurzel role as Kelly Gang's Constable Fitzpatrick.
Paired once again with cinematographer Adam Arkapaw, Kurzel zeros in on the fascist fantasy of a prelapsarian America; the wide compositions beckon towards an abundant landscape of ethereal woodlands, crystalline lakes and fields yawning into infinity.
When violence erupts, it does so in swift, thunderous bursts. Bullets don't just pierce flesh — they mangle clothing, splinter wood and kick up dust, lending weight and texture to gunfights. The action tends to be more economical than flashy, trading elaborate camera movements for precise compositions, such as an assassination captured through the window of a car, or the high-angle slaughter of hapless armoured gunmen.
"I was surprised that I didn't know this story," Hoult told W Magazine, "It's a true story that took place in the 80s, and it seemed very relevant to what is happening in the world now. So... how did I not know anything about this part of history?" (Supplied: Amazon Prime)
It's the kind of pounding, no-frills crowd-pleaser that should be tearing up a big screen, with Jed Kurzel's thrumming electronic score played loud. Despite its overseas theatrical rollout, however, local audiences will have to make do with streaming The Order online.
Like the rom-com and adult drama, the crime thriller is a genre in crisis. So long as mid-budget movies are routinely dumped on streaming services alongside shows that are actively designed to be ignored, audiences will perceive them as being less worth their attention and money.
The Order still plays like gangbusters at home — but in the middle of summer, nothing hits like watching sweaty alcoholics, vehicular heists and Nazi hunting in an air-conditioned theatre.

title: Daniel Craig shrugs off Bond with bold, unsettling performance in Queer
content:
In the 1985 introduction to William S Burroughs' semi-autobiographical novel Queer — which he wrote 30 years prior, but hadn't been published until then — the author reveals that the book's core reason for being is an "event that is never mentioned, in fact, is carefully avoided" throughout its pages.
What: An adaptation of Beat Generation figure William S. Burroughs' controversial 1985 novel Queer.
Starring: Daniel Craig, Drew Starkey, Lesley Manville, Jason Schwartzman, Omar Apollo
Director: Luca Guadagnino (Challengers, Call Me By Your Name)
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: Swept away then hollowed out.
He's referring to his allegedly accidental, fatal shooting of his wife, Joan Vollmer, in 1951, supposedly part of a William Tell trick gone wrong. Not only did her death shape Queer, he writes, but his entire career (his debut novel, Junkie, came out in 1953): "I am forced to the appalling conclusion that I would never have become a writer but for Joan's death."
The admission isn't necessarily new information, but it's the counterweight that Queer protagonist (and Burroughs' conduit character) Lee fails to float away from because he can't name it, even as he attempts self-obliteration and distraction in Mexico City.
William S. Burroughs, circa 1964, in Paris, France. (Getty Images)
Without spoiling specifics, Burroughs' book ends abruptly. There's no great release or even much of a plot. Nor is Queer a love story between him and Allerton, a young man also aimless, having recently been discharged from the US Navy. Instead, it's a high-frequency howl of desperation, loneliness and self-loathing, one that puts hairs on end, even if we can't always hear it directly.
Queer, then, is intriguing fodder for Italian director Luca Guadagnino, a filmmaker who specialises in transformative, all-eclipsing desire. (The throbbing Italian summer romances of Call Me By Your Name or I Am Love are the most immediate examples. But irresistible desire also runs underneath the supernatural awakening of Guadagnino's Suspiria remake, Bones and All's gory cannibalism, and the frenetic love triangle that pushes Challengers's tennis players to glory.)
Unlike previous Guadagnino films, Queer is about a failure of transformation — as Lee's alcoholism, heroin use and unknowable feelings about Vollmer's death make for an unbridged barrier. Here, Guadagnino's ability to create gorgeous, intoxicating worlds of vibrant colours and passions only underscores Lee's emptiness.
At its centre is Daniel Craig, whose Lee is removed from Peter Weller's dead-eyed version in 1991 film Naked Lunch, a hallucinatory adaptation of Burroughs' novel of the same name. Craig's Lee is pathetic: A man whose bruises are only all the more obvious in his attempts to hide them.
Daniel Craig told W Magazine he "didn't think twice" about taking on Queer, as he was eager to work with director Luca Guadagnino. (Supplied: Yannis Drakoulidis/Madman Entertainment)
Jittery and ever looking for the next hit of attention, he peacocks at bars late at night with rambling monologues on history and gossip.
His need for attention renders him a clown in a white linen suit, but there's genius in Craig's lightning-bolt blue eyes. He embodies the charm and cruelty of an addict — the intense, flattering focus that diminishes as you realise how you could be anyone. (See also: Ryan Murphy's season of Feud about Truman Capote, another queer mid-century writer, raconteur and addict.)
Still, Lee soon fixates on Allerton — played by Drew Starkey, a heart-throb previously best known for Netflix teen drama Outer Banks.
Starkey plays Allerton with icy remove, both disgusted by and intrigued by — although not necessarily attracted to — Lee's effete mannerisms and explicit ramblings.
"In some ways, I see [Queer] as a comedy about this lovelorn person," screenwriter Justin Kuritzkes told the Guardian. (Supplied: Yannis Drakoulidis/Madman Entertainment)
The two, eventually, go on a journey into the Ecuadorian jungle in search of yagé, used to make ayahuasca. (An unrecognisable Lesley Manville pops up in here as a white witch doctor, in a brief, completely terrifying role worthy of a Best Supporting Actress nomination.)
It's not exactly clear why Allerton entertains Lee but, while the humidity makes Lee look dishevelled, Allerton's sweat is dewy; he almost glows in the humid air and the light of Lee's unadulterated attention. It's either an immensely attuned, underplayed performance or one that skates by on Starkey's handsomeness. Either way, it works, as Allerton seems to be more object than equal.
Craig has received Best Actor nominations for Queer from the Golden Globes, AACTAs, Critics's Choice, the SAGs and more. (Gilbert Flores/Variety via Getty Images)
When they're together at a dinner, voices echo, fade in and out: the content of their conversation doesn't matter as much as the contact. While staring, a ghostly apparition of Lee — a shot layered on top — pushes out of his body to caress Allerton's face.
It's a simple but effective visual representation of longing constrained by fear or shame, used repeatedly. But it's built upon in a late, choreographed dance between Lee and Allerton, for a scene that is both tender and horrifying, full of body horror. Haunting, tragic and disgusting, it's what will stay with you.
But Queer isn't all phantom connection. There are multiple explicit gay sex scenes — with one in particular created to shut up those frustrated by Call Me By Your Name's PG-13 tilt up from bed to the window.
American musician Omar Apollo makes his acting debut in Queer as a man Lee's character picks up in a bar. (Supplied: Yannis Drakoulidis/Madman Entertainment)
The moments where Lee lets go — via sex and drugs, essentially — are few and far between, even though mid-century Mexico City is rendered with an intentional sense of unreality.
Using miniatures as well as painted backdrops, the film is over-saturated, supple and sun-soaked. CGI was used to add a further artificiality for colours, while pristine mid-century costuming by Loewe designer Jonathan Anderson makes everything too pretty, even when collars are sweat-stained.
All in all, Queer carries a sense that Mexico City is just a dreamy playland for Lee — and other queer American men — to pass the days as sexual outlaws. The exploitative, colonial element of their hedonism lingers, echoed by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross's eerie score of uneasy piano, strings and deep, dark synths.
"We conceived the movie not as a period drama, but as a visualisation of the imagination of William S. Burroughs," Guadagnino told IndieWire. (Supplied: Yannis Drakoulidis/Madman Entertainment)
Queer retains many core collaborators from Guadagnino's last film Challengers — including Anderson, Reznor and Ross, as well as cinematographer Sayombhu Mukdeeprom and screenwriter Justin Kuritzkes. They're clearly in a groove, working to create both Queer's irresistible beauty and a growing sense that something is very wrong.
Slow-motion becomes eerie, colour overwhelms, suits muddy. Repeat needle drops of Nirvana's 'Come As You Are' thrash through the film's romantic take on the 1950s. The drug-fuelled surrealism of Burroughs' consciousness seeps in.
There is, of course, something wrong, and it isn't merely Lee's sense of shame over his queerness or the difficulty of escaping addiction — even if that may be what audiences will find relatable or heartbreaking.
As Burroughs writes in his introduction, Lee is "inexorably driven" to Vollmer's death. Because Queer doesn't mention it by name, he writes, "a smog of menace and evil rises from the pages, an evil that Lee, knowing and yet not knowing, tries to escape with frantic flights of fantasy."
Queer sits in that evil with great discomfort. It could be Guadagnino's most accomplished film yet, but it's far too unsettling to become his most adored, offering plenty of beauty but giving little release.
Queer is in cinemas now.

title: Why you're unlikely to see COVID mentioned in film for a while
content:
It's been five years since COVID-19 started to sweep the globe, sparking lockdowns, infecting communities and claiming millions of lives.
But for an event of its scale, the way the pandemic has been represented in culture — if at all — has varied wildly.
The COVID-19 pandemic has hardly been mentioned in any major Hollywood blockbusters, with the industry sidestepping the very thing that brought several productions to a halt.
It is a different story when it comes to literature, with multiple novels interrogating the pandemic's lasting effects on our lives and relationships.
Madeleine Gray is the author of Green Dot, which follows Hera, a 20-something who starts an affair with her older, married colleague.
In the middle of the novel, Hera attempts to flee the mess she's made in Sydney by moving to London — but strict COVID-19 lockdowns up-end her new life and force her back home.
Madeleine Gray wrote her debut novel Green Dot during Sydney's COVID-19 lockdown. (Supplied: Allen & Unwin/Zan Wimberley)
Gray wrote the novel when she was living alone during lockdown in Sydney, with her mental health "not exactly flourishing".
"I decided to include the pandemic section in the book because Green Dot is a contemporary novel, set before and during the pandemic time, and to me it would have felt strange to create a revisionist history of the present," Gray told ABC News.
"Green Dot is a story about yearning and love and not being able to connect with the person you love, so the pandemic was actually an amazing plot device for that.
Green Dot was published in 2023. (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)
"The isolation we all felt during the pandemic — that's a parallel to the kind of lovelorn desperation and pathos that my protagonist is experiencing."
Gray is far from the only author whose writing features the pandemic — see Dolly Alderton's Good Material, Curtis Sittenfeld's Romantic Comedy and Ann Patchett's Tom Lake.
But one of Gray's publishers suggested it "might be best" not to include the pandemic, the reason being that readers might not be ready to re-experience it.
"And while that is a perspective that I empathise with, at the same time, we did all go through it, and as a world we are still recovering from a deeply traumatic experience that connects all of us," Gray said.
"Fiction is a place in which we can see our world reflected back to us, enter the minds of others, understand that our experience of an event might be very different to someone else's, so I fought to keep the pandemic section.
In the years since 2020, plenty of TV series have weaved the pandemic into their episodes, such as Morning Wars, Superstore and Grey's Anatomy.
The pandemic has also cropped up in international films, including the Oscar-nominated Norwegian film The Worst Person In the World.
But COVID-19 is yet to feature much in mainstream Hollywood films, if at all.
Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery (2022) was one of the first films to mention the pandemic. (Netflix)
Glass Onion, Rian Johnson's sequel to Knives Out, featured the pandemic but only through the lens of rich people ditching their face masks in turn for a getaway on a tech billionaire's private Greek island.
Because the film was bought by Netflix, it went straight to streaming after a limited one-week run in theatres.
"It is estimated that over 1 million people in the United States died from COVID-19," said Lauren Rosewarne, an expert in politics and pop culture at the University of Melbourne.
Dr Rosewarne added there were "very little positives to draw from this period".
"All the incalculable loss and grief aside, the pandemic also destroyed businesses, significantly impacted livelihoods and further amplified sharp and ugly political divisions.
"Experiencing the whole thing again right now is probably something nobody wants. At least not now, at least not in our entertainment media."
This isn't the first time Hollywood has been reluctant to represent an unfolding crisis.
"The two classic examples of this are the Vietnam War and the AIDS epidemic," Dr Rosewarne said.
"Both topics took several years to make it to the big screen in a significant way."
After the terrorist attacks in the US on September 11, 2001, the Twin Towers were also digitally removed from the New York City skyline in several yet-to-be-released films to avoid re-traumatising audiences.
Lauren Rosewarne says COVID-19 lockdowns and the SAG-AFTRA strikes have hampered Hollywood's output in recent years. (AP: Richard Shotwell/Invision)
But there are other factors at play that may have contributed to a lack of COVID-19 content across film.
"Lockdowns, compounded with the Hollywood writers' strike, mean that the film and TV industries are still playing catch-up in a way that literature hasn't had to," Dr Rosewarne said.
For authors such as Madeleine Gray, representing the pandemic in novels is less of a risk because "to be honest, novels cost less money to make".
"That is why literature can be the wackiest, most exciting, most bizarre art form," Gray said.
The COVID-19 pandemic hit at the start of a new decade. Now at the halfway mark, what can we expect from film, television and literature in the next five years?
It's been about five years since the first case of COVID-19 was confirmed in Australia. This is what Australia living through "unprecedented times" looks like in numbers.
"Creators have tried — and will continue to try — to capture aspects of the Zeitgeist in their work," Dr Rosewarne said.
"Some of this will be about the pandemic and understanding its impact on us, even if not necessarily being about the pandemic itself."
Dr Rosewarne said it was likely the pandemic would be represented through metaphors, rather than direct presentations.
"During the early years of the AIDS epidemic, for instance, there were several horror films about viruses and bodily invasion — albeit without any direct mention of AIDS," she said.
"Films and TV shows can reference the legacy of the pandemic without needing to be about the pandemic itself.

title: This French restaurant is close to paradise — if you can afford it
content:
For a documentary centred on the behind-the-scenes travails of fine dining, Menus-Plaisirs — Les Troisgros is immediately notable for its absence of culinary clichés.
What: A tantalising, epic-length documentary on one of the greatest restaurants in the world
Directed by: Frederick Wiseman
Starring: Many generations of the Troisgros family
Where: Out now on DocPlay
Likely to make you feel: Hungry!
Grandstanding egos, bubbling chaos and blistering tempers are virtually absent. The kitchen soundscape never rises above a light percussive flow. Even amid the flurry of roaring stoves and rapid-fire dicing, barely a drop of sweat can be glimpsed throughout the entire run time.
Le Bois sans Feuilles is the latest iteration of legendary French restaurant La Maison Troigros, which has held onto three Michelin stars for a record 69 years.
The spectacle being offered isn't just of food porn — it's competency porn.
The gardens outside restaurant Le Bois Sans Feuilles (The Woods Without Leaves). (Supplied: Madman)
The open kitchen set-up that fixes each worker in plain, inescapable view, feels akin to a 19th century operating theatre. Armed with tweezers and a practiced dexterity, chefs huddle over grids of plates, twisting and layering and contouring each prepared element — kidneys and brains included — until the completed dish emerges.
When the restaurant was still operating out of Roanne, 90km north-west of gastronomic capital Lyon, second-generation brothers Jean and Pierre turned their parents' institution into an epicentre of nouvelle cuisine, whose philosophy gave precedence to fresh ingredients, invention and a delicate touch. Today, the restaurant operates in rural Ouches, with its seamless, ceiling-length windows gazing onto the surrounding farmland.
That same doctrine has been dutifully followed by Pierre's son, Michel Troisgros — now the stately patriarch of his family's restaurant dynasty — and Michel's own sons, César and Leo.
Michel Troisgros (centre) has played a major role in La Maison Troigros since 1983, restoring the original restaurant after the deaths of his father and uncle. (Supplied: Madman)
The minutiae of their practice is affectionately and attentively detailed: crisp artichoke hearts are paired with lamb, garlic flowers and sage; John Dory fillets are sliced into petals, decorated with squid ink, and floated atop green curry; strands of puff pastry are coiled into a nest, upon which trompe-l'oeil dessert eggs rest.
For a working environment with a sky-high margin of error, the inevitable mistakes only amount to minor, contained inconveniences. When a junior cook neglects to drain veal brains of their blood vessels, Michel directs him to a pair of hefty cooking bibles, from which Michel narrates the correct preparation of the dish from the page. The lesson is delivered in classically paternal fashion: encouraging, if lightly condescending.
Director Frederick Wiseman, who remains startlingly energised at 95 years of age, has long occupied an elder statesman status in his own artistic field. Produced with a minimal crew (often with Wiseman doubling as sound recordist), his films relentlessly eschew the kind of conventions that have become synonymous with the documentary form.
"The people who work there know a lot more than I do about the place and the routines," Wiseman told Screen Slate. "I deliberately use the moments when we're not shooting to talk with the people, as long as it doesn't interrupt their work." (Supplied: Madman)
His trademark style — an unobtrusive, fly-on-the-wall perspective unencumbered by music, titles, voiceover or talking heads — can have a hypnotically immersive effect.
His films bristle with personality and pointed commentary in how he weaves between institutions (spanning New York's welfare offices to the National Gallery of London) and the bureaucracies behind them. The incensing failures of dilapidated government services and utopic glimpses of their potential are contrasted across class lines.
With Menus-Plaisirs, his 47th feature and counting, Wiseman has seemingly captured the closest one can get to paradise — at least for those who can afford it.
"All the films that I've shot in France had to do with artistic creation ... Whatever the definition of an artist may be, they [the chefs] are artists," Wiseman told Film at LIncoln Center. (Madigan Heck)
Across its four-hour run time (at home, the film is likely best enjoyed with a charcuterie board and a self-imposed intermission), the director's curiosity takes the film to local fromageries, farms and greenhouses around the verdant countryside.
Speaking in inadvertently metaphorical terms, more than one practitioner expounds the significance of the soil on which they stand, and its importance in maintaining a "virtuous cycle". It's a small-scale ecosystem sustained by formidable passion, sustainable practices and technical rigour; the multifaceted aging process for goat's cheese extends back to the feeding of organic cow's milk to baby kids.
One can draw parallels between the pampered goats and César's own offspring, an infant daughter with a taste for mushroom pasta — the foundations of the Troisgros dynasty continue to be carefully nurtured.
Menus-Plaisirs relishes in the creative synchronicity shared between Michel and his kin, with the testing and discussion of new menu items kicking off a lively volley of ideas, feedback, and technical considerations.
Michel's father, Pierre, and uncle, Jean, transformed their parents' institution into an epicentre of nouvelle cuisine, whose philosophy gave precedence to fresh ingredients, invention and a delicate touch. (Supplied: Madman)
The film's abundant pleasures are nonetheless infused with an awareness of the immense privilege on display, evoking the inherent tension between artist and benefactor.
At the front of house, an army of waiters (accompanied by Michel himself) are tasked with entertaining the kind of patrons who can afford the €350 seasonal menu (or reserve a €15,000 bottle of wine).
One customer probes the staff about the presence of sulphites in wine, while another invokes Balzac in a philosophical tangent while ordering. Try not to cringe as an Australian businessman attempts to appraise the wine, or waves his hand above the plate to take in the aroma.
Most of us will never land a reservation at such an institution — but for those with the appetite for an epic-length run time, the film lovingly dishes up one of the purest, most joyful expressions of culinary creativity ever committed to screen.

title: Sophie Wilde went from an Adelaide horror to starring alongside Nicole Kidman
content:
Actor Sophie Wilde is an Amyl and the Sniffers mega fan.
She wears their merch to our interview and gushes about seeing them live twice in the past month, but admits she forgot to cast them her vote in triple j's Hottest 100: "Sacrilegious, I know".
But Sophie's had a busy year. Since her breakout role in A24's Aussie horror smash-hit Talk to Me, she's led the Netflix series Everything Now, won an AACTA award and was personally congratulated by Prince William after her nomination for BAFTA's Rising Star Award.
William, Prince of Wales, congratulated the nominees for BAFTA’s Rising Star Award, including Australian Sophie Wilde. (Getty: WPA Pool)
Now, the 26-year-old from Sydney's Enmore, on Gadigal land, stars alongside Nicole Kidman in the racy new flick, Babygirl, which premiered at the Venice International Film Festival to a six-and-a-half-minute standing ovation.
Babygirl is hooked on tech CEO Romy (Kidman) and her affair with a much younger intern (played by Triangle of Sadness's Harris Dickinson). Sophie plays Kidman's ambitious assistant, Esme, in a mentor-mentee relationship that mirrors the bond between the two actors.
ABC Entertainment caught up with Sophie to mark the release of Babygirl, hear more about her music obsessions, and to compel her to change her passwords.
After months of enticing memes, the film starring Nicole Kidman as a woman exploring BDSM with a younger man is here.
I mean she's just so cool, she's awesome. You know, it's Nicole Kidman, and I think for her to be so down to earth and warm and loving and welcoming, it's unreal.
I have loved the press tour and watching some of her answers to things. Like when she was like, "I love to go to a rave".
I wish! I need to text her.
Oh my god. I feel like she'd be into it. Absolutely.

title: Power, sex and drinking milk: Nicole Kidman has an awakening in Babygirl
content:
Babygirl opens with Romy (Nicole Kidman) in the throes of sex with her husband of 19 years, Jacob (Antonio Banderas). She's making all the right sounds, but as soon as it's over and Jacob has descended into a post-coital stupor, Romy steals away to watch porn on her laptop and pleasure herself. She didn't orgasm with Jacob and, it turns out, never has.
What: A sensual, often-funny, occasionally surprising exploration of one woman's journey of sexual reawakening
Directed by: Halina Reijn (Bodies Bodies Bodies)
Starring: Nicole Kidman, Harris Dickinson, Antonio Banderas, Sophie Wilde
When and where: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Titillated
The film cuts almost immediately from the intimate space of the home and its entombed secrets to the sterility of a warehouse. Romy is the CEO of a robotics company that trades in a rote automisation replicated in her characterisation.
Perennially put-together and guarded with nary a tendril of hair askew, Romy pursues perfection in every realm of her life, meticulously assembling lunch boxes with hand-written notes for her two daughters as seamlessly as she spouts meaningless corporate nothings in promotional videos and undergoes periodic botox injections.
Nicole Kidman plays Romy, who is apparently happily married to Jacob, played by Antonio Banderas. (Supplied: A24)
There's a touch of Severance in the world-building of Babygirl. Dutch writer-director Halina Reijn nails the humdrum details of everyday office life, from the insipid office small talk to Romy's swapping of pragmatic runners for teetering heels as soon as she steps into her office.
But Romy's aloof detachment starts to come undone with the arrival of a new intern, Samuel (Harris Dickinson), who is nearly 30 years her junior. Confident and impetuous, bordering on rude, Sam intuitively guesses what Romy wants from him, and the chemistry between them is palpable. So begins an affair conducted within the privacy of hotel rooms, in the obscured nooks and crannies of their office.
There's a clear power differential in an illicit relationship between a CEO and an intern, but Sam signals early on that he holds all the cards in this affair, subverting the dynamic from the outset. Not only is Sam the dom to Romy's sub, but he also warns her that he could easily dismantle her professional and personal life if he were to go public with their affair.
"[Harris and I] had to surrender to the material, understand the material and then also throw that out and allow our visceral nature as actors to exist," Kidman told Marie Claire. (Supplied: A24)
Romy is keenly aware of this dynamic — it's what imbues their escalating liaison with the electricity and sexual charge that's so sorely missing in her own marriage. That, and his commands for her to lap milk from a saucer, prostrate on all fours in an impossibly tight pencil skirt, and skulk in the naughty corner like a child being disciplined.
Babygirl is less sexually explicit than its trailer suggests. The moments of raw, unadulterated pleasure Romy experiences with Sam are carnal and guttural, but Jasper Wolf's camera angles fixate almost exclusively on Romy's face as she engages in these acts.
Babygirl is less intent on capturing these sexual acts in their entirety — the sex itself is never particularly risqué — and more concerned with Romy's interiority as she metamorphoses and has her most perverse sexual desires realised.
"I wouldn't have done this if I'd felt that it was a dangerous place for me to go, because it was very vulnerable and raw, emotionally as well as physically, but if that person [director Halina Reijn] is there going, 'I've got you, I'm never going to betray you', then it's incredibly safe," Kidman told Marie Claire. (Supplied: A24)
For a film riven by depictions of clandestine sex and unmitigated desire, Babygirl is surprisingly tender and funny.
Both Romy and Sam experiment with different ways of being as they fumble, at times, through their dominant-submissive relationship. Romy trying to communicate her sexual preferences to Jacob while draped in a bedsheet because she's too embarrassed is as humorous as it is painfully affecting.
Cristobal Tapia de Veer's soundtrack is one of Babygirl's greatest accomplishments, setting the tone for much of the film. Montages of Romy and Sam's affair unfold to the wonderfully apt 'Father Figure' by George Michael and INXS's 'Never Tear Us Apart'. Le Tigre's jaunty pop-punk anthem, 'Deceptacon', backdrops Romy's intensified discomfort as she catches Sam's eye while children dance between them at her daughter's birthday party.
"We [Kidman and Dickinson] didn't get to know each other too well beforehand, which I think helped," Dickinson told People. (Supplied: A24)
One of the film's most memorable scenes sees Romy joining Sam at a rave, with strobe lights illuminating their movements in haphazard flashes while jarringly discordant electro house music by Yellow Claw plays.
Costume design duo Kurt and Bart's work is another highlight — everything Kidman wears looks as though it was sculpted to her body.
Tangential details in the film carry acute symbolism as Romy's life unravels and is reflected by those around her. Her playwright husband, Jacob, is directing the Henrick Ibsen play Hedda Gabler, a narrative centred on a woman perilously trapped in a marriage and constrained by society's expectations of her.
On the surface, Romy appears perfect in almost every realm of her life. (Supplied: A24)
Romy's behaviour is mirrored on a more minute scale by her older daughter, who cheats on her own girlfriend with a neighbour and is caught surreptitiously smoking by Romy late one night, who then joins her. There's also a surreal quality to many of the scenes, begging the question: did some of it even happen?
Kidman goes above and beyond in a role where she bares herself metaphorically and physically in a heightened show of vulnerability, but the celebrated evolution of Romy herself may have been more convincing with a more sharply realised character. With a whisper of a backstory concerning a childhood spent on a commune, Romy's motivations and impulses remain opaque even as her actions escalate (though Babygirl, thankfully, never veers in the direction of kink-shaming Romy, as so many portrayals of BDSM do).
Ultimately, Babygirl may not be saying anything particularly new or subversive about female desire, the pursuit of pleasure over shame and sensibility, and questions of power and consent. Nor are the stakes so heightened that it feels like an erotic psycho-thriller — the absence of punishment for Romy is a clear departure from the 1990s films that Reijn took inspiration from.
But it's a rollicking ride all the way, a tour de force performance from Kidman, and an often-unexpected treatise focused less on the moral consequences of a woman transgressing, and more on the liberation afforded by the reclamation of self.

title: Angelina Jolie in career-high performance as opera legend Maria Callas
content:
To the extent that the Oscars even matter in recognising great movie artistry, if we're talking about snubs from last week's nominations, well, look no further than Angelina Jolie's portrayal of Greek-American opera legend Maria Callas.
What: A portrait of opera icon Maria Callas in her final week of life.
Director: Pablo Larraín
Starring: Angelina Jolie, Alba Rohrwacher, Kodi Smit-McPhee, Pierfrancesco Favino, Haluk Bilginer, Valeria Golino
When: In cinemas January 30.
Likely to make you feel: Moved by Callas's indomitable spirit — and Jolie's sublime performance.
It's a career-high performance that's by turns graceful, imperious, elusive and fabulously defiant.
"You have no idea," Jolie's Callas chastises a fan at one point, her eyes a pair of daggers behind tinted frames. "No idea of the pain to pull music through your belly, out your poor mouth. No idea!" She might as well be addressing the Academy.
Maria is the latest portrait of a 20th-century icon from Chilean director Pablo Larraín, and like his re-imaginings of Jackie Kennedy (2016's Jackie) and Princess Diana (2021's Spencer), it ditches conventional biopic tropes for an impressionistic approach that favours a kind of spiritual communion with its subject.
Angelina Jolie had seven months of singing class, Italian class and opera class to prepare for the role.  (Supplied: Kismet)
The film picks up in the week before Callas's death in September 1977, with the 53-year-old diva in her signature black and roaming her palatial Paris apartment — her only company her faithful butler (Pierfrancesco Favino), housemaid (Alba Rohrwacher) and the two poodles to whom she's been feeding most of her meals.
Crash dieting, popping pills and issuing hilariously prickly memos ("I need you to make me an appointment with a hairdresser that doesn't speak"), La Divina is adrift, morose, more than a little reflective — a star who, ailing from the rare autoimmune condition dermatomyositis, hasn't taken the stage in years.
"I can no longer perform miracles," she admits to the conductor (Stephen Ashfield) she visits in an effort to revitalise her voice.
"It doesn't take much to look [Callas] up and start to see everybody's opinion of her. But you don't really know her. I think she was misunderstood," Jolie told W Magazine. (Supplied: Kismet)
She might also be hallucinating. In lieu of an official memoir, Callas imagines a TV crew interviewing her for a documentary about her last days, led by a filmmaker named Mandrax (Kodi Smit-McPhee) — which also happens to be the name of her medication. That's right: Maria is effectively confessing her life, love and dreams to a prescription drug.
What does it take for actors to portray classical musicians?
"Madam, this television crew, is it real?" her butler enquires. Maria's response could double as the movie's playbook: "As of this morning, what is real and what is not real is my business."
As she surrenders to reverie, so the film flashes back, sometimes in black and white, to Callas's recollections of her younger self: as a teenager (Aggelina Papadopoulou) forced to perform for Nazi soldiers in occupied Greece; as a spectacular young singer breaking through in Europe; as an international superstar feted by shipping magnate Aristotle Onassis (Haluk Bilginer), a man who saw her as one of his many possessions.
Maria Callas and Aristotle Onassis were both married when they first met and started their on-again-off-again relationship. (Supplied: Kismet)
It moves effortlessly between the present and memories of the past, collapsing time and space as though all of history — Maria's history — is unfolding in a single, surreal moment where the private and public personae become indistinguishable.
"There is no life away from the stage," Maria says. "The stage is in my mind."
Fleeting musical sequences catch Callas at the height of her power, exaltation and fame, while others — like a rain-soaked orchestra that materialises on a sunny Parisian street — seem to unfold out of time altogether, emerging through the haze of a fever dream.
"We're both seen as strong, but actually we're very vulnerable and human," Jolie told The New York Times about her similarities with Callas. "I don't think either one of us is necessarily comfortable being public." (Supplied: Kismet)
Rich, expressive cinematography — by veteran director of photography, and the film's lone Oscar nominee, Ed Lachman (Carol, The Virgin Suicides) — and Larrain's gently rotating camera create a paradoxical sense of intimacy and dissonance; we're never quite sure what's real or imagined.
It's both a glimpse into Callas's frayed state of mind and a clear distillation of her essence, evoking her all-consuming relationship with the music that moved through her like an otherworldly life-force — and the prickly one she shared with her mother, the press and a world that wanted a piece of her.
In many ways Callas is a perfect match for Jolie, whose luminous talents have been chronically under-served by Hollywood in what feels like forever.
"I hope [people] have more empathy for [Maria Callas]. There was something very sad to me when I realised what this last week of her life must have been and how unloved and unseen she must have felt," Jolie told ABC News Breakfast. (Supplied: Kismet)
The actor relishes Maria's contradictions, her immaculate poise and her steely sense of self-possession, as though channelling her own celebrity and understanding of fame, the crippling demands of beauty and age, and a woman's need to author her own narrative at whatever cost.
Performing with a combination of her own voice and Callas's vocals, she captures the singer's gestural power, her pain, and the shadow that seemed to haunt her, even at the apex of success.
As Maria says to Mandrax: "We are Greek — death is our familiar companion."
It's a soulful, sometimes spooky glance at a diva at the edge of oblivion, and a portrait as rich, melancholy and moving as its subject.

title: One man's doll-like new girlfriend seems too good to be true — she is
content:
With so much of our daily life, love and even political leadership under the influence of a handful of tech companies, it isn't too much of a leap to imagine our memories — already slippery custodians of history — being manipulated by those in control.
What: A weekend retreat turns deadly when a subservient android develops self-awareness
Director: Drew Hancock
Starring: Sophie Thatcher, Jack Quaid, Megan Suri, Lukas Gage, Harvey Guillén, Rupert Friend
When: In cinemas January 30
Likely to make you feel: Like exterminating all huma— sorry, I mean amused and entertained
The idea has long been a staple of science fiction, and it's central to playful new thriller Companion, which opens on the memory of a meet-cute so generic that it can only be the work of programmers.
The reverie — of a girl and a guy instantly smitten in a supermarket aisle — belongs to Iris (Sophie Thatcher), flashing back to her first encounter with her boyfriend, Josh (Jack Quaid).
With her exaggerated, doll-like features and anachronistic 60s outfit, she's both vaguely out of time and way out of the league of the unremarkable Josh, who nonetheless — in a moment of pure straight-guy fantasy — miraculously catches her eye.
If the episode seems too perfect to be real, well, that's because — you guessed it — it isn't.
In the present, Iris and Josh are en route to a luxury lake house in upstate New York, where a group of successful, attractive 20-somethings have gathered for the weekend. There's Eli (Harvey Guillén) and his model boyfriend Patrick (Lukas Gage), seemingly a warm and loving couple, and the stylish and spiky Kat (Megan Suri), whose much older lover — a wealthy, cartoonish Russian by the name of Sergey (Rupert Friend) — owns the house and considers everything in its orbit his property.
Quaid (pictured with Thatcher) told The Hollywood Reporter Companion was one of the best scripts he'd ever read.  (Supplied: Warner Bros)
It's all banter and revelry until Sergey demands a sleazy sunscreen massage from Iris, who suddenly turns violent.
"Go to sleep," Josh commands her, and her eyes roll back into spooky-white screensavers.
Companion, which is the debut feature for TV writer and director Drew Hancock, is one of those movies that's best to go into knowing as little as possible. None of what follows is a spoiler, however — it's all present in the movie's marketing, which relies upon the story's few modest twists as its selling point.
Although she has no idea herself, it turns out that Iris is a robot who's been designed as a companion for men — and her memories have been tailored to flatter Josh's idea of the perfect relationship.
Quaid with co-star Megan Suri, whose first leading role was in horror film It Lives Inside (2023). (Supplied: Warner Bros)
"There have been two moments in my life when I was happiest," she says in the film's opening scene (and indeed, during its trailer). "The first was the day I met Josh, and the second, the day I killed him."
The line effectively frames events as being told from the perspective of technology, turning the movie into an origin story of robo-liberation.
That might sound like big tech's latest sinister plan to groom audiences into empathising with AI, but it's really just the latest in a long and storied tradition of movies exploring the existential nature of technology — from the likes of Blade Runner to recent variations such as M3GAN, The Creator and even last year's The Wild Robot.
"I've never felt so scared going to a project," Thatcher told The Cut. (Supplied: Warner Bros)
As played by Thatcher, star of TV's Yellowjackets and the recent Heretic, Iris makes for a worthy addition to the android club, whether she's stomping through the forest, bloodied and barefoot, or defiantly hacking into her system to bump up her intelligence — which Josh had set at a man-friendly 40 per cent — to its galaxy-brained maximum setting.
There are some amusing twists, nasty thrills and plenty of sass — think The Stepford Wives as retold in the style of Get Out, the latter now surely one of the most imitated genre movies of the past decade.
Companion is from the producers of 2022's house-bound horror hit Barbarian, and if you've seen that, you more or less know what you're getting here: a killer premise that devolves into something much more generic, though not without a certain unpretentious, B-movie charm.
Quaid followed his famous parents — Meg Ryan and Dennis Quaid — into acting. (Supplied: Warner Bros)
As sci-fi, it's pretty familiar stuff; Hancock doesn't have much interest in pushing the technological possibilities of his scenario, of digging into its repercussions for the future. But as a metaphor for domestic abuse — and the many ways in which men seek to control women — Companion is crudely effective, and at times even confronting in its imagery.
It'd be easy enough to take aim at Companion's veneer of "feminism" — the kind of superficial empowerment behind which so many filmmakers hide their cruelty and violence. And it's true that Hancock might have leaned harder into his film's underlying ideas, which are rich with potential.
Still, the movie is entertaining, and more than a little mischievous; it might not restore your faith in humanity, but it might make you warm to our replacements.

title: Cameron Diaz is Back in Action for first film in more than 10 years
content:
The last time Cameron Diaz was on screen, Obama was president, eyebrows were on fleek, and a girlboss Taylor Swift was ruling the pop charts with 'Blank Space'.
What: A pair of former spies are pulled out of their suburban retirement after a threat to global security resurfaces.
Director: Seth Gordon
Starring: Cameron Diaz, Jamie Foxx, Andrew Scott, Glenn Close, Kyle Chandler, Jamie Demetriou
When: Streaming on Netflix now.
Likely to make you feel: Entertained, if you're in an undemanding mood.
That's a long time away for a star who'd been a luminous, irrepressible fixture of Hollywood for more than two decades, though it's not like you can blame her for stepping aside to raise kids with a rockstar and run an organic wine label. The formulaic comedies on offer were failing her fizzy, firecracker talent; even a valiantly unhinged performance in 2014's Annie remake couldn't save an otherwise forgettable affair, nor her apparently waning interest in stardom.
Whatever possessed the Charlie's Angels icon to return with this splashy new Netflix spectacle — the imaginatively titled Back in Action — is anyone's guess, even as the breezy action-comedy works as a neat-enough metaphor for her career about-face.
"If I'm going to leave my family for 10 hours out of the day, I knew it had to be with someone I could count on," Diaz told Entertainment Tonight about working with Foxx again. (Supplied: Netflix)
Diaz and her Annie co-star, Jamie Foxx, play Emily and Matt, a married suburban couple who walked away from their glamorous, high-stakes lives as globetrotting CIA operatives after learning they were about to have a child.
Fifteen years later, they've disappeared into a vanilla American suburbia of SUVs and soccer practice, while raising two kids — 14-year-old Alice (McKenna Roberts) and 12-year-old Leo (Rylan Jackson) — who regard mum and dad as total squares.
Not that Emily and Matt can conceal their own boredom. She sells bespoke craft puzzles on Etsy, while he's busy scowling at Alice's 16-year-old boyfriend and his teenage moustache. Soon, they've stalked their daughter to a nightclub, where a scuffle with some older boys leads to the couple unleashing mayhem — and blowing their carefully constructed cover in the process.
"Jamie is, like, the cheerleader for the entire crew. Everybody loves him. We have so much fun ... and he's just a professional on every level," Diaz told Deadline of her co-star. (Supplied: Netflix)
Threatened by a gang of Belarusian terrorists on the hunt for a deadly cyber-security device, the family packs up and hightails it to London, where Matt has stashed the gadget at the manor of Emily's estranged, ex-MI6 mother (a plummy, tweed-clad Glenn Close, having what appears to be the movie's one genuinely great time).
Their ex-boss (Kyle Chandler) seems to be dead, and a shady British agent (Andrew Scott) is on their trail. You can more or less clock the ensuing plot beats with your eyes closed.
What is there really to say about a movie like Back in Action, which — for all its obvious expense and glossy surfaces — is designed to keep subscribers mindlessly engaged without disrupting them from folding their washing, cooking dinner, or whatever else they're doing while the streamer's key metrics chug along?
"The [first] moment you see Cameron Diaz look into the screen, that is movie magic," Jamie Foxx told Etalk. (Supplied: Netflix)
It's the movie equivalent of an inoffensive, algorithmically generated Spotify playlist — background in action. Take that for whatever it's worth.
Director Seth Gordon (Horrible Bosses; 2017's Baywatch), working from a script he co-wrote with Brendan O'Brien (the Bad Neighbours movies), keeps the slick, anonymous set-pieces rolling along at a clip.
There's a running thread of playful banter, plenty of CGI carnage, and a slew of diet-John-Wick brawls scored to old-timey standards from the likes of Dean Martin, Nat King Cole and Etta James — presumably so as not to upset dinner.
"It was a really fun character," Glenn Close told TODAY (US). (Supplied: Netflix)
Diaz and Foxx are immensely charismatic stars, and they share an on-screen chemistry that's not without its appeal. (Pity poor Andrew Scott, though, who seems vaguely pained as he goes through the motions, as though his cheque had yet to clear.)
As low-stakes filler, Back in Action is never less than diverting, especially for an audience in an undemanding mood.
But when the filmmaking is this generic, and the writing this uninspired, you do have to wonder how far we're away from a movie like this being entirely, and indifferently, generated by AI — when 'stars' can be digitally scraped from data, minus the exorbitant salary.
Director Seth Gordon keeps the slick, anonymous set-pieces rolling along at a clip. (Supplied: Netflix)
It's why Back in Action's better moments are the ones that remind us of the actors' distinctive personalities, when we get a glimpse — however briefly — of the human moments of performance. Diaz and Foxx rapping along to Salt-N-Pepa's 'Push It' while their zoomer kids roll their eyes back into infinity? It's just the sort of scene the movie could've delivered more.
It's a shame that Back in Action doesn't really tap into its stars' comedic abilities, nor into Diaz's talent for going unexpectedly dark and deranged — the kind of performances that would occasionally flare up in movies like Vanilla Sky and The Counselor.
Still, there's no denying that it's nice to have her back.
