title: The newest film from Forrest Gump director has Tom Hanks, age-reversing technology and dinosaurs
content:
Thirty years after they captured the Zeitgeist with Forrest Gump, director Robert Zemeckis, screenwriter Eric Roth and stars Tom Hanks and Robin Wright reunite for a new film that plays very much as a spiritual sequel to their Oscar-winning 1994 smash.
What: Life as it unfolds on a single plot of land in East Coast America, from the prehistoric age through to the 21st century.
Director: Robert Zemeckis
Starring: Tom Hanks, Robin Wright, Paul Bettany, Kelly Reilly, Gwilym Lee, Michelle Dockery, David Fynn
When: In cinemas now
Likely to make you feel: Misty-eyed, if manipulated
At the same time, it also feels considerably more melancholy, channeling the anxieties of a baby boomer generation as it reckons with time and mortality.
Adapted by Roth and Zemeckis from Richard McGuire's 1989 comic strip (and later, graphic novel) of the same name, Here unfolds in a single location as it goes from prehistoric jungle to a suburban living room that bears witness — not unlike Gump — to so much of 20th century history.
With its locked-off camera trained for the most part on a sofa, bay window and television, the movie could quickly lapse into filmed theatre or a single-camera sitcom, but Zemeckis — always one of the most inventive Hollywood storytellers — keeps things moving at a playful clip, sending the action flashing back and forwards in time.
We sit down with Tom Hanks and Robin Wright to ask them about their multigenerational epic Here, reuniting with their Forrest Gump director, and being made younger with AI.
Having swept through dinosaurs, asteroids and colonial America with the speed of a museum highlights reel, the movie settles into a turn-of-the-century Pennsylvania home occupied by a series of families. There's an early 20th-century suffragette (Michelle Dockery) and her aviation pioneer husband (Gwilym Lee); a jazz-age inventor (David Fynn) and his bohemian pin-up partner (Ophelia Lovibond); and the home's first African-American family (Nicholas Pinnock, Nikki Amuka-Bird and Cache Vanderpuye) in the 2010s, filming birthdays on iPhones against crisp cream walls.
But the bulk of Zemeckis's film, and its emotional focus, is devoted to three generations of the Youngs, a family who comes into existence post-World War II when a returning soldier (Paul Bettany) and his wife (Kelly Reilly) welcome a brood of little boomers, who scamper about the house like the 50s family of Back to the Future. (It's no surprise that Zemeckis, who was born in 1952, keeps returning to this apparently formative era.)
The eldest of these tykes grows up to be Richard (Hanks), who we meet at age 18 as he falls for high-school sweetheart Margaret (Wright) — both stars remarkably digitally de-aged, though betrayed, as usual, by the voices of their older selves. He's a budding artist who resigns himself to the working life of a salesman; her career aspirations are put on hold for home making.
A page from McGuire’s graphic novel shows how the story links disparate times, species and worlds together. (Richard McGuire)
The ups and downs of their lifelong love might be confined to a single room, but that doesn't stop Zemeckis from packing the film with incident. Births, deaths, marriages and funerals all miraculously happen in the living room; the TV helpfully beams in The Beatles, Nixon and Jane Fonda's aerobics; and the golden oldies just keep on rolling. (If you think a needle drop of Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young's 'Our House' is too obvious, you've clearly never seen a Robert Zemeckis movie.)
Meanwhile, the film cuts between timelines, often nesting different eras within the same frame via panels like those of the comic strip — kind of like watching the picture-in-picture function on a modern TV, only instead of the game, you might be checking in on a Founding Father or the Spanish flu.
Some of this, however well-intended, is tone-deaf, much in the way that Forrest Gump treated culture as an emotional sandbox. A Native American couple, seen in pre-colonial times (Joel Oulette and Dannie McCallum, respectively billed as "Indigenous Man" and "Indigenous Women"), gets little-to-no dialogue.
Richard and Margaret marry early after Margaret falls pregnant. (Supplied: IMDB)
But the worst scene situates the Black family entirely as social phenomenon, as dad explains at length to his son the correct procedure to avoid trouble when pulled over by the police. It's the only conversation of substance this family gets in the movie.
Otherwise, it'd be easy to dismiss Here as a cheeseball greeting-card movie, so syrupy and heart-string-tugging that it's impossible to believe there isn't a "Live, Laugh, Love" plaque somewhere in the background of the shot.
But for all his sentimentality, Zemeckis — a technical wizard with a career full of experiments in mainstream form — has always been a more interesting filmmaker than his worst tendencies suggest. His best movies engage technology to tangle with nostalgia and evoke the uncanny (Back to the Future and its 1989 sequel), to explore the cosmic (Contact), or simply to derange good taste (Death Becomes Her).
While Here is hardly his most boundary-pushing work, its formal playfulness is fascinating for the way in which it frames what is essentially a very unremarkable story — a life onto which audiences of a certain age and temperament will be able to project their own experience.
Robert Zemekis reunites with Robin Wright and Tom Hanks, who he directed in Forrest Gump in 1994 — although they're looking a little bit older than usual here. (Supplied: Sony)
That the movie's takeaway appears to be little more than "Time sure flies" — as Hanks's character is fond of repeating — lends it a feeling of generic relatability. That's not a criticism. Here's emotional effect is cumulative and, thanks to expert performances from the two leads, in many ways quite moving.
The film's ending might be as corny as any in Hollywood cinema, but in trying to tie a bow on a century of American life and family, it winds up leaving more threads hanging — and exposing the myopia of a post-war generation.
At its best, it's an essential piece of the Zemeckis puzzle — an attempt to reconcile life, for better and for worse, through the magic of the movies.
Here is in cinemas now.

title: Saturday Night is a love letter to the people 'who ripped TV out of the hands of the last generation'
content:
It's hard to imagine the face of American comedy, or indeed American movies, without Saturday Night Live. The show gave us Eddie Murphy and Will Ferrell. Steve Martin and Tina Fey. Adam Sandler and Kristen Wiig. Bill Murray and, er, Pete Davidson.
SNL has been part of the mainstream for so long that it's easy to forget it was once revolutionary.
Jason Reitman's Saturday Night goes back to the very beginning at New York's Rockefeller Center in 1975, as the first cohort of young stars — including Chevy Chase (Cory Michael Smith), Dan Aykroyd (Dylan O'Brien), Gilda Radner (Ella Hunt) and John Belushi (Matt Wood) — prepare for the maiden broadcast of an unlikely sketch show then titled NBC's Saturday Night.
The upstarts have been given a national slot thanks to a contract dispute between the network and its late-night star Johnny Carson, but the suits (led by Willem Dafoe) are looking on with undisguised scepticism. It doesn't help that creator Lorne Michaels (Gabriel LaBelle) is having trouble articulating exactly what his new show is.
The reason, Reitman tells ABC RN's The Screen Show, is that SNL "lacked specific definition". Unlike the shows that came before it, it couldn't obviously be categorised.
"[It had] these odd cold opens, and satirical news, and music from artists that young people really loved," the director explains.
Saturday Night trailer
Reitman's credits include such acclaimed dramedies as Juno and Thank You for Smoking. Most recently, he took on the 2021 reboot of Ghostbusters, which was originally directed by his father, Ivan.
It's perhaps no coincidence that he was drawn to his latest story: Saturday Night is ultimately about the new generation picking up the baton and running with it.
"Certainly when the original episode [of NBC's Saturday Night] went up, they were reacting to decades of television that had become very stale," he says.
"You know, you had an evolution from vaudeville, to radio, to variety television that had a very specific look, feel and sound that did not represent that coming generation.
"[A generation] who had already declared who they were at Woodstock, and declared who they were in early 70s cinema through films like The Graduate and Harold and Maude. Movies that really said: we are not our parents."
It's a measure of SNL's intergenerational impact that Reitman, 47, and his leading man Gabriel LaBelle, 22, share the same childhood memory: staying up late to watch SNL.
"My parents showed us all the National Lampoon movies," says LaBelle.
LaBelle had a star-making role in 2022's The Fabelmans as the young Steven Spielberg, and he brings some of the same boy-genius pluck to the role of Lorne Michaels.
The real Michaels was actually slightly older (30) when he created SNL, but the decision to cast the baby-faced LaBelle fits with Reitman's framing of the story as the kids running riot, thumbing their noses at the establishment.
The famously belligerent John Belushi (Matt Wood) only signed his contract the day of the show airing. (Supplied: Sony/Hopper Ston)
LaBelle is joined in the film by a who's who of young Hollywood talent, including Kaia Gerber (daughter of Cindy Crawford) and Cooper Hoffman (son of Philip Seymour).
But Michaels's most important sparring partner is Rosie Shuster, his wife, co-writer and creative partner, played by Rachel Sennott (Shiva Baby, Bodies, Bodies, Bodies).
Sennott is a comedian and a writer herself (she wrote last year's Bottoms, in which she co-starred with The Bear's Ayo Edebiri), and she revelled in the chance to meet the real Shuster and show how integral she was to SNL's birth.
"She was f***ing smart, a bad ass, and seemed to be cool in this really hectic environment," Sennott says.
"So, boy's club or not, the girls were rocking it."
Much of the surviving cast and crew from the first-ever episode of SNL were interviewed by Reitman for the film.
  (Supplied: Sony/Hopper Stone)
Sennott and the rest of the cast worked on a labyrinthine studio set built using the blueprints of the Rockefeller Center. It extended over two storeys, with real windows, stairs, lights and cables, which meant the cameras could follow the actors anywhere.
Reitman shot on film and handheld camera — the better to capture both the period, and the antic energy of preparing for showtime as everything goes wrong, Noises Off-style.
Michaels walks and talks between set and backstage, avoiding falling lights and suspicious executives, and the script (written by Reitman and Gil Kenan) pauses only to show a clock ticking over as potential doom nears.
The director once spent a week as an SNL guest writer, experiencing first-hand the adrenaline of putting together a 90-minute sketch show, and he wanted to bottle that feeling on screen.
The pressure of prime time is one thing, but the real squeeze in Saturday Night comes from the older generation of TV comics, figures like George Carlin (Matthew Rhys) and Milton Berle (J.K. Simmons). They're seen as dinosaurs by the new generation snapping at their heels, and they respond in kind.
"It's the first time we were getting this kind of absurdist sense of humour that clashed with the Sid Caesars of the world," says Reitman.
Vintage TV comic Milton Berle (JK Simmons) was reportedly banned from SNL after a disastrous turn hosting the show in 1979. (Supplied: Sony/Hopper Stone)
One scene sees Berle whip his penis out of his pants in front of Chevy Chase's girlfriend (Gerber) in an attempt to dominate the younger man.
Berle is "representative of the last generation", says Reitman.
The men of the subsequent one weren't exactly choirboys, either — nostalgia for the era has its limits. But Saturday Night is explicitly about smashing the old world to create a new one.
Reitman was inspired by the sheer confidence and bravado of "a group of genuinely young people in their early 20s who ripped television out of the hands of the last generation".
Though he's now a veteran filmmaker, it's clear Reitman identifies with them — and particularly with his film's hero, Michaels.
"What does it feel like when you have an idea in your head that you can't articulate to others, but [which] you know is right? That's something that I've felt as a director many times."
Saturday Night is in cinemas now.

title: Inspired by Muriel's Wedding, this 'irreverent and naughty' comedy is sure to be a cult classic
content:
In the first act of the new Australian black comedy film Audrey, the titular teenage character falls into a coma — and her family couldn't be happier about it.
What: An absurd black comedy about ambition and motherhood.
Starring: Jackie van Beek, Hannah Diviney, Josephine Blazier and Jeremy Lindsay Taylor.
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: Evil for wanting Audrey to remain in a coma indefinitely like the rest of the Lipsick family.
With Audrey (Josephine Blazier, Fires) in a coma, her sister Nora (Hannah Diviney, Latecomers) gets the attention she deserves from their parents for the first time, as well as from Audrey's boyfriend.
Her dad Cormack (Jeremy Lindsay Taylor, Heartbreak High) finally has the time to follow his completely normal dream of producing Christian-themed porn.
And it gives her washed up soap actor mother Ronnie (Jackie van Beek, The Breaker Upperers) a way to get her career back on track … by pretending to be Audrey.
It was this darkest of dark premises that drew van Beek to the movie, written by Lou Sanz and directed by Natalie Bailey in their feature debut.
"It's so irreverent and naughty and it's great to have a protagonist be a woman, be a mother, but not shying away from the darkness — creating it, in many ways," van Beek tells ABC Entertainment.
"I love that Ronnie's daughter goes into a coma but she's still got her eyes on the prize and that is her career, so she assumes her daughter's identity … and that's the most buoyant we see her in the film."
Audrey — official trailer
When van Beek first read the script and felt the third act approaching, she assumed it would be redemptive and involve the family reconnecting, which is how stories like this one normally end.
But that couldn't be further from what happens.
"[Sanz] does something very different to what we expect and doubles down on the dark," van Beek says.
The result is a uniquely Australian film that pays visual homage to Muriel's Wedding, set near the fictional Porpoise Spit on the real-life, sun-drenched Gold Coast.
Its plot — inspired by satirical black comedies including To Die For and Jennifer's Body — offers sharply written feminist commentary just as the deeply misunderstood Megan Fox classic did.
Ronnie is at her most "buoyant" in Audrey when she's pretending to be her daughter (which she obviously pulls off totally believably). (Supplied)
When she was younger, Ronnie scored a role on a long-running soap, and a 2004 Logie Award win that was going to help catapult her into mainstream Hollywood.
But that moment became the height of her career after she unexpectedly fell pregnant. Then came the second child, the mortgage, and the inescapable daily grind.
Somewhere along the line, Ronnie transferred her dashed dreams of super-stardom to Audrey, who couldn't want this any less.
A 2004 Logie Award win was never meant to be the height of Ronnie's career, and yet... (Supplied)
As a person, Ronnie "has a fun side, but she's very ambitious, quite singular, mentally unhinged, and delusional," van Beek says.
As a mother?
"She genuinely loves her children, but she's lost sight of her role as a mother because she relies a lot on attaining work goals to feel happy, which I personally find quite bad, but relatable."
Van Beek was trained as an actor to "always try to win the audience, whether you're playing a hero or a villain", and to find "truth" in every single scene.
So, her biggest challenge in portraying a character who is "reasonably abhorrent at times" was looking for moments of vulnerability and opportunities to charm, despite Ronnie's "horrific" actions.
"In the scene where Audrey has just gone into a coma, Ronnie says to one of the orderlies, 'Well, will she still be able to do an audition?'
"Ninety-nine per cent of mothers would be absolutely devastated if their child was in a coma and I [didn't] want to come off just like a cold-hearted bitch.
"And so I thought, 'I'll play delusion and see if I can get even a few members of the audience onside' … that felt more truthful than flippancy."
The Lipsicks begin to thrive after Audrey falls into a coma because she's a brat.
As the favourite child, she is carted around to dancing, singing and acting classes, which she sees as a personal attack. She is disgustingly ableist to her sister, Nora, who has cerebral palsy.
The best version of Audrey is comatose Audrey — that's how awful she is (and how well Josephine Blazier embodies the character). (Supplied)
Blazier's portrayal of the teenager was so good that it horrified van Beek.
"I was part of the recall process where there were four women auditioning that were shortlisted for Audrey … and they were all very good actors, but [Blazier] was the one of the four that truly scared me," van Beek shares.
Diviney agrees, saying she'd never seen someone put so much energy into a character before.
"Even though she's in a coma for half the movie, you can't take your eyes off her when she's on screen," she says.
Audrey (right) and Nora (centre) have the requisite sibling rivalry, with an added dose of ableism from Audrey's side. (Supplied)
Nora's snarky, sarcastic and dry sense of humour is a defence mechanism developed from a life spent as the forgotten child in the Lipsick family.
Those who caught Diviney's first acting role as the lead in the SBS dramedy Latecomers may notice similarities between Nora's humour and that of her 2022 character, Sarah. Apparently, this is by design.
"Disabled people have deserved stories since … forever! Now, we're finally getting them," writes Hannah Diviney.
"It has to do with the way I operate and the way I view my disability outside of playing a character, and how the writers have been influenced by that," Diviney explains.
The emerging actor, writer and disability and women's rights advocate was offered the role of Nora after Audrey's producers saw her speaking about Latecomers on breakfast TV.
"I was talking about how I was the first person [with disability] in Australia, as far as we know, to do a sex scene on television, and the comedic way I delivered that story … something about it said to the Audrey team, 'Yep, that's Nora'."
Diviney says this was equal parts terrifying, liberating and exhilarating.
"The thing that made it scary was having to rely on support workers, being forced by necessity to create very fast intimacy with strangers and to be thrust into a world that was a lot bigger, and ran a lot differently, to Latecomers."
While Latecomers was filmed over just 13 days, Audrey was shot over five weeks. The former was also created and written by people with disability, starring people with disability.
Hannah Diviney (left) says she built resilience and learned a lot about herself over the course of Audrey's five-week shoot. (Supplied)
Things were trickier on Audrey, Diviney says, "Because they had to be, for the plot to work."
The Lipsicks live in a two-storey McMansion that boasts a backyard pool. And yet, Ronnie and Cormack have failed to make the family home accessible for their daughter. Not only that, she is routinely told off for the damage her wheelchair inflicts on too-narrow door frames.
"There's a very specific reason why [the] location [team] chose the house they did — it fit the inaccessible comedy of the movie," she explains.
But this meant the Lipsick family home was as inaccessible for Diviney the actor as it was for Nora the character.
"I'm really proud of the fact that I got through that, built resilience and showed myself that I can do it. I learned a lot about myself," Diviney says.
"And people seem to be fans of my comedic timing, which is nice."
Audrey's ensemble cast of beautifully insufferable characters does more than just deliver. As does its dopamine dressing-heavy costume design, its acerbic script and its setting on the relaxed, slightly daggy Gold Coast.
It's so delightfully dark, absurd and uncomfortably relatable that Diviney has heard murmurings from viewers who think it has the potential to become a cult classic in the same vein as its major inspiration source, Muriel's Wedding.
She would love for this to be the case — but for now Diviney is basking in the glow of the movie's film festival success, from SXSW to the Melbourne International Film Festival and CinefestOz.
The latter stands out in particular, because actress and Muriel's Wedding star Rachel Griffiths was the head of the jury.
Audrey is in cinemas now.

title: The hidden architectural gems in pop culture
content:
Italian architect Carlo Scarpa is one of those architects you might study at university.
His incredible material detail and sense of celebration in design comes from his home city of Venice, and has always felt beyond the everyday.
But even if you're not an architecture fanatic like me, you likely already know his work.
One of his master designs, the Brion Tomb (1978) made a star cameo in the latest blockbuster Dune: Part Two.
YouTube: Dune: Part Two Movie Clip - This Is Our Doing (2024)
It's the scene(s) where the Bene Gesserit witches meet with the imperial princess Irulan in the garden and chambers of the Corrino home, which appears about 40 minutes into the film.
Its recognisable double moon gate windows, richly coloured ceramic tile trim, textured finish, and the stone that surrounds it all, are as beautiful today as the day they were finished.
The tomb is instantly recognisable to anyone who has studied architecture, but perhaps not to most people — until now, that is.
Of course, it's not the first time an audience has learnt about a celebrity architect's work through a blockbuster movie. But that's the point — so many architectural ideas make their way into our popular cultural imagination, not through the design press, but by stealth in movies and TV, becoming part of our visual and design cultural catalogue.
The Brion Tomb, designed by Carlo Scarpa, features in Dune: Part Two. (Getty Images: DeAgostini)
In the movies, we expect to see the landmark buildings that locate us in, or transport us to, a place, city or country; think the Empire State Building in New York (King Kong, The Day After Tomorrow or Oblivion) or the Opera House in Sydney (The Fall Guy and Anyone But You).
But it's the next tier of buildings that star in movies that are perhaps more interesting.
So does architecture 'speak'? Yes – and we've been trained through the movies and TV to listen when it does.
It's a cultural language we're now well trained to quickly pick up on, there are a couple of ways in which architecture does this.
First is architecture as a scene or backdrop.
In the case of Downton Abbey, for example, the architecture tells us the period, the style and the 'class' of the protagonists in the drama and importantly sets the expectations for behaviour of the protagonists within the film.
The setting for Downton Abbey tells us about the period and the class of the characters. (JBUK_Planet, CC)
Think of the Russian Spy TV series The Americans, and how the premise of pretending to be 'normal Americans' relied so much on the average house these Russian infiltrators took up residence in.
Or the Grand Budapest Hotel, where nothing is 'normal' and of course a superb Wes Andersen adventure takes place.
The second tell is where architecture is actually a protagonist itself.
In Amityville Horror, or any haunted house horror, the house is more an actor than a background.
The buildings take on a persona that is central to the narrative.
And finally, there is architecture as a metaphor or index for the action.
As the film progresses, the locations speak to the drama unfolding; metaphors of relationships falling apart as a city falls into ruin, for example. Or cities being 'folded' in Inception just like the minds of the key figures bending as they go deeper into their dreams.
In The Amityville Horror, the house is as much an actor as the people. (AP: Richard Drew)
I was introduced to the famous Sheats-Goldstein house by architect John Lautner as the living room of a porn mogul in The Big Lebowski, where 'The Dude' (Jeff Bridges) abided for a brief moment.
The house, one of the most celebrated Los Angeles homes of the late mid-century, was donated to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art by James Goldstein in 2016.
The coffered ceilings, hand-made by Lautner with glass jars embedded in the concrete to let in points of light, the dramatic triangular roof folding out from the internal courtyard to project over the pool into the view beyond, is unmissable.
It's more impressive in person, but its impact in the scenes in the movie is as much cultural as it is architectural.
Once you start to see famous and not-so-famous architecture in the movies, it only adds to the enigmatic quality of the designs.
Perhaps the ideas were so strong in the original architecture they organically found their way into the eternal life of film.
Perhaps these were ideas that were so far ahead of their time when they were built, that it's only now, in the exaggerated spaces of the movies, where culture is ready for them.
More likely they are just so out of the ordinary that their visual power and cultural load transcends any one medium.
It's interesting to note that there are people whose job it is to source these locations, and in that sense, a whole second life of architecture exists for some of our most inspiring buildings.
But what the movies tell us is that architecture is a medium for storytelling, as much as a place to live or a home for a family.
So next time you're at the movies, take a moment to think of the architecture that sets the scene; the power of design to shape culture, not just space, and architecture's ability to speak to us … and the design education you're enjoying without realising it!
Anthony Burke is a professor of architecture and the host of ABC iview's Grand Designs Australia.

title: 'We're not here forever': George Harrison's advice that Eric Idle still lives by
content:
Eric Idle is proud that Always Look on the Bright Side of Life is one of the most popular funeral songs in England.
"I find that very, very moving actually," he tells ABC RN's The Stage Show. "It's rather nice that people want to be cheered up a bit."
Two years ago, in 2022, Idle revealed he had survived pancreatic cancer after early diagnosis and treatment.
It was a song borne of need: Monty Python — the British comedy collective made up of Idle, Graham Chapman, John Cleese, Terry Gilliam, Terry Jones and Michael Palin — had no idea how to end their 1979 comedy, Life of Brian.
By the end of the movie, "very naughty boy" Brian, who has been mistaken for Jesus, is sentenced to death and strung up on the cross. It was Idle who suggested ending the movie with a song and raced home to write it.
"It should be like a cheery-uppy song, ridiculously optimistic … like a Disney song," Idle recalls to ABC RN Breakfast. "Maybe it should even have a whistle."
The song has since taken on a life of its own — and often pops up in unexpected places.
"I was watching a football match, and Liverpool supporters suddenly started to sing it to Manchester United fans when they were beating them. I thought, 'Isn't that lovely to be able to sit there in your home and somebody's singing your song on the terraces?'" Idle says.
Watch: Eric Idle on 7.30 (David Speers)
It's also the name for the 81-year-old's latest tour, which travels across Australia this month.
Always Look on the Bright Side of Life, Live! features anecdotes, one fart joke, a new song about not recording his show and uploading it to YouTube, and even a virtual band.
"They're much cheaper than real musicians. I've got them on screen and they're behind me and I play along. I'm hoping to have a virtual symphony orchestra next time I come," he tells ABC TV's 7.30.
At Cambridge University, as part of theatre society the Pembroke Players and the Footlights sketch comedy troupe, Idle found not just comedy but community, including some of his future collaborators like Cleese and Chapman.
The Stage Show brings you in-depth conversations with the world's top directors, performers and writers for the stage.
"I discovered my true quest," Idle says. "I was auditioned by two of the Goodies [Tim Brooke-Taylor and Bill Oddie] in my first term, and I was in a sketch which John Cleese had written, and he was at my first-ever performance in public.
"I spent all my time there [at Footlights]. It was very interesting because you learn by doing in comedy — you watch people, and you learn."
After university, Idle joined the cast of Do Not Adjust Your Set, a kids show that found an adult following and also featured future collaborators, Jones, Palin and Gilliam. The show soon led to the creation of Monty Python in 1969 and their sketch series Monty Python's Flying Circus.
Monty Python in 1969. Left to right: Terry Jones, Graham Chapman, John Cleese, Eric Idle, Terry Gilliam and Michael Palin. (Getty Images: Michael Ochs Archives)
The group found mentors in Dudley Moore and Peter Cook, the men behind 1960s sketch comedy show Not Only…But Also and Beyond the Fringe.
"They were the people who made me want to be a comedian," says Idle.
Monty Python's Flying Circus, which aired on the BBC from late 1969 to 1974, was a mishmash of styles: of songs, slapstick, and satire, often taking aim at those very institutions. Idle puts their enormous creative freedom down to their 10:55pm Sunday timeslot.
"We would write and then we'd read it out to each other and if we made ourselves laugh, it was in the show," he says.
Michael Palin, John Cleese, Terry Jones, Terry Gilliam and Eric Idle in 2009, at the premiere of the documentary Monty Python: Almost the Truth (Lawyer's Cut). (Reuters: Lucas Jackson )
"We were allowed to do daft things without anybody saying, 'Oh, come on' and interfering.
"[Executives] didn't really care … They thought, who was going to watch anyway?"
The sketch series soon led to several movies, including 1975's Monty Python and the Holy Grail. Little did Idle know he'd still be talking about the Holy Grail 50 years on.
In October, he released The Spamalot Diaries, a collection of journal entries written in the lead-up to the Broadway premiere of his musical Spamalot in 2005.
"I didn't know it was going to be a hit," says Idle of his musical Spamalot. (Supplied: Penguin)
The musical, based on the Holy Grail and starring Tim Curry (The Rocky Horror Picture Show; Charlie's Angels), went on to win three Tonys from 14 nominations, including Best Musical.
Two years ago, when Idle was moving house, he found the diaries and discovered an interesting perspective inside.
"It's about putting a show together, [about] anxieties and people arguing and fighting and some people being fired. It's the making of a show," he says.
"It shows you how something successful, that obviously looks easy, is actually a lot of hard work and conflict."
In an early scene in Spamalot a man collecting the bodies of people who have died from the Black Plague tries to dispose of a man who declares, "I'm not dead!" His protestations, as he tries to prove he's still alive, lead into the toe-tapping musical number He Is Not Dead Yet.
Idle thinks the scene is funny because it's "literally laughing in the face of death".
"And it naturally led into a song," Idle says. "It does start the musical off rather nicely."
Audiences can expect Idle to sing about death — and about his late friends — in Always Look on the Bright Side of Life, Live!
These tributes include a song he wrote for Robin Williams's memorial, and one for Beatles guitarist George Harrison, who Idle met at a screening of the Holy Grail, and who even financed Life of Brian.
Idle describes Always Look on the Bright Side of Life, Live! as a one-man musical. (Getty Images: Frazer Harrison)
"The sad thing about getting older is you lose all these friends," says Idle.
He recalls something Harrison used to say: "It doesn't matter how famous you are or how much money you have, you're all going to have to die."
Idle continues: "A lot of my songs are actually about death … It is important to remember that we're not here forever. It's a very privileged thing to be alive in these bodies and have these experiences with other people on a strange planet."
Eric Idle: Always Look on the Bright Side of Life, Live! is at Hamer Hall, Arts Centre Melbourne, on November 4, before touring to Brisbane, Gold Coast, Newcastle, Sydney, Perth and Adelaide.

title: Happy 70th birthday, Godzilla: Tourism ambassador, Oscar winner and metaphor for environmental dread
content:
A nuclear-charged reptile, a Tokyo tourism ambassador and an Oscar winner with a Hollywood star to its name – truly, no-one in showbiz works harder than Godzilla, who shows no sign of slowing upon its 70th birthday this year.
This latest anniversary sees Godzilla riding the wave of a formidable, decade-long comeback story.
Gareth Edwards's 2014 reboot broke a protracted dry spell and kicked off its own prospering cinematic universe, while Japan reinvented the iconic monster to truly terrifying ends with 2016's Shin Godzilla and last year's barnstorming, box-office-breaking Godzilla Minus One.
Its renewed fame has accompanied a major face-lift, too. Even as late as 2004's Godzilla: Final Wars, the Japanese films stuck to the tradition of filming Godzilla in-camera rather than rendering the scaly leviathan through increasingly common digital effects. For a monster firmly planted in the tradition of the low-budget B-movie, whose ingenious practical effects and men in rubber suits were integral to its charm, the recent CGI blockbuster treatment has marked a radical departure from its roots.
Godzilla Minus One redefined what you can do with visual effects on a small budget.
But as the age of the Hollywood mega-franchise began to swallow the entertainment industry whole, the loveable apex predator faced a choice: evolve or risk falling to the bottom of the food chain.
What endures is Godzilla's appetite for pure destruction. Eschewing the uneasy contradictions of contemporary superhero cinema, which frequently sees acts of heroism overshadowed by apocalyptic spectacle, Godzilla is embraced in all its gloriously chaotic behaviour, both as villain and reluctant saviour.
Even when protecting the world, as has become the norm in the American MonsterVerse universe, its presence is never less than a potential extinction event unable to be reasoned with.
When Godzilla decides to curl up in the Colosseum for a nap, who are we to deny it?
Godzilla sleeping in the Colosseum
The appeal of Godzilla has many strands. For children, the excitement of whole cities being levelled by this raging monstrosity has always realised an innate power fantasy, all while articulating the sensation of intense, unrestrained emotion.
For adults, the unyielding carnage — wrought over 38 movies and counting — is a reminder of our own boundless capacity for annihilation on a global scale, embedded within Godzilla's famously bleak origins.
Those fears can be traced back to the aftermath of World War II. Ishirō Honda, the director of the very first Godzilla film, returned home as a Chinese prisoner of war, passing through the devastated ruins of Hiroshima. As his wife, Kimi Honda, put it: "Without the bomb, there could not have been a monster."
Another high-profile nuclear disaster would become a direct inspiration for the film. In 1954, the world's first hydrogen bomb was detonated in the Bikini Atoll with unexpectedly cataclysmic results; its irradiating shock wave extended far beyond its testing zones, striking a nearby Japanese fishing trawler, the Lucky Dragon No. 5.
The director of the original 1954 Godzilla, Ishirō Honda, was a Chinese prisoner of war and passed through the devastated ruins of Hiroshima on his return home.
The incident and the subsequent poisoning of the crew would be widely documented in the press, reaching Toho producer Tomoyuki Tanaka who, at the time, was in pre-production on a monster movie inspired by The Beast from 20,000 Fathoms. The project would soon take shape as the original Godzilla movie, which would open on a group of sailors witnessing a brilliant explosion that sinks their ship, leaving few survivors.
Under Honda's austere direction, Godzilla's scenes of widespread destruction are evoked through loaded imagery, often doused in shadow and fog. Civilians take shelter in hospitals; tanks roll onto the streets; children are tested with Geiger counters.
Viewed under modern eyes, the original design of Godzilla is unavoidably goofy; at times, Tokyo can look like a toyset. Despite being the most expensive Japanese film ever made at the time, it's hard not to be spoiled by the advancements in special effects in the second half of the century.
But Godzilla nonetheless resembles an unknowable, prehistoric force of nature. The impact of its 20,000-tonne weight can be felt as it tears through the city; its screams remain genuinely haunting.
Godzilla in a scene from the 1971 movie, Godzilla vs Hedorah. (IMDB)
Following Godzilla's pitch-black debut, which became a thunderous success among audiences, it would only take a decade for this fearsome incarnation of nuclear wrath to transition into a saviour of planet Earth.
In the 1960s, Toho developed a cinematic kaiju empire populated by other gargantuan beasties, and found massive success in crossovers that pitted Godzilla against beloved icons like King Kong, the luminescent deity Mothra, and the Pteranodon Rodan.
As the initial target audience of adults was aged down, Godzilla would become steadily (and infamously) anthropomorphised. New generations of children would grow up largely unburdened by their parents' atomic anxieties, finding greater interest in Godzilla's interstellar beefs.
Godzilla victory dance
While the threat of nuclear holocaust has never truly subsided – current stockpiles are substantially larger than they were 70 years ago, after all – Godzilla has expanded its initial subtext.
In the 1971 gonzo cult favourite Godzilla vs. Hedorah, it would throw down with an alien toxic sludge that thrives off earthbound pollution, a direct response to Japan's Minimata outbreak. In 1991's Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah, time travellers from the future attempt to disrupt a timeline that sees Japan become an economic superpower.
But Godzilla, like other kaiju, represents something more elemental. Japan's history has long been shaped by its tectonic volatility, materialising through regular occurrences of earthquakes, typhoons, and other natural disasters. On Godzilla's tempestuous home turf, the horrifying spectacle of flattened cities uniquely strikes a chord, resonating much further back than the 1940s.
2016's Shin Godzilla drew inspiration from the devastating 2011 earthquake and the bureaucracy that failed its victims. (Supplied: Toho Co)
More recently, 2016's Shin Godzilla (written and directed by Evangelion creator Hideaki Anno) drew its power not just from the 2011 Tohoku earthquake and the Fukushima meltdown, but the byzantine, modern-day bureaucracy that failed its victims.
In spite of, or perhaps because of its sheer bluntness, expressed at a colossal, 100-metre-tall scale, Godzilla has become a load-bearing metaphor for modern terrors and ancient anxieties.
As its birthday approaches, pour one out for the big guy – it's tough work being King of the Monsters.

title: A Different Man is one of the year's finest explorations of identity, and is also bleakly funny
content:
It's been a pivotal year for Sebastian Stan, who — after 13 years of MCU films (and counting) — has made a compelling, go-for-broke pivot into indie cinema with two meaty leading roles.
What: A bleakly funny psychodrama about an actor with a rare genetic disorder who undergoes a miraculous face surgery.
Directed by: Aaron Schimberg.
Starring: Sebastian Stan, Renate Reinsve, Adam Pearson.
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: Terrible for laughing.
Earlier this month, he donned one of history's most infamous blonde wigs to play Donald Trump in Ali Abbasi's 1970s biopic, The Apprentice. With A Different Man, he commits to a different transformation altogether as Edward, an actor living with neurofibromatosis: a rare genetic disorder that manifests as a spread of benign tumours on his face.
Despite being a capable performer, Edward finds himself relegated to undignified bit parts specifically aimed at those with a "unique and unusual physiognomy".
An estimated one in 3,000 people in Australia have Neurofibromatosis, according to the Royal Children's Hospital, but the large benign tumours seen here are very rare. (Supplied: Kismet)
His new, sweetly oblivious neighbour Ingrid (Renate Reinsve; The Worst Person in the World), pries open his otherwise solitary personal life in ways both hilarious and horrifying. An aspiring playwright herself, they bond over their creative struggles, though the extent to which she shares his romantic interest is vague.
Initially presented as a wry portrait of isolation and disability, A Different Man finds itself methodically escalating into pitch-black psychodrama when Edward begins an experimental treatment that promises to alleviate him of his condition.
Stan's consummate performance extends well beyond the sort of laboured mimicry that tends to get mistaken for dramatic skill. His wilting physicality carries a man entombed in his own anxiety, sealed by the othering gazes of friends and strangers alike.
The former US president attempted to stall The Apprentice's release ahead of the 2024 election, citing Hollywood interference. Does he have a point?
So detailed are his prosthetics (designed by The Penguin's make-up maestro, Michael Marino), viewers going in cold may not even realise who they're watching.
The trial proves to be a success, if not without its own gruesome tribulations. Edward's face agonisingly stretches and peels off in mangled globs; much of the process is spent screaming and keeled over in bed.
Unlike, say, The Substance — another recent movie centred on a miraculous cosmetic procedure — the bursts of body horror are fleeting and generally incidental, as opposed to being a juvenile, droning obsession.
The film is closer aligned with John Frankenheimer's 1966 existential thriller, Seconds; when Edward metamorphoses into a man with Sebastian Stan's enviable movie-star features, he fakes his own death and begins life anew, only to encounter an internal malaise less easily cured.
Both Stan and Schimberg suggested casting Reinsve as Ingrid, having been impressed by her performance in The Worst Person in the World. (Supplied: Kismet)
His makeover is accompanied by a new-found swagger and a voice more recognisably in Stan's register. The new Edward (under the objectively hilarious alias of Guy) thrives as a real estate agent, his sculpted face now plastered on billboards and subway ads; for the first time in his life, he invites and celebrates his own objectification, even as it erodes his personhood.
When Guy discovers a casting call for a new play written by Ingrid – titled Edward, no less — he auditions for the main character role, despite no longer looking the part. Life becomes stranger than autofiction upon the arrival of Oswald (Adam Pearson; Under the Skin) — another actor with a strikingly similar resemblance to Edward, who also vies for a part he was seemingly born to play.
While Stan's dual performance is the spectacular centrepiece of A Different Man, the film's true breakout star arguably ends up being Pearson, an actor and campaigner who lives with neurofibromatosis in real life.
In production notes, Stan recalls Schimberg advising him to "lean more into what it feels like to be a celebrity" to find the character of Edward. (Supplied: Kismet)
Last seen in writer-director Aaron Schimberg's previous film, Chained for Life (2018), he practically levitates on screen as the radiantly happy-go-lucky Oswald. His chummy, unselfconscious charm enlivens a character who's far more comfortable in his skin than Edward or Guy has ever been; a doppelganger of sorts who unwittingly contorts Guy's life into a delirious torment.
Schimberg is too canny a writer to let the film fall into broad aphorisms concerning confidence and self-image. He attentively homes in on the everyday indignities inflicted on Edward, whose permanently defensive, diminutive stature forms a much-needed safety mechanism.
Oswald may be precisely configured as Edward's mirror opposite to amusing extreme — he's well-liked, romantically attuned, and talented (the film makes a running joke out of his numerous hobbies) — but Schimberg notes how his own defences make him susceptible to a less overt exploitation.
Wyatt Garfield's 16mm cinematography becomes central to evoking the film's identity crisis; with drawn-out, inquisitive movements, the camera mercilessly probes its subjects, often squashing Edward within the confines of the frame, or conjuring simmering resentment from sparse compositions. (In contrast, the camera revolves around Oswald's centre of gravity.)
Schimberg has a corrected bilateral cleft lip and palate. In production notes he said he wondered: "How do I present someone like myself positively, or at least realistically to my own experience?" (Supplied: Kismet)
Umberto Smerilli's jazzy, foreboding score brilliantly matches the film's mounting absurdity, descending into a soundscape best described as chaotic noir.
A Different Man also makes a few timely jabs at theatre, particularly in what it means for someone to authentically portray and embody disability – an in-built, perhaps too-aware acknowledgement of the film's own potential pitfalls, and how stories about disability told by able-bodied creatives can suffer from intense, patronising projection.
The film remains bleakly funny throughout, lest anyone take its premise too literally; it's one of the year's finest explorations of identity, a slippery parable of dysmorphic horrors that takes our own biases and delusions to task.
After all, what's in a face?
A Different Man is in cinemas now.

title: Deeply disturbing and shockingly beautiful: Texas Chain Saw Massacre still resonates after 50 years
content:
Described as a "grisly little item" by Roger Ebert upon its controversial 1974 release, and deemed too extreme to be screened in Australia for 10 years, The Texas Chain Saw Massacre is one of the unlikeliest films to have become a household name.
Fifty years on, the film's premise remains the stuff of nightmares: while travelling through the sweltering American South, a group of hippies are brusquely slaughtered by Leatherface (played by Gunnar Hansen and inspired by Ed Gein), a hulking, brutish butcher who provides for his family of cannibals.
Despite indie horror being relegated to grubby grindhouse theatres and drive-ins at the time, Tobe Hooper's micro-budget carve-em-up broke into the top 15 highest-grossing films of the year.
As one of the first films to handsomely profit from the gruesome demise of young adults on screen, The Texas Chain Saw Massacre paved the way for the slasher movie, which would rapidly explode in popularity upon the arrival of Halloween and Friday the 13th in the late 70s and early 80s.
The film may no longer be the boundary-pushing event it once was — yet its primordial terror endures.
Edwin Neal was a college student in Texas when he landed the role of the hitchiker. (Supplied: Second Shot)
"From the day it was released, The Texas Chain Saw Massacre endured as an unwavering testament to the very ferocity of the creative vision," says film critic and historian Alexandra Heller-Nicholas of award-winning horror doco Chain Reactions.
"It is unflinching and unrepentant in its determination to shine a light on humanity at its darkest and most desperate."
For a horror film whose brief narrative can be summed up by its title, Texas Chain Saw is often disarmingly beautiful, resplendent in images of blooming sunflower fields, young, carefree bodies, and Leatherface's idyllic Edwardian farmhouse. Shot on vibrant 16mm film stock, with frequent use of handheld and wide-angle framing, the film often feels like a home movie shot on vacation.
It's an approach that makes the intrusions of violence — from a deranged hitchhiker brandishing a razor to the fleeting appearances of Leatherface — feel all the more upsetting.
"There is actually very little blood or gore across the film, but the fear of the unknown and the unexpected is what has continued to disturb audiences," argues critic and curator Zak Hepburn.
"It's not so much a horror film, like Wake in Fright; it's a prismatic reflection of the darkness bubbling away underneath perceived normality."
Texas Chain Saw Massacre is surprisingly beautiful, capturing the 70s landscapes with an Eclair NPR 16mm camera. (Supplied: Second Shot)
Despite being an inherently disposable cast of free-wheeling youngsters, it's easy to identify with the film's unwitting victims as they bicker about the meaning of Saturn in retrograde and blithely discuss the specifics of animal slaughter, their road trip set to the soundtrack of grisly police reports on the radio.
Hooper and co-screenwriter Kim Henkel depict a generation coming of age into the existential turmoil of the 1970's, and as lurid stories of war and crime have gone on to saturate culture, their character's desensitisation to violence has only grown more resonant; the cruelty of their deaths are a potent reminder of what we risk growing numb to.
In the half-century since Texas Chain Saw's release, the horror genre has simultaneously grown more violent and less stigmatised, a trajectory reflected in the film's tireless franchising efforts.
After several increasingly outlandish sequels (culminating in a go-for-broke performance from a young Matthew McConaughey), it was treated to a glossy remake in the 2000's, like countless other horror classics. In 2022, an Elsie Fisher-starring legacy sequel dropped on Netflix, and boasted the series' highest body count yet.
What's an early-2000s classic horror remake without Jessica Biel in a midriff top?  (Supplied: IMDB)
While the post-pandemic movie-going landscape has been saddled with cost-of-living woes and audience fatigue, horror has only continued to thrive in cinemas.
Historically, the genre has come out on top in times of economic turmoil.
The films are usually much cheaper to produce, and audiences show up in droves, even in the face of harsh critical reception. Data from Parrot Analytics shows that horror films get the most return in opening weekend box office revenue compared to production budgets.
After peaking in 2021 at 12.91 per cent, horror films have steadily held about 10 per cent of the market share per year, up from 2.69 per cent in 2014.
The original Texas Chain Saw Massacre was itself produced and released amid the 1970's recession. And, from a box office perspective, the enduring lesson appears to be that extremity loves company; in 1974, it would've been unthinkable that the glorious, nausea-inducing carnage of Terrifier 3 and The Substance could have ever played in multiplexes.
Roger Ebert would have been shocked that graphic films like The Substance are getting mainstream release. (Supplied: Madman)
"During times of economic hardship, horror allows viewers to confront their anxieties in a cathartic way, reflecting the instability and uncertainty they may be feeling in their daily lives," Harrison says.
"It's also best enjoyed as a group, whether that's in the cinemas or on the couch at home."
Perhaps it's that same pinch of financial distress that makes The Texas Chain Saw Massacre feel so timeless; Hooper's film reflects a palpable societal decay, wrenching the discarded remnants of rural America onto the screen in all their unadulterated fury.
"Often lost in the shock-and-awe of it all is the fact that this film is fundamentally a nightmare about capitalism in its death throes," says Heller-Nicholas.
Sally Hardesty — played by Marilyn Burns in the original film — is said to be the inspiration behind the 'final girl' trope. (Supplied: Second Sight)
"You literally cannot talk about The Texas Chain Saw Massacre in any depth and not talk about class. Focusing as it does on a disenfranchised family of now-unemployed abattoir workers who turn to the unimaginable to fill the void their jobs once filled, the inescapable question at its heart of the film is this: what happens to the people that capitalism leaves behind?"
So long as people are starving, Hooper's cannibal masterpiece will continue to haunt horror cinema.

title: The Moogai looks like a horror movie, but it's really about the horrors of the Stolen Generation
content:
Filmmaker Jon Bell says his horror film The Moogai (2024) is a love letter to the Aboriginal women in his family.
Interweaving the history of the Stolen Generations with Aboriginal lore, The Moogai is about a young Aboriginal couple, Sarah (Shari Sebbens) and Fergus (Meyne Wyatt), who are terrorised by a child-stealing spirit following the birth of their second baby.
"There's something that's so primal about women literally creating these other people, and then these people being stolen and [by extension] stealing a part of that [mother]," Bell says.
And so, when the Wiradjuri, Bundjalung and Yaegl man considered the way Aboriginal women have continued to create families and hold families together in the face of "hundreds of years of genocidal practices and policies," he wanted to acknowledge it.
Daughter Chloe is played by Jahdeana Mary, a granddaughter of director Jon Bell. (Supplied: Maslow/Elise Lockwood)
"Aboriginal women have held on through the flood and through the deluge of hate and mistreatment and destruction and all of those sorts of things, and this is really just a personal thing for me to say to the women in my family, thanks," he explains.
"Because, to be honest, I just wouldn't be here if you hadn't done that."
There are three Bundjalung words traditionally used to describe spirits — Moogai, Wongai and Dogai.
Bell says Moogai is still used today to describe monsters (similar to a bogeyman), while the word Dogai has become a colloquialism for "white people".
It's the resonance between these two words that formed the basis of Bell's story: On one hand, the Moogai (Paul Chambers) is a supernatural creature; while on the other, systemic racism is very real.
"I made this movie for the stolen mob," director Jon Bell told the Brisbane Times, "to say, 'you will always belong with us. That can never be broken, as much as it may feel like it has'." (Supplied: Maslow/Elise Lockwood)
In thinking about these dual horrors and the "inhumanity of taking somebody's children", Bell felt like the horror genre best provided him the space to explore what's at stake.
When Sarah's perfect life as a high-achieving lawyer, wife and mother starts to unravel, Bell's camera shows his audience the same unsettling visions she is experiencing, forcing them into Sarah's shoes without the luxury of emotional distance.
"The way the Moogai pursues Sarah in the film – it tries to get into her head, and in the end, they have to physically move to get away from it. Horror is the genre most suited to be able to explore these kinds of societal concerns," he says.
Bell also wanted to make sure each character has a valid explanation for why they act the way they do.
Actor-turned-director Shari Sebbens is best known for her film and TV work, but her first love is theatre.
He describes these moments as "a bit of a Rorschach test". People will see themselves and either push away from the film or lean into it, depending on who they identify with — or if they're even willing to look.
A particularly tense example is a scene in which a teacher questions Sarah about bruises on her eldest daughter's arms. As the interaction escalates, the police are called to the school.
"It's important to put [valid explanations] in because that's the real examination of the system, like that the system can validate itself … You might be getting pressed in on all sides, and you say, 'but this is unfair' and then the system can say, 'it's not unfair'."
Much later, when the Moogai tries to entice Sarah's daughter Chloe (Jahdeana Mary) away with assurances of protection and safety, the message is clear: the Moogai itself is equally entangled in this idea of the system.
Its promise is reminiscent of those from authorities who would insist that forcibly removing Aboriginal children was giving them a better life, making it a personification of the darker elements of government and government reach.
Young actor Precious Ann is terrifying in her role as Agnes. (Supplied: Maslow/Elise Lockwood)
The fact that Sarah – who was forcibly removed from her biological mother – is desperate to keep her children close doesn't seem to matter.
"When people aren't actually being listened to they're being invalidated, because that's what the system needs to do to continue," says Bell.
"And it's not even a good or bad thing or anything like that. It's just what the system needs and wants."
Reflecting on the genre conventions and tropes he drew on for The Moogai, Bell is clear: he wanted to bring these ideas and iconographies into Aboriginal expression.
"So often our stuff gets co-opted for other things, so I wanted to do the reverse — where I was pulling from different influences, and then put them into the film," Bell explains.
Moogai is a Bundjalung word still used to describe monsters similar to the bogeyman. (Supplied: Maslow/Elise Lockwood)
He argues one of the results of this co-opting means Indigenous filmmakers are often accused of being "didactic or depressing" when attempting to tell stories that deal with "cultural demons".
"At times it might feel a bit hacky [to draw on these conventions] … but I'm repurposing them. And that is the commentary. The commentary is the repurposing," he says.
Bell says that making a proof-of-concept short film version of The Moogai (2020) helped him refine his skills in the horror genre.
"When I started the feature I had more of a sense of what function [each] character performed in the overall sort of ensemble … And there was some of those kinds of filmmaking director-y lessons that I learned," he says.
"Especially because, when you do dark horror stuff it doesn't feel scary until you put it all together."
And when it came to the design of the Moogai itself, Bell and his creative team wanted the figure to retain human qualities amongst the makeup and prosthetics, to heighten its menacing presence.
Locating a birthing tree, key to the final scenes of the film, was a challenge, but the right tree was finally found on Jon's family's land. (Supplied: Maslow/Elise Lockwood)
"Paul made the Moogai move in such freaky ways … Even during rehearsals, he'd get down and start moving towards me, and I'd say; 'That's enough. Please just stand up now,'" Bell says.
Still, its head has a mask-like aesthetic, with a "top face" that mesmerises while the "bottom face" is looking down at the child, ready to snatch them and go.
"It blinks, it smiles, it mimics, as best it can human emotions … It is simply something that has a goal, and in that sense, the Moogai itself isn't evil. It's just invested in its own survival, and it just does what it does," Bell says.
Unlike some other genres, in horror there is no definitive social contract between creator and audience when it comes to endings. A horror film is just as likely to end in triumph as it is in tragedy.
However, Bell – a fan of early Steven Spielberg films like Poltergeist – wanted to bring a "positive uplift" to his horror film.
Meyne Wyatt plays father Fergus alongside Shari Sebbens, who is his long time friend and creative collaborator. (Supplied: Maslow/Elise Lockwood)
"I knew that [the producers] were interested in horror narratives which had something to say. We found common ground in terms of trying to bring – this sounds weird – but some heart to horror," Bell says.
The developing relationship between Sarah and her biological mother, Ruth (Tessa Rose), was integral to this goal.
Sarah and Ruth are in constant tension as they each straddle opposite sides of a cultural divide. While Sarah is willing to hang an Aboriginal painting worth several thousand dollars in her living room, she won't allow Ruth to perform a smoking ceremony to cleanse the home because it might set off the smoke detectors.
Tessa Rose — who has starred in everything from Top End Wedding to Bloom — plays Sarah's biological mother, Ruth. (Supplied: Maslow/Elise Lockwood)
Their tension results in a beautiful mise en scène as Ruth (making one of a number of attempts to protect the children from the Moogai) wipes a stripe of yellow ochre down the wall next to Sarah's painting.
"When [Sarah's] trying to scrub it, she's trying to break that bond, but it's been made. It can't be unmade, no matter even if you clean the wall, you'd have to tear the wall down, or you'd know that the thing was [still] there," Bell says.
The mark creates a bridge between Sarah's performative life and her cultural truth. One that binds mother to child and – as Sarah prepares to make her stand against the Moogai – invites three generations to unite their strengths.
"In the face of that crashing wave of destruction that's come down on Aboriginal families, women … in that moment she understands what her mother's been through."

The Moogai is in cinemas from October 31.

title: Ever wondered how Saturday Night Live got so huge? This film takes us back to its bizarre beginnings
content:
It might seem difficult to imagine that Saturday Night Live — the cultural behemoth now regularly derided for its turgid punchlines and bloodless gags — was once one of the most risqué, risky events on television.
What: The chaos and calamity of the 90 minutes leading up to the first broadcast of Saturday Night Live in 1975.
Directed by: Jason Reitman.
Starring: Gabriel LaBelle, Rachel Sennott, Nicholas Braun, Cory Michael Smith, Cooper Hoffman, Dylan O'Brien, Ella Hunt.
When: In cinemas from October 31.
Likely to make you feel: Stressed, crazy, but maybe a little bored?
So it was when it premiered in 1975 with a cast of practically unknown comics performing sketches that were, by turns, nutty, absurdist, countercultural and borderline hostile.
A New Yorker review published a few months after the show's debut called it a "huge, darkened, lively TV cabaret" and a welcome alternative to the anodyne "rituals of mass-entertainment television".
Rolling Stone went even further. "The audacity of its concept and execution," wrote an early critic, "alter not so much the visual and audio centres as the central nervous system itself."
The mania and the mayhem, the terror and the transgression: these are the stakes that Jason Reitman attempts to re-create in Saturday Night.
Matt Wood plays John Belushi, who famously picked fights and even threatened to quit on the first night of Saturday Night Live. (Supplied: Sony/Hopper Stone)
The film, though, faces the same problem that dogs its protagonist: the search for meaning.
Set over one madcap evening in the lead-up to the show's first broadcast, Saturday Night relishes the discomfort of a young Lorne Michaels (The Fabelmans' Gabriel LaBelle), squirming as he's interrogated again and again by producers, peers and studio bigwigs.
The question is the same each time: just what is this thing he's created?
Michaels struggles to answer, though there's no shortage of suggestions. It's a "variety spectacular," says a network staffer selling the show to confused passers-by. Another character calls it "a three-hour sketch comedy revue".
NBC executives had little faith in Saturday Night Live when it debuted. Even so, it's lasted 50 seasons. (Supplied: Sony/Hopper Stone)
Or maybe it's something entirely less tangible.
"It's postmodern, it's Warhol, it's iconic," offers Rosie Shuster (Bottoms' Rachel Sennott), Michaels's co-conspirator and wife, gazing upon a stage full of bee costumes.
Young Michaels is far from his contemporary persona as the grizzled industry Svengali. LaBelle plays him both nervy and fusty, somehow simultaneously, with his sweater vest threatening to burst with a flurry of butterflies at any given catastrophe.
And catastrophes abound. As the clock ticks ever more ominously towards 11:30pm, the antics heighten: a sofa bursts aflame; a lighting rig comes crashing down in a wild kaboom; a puritanical network censor promises to strike every not-so-PG one-liner.
To make things worse, they're haemorrhaging money like it's payday, the execs are breathing down their necks, and a leading man has just gone AWOL. What's a guy to do?
These hijinks are certainly suffused with a deranged glee – as are the sheer feats of casting here.
Alongside recent breakout stars LaBelle and Sennott, we see Cooper Hoffman (Licorice Pizza) as a gormless NBC advisor, Cory Michael Smith (May December) as the all-American star Chevy Chase, and Nicholas Braun (Succession) in double duty as gonzo provocateur Andy Kaufman and puppetmaster Jim Henson.
Braun was first cast as Henson, and then as Kaufman after Benny Safdie pulled out of the movie. (Supplied: Sony/Hopper Stone)
It's an ensemble comprising Hollywood's pluckiest upstarts – a canny decision, given Saturday Night Live's own kingmaking legacy.
But their performances can often feel like cosplay rather than true characterisation. Despite the film's painstaking efforts to transform its actors into their real-life counterparts – a hair piece here, a moustache there – we glean precious little about the interiority of these figures.
Indeed, Saturday Night is so invested in reproducing reality that it seems curiously disinterested in actually understanding it.
By no means is it the wittiest account of NBC's hallowed hallways; its walking-and-talking executives and hapless page boys, its peacocking stars and green room conniptions. That would be 30 Rock.
Nor is Saturday Night – despite its pinwheeling camera work and blathering density – the giddiest backstage drama that reveals the lunacy always, always looming behind the spectacle. That dubious honour would belong to Birdman.
Lamorne Morris (New Girl) plays Garrett Morris, the first Black cast member on Saturday Night Live. (Supplied: Sony/Hopper Stone)
Instead, Reitman's film is so besotted with the mythology of SNL that it is difficult to pinpoint exactly what it wants to say.
It's part-historical archive, part-biopic, and part-Easter egg hunt for comedy diehards.
It's also, perhaps, personal wish fulfilment for Reitman, who has said that working on SNL was a lifelong dream – one he achieved as a guest writer in 2008, shortly after making his Oscar-winning film Juno.
Saturday Night, as a result, can veer towards self-indulgence.
There's only so much tension Reitman can sustain when he's hurtling towards a foregone conclusion.
Unlike the thrilling gamble of SNL's debut, we know how this story ends – with Michaels pulling it off. Seeing precisely how it happens can feel trivial.
Saturday Night is in cinemas from October 31.

title: Much-loved cinema's rent slashed by Sydney council after national chain threatens closure
content:
The City of Sydney has slashed the rent for a national cinema chain to ensure the much-loved Chauvel Cinema in the eastern suburbs stays open.
Palace Cinemas last month warned it would be forced to close the Chauvel Cinema housed in the Paddington Town Hall due to the poor state of the building and low ticket sales.
It was a sad prospect for film-goers, who farewelled the Palace Verona from Oxford Street in February.
On Monday night, the City of Sydney voted to approve a substantial rent reduction for the remainder of Palace's lease, which expires in March 2026.
Palace CEO Benjamin Zeccola said the two-screen cinema had been running at a loss, in part because the state of the building was "dilapidated", which was putting people off coming to the cinema.
"We would either need to exit [the lease] early or council approve a reduced rate."
The council says it can't renew Palace Cinema's lease without a new tender process. (Supplied: Palace Cinemas)
Mr Zeccola said they had been trying to resolve long-running maintenance issues for nearly 10 years.
"It's owned by the council and the building's been affected by inundation … that's caused all sorts of issues."
A City of Sydney spokesperson said Palace was responsible for the upkeep of the cinema interiors, including seats and carpets.
Mr Zeccola said the rent reduction would save the cinema in the short term, but its long-term future was still in doubt.
The council committed $25 million in June to upgrade the 120-year-old Paddington Town Hall, but it's unclear if Palace will remain as a tenant.
Mr Zeccola said the company had proposed extending its lease beyond 2026, but had been told it must be put out to tender.
Ever wondered why small cinemas aren't showing the films you want to see at a convenient time?
A council spokesperson said Palace took over the Chauvel in 2006 and would soon reach the 21-year limit for leases on "community land" under NSW legislation.
"Where a business wishes to stay in the space after 21 years, they need to re-tender under a regulated application process," a council spokesperson said.
Neither the council or Palace would disclose the amount of the rent reduction but the ABC understands it is "significant".
Lord Mayor Clover Moore supported the decision to provide "essential support" to ensure the Chauvel continued until the end of its lease.
"The city has also committed $25 million to restore this wonderful example of Victorian classical architecture and cornerstone of Oxford street, so it can cater for a wide range of community uses and events for another 100 years."
New Greens councillor Matthew Thompson was one of two councillors who voted against the rent reduction.
He said the council should support the arts but prioritise not-for-profits and community organisations.
"If the cinema were to close there are so many other opportunities for the space," he said.
"Palace are a for-profit company. If they can't afford the rent they should make way for community groups that could activate and reinvigorate the venue."
Independent councillor Yvonne Wheldon also voted against the rent reduction.
She said she was conscious neighbouring restaurants and bars would lose out if the site was left vacant, but there was "not enough information to justify a rent reduction for a large and profitable company".
"We need to expedite maintenance works and find a new operator or a good community use for the theatre."

title: Teacup is a slightly silly horror TV show and the perfect comfort watch
content:
It's a great time to be a fan of horror.
If you're into serial killers, hammy melodrama and religious symbolism, Ryan Murphy's Grostesquerie (Disney+) will give you all that and Travis Kelce playing a nurse. If you prefer supernatural monsters, survival horror and intricate worldbuilding, then you can't go wrong with From (now in Season 3 on Stan).
And if you want more of From but you also like conspiracies, an (un)healthy dose of body horror and a touch of family drama, then Teacup may just be the new horror show for you.
What: Puzzlebox mystery horror about a family stuck on their farm with a mysterious entity hunting them down. Produced by James Wan and loosely based on Robert R. McCammon's book Stinger.
Starring: Yvonne Strahovski, Scott Speedman, Chaske Spencer and Caleb Dolden.
When: Streaming on Binge now.
Likely to make you feel: Intrigued, anxious, thrilled.
Teacup and From are cut from the same cloth. A cursory Google didn't result in a clean collective term for this horror/thriller subgenre, but you know it when you see it:
Take a group of people with disparate personalities and/or pre-existing tensions; stick them in a single location they can't escape from; give them a mysterious existential threat to survive, overcome and solve.
There are also elements of puzzlebox mystery and survival horror at play, and they usually hinge on the interpersonal drama between the characters.
This is not a new phenomenon; think of shows like Lost (2004-2010), Under the Dome (2013-15), Wayward Pines (2015-16) or The Society (2019). And there are countless more.
The Chenoweths must cast aside their internal tensions to protect their home. (Supplied: Binge)
Most of them, if we're being honest, end up failing to give satisfying answers to the tantalising questions they ask at the beginning of their runs. Some even get cancelled before being able to provide any answers at all.
But we keep being drawn back to them, over and over again.
As most of these shows are, Teacup is centred around an isolated rural property. This one is in Georgia, USA, owned by veterinarian Maggie Chenoweth (Yvonne Stahovski, Handmaid's Tale) and her husband James (Scott Speedman, Felicity). The pair start to notice the animals on their farm acting erratically, but when their neighbours come to Maggie with a distressed and injured horse, things really begin to spiral.
The Chenoweths' young son goes missing while chasing after one of the animals and, meanwhile, there's a mysterious stranger wearing a gas mask lurking about with a paint gun spraying a line around the property's perimeter.
So what's going on? It all certainly seems mysterious. And the show does a good job of creating a sense of dread during that first night, drawing you in.
Is the masked stranger friend or foe? (Supplied: Binge)
But if you think you've seen this set-up before, you're not wrong. Teacup can feel like a veritable bingo card of genre tropes.
A strained marriage between the protagonists? Check. A child becoming a conduit to a mysterious entity and saying spooky things? Check. A stranger telling the main characters to "trust no one"? Check.
But familiarity is not necessarily a bad thing.
There's a comfort in watching a show hit the familiar beats of its genre. And having that framework lets a new series get on with telling their story without having to spend too much time setting the table.
Produced by horror master James Wan (Saw, The Conjuring) and written by Ian McColluch (Yellowstone), Teacup is loosely based on Robert R. McCammon's book Stinger — so if you know what the book's about, then you have some idea of where the show is going.
In these early episodes, the pacing of the show takes a leaf from The Walking Dead: short bursts of mayhem interspersed between stretches of quiet and contemplation. It's a lot of two people walking through the woods talking about their feelings while trying to figure out what's going on.
Ruben (Chaske Spencer) and James (Scott Speedman) reluctantly work together to figure out what's going on. (Supplied: Binge)
But the half-hour episodes ensure things never get too bogged down and it only has eight episodes — with two released each week so the final episode airs on Halloween (of course!)
By the middle of the series, a lot is revealed through exposition and flashbacks, which moves the series into a different direction.
This means the show doesn't lead you into multiple annoying red herrings, as others in the sub-genre are wont to do, but you also never feel like you're an active participant in figuring out the mystery, which is really half the fun of these shows.
Strahovski is effective as the protagonist Maggie — a strong, calm, natural leader in the face of adversity on multiple fronts, and a far cry from the often monstrous Serena Joy she played on The Handmaid's Tale.
Yvonne Strahovski plays Maggie, a veterinarian who must lead her family out of crises on multiple fronts. (Supplied: Binge)
Chaske Spencer (The English) is the other stand-out on the show, playing the Chenoweths' neighbour Ruben Shanley, who is reeling from his own personal dramas and wants nothing more than to get off the farm and be as far away from the people on it as possible.
Teacup ultimately doesn't have much that's new to say, and the reveals are disappointing given the great promise of the set-up. But there is still plenty of fun to be had, with a handful of genuinely creepy, thrilling sequences and solid performances.
It might be strange to think of a horror show as a comfort watch, but that's what Teacup is. If you're a fan of the sub-genre then you will definitely relish this show. All the elements are there.
From a twisted take on Freaky Friday to a deeply satisfying 'eat the rich' fable, here are some Halloween movies that might give you a jolt but won't keep you up at night.
And being only four hours long, it's easily bingeable over a weekend (or a long Halloween night). Teacup never overstays its welcome.
As one mysterious character on the show says: "Coming over to this side's a piece of cake. Heading back the other way, that's the problem."
That could apply to the show's creators, as well as your experience of it as a viewer.
Teacup is streaming on Binge.
