title: BTS' Jung Kook may be a K-pop juggernaut, but a new doco shows he's just as insecure as the rest of us
content:
Pop music history is littered with the stalled careers of former world-conquering boy band members; not everyone gets to be a Harry Styles or a Justin Timberlake, let alone a Michael Jackson (just ask Liam Payne, Lance Bass or Jermaine Jackson).
What: A documentary following BTS vocalist Jung Kook as he prepares to launch his solo career.
Directed by: Jun-Soo Park.
Starring: Jung Kook.
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: Like joining the BTS ARMY — or renewing your membership.
That knowledge seems to weigh heavily on BTS main vocalist Jung Kook in the new documentary I Am Still, which follows the K-pop superstar as he prepares to launch his solo career with his debut album, Golden, in November 2023.
Early on in the film, the then-25-year-old singer rides in the back of a limousine, en route to a showcase for the forthcoming record, wracked with anxiety over stepping out from the safety of his juggernaut band. The music — the work — he says, is not enough; he needs the approval of the fans, collectively known as ARMY.
Directed by Jun-Soo Park (who helmed many of the previous BTS films, including 2018's Burn the Stage), I Am Still is the first official documentary dedicated to the dreamy vocalist.
'Seven' is the fastest song to ever surpass 1 billion Spotify streams. (Supplied: Trafalgar Releasing)
Unfolding over a period of roughly eight months, from early 2023 through to the launch of the album, it offers a compelling snapshot of a star in transition.
The film follows the recording of Jung Kook's chart-topping solo singles 'Seven', '3D' and the Jackson-esque banger 'Standing Next to You', incorporating a wealth of studio and rehearsal footage, live performances and candid moments captured behind-the-scenes (and sometimes, it seems, on Jung Kook's own cell phone).
What emerges is a portrait of an artist in search of his identity, driven by a desire to satisfy his audience — and the precision work ethic embedded in his K-pop training — while yearning to break free as a solo performer, trying new musical styles and pushing himself as a vocalist.
"The general public do not know me," Jung Kook says at one point, before wondering if he can launch his solo career without, he says, "the power of BTS". Just how does he break out of a massively successfully group who have their own identity as a unit? Will he — as the title implies — "still" be on top?
In a whirlwind year filled with multiple city stops, studio sessions, music video shoots and outfit changes (check that ponytail-and-denim-jacket combo in the LA recording of 'Seven'), we get a glimpse into Jung Kook's musical process — into what drives him as a performer and an vocalist.
Jung Kook ft Latto — Seven
"Jin and Jimin drive me crazy," Jung Kook declares of his BTS band mates in an amusing aside, "because they write the keys too high." Yet his talent offers evidence to the contrary, especially during a remarkable vocal session for 'Standing Next to You', as the producers push his angelic tenor to its uppermost register. ("Why is every song so hard?" he wonders, and not for the last time.)
He's playful, anxious, and sometimes delightfully cheeky, as when an American morning radio host tells him that 'Seven' is a great song, and he replies "I know." In another scene, he seems genuinely awed that there's a cardboard standee of himself in a Barnes & Noble bookstore.
Jung Kook has said he's influenced by artists including Justin Bieber, Usher and Justin Timberlake. (Getty Images: Daniel Zuchnik)
It goes without saying that there's an in-built cute factor, as any film that opens on a close-up of its star's baby photo is apt to deliver. And it's hard not to be charmed by the sight of Jung Kook dangling his legs off a hotel bed as he scrolls through his phone, or hugging his teary-eyed hairdresser after having his locks shorn off in preparation for his South Korean military service.
But we also get a classic document of the star in emotional and geographic flux as he shuttles across continents and between shows — a life seen through the liminal spaces of hotel rooms and car rides.
In one of the film's most poignant scenes, we see Jung Kook alone in the back of a limo post-concert, his face illuminated by the social media reactions on his phone. Even in his private moments, the fans — and the pressures of stardom — are right there with him.
With '3D', Jung Kook became the first South Korean solo artist to have two consecutive songs in the top five of the UK Singles Chart. (Supplied: Trafalgar Releasing)
I Am Still remains a largely celebratory work, and it's a tapestry of riches for any fan of Jung Kook or BTS. As an insight into the life of its star, it proves to be much more guarded.
Unlike some of the more intimate pop documentaries, like Billie Eilish's 2021 emotional deep-dive The World's a Little Blurry, I Am Still is a polished portrait of a diamond-cut star synonymous with his public persona.
In that sense it's a traditional pop star movie, one that preserves its subject's sense of mystery — an essential unknowability that is key to any great superstar — within its playful, semi-confessional exterior.
When Jung Kook appears on stage framed in a pyramid of light, his "real" self doesn't matter — he's spectral and mesmerising, almost a hologram of a pop star.
Jung Kook: I Am Still is in cinemas now.

title: Stand-up comedian Lizzy Hoo is looking for new ways to make jokes about her identity
content:
Lizzy Hoo and Shaun Micallef had never met before they boarded a 17-hour flight to Ireland together back in April.
Hoo is an established comedian, presenter, writer and actor, who has appeared on ABC TV's Question Everything and The Weekly, and released a Prime Video comedy special called Hoo Cares. She hosts a podcast for SBS Audio, Grand Gestures, where she asks famous Australians about their grandparents. Next month, she takes her stand-up on the road again.
But she'd never had the chance to work with Micallef, a veteran of the Australian comedy world, until they were thrown together for a week to explore Hoo (and Micallef's) Irish heritage for the new SBS documentary series, Shaun Micallef's Origin Odyssey.
We caught up with Hoo to find out what it was like learning more about her family's cultural background, and how that impacted her feelings about identity as a mixed-race person. We also found out what Micallef watched on the long flight, and what her favourite meme is. (It's deliciously dark.)
No, we got flown business class, which was very nice. But we flew from Melbourne to Dublin in pretty much one hit and then we started filming as soon as we got off the flight.
When I watched the episode recently, I kept looking at myself like, "Wow, not too bad given I'd just got off a 17-hour flight." I'm still surprised words actually came out of my mouth.
I guess we got to know each other on the way there. Yeah … we did lose Shaun in the airport. He would just wander off [laughs] and we'd be walking around like, "Where's Shaun? We've lost the old man." We could always find him because he was this tall guy with a hat on.
We don't know [laughs]. He would just go AWOL. He would be waiting for someone to tell him what to do and he would just walk off, and then he'd get distracted by something, I think. It was quite fascinating.
Not having met someone, then having that 17-hour flight, then spending a whole week with that person was quite a daunting idea, but we got on quite well. We were quite well-matched in energy and style.
Hoo and the rest of the SBS team frequently lost track of Micallef in the airport on the way to Ireland. (Supplied: SBS/Rob Meyer)
Oh gosh, I can never remember book names because I have a Kindle and you know, the book name is just not important. You just keep reading. But let me look at what it was … Oh! What a book … that I can't remember the name of [laughs].
Stay True — it's by Hua Hsu and it's about growing up Asian in America. It's a really interesting story … I think me and the author are the same age because he references all this 90s grunge music throughout the book that formed a lot of his identity, and it's exactly the same music that I used to listen to growing up.
And I'm currently reading a book called I'm Supposed to Protect You From All This, which is kind of heavy — it's a memoir by Nadja Spiegelman. Her dad wrote that graphic novel Maus about the Holocaust. I wish I'd read it before I'd gone to Ireland, if I'm honest, because it's her asking her grandparents everything and why they are like they are and why her mum's like she is and it's a really interesting way of writing a memoir.
It would appear that way! I think I'm always sort of thinking about it because my comedy has largely been about identity — not so much anymore, but it has been. The Ireland trip sparked something in me, and my parents are old now. My dad's 85 and my mum's almost 79 and I really want to know everything I can about them before it's too late.
It was 'Dancing in the Shadows' by Tsha. I was listening to it so much because I went through a break-up at the end of 2022 and this is one of the songs I had on repeat all the way through 2023.
TSHA ft Clementine Douglas — Dancing in the Shadows
I'm a big Below Deck fan. I got really into it in lockdown and I'm loving the new season at the moment. And I watched America's Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders. Loved that, it was a bit crazy but I mean, I enjoyed it.
What else … that's kind of it from memory, but TV just leaves your head now after you've watched it. It's hard to remember.
Yeah, he was telling me about the idea on the tour … I love the idea. I do think it could be a podcast. But I mean, people love Shaun … Yeah, they love Shaun. They love watching Shaun … He's got such a big following … I think everything he does is great. So, I think people will enjoy his return to the screen. Um, yeah … But he didn't get me on as a guest so, whatever.
I don't know if it even is a meme … it's this video of a group of friends and one of them gets something out of the oven and she catches on fire but then the other girls are filming it, just laughing at her.
It's so evil [laughs] and then the girl who's on fire is like, "Stop laughing at me, I'm on fire!" but they can't stop laughing, it's so funny [laughs].
[Still laughing] I think it just reminds me a bit of my friends.
When you're mixed you can't align with one or the other. You're bits of this and bits of that.
But when I tell people, "I did this show that's tracing your origins" and people are like, "Oh, why'd you go [to Ireland]? Why wouldn't you go to the Malaysian or Chinese side?" But I'm as white as I am Chinese.
Hoo (pictured left as a child with her family) is still coming to terms with her mixed-race identity.  (Supplied)
It's such a difficult thing and I've tried to come to terms with it over the years. It's definitely something I didn't start exploring properly until my early 30s, when I started comedy. And it's something I continue to grapple with. Did I answer the question?
I think for so long I didn't feel comfortable talking about it, and comedy was a vehicle to talk about it in a lighthearted, funny way, while also helping me make sense of it.
I started comedy at a time when lots of people were reconsidering their identities. Learning more about yourself and being proud of who you are was kind of in the zeitgeist.
But I think talking about where you're from has kind of been done now, especially from a comedy point of view. We've got to find new ways of telling stories [about identity].
So, now I try not so much to talk to it directly, but be more like, "Here's a story about my dad," and obviously he's not from here.
The world knows her best as teenager Amerie Wadia, but Ayesha Madon is now reintroducing herself as a pop star.
We've got people getting their backs cracked. I'm really into back cracking. I'm into pimple popping, too. I love it all! I love earwax removal. I'm gross. The other thing I get a lot of is greyhounds because I have one and I'm always looking at them, and then a lot of pop psychology around dating.
He watched Poor Things on the plane. There are some hectic scenes there…

title: Bisexual people rarely see themselves portrayed accurately on screen. Here's why that's a problem
content:
The world of entertainment feels vehemently bisexual in 2024, with some of the biggest TV shows and films focusing on bi+ characters — think sexy tennis romp Challengers, or that kiss in House of the Dragon.
But even though bisexual people make up a large part of the queer community, when it comes to the television world, we account for just 24 per cent of LGBTQIA+ representation. Not only that, bisexual representation has decreased in 2023 and 2024.
This Bisexual Visibility Day — a day dedicated to recognising and celebrating the bisexual community — we look a bit closer at how bi+ people are represented on our screens.
It may feel like bisexual characters are more common in mainstream media, but representation goes beyond just visibility.
Benedict Bridgerton's (Luke Thompson) scenes are largely limited to the bedroom. (Supplied: Netflix)
Take season three of Bridgerton. While some fans celebrated (and others rioted) over the decision to make the character Benedict (Luke Thompson) bi-presenting, the execution left much to be desired.
Bisexual stories are often limited to bedroom scenes, where characters suddenly shed their "straight" identities in fantastical threesome scenarios and enter a murkier, unknown territory.
Bridgerton falls into this trap, with Benedict's story focused on pleasure and steamy make-outs, reinforcing tired stereotypes of bisexuals as promiscuous, confused, irrefutably horny, and incapable of monogamy. I don't know a single bi+ person who discovered their identity through a threesome.
Then there's House of the Dragon, which made waves with a surprise kiss between Rhaenyra (Emma D'Arcy) and her adviser Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno). Entirely improvised, they kiss and then it is never mentioned again, as if it never happened.
The kiss between Rhaenyra (Emma D'Arcy) and her adviser Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno) in House of the Dragon reinforces damaging stereotypes about bisexual infidelity. (Supplied: Binge)
As far as I'm concerned we should make the whole Seven Kingdoms queer, but the fleeting moment still plays into old tropes. Mysaria's political scheming and Rhaenyra's infidelity reinforce the idea of transactional romance, painting bisexuals as morally ambiguous plot devices rather than real people.
Even one of 2024's biggest films, Challengers, isn't immune. Watching two men aggressively chomp on a churro while gazing deeply into each other's eyes delivers the queer energy we want, but the decision to make Patrick (Josh O'Connor) the most outwardly bisexual character and the biggest villain of the three is certainly a choice.
Challengers' iconic churro scene. (Please be advised this video contains some swearing.)
While others might argue that Zendaya's Tashi or Mike Faist's Art is the real villain, it's queer-coded messiness that permeates the film.
It's a familiar narrative — bisexual characters as unpredictable, morally grey, and tangled in love triangles. But don't we deserve more than just another "disaster bisexual"?
It might be tempting to celebrate any bisexuality on screen, but reducing someone's identity to stereotypes has real consequences.
It's a common experience for bisexuals to feel like we never fully belong. We're too straight for some, too queer for others. We're constantly subjected to queries about our sexuality, as if we're in denial, or we need to "prove" our queerness with a hypothetical kiss quota.
Many still don't believe bi+ sexualities are authentic, Shannon writes.
A study from queer dating app HER found 34 per cent of bisexual people had been labelled "greedy" or "confused" because of their sexual orientation, while 40 per cent admit to feeling invisible in LGBTQIA+ spaces due to bi-erasure they have faced. And 28 per cent of bisexual women have faced accusations they're more likely to cheat because of their sexuality.
This lack of understanding has damaging real-world effects. Bisexual people are more likely to binge-drink, self-harm and have suicidal thoughts than their straight peers. Only 33 per cent of bisexual people in the UK said they were comfortable telling their medical providers their sexual orientation, and almost half of those people experienced biphobia while accessing health services.
When we see characters that are meant to represent us, it matters. It shapes public perceptions, either breaking down or reinforcing negative stereotypes.
Thankfully, it's not all bad. While global shows continue to struggle, Australian gems including Heartbreak High are showing how sexual representation can be done right. Bisexual characters feel fully realised in the reboot of the classic Australian 90s series, with their sexuality naturally woven into their lives.
In Heartbreak High, Malakai (right), played by Thomas Weatherall, proudly embraces his identity, openly correcting those who incorrectly label him. (Supplied: Netflix)
Among the group of diverse characters are Missy (Sherry-Lee Watson) and Malakai (Thomas Weatherall) — two self-proclaimed "bloody bisexual icons". Both characters proudly embrace their identity, openly correcting those who mislabel them.
Still, Malakai grapples with bisexual impostor syndrome – an experience familiar to many bi+ people who feel they never fully fit in. Darren gently reassures him (and us) in a scene that speaks directly to this insecurity.
"Literally everyone is queer now," he tells Malakai. "I know that doesn't make things easy, and I'm proud of you."
And in the UK, shows aimed at gen Z audiences, including Heartstopper, are getting bisexual representation right. The show follows Nick (Kit Connor), a teenager discovering his own bi identity through a heartwarming relationship with Charlie (Joe Locke).
Nick faces the same frustrating questions many of us hear: "Admit that you're gay," his brother says, while his mother reassures him, "You don't have to say you like girls if you don't."
Nick's response is simple but powerful: "I'm bi, actually."
In Heartstopper, Nick (Kit Connor, right) is openly bisexual, navigating his identity without being reduced to a cheap plot device. (Supplied: Netflix)
With Heartstopper bathing Nick in pink, purple and blue lighting and using the term "bisexual" explicitly (rather than simply hinting at it), the show chips away at bi-erasure, one scene at a time. The impact is clear, with countless stories emerging of people coming to terms with their own sexuality after seeing it depicted so lovingly on screen.
In both these shows, the characters' sexual identities are kaleidoscopes of experiences, where being bisexual is just one part of a much bigger picture. Their sexuality isn't there to tick a box – it's part of a fully developed character who reflects the multifaceted experiences of being a bisexual person in the world.
While 2024 hasn't exactly been a banner year for bisexual representation, shows including Heartstopper and Heartbreak High are finally starting to get it right.
Things can only go up from here.
Alexandra Koster is a Melbourne-based writer and former Culture Editor at Refinery29 Australia. Her work has been featured in The Age, Sydney Morning Herald, PEDESTRIAN.TV, VICE, Body+Soul, Kotaku and more.

title: Erik and Lyle Menendez were sentenced to life for killing their parents. Now Netflix is telling their story
content:
Warning: This article discusses abuse.
Netflix just can't keep TV hitmaker Ryan Murphy away from true-crime retellings — and why would they?
After working on Glee, American Horror Story and American Crime Story, Murphy came out with the confusingly titled Dahmer – Monster: The Jeffrey Dahmer Story. It raked in 13 Emmy nominations (plus one win for actor Niecy Nash) and notched up 1 billion view hours within its first 60 days on the platform — one of only four shows to ever achieve this feat.
Now, the streaming giant is unleashing Murphy on another dark chapter in American history, with his anthology series Monster next taking on the true story of brothers Erik and Lyle Menendez, who were sentenced to life without parole in 1996 for murdering their parents.
Here's what you need to know.
Up until 1989, Erik and Lyle Menendez were normal, albeit privileged, young men. They lived in a Beverly Hills mansion with their parents, Mary Louise (better known as Kitty) and José, an entertainment executive.
On August 20, 1989, the brothers — Erik, 18, Lyle, 22 — shot their parents multiple times at home, killing them both. Then they left the property.
After returning home and alerting the police of their parent's bodies, the brothers feigned innocence. This lead police to spend months investigating if the murders were mob-related, due to José's connection to the entertainment industry.
Erik Menendez (R) and brother Lyle listen to court proceedings during a May 17, 1991 appearance.  (Reuters: Lee Celano)
In the months after their parents' deaths, Erik and Lyle went on a shopping spree, buying businesses and luxuries like sports cars.
It wasn't until March 1990 that the brothers were arrested and it would be another three years before they both went to trial.
After their arrest, the brothers confessed to shooting their parents. During their first trial, which began in 1993, Erik's lawyer Leslie Abramson claimed they had been pushed to the crime out of fear for their lives.
The brothers testified that José had molested Lyle from the ages of six to eight, and Erik from ages six to 18; that their father's abuse and their mother's neglect led them to live in constant fear; that, in their eyes, shooting and killing their parents was an act of defence.
Prosecutors argued the brothers had killed their parents in order to get their hands on their $US14 million inheritance sooner.
The high profile of the case saw it broadcast on cable channel CourtTV, and the brothers' tearful testimony turned the murder trial into an international spectacle.
Erik Menendez Takes the Stand - (1993) CA v. Menendez Brothers | COURT TV
After months of testimony, two separate juries could not make a decision on whether the brothers were guilty of voluntary manslaughter or murder.
A retrial began in late 1995, with both men tried in front of a single jury and without any cameras inside the courtroom. Judge Stanley Weisberg ruled that the defence had not adequately provided proof of the brothers' prolonged abuse at the hands of their father.
Twenty weeks later, a jury found Erik and Lyle guilty of first-degree murder. They were later sentenced to life without parole.
Erik and Lyle, now both in their 50s, are still in prison, having made multiple unsuccessful appeal attempts.
In 2018, more than 20 years after their convictions, the brothers were moved into the same housing unit in a Southern California prison. A prison spokesperson said they can and do interact.
Like the previous season of Monsters, this iteration follows the Menendez brothers as they deal with the aftermath of their crimes while also luxuriating in their parents' money pre-arrest, before delving into their seven-year court run.
MONSTERS: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story | Official Trailer #1 | Netflix
But it also looks further into the time that led up to the crime, focusing on Erik and Lyle's restrictive life with their parents, and the actions that drove them to the murders.
MONSTERS: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story | Official Trailer #2 | Netflix
Relative newcomers Cooper Koch (Swallowed) and Nicholas Chavez (General Hospital) play Erik and Lyle, respectively.
Nicholas Chavez as Lyle (L), Cooper Koch as Erik and Ari Graynor as lawyer Leslie Abramson. (Supplied: Netflix)
But beyond the brothers, the cast is stuffed full of A-listers. Javier Bardem (Dune, No Country For Old Men) and Chloë Sevigny (a Murphy mainstay since 2011's American Horror Story: Asylum) play parents José and Kitty.
Ari Graynor (I'm Dying Up Here) will feature as Leslie Abramson, LA defence attorney and eventual lead counsel for Erik.
Nathan Lane (The Lion King, Beau is Afraid) plays late Vanity Fair reporter Dominick Dunne, who extensively covered the murders. Lane recently told the Hollywood Reporter that the show opened his eyes to the real-life ordeal.
Javier Bardem and Chloë Sevigny as Menendez parents José and Kitty. (Supplied: Netflix)
"I think it was easy for people in the beginning to think these two spoiled rich kids will kill their parents for the money, for the inheritance, but it's much more complicated," he said.
"It doesn't change the fact that they committed this horrific act, but I think maybe you start to understand what led to that."
Despite the popularity of his first Monsters show, Dahmer copped flack for exploiting the victim's real-life tragedy in the name of entertainment.
Here's why Netflix's new serial killer show about Jeffrey Dahmer is dividing viewers.
This time around, early reviews question the necessity of rolling out the Menendez's story again, while still praising the core actors.
"Despite the gripping subject matter and the outstanding performances, Monsters… has no idea what it wants to be. Therefore, it just dissolves into a retelling of unspeakable abuses and gruesome crimes," Variety's Aramide Tinubu said.
"When we engage in the platforming of murderous and unwell people, no matter how heinous their upbringings may have been, we lean into our own unchecked monstrosities."
The Independent's Katie Rosseinsky echoed these sentiments.
"[Monsters…] feels like a muddled mix of the best and worst of Murphy's oeuvre. It's likely to please his legions of fans, but may leave his detractors feeling a little queasy."
Meanwhile, Murphy has already moved onto his next grizzly tale, announcing that the next Monsters series will focus on the Butcher of Plainfield Ed Gein, who will be played by Charlie Hunham.
Monsters: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story is streaming on Netflix now.

title: Would you take a miracle drug for eternal youth? Demi Moore does in The Substance, with horrific results
content:
Would you take a miracle drug that guaranteed eternal youth? That granted poreless skin and supple limbs? That reversed all the violence of the world and restored the body to its smoothest, its tautest, its lithest?
What: An ageing movie star trades her body for a younger, more perfect specimen – with dire consequences.
Director: Coralie Fargeat.
Starring: Demi Moore, Margaret Qualley, Dennis Quaid.
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: Nauseous.
What if it wasn't so eternal after all? What if it came with a raft of unknown – and grotesque – side effects? What if the flesh rotted and bruised, peeled off like mandarin skin? Would you keep taking it? Would you?
This is the Faustian bargain that powers The Substance: French director Coralie Fargeat's fantastically nasty, proudly gaudy piece of body horror that instantly cleaved audiences into loud, warring factions at its Cannes premiere earlier this year – and then won the festival's best screenplay award.
Director Coralie Fargeat creates a sci-fi neon dystopia fused with the excesses of 1980s Wall St. (Supplied: Madman)
Demi Moore is the film's beating heart – and its sinew, bone and tendon – as Elisabeth Sparkle, a one-time Hollywood idol now suffering the consequences of an industry where ageing is worse than dying.
Fargeat's world is halfway between the 1980s excess of Wall Street and the neon dystopia of countless sci-fi ventures. It is a world where network television still reigns supreme and audiences still tune into a Jane-Fonda-lite aerobics show fronted by Sparkle in shimmer tights and a megawatt grin. Then, she is unceremoniously axed on her 50th birthday.
This is not a subtle film by any measure. A lecherous, chauvinistic studio exec called Harvey (Dennis Quaid) ushers Sparkle out of the building faster than you can say "Weinstein". Seconds later, Sparkle drives past her own obsolescence on her way home: a billboard of her beaming face being torn down.
Dennis Quaid plays a lecherous, chauvinistic studio exec called Harvey. (Supplied: Madman)
The former leading lady gazes up at her past glory. Her face in the sky falls to the pavement in one long shred. Then the scene explodes: another car T-bones Sparkle's in a deranged chorus of ear-splitting screeches.
The ground seems to quake so violently you might wonder if you've accidentally entered a 4D session. It is a brutal, almost excruciatingly long sequence – though it's a stroll in the park compared to the rest of the film's hellish delights.
In the aftermath, a doctor slips Sparkle a USB containing an ad for The Substance: a mysterious panacea promising "a better version of yourself". Like any horror heroine, Sparkle immediately dispenses with any reasonable logic and succumbs to temptation.
Soon enough, she's staring at a highlighter-hued elixir and all manner of sharp objects: syringes, scissors and sewing needles.
The Substance is best viewed on an empty stomach. (Supplied: Madman)
She "activates" by injecting The Substance and her spine ruptures to birth a glistening creature onto bathroom tiles. As the USB claims: it's Elisabeth, only "younger, more beautiful, more perfect" – and now played by a dead-eyed Margaret Qualley (Kinds of Kindness, Poor Things).
This new specimen calls herself Sue and quickly usurps her counterpart's life, replacing her television spot and swanning around her palatial apartment.
Sue (Margaret Qualley) quickly usurps her counterpart’s life. (Supplied: Madman)
The rules of engagement are clear from the outset: Elisabeth and Sue are one brain split across two bodies. Only one can be conscious while the other lies dormant – and they must swap every seven days.
Rules, though, are designed to be flouted – particularly when you're Tinseltown's latest discovery and there's always another party, promotion and Vogue cover on the horizon. In a blink, Sue's seven days become eight, then a month, then three months.
Elisabeth, meanwhile, rapidly decomposes. It's a feat of physical acting from Moore, covered in head-to-toe prosthetics and unleashing an animal ferocity after a decade of mostly thankless movie roles.
Fargeat's targets are many and varied. There is, of course, the meta-commentary on Hollywood's treatment of actresses who dare to – shock horror – age. There's the satire of our age-old pursuit of beauty at all costs – like Dorian Gray meets Botched. There's the skewering of Big Pharma and all its magic pills.
There's nothing more disgusting in The Substance than the prawn shells flung into a fish-eye lens from the squelching teeth of Harvey (Dennis Quaid). (Supplied: Madman)
Trumping its polemics, however, is the film's commitment to spectacle. Each sound – an olive plunging into a martini, the crack of a soft-drink can (or a bone) – is amplified to an arena-ready roar. The camera gawps at skin and saliva with frenzied glee; there's nothing more disgusting in The Substance than the prawn shells flung into a fish-eye lens from Harvey's squelching teeth.
It is pure pageantry. Go in with an empty stomach.
The Substance is showing now in cinemas.

title: Vivaldi gets a contemporary pop treatment in Gloria! a joyful film set in 19th-century Italy
content:
When American musician Billie Eilish and her producer brother Finneas O'Connell first heard the rapid staccato of a pedestrian crossing signal while visiting Sydney, they were so blown away by the musical potential of this seemingly mundane sound it wound up as the beat to her hit single Bad Guys.
What: Opening-night movie of the Italian Film Festival, following a group of young orphans in 19th-century Italy who discover the power of music.
Starring: Galatéa Bellugi, Carlotta Gamba, Paolo Rossi, Elio, Natalino Balasso
Director: Margherita Vicario
When: In cinemas September-October
Likely to make you feel: Like dancing!
Italian actor and singer-songwriter Margherita Vicario also transforms humdrum background noise into the fantastical in her debut directorial feature, Gloria! The peppy, toe-tapping film flourishes with a joyous fusion of pop and Vivaldi, and it opens this year's Italian Film Festival in states across Australia.
Set in Venice at the turn of the 19th century, it thrusts us into the stuffy confines of Sant'Ignazio, a religious institution housing orphaned young women and training them to be musicians. While the halls that host guests are resplendent, the girls' quarters are more like prison cells. But even within their ranks, not all are equal.
Teresa, portrayed by The Taste of Things actor Galatéa Bellugi, is a Cinderella figure. She has an illegitimate son — who was taken from her — and isn't deemed reputable enough by Perlina (Paolo Rossi), a mean-spirited priest with his own secrets to keep, to join the other girls in their lessons. Instead, she must tidy up for everyone.
Teresa, played by Galatéa Bellugi, is a Cinderella figure in Gloria! (Supplied: RAI)
During one such monotonous courtyard sweep, Teresa suddenly becomes aware of every brushstroke, sneeze and bucket splash, coalescing into a percussive musical number of sorts, until her reverie is rudely interrupted by a slap about the head.
"The movie is about her imagination," Vicario says. "At the beginning, it's all in her mind, and then it's like the arc of a songwriter. Her imagination is her escape from reality."
That escape opens further when a beautiful piano is donated to the orphanage. Perlina banishes it to the basement in a moral paroxysm, but when Teresa is forced to clean out the basement in preparation for a Papal visit — at which they must perform a concert for the cruel governor (Natalino Balasso) — she stumbles upon the instrument.
The girls are required to perform a concert for a visiting governor. (Supplied: RAI)
Even though she has never been trained, Teresa wills incredible music into being, as if by magic, bringing all the other girls to her in the middle of the night.
With Perlina distracted by the impending visit, the girls gather together around the piano, composing something just for them as the seeds of a rousing rebellion are sown. One girl even invokes the spirit of the French Revolution.
"Through the piano, Teresa's imagination goes outside her," Vicario says. "And like every singer-songwriter I know, the biggest dream is to have your music played by an orchestra."
Vicario may have two hit albums to her name, but she comes from a long line of filmmakers and went to theatre school, so it seems inevitable these paths would cross professionally.
"I wanted to do like this musical movie that wasn't a musical," she says. "In Italy, they don't really like it if someone starts singing. They're quite sceptical."
In Gloria! Mary Montalto's costumes are both beautiful and believably worn. (Supplied: RAI)
The handy thing about historical fiction, Vicario suggests, is that you can dispense with a great deal of scepticism surprisingly easily — with a little help from a great team, including cinematographer Gianluca Palma, production designers Susanna Abenavoli and Luca Servino, and Mary Montalto's costumes, which are both beautiful and believably worn.
"My biggest talent is to talk, talk and talk, telling you what I'm thinking, but then I can do nothing," Vicario laughs. "To have this balance between the contemporary pop and the historical, the aesthetic had to be perfect, and by perfect, I mean dusty and dirty. Of course, it's like a fable, a tableau."
Margherita Vicario has two hit albums to her name but Gloria! is her feature directorial debut. (Supplied: Italian Film Festival)
Casting Bellugi was an artistic decision for Vicario, too: "I did a lot of auditioning, and she has these cool eyes, as if she comes from a Vermeer painting."
Other than her music videos, Vicario had never worked as a director. But she took the complicated musical scenes with Teresa in her stride.
"I felt really comfortable going to all the actors and saying, 'Trust me, I know what I'm doing' because it was all in my head," she says. "They were the simple scenes for me. Whereas the ones with dialogue were much more difficult to find the rhythm."
Vicario says the six weeks of shooting Gloria! were the most difficult of her life. (Supplied: Italian Film Festival)
And she drew on elements of her story for Teresa's journey, too.
"It's a little bit autobiographical, because I cannot read or write music," she reveals. And yet, Vicario composed the film's magnificent score alongside fellow musician Davide Pavanello, who also can't read or write sheet music.
"In pop music, there's like a grammar where, if you work together, you have to say, 'The chorus is not working', or 'We need the hook'," Vicario says.
"But in music for cinema, you don't need that grammar. Davide and I were like two children of six or seven years old, building whatever they want. You just need to reach the feeling."
Gloria!'s empowering story of young women grasping their moment also contains a sobering nod towards the many whose music was obscured throughout history.
"In this case, the villain is the one who holds all the power," Vicario says. "I'm sorry to say that it's very normal in that century, and not that far from today, at least in Italy, for that power to be held by the church and the nobility. They had a lot to do with the conditions of women."
Gloria! official trailer.
Vicario is thrilled she got through the endurance test of her first directing job.
"The six weeks of shooting were the most difficult of my life and I'm not the same person anymore," she says. "It was like climbing a big mountain."
Well worth it, though.
"I'm so excited to come to Australia. I haven't travelled that much in my life, because in summertime I'm always touring or shooting, so it's wonderful to share these women and their music."
The Italian Film Festival begins on the 18th of September in Sydney, with screenings also happening across September and October in Canberra, Brisbane, Melbourne, Byron Bay and Ballina, Adelaide and Perth.

title: Grand country cinema saved by Australia's largest independent theatre chain
content:
The near-century-old Regent Cinemas in Ballarat have been saved from closure after Australia's largest independent movie theatre group Palace Cinemas purchased the historic business for an undisclosed sum.
Rebranded as the Palace Regent Ballarat, the cinema will open its doors on October 3 and showcase international film festivals, upmarket movies and big blockbusters.
In June, the Regent Cinemas, once labelled the largest "movie palace" in regional Victoria closed, citing several factors leading to the "heartbreaking" decision.
Ballarat's Regent has six cinemas including the main theatre room. (Supplied: Bronwyn Blaiklock)
The Regent was first opened by the Hoyts theatre chain in 1928.
Liquidator Justin Howlett said the cinema's sale was a "fantastic result", following a two-and-a-half-month process that involved conversations with 16 interested parties.
Crippled by the pandemic, film distribution deals and the online streaming boom, a "conga line" of regional cinemas are shutting their doors. But could there be a way to reverse the trend?
Mr Howlett said during the sale process he had many interactions with locals who expressed their love for the historic building."Whether it be social gatherings, groups — and for some people, it was their only real social outlet," he said. "It's a great day for Ballarat and for the cinema public.
"The ongoing support that we've had from the Ballarat community has no doubt played a massive part in the attractiveness of the business."
Mr Howlett said some of the interested parties just wanted to purchase items from the cinema, whereas Palace Cinemas intended to reopen the theatre.
Palace Cinemas head of marketing Alex Moir said he understood the compounding pressures independent cinemas had faced over the past few years.
"The actors and writers strike last year [also] carried on for several months and disrupted the entire release calendar for 2024."
Palace Cinemas head of marketing Alex Moir is excited to revive the historic Ballarat cinema. (Supplied: Alex Moir)
Mr Moir said over the past year he had seen signs of growth within the industry and in demand for the big screen in regional Victoria.
"We were equally as shocked as the community to see the cinema close, but completely understood," he said.
"Moving forward, we thought we could make something special.
Movie-goers have been enjoying films at the Regent Cinemas in Ballarat since 1928. (Supplied: Regent Cinemas Ballarat)
Ballarat Arts Community member and movie buff Liana Emmerson said she was excited to see a culturally diverse range of films being offered locally.
"We haven't had something locally that's had that range," Ms Emmerson said.
Ballarat resident Liana Emmerson is looking forward to watching culturally diverse movies locally. (Supplied: Liana Emmerson)
"The building itself is historically and culturally important, and to be able to be in that space experiencing cinema is amazing.
"Cinema as an experience, is so much more than what you're able to get access to at home."
The Regent has long been a social hub for the town, with almost 2,000 seats in stalls and balcony levels when it opened.
Melbourne architects Arthur W. Purnell and Cedric H. Ballantyne were responsible for the design.
Ballantyne also designed the Regent Theatre on Collins Street in Melbourne.
The Ballarat theatre survived a significant fire in 1943, after which the building was redesigned.
Hoyts closed the business in 1970 and it was reopened in 1976 by the Anderson family, who operated it until recently.

title: The book Uglies changed YA fantasy. So why did it take 20 years to be made into a movie?
content:
Scott Westerfeld's dystopian sci-fi novel Uglies is a rare sort of book.
Not only is it an engaging read, but the moral lessons it imparts also earned it a spot on many high school English class syllabi following its 2005 release.
And that's how an entire generation was forced to read Uglies … only to fall unironically in love with it.
To date, more than 6 million copies of the Uglies series (now comprising eight books) have been sold according to its publisher, Simon & Schuster. Some have suggested it started a trend of YA dystopian books, with The Hunger Games following in 2008 and Divergent in 2011. Both series were adapted into massively popular movie franchises within a handful of years, while Uglies faded into obscurity.
Now, almost 20 years later, the beloved story has finally been made into a film — albeit a direct-to-streaming mockbuster.
Uglies — official trailer
Approximately 300 years in the future, post-apocalypse society is divided into "Uglies" and "Pretties".
Everyone is considered unattractive until their 16th birthday, which is when they undergo extensive government-funded plastic surgery in accordance with official (unrealistic and largely Eurocentric) beauty standards to become a Pretty and move to Pretty Town. This is supposedly to eliminate discrimination.
Like everyone else, Tally (played in the film by Netflix darling Joey King, The Kissing Booth) has grown up dreaming of this day her entire life. That is, until a chance meeting with another 15-year-old named Shay (Brianne Tju, Light as a Feather) — the first person Tally has ever met who doesn't subscribe to the Pretties' beauty standards, and who refuses to go under the knife. She's planning to instead join a resistance group living in a settlement called "The Smoke" outside their city.
By the time Tally (second from left) decides against betraying the rebels, it's too late. (Netflix: Brian Douglas)
Unfortunately, Tally is too indoctrinated and desperate to move to Pretty Town, where her best friend and crush Peris (Chase Stokes, Stranger Things) recently moved.
But our protagonist doesn't get the cosmetic makeover she'd dreamed of on her birthday. Instead, secret police operatives forcibly take her to their mysterious Special Circumstances Unit, where the ultimate Pretty Dr Cable (Laverne Cox, Orange is the New Black) gives her an ultimatum: help officials find Shay and the rebel group, or stay an Ugly forever.
Unable to refuse, Tally journeys to The Smoke. But after Tally meets the rebels and their teenage leader David (Keith Powers, Straight Outta Compton), she learns the operation to become a Pretty is more than surface level — it also changes the way people think.
Too bad she's already led the officials right to them…
Uglies enjoyed weeks atop various bestseller lists and won countless prizes after it was published in 2005. By 2006, 20th Century Fox had bought the film rights.
It's been stuck in development purgatory ever since, for reasons that haven't been made public. And Westerfeld has spent years promising updates on the project (which changed hands and forms more than once).
One longtime fan of the series wrote on Screenrant: "My copy of the Uglies book has a 'soon to be a major motion picture' stamp on the cover, which I have looked at bitterly for nearly 20 years now."
It wasn't until 2020 that it was announced Netflix had acquired the film rights, with King to star and Joseph McGinty Nichol, who is known professionally as Mcg, to direct. But after King revealed in 2022 that production on the film had wrapped in 2021, fans started getting nervous the project had stalled again.
As of March 2024, Uglies the movie didn't even have a release date. Netflix finally announced the film's September 13 release date a month before it dropped.
Almost 20 years on from when Uglies was published, we have an entirely new set of outrageous beauty standards. Cosmetic procedures and surgeries have become a whole lot more accessible, and social media is virtually inescapable.
But there's also a wider acceptance of the idea that beauty is subjective and diet culture is real. Meanwhile, the discourse around the many "isms" that feed into those things (think: racism, ableism, etc.) has become an inescapable part of life online.
Despite this, director Mcg recently told Netflix the film's message sticks pretty thoroughly to the source material. Which is to say, it feels very 2005.
There is a lot of CGI in Uglies, and none of it is "good". But it is very funny in an ironic way. (Netflix: Brian Douglas)
"[It's] about beauty as interior," he said.
"It's a commentary on what we're experiencing today, where so many people can't just take a photograph and post it on social media.
Meanwhile, the movie's CGI, colour grading, set design and costumes are giving 2008 dystopian YA film. Which is to say they're Divergent/Hunger Games-coded. (Though in its defence, Uglies the book came first.)
The Pretties are the only thing that feel like they belong in the 2020s. They are laughably yassified. "Yassified to maintain anonymity" levels of yassified.
And all the Uglies are hot actors who no one would ever describe as ugly.
Powers has the bone structure of a god. Tju could ditch acting in favour of modelling. King is so hot that she counts babygirl Jacob Elordi among her exes.
It may be Hollywood, but this requires a little too much suspension of disbelief.
Brianne Tju, another hot actor who Netflix had the audacity to cast as an "Ugly". (Netflix: Brian Douglas)
In the book, the Pretties have an olive skin tone that's described as being an "average" of all the members of their society.
This element of the story doesn't feature in the film, which has a racially diverse cast. Powers, who is Black, plays the main love interest David, while Tju, who plays Shay, is Asian. And plenty of the background actors are people of colour.
And then there's Cox, who plays Dr Cable and functions as the evil arbiter of all things unrealistic-beauty-standards-via-mandated-surgery.
Laverne Cox plays the exceedingly beautiful villain, Dr Cable. (Netflix: Brian Douglas)
On one hand, it's refreshing to see a Black trans woman presented as the ultimate Pretty. On the other, it's another example of a trans person being cast as the villain.
At no point does the film actively discuss race or gender as drivers of discrimination.
In the world of the Uglies movie, yassification is apparently enough to eradicate racism, misogyny, transphobia, fatphobia, homophobia and ableism. Despite having one of the most famous trans women as a lead, there is no acknowledgement of queerness at all in Pretty Town, let alone characters with disability.
A real shame, especially considering King and Tju's versions of Tally and Shay share actual chemistry — unlike King and Powers.
The Uglies movie spends too much time trying to make us want David and Tally (pictured) to happen when Tally and Shay were already happening. (Netflix: Brian Douglas)
Given the film's direct-to-streaming release with minimal hype, many fans of the Uglies series were expecting the worst.
"Words cannot describe the pain I feel at the fact that this book is finally getting an adaptation … and it's being made by Netflix," one wrote in the comments section of the film's YouTube trailer.
There is plenty about the Uglies movie that is silly, shallow, unbelievable and cringe. As reviewers have pointed out in various publications like The Guardian and Variety, this issue is a vital and nuanced one that could have made for a great film. Unfortunately, the 20-year delay and lack of updates to the script have left it feeling outdated and unoriginal.
But longtime fans of the books are also finding watching it nostalgic, funny (not that it's trying to be) and feeling a sense of closure because it's finally happened. An Uglies movie finally exists.
One such fan wrote online: "If you keep in mind that the Uglies book came out in 2005 (BEFORE Hunger Games, Divergent, etc) then you'll see the movie's tropes not as cliché or overused, but realise they actually are the blueprint."
And another gushed: "I have read all of the books in this series as they came out, and re-read them multiple times … It has been a dream to see them do a movie/show adaptation of this series, though I always get nervous they'll ruin it for me. They did such a fantastic job bringing everything to life and for once I felt like it matched or was better than what I had imagined."
Netflix hasn't announced plans to adapt any of the seven subsequent books in the Uglies series for the screen.
The ending of the movie strikes the perfect balance between leaving the possibility for a sequel open, while also providing enough closure for fans should it never eventuate — or take another 20 years to see the light of day.
Uglies is streaming now on Netflix.

title: Three decades in the making, a new Australian movie dives into the fascinating world of tent boxing
content:
What: A boxing drama-romance set in 1970s Western Australia.
Starring: Billy Howle, Phoebe Tonkin, Tasma Walton, Tom Bateman, Shaka Cook, Hunter Page-Lochard, Mark Coles Smith.
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: Like putting on gloves.
Innawonga and Yindjibarndi man Shaka Cook grew up with his grandfather's gather-round retellings of glorious tent boxing fights.
"He tells it epically. He was this legend, this heroic figure to us growing up," the actor says. "To get an experience of what that life might have been like, and channel that in an actual boxing tent, is amazing. I couldn't pass it up."
Cook plays Armless in Kid Snow, a film set in 1970s Western Australia during the final days of tent boxing troupes before the sport was regulated largely out of existence.
Shaka Cook as Armless, whose name comes from his schtick: he’s so talented that he’ll still win with one arm tied behind his back. (Supplied/Madman Entertainment)
These troupes would travel from town to town across the country during the 19th and early 20th centuries, fighting those with enough bravado to enter the "ring" – a circus tent where their neighbours would cheer them on.
"A round or two for a pound or two" was a common tagline to bring in punters like Cook's grandfather, who came home from one Perth Royal Show with cash and bragging rights to burn.
A huge alligator owned by boxing tent promoter Fred Brophy's grandfather once sparked a peculiar mystery – but another tent-fighting maestro's mascot was even weirder.
Tent boxing continues to this day in limited capacity in Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory — mostly thanks to two men, Fred Brophy and Michael Karaitiana, whose family tent, the Roy Bell Touring Stadium, was used in Kid Snow.
While tent boxing has been the focus of multiple documentaries, Kid Snow marks the first major fiction film about the sport.
Three decades in the making, it was first written by actor and boxer John Brumpton in the mid-1990s, inspired by a television documentary featuring Karaitiana. Eventually, it found its way to director Paul Goldman (Ego: The Michael Gudinski Story), who was able to shoot the film in Western Australia in 2022, after COVID-19 delays.
"I'd always wondered why a film had never been made in the world of boxing tents," says Goldman. "It's such a rich part of Australian folklore and mythology."
The film follows Irish boxer Kid Snow (Billy Howle), a washed-up former lightweight champion who is burdened by a tragedy that ended the professional careers of himself and his brother Rory (Tom Bateman) and took their father's life (played by Brumpton, now aged out of the lead role).
Rory now unhappily runs their boxing tent, with Kid their star attraction.
As Kid begins to train for a rematch that could turn around both of their lives, a burgeoning relationship with Sunny (Phoebe Tonkin) — a single mother who joins the troupe as a dancer to escape her own dark past — awakens him to a life outside of throwing punches.
Goldman says he was drawn to the character of Sunny (Tonkin), with script reworks centred on developing her strength further. (Supplied/Madman Entertainment)
"I think Kid Snow's reluctantly a boxing film," says Goldman. "Clearly it is! But I hung my hat on the relationship between the two brothers."
For Goldman, whose previous credits include 2002 film Australian Rules and a Ben Cousins documentary, sport is a "wonderful microcosm" to explore bigger issues. Kid Snow covers many, honouring the glory of the ring while acknowledging its brutality.
The director is reluctant to use the term toxic masculinity, citing its overuse, but he says tent boxing "informs our notions of Australian masculinity".
Goldman (pictured) describes filming in Western Australia as a "non-negotiable" even when COVID-19 delays locked him out of the state, viewing the landscape as a character. (Supplied/Madman Entertainment)
"[Sport] is a way to examine society," says Goldman. "In Australia, many of [our] very vexing issues, whether it's racism or domestic violence, reverberate in sport, in a way that people feel more comfortable talking about.
"I've made a lot of films about men. I'm always haunted about a quote from AFL coach Ron Barassi: 'When men get together, wonderful things happen'. It's quoted in Australian Rules, and I can only ever see that being ironic. I'm interested in the damage that men do to one another."
Filming marked the first time in Australia for both Howle and Bateman, with Goldman telling the British actors to watch 1970s outback horror Wake In Fright as preparation.
Shot predominantly in Kalgoorlie and surrounds, Kid Snow's boxers are caked in sweat, desert dirt and, occasionally, blood. The film's colours, under the lens of cinematographer Gary Phillips, blast the day's relentless heat into the cinema, and the sharp relief of night before a foreboding, lonely chill settles in.
"Those two Irish characters should feel like they're shipwrecked," says Goldman. "I wanted it to feel like they were lost, that they were just going around in circles."
Howle had doubled down on a boxing hobby to prepare for the film, but arriving after nine months of fitness training, shooting had been rescheduled. His fighting scenes would no longer be shot first, meaning he had to resort to Kid's 'before' body, transforming into a washed-up chain smoker who is terribly out of shape.
"Smoking and boxing are not good bedfellows, really”, Billy Howle tells ABC Entertainment of his on-set training. (Supplied/Madman Entertainment)
Next came the transformation back to fitness, mirroring the journey we see Kid take, as Howle and his fellow tent boxers worked closely with Big Rigs, a Perth boxing centre.
But it wasn't as simple as learning how to box; Shaka Cook says they had to figure out how to add in the scrappiness and "personality" of a tent fight, all the while still keeping things choreographed and safe.
Shaka Cook, Hunter Page-Lochard and Mark Coles Smith stand behind Billy Howle on set of Kid SNow. (Supplied/Madman Entertainment)
"Boxing can be like a game of chess: If you're throwing this kind of hook, the opponent can move this way or dodge and parry like this. So you know what move they're going to make next," he says.
"In the tent, they're not being serious about destroying someone. It's all fun and games. We want everyone to have a good time, so they keep coming back to have a good time so that the boxers can make some money."
While Rory and Kid's relationship is strained, to say the least, the rest of the troupe try to make do and create joy.
"It's just a band of misfits that end up joining this boxing tent, and they create their own family in hard times," says Cook. "They're all struggling, but yet they have each other."
Armless is one of three Indigenous boxers in Kid Snow's troupe, joined by Lovely (Mark Coles Smith, Mystery Road: Origins) and Lizard (Hunter Page-Lochard, Cleverman). Where Sunny, Kid and Rory see tent boxing as a last resort, Cook says the tent offers "the safest spot" for Armless and co during the 1970s.
Goldman says the cast and crew formed a tight bond during filming, as the remote locations meant they, like the tent boxers, were stuck together during filming. (Supplied/Madman Entertainment)
"Out in the real world, it's like, 'No, you can't come into the pub'. Or, 'Hey, you have a curfew'. The tent represented a haven, a different world," says Cook. "It was like the tent was almost ahead of its time."
Historically, tent boxing offered a rare chance for Indigenous men and boys during the 19th and early 20th centuries to make a living and freely travel away from missions, though this didn't guarantee just treatment.
Kid Snow's moody score was a collaboration between prolific artist Warren Ellis and composer Peter Knight. (Supplied/Madman Entertainment)
While not the focus of the film, Goldman says he wanted to touch upon this legacy, which launched the careers of Indigenous champions Lionel Rose and Tony Mundine.
"I've never been that happy making films that are just there purely for entertainment's sake," says Goldman.
"I like films that get under people's skin, that, when you walk out of the cinema, are going to give you pause to stop and think."
Kid Snow is in cinemas now.

title: Actor, director and radio presenter Lex Marinos dies aged 75
content:
Australian actor, director and former Double J radio presenter Lex Marinos has died aged 75, his family has announced.
A post to his Facebook on Saturday said the former Kingswood Country actor died at home on Friday at his Sydney home, "at a moment of his choosing, surrounded by family and the sounds of Bob Dylan accompanying our vigil".
"There was so much love in the room," the post read.
A recipient of the Medal of the Order of Australia for his services to the performing arts, Marinos was the former deputy chair of the Australia Council as well as a member of the creative and production team for the Opening Ceremony of the Sydney 2000 Olympics.
Marinos started his career as a producer and presenter on 2JJ/2JJJ (the precursors to Double J and Triple J) in the 1970s, going on to present on ABC and commercial radio in the following decades.
But Marinos is perhaps best remembered for his role in the popular 1980s sitcom, Kingswood Country.
He played the role of Bruno, the Italian son-in-law of the main actor, Ted Bulpitt, whose Holden Kingswood car was the highlight of his suburban life.
Marinos was, in fact, of Greek origin. His father emigrated from Greece and his mother was Greek-Australian.
In 2013, Marinos reflected on his multi-cultural roots in the SBS TV series, Who Do You Think You Are?
Lex Marinos on Who Do You Think You Are?
Like his character Bruno, Marinos was born in Wagga Wagga before moving to Sydney and attending North Sydney Boys High School.
Kingswood Country ran for six seasons between 1980 and 1984, delivering 89 episodes and winning the Logie Award for best comedy in 1982 and 1983.
In the series, Bruno was the subject of racist jibes from his father-in-law, played by veteran actor Ross Higgins.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
Marinos also appeared on the small screen in other shows such as The Slap, S.C.O.O.P, Live and Sweaty, Ballzup, Good News Week and World Series Debating.
He also acted in theatrical productions with Nimrod, the APG Sydney Theatre Company and the Melbourne Theatre Company.
His directing credits included the films An Indecent Obsession and Boundaries of the Heart, the television series Bodyline and Embassy, and a number of documentaries and theatre productions.
His writing, meanwhile, appeared in The Bulletin, The Weekend Australian, and the Good Weekend.
To pay tribute to Marinos's career, Wagga Wagga's Museum of the Riverina is planning to hold an exhibition later this year, titled The Lex Factor: From Wagga to the World Stage.

title: Neneh Superstar shows the elite world of ballet through the eyes of a young Black dancer
content:
Famously exacting in the physical endurance, uniformity and precision it requires from its dancers, ballet has served as the heightened dramatic backdrop to many a film – Black Swan, Billy Elliot, Suspiria, The Red Shoes.
What: An uplifting story of a Black girl’s quest to stick it to institutionalised racism in the world of ballet.
Director: Ramzi Ben Sliman
Starring: Oumy Bruni Garrel, Maïwenn, Aïssa Maïga, Steve Tientcheu
When: In selected cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: At times angry and hopeful.
The latest addition to this oeuvre, Neneh Superstar, asks what would happen if a young, working-class Black girl were to attempt to break into the whitewashed and, by extension, white supremacist, world of ballet.
Neneh-Fanta Gnaoré (Oumy Bruni Garrel) is a 12-year-old French girl completely and unabashedly herself: a virtuously talented dancer as comfortable freestyling in the streets to hip-hop as she is performing a pirouette in the formal setting of a ballet school. She's cheeky, impudent, brash and confident.
When she's accepted into the prestigious Paris Opera Ballet School, she comes up against the racism of gatekeepers, hell bent on "guaranteeing the tradition" of the artform, which is another way of saying they're committed to preserving its whiteness.
The racism levelled at Neneh is sometimes so blatant it can seem cartoonish. (Supplied: Limelight)
In one particularly eye-opening sequence where the judges are debating whether to admit Neneh into their school, the racism on display ranges from veiled statements ("we need an aesthetic uniformity") to full-blown eugenics-informed vitriol that calls into question the Black body and the "risk" of Neneh developing hips and breasts in adolescence.
The racism depicted is so blatant it can seem cartoonish, but such are the race relations in an artform decried for lagging behind the rest of the world. The Paris Opera Ballet School specifically has been called out for staging dancers in blackface as recently as 2015, and French Black ballet dancer Chloé Lopes Gomes's experience at Berlin's principal dance company mirrors the racism Neneh faces in the film.
Neneh's Blackness is seen as a distraction in a sea of whiteness, a weakness that renders her incapable of amounting to anything more than an understudy, an aberration.
Neneh's Blackness is seen as a distraction in a sea of whiteness. (Supplied: Limelight)
This racism finds its apotheosis in Marianne Belage (Maïwenn), the ballet company's matriarch who goes out of her way to denigrate Neneh by belittling her or straight-out ignoring her. Neneh's trials and tribulations unfold in tandem with Marianne's, as the latter grapples with her own tortured entry into the ballet world and the way she was also regarded as an outsider.
That a 12-year-old has to shoulder all these malignant, unspoken prejudices while also being bullied by the other girls and without the support of her parents – the dancing company operates akin to a boarding school – is difficult to watch.
Pressures mount on Neneh from every direction: the pressure to be small, which is something all the girls face, though only Neneh's "morphology" is called into question by practitioners who regard her like an exotic exhibit; the pressure to obtain additional private tutoring on top of five days of rigorous training.
The ballet company's matriarch, Marianne Belage (Maïwenn), goes out of her way to denigrate Neneh. (Supplied: Limelight)
It's a credit to the film's nuanced portrayal that Neneh is painted as an anomaly in the ballet scene for reasons that extend beyond her race. Insolent and quick to anger, she's a disruptive force in rehearsals because she's inquisitive and stands up for herself – qualities not appreciated in a setting that values conformity and obsequiousness above all else.
Writer and director Ramzi Ben Sliman imbues the film with enough light-heartedness and joy that things never truly feel hopeless and bleak. The warm saturation of scenes capturing Neneh mirthfully dancing through a ballet shop, and the contentment she derives from belonging to a loving community — memorably captured in a hair salon in one scene — stands in stark contrast to the cool-tinged scenes in the ballet school, where almost everyone is seen as a threat.
Men surprisingly emerge as the biggest champions of Neneh. Her father, played by Steve Tientcheu in an exceedingly heartfelt performance, counters the (to be fair, extremely valid) concerns of her mother (Aïssa Maïga), who struggles to see the viability and feasibility of her daughter becoming a dancer.
Neneh's father, played by Steve Tientcheu, is her greatest champion. (Supplied: Limelight)
In one particularly moving scene towards the end of the movie, he expertly distils Neneh's discomfort in her own skin with resounding lines like: "You're not sick of being Black, you're sick of how Blacks are treated in France."
The amiable Jean-Claude Kahane (Cédric Kahn) is Neneh's main cheerleader within the institutionalised setting – though his ability to supersede the wishes of Marianne, the supposed headmistress of the school, is laughable at times.
If at times reductive and fairytale-like in its swift resolution of deeply entrenched attitudes, Neneh Superstar is perfect for the audience it's intended for – children the same age as Neneh, daring to imagine a reality that seems all but impossible for them.

title: Francis Ford Coppola sues Variety over allegations of misconduct on Megalopolis set
content:
Film director Francis Ford Coppola has sued Variety, saying that a July story that said he ran an unprofessional set with impunity and tried to kiss female extras during the production of his film Megalopolis was false and libellous.
The suit, which seeks at least $US15 million ($22.3 million) from the entertainment trade publication, was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Wednesday, two weeks before the director's long-dreamed-of and self-financed epic is to be released in US and Australian cinemas.
The suit calls the 85-year-old director of The Godfather trilogy and Apocalypse Now a "creative genius" and says others are "jealous" and therefore tell "knowing and reckless falsehoods".
The veteran director once called Megalopolis "a movie that costs a lot of money to make". So was it worth it?
It says Variety's "writers and editors, hiding behind supposedly anonymous sources, accused Coppola of manifest incompetence as a motion picture director, of unprofessional behaviour on the set of his most recent production, Megalopolis, of setting up some type of scheme so that anyone on the set who had a complaint of harassment or otherwise had nowhere to lodge a complaint, and of hugging topless actresses on the set. Each of these accusations was false".
The lawsuit also names the story's reporters, Brent Lang and Tatiana Siegel, as defendants.
It repeatedly says Variety was either knowingly publicising falsehoods or showing reckless disregard for the truth, echoing a standard for libel established by the US Supreme Court.
A Variety spokesperson, Jeffrey Schneider, told The Associated Press, "While we will not comment on active litigation, we stand by our reporters."
Coppola said in a statement on Thursday that nothing in his career compared to the difficult yet triumphant efforts to make Megalopolis.
"It was a collaboration of hundreds of artists, from extras to box office stars, to whom I consistently displayed the utmost respect and my deepest gratitude," Coppola said. "To see our collective efforts tainted by false, reckless and irresponsible reporting is devastating."
Coppola said he "consistently displayed the utmost respect and my deepest gratitude” for the cast and crew of Megalopolis.
The July 26 story used anonymous reports and videos from crew members of the shooting for Megalopolis of a nightclub scene in an Atlanta concert hall in February 2023. The story said Coppola tried to kiss young female extras and "appeared to act with impunity" on the set. It said the film's financial arrangements meant "there were none of the traditional checks and balances in place".
In one video, Coppola, wearing a white suit, walks through a dancing crowd, stopping to apparently lean in to several young women to hug them, kiss them on the cheek or whisper to them. Another video shows him leaning into a woman who pulls away and shakes her head.
All of the women have tops on. The Variety story mentions "topless" extras only in reference to an original report on the allegations in the Guardian.
In a subsequent story, about a week later, which is mentioned only parenthetically in Coppola's lawsuit, one of the women, Lauren Pagone, spoke to Variety and agreed to be identified, saying Coppola left her "in shock" when he touched, hugged and kissed her without her consent.
Pagone said she came forward because another of the extras, Rayna Menz, said in Variety's sister publication, Deadline, that Coppola did nothing to make her or anyone else on the set uncomfortable.
Pagone also filed a lawsuit Monday against Coppola in Georgia, alleging that her treatment on the set amounted to civil assault and civil battery.
Asked for a specific response to that lawsuit, a Coppola representative said there would be no immediate comment beyond the director's broader statement.
Adam Driver stars as architect and time turner Cesar Catilina in Megalopolis. (Supplied: American Zoetrope/Mihai Malaimare)
The AP does not typically name people who say they have been sexually abused unless they come forward publicly, as Pagone has.
Asked about the touching and kissing allegations by The AP before the lawsuit was filed, Coppola said: "I don't even want to [talk about it]. It's a waste of time."
Later in the same interview, without being asked about the subject again, Coppola said: "I'm very respectful of women. I always have been. My mother taught me — she was a little nuts — she said, 'Francis, if you ever make a pass at a girl, that means you disrespect her.' So I never did."
The lawsuit takes particular issue with an assertion in the Variety story that Coppola inadvertently got into a shot and ruined it. The suit says Coppola was well aware that some camera angles would include him, and that he was supposed to appear in the scene anyway.
"The average reader would understand that Coppola was so aged and infirm that he no longer knew how to direct a motion picture," the suit says.
Megalopolis is a Roman epic set in a futuristic New York, starring Adam Driver and Nathalie Emmanuel. Coppola sold off pieces of his considerable wine empire to largely finance it himself.
