title: Blood lust meets queer heart-throb canon in this noir revenge thriller starring Kristen Stewart
content:
Few modern stars radiate soft butch excellence quite like Kristen Stewart, and rarely has such a quality been put to greater use than in Love Lies Bleeding — a sweltering South-Western noir from British director Rose Glass.
What: A queer beefcake romance turned surreal noir thriller.
Starring: Kristen Stewart, Katy M. O'Brian, Ed Harris, Dave Franco, Jena Malone, Dave Franco.
When: In cinemas March 14.
Likely to make you feel: Sweaty and shocked.
Stewart plays Lou, a surly gym manager at the tail end of the 80s with an opaque past and a reputation as the town's "Grade-A dyke".
In one of the film's many lingering gazes, an out-of-town bodybuilder, Jackie (Katy M. O'Brian), catches her eye while training for an upcoming contest.
Following a blood-splattered meet-cute and a sensual introduction to steroids, Jackie moves in with Lou in U-Haul record time.
Having just drifted into town without a dime to her name, Jackie gets by as a waitress at the local gun range — a smuggling front run by the local underworld boss, Lou Sr. (Ed Harris).
Lou and her sister Beth (Jena Malone) steer clear of their dad's operation, but the fragile quiet of their New Mexico refuge is soon jeopardised by Beth's abusive sad-sack husband, JJ (Dave Franco).
Katy M. O'Brian told W magazine she got an audition for the role of Jackie after responding to an A24 tweet with a photo of herself working out and the caption "I'm free". (Supplied: VVS)
A repressed loner turned infatuated lover, Lou is the perfect vessel for Stewart's manic libidinal energy and gamine charm.
An instant entry in the queer heart-throb canon.
Director Rose Glass on Love Lies Bleeding, a lesbian romantic thriller starring Kristen Stewart as a gym manager whose love affair with a female bodybuilder puts her on a collision course with her violent criminal family.
O'Brian also astounds in her breakout role as Jackie, having paid her dues across bit parts in Disney blockbusters in the last decade.
As her protagonist's grind set becomes invigorated by new-found chemical enhancements, O'Brian impressively commits to her euphoric head spins and aggressive delusions without spiralling into schtick.
The less said about the plot, the better.
Love Lies Bleeding wears its inherited genre elements with pride, recalling anything from True Romance and Thelma & Louise to last month's Drive-Away Dolls. But the screenplay from Glass and co-writer Weronika Tofilska deftly rearranges its beats to slippery, sordid ends.
Like any great noir, the overlapping threads of murder, blackmail and betrayal satisfyingly coalesce around the bruising relationships at the film's core.
Love spills over into obsession, obsession calcifies into addiction, and addiction engenders abuse.
Ed Harris has the perfect menacing air, and skull shape, to play Lou Sr. (Supplied: VVS)
Ed Harris continues to demonstrate his aptitude for enigmatic, gravelly-voiced antagonists, this time sporting a mangy skullet. You've almost got to feel sorry for the crime kingpins of cinema and their dwindling dynasties, whose children can't help but trample over their best-laid plans.
Margaret Qualley and Geraldine Viswanathan star in Drive-Away Dolls as two queer women on a road trip who find themselves caught up in criminal activity.
Glass' debut film, Saint Maud, was a psychological thriller that was subsumed by the slow-burning horror trends of its day, but its tale of religious delusion still struck a nerve with its bursts of brutality.
Her follow-up act is no less agonising to watch, with jaw-shattering, flesh-mangling violence splattering across the jagged topography of this badlands revenge tale.
Similarly bracing (but uniquely enticing) are the film's sex scenes, which exude an unvarnished eroticism with inflections of kink. The camera candidly fixates on sweat, egg yolks, spit and other bodily runoff that cinema typically sweeps under the covers.
An earlier montage not-so-subtly splices together Lou and Jackie's shared rhythms of pumping, juicing, thrusting and flexing.
Film still from Love Lies Bleeding (2024) featuring Katy O'Brian (Supplied: VVS)
Glass occasionally approaches the film's excess with a surreal touch; not since the Alien franchise has someone crafted a more visceral, metaphorically loaded scene of bodily expulsion.
Other horror-inspired flourishes feel immediately dated. Lou is haunted by red, neon-drenched visions of her past that resemble a second-generation homage to Nicolas Winding Refn's filmography (Drive; Pusher).
It's a needless diversion from the film's gorgeously grimy patina, in which cinematographer Ben Fordesman finds a compelling middle-ground between period-specific grit and digital modern sheen.
Love Lies Bleeding arrives after years of gnawing hunger for complex female antiheroes — as evidenced by the coining of the "Good for Her" Cinematic Universe.
Not coincidentally, this embrace of women's wrongs has become near synonymous with A24's savvily branded, endlessly meme-able slate, to which this film belongs.
Jaw-shattering, flesh-mangling violence splatters across this badlands revenge tale. (Supplied: VVS)
The knotty dynamic between Jackie and Lou may not be as easy to swallow. Glass cleverly plays on the audience's own blood lust, dishing out satisfyingly gnarly punishments to deserving victims — but what happens when that rage and power no longer has a righteous outlet?
Amid all the film's pulpy pleasures, the pain they inflict on each other — and on each other's behalf — is genuinely unsettling. It's impossible to find a clean path through a story like this, where the threat of violence hangs on the end of every interaction and transaction.
Murder is a nasty, messy business, but it's nothing compared to love.
Love Lies Bleeding is in cinemas now.

title: From Beatlemania to Swifties: Why female fans aren't taken seriously, but males are considered 'experts'
content:
A few years ago, author and journalist Tabitha Carvan became obsessed with British actor Benedict Cumberbatch.
Fuelled by the worldwide success of the TV show Sherlock, she joined the ranks of the "Cumberbitches", a community of women of all ages who, quite simply, adored Benedict Cumberbatch.
At the height of her "Cumbermania", she would seek out Cumberbatch in films and TV, watch online interviews with him and print out photos of him to adorn her desk.
"It coincided with a personal time of my life which was being at home with my young kids and not having much of an outlet," she says.
"It was about finding something that was just for me, that lit me up for no reason other than it just fired up all the synapses that bridge pleasure and happiness and joy and connection."
Carvan happily displayed her Cumbermania at her work desk. (Supplied: Jimmy Walsh )
But the more joy her obsession brought her, the more suspicion it elicited.
Friends and strangers alike would interrogate her: Why was she acting like a starstruck teenager? Shouldn't she be spending her time more productively? And what on earth did her husband think?
It prompted her to write a book about her and others' journeys into Cumbermania, titled This Is Not A Book About Benedict Cumberbatch.
What she discovered was not a desperate coven of delusional women, as they were often portrayed, but a radical expression of female joy — and the fight to keep it alive.
Carvan is well aware that Benedict Cumberbatch likely has no idea who she is.
In 1956, sociologist R. Richard Wohl and anthropologist Donald Horton coined the term "parasocial relationship" to describe a one-sided relationship with a public figure that springs out of exposure to mass media.
"The definition of parasocial is non-reciprocated: I know the person, they don't know me back," explains Gayle S Stever, a professor of social and behavioural studies at Empire State University of New York.
Parasocial relationships can be intense. But what's it like to be on the receiving end?
"Parasocial interaction happens while you're consuming media. [The person] is talking to you from the screen and you're listening, and it feels like they're talking to you … We refer to that as the illusion of intimacy."
While public figures have always attracted admirers, Dr Stever says parasocial relationships as we now know them can be traced back to the popularisation of network television.
"In the 70s, soaps were on every day, so if you were interacting daily with your favourite celebrity, there was a tremendous potential to develop an affinity for that person," she tells ABC RN's All In The Mind.
This was furthered by the rise of talk shows, in which hosts would address the audience directly, and later, by social media.
"It feels personal, it feels intimate, and so the parasocial relationship grows from that mediated interaction. You walk away from the TV and you're still mentally interacting with the character, or the actor or both," Dr Stever says.
That sense of comfort and connection drives us to "seek proximity" to that person or character.
"If it's a singer, you go to one of their concerts. If it's an actor and they're going to appear at a convention, you go meet them," Dr Stever says.
Taylor Swift greets fans on the red carpet of the ARIAs. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)
Carvan says this dynamic is often misunderstood.
"People think … that the relationship is a kind of delusion and that if you have a parasocial relationship, you don't have a grasp on reality," Carvan says.
"But if you have ever read a novel and thought about a character in that novel, you understand that you can have a connection and an investment in a person you don't know or a person who's not even real.
And while female fans are often depicted as obsessive, creepy or downright dangerous — think sadistic superfan Annie Wilkes in Stephen King's cult classic, Misery, for example — Carvan says the vast majority are enacting a safe, enjoyable fantasy.
"I think most fans are aware that the person they love or are interested in is the public projection of that person, as represented by the movies they're in or the songs they make, and it's not real," she says.
Experts have long identified that male and female fans are viewed very differently in the popular imagination.
"When women get obsessed with or passionate about a musician or an actor or a celebrity, they're represented as having this kind of maniacal, hysterical interest in it which overtakes their entire life … but men have been doing this for a very long time," Carvan says.
Carvan says male sports fans are judged less harshly than female pop music fans, although their behaviour is similar. (AAP: Joe Castro)
She gives the example of "Dylanologists", a subset of the largely male fanbase of musician Bob Dylan, who define themselves as music critics.
"The detail with which Bob Dylan has been documented by these fans is unprecedented and unsurpassed by any other fan group and it's regarded as the height of music criticism," she says.
"They might like to say that they have an objective appreciation of his art — and I'm sure they do as well — but they love him. Of course they love him; they couldn't invest that much time in the project if they didn't love him."
While male fans are seen as taste-makers and aficionados, female fans are often described as mindless hordes — despite driving massive economic and cultural change (hello, Swifteconomics).
In an infamous 1964 essay, English journalist Paul Johnson described Beatles fans "who scream themselves into hysteria" as "the least fortunate of their generation, the dull, the idle, the failures".
The term 'Beatlemania' was coined to refer to the fervour of the band's mostly female fanbase. (Getty: Mirrorpix)
Skip to 2012, and experts described the mostly female Justin Bieber fandom as "a group response set off by emotions and hormones", which young men don't experience because they are "wired differently".
Sascha Samlal, a PhD candidate in cultural studies at the University of Melbourne, says female fans are shamed both by mainstream culture and within their own communities.
"The top-down shaming … is this idea that any sort of feminine cultural product is seen as less than," she says.
"A lot of our ideas about what constitutes good taste really centres around what is masculine, what is intellectual, and what should be taken seriously."
Despite the prevailing idea that fandom is the domain of teenagers, Dr Stever says research shows that parasocial relationships are part of life across all age groups.
"One of the misconceptions about this is that this is an adolescent thing," she says.
"Developing a crush on a celebrity is a common lifelong thing, and for most people, it's just a fun thing."
Harry Styles fans show off their feather boas before a show. (Supplied)
Carvan says that for women particularly, there's pressure to grow out of fandom as they age.
"You're supposed to become more well-rounded; you like things in a balanced way, [you have] productive hobbies and you become a professional and maybe a partner or a mother or caregiver," she says.
That's particularly true when time becomes a precious resource. In Australia, Treasury statistics show women have an average of 31 minutes less free time per day, with that gap widening to an hour and 17 minutes for women aged 15 to 24.
"It is difficult for women to maintain that culture of leisure, full stop, and then to maintain a culture of leisure around something that society deems should be left behind in adolescence, that's doubly hard," Carvan says.
Yet there's a certain power in finding kinship and community with other fans, whether Swifties, Harries [fans of Harry Styles] or members of the BTS ARMY or BeyHive, Ms Samlal says.
"One of my participants in my research described the intensity of the relationship as having sisters — and she's talking about people she's never even met," she says.
"That sense of belonging often results in a sort of effectual power, so often fans can be the impetus for social change."
Devotees of K-pop — short for Korean pop — have made fighting for social issues a core part of their identity.
That's particularly true of K-Pop fans, whose political activism has been widely documented.
Ms Samlal says creative practices like writing fan fiction can be another form of political power, by "mapping onto a celebrity what you want to see in the world".
She gives the example of "Larries" in the 2010s, the fans who imagined a romantic relationship between former One Direction bandmates Harry Styles and Louis Tomlinson.
"I view that as … a lot of people mapping a queer future onto a mainstream media star, something that at the time was not often seen and not accepted," she says.
For Carvan, devoting time to loving Benedict Cumberbatch was radical in a more personal way.
Since Benedict Cumberbatch, Carvan has fallen for Harry Styles. She and her husband attended his Sydney show last year. (Supplied)
Her advice is to welcome that joy with open arms.
"If you're surprised by how good it feels or how much fun it is … let it happen," she says.
"That's what makes it transgressive, to keep it alive and say, 'No matter what age I am, no matter how I look, no matter where I live, I can actually just feel feelings that are good for me'."

title: Can Godzilla Minus One's Oscar win disrupt the Marvel machine?
content:
When American Fiction writer and director Cord Jefferson collected his best original screenplay Oscar he used his speech to call Hollywood out.
"I understand that this is a risk-averse industry," he told the audience.
"But $200 million movies are also a risk. But you take the risk anyway. Instead of making one $200 million movie, make 20 $10 million movies. Or 50 $4 million movies."
Jefferson might have said it out loud, but the films sweeping the statuettes quietly confirmed the potential low- and mid-budget films have in an industry that won't stop pushing mega-blockbusters with enormous price tags.
While mega-budget blockbusters are often locked out of the more artistically prestigious Oscar categories, one place they get a look in is visual effects: Impressive budgets frequently means slicker effects.
This year's contenders were:
Despite costing a fraction of its competitors, this epic Japanese-language Kaiju production took home the award, becoming the first Godzilla film to win an Oscar in the character's 70-year movie history.
Even director Takashi Yamazaki seemed surprised when he and his team — carrying tiny golden Godzillas and wearing matching Godzilla shoes — took to the stage to accept the award.
"This is proof everyone has a chance."
The Godzilla Minus One team accept the award for best visual effects at the 96th Academy Awards with their mini Godzillas. (Getty Images: Kevin Winter)
Godzilla Minus One sees the giant lizard terrorise post-WWII Japan and has been universally praised for its larger-than-life effects, a lot of which happen on water — a notoriously tricky VFX challenge.
Not only was Godzilla Minus One critically acclaimed, it made a fair chunk of change too, recouping $161 million ($US107 million) internationally.
"There is a history of low-finance horror finding mass audiences in congested film distribution markets," explains Steve Gaunson, an associate professor in cinema studies at RMIT.
With youthful energy and a quintessentially Australian soundtrack, the debut film from the RackaRacka brothers hits all the right notes.
"The Blair Witch Project was shot for $US60,000 and grossed $US250 million at the box office. In Australia we had similar, albeit [on a] smaller scale, with Talk to Me grossing $US92 million from a budget of $US4 million."
Gaunson says the issue smaller films face in a blockbuster world is not so much their production budgets, but their marketing budgets — which can add upwards of $150 million to the overall cost of a film.
"Unless a film can find an audience early into its release who can build a strong social media buzz, most films will often struggle to recoup their budget," he says.
Essentially, lower budget films like Godzilla Minus One or last year's best picture winner Everything Everywhere All at Once ($38 million budget) need substantial organic support before they can even dream of reaching the exposure of one Marvel marketing budget.
When Marvel VFX workers in the US voted to unionise late last year, it brought to light the poor treatment of employees.
"It was almost six months of overtime every day. I was working seven days a week, averaging 64 hours a week on a good week," one anonymous whistleblower told Vulture.
In comparison, Yamazaki told Vulture that he works hard to make sure he runs a "white" company: one that doesn't exploit their workers.
"We really try to avoid long hours but, if you do, it's a very welcoming environment in which to spend a few extra hours," he said.
"Hopefully, in due time, VFX budget increases will allow for more improvements. I am looking forward to the day when we can pay creatives more."
But nothing highlighted the disparity, between the size of blockbuster budgets compared to their quality, than the release of Dune: Part Two earlier this month.
At a production cost of $287 million ($38 million more than the first edition, thanks to pandemic-related costs) Dune: Part Two is considered towards the lower end of blockbuster budgets.
However, Denis Villeneuve's film is being lauded for its stunning special effects, especially compared to the look of recent films like Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania ($416 million) with its disturbing CGI villain, or even recent Universal tentpole Argylle ($302 million) which, you know, featured this scene.
Both these films underperformed at the box office: Quantumania became one of the rare Marvel films not to break the half-a-billion mark (a flop in Marvel's eyes); Argylle brought home a paltry $142 million worldwide — half of its reported production budget.
Despite the diminishing returns on mega-budget films, Gaunson says Hollywood seems committed to staying the course.
"Ultimately, studios are now producing few films but with high productions," he says.
We asked two experts to dish on the reasons it can sometimes take days, weeks or months until international films make it to our cinemas.
"Rather than produce five action movies in an iffy market, they are pooling all of their budgets into one mega film with an all-star cast."
It gets even tougher for low- and mid-budget films to break through in a smaller market like Australia, where our number of cinema screens pales in comparison to the US.
"Audiences have never had such a wide choice of films, which is causing issues for theatrical distribution. With ticket prices also at an all-time high [Australia's are some of the most expensive worldwide], audiences are cautious on spending money on a mediocre film," Gaunson says.
"Therefore theatres are tending to book out known popular and crowd-pleaser films, rather than offer a wider selection for its audiences."
For a long time, it was unclear if Godzilla Minus One would even make it to Australian cinemas. But by the film gods' grace it debuted locally in December 2023 (a month after the Japanese premiere) to a very short run in select cinemas.
As Yamazaki confirmed in his post-Oscars interview, we still don't know when or if the film will come to streaming.
Interview with the Godzilla Minus One team after their Oscar win
But while Godzilla Minus One's Oscar victory might notch one up for the little guys, Gaunson isn't confident it will bring around industry-wide change.

title: Oscars producer apologises for Best Picture slip-up and Kimmel reveals he was told not to mention Trump
content:
A producer for the Oscars has apologised for how the winner of Best Picture was announced.
Hollywood great Al Pacino was in charge of handing out the final award for the night but confused many people because he only read out the winner and not out any of the nominees.
As he opened the envelope to reveal the winner, Pacino said, "My eyes see Oppenheimer," without mentioning anything else.
The cast and crew of Oppenheimer then looked at each other confused before going on stage to collect their seventh award of the night.
In an interview with Variety, Oscars producer Molly McNearney said it was a "creative decision" to not have the actor read out all 10 nominees due to fears the show would have been too long.
"By the time you get to the end of the show, you've seen all 10 best picture clip packages," she told Variety.
"People just want to hear who wins, and they're pretty ready for the show to be over."
The cast and crew of Oppenheimer accepts the award for Best Picture. (Reuters: Mike Blake)
She said that was why Pacino's speech did not include a clip package showing all the nominated films.
"I apologise if our decision to not have to read through all those nominations put him in a tough spot," she told Variety.
Ms McNearney added that Pacino's decision not to use the traditional "And the Oscar goes to …" did make things "a little confusing".
She noted, however, it added some excitement, saying it was live television and you never knew what could happen.
The Godfather actor also addressed how he announced the winner of the Best Picture award, saying he was following the instructions of the producers.
"There seems to be some controversy about my not mentioning every film by name last night before announcing the best picture award," Pacino said in a statement.
"I just want to be clear it was not my intention to omit them, rather a choice by the producers not to have them said again since they were highlighted individually throughout the ceremony.
"I realise being nominated is a huge milestone in one's life and to not be fully recognised is offensive and hurtful."
In his statement, Pacino said he "deeply empathises" with the people who were slighted by the oversight.
This year's Oscars has had plenty of iconic moments, from John Cena streaking through to Ryan Gosling glamming it up as Ken.  Here are the key moments from the 2024 Academy Awards.
Oscars host Jimmy Kimmel also weighed in on the announcement controversy while speaking to ABC America talk show hosts Kelly Ripa and Mark Consuelos after the show.
"I guess he's never watched an awards show before. It seems like everyone in America knows the rhythm of how it's supposed to go down to the, 'And the Oscar goes to …' But not Al Pacino! God bless him."
The Oscars host also discussed former US president Donald Trump's social media rant about him, saying he was told by people backstage not to say mention it on stage.
"They're like, 'You've got a little bit of time,' and I was like, 'I'm reading the Trump tweet,' and they're like, 'No, no, don't read that,'" Kimmel told the ABC America talk show hosts.
Jimmy Kimmel has hosted the Oscars four times. (Photo by Rick Polk/ Variety via Getty Images)
However Kimmel read out Mr Trump's post from his phone.
"Has there EVER been a WORSE HOST than Jimmy Kimmel at The Oscars," Kimmel read.
"His opening was that of a less than average person trying too hard to be something which he is not, and never can be."
Not missing a beat, Kimmel thanked Mr Trump for his viewership before asking: "Isn't it past your jail time?"
The former president also said on his Truth Social account that having a different host would increase audience and TV ratings.
Variety said the 96th annual Academy Awards ceremony drew in 19.5 million viewers.
The viewership was up by just under 4 per cent from 18.8 million viewers in 2023.
Kimmel has hosted the award show three other times, in 2023, 2018 and 2017.

title: Oppenheimer dominated the 2024 Academy Awards. But did it break the record for most Oscar wins of all time?
content:
After blazing its way through awards season, the blockbuster biopic Oppenheimer took home the most Oscar trophies this year, including Best Picture.
The film, which grossed more than US$953.8 million ($1.4 billion), had 13 nominations ahead of the 96th Academy Awards.
This gave it a strong chance of breaking a decades-old record for the most Oscar wins by a single film.
So how did it fare? We take a look at whether Oppenheimer dominated the all-time list of award-winners too.
If you still haven't seen it, Oppenheimer is a three-hour historical drama that follows the life of American theoretical physicist J Robert Oppenheimer.
The movie focuses on how Oppenheimer, played by Cillian Murphy, spearheaded the invention of the atomic bomb during World War II.
J Robert Oppenheimer (left) is portrayed by Cillian Murphy (right) in the Oppenheimer film. (AP/Universal)
It also explores the moral and political issues he faced in creating this deadly weapon, which would later be used in the US bombings of Japanese cities Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
"We made a film about the man who created the atomic bomb, and for better or worse, we are living in Oppenheimer's world," Murphy said as he held his first Oscar for Best Actor on Monday.
"So I would really like to dedicate this to the peacemakers everywhere."
Cillian Murphy clinched his first Oscar for his performance in Oppenheimer. (Reuters: Carlos Barria)
The win caps a successful awards season for the 47-year-old Irish actor who also picked up a Golden Globe, a BAFTA and a Screen Actors Guild award for his performance.
While Oppenheimer is steeped in nuclear science, Murphy had previously said he "didn't really waste too much time on the physics" to prepare for the role.
Instead, he honed in on the "humanity and the emotion, and the complexity and the morality of the character".
Oppenheimer has won seven Oscars after being nominated in 13 categories, making it the biggest victor of the year.
Having clinched 22 other awards at this year's major ceremonies, the film now has a total haul of 30 trophies.
This brings to a close the Barbenheimer battle, which began when Barbie and Oppenheimer were released at the same time in July last year.
The Mattel doll movie won out at the box office after grossing US$1.45 billion ($2.2 billion).
But it lost on the awards front after it failed to pick up major award categories this season and only nabbed a single Oscar for Best Song.
British-American filmmaker Christopher Nolan had been favoured to win the Oscar for Oppenheimer after racking up Best Director trophies all season.
Known for his cerebral films, Nolan had lost out on Oscars for Memento in 2002 and Dunkirk in 2019, but he finally clinched the statuette on Monday.
In his acceptance speech, he thanked the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences for the honour and noted that movies are just a little over 100 years old.
"We don't know where this incredible journey [of film] is going from here," Nolan said.
"But to know that you think I am a meaningful part of it means the world to me."
Christopher Nolan won the best director trophy at every major awards show this year. (Reuters)
In the Supporting Actor category, Robert Downey Jr also claimed his first Academy Award.
The 58-year-old actor, who was nominated for an Oscar in 1993 before his career was derailed by drug use, won his honour for playing Oppenheimer's professional nemesis Lewis Strauss.
"I'd like to thank my terrible childhood and the Academy, in that order," Downey joked before he saluted his wife, Susan.
He said she had found him as a "snarly rescue pet" and "loved him back to life".
Three films are tied for most Oscar wins in history.
Ben-Hur, Titanic and The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King hold 11 Academy Awards each.
Oppenheimer has fallen short of that, after losing six of its 13 nominations.
It did not win Best Adapted Screenplay, which went to Cord Jefferson for American Fiction. It also lost Best Costume Design, Best Makeup and Hairstyling and Best Production Design, which were all won by Poor Things.
Emily Blunt lost to Da'Vine Joy Randolph in The Holdovers in the Best Supporting Actress category and Oppenheimer lost to Zone of Interest for Best Sound.
While seven Oscars still puts Oppenheimer among the most accomplished films ever, it's a pretty long list.

title: Cinemagoer 'shaking with rage' after screening of Oscar-winning Holocaust film allegedly disrupted by Nazi salute
content:
Victoria Police is investigating after a group of people allegedly voiced hate speech and performed a Nazi salute during the screening of a film about the Holocaust at a Melbourne cinema.
The group were watching The Zone of Interest — a film based on the story of real-life Auschwitz commander Rudolf Höss and his family — at Cinema Nova in Carlton, on Saturday night.
The UK film this week won the Oscar for best international film and for best sound.
The Zone of Interest became the first British movie to win best international film in this year's Oscars. (Supplied: Madman)
A Cinema Nova spokesperson said staff were informed of a disturbance during the film and investigated immediately.
They said a group of four men and one woman were "vocalising hate speech to create a scene inside the auditorium".
"While staff did not catch these individuals in the act despite spending an extended time in the cinema on two separate occasions, the group admitted to creating a scene when confronted by management at the conclusion of the session," the spokesperson said.
The group were then escorted out of the premises by security and the incident was reported to police.
In a statement a Victoria Police spokesperson said the circumstances surrounding the incident were yet to be determined and encouraged any witnesses or anyone with vision of the event to contact Crime Stoppers.
Louise Shuter said her daughter was at the screening of the movie and witnessed the event.
"It was a pretty upsetting incident," Ms Shuter told ABC Radio Melbourne.
She said the group were heard laughing throughout the film before performing a Nazi salute and making inflammatory comments.
Ms Shuter said her daughter was harassed by the group after complaining to cinema staff.
"She was just shaking with rage, upset, just shocked," she said.
Performing a Nazi salute is a criminal offence in Australia after the government outlawed the radically offensive gesture last year.
Those found guilty of the offence face up to 12 months' imprisonment and a $23,000 fine.

title: Emma Stone's broken dress, John Cena's lack of any clothes — here's what went down at the Oscars
content:
This year's Oscars had an almost naked John Cena gingerly stepping across the stage to present an award, a wardrobe malfunction from Emma Stone and a cameo from Messi the dog. But it will be remembered for something else entirely.
As the three-hour ceremony neared the business end, the show ground to a halt to clear the way for Ryan Gosling to glam it up with a rousing rendition of I'm Just Ken, complete with a singalong and some special guests.
Here are the key moments from the 2024 Academy Awards:
After the roster of Original Song nominees performed earlier in the show, Gosling took to the stage to perform Barbie movie hit I'm Just Ken in a show-stopping performance.
Opening the performance from his seat in the audience behind a giggling Margot Robbie, Gosling — sporting a sparkly pink suit with matching gloves — made his way to the stage to be joined by a troupe of cowboy-hatted dancers.
As the number shifted from power ballad to operatic rock, Gosling disappeared under giant Barbie masks, emerging in time for Guns and Roses guitarist Slash to let rip with a typically frenetic solo.
Slash joined Gosling on stage, showing he is also just Ken.  (Getty: Kevin Winter)
Gosling then descended into the crowd to pass the mic around for a singalong, first joined by Robbie, America Ferrera and Greta Gerwig before he made his way to Stone. The performance ended with Gosling back on stage with the other Kens, including Simu Liu and Kingsley Ben-Adir.
Margot Robbie stunned fans as she opted out of a final pink Barbie number. (Getty: Mike Coppola)
Stepping away from the Barbie pink once again, Robbie stepped onto the red carpet in a gorgeous black Versace dress.
There was some suggestion the outfit could be a nod to Princess Diana's iconic black revenge dress because Robbie was not nominated for the Best Actress award.
Previous red carpet appearances from Robbie this awards season have been themed around iconic Barbie looks from past decades.
Emma Stone blamed the Kenergy for her wardrobe mishap.  (Reuters: Mike Blake)
After making her way to the stage to accept the Best Actress award, Stone opened her speech by warning the crowd that the back of her dress had "broken".
She blamed the I'm Just Ken moment for the costume drama.
A visibly shaken Stone — whose win is her second in the category — also told the crowd to avert their eyes as she walked offstage.
And no we aren't talking about the Argentinian footballer.
This is Messi.
The Anatomy of a Fall star looked adorable in the audience and was even spotted clapping for some of the winners.
Sadly, there was no award for Best Good Boy at the Oscars.
John Cena made a last-minute attempt to get out of appearing naked on stage.  (Getty: Kevin Winter)
From Versace to vastly naked, John Cena took to the stage in nothing but a pair of sandals to hand out the Best Costume Design award.
Cena tried at the last minute to bail out of the streaking bit before reluctantly coming on to the stage.
The wrestling star asked host Jimmy Kimmel to help read out the awards — given he couldn't quite move the envelope without the show becoming R rated.
And in case you were wondering, no, he wasn't fully naked. We have proof.
So it turns out John Cena was not entirely naked after all. ( Photo by Al Seib/AMPAS/Getty Images)
Well, at least Emily Blunt and Ryan Gosling tried to end it.
Emily Blunt and Ryan Gosling tried to end their rivalry. They did not succeed.  (Getty: Kevin Winter)
Gosling started by suggesting to Blunt it was time to end the rivalry.
Blunt agreed and said there wasn't much of a rivalry with the way the awards season had gone. But Gosling's Ken-splanation of why it's Barbenheimer and not Oppenbarbie didn't go down well:
"I think you guys are at the tail end of that because you were riding Barbie's coat-tails all summer."
The Iron Man star won his first Oscar, taking the gong for Best Supporting Actor for his role in Oppenheimer.
"I would like to thank my terrible childhood and the academy in that order," Downey Jr said to open his acceptance speech.
"I would like to thank my veterinarian … I meant wife Susan Downey over there.
"She found me a snarling rescue pet and you loved me back to life, and that is why I am here."
He admitted in the speech he needed the film more than it needed him.
Also taking home his first Oscar tonight was Wes Anderson. He won Best Live Short Film for The Wonderful Story of Henry Sugar, but was not at the show to accept the award.
Godzilla's not so scary when in mini form.  (Getty: Kevin Winter)
Masaki Takahashi, Takashi Yamazaki, Kiyoko Shibuya and Tatsuji Nojima accepted the Best Visual Effects award for Godzilla Minus One by bringing mini Godzillas on stage with them.
In his acceptance speech, director Yamazaki said: "Even then the possibility of standing on this stage seemed out of reach, and the moment we were nominated we felt like Rocky Balboa.
The Academy Awards began with a political statement from some entertainers on the red carpet.
Ramy Youssef, Billie Eililsh and Finneas O'Connell on the Oscars red carpet.  (Getty: Alberto Rodriguez)
Billie Eilish, Ramy Youssef, Mark Ruffalo, Ava DuVernay and Mahershala Ali were among the performers who wore pins as part of a movement launched by Artists4Ceasefire, which is a group of people in the entertainment industry demanding a ceasefire in the Gaza-Israel conflict.
During the ceremony, when the Holocaust drama The Zone of Interest was the first British movie to win the Oscar for Best International Film, director Jonathan Glazer, who is Jewish, used his speech to speak out against Israel's "occupation" of the Palestinian Territory and its attacks on Gaza, as well as the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel.
"All our choices were made to reflect and confront us in the present, not to say, 'Look what they did then,' rather, 'Look what they do now,'" Glazer said.
"Our film shows where dehumanisation leads, at its worst. Right now, we stand here as men who refute their Jewishness and the Holocaust being hijacked by an occupation which has led to conflict for so many innocent people.
"Whether the victims of October the 7th in Israel, or the ongoing attack on Gaza, all the victims, this dehumanisation, how do we resist?"
The Zone of Interest explores questions of complicity, while depicting the mundane lives of a Nazi family who live adjacent to the Auschwitz death camp.
From Anatomy of a Fall and Barbie to Oppenheimer and The Zone of Interest, here is the full list of nominees for the Academy Awards.
When director Mstyslav Chernov accepted the Documentary Feature Film award for 20 Days in Mariupol, his acknowledgement of the award came with a caveat.
"I'm honoured," Chernov said. "But probably I will be the first director on this stage who will say, 'I wish I never made this film.'
"I wish to be able to exchange this to Russia never attacking Ukraine, never occupying our cities.
"I wish to give all the recognition to Russia not killing tens of thousands of my fellow Ukrainians. I wish for them to release all the hostages, all the soldiers who are protecting their land, all the civilians who are now in their jails. But I cannot change the history. I cannot change the past."
The In Memoriam part of the ceremony was introduced in Russian with a clip from late opposition leader and activist Alexei Navalny.
His words, "The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good people to do nothing," were flashed on screen.
Jimmy Kimmel hosted the Oscars, held in Los Angeles. (Photo by Rich Polk/Variety via Getty Images)
Host Jimmy Kimmel took a jab at Alabama senator Katie Britt, who gave the Republican response to US President Joe Biden's State of the Union address last week.
In reference to Emma Stone's role in Poor Things, in which she's child-like, Kimmel joked: "Emma Stone played an adult lady with the brain of a child, kind of like the lady that gave the State of the Union rebuttal."
He later finished the ceremony by reading out one of the first reviews of his performance, panning Kimmel as "a less than average person trying too hard to be something he is not".
Kimmel then revealed the anonymous review to be from a Donald Trump social media post, before quipping "Isn't it past your jail time?".
Hollywood great Al Pacino appeared to have slipped up a little as he announced the winner of Best Picture by forgetting to read out the nominees.
He told the audience to announce the winner he had to "go to the envelope."
He called out the winner by saying "my eyes see Oppenheimer" without mention of any of the other nominations.
A slip up, or straight to the point? Who knows.

title: Why do we still have to wait so long for films when they're already out in the US?
content:
Of the 10 films up for Best Picture at this year's Oscar awards, half were released in Australia in an entirely different calendar year than in the US.
Just three of the films were released in Australia before they aired in US cinemas. And, even then, Australian audiences only got Barbenheimer and Killers of the Flower Moon a day earlier.
In an increasingly globalised and extremely online world, why is this still happening?
"It used to be the case when films were 35-millimetre prints, a studio or distributor could only afford to print a limited number of films," explains Lori Flekser, executive director of the Motion Picture Distributors Association of Australia.
"And those films would then literally travel across the seas to other countries."
So, for example, a US film print would start off in America, then travel overseas to the UK, and eventually end up in Australia. Australian films would have the opposite journey: starting here and then travelling the rest of the globe.
But that all changed with the advent of digital cinema. These days, distributors each have their own digital film master files.
"With the big Hollywood films and the big studio blockbusters, it's become more and more essential to release them on what we call 'day and date', which is a simultaneous day and date release," Ms Flekser says.
"This actually usually means Australia gets the films sooner, because we are a day ahead of the US."
In an "ideal world", she says all films would use the day and date release strategy, like the (relentless) ones we saw for Barbenheimer. Simultaneous releases allow for global marketing campaigns, particularly pertinent in the age of social media and platforms like Letterboxd. Distributors also believe simultaneous releases help decrease piracy.
Martin Scorcese's Killers of the Flower Moon (pictured) was one of three 2024 Best Picture-nominated films that enjoyed a simultaneous release — out of 10.  (Supplied: Apple+)
"We often lead audiences to believe they're hard done by in Australia and the result of that is often a sense of resentment about cinema, and it also leads people to feel more entitled about piracy due to the idea there's a lack of care that results in films not being released here," Ms Flekser says.
"That is so far from the truth … cinema is a business with a lot of current challenges."
"To go global and release a film big, you need the budget. The smaller films just don't have that and it's just a lot easier to do it country by country," explains Steve Gaunson, an associate professor in cinema studies at RMIT.
And there are only so many days in a week, and so many cinema screens.
Stephen Gaunson says simultaneous releases like the one engineered for Oppenheimer (pictured) require a huge budget.  (Supplied: Universal)
"We have around 2,100 screens in Australia, while the US has over 40,000," Ms Flekser says.
"Competition for screens here is intense. [On top of that,] distributors and exhibitors have to try and find times that are likely to attract the biggest audiences. Then they have to put a lot of money into marketing the film in a way that brings audiences to those films at a time that is convenient for those audiences."
The Holdovers won Golden Globes for Paul Giamatti and Da'Vine Joy Rudolph. Now the movie is finally in Australian cinemas, is it any good?
"Our holiday periods don't really match up [with most of the world]," Dr Gaunson adds.
Stars also have a huge impact on marketing. Unfortunately, they have exceedingly busy schedules.
Say distributors wanted Da'Vine Joy Randolph of the Oscar-nominated dramedy The Holdovers in Australia to do promotion.
"If that film was released in Australia at the same time as the US, she can't be in two places at once. But if there's a bit of a lag, she can do the US press tour, then come to Australia and do Australian press," Dr Gaunson explains.
So that's possibly part of the reason a film that is all about Christmas ended up being released here on January 11.
Actor Da’Vine Joy Randolph reacts to Oscar buzz around her performance in The Holdovers
Then there's the issue of competition.
"Generally, [distributors] won't want to release films at a period of high competition. The Barbie-Oppenheimer moment was really interesting," says Dr Gaunson.
"Wes Anderson's Asteroid City was going to come out a couple of weeks later in Australia, but they decided to hold back on the film because it had been released in the US and hadn't been performing well and they thought, 'Well, everyone's off to see Barbie and Oppenheimer so they must be a big fatigued with the cinema'."
He's the screenwriter behind The Favourite, Cruella and The Secret Life of Us. Now Australian Tony McNamara is up for an Oscar for his work on Poor Things.
This is where Ms Flekser thinks the perception that films are automatically released later in Australia (which she says is a "myth") comes from.
"[Independents] are often distributed by smaller businesses who don't have a lot of money for marketing and publicity," she explains.
"Often they want to wait until films have been released internationally to see how they perform.
After an international run, Ms Flekser says "distributors can better determine who went to see the film overseas and who they should aim their marketing at here".
This strategy also sees them benefit from any hype films garner during international showings.
Lori Flekser says distributors have no way of knowing which film festival darlings like Anatomy of a Fall (pictured) will break through to the mainstream. (Supplied: Madman)
And, in some cases, distributors are playing catch-up.
"If we look at May December, which was released [here] by Transmission Films. It went onto screens in America on November 17, but Transmission already had a local film, The Royal Hotel, releasing a week later, and two other releases in the following month.
"They're a tiny operation. The resources and the funds to put into another big release would have been an enormous burden, so they were forced to wait."
The Australian actor stars as detective Aaron Falk in the second movie in The Dry series, adapted from Jane Harper's murder mystery series.
And even if smaller distributors do have the capacity to go ahead with screenings for independent films, it doesn't mean there are screens available for them amid the deluge of Hollywood blockbusters.
"An independent cinema in Sydney was only screening Dune [right after its release]," Ms Flekser says.
It might be tempting to look to the streaming industry's widespread adoption of the simultaneous release model as proof cinema could do the same if it really wanted to.
But Dr Gaunson says it's not that simple.
While he admits it's hard to predict exactly where cinema will go with its distribution strategies, Dr Gaunson thinks we may see more simultaneous blockbuster releases, but a continuation of holding holiday and children's movies for the right time.
As for the rest of the world's theatrical offerings?
Echoing Harry Styles, he says: "I think it will be a matter of working out — what do people want to see at the cinema? Because it's been made for the cinema experience, and if you don't see it on the big screen you're missing out on what the film is really doing."
In which case, waiting will likely still be involved.

title: Who can pick the 2024 Oscar winners more accurately — a film critic or a mathematician?
content:
Last year, we asked a film reviewer and a mathematician to use their very particular skill sets to predict who would win the top prizes at the 95th Academy Awards.
The results were a draw — both managed to get seven out of 10 correct — so we've invited them back for another crack at forecasting the outcome of Hollywood's night of nights.
In one corner is film reviewer Luke Goodsell, who has critiqued movies for the ABC, The Monthly, Empire, and more.
In the other is American mathematician Ben Zauzmer, who penned the book Oscarmetrics: The Math Behind The Biggest Night in Hollywood, and whose computations are sought out every year by The Hollywood Reporter.
Here are their predictions, and you can see if they're correct on Monday, March 11 from 10:30am AEDT.
Oppenheimer, featuring Matt Damon and Cillian Murphy, is the favourite to win best film at the Oscars. (Supplied: Universal)
The critic says: Oppenheimer
Unless voters unite for Barbie on behalf of the unnominated Greta Gerwig and Margot Robbie (which would be pretty funny) — or some weird preferential distribution crowns The Holdovers, a nice movie everyone can agree on — it's safe to say Oppenheimer has this one on lock. Christopher Nolan's epic has swept pretty much everything, which makes this category a little anticlimactic — but the film is a solid choice for the prize.
The mathematician says: Oppenheimer
No doubt about this one. Oppenheimer won nearly every award there is to win down the home stretch of awards season, and any other result would be a major upset.
Christopher Nolan looks likely to win his first Oscar from his second nomination for best director. (News Video)
The critic says: Christopher Nolan (Oppenheimer)
As a former Nolan skeptic, I never thought I'd see the day where I'd say he's every bit deserving of winning this (even if Martin Scorsese probably deserves it more). Between his two decades of delivering smart blockbusters and fighting to preserve the theatrical experience, he commands a massive amount of peer respect; plus, he's been totally charming and gracious on the awards trail.
The mathematician says: Christopher Nolan (Oppenheimer)
Just like best picture, best director is Oppenheimer's category to lose. Nolan is in a strong position after winning the Golden Globe, BAFTA, Directors Guild, and plenty of other honours.
Our experts predict a few easy wins for Oppenheimer at the Oscars. (Supplied: Universal)
The critic says: Cillian Murphy (Oppenheimer)
It kinda looked like Paul Giamatti might have a shot here but at this stage — with Murphy collecting the Screen Actors Guild (SAG) honours, on top of pretty much everything else — the Oppenheimer lead has got this one. I mean, the man starved himself, cracked his head open, and kept a straight face while quoting the Bhagavad Gita to Florence Pugh during a sex scene — he's earned it.
The mathematician says: Cillian Murphy (Oppenheimer)
Murphy, but Paul Giamatti (The Holdovers) is in the running. The two Golden Globe winners started out neck and neck, but Murphy's recent winning streak and Oppenheimer's overall momentum are enough to make him the frontrunner.
Lily Gladstone (left) has been locked in a tight battle with Emma Stone for the best actress gongs this awards season. (Supplied: Apple TV+)
The critic says: Lily Gladstone (Killers Of The Flower Moon)
Tough call. Gladstone and Emma Stone (Poor Things) have split the awards to date (let's just ignore the BAFTAs, which didn't even have the sense to nominate the former), with the Killers of the Flower Moon star's SAG win pushing this back toward a close race. Gladstone's win would be historical (whereas Stone won the category only a few years ago), and I suspect a lot of voters might be moved by that — assuming the Academy can get over its bias against quiet, internalised performances (and not fall for actors saying "naughty" words in period pieces yet again).
The mathematician says: Lily Gladstone (Killers Of The Flower Moon)
By my calculations, Gladstone is nearly tied with Emma Stone (Poor Things). This is the single closest race of the night. My model gives Gladstone a 1.3 per cent edge over Stone, but that's pretty close to saying it's a coin toss.
Robert Downey Jr. is the hot favourite to win his first Oscar for his role in Oppenheimer. (Supplied: Universal)
The critic says: Robert Downey Jr. (Oppenheimer)
Does anyone really wanna see him go back to making Marvel movies? Give this man his award already, so we can all move on.
The mathematician says: Robert Downey Jr. (Oppenheimer)
Unlike the lead acting categories, the supporting roles are easy. Look for Robert Downey Jr. to finally win his first Oscar, short of a major upset.
Da'Vine Joy Randolph has already won a Golden Globe for her role in The Holdovers. (Supplied: Universal/Seacia Pavao)
The critic says: Da'Vine Joy Randolph (The Holdovers)
It's pretty much a given that Randolph has this in the bag, but I wouldn't be entirely surprised (nor unhappy) to see America Ferrera pull an upset in this category, considering both its historical track record and the fact that people really, really love that Barbie speech. Then again, last year's surprise Oscar winner, Jamie Lee Curtis, also won the SAG — and Randolph's recent win there seals the deal.
The mathematician says: Da'Vine Joy Randolph (The Holdovers)
Just like Downey Jr., Randolph swept every major award for supporting actress this awards season, and there's no reason to believe she won't wrap up her run with an Oscar statuette.
The critic says: Past Lives
The mathematician says: Anatomy Of A Fall
The critic says: Oppenheimer
The mathematician says: American Fiction
Spider-Woman and Spider-Man 2099 in action in Spider-Man: Across The Spider-Verse. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
The critic says: Spider-Man: Across The Spider-Verse
The mathematician says: Spider-Man: Across The Spider-Verse
The critic says: The Zone Of Interest
The mathematician says: The Zone Of Interest

title: How an obscure Star Wars beer campaign became the internet's funniest new viral meme
content:
The force is strong with this one.
An obscure early 2000s ad campaign for South American beer brand Cerveza Cristal is currently the internet's newest obsession, spawning a number of hilarious memes.
Prompted by some hokey product placement edited into the original Star Wars trilogy, the viral trend (and infectious jingle) has extended to other blockbusters, from Dune to Lord of the Rings.
So, if you were wondering why Cerveza Cristal is dominating your social feeds, we're here with everything you need to know.
The story begins a long time ago — well, 2003 — in a galaxy far, far away (re: South America). When the original Star Wars trilogy first aired on Chilean TV in December 2003 without traditional commercial breaks.
Instead, product placement was awkwardly edited into key scenes of the films to advertise Cerveza Cristal.
The result? Iconic characters like Luke Skywalker, Obi-Wan Kenobi and Emperor Palpatine reaching for a cold one to amusing effect.
The footage resurfaced thanks to X user @heyitswindy, who shared an English dub of one such Cerveza-edited scene.
They went on to share other edits, featuring scenes from 1980's Empire Strikes Back and 1983's Return Of The Jedi — all with the addictive, absurd Cerveza Cristal jingle ringing out.
In our current AI age, many commentators understandably thought that this was all fake. But nope, it's legit.
For starters, there's documentation of Star Wars fans chatting about the 'Cerveza Cristal' edit on forums back in 2004. Plus, footage was shared on YouTube as far back as 2009.
The campaign — known as La Fuerza está con Cerveza Cristal (translating to The Force is with Cerveza Cristal) — even scooped the top award at the 2004 Cannes International Advertising Festival, recognising the "genius" of its creators, ad agency OMD Santiago.
According to video game and pop culture site Vida Extra, the success led to alcohol empire CCU (Compañía de las Cervecerías Unidas) to use the same move in broadcasts of 1999 Oscar Best Picture winner American Beauty, Julia Roberts romcom Notting Hill, and 2000 swords-and-sandals blockbuster Gladiator. (We NEED that footage!)
However, creator George Lucas was not happy about the edits, and Lucasfilm's lawyers successfully lodged legal action, arguing it misled viewers into believing there was an official link between Cerveza Cristal and Star Wars.
As a result, the TV edit was never broadcast again and largely lost to time. But as with many pop culture obscurities, the internet never forgets.
On social media, crafty editors latched onto the bizarre beer-ification of movie blockbusters, beginning with inserting Cerveza Cristal into the Star Wars prequels and J.J Abrams-helmed sequel trilogy.
The next logical step was bringing the idea into other sci-fi and fantasy franchises, including the ever-popular Lord Of The Rings cinematic trilogy and the current appetite for Denis Villeneuve's Dune.
Why stop there? Within a week of the Star Wars edits surfacing, we now have cerveza showing up in Back The Future, Alien, Ghostbusters, Iron Man, Se7en — you name it.
Some have even gone above and beyond, creating universe-accurate models of the longneck bottle that seamlessly merge into The Lego Movie and videogame franchises such as The Legend of Zelda and Metal Gear Solid.
'Tis the gift that keeps on giving. Now, if you'll excuse me, I need to go slake this strangely urgent thirst I've suddenly developed.

title: 'I think this is a warning': Zone of Interest star on what audiences take from the horrifying film
content:
If you watched the Best Picture-nominated film The Zone Of Interest on mute, you could be forgiven for thinking that it's a simple period family drama.
A soldier father, a stay-at-home mother and five perfect children all enjoying a large estate with bountiful access to nature as the European seasons gracefully change.
Of course, once you crank the volume, the unspeakable horror bubbling underneath director Jonathan Glazer's familial nightmare reveals itself most harshly.
The picture-perfect family we follow in the film isn't a normal family.
The father is Rudolf Höss, a real-life Nazi commander, his wife Hedwig gleefully accepts the title Queen of Auschwitz in the film, and the lively garden the children play in shares a wall with a concentration camp that is actively killing hundreds — if not thousands — of people a day.
The Höss family lives in wilful ignorance, just steps from the Auschwitz concentration camp. (Supplied: Madman)
Not that the audience ever sees the atrocities occurring just over the garden wall — but they do hear them. Despite its ghoulish setting, sound designer Johnnie Burn transforms the audio landscape into the biggest source of horror in the film.
"[Jonathan Glazer] said 'I never want to go to the camp and show people images that they have already seen'," says Burn who, alongside sound engineer Tarn Willers, are up for an Academy Award for their work on the film (the pair has already secured a BAFTA for Best Sound this season).
This film set in a family home next to Auschwitz during WWII has been nominated for five Oscars, including Best Picture.
"He said, 'We're only going to do it through sound… I'm basically going to go and film a family drama and you've got a year to become an expert on the sound of 1943'. So that was panic stations."
What followed for Burn was a year of intense research, combing through real-life accounts and the Auschwitz Memorial archive to figure out what it sounded like to live next to a concentration camp in WWII Poland.
"There were many incidents of things that specifically had sound attributed, like survivors saying when someone threw themselves at the electric fence that would make a screaming sound," Burn says.
"When they put people in the gas chambers, they used to start motorbikes and rev them really loudly, two at a time, in order to drown out the sound of people screaming in pain to their death and the banging on the doors of the chamber.
"[I was] basically copying and pasting little stories that I found that I felt could have had sound attributed to them."
Johnnie Burn (left) and Tarn Willers at the 2024 BAFTA awards. (Getty: Gareth Cattermole)
Zone of Interest was shot on location in Auschwitz (in a recreation of the original Höss house, which has been a private residence since the war), allowing Burns to meticulously map the area.
"You can use a sound source like a hand clap, or a gunshot and you can show that to a computer. It will recognise the reverb pattern and the echoes within that recording, and can then faithfully reproduce them," Burns says.
The result is an nightmare surround-sound experience that juxtaposes the domestic bliss appearing on screen.
One of the keys to Zone Of Interest's chilling success is the characters wilful ignorance of the sounds of death nearby.
The concept is a through-line that Burn wanted to impress with his sound work.
"It's shocking the idea that people were blind to it, they felt that they were doing the right thing, they were just following orders," Burn says.
To achieve this effect, none of the actors knew about the abhorrent soundscape that would hang like the darkest storm cloud over their performances.
This means they seem to just not react while the audio horrors unfold.
"Our behaviours are really normal; [it makes the audience ask], are we not listening or are we pretending not to hear?" says Christian Friedel, the German actor tasked with embodying Höss, the ruthless commander of Auschwitz between 1941 and 1943 and one of the willing architects of Hitler's Final Solution.
Friedel says he was "maybe a little naive" when he first accepted the role, but the gravity of the story they were trying to tell hit him hard once filming started.
"I felt the responsibility every day. I was thinking, 'oh my god, we're what we're doing here — is it right? Or is it wrong?'," he says.
Christian Friedel plays Rudolf Franz Ferdinand Höss, a real-life German SS officer and commandant of the Auschwitz concentration camp. (Supplied: Madman)
"Jonathan said to me, keep the darkness inside of you, but don't show me that. For the first time in my life, I had some panic attacks."
But despite the difficulties of executing it, Friedel says the film is a timely and important reminder of the deadly consequences of political and moral apathy.
"For me, the message is to watch an example of people who decided to use political fascism for their own good… [The Hösses] believed in the system and they ignored what they were doing, they compartmentalised," Friedel says.
The Zone of Interest is in cinemas now.

title: Delayed by war, the Palestinian Film Festival re-emerges to present images of hope
content:
Naser Shakhtour says it has been the hardest year to organise the Palestinian Film Festival since he began running it in 2008.
It was due to begin in mid-October, but that plan changed when the October 7 attacks on Israelis happened.
After the Hamas attack — in which 1,200 Israelis were killed and the invasion and siege of Gaza followed — the festival director felt the community needed time to mourn.
"Our community, especially our friends from Gaza, they were mourning their families," Mr Shakhtour said.
One of the films, Alam, is a story about Palestinian people living in the state of Israel. (Supplied: Palestinian Film Festival Australia)
More than 30,000 Palestinians have been killed since Israel began bombing and sending ground forces into Gaza, according to local health officials.
The events of the current cycle of violence have prompted an "extensive surge" of interest in what life is like in the Occupied Palestinian Territories, according to Mr Shakhtour.
He said the decision to go ahead with the festival was inspired by a journalist in Gaza who reported that people were still celebrating birthdays despite the devastation.
"That's quite significant, that you celebrate life," Mr Shakhtour said.
The Palestinian Film Festival begins its national tour on Thursday, starting in Sydney then visiting Brisbane, Canberra, Adelaide, Hobart, Melbourne, and Perth.
Many of the twelve films at the Palestinian Film Festival focus on the daily lives of Palestinian people in both Israel and the occupied territories of Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem.
Mr Shakhtour said he felt an audience in Sydney may be able to relate to Gazans trying to enjoy the sea in the film Gaza Surf Club.
Audiences may be able to connect to the surf culture seen in Gaza Surf club, the festival organiser said. (Supplied: Palestinian Film Festival Australia)
The documentary focuses on the residents of the coastal strip and how they developed a surf culture despite hazardous waters and a blockade.
"The point of programming this film is to show Palestinians, Gazans specifically, their aspirations to lead a normal life," Mr Shakhtour said.
The film Lyd combines documentary and science fiction elements. (Supplied: Palestinian Film Festival Australia)
The festival, which has been curated for a broad Australian audience, is also curated to inspire a better future for people in the region.
One example of this is the film Lyd, a film combining documentary and science fiction techniques in picturing a world where the eponymous city was never taken over in 1948 by Israel.
"To inspire people, you have to start to imagining something good.
"Yes, acknowledge what has happened. But then, where to?"

title: Jury finds armourer guilty of involuntary manslaughter in fatal shooting on set of Alec Baldwin movie Rust
content:
A New Mexico jury has found Rust armourer Hannah Gutierrez guilty of involuntary manslaughter, ending a trial over Hollywood's first on-set fatal shooting in nearly 30 years.
Ten days of testimony had focused on whether the relatively inexperienced armourer endangered fellow crew and cast members in her handling and supervision of firearms on the low-budget production set in New Mexico.
Judge Mary Marlowe Sommer ordered that Gutierrez be taken into custody immediately. She faces up to 18 months in state prison.
As deputies led her from the courtroom, Gutierrez told her distraught mother, "I'll be okay".
Jurors, who reached their decision in just three hours, acquitted Gutierrez on a second charge of evidence tampering.
Just after lunch on October 21, 2021, Gutierrez mistakenly loaded a live round into a reproduction Colt .45 revolver that actor Alec Baldwin was using inside a movie-set church outside Santa Fe.
Baldwin cocked the gun, pointed it toward the camera and it fired one live bullet that killed cinematographer Halyna Hutchins and wounded director Joel Souza.
Halyna Hutchins was killed on the set of the movie Rust when a prop gun misfired. (Instagram: Halyna Hutchins)
Baldwin denies having pulled the trigger. His own manslaughter trial is set for July 10.
"This case is about constant, never-ending safety failures that resulted in the death of a human being and nearly killed another," New Mexico state special prosecutor Kari Morrissey said in her closing statements on Wednesday.
Gutierrez's lawyer Jason Bowles said he would appeal the decision.
"My sense was the evidence was insufficient and it was a lot of speculation," he said outside the courthouse following the decision.
During the trial Mr Bowles argued that the movie's production company tried to cut costs by employing Gutierrez as both a part-time armourer and a props assistant in the gun-heavy Western.
Rust movie armourer Hannah Gutierrez faces up to 18 months in prison. (AP: Jim Weber/Santa Fe New Mexican)
Movie-set firearms safety expert Bryan Carpenter testified during the trial that more armourers were needed on the set.
New Mexico's worker safety agency in 2022 fined the company, Rust Media Productions, the state's maximum possible penalty for ignoring industry firearm safety guidelines.
As one of the least experienced, least powerful people on set, Mr Bowles said his client was taking the blame for management.
"You've got a convenient fall person, a convenient scapegoat," he said.
Alec Baldwin was photographed on set shortly after the shooting. (AP: Jim Weber/Santa Fe New Mexican )
Throughout the trial witnesses ranging from director Souza to assistant director Dave Halls said it was beyond anyone's imagination that live rounds could be mingled in with dummy rounds on the production.
State prosecutors and defence lawyers have fought over the source of live rounds, which are strictly forbidden on movie sets.
What actually happened during rehearsals at the ranch on the outskirts of Santa Fe and why is Alec Baldwin being charged?
During the trial a Santa Fe detective cited "circumstantial evidence" that Gutierrez unknowingly brought the live rounds to Rust from a previous production in a white cardboard box.
Ms Morrissey gave jurors photos taken up to 10 days before the shooting showing a live round in the box and one in Baldwin's bandolier.
"That's a mountain of circumstantial evidence," Ms Morrissey said.
Mr Bowles repeatedly blamed props supplier Seth Kenney, who has not been charged, as the source of the live rounds.
He said Mr Kenney, a weapons consultant on movies like Man Down and a props supplier to The Walking Dead, was not searched until a month after the shooting, allowing him to potentially dispose of evidence from his Albuquerque office.
Without knowing live rounds were on set, Mr Bowles said Gutierrez did not show "wilful disregard" for the safety of others, a requirement to convict her of involuntary manslaughter or a lesser charge of negligent use of a firearm, which carries up to six months in jail.
Half a dozen Rust crew members called by prosecutors testified that safety meetings were skipped, that Gutierrez sometimes failed to check whether weapons were loaded, and that Baldwin broke basic firearms safety rules.

title: Colin Firth's Mr Darcy shirt makes a splash at auction, selling for $38,000
content:
What is arguably the most famous wet shirt in television history sold for 20,000 pounds ($38,000) on Tuesday — water not included.
The white linen garment worn by Colin Firth as Mr Darcy in the BBC's 1995 TV adaptation of Pride and Prejudice was the star item at an auction of film and television costumes.
The costume which included boots, moleskin breeches and velvet waistcoat fetched double its top pre-sale estimate of 10,000 pounds during a sale at Kerry Taylor Auctions.
The scene from the 1995 television show was once voted the UK's most memorable television moment.  (Supplied)
The total price is 25,000 pounds once an auction house fee known as the buyer's premium is added.
The scene in which Firth's brooding heart-throb emerges from a pond, startling soon-to-be true love Elizabeth Bennet (Jennifer Ehle), was once voted the UK's most memorable television moment.
It was later re-imagined in Bridgerton in a scene featuring British actor Jonathan Bailey.
Jonathan Bailey as Anthony Bridgerton in episode 205 of the popular TV series Bridgerton. (Netflix: Liam Daniel)
Firth referenced his own performance with further romantic soakings in Love, Actually and Bridget Jones: The Edge of Reason.
Other items up for sale include a 1950s Christian Dior taffeta ball gown worn by Madonna in the 1996 movie Evita, which sold for 40,000 pounds and Johnny Depp's costume for Ichabod Crane in Sleepy Hollow, which fetched 24,000 pounds.
Madonna's pink satin evening coat used in the film Evita.  (AP Photo: Kirsty Wigglesworth )
Clothes worn by Depp as the Earl of Rochester in The Libertine and as writer JM Barrie in Finding Neverland were also among some 60 items that went under the hammer.
Drew Barrymore's costume as Danielle in the film Ever After released in 1998 was also sold.
The dress (centre) from the ball scene of Ever After.  (AP Photo: Kirsty Wigglesworth)
Proceeds from the auction will go to the Bright Foundation, an arts education charity founded by Academy Award-winning costume designer John Bright.
The items have been donated by his costume house, Cosprop.
"My life's work has been committed to costume design for film, TV and theatre, and I feel incredibly fortunate to have been able to pursue this path," Bright said.
"It is my firmly held belief that the arts and creativity can shape happier and healthier children and enable young people to reach their full potential."

title: How to Have Sex is not an instruction guide but will teach teenagers vital lessons about sex
content:
Warning: The following story discusses sexual assault.
Director Molly Manning Walker knew she wanted to tackle the spiky issues of consent and sex among young adults in her debut feature film, How to Have Sex.
"I was assaulted when I was 16 in a nightclub. [It's] very different to this story, but it's something I have always wanted to talk about very openly," Manning Walker says.
"Whenever you do talk about it, it sort of sucks the air out of a room. I wanted to change that."
The result is a vividly nuanced exploration of sex told through the eyes of three teenage girls — best friends Tara (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Skye (Lara Peake) and Em (Enva Lewis) — who fly to a Greek party island to celebrate the end of their high school exams.
Sixteen-year-old Tara is a virgin, and much less experienced than her two besties — and her friends don't let her forget it. She's hoping to finally have sex during the group's "summer to remember".
"Whoever gets laid the most gets the main room," one girl screams when they reach their resort.
Manning Walker drew upon her holidays to Majorca and Ibiza as a teenager and in her 20s to bring the movie to life. (Supplied: Ahi/Nikos Nikolopoulos)
Manning Walker says that kind of narrative was everywhere when she went on  holiday with friends when she was younger.
"It came from within our friendship group, or from ourselves, like, 'Oh, this is what we're meant to do,'" she says.
"There was always a chat about 'who's gonna get with who' or like 'how many people you've got with'."
Sex, and the pressure to have it, is ubiquitous here, and not just from the teenagers.
"In the film we tried to get all this tourist stuff that's got naked women on it — lighters, towels," Manning Walker explains.
"We tried to, props-wise, influence them, and put it in the background of the shot as well, because it feels like even the environment has a pressure on them."
Manning Walker deliberately focused the action on the clubs and party scene of the island, rather than on the surrounding areas.
"It was depicting this Disneyland for teenagers where you can leave your parents and party, and the first half is meant to be really joyous and fun and you get this sort of freeing experience, where you're free for once," she told ABC RN's The Screen Show.
"And then you see the underbelly of it, and how sex pressures these kids from all angles."
An intimacy co-ordinator, a therapist and counsellors were part of the shoot in Crete. (Supplied: Ahi/Nikos Nikolopoulos)
Manning Walker wanted her movie to be relevant to young people, so she invited groups of teenagers from all over the UK to workshops to give their input.
"We asked them about everything from, 'what music are you listening to?', to 'what are you wearing?', to 'what is your concept of consent?'," she told The Screen Show.
Listen: Molly Manning Walker on ABC RN's The Screen Show
She also showed them scenes from the film, with a particular focus on one moment.
After a night clubbing, Tara is separated from her friends, and ends up alone on the beach with a boy who becomes increasingly forward — touching her, picking her up (and refusing to put her down when she tells him to), and, eventually, pressuring her to have sex.
And while she agrees, the close-up camera work on her hands gripping the sand and on the tension in her face makes it clear that it's not what she wants.
Manning Walker's parents work in the film industry — her mother as a director and her father as a writer and animator. (Supplied: Ahi/Nikos Nikolopoulos)
"We were really trying to ride that fine line: some people would instantly think, 'OK that's really uncomfortable, that's an assault', and some people would recognise themselves in it," Manning Walker explains.
Even so, the director was not ready when one young woman remarked that "girls need to take responsibility, and not get so drunk".
"I thought things might have changed, it was pretty shocking to see that," Manning Walker says.
She says there was also a split in responses when the film was screened at Cannes in 2023.
"Lots of women would come into the room and say 'thank you for making this film, I've been through that, I feel seen', and a lot of men would come in quite defensive and say, 'It's not an assault because she said yes'," Manning Walker says.
"It was fascinating, but also deeply worrying. It just makes the conversation feel more important and more relevant."
"We really wanted men to see themselves in these characters," Manning Walker told The Screen Show. (Supplied: Ahi/Nikos Nikolopoulos)
Manning Walker says she loved actor Mia McKenna-Bruce (who recently won the BAFTA Rising Star Award) from the moment she saw her first audition tape, and knew her smile and infectious vibe would be perfect for the role of Tara.
"She’s full of joy and energy and she can make everyone laugh; she’s not a victim that we know traditionally on screen," Manning Walker told The Screen Show.
"I think so often people who have gone through terrible things are depicted on screen as quite meek, and actually she’s the life and soul of the party."
After the assault, Tara goes back to a club and ends up staying with a different group of people. The boy assumes Tara wants to have sex a second time, and her friend Skye suggestively asks Tara when they'll hook up again.
McKenna-Bruce beat Jacob Elordi, Ayo Edebri, Phoebe Dynevor and Sophie Wilde to win the Rising Star Award at this year's BAFTAs. (Supplied: Ahi/Nikos Nikolopoulos)
It's only days later, when they're at the airport on their way home, that Tara confides in Em about what happened.
"There's so much pretence when you're a teenager and you're sort of making stuff up and pretending to be something you're not," Manning-Walker explains.
"I think if there was less of that, then there would be less pushing each other in situations that no one really agrees with anyway."
Manning Walker says she wants to encourage more young people to talk to their mates, and to listen.
"I hope it starts a conversation around how we can have better sex, especially for women," she says.
If you or someone you know needs help, assistance is available at the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Violence Counselling Service 1800 RESPECT:  https://www.1800respect.org.au/.
How to Have Sex is in cinemas from March 7.
