title: Actress drops 50kgs for Chinese film hit You Only Live Once
content:
The weight-loss journey of a Chinese film star who shed an astonishing 50 kilograms in a year has captivated the internet in China.
Jia Ling unveiled her remarkable transformation in her latest film You Only Live Once (YOLO).
YOLO's main character becomes a fan of boxing and weight training. (Supplied)
It's been a hit in China, and in less than a month has made more than $726 million at the box office.
YOLO opens in Australia on Thursday.
Jia said her film is more about "self-love" than "body transformation".
However, many have questioned whether the film, which is meant to be uplifting, has exposed audiences to another round of content that could drive body-image anxiety.
The buzz around the film and Jia's transformation was fuelled by her year-long absence from the public eye.
She had vanished to dedicate herself to a program of intense strength training.
Video clips showcasing Jia's work-out routine, featuring body-weight training that she calls animal flow, and her deadlifting 120kg, have gone viral.
The (translated) tag #Jia Ling losing 50kgs has received more than 800 million views on Weibo.
On Douyin, China's version of TikTok, short videos of people talking about her weight loss have been viewed more than 1 million times.
Her year of low-carb, high-protein, intermittent dieting, combined with her intense training led to her dropping from 105kg to 55kg.
She's inspired people across China.
Since the movie's premiere in early February, interest in gym memberships and personal trainers has surged across China, according to local reports.
Adapted from the award-winning Japanese movie 100 Yen Love, YOLO's main character is Du Leying.
She is an obese woman who hits rock bottom then falls in love with boxing and achieves her dream of getting in shape.
Some young feminists in China are rebelling against mainstream beauty standards by embracing buzz cuts and ditching make-up.
Despite Jia's insistence that the message is "you win as long as you spare no efforts", it is her weight loss that caught the eye of the public.
With the controversy surrounding the movie, a documentary recording Jia's year of weight loss, due to be screened across China last week, was cancelled without explanation.
Wang Pan, an expert on China's gender issues at the University of New South Wales, has suggested the feminist impact of the movie is immense.
Since the premiere of the movie, more young women are taking up boxing, which is traditionally a male sport, Dr Wang said.
More women are also reportedly taking up strength training.
Wang Pan said YOLO may help to motivate some women who want to change. (Supplied: Wang Pan)
"So many young women are anxious about their bodies, unhappy with their weight and appearance, resulting in a lack of self-confidence," she said.
"These women are desperate for a change and want to be redefined.
Discussions around the 41-year-old star's transformation has exploded on social media. (Supplied)
In China, "pale skin, skinny body and youthful looking face" are still seen as traditional beauty standards.
As YOLO continues to lead the box office, people across China have been posting weight-loss goals as their New Year resolution on social media.
Jia Ling underwent a remarkable body-shape change for YOLO. (Supplied: YouTube)
Experts have warned that despite the inspirational message the film intended to convey, the social impact has not been completely positive.
YOLO has been criticised for overstressing the link between weight loss and self-achievement.
"While we were in the cinema, my mother was criticising me for not working hard enough [to lose weight] while praising how great Jia's achievement was," a woman wrote on Chinese social media platform Red.
Chinese film star's extreme weight loss sparks online controversy.
Li Yawen, a professor of social work at California State University San Bernardino, said a movie like YOLO could worsen peoples' perceptions of their weight.
"Potentially [it's] leading to more young women believing they are overweight, experiencing low self-esteem, or engaging in unhealthy weight loss behaviours," Dr Li said.
Dr Li has studied the body-image perception of female Chinese university students.
She found that about 70 per cent of participants who considered themselves overweight didn't meet the World Health Organization's criteria.
Li Yawen says discussions around YOLO could promote unhealthy and unrealistic weight-loss plans. (Supplied)
"Chinese young women often have a tendency to misperceive their weight, viewing themselves as heavier than their actual weight," she said.
The discussion around the film also has the potential to promote unrealistic weight loss goals, which is not feasible or healthy for most, Dr Li added.
"Many weight-control programs have limited long-term effectiveness, with individuals often regaining their original weight — or even more after 12 months," she said.
"Setting unrealistic goals, combined with the likelihood of weight regain over the long term, can lead individuals to blame themselves for perceived shortcomings in determination, effective behaviour regulation, or personal control."
Dietitian Lisa Chen outlined some of the bad side effects of an unhealthy weight loss plan, including depression and eating disorders. (Supplied)
Dr Li and others have concerns about the often unhealthy strategies used to lose weight.
After Chinese models with small eyes were blasted for insulting China by nationalists online, the government has urged TV companies to conform to the "correct aesthetic".
Many netizens have questioned whether Jia's efforts were helped by the use of Ozempic — a drug for diabetics that has become incredibly popular for weight loss.
Sydney-based dietitian and diabetes educator Lisa Chen told the ABC weight-loss medication may have side effects, including "diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, low mood, or even poor sleep".
"The impressive weight-loss results have led people to discuss how she achieved the amazing results," Ms Chen said.
Unhealthy weight-loss plans can increase the risk of anxiety, depression, eating disorders — even suicidal thoughts, Ms Chen warned.

title: 'I must go punch that baby': Meet the Aussie writer behind Emma Stone's best line in Poor Things
content:
Australian screenwriter Tony McNamara loves Poor Things, but he didn't think millions of other people would too.
"In my mind, I thought, 'we're probably made a very polarising movie,'" he says. "We didn't think it would be the general hit it's been."
While McNamara awaits to see whether Poor Things takes home Best Adapted Screenplay at the 2023 Academy Awards — or any of the 10 other gongs it is nominated for, including Best Picture — the film has broken the $100-million-box-office milestone.
It's the fourth-biggest box office of any Best Picture nominee, behind Barbie, Oppenheimer and Killers of the Flower Moon. But given it was made with a fraction of their budgets, at $35 million, it's no small feat.
Poor Things marks the writer's second collaboration with director Yorgos Lanthimos, following 2018's The Favourite – an ultra-dark comedy about an 18th-century love triangle between Queen Anne and two cousins (including Emma Stone), which saw Olivia Colman take Best Actress at the 2019 Oscars.
The film's interior scenes were only lit with candles and available window light as director Yorgos Lanthimos had banned the use of artificial lighting. (Supplied: 20th Century Fox)
"I'd worked with Yorgos before, so I knew he's brave," McNamara says.
"He just wants to make something unique. I loved working with him and he was keen to do it again. But it was really Bella Baxter's character [that drew me in]."
Adapted from Alasdair Gray's 1992 novel of the same name, Poor Things follows Bella Baxter (Emma Stone), a fully grown woman born in Victorian London from a Frankenstein-esque experiment by oddball surgeon Godwin Baxter (Willem Dafoe).
Across the film, Bella learns to be human: To walk, talk and think, as well as discover the pleasures of living — from Portuguese tarts, to philosophy, to "furious jumping" (her term for sex).
A series of men she meets (Dafoe, Mark Ruffalo, Ramy Youssef, Christopher Abbott) are enraptured by her beauty and/or off-kilter view of the world. Each, in their own ways, want her all to themselves, while Bella remains beholden to only one thing: experiencing it all.
In Poor Things, Mark Ruffalo convinces Emma Stone to join him on an adventure that takes them from London to Marseilles via Lisbon. (Supplied: 20th Century Studios)
"The novel is wild and crazy, it has a great premise," McNamara says. "It also offered an opportunity for us because the book is [largely] told by the men. You're never with her in her experience.
"So [I thought], 'If we put her at the centre, you've got this character without the fingerprints of childhood or society on her.' You've got a great comic coming-of-age story and satire about control."
Poor Things trailer
Much of McNamara's career has revolved around those twin themes: coming-of-age and control. They're not only prevalent in just Poor Things and The Favourite; they're even in his co-write on Disney villain origin film Cruella, also starring Stone.
It's also central to The Great — McNamara's three-season comedy-drama series about Catherine The Great starring Elle Fanning and Nicholas Hoult, which ended last year. Based off his 2008 play of the same name, The Great's script was what first caught Lanthimos's attention, something of a companion piece to The Favourite.
In The Great, Elle Fanning and Nicolas Hoult play Russian empress Catherine the Great and her husband Emperor Peter III. (Supplied: Stan)
Lewd and delightfully ahistorical, The Great, The Favourite and Poor Things all revel in witty wordplay and imaginatively vulgar swears, with McNamara on hand during rehearsals for all three, locking in the script with the actors line by line.
A lesbian love-and-power triangle causes havoc in the court of Great Britain's 18th century Queen in this latest caper from the director of The Lobster.
"We were pretty meticulous," he says specifically about Poor Things' language. "It was about making sure it matched her evolution and how she could articulate herself."
"In rehearsal, we would adjust with Emma … About whether we wanted a more sophisticated word there, or if it was too sophisticated for where we're at. It's quite an exacting process, but it was fun."
Born in 1967 and raised in the regional Victorian town of Kilmore, McNamara was an avid reader as a child, though says that didn't translate to great grades in English, repeatedly joking in the press that he could never grasp grammar – and still can't, referencing his character's odd cadence.
Poor Things won best motion picture musical or comedy at this year's Golden Globes. (Pictured: director Yorgos Lanthimos accepting the award.) (Rich Polk/Golden Globes 2024/ via Getty Images)
That tendency to play with language — to find unique, funny and often profound ways to describe everyday moments — has been key to McNamara's career, beginning with writing on beloved 00s Australian TV shows such as The Secret Life of Us, Love My Way and Offspring.
"His dialogue on Secret Life was always distinctly Tony," actor Claudia Karvan told The Australian. "It had a particular rhythm and real smarts. It worked when it was delivered fast. No pauses. It had a theatricality and self-awareness, but was also cool and sassy."
There's a through-line from Ben Lee's quirked-up, axe-wielding teen in McNamara's 2003 indie cult favourite The Rage in Placid Lake (which McNamara also directed), to Stone's deadpan delivery of "I must go punch that baby" in Poor Things.
He's fascinated by characters who see and view the world from a different angle, who articulate themselves in odd ways that jolt and delight audiences, satirising normal conventions of politeness, revealing the vulgar power plays underneath how people interact.
Emma Stone thanks the Poor Things writer for the line: "I must go punch that baby."
And yes, much of that is through swearing and innuendo more graphic than Poor Things' many sex scenes.
"I grew up going to a school where insulting each other was the curriculum," McNamara says of where his love of swears comes from.
"I think that's part of the [Australian] culture. And with Yorgos, the Greek culture has a bit of that as well, like teasing."
McNamara is already working on several new projects, including an adaptation with Lanthimos of Richard Brautigan's novel, The Hawkline Monster: A Gothic Western. When asked if he has any urge to return to directing, he answers with a single word: No.
"I think I like writing too much," he elaborates when pressed. "I felt like I can be a better writer if I'm just focused on one thing.
"There are people who are better than me at [directing]. So I thought, 'What are you good at? Just do what you're good at, and maybe you'll be really good at it'.
"I thought I'd be an OK director, but I was never going to be a great director. But I thought, 'If you focus on writing, you might be a great writer.'"

title: ICYMI: Sydney Sweeney adds to rumours, Euphoria star arrested, and Rihanna plays for billionaire
content:
Welcome to March!
We're tantalisingly close to this year's Oscars (awards season goes so fast!), which happen next Monday, Aussie time.
While we wait to see if Oppenheimer has a record-breaking run, here's the most important pop culture news you may have missed over the last few days.
There's only been one thing more popular than the Sydney Sweeney and Glen Powell rom-com Anyone But You, and that's trying to figure out if Sweeney and Powell hooked up while filming Anyone But You.
Sweeney revived the trend over the weekend while hosting Saturday Night Live. The Euphoria star used her monologue to stamp down various rumours, including her very heavily implied affair with Powell.
While reiterating that she loves her fiance (producer Jonathan Davino) and he was in the studio supporting her, the camera then did a quick cut to the human capybara himself, Glen Powell.
So did they hook up? We don't know! Do they want us to think they hooked up to keep interest in more Sweeney/Powell rom coms? Yes, probably!
Viva la fake Hollywood romance.
Throughout the show, Sweeney got the Jacob Elordi treatment, with a good chunk of her skits revolving around her looks, including one sketch where she just can't figure out why she's so good at being a Hooters waitress.
There was a moment or two where she was actually allowed to be funny as well as hot, helped by the always spot-on Bowen Yang.
— Velvet Winter
Just when you thought you were safe from Tones and I's massive single Dance Monkey, it goes and breaks another record.
The viral 2019 hit reached 3 billion streams on Spotify last week, making Tones the first woman and the first Australian to join the 3 billion club.
Only eight songs have notched over 3 billy on Spotify — The Weeknd's Blinding Lights takes the top spot with more than 4 billion streams.
This comes off the announcement last year that Dance Monkey has been streamed more than 10 billion times across all platforms.
Tones is currently accompanying P!nk on her Summer Carnival tour through Australia and New Zealand.
— Velvet Winter
Rihanna hasn't done a tour or released a new album in eight long years. Seems like the only way to get RiRi to perform in public nowadays is to be the Super Bowl or — as we found out over the weekend — a billionaire whose son is about to get married.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
Videos began popping up on social media on Saturday of Rihanna performing at the pre-wedding celebration of Anant Ambani and his soon-to-be wife Radhika Merchant.
Anant is the son of Mukesh Ambani, chairman of conglomerate Reliance Industries and the richest man in Asia — with a net worth of $179 billion ($US117 billion) as of 2024, according to Forbes. (You may also remember him for being fined millions of dollars for historical business fraud in 2021.)
Hiring Rihanna might have just been an attempt to even out sibling rivalry, after Mukesh booked Beyoncé to sing at his daughter's wedding in 2018.
Anyway, Rihanna performed 19 songs at the lavish Ambani event, including Pour It Up, Bitch Better Have My Money, All of the Lights and Birthday Cake.
There's been no confirmation on how much Rihanna was paid for the pop-up performance, but Ambani's Reliance made a partnership deal with Sephora India last year and Ri's currently in her billionaire make-up mogul era, so it's probably safe to say it was a good business deal.
Euphoria star Hunter Schafer was protesting US President Joe Biden's slot on Late Night with Seth Meyers, with the Jewish-led, anti-Zionist organisation Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP), when she was arrested on Monday.
The 25-year-old was taken into police custody at 30 Rockefeller Center in New York, along with 50 others, the organisation told Vulture in a statement last week.
"We commend her commitment to Palestinian freedom and to a future of justice for everyone," the statement read.
"As Jewish New Yorkers we are absolutely outraged that President Biden is actively supporting a genocide against the Palestinians of Gaza."
Schafer's arrest comes as the reported Palestinian death toll has surpassed 30,000, with the humanitarian crisis worsening in Gaza.
The star, who is trans, has not publicly commented on her arrest. But that hasn't stopped people from flooding the comments sections of her older posts with a mix of condemnation and support.
One person commented on Instagram: "The amount of courage it takes for a TRANS WOMAN to stand against this, risking her career in the process, is not lost on me 🏳️‍⚧️ nobody is free until we are all free."
Schafer's move to protest in support of Palestine comes as other Hollywood stars, including Melissa Barrera and Susan Sarandon, have lost jobs and representation for voicing similar sentiments.
In January, And Just Like That… actor Sara Ramirez (who played Che Diaz) called out the "duplicitous" entertainment industry on Instagram for "making black lists of actors and workers who post anything in support of Palestinians and Gaza to ensure they will not work again".
— Yasmin Jeffery
Romantasy BookTok and Bookstagram are in overdrive pondering what the Barbie star and bestselling author's apparent meeting at a cafe last week might mean.
Sarah J. Maas is the author of the hugely popular A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) series, the first of which was published in 2015, but has recently exploded in popularity, thanks to the internet girlies discovering that fantasy books are full of smut.
Just last month we found out the future of the ACOTAR TV series that's been in development at Hulu for years is apparently "murky", following reports it had been scrapped altogether.
According to Variety, that project isn't currently being shopped elsewhere in its current form. But that hasn't stopped the internet from wondering whether Robbie might have met with Maas to discuss the possibility of producing or starring in a different version of ACOTAR.
Or could they have met to talk about the possibility of bringing one of Maas's other ridiculously popular fantasy series — Throne of Glass (ToG) or Crescent City (CC) — to life?
The options are practically endless and we have absolutely zero confirmation of anything, folks.
Margot, if you're reading this, I would love to see you play Ianthe or the Morrigan in ACOTAR or Aelin in ToG or Bryce Quinlan in CC, thank you in advance.
— Yasmin Jeffery
Bring out your Dune 2 popcorn buckets, it's time to celebrate.
The highly anticipated second part of the Dune cinematic series has arrived, complete with sandworms, commentary on war and a star-studded cast.
The highly anticipated sequel to Denis Villeneuve's 2021 sci-fi freak out has made bank on its opening weekend. It raked in $273 million ($US178.5 million) worldwide, with more than half of the profit coming from international markets.
It's the biggest opening weekend for any of Villeneuve's films and the biggest for star Timothée Chalamet in 58 countries, including Australia.
Speaking of Australia, this sandworm nature documentary was number one at the box office over the weekend, pulling in $9 million.
This all bodes well for a potential third film in Villeneuve's series, Dune Messiah, which is contingent on a high box office performance despite the script being "almost finished", according to the director.
The first Dune pulled in around $612 million ($US400 million) worldwide in total, so we're almost halfway to seeing even more hot sandworm action.
— Velvet Winter
In happy news for sad girls everywhere, a new Sally Rooney novel will hit shelves on September 24.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
Rooney's publishers have posted a tantalising taste of the forthcoming novel — titled Intermezzo — to X (formerly known as Twitter), sharing its opening lines:
"Didn't seem fair on the young lad. That suit at the funeral. With the braces on his teeth, the supreme discomfort of the adolescent."
Intermezzo centres on Peter and Ivan Koubek, two brothers grieving the death of their father. In true Rooney style, complicated romantic relationships ensue.
Rooney, 33, is an Irish novelist and self-described feminist and Marxist, who attained international fame in 2018 with the publication of her second book, Normal People, which was longlisted for the Booker Prize and later turned into a critically acclaimed TV series, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal as the lovelorn Marianne and Connell. Her debut novel, 2017's Conversations with Friends, was also adapted for the screen in 2022.
Rooney was labelled "the first great millennial author" by the New York Times and earned a spot in Time's list of the 100 most influential people in 2022.
Intermezzo is Rooney's first novel since Beautiful World, Where Are You in 2021, which was accompanied by a huge marketing campaign that saw bookstores opening early to accommodate the anticipated rush of dedicated fans.
We can't wait to see if Rooney's new novel elicits a similar frenzy among the book-loving world come September. Maybe there'll even be a new bucket hat.
— Nicola Heath
Imagine leaving your morning Pilates for a coffee only to be swarmed by a mass of electronic music fans racing to a nearby club.
That was the scene on Saturday (March 2) at around 9am in Melbourne's iconic Chapel Street as a huge audience flooded southside institution Revolver Upstairs (which, notoriously, does not close over the weekend) for an audience with Fred Again..
Later on Saturday night, the British DJ and producer played a second "secret rave" at The Timber Yard, a 1,500-capacity warehouse in Port Melbourne, with cult Australian Sudanese techno favourite Skin on Skin.
Oh, and he also played Sydney's Club 77 on Thursday (February 29) in the lead-up to Mardi Gras for good measure.
These secret shows come hot on the heels of Fred Again.. playing an impromptu show at the Sydney Opera House last week, which saw more than 100,000 people try to buy tickets online. Shortly after, he announced a (pricey) east coast arena tour that sold out in a matter of hours.
These kinds of impromptu shows are Fred's thing. But why the hype? Well, the man born Frederick John Philip Gibson has been producing for the past decade, for hit-makers including Ed Sheeran, Rita Ora and his mentor Brian Eno.
However, his popularity exploded during the COVID years with his Actual Life album series, which mix house and dance music with emotive snatches of conversation and singing, including Australia's own singer-songwriter Angie McMahon and her ode to lethargy, Pasta.
His beats are accessible, making him a fixture on TikTok, and his music moves your hips and your heart, resonating with a generation who missed out on the ecstasy of the dancefloor during lockdowns.
Our nation is only just recovering from Taylor Swift fever, and now it seems we're experiencing an epidemic of Fred-mania.
— Al Newstead

title: Will Oppenheimer make a bang with a record-breaking Oscar haul?
content:
Some big records could fall at this year's Academy Awards, which Oppenheimer enters with an impressive 13 nominations.
The 96th Academy Awards will be held in Hollywood on Monday,  March 11, Australian time.
That means lots of amazing outfits, mile-a-minute speeches, and new Barbenheimer memes.
It might also mean some records will get broken, and if that's your cup of tea, then read on.
Cillian Murphy stars in Oppenheimer, which is nominated for 13 Academy Awards. (Supplied: Universal Pictures)
Most years, there's one film that gets a huge swag of nominations and the chance to have a crack at the biggest record of them all — most awards for a single film.
That record is 11 Oscars, a title shared by Ben-Hur, Titanic, and The Lord Of The Rings: The Return Of The King.
Recent films that have had an opportunity to equal or better that record have included Everything Everywhere All At Once (11 nominations), The Power Of The Dog (12), Joker (11) and The Shape Of Water (13), but all have fallen short.
This year, Oppenheimer has a shot at the title, with 13 nominations — two more than Return Of The King had when it won 11 Oscars.
Of course, Poor Things also has 11 nominations, so theoretically it has a shot too, but it's fair to say that would be a big upset.
Lily Gladstone (left) starred with Robert De Niro and Leonardo DiCaprio in Killers Of The Flower Moon. (Supplied: Apple TV+)
Lily Gladstone has already blazed a trail with her nomination for best actress for Killers Of The Flower Moon, becoming the first Native American to make that shortlist, as has fellow Native American Scott George in the best original song category.
If either of them win, they could be the first Native Americans to win a competitive Oscar, though this is somewhat controversial.
Buffy Sainte-Marie, who won the best original song Oscar in 1982 for An Officer And A Gentleman's hit single Up Where We Belong, claims to have been born to Cree parents and adopted — a claim disputed by a CBC News documentary, other media outlets, and members of her own family.
Her status as the first Indigenous person to win an Oscar is "under review", but either way, a win for Gladstone and/or George would be seen as a win for diversity.
Gladstone is also the first openly non-binary actor to be nominated for an acting Oscar — another milestone for the academy.
Martin Scorsese now has the most nominations for the best director Oscar of any living person. (AP: Evan Agostini/Invision)
Martin Scorsese, 81, could become the oldest person to win the best director Oscar, surpassing Clint Eastwood, who was 74 when he won it for Million Dollar Baby.
Scorsese's 10th nomination in the category (for Killers Of The Flower Moon) gives him the most nominations of a living person, and puts him just two nominations behind the late William Wyler.
The oldest winner of any Academy Award is James Ivory, who was 89 when he won for best adapted screenplay (Call Me By Your Name) in 2017 (sidenote: Ann Roth was also 89 — but three months younger than Ivory — when she won for best costume design in 2021).
John Williams has a shot at surpassing Ivory if he wins. The 91-year-old has been nominated for best original score for Indiana Jones And The Dial Of Destiny.
John Williams could set a new record for the oldest winner of any Academy Award if he wins. (AP/Invision: Chris Pizzello)
Williams holds the record for most nominations by a living person, with 54, but it also means Williams holds the somewhat ignominious record of most Oscar losses of all time.
He's won five Academy Awards, so that means 48 losses — another loss this year takes that total to 49.
Billie Eilish and Finneas O'Connell are strong favourites to take home the Oscar for best original song for their Barbie tearjerker What Was I Made For.
Finneas O'Connell and Billie Eilish have a shot at becoming the youngest people to win two Oscars. (Supplied: Apple TV+)
The siblings will set an impressive record if they win — they will be the youngest people to win two Oscars, having already won for the James Bond song No Time To Die.
Eilish and O'Connell will be 22 and 26 respectively on Oscars night.
The current holder for the record of youngest two-time winner is Luise Rainer, who won best actress Oscars for The Great Ziegfeld (1936) and The Good Earth (1937) by the time she was 28.

title: India's richest man brings Rihanna, Mark Zuckerberg and more to a pre-wedding bash for his son
content:
The nearly 1,200-person guest list includes Bill Gates, Mark Zuckerberg, Rihanna and Ivanka Trump.
It might be the biggest party this small west Indian city has ever seen.
Billionaire Mukesh Ambani is kickstarting big fat Indian wedding celebrations for his son, Anant Ambani, 28, who is set to marry his longtime girlfriend Radhika Merchant.
He's expecting billionaires from around the world, heads of state, and Hollywood and Bollywood royalty to attend a three-day bash in the family's hometown, which kicked off on Friday.
The occasion that has India transfixed is a three-day pre-wedding jamboree for his youngest son.
Radhika Merchant (left) pictured with her fiancé Anant Ambani and the Ambani family. (Reuters: Francis Mascarenhas)
The party is in Jamnagar, a city of about 600,000 in a near-desert part of Gujarat state.
It's the family’s hometown, and the home of the main oil refinery of their business empire, Reliance Industries.
There will also be traditional ceremonies in a temple complex.
On Wednesday, the Ambani family organised a community food service for 51,000 people living in nearby villages.
The wedding itself does not take place until July.
The three-day pre-wedding bash provides a glimpse of the opulence expected at the wedding itself.
The nearly 1,200-person guest list includes Bill Gates, Mark Zuckerberg, Sunder Pichai and Ivanka Trump.
Indian billionaires Gautam Adani and Kumar Mangalam Birla are also expected to attend, along with retired cricketer Sachin Tendulkar.
Bollywood celebrities such as Deepika Padukone, Shah Rukh Khan and Rani Mukherjee will also attend.
Bollywood actors Ranveer Singh and Deepika Padukone arrive at the airport to attend the pre-wedding celebrations. (AP Photo: Ajit Solanki)
They'll be entertained by pop superstar Rihanna, magician David Blaine and famous Bollywood singers.
Pop and R&B superstar Rihanna will perform at the pre-wedding celebration. (Getty Images/Roc Nation: Kevin Mazur)
Bob Iger, CEO of Disney, is also likely to attend following an announced $8.5 billion merger of its India media assets with Reliance's on Wednesday.
The guest list also includes Mohammed Bin Jassim al Thani, the prime minister of Qatar; Stephen Harper, former Canadian prime minister; and the king and queen of Bhutan.
Guests to the couple's celebrations are set to savour 500 dishes created by about 100 chefs.
They will also be pampered, with hair styling, makeup artists and Indian wear drapists available but only on a "first come, first serve basis", according to a planning document provided to invitees and seen by Reuters.
Guests will also don jungle-themed outfits to visit an animal rescue centre run by Anant Ambani.
Known as Vantara, meaning Star Of The Forest, the 3,000 acre (1,200 hectare) centre houses abused, injured and endangered animals, especially elephants.
The invitation says guests will start each day with a new dress code, with mood boards and an army of hair stylists, makeup artists and Indian wear designers at their hotel to help them prepare.
Return charter jet flights from New Delhi and Mumbai are on offer, but guests have been asked to limit themselves to only two luggage items or three suitcases per couple.
The document cautions that "if you bring more", there's no guarantee it will arrive on the same flight.
Forbes lists Mr Ambani as the richest person in Asia.
His Reliance Industries is a massive conglomerate, with $US100 billion ($153 billion) in annual revenue and interests ranging from oil and gas to telecoms and retail.

title: Adam Sandler befriends a giant alien spider in Netflix's latest sad man in space sci-fi drama
content:
Adam Sandler is a man who prioritises comfort — this much can be deduced from his perennial preference for dressing in billowy tees, basketball shorts, and sneakers (he finds suits intolerably "itchy") — and this priority has been reflected, more often than not, in his career choices.
For decades, he's been plying variations of the man-child, the wacky savant, the weirdo-naïf. His films are always peopled with the real-life pals he forged all the way back in his SNL days and are often set in luxe tropical locales.
The comedian doubles down on his acting credentials in this propulsive, tragicomic odyssey through New York City's gem district, streaming on Netflix.
Since 2014, he's been putting out a steady stream of goofy-sweet comedies for Netflix; comfort viewing for millions cosied up on the couch at home.
There have been notable exceptions: Sandler's performance as compulsive gambler Howard Ratner in Uncut Gems in 2019 was an electrifying left turn on the level of, if not greater than, his first dramatic role, in Paul Thomas Anderson's Punch-Drunk Love (2002).
As lonesome small-fry entrepreneur Barry Egan, Sandler swung between anxious mess and exploding with rage, and proved to the haters — though he didn't owe them anything — that he could do more than funny voices.
The latest Sandler-Netflix venture — directed by Chernobyl's Johan Renck and based on a book by Jaroslav Kalfar, Spaceman of Bohemia (2017) — represents new territory again for the actor. Although, it must be noted, it's territory that has recently been trod by other big names, including Matthew McConaughey (in Interstellar), Ryan Gosling (in First Man), and Brad Pitt (in Ad Astra).
As Jakub Procházka, a Czech astronaut on a solo mission, Sandler joins the ranks of sad men in space, appearing drained of his characteristic geniality and rage alike. (Nor is he doing an accent — sorry folks, Renck doesn't believe in them.)
Sandler wore a harness suspended from wires to create the effect of zero gravity while his character was in space. (Supplied: Netflix)
Millions of miles from any beach resort or sprawling suburban home or, indeed, from any jokes, Sandler accesses a resolutely hushed, contemplative mode — leaning all the way into the depressive midlife slump he brushed up against in 2022 basketball drama Hustle.
"I used to be able to write these romantic comedies and comedies about people struggling with what they're going to do with their life," Sandler tells ABC Arts. He appears to be in quite a contemplative mood himself on the day we speak, though he's decked out in Miami-hued neons.
Sandler also professes a certain suggestibility. "Every time I watch a movie that I could act in, I say, 'Oh shit, I'd like to do something like that'. I get influenced quickly."
It's an endearing and perhaps rare quality for a wildly successful man in his fifties to have — suggestive of a curiosity and capacity for excitement that rhymes with the naiveté of his most iconic characters.
"Carey is the most exquisite actor I've ever worked with. She's so technically perfect and so delightful as a human being," Renck told The Hollywood Reporter. (Supplied: Netflix)
Jakub's mission in Spaceman is to retrieve a sample of a magenta cloud of space dust, a beautiful but ominous new presence in the sky over Earth. Man and movie alike, however, are far more interested in the mysteries of the human heart than in those of the cosmos.
We meet Jakub six months into his journey, at which point his wife, Lenka (Carey Mulligan), has stopped answering his calls, and the pining astronaut is seeking comfort in the forms of liquor and choc-hazelnut spread.
It's the unexpected appearance aboard the ship of Hanus, a giant, extraterrestrial arachnid voiced by Paul Dano, that shakes Jakub out of his growing stupor.
In a warm monotone, Hanus prods Jakub to consider his relationship with Lenka, from the magic of their first encounter through to its present state of distance and disrepair.
Hanus functions as something like a benevolent, eight-legged Ghost of Christmas Past, nudging Jakub towards the revelation that — at least as far as Lenka is concerned — he's been kind of a Scrooge.
Necessarily acting against a tennis ball for his scenes with Hanus, Sandler speaks fondly of seeing his unlikely companion come to life for the first time.
Film still from Spaceman (2024) featuring Hanus (voice by Paul Dano). (Supplied: Netflix)
"I saw drawings, so I knew what it was possibly going to look like — but getting to see the movie, and how fluid Hanus is movin' around the ship, and how warm his eyes are, and his little teeth that seem like they could eat corn on the cob …" he says, drifting off, tickled by the mental image.
While Dano recorded Hanus's lines in a darkened room, Sandler's role was a little more physically demanding — again taking the actor out of his comfort zone.
"When I read the script and saw this movie in my head, I was so excited," he says.
"Two weeks before we started shooting, Johan told me, 'Of course, you know this isn't Star Trek — you're not walking around on the ship. There's no gravity.'
"So then I realised that I had to do all these beautiful scenes while floating and having people twist me around.
Despite these new and trying conditions, Sandler gives a performance that is remarkable in its restraint — all the more so for the way in which it contrasts his public persona.
In Spaceman, the waggish comedian and devoted family man is left without any old friends or loved ones to bounce off or perform for.
Isabella Rossellini appears in Spaceman as Commissioner Tuma, Jakub's commanding officer. (Supplied: Netflix)
A little bit of that energy, however, would have leavened Spaceman — just a bit of the Adam Sandler seen in, say, Mr Deeds (2002); breaking out into a rendition of Space Oddity while on a private jet, singing into a banana, charming the pilots. But, as Bowie sang (more or less), the star looks very different today.
"The inner peace is here now — I'm calmer," Sandler says.
"There's less screaming in my house."
Spaceman is streaming on Netflix from March 1.

title: It's up for five Oscars and has attracted a wave of publicity in the United States. Now American Fiction arrives in Australia
content:
American Fiction didn't make it to cinemas in Australia, and while that needn't lessen the experience of people watching it locally when it debuts on Prime Video on Tuesday, it's likely to be a vastly different affair.
When Jonathan W. Gray saw the movie for a second time, he was at a cinema in Brooklyn, New York.
The associate professor of English at John Jay College-CUNY and the CUNY Graduate Center told ABC News that having people of different hues in the room resulted in quite the scene.
"It's a pity that you can't get the experience of having Aboriginal people and [other] black people and white people in Sydney all watching this film together," Dr Gray said.
"Because I think there are moments when you watch it with an audience, there's some uncomfortable laughter coming from some of the white people.
"And there are moments where they don't laugh at all, and we are laughing. We're cracking up.
"It was just interesting to hear the waves of laughter based on the people in the room."
Dr Gray says American Fiction cleverly uses humour as a vehicle, without resorting to slapstick. (Supplied)
American Fiction tells the story of Thelonious "Monk" Ellison (Jeffrey Wright), a frustrated novelist and professor, who is sick of the tired and offensive tropes in black literature and the industry that profits from them.
He writes the type of stereotypical black book he disdains to mock the establishment, but this book propels him to a level of success he could only previously have dreamt of.
The film has been nominated for five Oscars including Best Picture, Best Adapted Screenplay and a Best Actor nomination for Wright.
Dr Gray took to social media to crown American Fiction "the best film of the year" when he shared his review, published by The New Republic.
Based on the 2001 novel Erasure by Percival Everett, American Fiction was adapted for the screen by director and screenwriter Cord Jefferson (The Good Place, Watchmen).
"The book comes out in, I believe, February of 2001," Dr Gray says.
"It comes out before 9/11. It comes out before Oprah's book club becomes this cultural juggernaut.
"It comes out before the rise of Barack Obama. It comes out before Jay-Z and Beyonce, all of the things that would wind up shaping the 20-something years since its publication.
"I think that Cord is sensitive to the frustrations in the book and the frustrations are real.
"But those frustrations only make sense if you cast your mind back. This is 2001. This is the stolen election – that's really, in terms of history, that's the tangible thing in this cultural moment is the Bush versus Gore election.
"And there wasn't a lot of black representations. And there wasn't necessarily a lot of black empowerment when [Everett is] writing Erasure, so you see that sense of frustration there."
Dr Gray says despite the rise of black Twitter and far more visibility, black people are still vulnerable to the same kinds of misapprehensions they faced in the past.
"Cord's coming at it from a different point of view, because it's like, 'Oh, we actually have way more than we did when this book came out 20-something years ago, but how are we still dealing with the same shit?'
"And as soon as you ask that question, that's the question that allows him to then say let's update it because we are in some really important ways still dealing with the same foolishness, just calibrated differently."
Dr Gray says the humour comes from the absurdity in some of the scenarios presented in the film.
"There's a certain stratum of educated white people who do not understand that middle-class black people exist," he said.
He says in the film, both Monk and author of the hit novel We's Lives in Da Ghetto Sintara Golden (Issa Rae), are tapping into a set of expectations they themselves don't represent, and that tension is where the humour and pathos comes from.
"There are always talented people who are going to identify what the market wants and give them what they want."
Sintara Golden (Issa Rae) penned the novel We's Lives in Da Ghetto. (Supplied: Prime Video)
But Dr Gray says it works the other way too.
"Australia's favourite daughter, Margot Robbie, could make a career playing beautiful, vapid, blonde creatures. That's kind of how she got her start in The Wolf of Wall Street.
"But she's like, 'No, no, no, no, no, I'm not interested in that,' which is laudable for her not to be interested in continuing to play that stereotype. But that stereotype exists and is lucrative. And you could just keep doing that for the rest of your career and make money off it, right? And that's kind of what Sintara Golden is doing."
Dr Gray says one of the most telling parts of the movie is when Monk is writing his novel My Pafology and there is a father in conflict with his son acting out the scene in front of him.
The actor who plays the son is Okieriete Onaodowan, who played the Shakespearean dual roles of Hercules Mulligan and founding father James Madison in the musical Hamilton.
"That for me was a really brilliant and subtle, like, look at what we're asking these incredibly talented people [to do], right? We're asking them to play these stock stereotypes.
"How many other actors find themselves in the same situation where they could play this incredible thing, but you're asking them to play [a part] so diminished from that?"
American Fiction official trailer.
American Fiction is available to stream on Prime Video

title: ICYMI: Breaking Bad reunion, Dolly Parton pisses off country fans and Aussie actor's starring role
content:
This Sunday's SAG Awards didn't just make the Oscars' best actress race considerably more interesting, with Emma Stone and Lily Gladstone now equal frontrunners, it featured a lot of reunions, too.
You probably saw that Emily Blunt, Meryl Streep and Anne Hathaway reunited on stage in a Devil Wears Prada bit (not only was Streep wearing Prada, but Hathaway's blue dress felt like a nod to the cerulean top monologue).
But that was far from all. The casts of both Modern Family and Breaking Bad also reunited, to present ensemble cast awards. Better yet, between the Modern Family cast pondering whether it was too early to cash in with a reboot, and Bob Odenkirk refusing to do an acrostic poem about the word "ensemble", the bits were genuinely funny.
And in other entertainment and culture news? ICYMI:
The Indie Spirit Awards, in contrast to more well-funded award season ceremonies, is infamously held in a tent on the beach.
Which means it's not only "freezing cold" but it's a lot more accessible than your average event — as they found out today.
Streamed live via YouTube, the ISAs were all but drowned out by pro-Palestinian protesters — seemingly one guy with a very loud megaphone.
Although muffled, the protesters' chants were heard clearly as winners attempted to accept their awards. Host Aidy Bryant touched on the disruption, opening a bit about beach parties by saying, "Look we're at the beach and people are practising their freedom of speech."
Director Babak Jalali also acknowledged the outside protest while accepting the John Cassavetes Award for his film Fremont.
"There are people speaking outside, whatever they're saying is far more important than what I'm about to say," he said.
The loud protest has been operating throughout the whole ceremony, with many questioning the sounds on the ceremony's live stream. This is what Film Independent has to say about that:
Film Independent downplay the disruption to the Independent Spirit Awards.   (Supplied)
Protests over the war in Palestine have been a semi-constant presence at film and TV events this awards season. Earlier in February the Grammys red carpet was stalled due to a protest, and protesters shut down a street at this year's Sundance Film Festival.
— Velvet Winter
Shock eliminations on Survivor are one thing, but nobody expected Titans V Rebels contestant Scott to voluntarily leave during last night's episode.
Scott, a self-professed Survivor super fan and art director at MONA in Hobart, asked to leave during an already intense tribal council.
"I don't want to take this chance to play the game from someone else when I might not mentally be in the game right now," he said, adding, "You have no idea how bad my head's been these last 24 hours and the war that's going on up there. So I don't think I'd feel right sitting here in potentially someone else's stool after tonight."
Scott's decision was praised by cast mate Eden: "He's such an amazing person with such a kind energy and he knows what he needs. And mental health is such a huge hurdle that we all face. And for someone like yourself to know what you need right now — hat's off to you."
It was a teary farewell, with several other contestants commending Scott's decision both in the moment and on social media.
"I 100% support Scott," wrote fellow competitor Aileen on Twitter. "Kudos to him for being so brave, vulnerable and knowing when to prioritise his health. Survivor is an extremely tough game. You can prepare and dream to play the game all you want, but the mental battle can be the toughest challenge out there."
Watch his emotional farewell below.
— Jared Richards
It started as a counter-culture magazine (that was unfortunately co-founded by a Proud Boy), but now online outlet Vice could cease to exist completely.
Vice CEO Bruce Dixon signalled several hundred lay-offs and the shuttering of Vice.com in a memo to staff last week.
"I know that saying goodbye to our valued colleagues is difficult and feels overwhelming, but this is the best path forward for Vice as we position the company for long-term creative and financial success," Dixon said.
He said it was no longer cost-effective to distribute digital news via the website and they will be focusing more on their social offerings. Dixon also said they were looking to sell off its Refinery29 publishing business.
Vice filed for bankruptcy in the US in May, before being sold for $533 million ($US350 million) to a consortium led by the Fortress Investment Group.
In Australia, Vice and Refinery29 have an exclusive publishing deal with the Nine-owned Pedestrian Group. At the time of the bankruptcy announcement, former Vice staff members confirmed the Asia-Pacific newsroom had been closed, however Nine told Mediaweek at the time the change would not affect the deal they have with Vice.
ABC Entertainment has reached out to Pedestrian Group to confirm what the US changes mean for Vice and Refinery29 in Australia.
— Velvet Winter
Newcastle must be feeling a bit smug right now, as the new film starring locally raised comedian Geraldine Viswanathan was released globally.
Drive-Away Dolls is in cinemas now. It's directed by Ethan Coen, who split off from brother Joel to helm a goofy, queer road movie.
It's Viswanathan's first lead role in a major Hollywood flick, though you probably recognise her from movies including Blockers and Bad Education, or from TV shows including ABC drama Janet King and Miracle Workers (alongside Daniel Radcliffe).
Margaret Qualley and Geraldine Viswanathan star in Drive-Away Dolls as two queer women on a road trip who find themselves caught up in criminal activity.
Viswanathan plays uptight Marian, who agrees to a spur-of-the-moment road trip when BFF Jamie (Margaret Qualley of Maid) is dumped by her girlfriend (Beanie Feldstein, Booksmart). But their borrowed car's boot contains a severed head and some stolen items criminals want back.
Add in Miley Cyrus, Pedro Pascal, 2024 Oscar nominee Colman Domingo and Matt Damon, and you've got a star-packed, 84-minute comedy. ABC Entertainment reviewer Jamie Tram praised the film, calling it a "disarmingly sweet, lowkey jaunt" with "a potential record number of sex toy gags".
— Jared Richards
An endorsement from the legendary Dolly Parton is the stuff dreams are made of for any country music singer.
So, when the country music legend posted a message in support of Beyoncé after her debut on top of the Billboard Hot Country Songs chart last week, it felt like a significant moment in the Texas Hold Em singer's recently announced country turn.
"I'm a big fan of Beyoncé and very excited she's done a country album," Dolly wrote in a note on social media over the weekend.
"So congratulations on your Billboard Hot Country number one single. Can't wait to hear the full album."
You might imagine that such a legendary artist loudly professing their support of another singer would warm the hearts of music fans of all persuasions.
Thankfully, Parton's post did receive plenty of support, with a string of comments demanding a Dolly and Beyoncé collaboration, and others praising Parton's support of a fellow woman in music.
But, this is the internet in 2024, so there were also comments like this:
Each to their own, but if you ever find yourself trying to tell the woman who wrote Jolene what is and isn't country music, it's probably time to take a look in the mirror.
— Dan Condon
We promised this would be a Swift-free zone, but this story's too cute to not include.
If you've seen ABC's docuseries Better Date Than Never, which follows a set of diverse people on their first-ever dates, you'll remember Zach and Olivia – a couple who quickly bonded over both loving Taylor Swift.
Two years later, the two are engaged, with Zach proposing mid-Swift concert in time with the lyrics to Love Story: "He knelt to the ground and pulled out a ring."
Watch the heart-melting moment below, featuring a cameo from G Flip cheering the couple on.
Better Date Than Never's second season is currently airing Tuesdays 8:30pm on ABC TV, with all episodes streaming on ABC iview.

title: Star Trek: Discovery actor Kenneth Mitchell dies aged 49
content:
Kenneth Mitchell, an actor best known for playing several roles in Star Trek: Discovery, has died aged 49.
Mitchell died more than five years after being diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), his family announced on Sunday.
"With heavy hearts we announce the passing of Kenneth Alexander Mitchell, beloved father, husband, brother, uncle, son and dear friend," the family wrote in a statement posted to Instagram.
"For five-and-a-half years, Ken faced a series of awful challenges from ALS.
"And in truest Ken fashion, he managed to rise above each one with grace and commitment to living a full and joyous life in each moment."
Mitchell is best known for playing four Klingon characters in Star Trek: Discovery from 2017-2021.
During the first two seasons of Discovery, Kenneth played three Klingon characters — Kol, Kol-Sha, and Tenavik.
In season three, Mitchell returned as Aurellio, a character whose storyline carefully incorporated the personal use of a power wheelchair.
In an Instagram post in 2021, the actor said he was "incredibly grateful" to play Aurellio — a scientist born with a genetic defect.
He described the role as "a reminder that despite one's disabilities there is always room for possibility and ability".
Kenneth Mitchell also voiced several characters in an episode of Star Trek: Lower Decks. (Instagram: Kenneth Mitchell)
Mitchell also starred as Eric Green on the post-apocalyptic TV drama Jericho, and most recently in the 2019 film Captain Marvel.
The Star Trek world paid tribute to Mitchell following the news of his death.
"The entire Star Trek family sends their condolences to Mitchell's family, friends, loved ones, and fans around the world," StarTrek.com wrote.
The TV star was diagnosed with ALS in 2018. He revealed it to the public in a 2020 interview with People.
"The moment they told us it was ALS, it was like I was in my own movie," Mitchell said.
"That's what it felt like, like I was watching that scene where someone is being told they have a terminal illness."
The neurodegenerative disease, which causes the loss of physical function, led Mitchell to require the use of a wheelchair from 2019.
He is survived by his wife, Susan, and their two children.
ALS is the most common type of motor neurone disease (MND) that affects nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord.
The disease attacks the body in such a way that it becomes weakened, movement is affected, and it eventually leads to muscle paralysis.
To clarify, MND is the widely used generic term in Australia, the UK, and parts of Europe. ALS is used more generically in the United States, Canada, and South America.
The Mayo Clinic says:
The exact cause of the disease is still not known.
A small number of cases are inherited.
Researchers continue to study possible causes of ALS. Most theories centre on a complex interaction between genes and factors in the environment.
According to the Mayo Clinic, ALS often begins with muscle twitching and weakness in an arm or leg, trouble swallowing, or slurred speech.
As the condition progresses, the symptoms get worse and include:
Eventually, ALS affects control of the muscles needed to move, speak, eat, and breathe.
Eyesight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch are not affected. Nor are bladder and bowel function.
According to the Mayo Clinic, there is no cure for this fatal disease.
Half of people with ALS die within 14 to 18 months of diagnosis. However, some people with ALS live 10 years or longer.

title: This lesbian road movie from Ethan Coen embraces debauchery and sex positivity — and it's hilarious
content:
What: A raunchy lesbian road movie about two besties who are inadvertently pursued by bumbling criminals.
Starring: Margaret Qualley, Geraldine Viswanathan, Beanie Feldstein, Colman Domingo, Pedro Pescal.
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: In a state of constant, juvenile giggles.
It once seemed inconceivable that the Coen Brothers — affectionately described as "a monster with two heads" by Javier Bardem — would creatively part ways.
The duo's fixations on genre remixing, mordant humour and screwball antics spanned 34 fruitful years, and last converged in 2018's Western portmanteau The Ballad of Buster Scruggs.
In the temporary hiatus that's followed, their choice of individual narrative projects couldn't be starker.
Joel Coen went for a severe, minimalist rendering of Shakespeare with 2021's The Tragedy of Macbeth.
Meanwhile, Ethan revisited the screenplay for Drive-Away Dykes, a raunchy lesbian road movie he co-wrote with his wife (and long-time Coen editor) Tricia Cooke in the 2000s, which had previously languished in pre-production.
In the film's opening, a skittish collector of exotic goods (Pedro Pascal; The Last of Us) is cornered in an alleyway by an assassin who's intent on teaching a crucial Coen moral: bad things happen to those with valuable suitcases.
Coen and Cooke told ABC RN's The Stage Show they deliberately set the movie in 1999: "Making it a period thing makes it a little more innocent." (Supplied: Universal/Wilson Webb)
We're subsequently introduced to Margaret Qualley's (Maid) horned-up, motor-mouthed Jamie while she's tongue-deep in a sweaty tryst, her libido getting in the way of her relationship with cop girlfriend Sukie (Beanie Feldstein, Booksmart).
When she's quickly and inevitably dumped, she moves in with her buttoned-up bestie Marian (Australian Geraldine Viswanathan, Blockers), and they embark on a road trip to see Marian's aunt and escape their current funk.
Unsurprisingly, those best-laid plans are hijacked in service of a more urgent goal: to end Marian's terminal dry spell ("You can always find reasons to not have sex," Jamie chides).
Danger and opportunity arise when fate (or merely just incompetence) places the suitcase's hot goods — as well as a frozen head — into their "drive-away" rental car.
This fixes them in the crosshairs of an urbane criminal called The Chief (Colman Domingo; Rustin) with suspiciously deep pockets, who sets two bickering goons (Joey Slotnick and C.J. Wilson) on their tail.
Coen and Cooke asked Australian cinematographer Ari Wegner (The Power of the Dog) to shoot the movie, after seeing her work on the black comedy Zola. (Supplied: Universal/Wilson Webb)
What's not immediately apparent is that Drive-Away Dolls is a period film, situated at the tail end of the millennium.
Just as Nicolas Cage monologued about "that sumbitch Reagan" in Raising Arizona (whose zany comedic stylings and harebrained schemes are drawn upon here), a certain presidential scandal looms in the background of the Dolls' sexcapades.
Other Coen films like Fargo and No Country for Old Men may not have pointed fingers so directly, but they unmistakably illustrated the moral decay of modern-day America with quiet despair.
Dolls offers a refreshingly anarchic approach, instead sending up the stultifying sexual codes of yore to embrace debauchery of all stripes — resulting in a deliriously funny, unabashedly sex-positive ride.
In this way, Coen and Cooke leave any previous yearning for normality in the dust — a conviction reflected in their unconventional real-life marriage.
Listen to Ethan Coen and Tricia Cooke on ABC RN's The Screen Show
There's still melancholy to be found on the margins, however. A key marker of Dolls' period setting is the prevalence of lesbian bars in its southern road trip; Jamie aims to hit up every establishment from Philadelphia to Tallahassee, as well as other notable attractions like the world's largest dixie cup.
On ABC RN's The Screen Show, Cooke (who informally co-directed the film) recently discussed how the movie also draws upon her own experiences of lesbian bars in the same era — many of which are no longer around.
It's a nostalgic glimpse into the golden age for these safe havens, gesturing towards the wealth of lesbian history, culture and communion that has disappeared with these spaces.
It's always been rare to see a bawdy, queer comedy in cinemas. Rarer, still, is for this kind of mid-2000's material to be imbued with the sophistication of Coen and Cooke's direction.
Viswanathan prepared for the movie by re-watching Coen Brothers movies. "It just made me super intimidated," she told The Hollywood Reporter. (Supplied: Universal/Wilson Webb)
The script leans hard into regional vernacular to deliver a rapid-fire stream of colourful, scatological quips, typically dished out by Qualley with a "Honey Darlin'" drawl.
Her breathlessly hysterical performance is complemented by Viswanathan, an emerging Australian star (her comedic prowess previously graced another quality sex comedy, Blockers) who makes Marian's unusually pacey deadpan intonation sing.
For all the film's layered set-ups and its overarching noir riffs, Drive-Away Dolls gradually diffuses into a disarmingly sweet, lowkey jaunt across its 84-minute run time.
Crucially, the loose, frisky fun never lurches ahead of Jamie and Marian's lively rapport — a remarkable feat for a film stuffed with a potential record number of sex toy gags.
It's yet to be seen whether Dolls will be a box office hit, as even the best Coen films are often temperate in their financial successes. But the dismissive, inaccurate labelling of Gen Z audiences as "puriteens" ignores that there's a healthy appetite among young adult audiences, especially women, for ribald studio comedies.
As studio comedies claw back marquee space from the imploding superhero genre, let's hope Hollywood continues to tap into films like Drive-Away Dolls, which celebrate the sexy and unserious joys of queerness.
Drive-Away Dolls is in cinemas now.

title: SAG awards best moments: Fan favourites reunite, 'drunk' acceptance speech and a reignited Oscars race
content:
Oppenheimer has won best cast in a motion picture at the Screen Actors Guild awards to continue its dominance this season ahead of the Oscars.
Australian Elizabeth Debicki won for her portrayal of Princess Diana in The Crown, beating fellow Australian Sarah Snook who was nominated for her role in Succession.
But it was Lily Gladstone's win in the penultimate award of the night which will shake up the race for best actress at the Academy Awards next month.
Let's take a look at some of the key moments.
Emily Blunt, Meryl Streep, and Anne Hathaway reunited for a skit at the Screen Actors Guild awards. (Getty Images: Matt Winkelmeyer)
Meryl Streep stumbled on stage to present the first awards of the night, but somehow she'd forgotten her glasses and the card to read from.
But luckily Anne Hathaway and Emily Blunt were on hand to help our old friend Miranda Priestley.
And then Hathway and Blunt started quoting her lines back to her.
"By all means, move at a glacial pace!" and "No, no that wasn't a question."
And as it turns out, Streep was in Prada!
It was one of many reunions with the casts of Modern Family and Breaking Bad also taking the stage.
Billie Eilish autographs Melissa McCarthy's face before presenting an award. (Getty Images: Matt Winkelmeyer)
And it turns out it's Melissa McCarthy!
Eilish refused to sign her dress, saying she didn't want to ruin it, but had no such qualms autographing McCarthy's face.
She put her hand over McCarthy's mouth as she feverishly asked about Eilish's songwriting process.
Pedro Pascal accepts the outstanding performance by a male actor in a drama series award for The Last of Us. (Getty Images: Matt Winkelmeyer)
Pedro Pascal beat out the Succession trio of Brian Cox, Kieran Culkin and Matthew Macfadyen to take home the award for best male actor in a drama series.
It's fair to say the star of The Last of Us wasn't expecting it. "This is wrong for a number of reasons," he said on stage. "I am a little drunk, I thought I could get drunk."
He said as a member of the union since 1999 it was an incredible honour.
"I am making a fool of myself," he said before abruptly ending the speech and exiting the stage.
He later said he didn't remember what he said when accepting the award and was "very surprised".  "Let's YouTube it later," he said backstage.
There's nothing quite like seeing an actor in shock when their name is called out and that was the case for Australian Elizabeth Debicki.
She won best female actor in a drama series for her portrayal of Princess Diana in The Crown to add to her Golden Globe she won earlier this year.
And in doing so she beat fellow Australia Sarah Snook who took home the awards at both the Golden Globes and the Emmys this year.
Lily Gladstone accepts the outstanding performance by a female actor in a leading role for Killers of the Flower Moon. (Getty Images: Matt Winkelmeyer)
Lily Gladstone beat out Emma Stone to take home the best actress award and leave everyone asking, who will win the Oscar?
Stone took home the award at the Critics Choice and BAFTAs while both actors won at the Golden Globes in their respective categories — drama and musical/comedy.
But next month one will miss out.
Meanwhile, Oppenheimer duo Cillian Murphy and Robert Downey Jr. continued their dominance this awards season while The Holdovers star Da'Vine Joy Randolph also picked up another award.
This firms their grasp on their respective awards at the Oscars but other categories remain open.
Picking up best ensemble is a strong sign for Oppenheimer with three out of four Best Picture winners since 2020 also taking out this SAG Award.

As the last major award ahead of the Oscars on March 11, the SAGs take place just two days before voting closes.

With Jeremy Strong, Sarah Snook and Brian Cox absent tonight, Alan Ruck took the mic to speak on behalf of the cast. That's a win for Con-heads everywhere.

Fran Drescher takes the stage to give a rousing speech reflecting on last year's SAG-AFTRA strike, which lasted 118 days.
"I hold you all with the highest esteem and greatest respect, for you are the champions," she said to a silent room.
"You survived the longest strike in our union’s history with courage and conviction. The journey was arduous, came with great sacrifice and unrelenting stress.'
"Your collective dignity and perseverance to stand up and say, “We deserve better because we are better,” resulted in an historic 'Billion Dollar Deal.' Your solidarity ignited workers around the world, triggering what forever will be remembered as 'The Hot Labor Summer.' You survived the longest strike in our union's history with courage and conviction."
"You took the hero's journey and stood at the front lines, strike captains led the march on the picket lines and we all showed up to the rallies because you understood what our massive contribution means to this marvelous industry."
"And now, here we stand, tall and proud."
Drescher also called out the specific issue of AI in art.
"AI will entrap us in a Matrix where none of us know wha'ts real. If an inventor lacks empathy and spiriutality, then perhaps that's not the inventor we need."
"Dystopia stories can also become a self-fulfilling prophesy. We should tell stories that spark the human spirit, connect us to the natural world and awaken our capacity to love unconditionally."
She then called for female leadership that doesn't "emulate male energy" and leads with intellect, compassion and wisdom.
She ended with a hope for peace, and remarked on SAG-AFTRA's strength.
"I am honoured to be your president as we now enter our golden age."

Police are searching for Luke Davies, left, and Jesse Baird, right. (Instagram)
At Mr Baird's Paddington home, police discovered a "significant" amount of blood.
NSW Police Officer Beau Lamarre, 28, presented himself to police at Bondi police station at 10:30am on Friday, after a search.
In a statement, police have said they are "looking at a line of inquiry that a third person may be able to assist with the investigation".
Beau Lamarre in custody over disappearance of Sydney couple

A YouTube account associated with the blog site remains online.
Constable Lamarre's social media accounts show a long history of celebrity chasing and an inactive page for amateur actors.

title: This Oscar-nominated film about an Auschwitz commander's family is 'nothing short of nightmarish'
content:
The reeds by the river sway and shiver. They are soft, like carpet, and they arc up towards the knees of a family whose pale skin turns blinding under a noonday sun.
What: The story of real-life Auschwitz commandant Rudolf Höss and his family.
Starring: Sandra Hüller (Anatomy of a Fall; Toni Erdmann); Christian Friedel.
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: Like you need to stare at a wall for a couple hours.
It is a bucolic fantasy: a picnic unfurls itself in the grass; overhead, the faint echo of birds chirping — the kind of melodic chirps only heard in fables.
The family — a mother, father, and their sprawling nest of children — takes turns splashing in the water. When they've expended the last of their bliss, they traipse back through woodlands, nary a sound passing between them.
They drive down a darkening road that will lead them home, back to their immaculate estate with verdant lawns and blooming dahlias, back to their mannered conversations and pastoral luxuries — all the while happily, wilfully ignoring the horrors that lie in the concentration camp just beyond their garden wall.
These are the opening minutes of Jonathan Glazer's The Zone of Interest, a work so elusive, so uncanny, that it seems flung out of space.
The Höss family lives an idyllic country life, as long as you can ignore the concentration camp next door. (Supplied: Madman)
It's a film that is cool to the touch, expunged of anything as prosaic as a heartbeat or human warmth. It neither seduces nor repels its viewer, but rather wields something far more disquieting: a calculated detachment.
Truth be told, it is difficult to write about. How does one review a work that's so indifferent to its audience, a work that wrestles against its own classification as a film?
We might begin with its crude fundamentals. It is a holocaust film, but categorising it as one feels instantly crass. A holocaust film implies a certain sentimentality — the mawkish stylings of Schindler's List, or the rapture and devastation of Life is Beautiful — which is entirely absent in The Zone of Interest.
The brutalities and atrocities remain largely unseen here, muffled beneath the patter of domesticity.
It is, nominally, based on Martin Amis's 2014 novel of the same name — though, despite picking up an Oscar nomination for best adapted screenplay (one of its five nods, including best picture), it shares little with Amis's heightened, almost pulpy prose.
Christian Friedel plays Rudolf Franz Ferdinand Höss, a real-life German SS officer and commandant of the Auschwitz concentration camp. (Supplied: Madman)
Where the British author narrates a tale of love, lust and doom through a trio of men in and around Auschwitz, Glazer sharpens his focus to just one: Rudolf Höss, the real-life commandant of the Auschwitz concentration camp, played by Christian Friedel with a surgical and steely composure.
At a stretch, it is also a family drama, peering into the machinations of the Hösses as all around them, the air is punctuated by gunshots and shrieks. Their movements grow increasingly haunted: a daughter sleepwalks; an elder son punishes his brother by locking him in a greenhouse — a chilling mimicry of the savagery next door.
Their mother Hedwig (Sandra Hüller, in another tour de force after this year's Anatomy of a Fall) retains an iron grip on the proceedings, tempestuous and menacing in her rule over the manor.
"I could have my husband spread your ashes over the fields," she sing-songs to a young, stumbling housemaid.
The barbed-wire of a concentration camp make for a strange backdrop to a garden party. (Supplied: Madman)
It's only when her idyll is threatened that she cracks, stomping and convulsing in an infernal tantrum when she learns her husband may be deployed to another region. "They'll have to drag me out of here!" she wails in a painfully vacuous diatribe.
Glazer offers no interiority to these characters, and certainly no redemption.
There is little attempt to decipher their motives: how, for instance, Hedwig gleefully accepts her title as "Queen of Auschwitz", or how the couple sleeps soundly at night even as their house is lit by the glow of neighbouring flames.
Like Glazer's previous films — the oblique alien horror Under the Skin, or his sun-bleached gangster debut Sexy Beast — The Zone of Interest is formally tricky. At times, he cuts to a wide expanse of solid colour — white, red, black — in a deliberate act of distancing, preventing any tangible investment in the subject matter.
It is all artifice, all staging, bolstered by the score from previous Glazer collaborator Mica Levi, which gurgles like it's coming from the earth's core itself, or else rumbles with doleful bellows.
The cumulative effect is nothing short of nightmarish. It is a difficult, often distressing watch — a film that exhumes the villainies of the past, and reveals their lingering aftershocks in the present.
The Zone of Interest is in cinemas now.

title: Four Beatles, four biopics: How director Sam Mendes secured the rights to tell their stories
content:
John, Paul, George and Ringo are each set to get their very own biopic.
English director Sam Mendes plans to make four separate movies about the Fab Four, one from each Beatles' point of view, leading up to the group's break-up in 1970.
The project marks the first time The Beatles and their company Apple Corps have granted full life story and music rights to a scripted film, according to a statement. And Mendes is reportedly thrilled to have the blessing of Paul McCartney, Ringo Starr, and the families of the late John Lennon and George Harrison.
"I'm honoured to be telling the story of the greatest rock band of all time," said Mendes in a statement, adding that he was "excited to challenge the notion of what constitutes a trip to the movies".
Mendes is the Oscar-winning filmmaker behind American Beauty, 1917 and James Bond entries Skyfall and Spectre.
Produced, financed and distributed by Sony Pictures Entertainment and Mendes's Neal Street Productions, the four films are set for release in 2027.
Paul McCartney, Ringo Starr, John Lennon, and George Harrison pose for a Beatles photoshoot in 1963. (Supplied)
Music biopics have become a hugely popular fixture of the box office, with recent features including Baz Luhrmann's Elvis Presley blockbuster Elvis, Bradley Cooper directing and starring in Leonard Bernstein feature Maestro, and the Whitney Houston film I Wanna Dance with Somebody.
Plenty of other musical icons are about to get the silver screen treatment, including Bob Marley, Amy Winehouse, Michael Jackson and Bob Dylan. Ridley Scott is even in talks to helm a film about the rise of the Bee Gees.
The news is already prompting some great responses on social media, with many playfully likening the Beatles tetralogy to the interconnected blockbusters of the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

There's also an amusing trend emerging making light of what Ringo Starr's cinematic entry will be like.
A number of posts recall a scene from Walk Hard: The Dewey Cox Story – the 2007 biopic satire starring John C. Reilly – which lampoons The Beatles' 1968 spiritual trip to Maharishi Mahesh Yogi's ashram in Rishikesh, India.
The Fab Four have a storied cinematic history already.
Most recently, they were the subject of Peter Jackson's epic Get Back, chronicling the making of their final album Let It Be. There's also been documentaries about the band, including Ron Howard's 2016 film The Beatles: Eight Days A Week, covering the band's touring years, 2013 doco Good Ol' Freda, about the band's secretary and friend Freda Kelly, and Martin Scorsese's 2011 documentary on George Harrison, Living in the Material World.
John Lennon's early life was dramatised in 2009 biopic Nowhere Boy, while 1994's Backbeat fictionalised the group's pre-fame days in Hamburg, through the story of the band's original bassist Stuart Sutcliffe.
The Beatles during their Magical Mystery Tour. (Wikipedia Commons: Parlophone Music Sweden)
The Beatles' music also inspired two jukebox musicals: 1978's Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band and 2007 box office flop Across the Universe. They also inspired Danny Boyle's 2019 rom-com Yesterday (set in an alternate reality where The Beatles never existed, so a struggling musician takes credit for their songs) and 2001's I Am Sam, whose soundtrack is made entirely of cover versions of their music.
Of course, John, Paul, George and Ringo themselves starred in their own series of movies tied to their albums, beginning with 1964's madcap, groundbreaking A Hard Day's Night, 1965's surreal Help!, 1967's psychedelic Magical Mystery Tour and 1968's animated cult classic Yellow Submarine.
