title: Why Hugo Weaving likes making indie movies in Australia rather than blockbusters overseas
content:
Hugo Weaving will never say never to signing onto another big-budget, international blockbuster — but he'd rather be here, telling Australian stories.
"I've had enough of Red Skulls, Agent Smiths and Elronds," he says.
"It got to the stage where the only things I was being offered were uber-villains, so I thought, 'Let's just put that to one side.'"
Happier on home turf, he may well have fallen, inadvertently, into another typecasting stretch.
Weaving appeared as a cranky, drunken pub owner in last year's gripping outback thriller The Royal Hotel, from Melbourne filmmaker Kitty Green. Now, he pops up as a cranky, drunken recluse living in the Victorian bush in the soulful dark indie comedy The Rooster, from actor-turned-director Mark Leonard Winter.
"It's my year of crazy drunks," Weaving chuckles.
SMH's review of The Royal Hotel described Weaving's character as having "some of the hyperbolic blokiness of John Jarratt in Wolf Creek". (Supplied: See Saw Films)
Premiering at last year's Melbourne International Film Festival, The Rooster co-stars Iranian-born, Perth-raised actor Phoenix Raei. The Heights lead plays Dan, a country cop nursing an already bruised heart when his best mate unexpectedly dies.
Heading deep into the woods in search of answers, he stumbles across Weaving's shotgun-slinging character, wild man Mit. An unruly, if ultimately rewarding, bond is forged.
The pair has captivating on-screen chemistry, even though Weaving and Raei only met briefly before shooting, over Zoom.
"So it was lovely to finally meet him in the flesh, give him a big hug and say, 'Let's jump in and see where this journey takes us,'" Weaving says.
One of the film's most affecting moments involves an emotional breakthrough during a long, dark night when the pair drink a few too many whiskies.
"I remember being in that freezing cold hut, dancing to fabulous jazz with Phoenix, laughing and going 'Aww nooo,' a line my character says that became the accompanying catchcry for the whole film," Weaving recalls.
"Everything was always 'Aww nooo,' and we laughed a lot."
The Rooster was shot in the Macedon Ranges in Victoria. (Supplied: Bonsai/Sarah Enticknap)
With their oft-modest budgets, there's an all-in camaraderie on many Australian movies. That was certainly true of The Rooster, which was basically run out of the home Winter — who starred alongside Weaving in The Dressmaker, Healing and Measure for Measure — shares with his partner, producer and fellow actor Geraldine Hakewill.
Weaving says their generosity galvanised the cast and crew: "Having their mum and dad there every day, working away, was a real joy. Everyone bunked together, worked together and let off steam together."
He's known the pair personally for years, so was easily convinced when Mark called: "He's an actor I admire hugely, a really fabulous theatre-maker as well and he's got an out-there sensibility as well as being a soulful human being."
The film's focus on men and their mental health is important for Weaving and Winter.
In 2018 Weaving was set to feature in Paul Ireland's Measure for Measure — a retelling of the Shakespeare play set in a housing commission block in Melbourne — when the movie's co-writer and star Damian Hill died two days before filming was due to start.
Weaving agreed to star in Measure for Measure because he loved Pawno, the previous movie from Ireland and Hill. (Supplied: Umbrella)
Winter stood in for the beloved actor and writer, with production only delayed for a week.
"The trauma of that, for Paul and for Mark, who were very, very good friends of Damo, and for everyone on set, was shocking," Weaving says.
"It was really difficult for Mark to go through that process, so this film is informed by that experience."
That pain and grief is something we need to talk about more, Weaving says.
"Mark's exploring something which still has a lot of shame attached to it and remains such a strange taboo, this idea that men aren't allowed to express their feelings," he says.
"How, then, can men move forward? You've got to keep reassessing who you are, and so that becomes the reason why I do a film like The Rooster."
First-time filmmaker Winter wrote the role of the reclusive Mit with Weaving in mind. (Supplied: Bonsai/Sarah Enticknap)
Weaving follows his gut when choosing projects.
"I've always thought, 'Oh, this is a great script, I want to do it,' and I never think about the trappings," he says.
"If that means you're on a massive set built in a studio somewhere and there's masses of money, then cool.
"And if it means you're in someone's neighbour's hut in the middle of country Victoria, shivering your tits off, that's cool too."
Performing in film and TV projects here in Australia — and stage shows like Sydney Theatre Company's upcoming production of Thomas Bernhard's play, The President, alongside The Tourist star Olwen Fouéré — is the soul food Weaving craves.
Darkly comic classic The President is a co-production with Gate Theatre in Dublin. (Supplied: STC/Rich Gilligan)
"I'm not out to bang my own drum, but it makes sense to me that I should be wanting to do films like The Royal Hotel with Kitty and The Rooster with Mark.
"If you're an artist, actor, director, writer or a musician living in this country, I don't know why you wouldn't be focused on working here, telling our stories and prosecuting our culture," he says.
But working at home isn't necessarily the easiest route, even for a movie star of Weaving's calibre.
"This might sound weird for me to say, but it's been harder to get traction in my own country, even with my track record," he says. "So how hard is it for a young actor who wants to work here? For someone who hasn't been embraced overseas?"
For all his success, Weaving still gets the wobbles.
"I find myself getting more and more beset by nerves the older I get. But that's fine. It means you're actually caring more and more about all the complexities and nuances. Life's not simple," he says.
The Rooster is in cinemas from February 22.

title: We unpack Zendaya and Anya's Dune looks and try to understand this Hemsworth's Met Gala role
content:
Welcome to your Taylor Swift debrief, where we unpack everything Swiftie in the wake of the biggest and most monumental weekend of all time.
JK, this is a T-Swift-free space. For Eras tour content, we've got you covered here.
Zendaya has come a long way since Shake It Up's fedoras, pumped-up kicks and bangles. At the worldwide premiere of Dune: Part Two in London, the actor wore sci-fi couture perfection — a robotic suit of armour with daring see-through panels.
Sourced by stylist Law Roach, the suit is the original runway piece from designer Thierry Mugler's fall 1995 collection. (FYI, this is a pretty major coup. Few would be allowed to wear a vintage piece like this.)
The Queen's Gambit actor Anya Taylor-Joy also confirmed rumours she cameos in the film, popping up at the premiere in a white Dior cape featuring a hood, with a pleated gown. Some saw it as a nod to the character, but others have criticised Taylor-Joy for appropriating Muslim dress, pointing out the futuristic ensemble resembles a chador or khimar.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
For those (somehow??) more interested in the film than the fashion, critics are sharing their very positive reactions on socials. Top praise went to leads Timothée Chalamet and Zendaya alongside Part Two newcomer Austin Butler — as well as Australian cinematographer Greig Fraser and director Denis Villeneuve.
"[Denis] has delivered his magnum opus directing one of the best sci-fi films for generations to come," wrote Variety's senior artisans editor Jazz Tangcay.
Others are predicting a heap of nominations next awards season, including best picture.
You'll be able to see whether Dune: Part Two is worth the hype when it hits Australian cinemas on March 14.
— Jared Richards
The theme for fashion's biggest night out in 2024 is The Garden of Time, inspired by JG Ballard's 1962 short story.
Chris Hemsworth, who has never attended the ball, appears to be taking his co-chair duties super seriously.
"Anyone got a Garden of Time outfit I can borrow?" he wrote in an Instagram post/text chain shared across Vogue's social channels.
Thankfully, the Australian actor — who has a penchant for cycling through samey black/navy/maroon/grey suits on the red carpet — will share his co-chair duties with the uber-fashionable Zendaya, Bad Bunny and J.Lo, who have each attended the fundraising benefit in the past and are experts at taking red carpet risks.
This year's event coincides with the opening of the Metropolitan Museum of Art's new exhibition, Sleeping Beauties: Reawakening Fashion.
— Yasmin Jeffery
U2 vocalist Bono made an impassioned tribute to recently deceased Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny during the band's tenure at the billion dollar Las Vegas Sphere.
Navalny, who was fiercely critical of President Vladimir Putin, was reported dead on Friday while serving a 30-year jail sentence for charges he said were politically motivated. He was 47.
Bono, along with U2, has been vocally supportive of Ukraine as they battle for freedom against Russian forces. The singer took a break before their cover of Crowded House's Don't Dream It's Over to address the situation.
"Apparently Putin would never, ever say [Navalny's] name. So I thought tonight, the people who believe in freedom must say his name. Not just remember it, but say it," the singer said before leading the stadium in a chant of the fallen dissident's name.
Bono and Edge Tribute to Alexei Navalny with Don't Dream It's Over
— Velvet Winter
Twenty-one years after her first cover shoot for the Black women's lifestyle magazine, the queen is back. With a new hair product line to shill, yes.
But also with some insights into her experiences growing up in her mother's salon at the back of the Knowles family home, a smattering of musings on the connection between Black women's sense of self and our hair, and an achingly pure intergenerational photo shoot.
When she wasn't running what would become Destiny's Child routines in Ms Tina's shop, Beyoncé was watching her mother shampoo and trim women's hair, "transforming" them in the process.
"Looking back, it was more than just a hair appointment — it was therapy … It was a sacred space for these women," she says in the upcoming issue, which will drop on February 27.
Today, she sees Black hair salons as "a place to feel beautiful and vent, laugh, share secrets and pass down wisdom. It's the most consistent community gathering we have. It's so important that it's a sanctuary." And we couldn't agree more (multimillionaires — they're just like us?!)
"From spending my childhood in my mother's salon to my father applying oil on my scalp to treat my psoriasis — these moments have been sacred to me," Beyonce continues.
Yes, Beyonce is only telling us these things because she wants us to buy her new product. Yes, we're still in our feelings about it.
— Yasmin Jeffery
The family of the 81-year-old founder, producer and songwriter of the deeply revered Beach Boys, Brian Wilson, are seeking to place him under conservatorship.
This comes after the death last month of his wife, manager, and carer, Melinda Ledbetter.
"This decision was made to ensure that there will be no extreme changes to the household," the Wilson family said in a statement.
The Beach Boys — Good Vibrations
According to documents filed with the Los Angeles Superior Court, Wilson is "unable to properly provide for his own personal needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter" due to a neurocognitive disorder similar to dementia.
A hearing is scheduled for April 26 to determine whether the conservatorship can go ahead.
The news feels especially significant after the public's recent acquaintance with the problems of conservatorships, with Britney Spears successfully removing herself from an "abusive" conservatorship run by her father and legal team, who controlled her finances and career for 13 years.
— Al Newstead
Just call Geroge Santos a bad smell, 'cause this guy will not go away. Last year, the serial liar went from being voted out of congress (for being a serial liar) to hocking minute-long shout-outs on Cameo for $US500 ($764).
Late night host Jimmy Kimmel decided to take advantage of this opportunity with the segment Will Santos Say it?
Basically, Kimmel's staff paid for a bunch of Santos's Cameos to see if he would happily repeat the increasingly unhinged prompts requested by Kimmel (which included things like shouting out an uncle for eating "six pounds of loose ground beef", and congratulating a mum for the successful cloning of her schnauzer, Adolf).
Jimmy Kimmel pranks George Santos on Cameo, Trump wants "loyalists" only and the Chanucorn returns!
Enraged by the attention (or delighted, it's hard to tell with Santos), the former Republican congressman/drag queen has filed a lawsuit against Kimmel for "copyright infringement".
Santos is seeking statutory damages totalling $US750,000 ($1.1 million) for the five videos he created, which were played on the show and various social media platforms. He also asks for other damages, to be determined at trial.
It's an important reminder of the dangers of Cameo, just ask Flavor Flav…
— Velvet Winter
Not content with coining the term "Stan", Eminem is co-producing a documentary on the parasocial super-fan phenomenon.
Since Eminem's 2000 track Stan, where the rapper corresponds with an unhinged fan, the word has become synonymous with self-professed super-fans and those who identify as part of an artist's standom — such as Swifties, Barbz, Beehive, and the BTS Army and Rihanna's Navy.
The doco, tentatively titled Stans, will feature Eminem's biggest fans, and dive into the complex relationship between artist and audience.
Eminem — Stan ft. Dido
Directed by Steven Leckart, it's due out later this year. Here's hoping Mariah Carey makes an appearance, turning the spotlight on Slim Shady to ask the eternal question: "Why are you so obsessed with me"?
— Jared Richards
Oppenheimer star Cillian Murphy's new film Small Things Like These has opened the 2024 Berlinale to rave reviews, prompting Oscar rumblings already.
After taking home the BAFTA and Golden Globe for Oppenheimer, it's looking like he'll win the Oscar in a few weeks too — unless Paul Giamatti sneaks in for The Holdovers. So if the rumblings are true and Murphy won the best actor award back-to-back, he'd join a hallowed group of just four actors to do so, including Tom Hanks and Katharine Hepburn.
When asked post-screening whether he'd prefer to nab an Oscar for Oppenheimer or Berlinale's Golden Bear, Murphy said "Can I have both?"
As for the film itself? Small Things Like These is adapted from the celebrated 2021 novel of the same name by Irish writer Claire Keegan, and is directed by Belgian Tim Mielants, who worked on Murphy's show Peaky Blinders. It focuses on the Magdalene Laundries, cruel asylums across Ireland that housed "fallen women" who lived outside the boundaries of conservative beliefs.
The film is set in 1985, with Murphy playing a man who uncovers the truth of what occurs at a local convent. There's no cinema release date just yet, but expect to hear more soon.
— Jared Richards

title: Taylor Swift, Travis Kelce, Barbie win People's Choice Awards. Here are the key moments
content:
Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce have both won People's Choice Awards.
But of course, both were absent from the awards show. In case you missed it, Swift is in Australia for her Eras tour.
Okay, fine. It's been impossible to miss.
Kelce won the Athlete award after last week taking out Super Bowl LVIII with the Kansas City Chiefs.
Swift won the Pop Artist award, the Social Celebrity award and the Concert Tour award for the Eras Tour.
Barbie star Simu Liu's opening monologue made reference to Golden Globes host Jo Koy when he described himself as: "An Asian host of a major awards show, what could possibly go wrong?" before he seemingly referenced Barbie when he spoke about "the most iconic pop culture moment of the year".
"Who could forget that one little movie about a blonde American icon that had the entire country dressing up, dancing the night away and making huge waves at the box office," he said.
"I was a Swiftie long before I was Ken," he clarified to applause.
Just hours earlier, Barbie went home empty handed at the BAFTAs.
America Ferrera won the Movie Performance of the Year award. (REUTERS/Mario Anzuoni)
But at the People's Choice Awards, Barbie won the Movie award, the Comedy Movie award, Barbie World by Nicki Minaj & Ice Spice with Aqua won the Collaboration Song award, Male Movie Star went to Ryan Gosling, Margot Robbie won Female Movie Star and America Ferrera won the Movie Performance of the Year trophy.
"You, the audience, the people, you made Barbie a global cultural phenomenon, thank you," Ferrera said.
Here are the nominees for the People's Choice Awards, where Barbie leads the film nods and Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce are both nominated.
Ferrera thanked the "incomparable" Greta Gerwig and Margot Robbie who she said deserved "all the flowers".
"It feels like a once in a lifetime opportunity to be part of a bold and inspiring masterpiece and to get to speak words of truth that so many of us needed to hear out loud, so thank you Margot and Greta. I love you."
She also acknowledged how deeply Barbie resonated with fans.
"This movie Barbie, at the heart of what it is, it is an invitation to all of us to embrace our full selves."
Billie Eilish, who was on stage for the speech, was also a winner on the night.
Eilish took home the TV Performance award for her role in Swarm – her first acting gig.
Adam Sandler was crowned the People's Icon and in his acceptance speech, he did what he did best — entertained — delivering a self-deprecating acceptance speech… for the wrong award.
Adam Sandler thanked his wife Jackie after he gave a speech in which he accepted the wrong award. (REUTERS/Mario Anzuoni)
"This is going to be a little humiliating," he started.
"When my agent called me and said I won the People's Choice Icon Award, I was driving. I had him on speakerphone and I was also eating frosted flakes and… I think I misheard him.
Sandler said it was "about time," putting on a voice and giving a lengthy speech in which he called on the audience to respond to his proclamations with a "hell yeah".
"To the People Magazine's academy members of hotness and sexual attractiveness," Sandler said.
"I would like to say thank you for recognising me as the man who made our entire country the horniest this year. And was by far the most talked about person in the bedroom by couples or throuples during fantasy role play and slappy time."
Sandler has mostly played comedic roles throughout his decades-long career, starting with Saturday Night Live in 1990, before moving on to star in films such as Billy Madison and Happy Gilmore.
More recently, he's starred in the Netflix comedy Murder Mystery and the crime thriller Uncut Gems.
And as a true mark of pop culture relevance, he's been referenced on The Simpsons, South Park and Family Guy.
Lenny Kravitz said he's never followed trends. (REUTERS/Mario Anzuoni)
Lenny Kravitz was recognised as the Music Icon and gave a vastly different speech.
"When I was thinking of what to say tonight, I kept going back to that word icon," Kravitz said.
"And it means a lot of things to a lot of people.
"But to me, it means you've made an indelible mark by being who God created you to be and daring to be different.
"When I was first coming up, a lot of people offered me a lot of deals, but they wanted me to change.
"My music wasn't black enough. It wasn't white enough. It didn't fit nicely inside a box or sound like what was on the radio at the time.
"And I turned down the money and the goods and promises of fame and stardom because I couldn't live with myself doing something inauthentic."
The awards which brings together the biggest names in movies, television, music and pop culture in general. Here's some of the looks we've seen so far.
He said an icon to him is someone who inspires and teaches others to believe in themselves and their direction.
"I was a fan of music long before I was a musician," Kravitz said.
"And my mantra now is the same as it was 35 years ago.
"Never follow the trends, set your own pace and recognise that the best is right here, right now, in front of you."
Kravitz performed a medley of his hits including It Ain't Over 'till It's Over and Are You Gonna Go My Way.
Dressed in all red, including long red leather boots and singing into a red microphone, pop star Kylie Minogue sang her hit Padam Padam.
Kylie Minogue performed Padam Padam. (REUTERS/Mario Anzuoni)
She was earlier seen on the Red Carpet wearing a shiny teal dress.
The 49th annual People's Choice Awards took place in Santa Monica. As many expressed when winning a gong, this awards show holds a special place in the hearts of creatives because, as the title suggests, it is voted by the people.
That essentially means the awards show recognises film, TV, sport personalities and comedians – who are popular.
Fan voted, and open to those 18 and above worldwide, the public votes take place online.
There are 45 categories.

title: When Jennifer Lopez dance-montages her way through three failed marriages, it's breathtaking
content:
When the trailer for This Is Me … Now dropped last month, collective confusion ensued, with headlines describing it as "total chaos" and asking, What in the hell is going on?.
What: A genre-bending musical co-written, produced by and starring Jennifer Lopez.
Starring: J.Lo, OFC. And a host of cameos including her hubby Ben Affleck, Kim Petras, Post Malone, Fat Joe, Trevor Noah, Sofia Vergara, Jane Fonda, Keke Palmer, Jenifer Lewis, Neil deGrasse Tyson (yes, the astrophysicist) and Indian spiritual figure Sadhguru.
When: Streaming now on Amazon Prime.
Likely to make you feel: Bamboozled.
Was this Lopez's Everything Everywhere all at Once moment, but with singing, dancing and talk therapy instead of butt plug and bum bag martial arts fight scenes? Or was it, as Stop Everything! guest critic Maria Lewis suggests, "J.Lo's Cats"?
Well, I've watched This Is Me … Now, I've listened to Lopez during a press event for the film, and my answer is a very firm, "yessss, maybe?" to both.
Billed as emanating "from the dreams of Jennifer Lopez", This Is Me … Now is Lopez's US$20 million ($31 million) self-funded feature companion to a new album, which shares the same name. Both were released last week.
Lopez is a woman in her 50s, dancing like someone less than half her age in This Is Me … Now. (Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios)
The title is a nod to This Is Me … Then, Lopez's 2002 album, released at the height of Bennifer 1.0, her first, failed relationship with now-fourth husband Ben Affleck.
Co-written by Lopez, it reads as a genre-mashing steampunk musical x fragrance ad x rom-com dance movie x speculative psychodrama — and included the eyebrow-raising line: "We think you might be a sex addict."
Jennifer Lopez has teased upcoming movie-musical, This Is Me… Now: A Love Story, with an outrageous trailer that makes it hard to say what, exactly, the film is.
In the 90s, I watched Lopez on In Living Color, the Wayans brothers' hip-hop infused sketch comedy show. This was pre J.Lo, and she and her fellow fly girls — a multiracial crew of cute and mega-talented dancers — embodied everything I wanted to be but also found completely intimidating.
Pop culture is everywhere. But it's also a lot. If you need help making sense of like, everything in your feed, Beverley Wang is here to help.
Then came her breakout film role in Selena, and next minute she was acting opposite George Clooney in Steven Soderbergh's Out of Sight. After that, she was everywhere.
Lest we forget — the early 2000s were peak J.Lo-saturation years. She starred in rom-coms like The Wedding Planner and Maid in Manhattan. On the music industry side, she became Jenny from the Block with the flawless skin and signature hoops. Her fashion choices gave us Juicy Couture tracksuit ubiquity and Google Images.
Between marriages one and two, she dated Puff Daddy. And she made huge business moves — launching Glow, her first bestselling fragrance — setting a template for affordable branded fragrances that celebrities have followed ever since.
What this means is that J.Lo has been marketed to me as a celebrity brand for roughly half my life. Even if I've never bought her fragrance or watched all her films, I can't insist, like Mariah Carey, that I don't know her.
The new film is billed as emanating "from the dreams of Jennifer Lopez". (Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios)
And that's why, 30 years into my parasocial relationship with J.Lo, I won't pretend I'm not invested in the wild swings of her love life.
I won't deny knowing the names, in order, of her three ex-husbands. I've been stuffing my face with J.Lo relationship news for decades (and maybe you have too?).
And that's also why, when Lopez and Affleck reformed as Bennifer 3.0 (Affleck's marriage to actor Jennifer Garner was Bennifer 2.0), and married in 2022, 18 years after breaking up, it felt like a prank and a grand reward: an unbelievable redemption arc! And I was there from the beginning!
When, in the film, Lopez dance-montages her way through three failed marriages, while a cast of friends crack jokes about a cursed wedding bouquet, it's breathtaking.
Lopez and Affleck reunited after 18 years felt like an unbelievable redemption arc. (Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios)
Where before we may have read the gossip posts and gasped, gawked or rolled our eyes from afar, in This Is Me … Now, Lopez lets us know that yes, she thought it was a lot, too. The punchline becomes the power move.
"There's not a project that I've ever been involved with, music or movies or anything, that I didn't put a bunch of my life into and a lot of my personal experience," Lopez said at a pre-release press event.
"I was at a point in my life where, as a person and as an artist, I could really look at all of the things that I was good at and the things that I felt and knew about myself, and put them all into this project in a way.
Jennifer Lopez says her genre-mashing new musical film This is Me...Now is "kind of meta". (Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios)
Jennifer Lopez also produced, co-wrote and self-funded the semi-autobiographical film. (Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios)
While the result is baffling, I can't help but appreciate the reach and ambition of This Is Me … Now.
This is Me...Now is a genre-mashing steampunk musical x fragrance ad x rom-com dance movie x speculative psychodrama. (Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios)
Lopez is a woman in her 50s, dancing like someone less than half her age, singing, acting and processing her way through a musical feature about her often-mocked love life, that she co-wrote and self-financed.
As far as choices go, this one is intriguingly crazy-brave and exposing.
After the premiere of This Is Me … Now, it was announced that a documentary about the feature will be released on February 27, also on Prime Video. Humbly titled The Greatest Love Story Never Told, the documentary will tell the behind-the-scenes story of the making of This Is Me … Now.
Has Lopez turned her addiction to love into an addiction to talking about love?
There's a risk that all this multi-layered meta storytelling of this grand love story – me looking at J.Lo, looking at J.Lo, looking at J.Lo looking at her love — could cause a vortex that will shatter the space-time continuum, and my mind. But I won't rule out watching "The Greatest Love Story Never Told."
If J.Lo wants to share, who am I to decline?
This Is Me … Now is streaming on Prime Video.

title: Oppenheimer, Poor Things dominate BAFTAs as Barbie goes home empty handed — as it happened
content:
Oppenheimer and Poor Things take out the top awards at the BAFTAs, with all Australian nominees going home empty-handed.
Look back on the blog as it happened.
By Shiloh Payne
Thank you for joining in, we know it was an early morning.
You can continue to stay up to date with the latest news here on the ABC News website and on our app.
If you're looking for more red carpet fashion, we've got you covered at the link below.
By Jared Richards
Actor Michael J. Fox presented the BAFTAs final award, Best Picture, to rapturous applause and a standing ovation.
The 62-year-old actor was recently the subject of Still, a documentary about his experience living with Parkinson's.
"There's a reason why they say movies are magic, because movies can change your day," he said. "They can change your outlook, and sometimes even your life."
Watch the moment and host David Tennant's introduction below:
By Georgie Hewson
Emma Stone for Best Actress:
By Jared Richards
You're in luck. Here's a round-up of our reviews and interviews.
Luke Goodsell's review of Oppenheimer spells out why it's sweeping the awards season:
By the film's final moments it has, often by sheer force rather than any kind of elegance, cemented itself as an enormous, ugly-beautiful object infused with as much melancholy as bombast.
Looking for a more wholesome watch? Try The Holdovers, "a comfort movie, executed with the emotional precision of an old hand".
(GIPHY)
In my chat with Anatomy of a Fall director and co-writer Justine Triet, she explained why she'll never tell whether or not the lead character killed her husband:
"When we started to show it to audiences, sometimes people were saying 'she's so guilty', you know, sometimes the opposite. It was my goal to be in the middle; to divide opinions."
We also raved about The Boy and The Heron, the latest from Japanese animation titans Studio Ghibli that saw director Hayao Miyazaki return after retiring a decade ago:
Like Miyazaki's best work, The Boy and The Heron isn't merely nostalgic for its creator's childhood. It's a challenge to that next generation to rethink the way the world works. That's what keeps him vital, seven decades into his career.
Bookmark them for later!
And stay tuned for my interview with Poor Things' Oscar-nominated Australian screenwriter Tony McNamara later this week.
By Georgie Hewson
By Georgie Hewson
If you didn't get a chance to watch some of the big speeches from the night, have a look here.
Christopher Nolan for best director:
Robert Downey Jr. for Best Supporting Actor:
By Jared Richards
With the Oscars three weeks away, the BAFTAs have helped cement some category frontrunners.
Best Picture is seemingly Oppenheimer's to lose, now it's taken home the title (or its slightly differently worded equivalent) at the BAFTAs, Golden Globes, Critics Choice, DGAs and a heap of smaller (but respected) critics awards.
Other Oppenheimer locks? Robert Downey Jr. is a sure thing for Best Supporting Actor and Cillian Murphy is likely for Lead Actor, though Paul Giamatti is still in the running there.
Best Director is probably down to Christopher Nolan and Martin Scorsese, even if Killers of The Flower Moon didn't take home anything tonight. Its best chances remain there and Best Lead Actress for Lily Gladstone, though Emma Stone keeps raking in wins. It'll be tight.
But there's absolutely no competition in Best Supporting Actress. Da'Vine Joy Randolph has won it for her turn in The Holdovers at the BAFTAs, Golden Globes, Critics' Choice, New York Films Critics Circle and more. You can read Thuy Ong's interview with her here.
Best International Feature is likely going to Zone of Interest, given that Anatomy of a Fall isn't nominated. (France opted to nominate a different film, which didn't make the final cut.) .
Both are two of the best films of the award season. They also are likely to receive their flowers for their scripts, with Zone nominated for Best Adapted Screenplay and Anatomy for Best Original.  Anatomy has more chatter online thanks to its fun elements (beautiful border collie Messi, a 50 Cent earworm, a sexy French lawyer), while Zone is an important, harrowing and uncomfortable watch.
Keep an eye on Zone for Best Sound too. Once you've seen the movie, you'll see why, but as a glimpse: director Jonathan Glazer repeatedly calls the soundscape "movie 2" in press, as terrible screams break through an idyllic family home setting. It's essential to the film.
The Boy and The Heron is pretty much guaranteed for Best Animated Film, but we've known that for a while.
Barbie fans, don't worry. It's not looking good for the big categories, but it's on lock for Best Original Song and will likely sweep a few technical/production awards, too.
But what's the fun of knowing all? The Oscars love a random winner, so perhaps it's Maestro's night to sweep. (Just kidding, there's no way that's happening.)
By Shiloh Payne
Here's a peek behind the curtain to see what the stars get up to behind the camera at award ceremonies.
By Shiloh Payne
We've got you covered.
You can see our full winners list with this link:
By Georgie Hewson
So many gowns and so little time.
Here are some more fabulous frocks.
By Jared Richards
A few winners are still in cinemas, including The Boy and the Heron (best animated film), Anatomy of a Fall, Poor Things and The Holdovers (best supporting actress).
Oppenheimer is available to rent/buy online, and will be streaming on Binge from March 22.
Earth Mama (outstanding debut by a British writer, director or producer) is available to rent/buy online.
As for Crab Day (best Britsh short animation) and Jellyfish and Lobster (best British short), you can watch them on YouTube (for now). Why not take 10-20 minutes out of your morning — we won't tell your boss.

As for films to come?
The Zone of Interest is out in cinemas on February 22.
American Fiction (best adapted screenplay) is out in cinemas February 27.
Unfortunately, 20 Days in Mariupol (best documentary) has no Australian release yet, but just played at Antenna Documentary Film Festival last week. If you're in Melbourne, it's playing at ACMI on March 4.
By Shiloh Payne
By Georgie Hewson
Here's Sophie Ellis-Bextor's performance of Murder on the Dancefloor we told you about earlier.
Before the performance on the red carpet she joked that hopefully Barry Keoghan would "have his clothes on" in the performance, making reference to the film Saltburn.
There were of course no actual murders, but she did slay.
By Georgie Hewson
It's been a huge night for actors including rising star award winner Mia Mckenna-Bruce who's pictured here celebrating the win with her parents.
Aw.
Da'Vine Joy Randolph shot her first film in London and said the win was a full-circle moment.
Some winners even got to meet The Prince of Wales backstage.
By Jared Richards
Quite a few films were left awardless despite multiple nominations.
The biggest snub goes to Killers of the Flower Moon, nominated nine times and going home without a single win. Ouch.
Maestro missed out big too, with seven nominations and no trophies. I haven't done the math yet, but it has to be one of the most-snubbed films across the awards circuit so far.
And if you're still stuck in Barbenheimer discourse, it might be time to move on: Barbie didn't win in any of its five categories tonight.
Saltburn also lost out in five categories but it was quite simply never really going to win. Sophie Ellis-Bextor performing Murder on The Dance Floor was a nice nod to its cultural capital though.
A24 drama Past Lives also missed out on an award despite three nominations.
By Georgie Hewson
Remember earlier when we told you David Tennant couldn't get a dog sitter for the BAFTAs?
Here's Bark Ruffalo on his ruff journey to the stage.
By Shiloh Payne
Get yourself a Barbie that looks at you like this! Love this dynamic duo.
By Jared Richards
Oppenheimer swept this year, with seven BAFTAs. That includes some of the biggest categories of the night, including Best Film, Best Director and Lead and Supporting Actor for Cillian Murphy and Robert Downey Jr.
It marks British-American director Christopher Nolan's first BAFTA, bar an honorary award in 2010. That's worth losing your hat over.
Another big winner was Yorgos Lanthimos' odyssey Poor Things, taking home five golden masks. That included Best Leading Actress for Emma Stone and four production awards.
In third place was The Zone of Interest with three awards: Outstanding British Film, Best Film not in the English Language and Best Sound.
By Georgie Hewson
David Tennant closes the ceremony.
"Thankyou to everyone at home for supporting film because without an audience making movies would be a lot less fun," he says.
"Some people have won tonight, some have not but whatever the outcome, it's always a pleasure to gather together and celebrate cinema in all its forms.
"Now as a wise person once said, come on Barbie, let's go party!"
The ceremony might be over but our live coverage isn't.
Join us as we delve into the winners, snubs and what this might mean for the Oscars.
By Shiloh Payne

title: Original draft of Star Wars script left in London apartment by Harrison Ford fetches $20,821 at auction
content:
An original draft Star Wars script left in a London apartment by Han Solo actor Harrison Ford sold at a UK auction for 10,795 pounds ($20,821) on Saturday.
The script was used when Ford was in London for the filming of the first instalment of the epic saga, originally titled The Adventures Of Luke Starkiller, at Elstree Studios north of London.
Ford was given a budget by the film studio and chose a flat to rent in London's Notting Hill, where he formed a genuine friendship with the landlords and their family.
Harrison Ford starred in four of the Star Wars movies as Han Solo.  (Luscasfilm)
The grandchildren of the landlords say the owners lived on the bottom floors of the house, while Ford occupied the top two floors and they had no idea who he was — their only comment was he was "an excellent tenant, very tidy".
With no idea who their guest was, the owners mentioned to their cleaner that they had a lodger staying. She fainted on encountering the actor and realising who he was.
During his stay, many other Star Wars actors visited, including Carrie Fisher and Mark Hamill.
The grandchildren say as the owners got to know their famous tenant, they struck up a genuine rapport.
Harrison Ford formed a genuine rapport with his landlords.  (Supplied)
One touching story the owner recalls is Ford giving them money to purchase new plants for their garden, as they all spent so much time there. Ford even attended her son's first birthday party in said garden.
The landlords found the script and other items when Ford left and kept them for decades.
The fourth draft of the screenplay, dating from March 15, 1976, was snapped up by an Austrian collector when it went under the hammer at Excalibur Auctions in Hertfordshire, north of London.
A typed letter believed to be from an agent or friend of Harrison Ford sold for 177.80 pounds.  (Supplied)
Ford left the script at the London flat he rented at the time along with shooting schedules, which sold for 4,826 pounds, and a letter from an agent or friend, which sold for 177.80 pounds.
The incomplete and unbound script contains revisions, and introduces Han Solo on page 56.
The 1977 film catapulted Ford to international fame and he starred in sequels The Empire Strikes Back (1980) and Return Of The Jedi (1983), before taking on the role again in The Force Awakens (2015).
Harrison Ford’s shooting schedule for the first Star Wars film were among a group lot that sold for 4,826 pounds. (Supplied)
Excalibur Auctions' auctioneer Jonathan Torode said this sale saw a new record set for a Star Wars script, "which shows how a personal link to the items is so enticing to Star Wars fans".
ABC/AFP

title: If corporate team-building exercises aren't enough of a nightmare, what happens when someone disappears into the forest on one?
content:
The harshness of Australia's landscape and the caprices of a hostile climate have always been a preoccupation of bestselling crime author Jane Harper's novels.
What: The second whodunnit in Jane Harper's Aaron Falk trilogy.
Starring: Eric Bana, Anna Torv, Deborra-Lee Furness.
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: Cold and intrigued.
In Force of Nature, she exchanges the scorching heat of a drought-stricken regional town with the stinging cold and forceful gales of a dense rainforest.
Located in the fictional Giralang Ranges (but shot across Victoria's visually stunning Otway Ranges, the Dandenongs and Yarra Valley) lush greenery and the perennial sensation of being cold and damp permeate the second film adaptation of Harper's Aaron Falk trilogy — dubbed The Dry 2.
The Australian actor stars as detective Aaron Falk in the second movie in The Dry series, adapted from Jane Harper's murder mystery series.
The film's cinematography is breathtaking — the thick canopy of trees lends the film a claustrophobic feel, juxtaposed against an uneasy remoteness that heightens the tension as things start to go awry.
Five women of various dispositions, social backgrounds and hierarchical positions within the company BaileyTennants find themselves on the very worst thing you can imagine: a multi-day hike/corporate team building exercise for people essentially under performance management.
If there's one thing worse than having your every move scrutinised in a repressive office atmosphere, it's transplanting that to an impenetrable forest under immense physical duress with no way out.
Harper crafted a mystery thriller, but parts of Force of Nature feel more like a capitalist nightmare.
The dial is turned up to 11 when you throw in a whistleblower, a former substance abuser, a suspicious wife, a resentful childhood acquaintance, an adverse physical environment and long-held, simmering resentments — all of which find their focal point in Alice Russell.
Played by Anna Torv with a believable prickliness, Alice is an ambitious and ruthless senior leader, reluctantly acting as an informant on BaileyTennant's money laundering activities.
Anna Torv is a scene-stealer as the prickly Alice, who goes missing while the group is on a hike. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Cruel and stubborn, Alice is loathed by everyone, which makes the mystery of her disappearance during the hike all the more difficult to pinpoint.
Could her snooping around have landed her in trouble, or was it her unbearable personality?
De facto head of the group, Jill Bailey (a delightfully imposing Deborra-Lee Furness) is the wife of slippery family business scion and BaileyTennants CEO Daniel Bailey (Richard Roxburgh).
Bright-eyed ingénue Bree (the breathy Lucy Ansell) is Alice's assistant, while the meek, vacillating Lauren (Robin McLeavy) is Alice's schoolmate from decades back.
And rounding up the quintet is Beth (Sisi Stringer), Bree's chain-smoking sister, barely keeping a lid on her dark past.
Sissi Stringer, Robin McLeavy, Deborra-Lee Furness, Lucy Ansell and Anna Torv star as a group of women on a corporate team-building exercise in the wilderness, where one of them goes missing. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Enter our detective duo, Aaron Falk and Carmen Cooper (Jacqueline McKenzie). Reprising his role from The Dry, Aaron — unassuming and pallid in the books, but played antithetically by the dark, strapping Eric Bana — is investigating Alice's disappearance.
Armed with a guilty conscience that he pushed her too far in his efforts to unearth BaileyTennant's financial crimes, Bana raises some of the film's more interesting moral quandaries, the ethical grey areas of law enforcement.
Oscillating between three different timelines, the film, while not exactly propulsive, unfolds at an enjoyable pace. Twists and turns are revealed in each timeline, coalescing to paint a gradually forming picture of what happened to Alice.
Robert Connolly's film adaptation hews closely to the book, right down to several snatches of dialogue lifted verbatim, but there are a number of key changes — both to the detriment and benefit of the film.
Eric Bana and Robert Connolly return to the big screen in Force of Nature: The Dry 2 (Laura Tingle)
The cast is updated to be more culturally diverse — sisters Bree and Beth are women of colour, though Bree is defanged of her edge — and key relationships are reconfigured.
There's a shoe-horned, clumsy backstory that delves into Aaron's familiarity with the Giralang Ranges — honed over one fateful weekend hiking there with his parents — that doesn't add much to the narrative.
The cinematography of Force of Nature is breathtaking, as the dense canopy of trees lends the film an oppressive feel. (Supplied: Roadshow)
But where the film falters most is in its omission of a key plot point from the book that involved Alice's daughter and lent the book much of its urgency.
Faced with a heartbreaking revelation in the book, Alice is mired in personal crisis and desperate to leave the rainforest, which explains her inexcusable behaviour. Without it, much of her characterisation is lost.
There's a literary crime spree underway in Australia thanks to authors such as Jane Harper and Chris Hammer.
And for all of Harper's evocatively conjured backdrops in her books, the film's adaptations are never quite as successful at evoking the deleterious effects of the brutal physical environment on the psyche of the characters.
Despite being called The Dry 2 — a misleading moniker for so many reasons and undoubtedly a marketing move more than anything — the Force of Nature film feels more like a standalone. Without the throwaway lines and key details that evoked The Dry in the book, the film loses a crucial sense of continuity.
The Dry, like all the best crime thrillers, had two whodunnits unfolding in tandem: the mystery of Aaron's friend Luke's murder-suicide, and the cold case disappearance of Aaron's childhood sweetheart Ellie.
Force of Nature attempts to do the same, with a secondary mystery revolving around a long-dead serial killer and his unearthed hideout in Giralang Ranges, but it lacks heft.
If Force of Nature doesn't scale the heights of The Dry, it's predominantly because the story isn't nearly as good in the first place.
Force of Nature: The Dry 2 is in cinemas now.

title: The Fantastic Four franchise has had a chequered history. It's back with Pedro Pascal at the helm
content:
Marvel has unveiled its new cast for the Fantastic Four.
Pedro Pascal (The Last of Us, The Mandalorian, Game of Thrones, Narcos) has been announced as the new Reed Richards, also known as Mister Fantastic.
English actress Vanessa Kirby (The Crown, Napoleon) will play the role of Susan Storm, also known as the Invisible Woman. Joseph Quinn (Stranger Things) takes on the role as Johnny Storm, the Human Torch, and Ebon Moss-Bachrach (The Bear) will be Ben Grimm, the Thing.
Vanessa Kirby, seen here alongside Mission: Impossible star Tom Cruise, is the new Sue Storm. (Supplied: Paramount)
Joseph Quinn, who was Eddie Munson in Stranger Things, will become the Human Torch.
Ebon Moss-Bachrach (left), with The Bear co-star Ayo Edebiri, will transform into orange wrecking ball The Thing. (Supplied: Disney+)
It's set to be directed by Matt Shakman (WandaVision).
The Fantastic Four comics series is one of Marvel's longest running and is popular among fans.
It debuted in 1961 and was created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby.
Ioan Gruffudd played Mister Fantastic in 2005 and 2007. (Photo by Arnold Jerocki/WireImage/Getty)
The scientists-turned-superhero team's history has included false starts and bad reviews in past transitions to the big screen.
A low-budget 1994 movie adaptation was shelved. A year later, 20th Century Fox began developing two films that would take 10 years to make. Those were 2005's Fantastic Four starring Ioan Gruffudd and Jessica Alba, and the 2007 sequel Rise of the Silver Surfer.
The 2015 remake starring Miles Teller and Michael B. Jordan was a disaster, so much so there was no sequel. It was panned by critics and the studio lost more than $US80 million ($123 million).
The 2015 reboot of The Fantastic Four, starring Miles Teller, was not well received. (Photo by Gary Gershoff/WireImage/Getty)
Disney acquired Fox a few years later, with most Marvel characters re-united under its corporate umbrella to form the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
Fantastic Four is expected in theatres on July 25, 2025

title: Dakota Johnson has charisma to burn, but even she can't save this abysmal superhero movie
content:
While it's hard to feel too sorry for the multi-million-dollar superhero industrial complex, 2023 was such an annus horribilus for comic book movies that their sudden underdog status is almost endearing.
What: The latest Spider-verse spin-off that weaves the origin story of lesser-known mutant Madame Web.
Starring: Dakota Johnson, Sydney Sweeney, Isabela Merced, Celeste O'Connor.
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: Like finding Dakota Johnson a new agent.
At the very least, you'd hope the genre's flop era might yield the kind of imaginative filmmaking that can happen when all creative bets are off.
Sadly, Sony's new Spider-Man spin-off — the DOA Madame Web — isn't about to reverse the downward spiral.
As if to acknowledge the need for some sort of rebirth, the latest in the studio's extended Spidey series — which runs the quality gamut from Across the Spider-Verse to Morbius — takes place all the way back in good old 2003, right before superhero cinema's two-decade reign of terror gripped the multiplex.
There's not even a post-credits teaser at which audiences can hoot and holler like excitable shareholders in an annual meeting. Quelle horreur!
Madame Web is the sort of boilerplate storytelling that can't even summon the trashy, retro fun of the Venom films. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
With her indie-rock bangs and skinny jeans, Fifty Shades of Gray star Dakota Johnson plays Cassie Webb, a 30-ish paramedic zipping through post-9/11 New York to the sound of the Yeah Yeah Yeahs — right past an old-school Blockbuster and an awkwardly conspicuous Beyoncé billboard, Tobey Maguire's web-slinger presumably swinging by somewhere just out of shot.
After a brush with death, Cassie starts to experience visions of the future — no, not of The Apprentice host running for US President or boot-cut jeans returning to fashion, but flash forwards in time that portend some violent, soon-to-occur event. (In what might be the movie's cleverest moment, Johnson watches a pigeon crash into her apartment window, not unlike her grandma 60 years earlier.)
Celeste O'Connor, Dakota Johnson, Sydney Sweeney and Isabela Merced in Madame Web (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
As we learn in a prologue set in 1973, Cassie's mother died giving birth to her daughter in the Peruvian jungle, where she'd been searching for a rare species of spider said to have magic healing properties.
Saved by a mystical race of Amazonian spider-people — the kind of cartoonish Indigenous folk movies use to gift the white hero with powers — the young infant was unknowingly possessed with the insect's strange visions.
But mum's already notorious companion Ezekiel Sims (Tahar Rahim, A Prophet) stole the spider, and 30 years later he's been cursed with nightmares in which three teenage spider-girls — played by Sydney Sweeney (Anything But You), Isabela Merced (Dora and the Lost City of Gold) and Celeste O'Connor (Ghostbusters: Afterlife) — bring about his untimely death.
Tahar Rahim stars as the villainous Ezekiel Sims.  (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
Looking like a Sweet Valley High cosplayer at a Halloween party (and one montage away from a nerdy girl makeover), the 20-something Sweeney gets one of the movie's biggest unintentional laughs as a purportedly mousey teenager.
Lucky for these very authentic high school girls, Cassie's psychic glimpses are one step ahead of the murderous Ezekiel's — and she's soon rescuing them from his evil webby clutches, drawing them into a tentative, nurturing sisterhood.
Sydney Sweeney plays one of three teenaged spider-girls that play sidekick to Dakota Johnson in Madame Web. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
Although her name sounds like a sexy CD-ROM avatar from Web 1.0, Madame Web dates back to 1980, when the character was introduced to Marvel comics as an elderly, web-dwelling mutant with clairvoyant powers.
It's a cool bit of Marvel arcana from which to spin an eccentric standalone movie; throw in a little Britney Spears on the soundtrack and it all sounds pretty… fetch, right?
Madame Web may well be a welcome throwback in theory, but the result is worst possible version of a superhero movie from the era — the sort of boilerplate storytelling that can't even summon the trashy, retro fun of the Venom films, let alone Sam Raimi's vibrant Spider-Man instalments.
As always, Johnson has charisma to burn (if nothing else, the movie has given us her delightfully candid press tour). But her talents are no match for an abysmal screenplay — credited to director S.J. Clarkson, Claire Parker, and Morbius writers Matt Sazama and Burk Sharpless — that fails to establish the most basic rapport between its characters.
Where Cassie's den mother relationship with her teen sidekicks should be the soul of the movie, Sweeney, Merced and O'Connor's burgeoning superheroes are so hopelessly one-dimensional that you wonder whether the writers have ever encountered a teenage girl.
"Isn't it sad what happened to Martha Stewart?" says Sweeney's future Spider-Woman at one point, referring to the cooking mogul's then-indictment on stock fraud charges — words spoken by no teenager, in 2003 or otherwise.
This new Spider-Man spin-off Madame Web isn't about to reverse the downward spiral of all recent superhero/comic book-adaptations. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
TV veteran Clarkson directs with the visual wit of an anonymous streaming series (she previously helmed episodes of Jessica Jones and The Defenders), even managing to flub a sequence cut to Britney's all-timer Toxic — surely one of the easiest slam-dunks in movie music-cue existence. (That said, a pair of product placement moments — one right out of Wayne's World and another in which the sponsor's logo gets destroyed in a climactic battle — practically drip with cheeky, deliberate irony.)
Celeste O'Connor, Sydney Sweeney, Dakota Johnson, Isabela Merced and Writer/Director/Executive Producer S.J. Clarkson at the film's premiere in Los Angeles. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
Every time the movie threatens to build momentum — the sense of relentless pursuit essential to up the characters' mortal peril — Clarkson lets the tension slacken. Like the Madame herself, the audience is always two steps ahead of the action.
Instead, the movie eventually reveals itself to be yet another dreary preamble to a would-be franchise, with uncle Ben Parker (an underused Adam Scott) on reliable stand-by and his sister-in-law, Mary Parker (Emma Roberts), pregnant and about to pop — gee, wonder who that kid will turn out to be?
As Ms. Webb tells her colleague at one point, "I just wanna go home and watch Idol."
You and me both, Dakota. You and me both.
Madame Web is in cinemas now.

title: This heartwarming rom-com about finding love in the hellscape of capitalism won the Cannes Jury prize
content:
The minimalistic, heartwarming oddity of a film Fallen Leaves is a rom-com unlike any other.
What: An offbeat rom-com about two down-on-their-luck Finns.
Starring: Alma Pöysti and Jussi Vatanen.
When: In cinemas now.
Likely to make you feel: Simultaneously despondent and hopeful.
Fixated on two people who carry out their lives on the margins of society, this film has as much to say about love and hope as it does about the nature of work and the pursuit of joy in a world stripped of meaning.
Finnish auteur Aki Kaurismäki brings us the story of Ansa (Alma Pöysti) and Holappa (Jussi Vatanen), who catch each other's eyes in a karaoke bar and keep encountering one another thereafter.
Wintery Helsinki is rendered like a small village, where happenstance and serendipitous run-ins aren't uncommon. When they finally make plans to go on a proper date, their romancing is punctuated by misfortune, calamity and mismatched expectations.
Scenes from the movie were shot in one take, on 35mm film. "That heightens everyone's performance," Pöysti told the Sydney Morning Herald. (Supplied: Palace/Malla Hukkanen)
The worlds inhabited by Ansa and Holappa are small and mired in indignities and hardship. They're marked by poverty, alcoholism, mental illness, loneliness and transient living situations, but also the kinship offered by friends and the collectivism of workers in solidarity with one another.
The hellscape of capitalism and the extraction of humdrum work for meagre rewards and little-to-no personal safety is at the forefront of this rom-com.
Ansa works in a supermarket but is soon dismissed for what is deemed an affront by upper management, though the only discernible crime is the high volume of waste generated by industrialised food production. Holappa is a metalworker on a construction site that cuts costs by refusing to update their equipment, at great danger to their employees. Work doesn't define either character, but it occupies an outsized presence in their lives nonetheless.
Ansa and Holappa's dour, monotonous lives are captured in an impressionistic manner, not unlike the trappings of a Wes Anderson film. Highly stylised characters spout aphorisms in a deadpan monotone, background actors are often frozen in place.
Kaurismäki cast his own dog, also named Alma, as Ansa's dog Chaplin. Pöysti kept a sausage for her in her pocket. (Supplied: Palace/Malla Hukkanen)
Ansa and Holappa also have exceedingly distinct styles — she is forever ensconced by her full-length teal trench coat, while he is never pictured without his leather jacket, adding a certain debonair quality to his otherwise ramshackle appearance.
Russia's invasion of Ukraine is a constant backdrop to the two characters' lives, news of which filters into their homes through the radio — in Ansa's case, an anachronistic transistor radio that is still central to her life, despite the presence of phones and the internet.
If it wasn't for the war's signposting of time and place, you'd be forgiven for thinking the film was set in the 80s; characters reference telephone directories and exchange numbers by virtue of pen and paper, a handy archaism that ups the drama when the piece of paper flutters away in the wind. Here, Fallen Leaves most has whiffs of Richard Linklater's Before trilogy.
Fallen Leaves is Kaurismäki's 20th movie, and the latest in his series of working-class movies, which also includes 1986's Shadows in Paradise. (Supplied: Palace/Malla Hukkanen)
Dramatic, sweeping music underscores many of the scenes, at odds with the nondescript sufferings that make up the characters' worlds. It elevates their small lives into something cinematic, something worthy of attention.
The numerous film posters peppered throughout the film similarly imbue it with an old-world glamour and melodrama at odds with the harshness of Ansa's and Holappa's lives and the severe way in which Helsinki is cast.
The sound design is striking, matching the jarring scene transitions. The soundtrack oscillates between diagetic and non-diagetic music — a highlight of the former is Finnish girl group Maustetytöt serenading disaffected patrons in a bar with a catchy arrangement about the futility of loving someone when you can't love yourself.
Every word in Kaurismäki's dry, sardonic script is meticulously and deliberately placed — there is no mindless chatter or endless gabbing in Fallen Leaves.
There were no rehearsals ahead of filming. To prepare, Pöysti watched all of Kaurismäki's movies "to get into his world", as she told The Hollywood Reporter. (Supplied: Palace/Malla Hukkanen)
It's a film of intention and many silences — spaces for the emotionally restrained characters to contemplate one another and their lives, intervals that imbue each spoken word with the gravity they deserve. It's exceedingly funny in the most understated way, with a bleak, biting humour that injects levity into what is, at times, a despairing watch.
The imagery of fallen leaves signifying the turn of seasons and an air of rejuvenation is perhaps one of the few aspects of the film that's too on-the-nose.
Otherwise, the film plays in the margins of understated emotion conveyed through simple, profound imagery: the additional plate and set of cutlery Ansa buys to accommodate Holappa; the mound of cigarette butts squashed upon the asphalt as Holappa spends hours desperately waiting for a possible sighting of Ansa.
Contained, transporting, affecting and somehow never devoid of hope despite the many curveballs, this film leaves viewers with the distinct feeling that Ansa and Holappa will not only discover each other again, they'll be OK.
It's a beautiful thing to find your person in a world that pays you no heed.
Fallen Leaves is in cinemas now.
Fallen Leaves trailer
Editor's note: This article mistakenly said Fallen Leaves was nominated for an international Oscar. While it was shortlisted, it did not make the final list.

title: 'I wanted to showcase the Asian Australian experience': A new Aussie rom-com hits streaming
content:
Five Blind Dates begins with a PowerPoint-style presentation of polaroid images surrounded by tea leaves. It's our introduction to our protagonist, Lia Ling, her grandmother Popo, and her ex-best friend/"first let-down", Richard.
"This is a story about me, Lia! And, well, tea! Oh, no, not that kind," Lia narrates, frowning as an image of bubble tea swims into focus. Because Lia hates bubble tea.
Growing up in Townsville as a first-generation Chinese Australian, we're told Lia (played by Shuang Hu, who also co-wrote and produced the movie) and Richard (Yoson An) would listen to Popo talk about tea for hours.
When Popo died, she left Lia enough money to start her own tea shop, which Lia named in her honour.
Fifty-five seconds later, Lia's backstory is complete and we are thrown into her present-day Sydney teashop, where it becomes immediately apparent Lia is in a pretty bad place.
Five Blind Dates trailer
Popo's Tea Time is failing. The few potential customers who do walk through the door all seem to want bubble tea (which originated in Taiwan) and couldn't care less about the authentic handcrafted Chinese tea experiences Lia wants to share with the world.
But Lia is too proud to tell anyone or ask for help. She's exhausted, she feels like she's letting everyone down, her mummy issues keep surfacing and she frets she'll end up an "unloved crone".
At the same time, her sister Alice (Tiffany Wong) is getting married to the man of her dreams.
Alice's (pictured) decision to take the conventional path in life (staying in Townville and getting married) makes Lia feel inadequate.  (Supplied: Prime Video)
That's the hook for director Shawn Seet's Five Blind Dates, the first Amazon Original movie to be produced in Australia.
The five blind dates idea came from Hu's co-writer, Nathan Ramos-Park: "Before we met, I was randomly shopping around a reality show called Five Blind Dates where five people from your life get to choose a person that they think could be your soulmate," he said in a statement from Amazon.
When Lia (bottom right) gets her fortune told, she's in a pretty bad place in terms of her career, love life and relationship with her family. (Supplied: Prime Video)
Each member of Lia's family takes great delight in picking a blind date for her, with Lia's best friend Mason (played by Ilai Swindells of Retrograde and Bay of Fires) helping out too.
While we're on Mason: Swindells's character is unfortunately an exercise in the GBF stereotype, always at his friend's beck and call, with a penchant for calling people "boo", and apparently endless spare time for a makeover montage. That makeover sees Lia "transformed" from the beautiful tea shop owner with her hair in a pony to the beautiful tea shop owner in a red dress and lipstick with her hair down.
Mason's (pictured) character pretty much exists to help Lia towards success in love and business, with few of his own hopes, dreams or desires spoken of. (Supplied: Prime Video)
The first, set up by Lia's dad (played by the legendary Tzi Ma, who has starred in so many hits including The Farewell and Rush Hour), teaches Lia that what our parents think will be good for us might not be what we actually need.
"[Lia's] dad thinks money is important, because money comes with power … so he [sets her up with billionaire heir Apollo] because he thinks money is going to make her happy," Hu says.
"Lia learns through that that love is important to her even though money is nice."
Lia's second date, set up by her mum (Renee Lim: The Dry; Bali 2002; The Tourist), bombs because he turns out to be in love with redacted.
"[Ezra] helps [Lia] ask herself: What do I want? What makes me happy?"
Lia's third date, Curtis, sent by sister Alice, helps her "overcome her fears and become more empowered".
Beef, Always Be My Maybe, and Crazy Rich Asians are recent exceptions of TV shows and films with nuanced Asian female leads. But Joy Ride takes this one step further, with an emphasis on crass humour.
"[Lia realises] she doesn't need to feel pressured or held down by the expectations other people have of her. And [she realises] some of these expectations aren't even real — they're just figments of her imagination," Hu says.
The movie leaves you thinking about how the pursuit of happiness in life is a glorious, vital thing, about the beauty of cultural traditions, and about how important it is to show up to our family and friends as we truly are.
But something happens at the end of the film that will also leave you frowning at the apparent message that it's OK to completely compromise your dreams and values to make $$$.
This movie is billed as a rom-com, but feels desperately lacking when it comes to the "butterflies" feeling audiences may expect.
Swaths of it are poorly written, and the dialogue is often stilted, in the unique way of Australian productions. At times scenes feel rushed and mish-mashed together.
And it's clear from the outset who Lia will end up with, and what she will have to do to get there.
This is because Five Blind Dates is a Hallmark movie — the sort you watch when you're feeling bored and lonely over the holidays. (Which may have something to do with why Prime Video released it 24 hours ahead of Valentine's Day.)
This isn't a bad thing. Hallmark movies are a beautiful time when you're in the right mood. And they have a mass following for a reason.
They exist to provide an easy, feel-good, butterfly-inducing time. Which Five Blind Dates definitely tries to achieve.
There are a handful of comedic moments along the way. See: Mason's declaration: "I don't kink-shame but … straight people are wild" (Where's the lie?); Lia's dad unwittingly trying to set her up for a life as a billionaire businessman's beard; Lia's mum boasting openly about her new boyfriend's cunnilingus capabilities. And Lia's attempt at surreptitiously thirsting over Richard's six-pack being interrupted as he demands to know: "Are you staring at my body?"
Tzi Ma provides much-needed comic relief as the bumbling dad who doesn't quite understand dating apps or non-traditional marriage arrangements.  (Supplied: Prime Video)
As is the fact a rom-com created and penned by two Asian writers was chosen as Amazon's first Australian original film.
And the fact that so many talented Asian actors from myriad backgrounds could come together to tell such a uniquely Chinese Australian story is a beautiful thing, regardless of any critiques of the finished product.
It's the cultural elements of the story that shine brightest in Five Blind Dates, from the depiction of the traditional Chinese tea ceremony, to Lia's memories of Popo.
"We wanted to create a story that hadn't been seen before in Australia," Hu says.
A successful viral hoax generated a lot of buzz for star-studded movie Argylle. Does it live up to the hype?
That's why she and Ramos-Park went to such lengths to look at themes beyond romance (and perhaps why it feels light on the rom of the rom-com side of things).
"We tried to incorporate themes [from] filial piety and some of the responsibilities we feel towards our families in this modern era of trying to make a career and chase our dreams, but also feeling the responsibility of getting married and having kids [and] for families to be really involved in that, and I wanted to showcase the Asian Australian experience on the movie screen," she says.
The desire to bring tea into it came from Hu, who had an online tea store in another life.
"I think most of Western culture only thinks of tea in the form of tea bags in hot water, but it runs much deeper," she explains.
"Tea is such an important aspect of Chinese culture. It originated in China and, for us, it's a way of socialising and also greeting people.
"When you go to someone's house, you offer them tea and the act of making the tea and pouring it for them, and the energy that is transferred is a really nice way we bond. [But] the whole tea ceremony is something that's not really publicised or understood in Australian culture.
"I wanted the world to know more about tea and the ceremony that comes with it and what it means."
Five Blind Dates is streaming on Prime Video.

title: ICYMI: An Aus red carpet reunion, P!nk fan goes into labour at gig and Moana is back to save us all
content:
Welcome to ICYMI, pop culture fanatics.
Before we get any further, after weeks of speculation, yes, Taylor Swift was at the Super Bowl today.
Praise be, the billionaire managed to fly her private jet from her tour stop in Tokyo allll the way to the US just to play WAG to Travis Kelce for The Big Game.
Truly a triumph for Swifties and CO2 emitters everywhere.
Are you ready to defy gravity? Our first look at the two-part Wicked movie is here — in the form of a minute-long teaser dropped at the Super Bowl.
Directed by Jon M. Chu (Crazy Rich Asians), the long-awaited adaptation of the Broadway smash musical tells the story of Elphaba, the so-called Wicked Witch of the West in The Wizard of Oz.
In the trailer, we see Cynthia Erivo as Elphaba, Ariana Grande as friend-turned-enemy Glinda, and snippets of the rest of the cast (including Jeff Goldblum and Michelle Yeoh) in a dark and moody CGI Oz. Part one is out November 24, with part two set to be released a year later.
Wicked Trailer
We also saw new trailers for Deadpool & Wolverine, Twisters, Kingdom of the Planet of The Apes and The Fall Guy thanks to the big sports game.
But there are more new film and TV teasers and trailers that didn't air at the Super Bowl.
Get ready to scream, cry and throw up because a Moana sequel is coming this year and the first teaser trailer for it has dropped.
Moana Trailer
The movie will follow Moana on a new journey "to the far seas of Oceania and into dangerous, long-lost waters for an adventure unlike anything she's ever faced".
It's currently scheduled for a November 27 release date in the US, but we don't have word on when it will hit cinemas in Australia yet.
BRB putting How Far I'll Go on repeat until then.
In more pure news, Abbott Elementary has been renewed for a fourth season. No official release date yet beyond "Fall 2024" (aka between September and November).
And in deeply *stressful* news, The Bear has been renewed too, with a third season set to air in June. At least this means more Ayo Edebiri.
— Jared Richards and Yasmin Jeffery
We regret to inform you that Kanye West, otherwise known as Ye, has a new album out.
Last week Ye and Ty Dolla $ign premiered Vultures I at a listening event in Chicago, following the release of single Talking/Once Again, featuring his daughter North West.
Then the scandals began.
Multiple artists, including Ozzy Osborne and Nicki Minaj, have bopped Ye for using samples of their music without their permission.
There's also the multitude of anti-Semitic lyrics Ye raps on the new album, which reportedly caused his Chicago event live stream to be aborted after just an hour.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
So, same old, same old from someone once considered the GOAT.
Of course, if you'd like to listen to a rap album that won't get you kicked off Twitter (pre-Elon Twitter, that is) might we suggest Little Simz's new EP Drop 7, which also came out on Friday.
— Velvet Winter
Margot Robbie well and truly conquered Hollywood in 2023, and now she's come back home over the weekend to collect the Trailblazer Award at this year's AACTAs.
Margot Robbie accepting the Trailblazer Award at the AACTAs.
Fellow Aussie legend Cate Blanchett presented Robbie with the award, appropriately dressed in a neon pink get-up that she quickly and hilariously christened "Middle-aged Barbie".
Robbie waxed lyrical about being a Gold Coast girlie (the AACTAs were held in Surfers Paradise) and found the time to reunite with her fellow Neighbours star Lincoln Lewis.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
Awards-wise, the night belonged to the RackaRacka brothers and their A24 hit Talk To Me. The horror movie took home nine awards including best film, best direction, best screenplay, and best lead actress for Sophie Wilde.
Tears were shed as the late Cal Wilson was honoured with the award for best comedy performer for her work on The Great Australian Bake Off.
She passed away suddenly last year, at the age of 53, prompting outpourings of grief from people across the country.
— Velvet Winter
How do you get Serena Williams, Jodie Comer, Naomi Campbell, Adwoa Aboah, Victoria Beckham, and Dua Lipa into one room?
You become the editor-in-chief of British Vogue, announce your retirement, and then gather the supermodels, movie stars, musicians, sporting legends and moguls "who have shaped British Vogue for close to 108 years now" for one last, epic cover shoot before you leave.
"It was clear to all of us on the team that no one woman could or should encapsulate these past few years for the magazine," Edward Enninful wrote of the shoot in his final editorial.
"What we needed was a group, to lean into the power of the collective to bring to life what I hope has been a daring, disruptive and evolutionary period in Vogue's history.
"They also – by dint of extraordinary impact, force of personality, style and influence – needed to have reached beyond fashion and culture to change the fabric of society in the 2020s, in ways small and large and always positive."
Despite his monumental impact on the world of fashion over the course of his boundary-breaking, six-and-a-half-year tenure at British Vogue, Enninful said he held his breath for weeks expecting a series of "No"s.
Instead, 40 stars turned up. And because we know you'll ask, here's the proof the cover wasn't Photoshopped:
Enninful will be succeeded by British journalist Chioma Nnadi, who is the first Black woman to lead the magazine.
— Yasmin Jeffery
Not content with dizzying fans as she flips and flies through the air, P!NK took audience engagement to new heights at a Sydney concert, sending a fan into labour.
On Friday February 9, P!NK – real name Alicia Moore — stopped her concert at Allianz Stadium when staff alerted her to what was happening, miming it out offstage.
The song that triggered the exciting moment appeared to be Our Song, a cut from new album Trustfall.
"Wouldn't have called that one!" P!NK mused.
"I thought it would've been Get the Party Started or Never Not Gonna Dance Again."
The woman was escorted out by medical staff to a hospital, where it's believed she gave birth. Funnily enough, this is the second time an audience member has gone into labour during P!NK's current Summer Carnival tour, the last being a fan in Boston in July. We'll raise our glass to that, I guess?
P!NK's Australian tour continues around Australia into March, if you're currently overdue and wondering how to hurry things up.
— Jared Richards
Even for the biggest Drag Race fan, it can be hard to keep up with the 20+ franchises, so you're forgiven if you missed the premiere of UK vs. The World season two this weekend.
But among the glut of currently airing seasons (US16 and España: All Stars), it's worth a watch, not only does it put queens from across the globe together in one competition, but Australia's own Hannah Conda is competing.
And by the first episode alone, it's clear she's gunning for the crown, after having just lost out in Down Under S2.
We particularly loved her home country runway, a beautiful nod to both Priscilla's frilled-neck lizard outfits and First Nations culture, via a handpainted print by Marrithiyel designer Paul McCann. The word "TREATY" is emblazoned on the back.
Hannah Conda representing Australian drag at its finest.  (Supplied: Instagram/Hannah Conda/Lozich Creative)
"This is what I think of when I think of what it means to be a drag queen in Australia!" she wrote on Instagram.
— Jared Richards
We didn't expect the Dune II rollout to be quite this salacious. But not only do we have the *ahem* dual-purpose popcorn buckets, but now Josh Brolin has written a steamy ode to star Timothée Chalamet.
"Your cheekbones jump towards/what are youth laden eyes that slide down a prominent nose/and onto lips of certain poetry," a line from the poem reads.
I mean, fair play to Brolin, who among us hasn't at one point admired lil' Timmy Tim's cheekbones?
Will we get any more loving passages before Dune II hits cinemas on March 14? Only time will tell.
— Velvet Winter
