title: The pioneering creative couple behind Australia's earliest explicit adult film in 1970
content:
In an outwardly unremarkable house in inner-city Sydney, a silver-haired woman in her 80s is looking back on an extraordinary life.
So you could be forgiven for feeling a little surprised when this well-spoken daughter of a Melbourne minister begins to discuss the role she and her great love and soulmate, George, played in Australia's sexual revolution of the 1970s.
George and Charis Schwarz were artists, photographers, film-makers and adventurers active from the 1960s through to George’s death in 2021.
It's almost a footnote in their dizzying CV, but between 1970 and 1975 George and Charis produced a series of ground-breaking pornographic films, including the first explicit Australian sex film to be cleared by the censors for distribution in cinemas.
Surrounded by artefacts from their adventures, artist Charis Schwarz regales ABC Arts with wild tales from a long-lost Sydney.
The Schwarzes' appetite for life took many forms — art-making, bee-keeping, mead-brewing and journeying around the world on their 1965 BMW R50 motorcycle.
Theirs was a ceaseless drive for creative expression that cheerfully ignored societal expectations and the high/low culture divide.
Newspaper advertisement for the premiere of Sex Aids And How To Use Them. (Supplied: Leon O'Regan)
In 2023 it's hardly a challenge to find porn. A recent study estimated that pornographic material comprises 4 per cent of the entire internet, and is the subject of a staggering 20 per cent of mobile searches.
But in 1970s Australia, the landscape for viewing — and making — erotic films was very different.
Our fledgling adult entertainment industry was a fast-moving cultural frontier, with defenders of "community standards" pitched against adult theatres seeking to profit from X-rated content.
The epicentre of this battle for the nation's morality was Sydney's Kings Cross area.
Artwork by George Schwarz. (Supplied: George and Charis Schwarz website )
George and Charis Schwarz (née McKittrick) moved to Kings Cross in 1968. They were attracted to the area's central location, bohemian reputation and — perhaps most importantly for budding artists — cheap rents.
"It was quite different [then]," Schwarz says.
"It was full of families, it was lovely.
"We could leave the groceries on the street and no-one touched them. A great community feeling."
Neither George nor Charis were Sydney locals. Charis was from Melbourne, the daughter of a minister, and George was born in Zurich, Switzerland. The couple met in 1963 while Charis was travelling in Europe and fell deeply in love.
George and Charis Schwarz on the set of The Widow (1970). (Supplied: Charis Schwarz)
Once settled in Sydney, they quickly became key figures in the rich creative milieu of the Cross.
"George was a passionate artist," Charis says. "And I was more or less his co-worker."
"[He] was a painter when I met him, but I had bought a camera and George used it to photograph on the way out here. That's when he started getting interested in photography."
George set up a home darkroom and discovered a novel way to finance his photography equipment — developing pornographic films from imported negatives, for display in the local sex shops.
"The Cross was very much alive in those times," Charis recalls.
The result of this first venture into blue movies was hardcore lesbian film The Dream (1970), the earliest explicit adult film produced in Australia. This dialogue-free short features a performance from Gretel Pinninger, AKA notorious dominatrix Madame Lash.
"It was highly popular with the clientele," Charis says.
"They would have a live sex show and a movie or two.
"They'd be country blokes I think, mainly, watching it. And the Vice Squad would come and confiscate the film, and it regularly got pinched and regularly got developed again.
The experience of producing The Dream kicked off a flurry of film-making activity from the couple.
Still image from About Love (1970). (Supplied: Charis Schwarz)
Around this time they also produced About Love (1970), a feature-length anthology film that displays George's European art-house sensibility. While not an explicitly pornographic production, the film did feature erotic themes and imagery.
Sex and sexual themes feature prominently in the artistic output of the Schwarzes — which, alongside film, consisted of books, drawings, photographs, mixed media works and site-specific installations.
Their uninhibited, sex-positive attitude was at odds with the prevailing conservatism in Australian culture of the time.
"I'd grown up sexually, I think, living in Europe. [There] people talk normally about sex every day, it's an everyday thing. It's not the shy or embarrassed attitude that we had here," Schwarz says.
On the set of Sex Aids And How To Use Them (1974). (Supplied: Charis Schwarz)
This frank and fearless attitude to sex was on proud display in the Schwarzes' most successful film — Sex Aids and How to Use Them (1974). Purportedly an instructional guide, the film features performers 'Winton' and 'Astrid' demonstrating various lovemaking accessories to the accompaniment of a wry voiceover.
"We had a whale of a time making it," Schwarz says.
"We used our upstairs flat as a studio, and George had the idea to create it against a black background, so as not to distract from the action.
"I developed this set in a colourful way with a few antiques and a different coloured cushion for each sex aid.
The instructional nature of the film was more than an act of public-spirited community service. Film historian Leon O'Regan explains that this method of framing the action was a tactic to evade the era's restrictive censorship guidelines.
"These films were what were known in the US as a 'white coater', where you would get someone in a white coat posing as a doctor to try and promote the perception that the films were educational," Schwarz explains.
George Schwarz on the set of Sex Aids And How To Use Them (1974). (Supplied: Charis Schwarz)
Sex Aids was the first locally-produced pornographic movie passed by the Australian censors, and enjoyed great popularity with audiences.
It stayed in distribution until the early 1980s, with prints touring around Australia's cities and rural areas (although they were having none of it in Queensland, where it became the first film banned by the newly-minted Queensland Films Board of Review).
Remarkably, it became the highest-grossing Australian short film of its time.
George Schwarz on the set of Well, My Dear! (1975). (Supplied: Charis Schwarz)
This success of Sex Aids led the Schwarzes to produce a follow-up, Well, My Dear! (1975). This time however, the nation's moral guardians were less sympathetic to the film's helpful tips for a healthy marriage.
"Unfortunately we went a bit far and it was not given a certificate of classification," Schwarz says.
"It was very difficult, I tried to get an answer: 'Which particular frames or episodes were you objecting to?' And they said 'Oh, we can't tell you that'.
"And I said, 'well, that's a bit rough because how am I going to improve it if I don't know what you find offensive?' So we reached a stalemate."
After the misfire of Well, My Dear!, George and Charis moved away from the movie industry and the film was left to wither away. Sadly, George Schwarz died in 2021.
Charis Schwarz on ABC TV in 1974. (Source: ABC Archive )
Now, many years since their heyday, the films are being carefully restored by Leon O'Regan for Blu-Ray release in 2024.
"Some of these films were in such a bad state that when they arrived at the lab, they had to move all the other materials out because the vinegar syndrome and the fumes were so bad," Schwarz says.
"These are the only known film elements that exist for some of these movies.
Charis Schwarz at home in 2023. (Image: ABC Arts)
Charis still lives in the home they shared together, unwavering in her commitment to honouring the memory of George's life and work.
"I don't know how I survive with running a relationship with in a metaphysical sense. I miss him desperately, the flesh and blood George," she says.
Contemplating the house's silent spaces, she says "…but he's here."
Schwarz says she is pleased that the films will soon be made available again.
"I'm quite happy in a way. They're obviously enjoyable to some people (and) I think George lives through them as well."

title: Speed, sleek cars and a persistent sense of impending doom: Adam Driver stars in Ferrari
content:
Michael Mann has made a career from sleek, muscular portraits of masculinity in crisis.
Beneath their cool, calibrated surfaces, the veteran American director's films — concerning cops and robbers (Heat, Miami Vice), hitmen and hackers (Collateral, Blackhat), gangsters and safe crackers (Public Enemies, Thief) — thrum with the existential dread of life's impermanence, the romance of seizing the moment.
("Don't let yourself get attached to anything you are not willing to walk out on in 30 seconds flat," goes Robert De Niro's famous line in Heat.)
No wonder he's long been drawn to making a film about motor racing driver turned auto designer Enzo Ferrari — a man whose predilection for speed and success was tempered by a persistent sense of impending doom. (Not for nothing is his 1964 autobiography entitled My Terrible Joys.)
Listen: Michael Mann on The Screen Show
Set in 1957, Ferrari finds its eponymous motor magnate — played by everyone's favourite Italian, House of Gucci star Adam Driver — at a professional and private impasse.
Nearing 60, he's built a company that's seen him become a national treasure, elevating him to near-godlike status.
"If he were alive today, Jesus wouldn't have been a carpenter but a craftsmen of metal," a priest tells a congregation of Ferrari and his mechanics, assembled in a church that borders the racetrack in the boss's hometown of Modena.
The film sees Ferrari wager his fortunes on the Mille Miglia, the legendary 1,000-mile race across Italy. (Supplied: Roadshow/Lorenzo Sisti)
The standing of Ferrari's brand — and his personal legacy — is less certain.
The business is on the verge of insolvency, with the output of Ferrari production cars insufficient to meet the company's spending on racing — where Enzo's true passion lies.
For years he's run the company with his wife, the steely firebrand Laura (a crackling Penélope Cruz), but personal tensions are beginning to threaten their business partnership.
They're both dealing with grief over the recent loss of their teenage son, Dino, who died from muscular dystrophy. Every morning, Ferrari visits the mausoleum where his son and late brother, Alfredo, are entombed. He's talking to ghosts.
And while Laura tolerates her husband's affairs, she's about to uncover a bombshell: For a decade Enzo has been seeing Lina Lardi (Shailene Woodley), a younger woman with whom he has another son, Piero (Giuseppe Festinese).
Shailene Woodley stars as Ferrari's secret lover of a decade. (Supplied: Roadshow/Lorenzo Sisti)
Under pressure to ramp up production or make a deal with a more commercial enterprise like Fiat or Ford — the latter the focus of Ford v Ferrari, a project Mann was once attached to direct — Ferrari decides to wager his fortunes on the upcoming Mille Miglia, the legendary 1,000-mile race across Italy.
The film's action scenes puts the audience right in the driver's seat. (Supplied: Roadshow/Eros Hoagland)
A contemplative, sometimes mournful film, Ferrari echoes Mann's career obsession with the high-stakes balance between the professional and the private, zooming in on the specialised details of both business and pleasure.
As the stoic but embattled figure at the centre of the drama, Driver embodies the movie's sombre, reflective mood. His quiet, detached performance — coupled with his eerily youthful appearance — can make him seem like a man out of time, haunted by the cosmic balance.
His scenes with Cruz are pure melodrama; the clash of acting styles generates a friction that gives their moments together an electric charge.
Penélope Cruz gives a crackling performance as Ferrari's wife, the steely firebrand Laura. (Supplied: Roadshow/Lorenzo Sisti)
Mann's staging of the racing sequences, meanwhile, is unsurprisingly gripping.
The action has a kinetic punch that puts the audience right in the driver's seat, while the filmmaker's attention to track-side details — from the leather jackets and sunglasses to Ferrari's choice of ties — reflect a craftsman's eye for authenticity. (At one point, Enzo tells a new driver to keep his actress girlfriends away from the track, because "they distract from my cars".)
Patrick Dempsey stars as race-car driver Piero Taruffi. (Supplied: Roadshow/Lorenzo Sisti)
Still, for all of Ferrari's craft and passion, the elements don't always coalesce in an effective whole.
Working from a decades-old script by the late writer Troy Kennedy Martin (The Italian Job), Mann sometimes struggles to find the film's centre of gravity, torn between the exhilaration of the cars and dramatic moments that can play as soap opera.
As a work about legacy, though, it's fascinating one — especially coming from an 80-year-old filmmaker who may well have cause to reflect on his own life.
Ferrari is a film in which triumph and tragedy are twinned, where the ghosts of the past can appear as vivid as the living. For fans of Mann's singular body of work, it's ultimately quite moving.

title: Nordic Noir TV has taken over the world. But how did it get so good?
content:
What do the TV series Broadchurch, Marcella and Mare of Easttown all have in common?
These top-rating shows have all been influenced by the genre of Nordic or Scandi noir.
And its tropes of disturbing crime, complex police investigations, bleak urban settings and great winter sweaters have become so recognisable to be almost spoof-worthy. Don't believe us? See Australia's own Deadloch.
Deadloch is a murder-mystery parody series set in Tasmania.  (Supplied: Prime Video)
The genre first emerged in the 2000s in Denmark, with the global success of The Killing and then The Bridge, and it has gone on to spawn countless international imitators.
So how did Denmark, with its population of less than 6 million people, create a genre that reshaped the global TV industry?
And just as importantly, what are the unmissable Nordic noir shows to binge watch this summer?
Nordic noir wasn't born from one visionary creator's brainstorm.
In fact, it was the result of direct intervention from Denmark's government and film schools that were concerned about the quality of Danish productions.
Rear Vision puts contemporary events in their historical context, answering the question: "How did it come to this?"
"It was carefully planned from the early to mid 1990s, all the way to the early 2000s," Tobias Hochscherf, Professor of Audiovisual Media at the University of Applied Sciences in Kiel, Germany, tells ABC RN's Rear Vision.
Film schools started changing their teaching practices, including the introduction of a concept called scaffolding, which forced students to create within a specific set of rules.
"Absurdly, if you reduce the level of freedom you have for a certain task, you are more creative," Professor Hochscherf says.
The result was Dogma (Dogme) 95, a film movement bound by a set of rules created by Danish filmmakers Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg aimed at returning Danish cinema to its roots, and reclaiming it from the slickness of Hollywood.
Vinterberg's 1998 film The Celebration and von Trier's The Idiots from the same year are considered some of the earliest products of the movement.
Professor Hochscherf says Dogma 95 then trickled down into television. It particularly influenced the way DR, Denmark's public broadcaster, created serial dramas.
Danish productions hire completely new crews for each show.  (Unsplash: Brands&People )
In fact, DR developed its own set of "dogmas" after producers spent time in the US studying crime dramas like NYPD Blue and adapted them for a Danish context.
They also focused on fostering homegrown talent by hiring a totally different crew for each new show.
"[They say] we want to have two very successful seasons, or even one, and then we have a new production with a completely new team," Professor Hochscherf says.
"And therefore, new people get a chance to produce and to write and to direct and to film."
The seminal moment for Danish television came in 2007 when The Killing first aired on DR.
The show centres on a troubled detective in Copenhagen, Sarah Lund, as she tries to solve the brutal murder of a young woman.
"The Killing was the breakthrough," Susan Turnbull, the University of Wollongong's Senior Professor of Communication and Media, says.
The Killing season one typified what became the Nordic noir aesthetic.  (Supplied: SBS)
Then DR, with Sweden's public broadcaster SVT, released The Bridge in 2011, which follows a Danish detective and a Swedish detective who are forced to work together when a body is found on the bridge that links the two countries.
"Those two [The Killing and The Bridge] side-by-side are what all the commentators subsequently have regarded as the moment when what has now come to be called Nordic noir became Nordic noir," Professor Turnbull says.
So what makes a Nordic noir show?
The aesthetic is one thing: dark and washed out colours, scenery from the cities' dilapidated outskirts, and what Professor Hochscherf calls "design porn".
"You have these lovely homes and great dining areas," he says.
"And then outside … just a few miles [from] the big cities, you have these gruesome crimes.
"It kind of breaks away from the idea of Scandinavia as being this very cosy society with very strong social bounds."
The Bridge explores the personal lives of the two leading detectives, Saga Norén and Martin Rohde.  (Supplied: SBS)
Another hallmark of a Nordic noir series is the complexity of the characters, with shows always exploring both the personal and the professional lives of the main characters.
"If we think about The Bridge for example, it's also the interplay of a Danish cop and the Swedish cop," Professor Hochscherf says.
"Because you have all that time, you can deal with these cultural differences, but also the different characters, in more detail."
The Killing, like other Nordic dramas, was shown in Australia on SBS from the beginning.
But it didn't break through to a global audience until it aired on BBC Four in the UK, says Anne Marit Waade, Associate Professor of Media and Journalism at Aarhus University in Denmark.
"[The BBC had] been buying American content, it was quite expensive, and they were looking for something else," she says.
"[The Killing] was not produced with [the] ambition to sell it internationally, [so] the beginning of the series was quite cheap."
These shows were quickly followed by other DR series, which weren't necessarily crime dramas but, with their now-signature Nordic flavour, they found global success nonetheless.
For example, Borgen, a drama about a politician who unexpectedly becomes Denmark's first female prime minister, has been watched in more than 100 countries.
"It was less about Denmark, and it was more generally about democracy and integrity," Professor Hochscherf says.
"And thereby, I think it could be told internationally."
Dr Karl knows the best app for free podcasts, radio, music, news and audiobooks … and you don’t need to be a scientist to find it!
Denmark's neighbours quickly sought to take advantage of the growing international interest in Scandinavian television.
Professor Turnbull says Norway, Sweden and Iceland all began producing high-quality dramas that attracted similar audiences.
She says Nordic noir's influence extended to other crime dramas, like the UK's Broadchurch, which drew inspiration from the genre.
"It's almost like a family tree," Professor Turnbull says.
"You can see all these offshoots in different countries as people adapt,and assimilate, and create their own version of what a Nordic noir would look like."
Professor Turnbull says one of the best examples of a local interpretation of the genre has come out of Australia, in the form of Amazon Prime's murder-mystery comedy Deadloch.
The show, created by comedians Kate McLennan and Kate McCartney, follows two vastly different detectives who are forced to work together to solve a series of murders in the titular Tasmanian town.
It's the formula from The Bridge, which has inspired so many international remakes. But, as Professor Turnbull says, it "flips the Nordic noir genre on its arse".
"What Deadloch did so beautifully was do what [The Bridge did] with the two detectives. But in this case, it was two women – one from Tasmania and then one from the Northern Territory," she says.
"And sent up that … cultural difference in very interesting ways."

title: First version of Disney's Mickey Mouse enters public domain, kind of
content:
Almost a century after his big-screen debut, Mickey Mouse in the cartoon Steamboat Willie has entered the public domain, opening the floodgates to potential remakes, spin-offs, adaptations and legal battles with Disney.
The copyright on Steamboat Willie — a short, black and white 1928 animation that first introduced audiences to the mischievous rodent who would become emblematic of American pop culture — expired after 95 years, on January 1, under US law.
The date has loomed on the calendars of everyone from filmmakers, fans and intellectual property lawyers to Disney executives, who in the past helped lobby to change law to prolong US copyright terms.
Infestation 88 - Video game trailer featuring Mickey Mouse.
A trailer for a video game called Infestation 88, which features the Steamboat Willie version of Mickey Mouse has been released since the cartoon entered the public domain.
"This is a deeply symbolic, highly anticipated moment," said Jennifer Jenkins, director of the Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain.
Anyone is now free to copy, share, reuse and adapt Steamboat Willie and Plane Crazy — another 1928 Disney animation and the early versions of the characters that appear within them, including Mickey Mouse and Minnie Mouse.
A vital caveat is that the later versions of the characters, like those in 1940 film Fantasia, are not in the public domain and cannot be copied without a visit from Disney's lawyers.
In a statement to AFP, Disney said it would "continue to protect our rights in the more modern versions of Mickey Mouse and other works that remain subject to copyright."
Indeed, the version of Mickey in Steamboat Willie is a spindly, roguish creature who would not be recognisable to many younger viewers.
"What's in the public domain is kind of a frightful little black-and-white animal," said Justin Hughes, a professor at Loyola Law School.
He added: "The Mickey Mouse that is most familiar to current generations of Americans will remain under copyright protection.
"I wouldn't be surprised if we see some legal skirmishes, and I wouldn't be surprised if we see Disney out there educating people on that point."
Cease-and-desist letters could be sent to artists producing "high-budget fan art" if they use elements from later Mickey cartoons, such as red shorts and white gloves, he predicted.
Pooh's shift into the public domain sees the loveable teddy appear in some unlikely material.
Additionally, while the copyright has expired, the trademark has not.
Copyrights prevent the unlicensed copying of the creative work itself, for example books, films and characters. They expire after a set time.
Trademarks guard the source of a work, preventing anyone else from making a product that could mislead consumers into thinking it came from the original author. They can be renewed indefinitely.
Disney said it will "work to safeguard against consumer confusion caused by unauthorised uses of Mickey and our other iconic characters."
The company has even added a clip from Steamboat Willie to the opening sequence of every Walt Disney Animation Studios film.
"They were very smart folks at Disney — they realised that the best thing to do was to establish that iconic sequence of Steamboat Willie as a trademark," Mr Hughes said.
Anybody using the classic image of Mickey at the helm of the boat on shirts, caps or mugs could be open to legal action, he said.
Anyone hoping to cash in on Disney's beloved mascot "should move cautiously and with counsel," added Mr Hughes.

title: Taika Waititi was once a renegade. Does his new movie measure up?
content:
Taika Waititi loves an underdog story.
From stunted geeks and rebellious kids to goofball vampires, the Oscar-winning Māori filmmaker has routinely championed outcasts of all shapes and species. Even Asgardian deities find themselves cut down to size in Waititi's idiosyncratic cinema: When handed the keys to Marvel's cosmic sandbox, he memorably stranded Thor on a trash heap at the edge of the universe.
Like any former indie darling, the director's cultivated, carefree persona has also been defined by its outsider status — he felt like a renegade auteur who defied the odds.
But, recently, Waititi's career has merged into another narrative: that of the artist swallowed by the Hollywood machine.
Next Goal Wins is his latest tribute to the loveable losers of the world. A sports movie about the American Samoa soccer team — once considered to be the worst in the world — is the kind of lowkey, offbeat material that should've teed up an easy win for this director.
Next Goal Wins is a classic Waititi movie, the director told Screen Rant: "There's humour, there's some drama, and a few tears." (Supplied: Searchlight Pictures)
Taking after the 2014 documentary of the same name, the film introduces the audience to the ragtag team via their record-breaking 31-0 loss against Australia in 2001. After enduring a decade without a single win, the weathered team finds fresh hope with the arrival of Thomas Rongen, a washed-up Dutch American coach.
Next Goal Wins: Interview with coach Thomas Rongen
It's a remarkable true story that's summarily flattened into pure formula, its fictional retelling calibrated with calculated charm and flatlining wit.
The film's problems begin with its reluctant central character, played by Michael Fassbender (The Killer).
Having been banished from America's Major League, as well as his own marriage, Rongen carries a heavy chip on his shoulder.
"I'm not God, but I may as well be because I've performed more miracles than him," he tells the national team upon his introduction.
Fassbender has long wanted to flex his comedy chops, as he told Collider: "Nobody would hire me, and Taika took a roll of the dice." (Supplied: Searchlight Pictures)
His attempts to whip the perpetual losers into shape fall short of that claim, and mostly consist of outbursts, eye-rolling platitudes and extensive references to The Karate Kid.
Like the rest of Rongen's self-pitying antics — which extend to incessant alcoholism and a blatant disregard for the island's customs — these beats are drolly played for laughs.
Two shining stars in Taika Waititi's latest comedy film, Oscar Kightley and David Fane chat to Sosefina Fuamoli for Nesia Daily.
While Waititi's comedic style was once loose and unpredictable, it feels one-note here, never rising above a patter of self-deprecating jabs. Occasionally, the humour succeeds in its darker inflections (glimpsed in a drunk-driving sequence set to Sia's Chandelier).
The flimsy material makes a poor match for Fassbender's talents; he excels in roles that demand a steely intensity and gesture towards deeply suppressed emotion, not dead-eyed despondence and glib one-liners.
At least the supporting players are easy to root for. The film's biggest emotional swings centre on Jaiyah (newcomer Kaimana), the team's striker who identifies as fa'afafine, one of the four gender identities recognised in the Samoan diaspora.
Kaimina told the ABC: "[Fa'afafine is] just a beautiful part of our culture that's specific to the Samoan people, but also to the region." (Supplied: Searchlight Pictures)
Like her real-life counterpart, Jaiyah is the first openly transgender soccer player to compete in a World Cup qualifying match and is widely accepted by her community, though she's limited to the men's team under FIFA's medical standards.
Exuberant and tirelessly good-natured, she makes a fitting foil for the coach — but the film fumbles when it defines their relationship with tired tropes.
Unlike the real-life coach, Thomas is virulently transphobic: When introduced to Jaiyah, he immediately asks for her "real" registered name. He regularly picks on her across the movie, which escalates into an ugly confrontation when he goads her with her deadname.
Kaimina met with the real fa'afafine woman on whom her character is based, Jaiyah Saelua. (Supplied: Searchlight Pictures)
Not only does Waititi handle transphobia with the infantilising morality of his 2019 film Jojo Rabbit, he blatantly models Thomas after Captain Klenzendorf, that film's alcoholic Hitler Youth leader who's gradually revealed to be a good-natured, closeted fool.
Taika Waititi on authenticity and the myth of success
Waititi seemingly has too much affection for either spiralling man-child to confront them with their prejudices, offering the kind of easy catharsis that he aptly withheld in earlier work including Boy. In both recent films, this noncommittal approach renders hate crimes as functionally indistinguishable from quirk.
Next Goal Wins positions Jaiyah as the real hero of the movie and aims for positive trans representation, but unwittingly strips this character of dignity by simplifying her story into a frictionless, feel-good narrative.
Once the movie pivots away from Rongen's all-consuming dysfunction, it picks up some much-needed momentum to deliver a relatively straightforward sports drama. Those looking for peppy montages, the conquering of personal demons on the soccer pitch and rousing speeches delivered at half-time may well be satisfied.
Next Goal Wins features Elisabeth Moss, Will Arnett and our own Luke Hemsworth, but its core is its ensemble of Pacific Islander actors. (Supplied: Searchlight Pictures)
It's still a resounding misstep from the director, who recently admitted to creative overcommitment (his extensive slate currently encompasses Klara and the Sun, two Charlie and the Chocolate Factory series and Star Wars, among other titles) and has described his relationship with cinema as "an arranged marriage".
It's no wonder Next Goal Wins feels like an unconvincing imitation of his previous films, which may have lacked polish but were unmistakably driven by an infectious passion.
Waititi's career reveals the faulty logic of the "one for them, one for me" filmmaking axiom, with his smaller passion projects becoming suffocated by the overlapping demands of IP-driven blockbusters and costly streaming TV shows.
Let's hope this losing streak doesn't last.
Next Goal Wins is in cinemas now.

title: Interstellar is 10 years old this year. The Godfather Part II is 50
content:
It's now 2024, which means 2014 was a decade ago and 1974 was half a century ago.
It also means a bunch of movies will turn 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 years old this year.
We looked at entertainment website IMDb's archive of highest-earning films from 2014, 2004, 1994, 1984 and 1974.
And we also dug up a list of which movies that came out in those years won the Academy Award for Best Picture.
Here are some of films that are now at least a decade old.
Interstellar was one of the most talked about movies of 2014.
In 2014, a bunch of dark, gritty and graphic films topped people's watch-lists.
Interstellar, Gone Girl, Fury, John Wick, American Sniper and Birdman were some of the biggest movies from the year.
Even some kids movies got dark, like when Angelina Jolie donned a set of horns for Maleficent — the retelling of the villain in Disney's Sleeping Beauty.
But it wasn't all grey-filtered, with Paddington, The Lego Movie and Big Hero 6 adding some colour to the year.
And we saw two big action franchises continue into their third chapters, with Taken 3 and The Expendables 3 blasting on to the scene.
Birdman
Birdman took out top honours at the Oscars in 2015. (Supplied: Fox Searchlight)
Rankings are according to US box office takings
Source: IMDb
Even if you haven't seen Mean Girls, the chances are you're familiar with some of the lines from the movie.  (Supplied: Paramount Pictures)
A lot of millennials' most-quoted movies are turning 20 this year, including Anchorman, Napoleon Dynamite and the eternally popular Mean Girls.
Movies in the slumber party category got a massive boost this year, which gave us classics including Cinderella Story, Suddenly 30 and Sleepover.
We also had a lot of sequels this year, with Princess Diaries 2, Ocean's 12, Shrek 2, Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed, Bridget Jones: The Edge of Reason, Meet the Fockers, and Spiderman 2 cashing in on their predecessors' popularity.
Major indie favourites Garden State and Eternal Sunshine of a Spotless Mind came out this year, which also kicked off the Saw horror franchise and put David Hasselhoff on big screens in The SpongeBob SquarepPants Movie.
Million Dollar Baby
Shrek 2 featured big names including Julie Andrews, John Cleese, Mike Myers, Eddie Murphy, Antonio Banderas and Cameron Diaz. (Reuters)
Rankings are according to US box office takings
Source: IMDb
Jonathan Taylor Thomas voiced Simba as a cub in The Lion King, while Matthew Broderick played adult Simba.
This was an epic year for movies, with The Shawshank Redemption, Forrest Gump and Murial's Wedding coming out in 1994.
It was also a big year for child stars, with Kirsten Dunst stealing scenes in Interview with a Vampire and a remake of Little Women and MacAulay Culkin starring in Ritchie Rich and Getting Even With Dad.
And it was also a big year for Jim Carrey, who bashed out three of his most iconic roles in Dumb and Dumber, The Mask and Ace Ventura: Pet Detective.
There were also some of those zany 90s family films like Baby's Day Out, Junior and Blank Cheque.
Forrest Gump
Forrest Gump is perhaps one of Tom Hanks's most iconic roles.  (Supplied)
Rankings are according to US box office takings
Source: IMDb
Arnold Schwarzenegger delivered his often quoted line "I'll be back" in The Terminator.
Some of the most iconic 80s film moments happened this year, which was when Ghostbusters, The Karate Kid and Footloose were released.
Some of the top comedy films like Beverley Hills Cop and Police Academy leaned into in-uniform humour.
But it wasn't all wacky antics, with dramas like The Killing Fields, A Soldier's Story and Places in the Heart hitting the screens.
The year also gave classic horror movies Nightmare on Elm Street and Children of the Corn, and science fiction flick The Terminator and Dune.
Amadeus
Ghostbusters came with cool costumes and its own theme song.
Rankings are according to US box office takings
Source: IMDb
Al Pacino in a scene from The Godfather Part II.  (Paramount Pictures)
Fifty years ago we had what many argue is one of the best sequels every made — The Godfather: Part II.
It was a year of disaster movies such as The Towering Inferno, Earthquake and Airport 1975.
Huckleberry Finn and The Little Prince brought literary classics to the big screen.
And this year also gave us Gone in 60 Seconds, The Great Gatsby and Texas Chainsaw Massacre — all films which were rebooted decades later.

title: Hunting profits or serving an audience? Why Hollywood is obsessed with remakes
content:
Everyone has experienced the bittersweet feeling of walking out of the cinema after watching a great film and realising you'll never get to experience it for the first time again.
But, if next year's list of Hollywood releases is anything to go by, you can.
Remakes, reboots and live-action interpretations make up the majority of big blockbuster films slated for release in the next 12 months.
Mean Girls, Mad Max's Furiosa, Planet of the Apes, Ghostbusters and not to mention the recent release of Wonka, may have audiences feeling like they're in a time loop.
But whether you like them or not, the numbers don't lie, with eight out of the highest-growing films in 2023 either remakes, reboots, sequels, or based on an existing market and brand name (we're looking at you, Barbie).
It's no secret that remakes and reboots are big business for Hollywood.
But has it run out of new ideas?
We spoke to a pop culture expert and author, a director and a film professor about what makes audiences continue to come back for more.
Looking ahead to 2024, there are several remakes slated for release.
But Constantine Verevis, an associate professor of film studies at Monash University, said their popularity was nothing new.
"Remakes have always been around in one form or another," he said.
"If you look at Hollywood trade papers from the 1930s they use the term remake, and they say things like if the film has been good or successful then this is a good reason to remake it for another audience.
"I guess there have been arguments at some times that there are more remakes at any particular period than another. I'm not sure that there are statistics there to demonstrate that that’s the case."
Willy Wonka from Roald Dahl's Charlie and the Chocolate Factory has appeared on our screens three times, 1971, 2005 and 2023.  (IMDB)
Most of the earliest Hollywood films weren't completely original.
Lauren Rosewarne, from the School of Social and Political Sciences at Melbourne University, said from Hollywood's very beginning, studios were producing adaptations of classic literature and stage plays.
"Remakes are something already proven successful in the marketplace," she said.
"It could be a thing that was successful on Broadway, a comic book or a novel or a documentary or a film version."
And as technology advanced and films gained bigger budgets, more remakes began to appear.
There are many reasons for this, but Dr Rosewarne said the main reason was money.
"They [remakes] are less risky because they are a known entity," she said.
"There is research that when a [something is a] new film that nobody knows anything about, something that doesn’t come from a successful novel, a completely new story, audiences are generally reluctant to embrace it and you’re having to sell audiences a story completely from scratch," she said.
"But remakes are already something proven successful in the marketplace."
Tom Cruise brings star power to Top Gun sequel, filmed with real jets and in g-force conditions
The highest-grossing film of 2022 was the sequel to 1986's Top Gun — Top Gun: Maverick — which made more than $US718 million ($1 billion).
Wonka, with major Hollywood star Timothée Chalamet attached, takes another stab at the Charlie and the Chocolate Factory films, which were released in 1971 and 2005.
The musical prequel, which delves into how the famous chocolatier began his factory, made $US39.9 million globally in its opening weekend.
Hollywood has always been a money-making enterprise but COVID-19, the introduction of streaming services, and the writers' strike have given studios an incentive to play it safe with stories that have an existing audience.
"In the context of film — and I think COVID is a factor to get people to actually go to the cinema now — you need to make it a spectacle, justifiable to be seen on the big screen," she said.
"That’s why you see remakes with bigger budgets and more special effects and that justifies why you need to see it on the big screen."
"Most Hollywood productions are a flop. We don't speak about this but one in a hundred TV shows actually gets a decent audience.
Another example is the prequel to the Hunger Games franchise this year, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.
Almost 10 years after the final film of the Hunger Games franchise, Mockingjay — Part 2, audiences old and new to the franchise, have headed to cinemas to see the film, which has sold more than $US300 million in ticket sales globally.
Darren Fisher, a director and the head of the film department at Bond University, said he knew firsthand that money was the main barrier to getting an original script into production.
"It's always further down the list if there's no existing IP [intellectual property] or fan base, it becomes harder and harder," he said.
"It's all about in-built audiences, whether it's a following the makers have or whether it's the following from the actual material."
And while the biggest factor is economics, Dr Rosewarne says nostalgia is and has always been a big motivation for revisiting old stories in Hollywood.
"Nostalgia in the sense there are stories that have always been important to the Western literature canon," she said.
"Think Shakespeare, Wuthering Heights, Little Women. They're always successful when remade.
"There are the stories we have always loved and continued to love because the new generation gets the new version."
Dr Verevis agreed.
"I guess if there's a 20-year interval between them," he said.
"As in the case of Mean Girls, perhaps they’re fulfilling a kind of cultural function where being able to recall earlier versions, there’s that reassurance I suppose where the remake becomes a kind of stabilising force for certain sections of the audience.
"It enables them to recall earlier viewing experiences, bring up their own personal memories of the history of a film."
The terms remake and reboot can be misleading as there is no way to create a perfect copy of a classic.
Dr Rosewarne says remakes can often be made to reflect shifts in culture and provide more diversity.
Lauren Rosewarne says adding more diverse characters in remakes and retellings signals a fresh take.  (Instagram: Paramount Pictures)
"Diversity factor, you could pretty much pick any remake in the last five to 10 years and it's generally going to be a more updated cast related to things like gender and race and even sexuality in a number of examples," she said.
"And that’s a way to say this is the story you know but with a modern twist.
"And the attempt is to counter how the audience feels to say, 'I’ve already seen this before.'
"We know this story, we like this story but this is the way we’re bringing it into 2024."
Dr Fisher agreed, adding that by having new voices and perspectives in the remakes, Hollywood had always understood there was a need for some diversity.
He said that despite the film industry knowing this, it still had a long way to go.
"There needs to be more [diversity] and need to have that kind of avant-garde side of what they're prepared to finance, to try stuff out, but you'll never see that experimentation with millions of dollars," he said.
"But I think there is an understanding that it is necessary that we have to be bringing those new voices through because that's also what the market wants to see.
"And I think that's what's interesting with stuff like Mean Girls and some of the latest kind of reboots on television and Netflix".
He said the Netflix series of Heartbreak High was a great example of a reboot the industry got right.
"You are seeing these amazingly far more diverse [characters who are] far more reflective of modern Australia and modern America on screen," he said.
"It was authentic, it is a reboot people loved, it's going to get more seasons".
"And ideally, if that [original] show had continued on, you'd like to believe that's what we ended up like as it reflects true Australia."
Dr Fisher said the 2022 reboot of Heartbreak High was an example of "getting it right". (Netflix/Supplied)
Dr Rosewarne said the decision to remake a film could also reflect a moment in culture.
Seen the posts on Facebook and Twitter? Thousands of women are taking to social media to share their stories of sexual harassment using the #MeToo hashtag.
When the #MeToo movement took over Hollywood, there were attempts to present feminist retellings of old stories.
Wonder Woman (2017), Little Women (2017), and The Beguiled (2017) were all spoken of as "feminist updates".
Dr Rosewarne said what was happening in politics and society could often dictate appetites for certain stories to come back.
"A good example is after 9/11 there were lots of remakes of Cold War films because the same anxieties within a culture are present," she said.
"What's going on in the world that we could look at that's already in the cupboard that we can tap into again?"
Dr Fisher has tested out the theory of cultural knowledge and come to the conclusion that the average 16-year-old has about five years of cultural knowledge.
He said this allowed for stories to be told to people who might not know about the original concept.
"You can literally reinvent the wheel every five years for a younger audience," Dr Fisher said.
Dr Fisher said despite there being such a huge market for reboots and remakes, Hollywood knew if an adaptation of a film did not reflect modern society, it would not do as well.
"I think if that was all we were making, it's horrific and you'll have no new voices, but ultimately the industry does also realise it needs the new blood," he said.
He said a producer once told him the film industry "feeds off its young".
Stars discuss diversity in Hollywood. (ABC News Breakfast)
"It needs the new generations, it needs the new filmmakers, it needs the new blood, It needs people to try stuff out," Dr Fisher said.
"But they'll try stuff out at the 1-million-dollar level, the half-a-million-dollar level, the 2-million-dollar level, the art-house level where they can try stuff out and be interesting and cool".
For Dr Rosewarne, remakes don't lack creativity, they're actually really creative.
"What really annoys me when people say there is no creativity is that being able to tell a story hundreds of different ways and securing an audience, that is its own kind of creativity," she said.
"It tells us how important certain stories are to our culture."

title: Oscar-nominated British actor Tom Wilkinson dies at 75
content:
Tom Wilkinson, the Oscar-nominated British actor known for his roles in The Full Monty, Michael Clayton and The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel, has died aged 75, his family says.
A statement shared by his agent on behalf of the family said Wilkinson died suddenly at home on Saturday, but it didn't provide further details.
Wilkinson was nominated for a Best Actor Academy Award for his work in the family drama In The Bedroom in 2001 and in the Best Supporting Actor category for his role in Michael Clayton — a 2007 film that starred George Clooney.
He is remembered by many in Britain and beyond for playing former steel mill foreman Gerald Cooper in the 1997 comedy The Full Monty, about a group of unemployed steel workers who form an unlikely male stripping act.
Wilkinson appeared in dozens of other movies including Batman Begins, Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind and Valkyrie.
The actor was recognised for his services to drama in 2005 when he was appointed a member of the Order of the British Empire.

title: Looking back at the celebrities who died this year
content:
From punk rockers to crooners, best friends to magicians, the world lost some well-known faces and creative geniuses this year.
Let's take a look back at who died in 2023.
Matthew Perry died this year, aged just 54.
Friends fans around the world were left heartbroken when Matthew Perry died unexpectedly in October at the age of 54.
The actor was best known for playing the bumbling and sarcastic Chandler Bing in the iconic sitcom, which rocketed him to stardom in the 1990s.
Following his death at his Los Angeles home, Friends co-star David Schwimmer praised Perry's "impeccable comic timing", while the show's co-creators and executive producer said "he was always the funniest person in the room".
"We will always cherish the joy, the light, the blinding intelligence he brought to every moment — not just to his work, but in life as well," Marta Kauffman, David Crane and Kevin Bright said in a statement.
Last year, Perry released a memoir in which he detailed his struggles with addiction and sobriety. In it, he spoke about how he wanted to be remembered for his work with people dealing with substance abuse.
"When I die, people will talk about Friends, Friends, Friends," he wrote.
"And I'm glad of that ... But when I die, as far as my so-called accomplishments go, it would be nice if Friends were listed far behind the things I did to try to help other people."
Lisa Marie Presley in 2012. (AP Image: Chris Pizzello )
Starting with her father Elvis Presley's untimely death when she was just nine years old, Lisa Marie Presley's life was marred by tragedy before her own early death this year. She was 54.
The singer and songwriter was suffering from complications related to an earlier weight-loss surgery when she went into cardiac arrest in January.
Her mother, Priscilla Presley, confirmed the news, describing her daughter as the "most passionate, strong and loving woman" she had ever known.
Throughout her life, Presley was married and divorced four times — including to Michael Jackson and Nicholas Cage — and lost her only son to suicide when he was just 27.
She detailed her grief in a 2022 essay, writing that she had "dealt with death, grief and loss since the age of nine years old". "I've had more than anyone's fair share of it in my lifetime and somehow, I've made it this far."
She was the rockstar's only child and the sole heir of the Elvis Presley trust.
Singer and civil rights activist Harry Belafonte dies at 96
Harry Belafonte, a singer, songwriter, and groundbreaking actor turned political activist, died in April, aged 96.
Belafonte was born in Manhattan but spent his early childhood in his family's native Jamaica.
Belafonte began his career as a calypso singer, best known for his 1950s hit "Banana Boat" song.
He was the first black person allowed to perform in many plush nightspots and also had racial breakthroughs in movies at a time when segregation prevailed in much of the United States.
His acting work pushed racial boundaries in a segregated US, which led him to the civil rights movement, working with his friend Martin Luther King Jr.
Belafonte travelled the world as a goodwill ambassador for UNICEF, the United Nations Children's Fund, in 1987 and later started an AIDS foundation.
Belafonte was also the driving force behind the celebrity-studded, famine-fighting hit song We Are the World in the 1980s, raising $62 million.
Sinead O'Connor performs in 2014. (AP: Antonio Calanni/ File)
Sinéad O'Connor topped international charts with her rendition of Nothing Compares 2 U, but for many, it is the Irish singer's outspoken views on religion, sex, war and feminism and staunch activism that will endure. She died in London in July, aged 56.
The performer began her career singing on the streets of Dublin and soon rose to international fame. Her 1987 debut album, The Lion and the Cobra, made her a star, but it was her powerful performance of Prince's ballad that made her a sensation and earned her four Grammy nominations and one win.
O'Connor declined the award, describing it as a commercial exercise. The following year she made headlines when, during an appearance on Saturday Night Live, she ripped up a photo of Pope John Paul II while performing a rendition of Bob Marley's War, in which she changed some lyrics to reference child abuse in the Catholic Church.
"I found her to be a very, very humble person, a very funny person, and someone who struggled with the injustices of the world," wrote Irish music promoter Fran Daly following O'Connor's death.
"I don't think anyone who's seen her perform has heard a sound like when Sinéad O'Connor opens up and sings."
Irish songwriter and Pogues frontman Shane MacGowan dies at 65
Shane MacGowan, the singer-songwriter and frontman of The Pogues, died in November, aged 65
MacGowan, who was born on Christmas Day, grew up in Tipperary, Ireland, and later in England. He founded the Pogues — originally Pogue Mahone, an anglicisation of the Irish phrase póg mo thóin, meaning "kiss my arse"— in 1982.
The band melded Irish traditional music and "Celtic punk" rock with McGowan's emotive songwriting and slurred, exuberant performances.
The band's most famous song, 1987's Fairytale of New York — with Kirsty MacColl —  is a bittersweet Christmas classic.
MacGowan struggled with alcohol and substance abuse, which lead to a tempestuous relationship with his band — he was kicked out in 1991 before rejoining a decade later. They disbanded in 2014.
MacGowan had years of health problems and used a wheelchair after breaking his pelvis.
Tina Turner performs in 2009. (AP: Hermann J Knippertz/File)
Tina Turner, the legendary queen of rock'n'roll, died in May after a long illness. She was 83.
The singer and songwriter was best known internationally for her hits What's Love Got to Do With It and (Simply) The Best, while her song Nutbush City Limits struck a particular chord with Australians, inspiring the now iconic dance routine.
Turner began her career in the 1950s performing with her husband Ike Turner — the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame has described them as "one of the most formidable live acts in history" — before embarking on a solo career after their split in 1976.
In the 80s she won six of her eight Grammy Awards and saw a dozen songs reach the Top 40 charts. She also used her platform to speak about the abuse she suffered at the hands of her ex-husband.
"Through her courage in telling her story, her commitment to stay the course in her life, no matter the sacrifice, and her determination to carve out a space in rock'n'roll for herself and for others who look like her, Tina Turner showed others who lived in fear what a beautiful future filled with love, compassion, and freedom should look like," said actor Angela Bassett, who played Turner in a 1993 film, following the singer's death.
"How do we say farewell to a woman who owned her pain and trauma and used it as a means to help change the world?"
Actress Raquel Welch dies aged 82
Golden Globe winning actor Raquel Welch died in February, aged 82.
She starred in about 30 films and 50 television series in a career spanning five decades.
Welch came to the wide attention of movie-goers for her role in the 1966 sci-fi adventure Fantastic Voyage, followed by her iconic appearance in the prehistoric drama One Million Years BC — where her fur bikini made her a bestselling pin-up.
She broke the mould of the traditional sex symbol with her strong female characters and went on to be an icon of the 1960s and 70s. She won a Golden Globe for best actress in a musical or comedy in 1974 for The Three Musketeers.
Her final film, How to be a Latin Lover, was released in 2017.
Sir Michael Gambon as Albus Dumbledore in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2005). (AFP: Warner Bros)
Harry Potter and The King's Speech actor Michael Gambon died in September, aged 82.
Gambon left school aged 15 to begin an engineering apprenticeship and by 21 he was fully qualified.
He was also a member of an amateur theatre group and in 1962, he auditioned for the great Shakespearean actor Laurence Olivier, who made him one of the founding members of the National Theatre at the Old Vic, alongside other young emerging greats including Derek Jacobi and Maggie Smith.
He moved into TV and film in the 1980s, and was best known to younger generations for taking over the role of Professor Albus Dumbledore in the Harry Potter movies.
He won four BAFTAs, three Olivier Awards and two ensemble cast Screen Actors Guild Awards — for 2001's Gosford Park and The King's Speech. He was made a Commander of the British Empire in 1992 and knighted for services to drama in 1998.
Gambon retired from the stage in 2015 after suffering long-term memory problems but continued to act on-screen until 2019.
Jimmy Buffett was still touring into 2023. (AP: Matt Sayles)
The US singer-songwriter Jimmy Buffett, best known for his hit songs Margaritaville and Come Monday, died in September, aged 76.
Buffett's "tropical rock" sound was popular with his boomer fan base — who called themselves Parrotheads — and featured songs like Cheeseburger in Paradise, It's Five O'Clock Somewhere and Why Don't We Get Drunk.
Buffett's most popular tune Margaritaville was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2016 for its cultural and historic significance, which helped brand Key West, Florida, as a holiday destination internationally.
One of the world's richest musicians, Buffett channelled the "island escapism" of his music into several business ventures, including the Jimmy Buffett's Margaritaville chain of restaurants.
Buffett continued touring into 2023 despite undergoing treatment for a rare and aggressive skin cancer — Merkel cell carcinoma — for four years.
Some key moments from Jerry Springer's life and career
Controversial afternoon TV host Jerry Springer died in April, aged 79.
Love it or hate it, The Jerry Springer Show changed afternoon television with its bleep-filled family confrontations, chair throwing and the chant of "Jerry Jerry, Jerry" — an early indication on how popular reality TV would become.
Springer was born in a London underground railway station being used as a bomb shelter in 1944, before his parents, German Jews who fled during the Holocaust, moved to the US when he was five.
He first worked in politics and ran for office many times, including a stint at the mayor of Cincinnati. He went on to become a local political reporter before starting his talk show in 1991.
In its 4,000-episode run, which ended in 2017, The Jerry Springer Show found rebuke and criticism for its salacious storylines, but it was ratings gold, even outperforming Oprah's show at one stage.
Legendary American composer Burt Bacharach dies aged 94
Composer of some of the world's biggest earworms, Burt Bacharach died in February, aged 94.
The Oscar-winner is best known for hit songs, Alfie and I Say a Little Prayer, I'll Never Fall in Love Again and This Guy's in Love with You, usually working in partnership with lyricist Hal David.
He had a run of top 10 hits from the 1950s into the 21st century. There were few rivals for Bacharach's songwriting genius for catchy songs, which were performed, covered and played long after they were written.
Bacharach considered Dionne Warwick among his favourites, though he also created songs for Aretha Franklin, Dusty Springfield, Tom Jones and many others.
Elvis Presley, the Beatles and Frank Sinatra were among countless artists who covered his songs.

title: Star Wars production company sues Chilean car wash company Star Wash
content:
Walt Disney production company Lucasfilm is suing themed Chilean car wash Star Wash, accusing it of plagiarising the galactic film saga Star Wars.
On a regular day at Star Wash, a car wash company on the outskirts of Chilean capital Santiago, patrons can see Chewbacca or a stormtrooper wiping down hoods or Darth Vader appearing to use The Force to summon cleaning cloths.
But the law firm representing the car wash said while owner Matias Jara was in the process of registering his brand with Chilean patent authority INAPI, he received a lawsuit from the franchise's creator, Lucasfilm.
Mr Jara's lawyers said Lucasfilm wanted to block the registration of the name and argued the brand could be confused as being affiliated with it.
It had not raised issues with the attendants, the lawyers said.
Lucasfilm, which was acquired by Disney in 2012, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Mr Jara is contesting the suit and argues the name is sufficiently different enough from the movie franchise to avoid confusion.
He also argues that while the production company's copyright covers products such as toys, furniture and non-alcoholic drinks, it does not extend to cleaning cars.
He said his young daughter had thought of the wordplay while on a family trip to a Disney theme park in the US which features a Star Wars area.
"We don't make movies or sell their products or anything like that," Mr Jara added.
He did note his business was, however, a "stellar" car wash.

title: Parasite actor Lee Sun-kyun found dead in Seoul amid drug allegations
content:
South Korean actor Lee Sun-kyun of the Oscar-winning film Parasite has been found dead by authorities following up a report that he had gone missing, according to an official.
Lee, 48, who played the head of a wealthy household in the film, had faced investigation over accusations of illegal drug use amid a government crackdown in which police questioned him three times, with one session running 19 hours over the weekend.
The actor had said he was tricked into taking drugs by a bar hostess trying to blackmail him, the Yonhap news agency reported.
Authorities found Lee in a search triggered by the report that he was missing, a Seoul official told Reuters on condition of anonymity, as the matter is sensitive.
Earlier, citing police, Yonhap said Lee was found in a car at a park in Seoul, after his manager told police the actor had left home, leaving an apparent suicide note.
Officials at Seoul's Jongno and Seongbuk police stations did not immediately respond to telephone calls from Reuters to seek comment.
Lee's agency, HODU&U Entertainment, also did not respond to calls.
Infringements of South Korea's tough drug laws can lead to six months in jail, or up to 14 years for repeat offenders and dealers.
Lee starred in Parasite, which won four Oscars in 2020 including Best Picture.
Parasite, a 2019 dark-comedy thriller directed by Bong Joon-ho, won Academy Awards in 2020 in the categories of best picture, best director, best original screenplay and best international feature film.
It received six Oscar nominations.
In the film, Lee acted as Mr Park, whose affluent home is infiltrated by members of a lower-class family posing as highly qualified domestic workers in a tangled scheme that leads to a gory end.
Lee, born in 1975, had leading roles in South Korean films such as the 2012 thriller Helpless and 2014's All About My Wife.
He played the lead in Apple TV+'s first Korean-language original series, which rolled out in 2021.
Dr Brain, a six-episode sci-fi thriller, was about a cold-hearted neurologist, Koh Se-won, who tries to find clues to a mysterious family accident through brain experiments.

title: 2001's Spy Kids is actually about a dad having a midlife crisis. Let me tell you why
content:
Kids movies are my favourite genre.
Do I have children myself? No. Am I a fan of little ones? Only occasionally. But quality kids movies are, IMHO, peak cinema. The perfect comfort watch.
Of course, not all of these films are created equal. Some are full of what I disdainfully call "kid humour": slapstick, fart jokes, you name it. Very cringe. Not for me.
But others – like the 2001 masterpiece known as Spy Kids – are different.
Incredible sets. Creative concepts that spark the imagination. Gadgets. Action. Wigs. Exciting chase scenes involving life-sized thumbs. You want it, Spy Kids has it.
And I believe this film has a deeper, true meaning behind all the kid movie chaos. But more on that later.
Spy Kids (2001) - Theatrical Teaser Trailer (2K)
The film opens on a dramatic clifftop house. This house is nice.  So nice that the primary school aged children in the movie have an ensuite bathroom.
ANYWAY.
Big sister Carmen is a bit of an asshole to her little brother Juni. He's scared of everything, and is getting bullied at school. His fingers are covered in Band-Aids because his hands get so sweaty, they grow warts.
The children's mother sits down to tell them a bedtime story about two spies from competing nations. These spies were tasked with killing each other (ft. cool wigs and tech glasses), but soon fell in love.
Shock horror: The story's actually about their real life. The spies in the story are Ingrid and Gregorio, Carmen and Juni's parents.
Thumb-thumbs looking iconic in red. (Dimension Films)
Meanwhile, Juni is obsessed with kids show Floop's Fooglies. Turns out, the show's host – played by the iconic Alan Cumming – is actually a bad guy! Developing military-grade weapons! No good.
He's been kidnapping spies and turning them into freaky characters on his show. Mum Ingrid and dad Gregorio are next. But, luckily, Carmen and Junie are off to save them.
Cue: A car that turns into a boat! Instant cement out of a hairspray bottle! And, of course, what you probably remember most from the movie: life-sized thumb henchmen known as thumb-thumbs (who sometimes use jet packs).
It is my sincere belief this movie is not about spy kids at all, but is in fact a product of Gregorio Cortez's mid-life crisis.
At the end of Ingrid's story, she says the spies "trade in one adventure for another", swapping "espionage for parenthood".
The kids promptly argue that the story needs monsters, and "a new ending".
Is this man having a mid-life crisis? (Dimension Films)
Soon enough, we're at the kids' school, where Juni's getting bullied, with the bully's father egging his son on. Gregorio fantasies about standing up to said dad, throwing him across the playground to the cheers of the children around him, winning the approval of his son.
But when the moment comes, Gregorio chickens out. He's just a normal guy now! He wears glasses and everything.
This makes me read the rest of the film as yet another Gregorio fantasy: He's reliving the glory days and imagining a plot where he gets to be a spy again, even as a dad.
To back up this theory, I point to the film's recurring theme of dreams.
Floop performs a charming song about them. Lyrics include:
"You can all be free, free … if you dream, if you dream.
"It's a cruel cruel world full of selfish, mean nasty people but there's a way you can make your day, you can laugh, you can smile … you can dream."
Spy Kids - Floop's Song
There's also a line (technically directed at Carmen) where we're asked: "Is that what you wanna be? Free from your family?"
Then there's themes around who we are, compared with who we want to be. There's messages about overcoming your fears, and the value of family.
There's even the moment when Gregorio reconnects with his estranged brother, and they all fight the bad guys together as one big happy family.
In my highly professional opinion, this all points to a film about a dad in an identity crisis.
I am obsessed with the puzzle piece windows!! (Dimension Films)
And to take this all one step further: perhaps Gregorio never was a spy to begin with? Maybe he's just a boring man, wishing his kids thought he was cool.
After all, Spy Kids has the iconic line: "My parents can't be spies! They're not cool enough!"
But maybe parents can be cool enough … all they have to do is dream.
Yes! There's a little, but not too much kid humour. It's directed (and its incredible soundtrack is composed by) Robert Rodriguez, and there's an insanely famous actor cameo towards the end. Most of the jokes are funny, and the chase scenes are exciting. Plus, the movie's so stylised, anything a little odd is camp. <3
Yes! The film's about a Mexican-American family, with snippets of Spanish used throughout. At one point, Carmen is embarrassed about how long her full Hispanic name is, but soon learns its #power when it's the password to a cool ass safe house.
This film passes the Bechdel test (measures the representation of women in a film), but all the evil investors and other spies are white guys in suits. We do see women doing a bunch of flips and martial arts though, and that's always fun.
Gadgets!!!!!! And the incredible creativity and detail of the set design (stained glass windows shaped like puzzle pieces?! So nice.)

title: 'I think she'll have a huge career': Indigenous model Charlee Fraser stars in blockbuster Anyone But You
content:
You might not have heard of the quietly successful international model Charlee Fraser, but you probably will soon.
The 28-year-old Awabakal woman from Newcastle, NSW has walked for fashion houses like Chanel, Dior and Prada, and now she's about to make her acting debut — in Anyone But You, a rom-com set and filmed in Sydney, which is one of summer's biggest tentpole films.
She plays ex-girlfriend and potential future love interest Margaret, alongside Sydney Sweeney (Euphoria; White Lotus) and Glen Powell (Top Gun: Maverick).
Directed by Will Gluck, Anyone But You deals with the mess, fun and intensity of situationships.
Fraser said she was obsessed with Gluck's 2011 rom-com Friends With Benefits as a young adult. She also watched his film Easy A (2010) every night before bed as a teenager.
She said she couldn't believe it when she found out she got the part in Anyone But You.
"I was beside myself, thinking that one day I'm going to be shooting a rom-com with the man himself — William Francis Gluck. It's a wild, very full circle," she said.
"I still struggle to find words for that one."
In Anyone But You, Bea (Sweeney) and Ben (Powell) are both attending a destination wedding in Sydney.
Having had a previous romantic encounter — that quickly turned hostile due to a misunderstanding — they are less than thrilled to see each other in the summery city.
Raunchy tension arises when ex-lovers Bea (Sydney Sweeney) and Ben (Glen Powell) meet, in Anyone But You. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
But, in part to ensure the wedding runs smoothly, and in part to trick people for various *reasons*, they decide to pretend they are a couple. (Sound familiar? This film is loosely based on Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing.)
Meddling parents, yearning exes and close encounters with Aussie critters means there's a good deal of drama and raunchy comedy before the big day.
In the film, Fraser's character Margaret is a free spirit in her own relationship-slash-situationship with Beau (Joe Davidson).
Fraser enjoyed the process of becoming Margaret.
"She carries herself in this way that she just has this shamelessness about her. And I loved that because that's something I feel is difficult to attain personally," she explained.
"It was fun to explore what it feels like to be shameless in all of her moments, and just truly be in her body."
Margaret is somewhere many people dating in the modern world have been: she's having fun, but is potentially ready for more commitment. That's when she bumps into her ex Ben, who's having some romantic tension of his own.
Will Beau ever commit to Margaret? (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
"She's looking for something more serious, then the ex pops back up and then she realises he's grown-up and he's changed and like, maybe there's potential there to rekindle an old flame," Fraser said.
"I think most of us at some point in our lives will be able to connect with her story — we all get to that point where we're ready to be serious, and we start looking for the one."
On days off from filming, Fraser would spend time with the rest of the cast — which also includes Dermot Mulroney (the romantic lead in My Best Friend's Wedding), Alexandra Shipp (Writer Barbie) and Australians Bryan Brown and Rachel Griffiths.
Sydney Sweeney was the film's self-appointed Chief Fun Officer.
"[Sydney] was incredibly generous and, on weekends, she would arrange group activities for all of us ensemble cast to spend time together and connect and grow," Fraser said.
Charlee Fraser came onto the set without any preconceived notions. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
This included bus tours around the city, and movie nights.
"We watched My Best Friend's Wedding, which was incredibly beautiful because as we were filming a rom-com movie, we're watching an iconic rom-com movie, with an icon from that rom-com movie, who's in our rom-com movie."
William Gluck had high praises for Fraser's silver screen debut, saying she was "so real" on set.
"She'd never acted before, and she didn't come with any preconceived notions; it just felt so great to have someone who [can] play something so authentic," he said at the film's premiere screening in Sydney.
Sydney Sweeney and Charlee Fraser at the Sydney Premiere of Anyone But You. (Photo: Thuy Ong)
As well as modelling and acting, Fraser is the ambassador for First Nations Fashion and Design, where she acts as a mentor for young Indigenous models. She is also an activist for creating sustainable and ethical fashion.
"I feel like I've been the first to do a lot of what I've done in certain industries, and the ones who have come before me have really paved the way for me to have a platform," she said.
"Now I feel as though everything that I'm doing contributes to paving the way for others."
Her next big film is slated for 2024, though she can't talk about it just yet.
"I am really focused on aligning myself with the work I do and always incorporating culture along the way, [with] representation being a big part of that," she said.
"I just hope that the things I do continue to inspire community to do what they love, and reach for the stars and be passionate.
Anyone But You is out in cinemas on Boxing Day, December 26.
