title: Sydney Sweeney in Sydney Harbour, and other Boxing Day films to check out
content:
The presents are unwrapped, belts have been loosened and in-laws have been sent on their way: it's time to go to the movies!
Now you can sit back and relax in the dark, not having to — and not actually being allowed to — talk to anyone.
But has the end of year brain fog made it hard to make any assessments or choices for yourself? (Relatable)
Don't worry, our critics have checked out the big Boxing Day releases just for you.
Sony Pictures Entertainment Youtube: ANYONE BUT YOU – Official Trailer (HD)
Our critic Michael Sun says:
For a movie about eye candy, Anyone But You is certainly quite sour.
The Hollywood production — one of many made in Australia during the pandemic — is ostensibly a rom-com, though it often plays like the longest tourism ad ever made.
Within its 100-minute runtime, it ticks off a requisite checklist of Sydney's finest: the Opera House, the Harbour Bridge, Bondi and the Sydney Cricket Ground, all filmed with increasingly gratuitous drone shots.
Each location provides an appropriately corny backdrop for a tale as old as time — or at least Shakespeare.
Loosely based on Much Ado About Nothing, Anyone But You plonks its two genetically blessed leads — mouthy law student Bea (Euphoria/White Lotus's Sydney Sweeney) and roguish finance bro Ben (Glen Powell, from Top Gun) — in a web of romantic intrigue.
After a meet-cute at a café turns into a meet-ugly, the pair become sworn enemies — until a destination wedding in Australia re-unites them, much to their disdain.
Because this is a rom-com, a plan is soon hatched: they agree to perform the machinations of a loving couple. She's trying to ward off a former flame; he's trying to woo one back.
All the ingredients for success are here. The skies are impossibly blue, Sweeney exudes her typical charisma, and Powell is, well, hunky.
There is something wooden, though, about the film. It's shorn of the easy charm of director Will Gluck's previous work — including his 2010 breakout and instant teen classic Easy A.
The gags fly thick and fast: a stray firework; a Titanic homage that ends with a crash-landing in Sydney Harbour; a misbehaving huntsman that made headlines earlier this month. But Gluck belabours the jokes until they're threadbare and punchlines become awkward silences.
The perfect night, Ben says at one point, is both stupid and fun. One wishes the film heeded its own advice.
Transmission Films Youtube: ONE LIFE | Official Trailer
Our critic Luke Goodsell says:
The real-life story of a valiant English aid worker who helped save hundreds of refugee kids from the encroaching Nazis, this World War II weepie arrives as a timely reminder of — and maybe even a cause for reflection upon — the plight of those displaced from their homeland by occupying forces.
A doddering Anthony Hopkins stars as Nicholas "Nicky" Winton, a retired 79-year-old stockbroker going through his personal archives in 1988 — and flashing back to his life half-a-century earlier.
It's 1938, and the rise of the Nazis in Germany and Austria has driven masses of refugees to take shelter in Prague, where their makeshift encampments are facing the imminent threat of German invasion.
There, the young Nicky (Johnny Flynn) joins the humanitarian relief effort — alongside his mother (Helena Bonham Carter), a Prague schoolteacher (Alex Sharp) and an academic (Romola Garai) — to mount a campaign to evacuate orphaned children and rehouse them in foster homes in England. That's if they can get them out before the Nazis come goose-stepping into town.
Based on a book by Winton's daughter Barbara, One Life is a moving true story executed in the kind of vaguely anonymous style of the mid-tier British historical drama. Making his feature film debut, veteran television director James Hawes lays the action out in unfussy style, while screenwriters Lucinda Coxon (The Danish Girl) and Nick Drake (Romulus, My Father) take aim at the tear ducts.
By the time One Life has built to its big, heartstring-tugging climax, there'll be plenty of watery eyes — even if the film doesn't always do the work to earn them.
But Hopkins is such a master that he's able to suggest the richness of a life with the tiniest of gestures or modulation to his voice, crafting a pretty affecting portrait of a man whose emotions finally overwhelm his reserved facade. He's both better than the film around him, and the reason to see it.
Poor Things trailer
Our critic Keva York says:
People recoiled from Victor Frankenstein's Creature — a tall, lumbering, ugly thing. Even the doctor himself, repulsed, fled from the scene of his reanimation. Not so for sentient science experiment Bella Baxter (Emma Stone), who, with her big eyes, brows on fleek and exhilarating lack of social graces, seems to inspire ardour in all those she meets – especially men.
Bella, the accidental provocateur at the centre of Yorgos Lanthimos's baroque-steampunk Barbie tale, is the project of one Dr Godwin Baxter (Willem Dafoe) — or, as Bella calls him, "God".
That God resembles a patchwork monster more than he does divine creator is of a piece with the film's sense of humour. His disfigured appearance is testament to his own father's perverse dedication to science; young God was his guinea pig.
In The Curse, Nathan Fielder and Emma Stone play an excruciating couple who make you laugh but also want to cry.
Though Dr God dotes on Bella, the finest and certainly the smartest of his surgically wrought progeny, she recognises that his home — also populated by various hybrid creatures and matronly surgical assistants — is her gilded cage, and runs off with the first visitor to make an amorous advance.
So, it's off to Lisbon with foppish lawyer Duncan Wedderburn (Mark Ruffalo), whose horniness for Bella is matched — exceeded, even — by hers for him, and for the world itself.
Poor Things reunites Lanthimos with not just Stone — who played a courtly usurper in his much-lauded 2018 dramedy, The Favourite — but also with that film's writer, Australia's own Tony McNamara. (McNamara here adapts the 1992 novel by Scottish postmodernist Alasdair Gray.) If it ain't broke, right?
This latest venture does, however, go a little hard with some of The Favourite's ticks, like having old-world characters spit new world curse words, and the distractingly liberal use of a fish-eye lens.
As shot by Robbie Ryan (also an alum of The Favourite), Poor Things boasts the rich glow of a Hans Holbein portrait – and features even puffier sleeves. If only the film itself was not quite so puffed-up.
From the lavish set design to the deeply mannered performances, every frame brims with a smugness that, over the course of the two-and-a-half-hour runtime, becomes enervating.
Palace Films Youtube: TWO TICKETS TO GREECE - Official HD Trailer (2023) - Only In Cinemas
Our critic Luke Goodsell says:
There may not be ABBA, but there's a healthy dose of cheesy disco on the soundtrack to this French comedy, a Gen-X romp in boomer drag about a pair of mismatched middle-aged women on a trip to the sparkling Greek islands.
Inseparable besties as teenagers before a falling out over a boy, forty-something Blandine (Olivia Côte) and Magalie (Laure Calamy) have taken very different life paths in the ensuing 30 years.
When My Big Fat Greek Wedding came out more than 20 years ago, it made me feel seen.
An uptight radiology technician, Blandine lives with her college-bound son Benjamin (Alexandre Desrousseaux), and is deep in depression after her husband divorced her for a much younger woman. Free-spirited Magalie, meanwhile, continues to conduct her life like she's still a teenager, eking out a living as a freelance writer while hooking up with hot men as it takes her fancy.
In an effort to cheer his mother up, Benjamin orchestrates a trip to Greece for the two estranged pals. Blandine reluctantly joins up with Magalie for a jaunt to the Greek island of Amorgos, which the two had once dreamt of visiting as teenagers obsessed with Luc Besson's diving adventure, The Big Blue.
Writer-director Marc Fitoussi (Folies-Bergère) keeps things bubbling along and the scenery postcard-pretty (it's the next best thing to actually taking a summer holiday to Greece), while the two leads — particularly the vivacious Calamy, star of Full Time — push past some creaky pacing and lacklustre banter with the force of their screen presence.
They get an expert assist from a third-act turn by the great Kristin Scott Thomas, who arrives like a hippie vision astride a quad bike and effortlessly toes the line between the movie's frothy comedy and tender life moments

title: Actor Charlie Sheen allegedly attacked in Malibu home
content:
Actor Charlie Sheen has allegedly been attacked in his home, with police charging a woman with assault.
Los Angeles police were called to the Two and Half Men star's luxury Malibu home on Friday, regarding a battery and disturbance incident.
The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department said suspect Electra Schrock was arrested and charged with assault with a deadly weapon and residential burglary.
"Upon contacting the parties involved, deputies identified Charlie Sheen as a victim of assault," the statement said.
Entertainment outlet TMZ said Ms Schrock, 47, is one of Sheen's neighbours.
Actor Charlie Sheen (right) has faced court numerous times, seen here in 2010 after he was sentenced for assaulting his wife during an alcohol-fuelled quarrel. (Reuters: Rick Wilking )
TMZ reported that Ms Schrock is alleged to have forced her way into Sheen's home before ripping his shirt and trying to strangle him.
It said the actor was seen by paramedics but not taken to a hospital.
Sheen, the 58-year-old son of actor Martin Sheen, is notorious for his Hollywood scandals, including episodes of substance abuse and destructive violence.
He was the star of television sitcom Two and a Half Men, and starred in films such as Platoon, Wall Street, and Young Guns.

title: Kid-friendly movies to go see this summer — that you just might enjoy
content:
It's the end of the year and everyone is exhausted and ready for rest — except for the kids, who are hyped up on candy cane sugar and the prospect of the long days of summer stretching out before them.
Fear not! There are a host of kid-friendly films coming out, which you can plonk the kids in front of while you sit in silence, and which you might actually enjoy yourself.
YouTube | Walt Disney Animation Studios | Wish | Official Trailer
Our critic Luke Goodsell says:
Disney's latest animated feature marks the studio's 100th year in the business, so it's probably fitting that it's defined by a strong feeling of familiarity — though whether that breeds comfort or contempt among audiences is another matter entirely. (The movie flopped in the US, if that's anything to go by.)
A grab bag of storytelling tropes, generic characters and musical styles from the well-thumbed Disney playbook, Wish unfolds in a one-size-fits-all fairytale land ruled by the sorcerer king Magnifico (a comedically underutilised Chris Pine).
Magnifico's benevolent dream of nurturing and granting the wishes of his constituency has curdled into selfish tyranny: He's keeping all the wishes in the kingdom's mystical vault, to be handed out whenever he deems one of his citizens worthwhile.
But when plucky teenager Asha (Ariana DeBose, doing the thing) wishes upon a star — which looks like a Miyazaki sprite reconfigured as a corporate emoji — she sets in motion a challenge to the sorcerer's supremacy, championing a humanist utopia where the dreams are reclaimed for the people.
No points for guessing that this analogy for the dangers of monopolising dreams is drenched in irony, coming from the corporation with a stranglehold on the childhood fantasies of generations.That's just business as usual for the Mouse House ("When it comes to the universe, we're all shareholders," is an actual lyric in one of the new songs here).
Set that aside and there are sprinklings of the old Disney magic to be found — including an amusing chorus of chickens, a talking goat who might have sprung from Pinocchio's Pleasure Island and a forest full of animals that even features a cameo from Bambi.
The showtunes — primarily penned by singer Julia Michaels and songwriter Benjamin Rice — are a little forgettable, though on occasion (This Wish; I'm a Star) they generate sparks. (Plus, it's hard to resist when the refrain from When You Wish Upon A Star is threaded into parts of the score.) Wish isn't about to challenge Frozen for kids' repeat-viewing supremacy, but you could do worse for a pre-teen movie diversion this summer holidays.
YouTube | Warner Bros. Pictures |Wonka | Official Trailer
Our critic Keva York says:
The impulse to account for how some fictional freak (complimentary) got to be the way they are — especially tempting when wading into that most cash-grabby of genres, the origin story — is one usually best avoided. As with a magic trick, to 'explain' this is to reduce a character to less than the sum of their parts – to sub out a tantalising mystery for a game of connect the dots.
It's rather a relief to be introduced to a young Wonka who, as incarnated by Timothée Chalamet, is already a fully formed chocolate wizard (slash magician slash inventor). He's just arrived in a new city after seven years at sea, ready to launch his confectionary career — even if the money-grubbing members of the local "chocolate cartel" (Paterson Joseph, Matt Lucas and Mathew Baynton) are less than welcoming.
Deep Roy played 165 Oompa Loompas (including an entire glam rock band) in Tim Burton's 2005 film adaptation of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. Will Hugh Grant in 2023's Wonka ever measure up?
Director Paul King (Paddington, Paddington 2) applies a fairly light touch when it comes to psychoanalysing his protagonist's obsession – unlike Tim Burton's 2005 Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, with its flashback to Willy's childhood under the thumb of a sugar-hating dentist.
King preserves and, in fact, amplifies Wonka's magic. What does gets muted in the translation, however, is the unnerving weirdness of Roald Dahl's character – his darkness, his off-putting humour.
The misadventures of the bratty Golden Ticket winners in the Wonka factory, as recounted in Dahl's 1964 book, reveal a candy man with a truly warped sense of "just desserts". Chalamet's Wonka, meanwhile, is willing to abandon his calling for the sake of new pal Noodle (Calah Lane).
The Dune star gamely gives Willy his all, and proves endearing in the role, convincing even, but he hasn't got a madcap bone in his body. He looks like he belongs in a pre-Raphaelite painting, not a zany sweet shop.
If the film isn't quite up to the preternaturally scrumdiddlyumptious standard of its namesake, then it would certainly still pass muster at any of Wonka's rival chocolate companies.
YouTube | Illumination |  Migration | Official Trailer
Our critic Luke Goodsell says:
It's ducks amuck in this animated adventure from family-friendly hitmakers Illumination Studios (Minions; Sing; The Super Mario Bros. Movie), as a flock of New England mallards find their feathers ruffled on an unexpected trip to the frightening big pond of New York City.
Convinced by his wife (voiced by Elizabeth Banks) and ducklings (Caspar Jennings and Tresi Gazal) to take a break from the winter doldrums, a beleaguered drake (Kumail Nanjiani) gathers up the family — and a tagalong deadbeat uncle (Danny DeVito) — and heads south for the warmer climes of Jamaica.
Best laid eggs soon go awry when a cloud of fog sends them off course and tumbling into Manhattan — where the mallard-justed skein run a-fowl of a deranged but resourceful pigeon (Awkwafina, channelling Natasha Lyonne), and fall into the clutches of a dastardly restaurant with Duck à l'Orange on the menu.
Much like their Minions and Sing series, Illumination's latest feature is bright and bouncy and largely pitched to audiences who've only recently learned to waddle, with plenty of sight gags that will quack up undemanding audiences.
Screenwriter Mike White (The White Lotus) lands a few serviceable jokes amid the standard-issue story beats, while French director Benjamin Renner (who was Oscar-nominated for 2012's Ernest & Celestine), garnishes the farce with the occasional visual grace note (there's a shot of the ducks cruising across the New York skyline that really is quite poetic).
Keegan-Michael Key, meanwhile, does an amusingly over-the-top accent as a caged Jamaican parrot who longs for his tropical homeland, and — proving it's been a banner year for heron representation — the legendary Carol Kane lends her voice to a trickster bird that gives Robert Pattinson a run for his squawking money.
YouTube | DC | Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom | Trailer
Our critic Luke Goodsell says:
Despite being a sequel to the biggest hit in DC's Extended Universe, Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom arrives as the ignominious end of the line for Warner Bros' troubled superhero franchise, with new bosses James Gunn and Peter Safran having officially announced the end for Jason Momoa's underwater beefcake.
On the strength of this action-packed but mechanical new adventure, it's pretty hard to mourn the loss.
Having ascended to the throne of Atlantis, Aquaman (Momoa) is dividing his time between regal duties and raising his new baby with Queen Mera (a barely present Amber Heard, not exactly dispelling those wild behind-the-scenes rumours.)
That is until David Kane (Candyman's Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) — hell-bent on avenging the death of his father in the first movie — happens upon an ancient, all-powerful trident and summons the dark magic of a fabled lost kingdom to wreak havoc upon Atlantis.
To protect his people, Aquaman must team up on a quest with his exiled brother Orm (Patrick Wilson), make a whole bunch of lazily written wisecracks and pound a few six-packs of Guinness with his dad (Temuera Morrison). (Let's just try and ignore the fact that they're drinking them straight outta the can.)
There's also a plot about global warming and an impending climate catastrophe, which has something to do with the villain burning chunks of a mythical substance called Orichalcum (stop sniggering, it's a thing).
In theory, any movie teeming with fantastical ocean creatures, neon-streaked underwater metropolises and Nicole Kidman riding a freakin' cybernetic shark should be a no-brainer blast of escapism.
But, for all its visual splurges, the Lost Kingdom never transcends the tedium of its green screen action.
The film borrows liberally from The Lord of the Rings, Jules Verne, Avatar and Star Wars (Martin Short voices a Jabba the Hutt-like gangster fish, bless), among others, yet can't summon much in the way of its own personality.
On the plus side, hopefully this means we'll see more of director James Wan in Malignant mode.

title: Bradley Cooper delivers Oscar-worthy performance in his 'swooning biopic' Maestro
content:
No one could accuse Bradley Cooper of lacking big-screen ambition.
After starring in and directing the smash remake of A Star is Born, the actor-turned-filmmaker returns with Maestro, a swooning biopic of the legendary American composer Leonard Bernstein that — at its best — reaches the ecstatic heights of the conductor's symphonies.
Cooper sets the bar high with an opening quote from Bernstein, one that cannily doubles as a built-in defence against the film's critics:
It also sets the stage for a heady plunge into the life of a remarkable, multifaceted American figure.
"Smoking was a real hobby for both of them," Carey Mulligan said of the Bernsteins in an interview with Variety. (Supplied: Netflix)
Charismatic and larger than life, Bernstein was a 20th century musical giant whose career of composing and conducting for orchestra and film scores saw him achieve a kind of global cultural ubiquity. (His inspirational Young People's Concerts were broadcast on national TV and syndicated in some 40 countries around the world, from the 1950s through the 1970s.)
He was also a gay man in an era where the closet was the preferred mode for public figures — a fact testified to by his 27-year marriage to a woman, which forms the focal point of Cooper's film.
As Bradley Cooper brings Leonard Bernstein to life in the new biopic Maestro, Australian musicians weigh in on his performance.
Maestro begins in time-honoured music biopic style, with the older Bernstein (also played by Cooper) taking a moment to think about his entire life. Moments later, the film careens back in time to a black-and-white 1943, where the young conductor has just received his breakthrough call to head up the New York Philharmonic at Carnegie Hall.
In the ensuing rush of stardom he falls — platonically, at least — for Felicia Montealegre (Carey Mulligan, wielding a mid-Atlantic accent), a rising stage actor who clocks precisely what she's getting herself into.
"I know exactly who you are," Felicia tells Lenny. "Let's give it a whirl."
Though Felicia is accommodating of her husband's extramarital affairs, their life of willing deception will eventually take its toll. It's this domestic tension that drives Cooper and co-writer Josh Singer's screenplay, which endeavours to build a private, rather than our more familiar public, sense of its subject.
"[Felicia] was his everything; she was his muse, his inspiration, his closest confidant, his best friend, his lover," Mulligan told Variety. (Supplied: Netflix)
Inhabiting almost 50 years of Bernstein's life, Cooper delivers a rich, immersive performance, transforming himself both physically — makeup designer Kazu Hiro's work goes far beyond that much-publicised proboscis — and technically, lowering his voice to reflect the conductor's melodically nasal, four-pack-a-day timbre.
There's considerable craft to his creation, born of an obvious passion. The star spent some six years developing the project and learning how to conduct an orchestra, and even directed the movie while remaining in character as Bernstein. (For those of you playing at home, the Best Actor Oscar seems to be pretty much his to lose at this point.)
Cooper is a warm, generous actor; it shines through in his portrayal of a man who was bursting with vitality, who was eager to please everyone around him — even when it came at the expense of loving himself.
Cooper worked closely with Leonard and Felicia's three children during the production of Maestro. (Supplied: Netflix)
As the woman bearing witness, Mulligan has the less showy but just as detailed role, conveying the experience of a wife unravelling in slow motion, the frustration of living in the orbit of a Great Man, and the years of pleasure she's forgone.
Together, their show-stopping moment arrives in an explosive argument set against a Thanksgiving Parade, which Cooper lets unfurl in a long take that practically screams Oscar clip — that is until he deflates it all with a droll sight gag, one of the best of the year.
It's evidence of Cooper's growing confidence and craft as a filmmaker, which was already on display in his debut. He favours long, dramatic push-ins and off-kilter framing that he might have gleaned from his Licorice Pizza director Paul Thomas Anderson, and designs seamless camera moves that seem to glide across space and time.
Cooper told Screen Daily conducting the London Symphony Orchestra in a live rendition of Mahler's 2nd Symphony at Ely Cathedral was "the most terrifying thing I've ever done". (Supplied: Netflix)
A bravura early sequence, shot with smoky Old Hollywood glamour by cinematographer Matthew Libatique, reimagines Bernstein's 1944 ballet Fancy Free as a dance between Felicia and Lenny intertwined with homoerotic sailors.
As you might expect, the score — supplied by the London Symphony Orchestra — enriches these and other moments, giving Maestro the sustained feel of a musical movement. Variations on classical pieces by Schumann, Mahler and Beethoven mix with nods to Bernstein's own compositions from On the Town and West Side Story, adding grandiose flourishes to the story.
It all reaches a crescendo in a miraculous sequence set inside England's Ely Cathedral in 1973, with Bernstein — and Cooper — leading the orchestra through Mahler's Resurrection Symphony and into sweaty, spiritual abandon. Those prosthetics really get a workout.
Maestro is available in cinemas and on Netflix.

title: Marvel Studios drops Jonathan Majors after he is found guilty of assaulting ex
content:
Marvel Studios has dropped actor Jonathan Majors after he was found guilty by a New York jury of violently assaulting his former girlfriend.
He was convicted by a jury of six on one count of assault and one count of harassment, after a two week trial in state court in Manhattan.
Prosecutors said Majors assaulted his then-girlfriend Grace Jabbari in a hired car in Manhattan in March, leaving her with a broken finger and swollen arm and ear.
He was charged with two assault counts and two harassment counts, and will face sentencing in February.
The two other charges were acquitted.
Majors pursed his lips and cast his face down when the first conviction was read but otherwise showed little reaction.
Since a breakout role in The Last Black Man in San Francisco, Majors became a major Hollywood player through roles in Creed III and his emergence as a key supervillain in the Marvel multiverse.
Jonathan Majors enters court with current girlfriend Meagan Good holding a gold-leafed bible in his hand.  (AP: Bebeto Matthews)
However, the allegations saw the 34-year-old's work pulled or postponed, including the release of Sundance award-winning film Magazine Dreams.
A spokesperson for Walt Disney, who owns Marvel, told Reuters the studio had dropped the actor from future projects.
Majors was set to headline the conclusion to the Multiverse Saga, 2025's Avengers: The Kang Dynasty.
It was expected to start shooting in early 2024.
During the hearing, Ms Jabbari said Majors attacked her after she grabbed his phone upon seeing a text from another woman.
She also described his "violent temper" and other incidents where he "exploded" in anger.
"She had shaped herself around the defendant, to cater to his personality, to avoid him being angry with her," prosecutor Kelli Galaway said during closing arguments.
Grace Jabbari leaves court after giving testimony in the assault case.  (AP: Bebeto Matthews)
Majors's lawyer sought to flip the script, claiming it was Ms Jabbari who victimised Majors by attacking him in the car and then falsely accusing him of assault after he broke up with her.
"You are here to end this nightmare for Jonathan Majors," lawyer Priya Chaudhry said through tears during her closing argument.
Majors did not take the stand, but Ms Chaudhry said her client was the victim of "white lies, big lies, and pretty little lies" invented by Ms Jabbari to exact revenge on an unfaithful partner.
Majors filed his own complaint against Ms Jabbari, prompting her arrest on assault charges in October.
But the Manhattan District Attorney's Office later closed the case because it "lacks prosecutorial merit."

title: Did the recent seasons of The Crown feel a bit off to you? It might have something to do with your age
content:
After 60 episodes and several different versions of Queen Elizabeth II, historical fiction drama The Crown has come to an end.
Beginning before the Queen's reign, the series rehashed some of the biggest events in the past 100 years and created a reputation of being a prestige drama.
However, after winning over the critics in the beginning, The Crown seemed to have lost its shine by the end.
But is the show badly done or is there something else at play?
We spoke to two pop culture experts and a psychologist to find out.
Olivia Colman, Imelda Staunton and Claire Foy played Queen Elizabeth II at different stages in her life.  (Netflix: Justin Downing)
To recap, the first four episodes followed the lead-up to Princess Diana's death and her funeral.
Those episodes came out as something like a four-chapter mini-series.
Part two of the final season covered Prince William meeting a young Kate Middleton at university, Princess Margaret's death, Prince Charles and Camilla's wedding and The Queen planning her own funeral.
The Crown is not a documentary — in fact, it makes a point of saying so in its description, which reads:
"Inspired by real events, this fictional dramatisation tells the story of Queen Elizabeth II and the political and personal events that shaped her reign."
However, for people who weren't around when these events happened, there might have been a sense of authenticity that built creditability.
Lisa Hackett and Jo Coghlan are part of the University of New England's Popular Culture Research Network (PopCRN) and have an academic interest in the royals.
They unpacked why the credibility of the earlier seasons appears to be missing from some newer episodes.
"When I watched The Crown originally, I sat there Googling the whole time, 'was that true? Was that happening?'," Dr Coglan says.
"I'm not doing that anymore … it's all embellished, it's just narrative.
"Ergo, it's just a soap opera."
Elizabeth Debicki appearing to Imelda Staunton as Queen Elizabeth as Princess Diana's ghost.
The final season covers from 1997 to 2005.
The first four episodes span across just a few weeks in 1997, while the second part stretches over a few years until Prince Charles and Camilla's wedding in 2005.
And this might have been why it felt a bit off to you.
A baby born in 2005 is now legally considered an adult, but is 18 years enough time between then and now for the series to not feel too soon?
That may depend on how old you are.
"It is very much generational, how we respond," Dr Coghlan says.
Both pop culture experts think the series should have stopped earlier — specifically, Dr Hackett reckons they should have ended it with the divorce of Charles and Diana.
"I don't know if that's a good time to stop or if that's reflective of my age," she says.
"It was far back enough as where I don't remember as much.
"There's that debate — when does history start and when is it now?
"So maybe that 30 years ago feels like history to me, whereas the rest feels contemporary.
"It kind of feels like I know too much."
So it might have something to do with how much you know about a period of time.
And the more you know about that period of time, the more pressure there is on the show makers to get it right.
"Those earlier episodes, as long as he's got the essence, it's [got] authenticity," Dr Hackett says.
"But once you actually get closer to what we actually have first-hand experience of rather than remote history, I think we don't just want authenticity, we want accuracy.
"Whereas before I think we would have forgone that."
The series might have felt 'too soon' for people who were around during the period in which the episodes were set.  (Supplied: Netflix)
The death of Diana was major moment in history, with a global outpouring of grief.
But it's not just Diana's death — the series also touched on the September 11 terror attack on the World Trade Center and the invasion of Iraq.
So if you remember that time, your memories of that might have impacted the way you experienced the show.
Australian Psychological Society president Catriona Davis-McCabe says people commonly react differently when re-exposed to "shared past events".
"Our emotions at the time of experiencing an event influence how memories of the experience are formed and shape how we remember and experience these memories in the future," Dr Davis-McCabe says.
"For example, when people rewatch their favourite childhood movies, they can be taken back to the feelings they felt when they first watched it, and this is similar for fiction or non-fiction.
"With mass media now common, it is a lot easier for people to form emotional connections to events that they had no direct experience of, and if these events are rebroadcast years later, it's not surprising that people may feel similar emotions to when they experienced the initial event.
"If particularly strong emotional connections were formed during the consolidation of these initial memories, then people may have a visceral reaction when re-exposed to this content if not enough time has passed from the initial event or the event has not been processed.
"This is especially true if feelings of trauma are associated with the initial event."
Dr Coghlan says the fact that they didn't stop earlier reflects the commercial pressures at play — suggesting show makers kept the series running to capitalise on its popularity.
That's something she says made the newer episodes feel "quite laboured".
"I thought they were … milking it," she says.
"I get they want to make a few bucks out of it but I think it's just become a commercial product and without anything new to say, it becomes very soap opera-y."
Claire Foy played Elizabeth in seasons one and two, but reprised her role in flashbacks later in the series. (Supplied: Netflix)
Not only that, it might have been erring too close to wish fulfilment — something that can make us feel good, but we know life doesn't often pan out that way.
And, previously, the show didn't either.
In the earlier seasons, many viewers might have wanted Princess Margaret to marry the man of her choice but that didn't happen — and the show didn't shy away from that character's heartbreak.
While the later seasons still depict horrible, tragic events, they appear to cushion the blow with minor concessions.
We see Charles and Diana patch things up before she goes to Paris, we see Diana and Dodi being honest with each other right before the crash and we see Harry and William making amends after bickering.
"I think they've made decisions on what the audience would like," Dr Hackett says.
"So they're making decisions guessing what the audience would want to see and maybe they've got it a bit wrong now because there's too many conflicting stories, there's too many ideas out there."
"I think that, for the most part, The Crown is a very pro-British, pro-monarch program," Dr Coghlan says.
"People were probably expecting it to be a bit more critical.
"And there are moments where they're critical of a character but they're rather fleeting or it's implied criticism.
"They show their flaws, but that said it's a very pro-monarchy, pro-Windsor piece of television."
There were times when the show could have been harsher in its depictions of the royals.
For example, one episode teases out an apparent scandal from a fictionalised retelling of a young Elizabeth and Margaret partying after the end of World War II.
But the reveal is quite charming and, by today's standards, quite tame and wholesome.
Viola Prettejohn, who played the teenage Elizabeth in a flashback episdoes, bears a striking resemblance to fellow actor Claire Foy. (Netflix: Justin Downing)
In the years since their mother's death, both Prince William and Prince Harry have been open about how difficult that time was for them.
And there's a much deeper cultural understanding of the importance of mental health in today's society than there was 20 years ago.
"Cultural sensitivities and whether people feel re-enactments trivialise past events also shapes how we respond," Dr Davis-McCabe says.
Prince William and Harry have both spoken about how hard their mother's death — and what followed — was for them.  (Netflix)
So people may have been more likely to consider Diana's sons as complex, multi-faceted people rather than one-dimensional characters on a screen.
That's something the series showed in earlier seasons, but perhaps the fact that many of us have had so much more exposure to the princes, it feels more personal.
Dr Coghlan says that, even though it's clearly fictionalised, filmmakers do inform people's opinions by retelling these stories.
"You do have some sort of responsibility to … in this case, a living family and the boys," she says.
"I found myself wondering if William and Harry had watched it and how they would react.
"As a mother I found that quite confronting … the idea that it's their mother's death that they're seeing portrayed."
Both Dr Hackett and Coghlan say the newer seasons were less of a political drama and more about personal relationships.
The scenes depicting the Queen having meetings with the prime minister seem to be less pivotal in the context of influencing historical events.
"We're not seeing the statesperson anymore," Dr Hackett says.
"That's a huge shift from the first four seasons to the last two — it's really just about what the tabloids are saying.
"That sense of ... 'the Queen is the head of state and she's involved in these big events' has fallen away it's become a very different show I think."
The costume department paid very close attention to detail in some of the royals' most iconic outfits.  (Netflix: Keith Bernstein)
Dr Coghlan compares The Crown's early seasons to the first few seasons of Game of Thrones — which was known for its complex power dynamics and political plotting.
"And I found that, in the early episodes of The Crown, there was a lot of that," she says.
"The machinations of the courtiers and the press people and between Margaret and Elizabeth and whether Margaret should marry or not.
"I found all of that quite intriguing against the historical backdrop of actual events — so the Suez Canal crisis and that sort of thing."
This may have made relationship-focused storylines a bit more trivial by comparison.
"The big events weren't there anymore so it just became the family and their little 'who's going to marry who' and 'who do we like and who don't we like' and it's all a bit passé," she says.
The show makes a point of telling viewers the series is a fictionalised dramatisation.  (Netflix: Alex Bailey)
There may be some ethical dilemmas coming into play as well.
Society seems to be in the midst of grappling with the way we viewed celebrities in the past.
Recently, we've heard from pop culture icons like Paris Hilton, Britney Spears and Pamela Anderson about the toll tabloid reporting took on them.
Princess Diana was a major target for the tabloid press, right up until her very last moments.
And it might be uncomfortable to be confronted with how we as viewers contributed to the culture that normalised that kind of harmful harassment.
We also have more of an idea of how much this chapter of history impacted Prince William and Prince Harry.
So watching it might have felt a bit wrong and a bit, as Dr Coghlan describes it, "tabloid-y".
"Almost they themselves are acting like the tabloid media in presenting this one version," she says.
"What the filmmakers and the directors are saying is it was a war of PR that was going on.
"But by episode four, they are the paparazzi.
"And that's almost that grubby feel."
The first part of season six was released in November.
The final six episodes were released on December 14.
Australians can watch the whole series in its entirety on streaming service Netflix.

title: Timothée Chalamet gives Willy his all in new Wonka movie. But does it work?
content:
A Willy Wonka origin story starring… tween dream idol Timothée Chalamet? And it's also a musical?
Surely you can't blame me for having thought that Wonka might be the Cats of 2023.
And yet unusual ingredients, when mixed by the right hands, can be transmuted into something quite delightful. Something that young Wonka — whose chocolate-making arsenal includes giraffe's milk and thunderbolt essence — knows full well.
The right hands, in this case, are those of Paul King, of the much beloved Paddington movies. Like Paddingtons 1 and 2, King's Wonka is sweet but not saccharine, light but not frothy, and pleasantly nutty — it is, in short, a treat the whole family can enjoy.
Timothée Chalamet on set with director Paul King, who gifted the world with the Paddington movies. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
If the film isn't quite up to the preternaturally scrumdiddlyumptious standard of its namesake, then it would certainly still pass muster at any of Wonka's rival chocolate companies.
Those rivals, you may recall, are Slugworth, Fickelgruber and Prodnose. Minor figures in Roald Dahl's timeless 1964 novel Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, they are brought to the fore as major villains in King's prequel.
This trio of corrupt confectioners, incarnated with relish by Paterson Joseph, Mathew Baynton and Matt Lucas, operate as a "Chocolate Cartel". It calls to mind the uniting of farmers Boggis, Bunce and Bean against the wily title character in Dahl's Fantastic Mr. Fox — but with a Mafioso twist.
They don't immediately clock Willy as a threat when he strides into the distinguished Galeries Gourmet, where each of the chocolate barons has his shopfront.
Paul King's Wonka aligns itself with the 1971 version through the repeated deployment of that film's most indelible musical numbers. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
The fresh-faced Wonka has just arrived in town after seven years on the high seas, during which he diligently gathered the flavours and the skills with which to enter the pantheon of top-tier chocolatiers — not that they know that.
A taste of his wares, however, sets the toffee-nosed moguls scurrying into action.
Particularly entertaining are their two main collaborators, whose complicity is bought with sweet, sweet candy: Rowan Atkinson plays a "chocoholic" priest and Keegan-Michael Key the similarly afflicted Chief of Police, whose ballooning waistline betrays his unsavoury conduct.
But being on the Cartel's hitlist isn't even the most pressing of Wonka's problems. First, he needs to figure out how to extract himself from a contract committing him to indentured servitude at a laundry (operated by Olivia Colman and Paddington 2 stand-out Tom Davis), which he signed in good faith and great naïvete upon arrival in his new, unnamed city.
Olivia Colman as a laundress is one of many captivating side characters in a star-studded line-up. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
There's also the "little orange man" (Hugh Grant, who apparently did not enjoy playing an Oompa Loompa, but does a good job of it), who keeps making off with jars of Willy's precious wares.
Deep Roy played 165 Oompa Loompas (including an entire glam rock band) in Tim Burton's 2005 film adaptation of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. Will Hugh Grant in 2023's Wonka ever measure up?
It was rather a relief to be introduced to young Wonka as an already fully formed chocolate wizard (slash magician slash inventor).
King applies a fairly light touch when it comes to attempting to psychoanalyse his protagonist's obsession — unlike Tim Burton's 2005 Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, with its flashback to Willy's childhood under the thumb of a sugar-hating dentist.
The impulse to account for how some fictional freak (complimentary) got to be the way they are — via that most cash-grabby of genres, the origin story — is one usually best avoided.
Hugh Grant apparently did not enjoy playing an Oompa Loompa, but does a good job of it. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
As with a magic trick, to 'explain' this is to reduce a character to less than the sum of their parts — to sub out a tantalising mystery for a game of connect the dots.
King preserves, and in fact, amplifies, Wonka's magic. What does gets muted in the translation, however, is the unnerving weirdness of Dahl's character — his darkness, his off-putting humour.
The misadventures of the bratty Golden Ticket winners in the Wonka factory, as recounted in the book, reveal a candy man with a truly warped sense of "just desserts".
Young Wonka, meanwhile, is willing to abandon his calling for the sake of new pal and fellow laundry inmate, Noodle (Calah Lane).
Timothée Chalamet's performance has little in common with that of Gene Wilder's, with the famous manic glint in his eye (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
King's film aligns itself with the Gene Wilder-starring adaptation of Dahl's book, Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory, through the design of Grant's Oompa Loompa, who sports orange skin and green hair, plus the repeated deployment of that film's most indelible musical numbers.
And yet, beyond a few turns of phrase, Chalamet's Wonka would seem to have little in common with Wilder's.
Nothing in Timmy's performance inspires anything like the impact of the manic glint in Wilder's eye as he showcases some delectable creation, or the tremulous, off-key waver in his voice in the film's terrifying tunnel sequence.
The Dune star gamely gives Willy his all, and proves endearing in the role, convincing even, but he hasn't got a madcap bone in his body. He looks like he belongs in a pre-Raphaelite painting, not a zany sweet shop.
Admittedly, Chalamet's playing a young Wonka, 25 years prior to the events of the 1971 film — the chocolatier has not yet become the recluse of Dahl's creation.
Still, I couldn't help but think of Wilder's inspired on-screen entrance — walking with a cane, frail-seeming, before then collapsing into a sprightly somersault — and his explanation for it: "From that time on, no one would know if I was lying or telling the truth."
Chalamet's Wonka is someone I feel I could trust completely — and where's the excitement in that?

Wonka is in cinemas now.

title: What is Rebel Moon, the new straight-to-streaming blockbuster by Zack Snyder?
content:
Rebel Moon is the latest big-budget movie from a big-name director to give most cinemas a miss and head straight to streaming.
So what's the film about, and why has Zack Snyder opted for the small screen to share his latest vision?
With a name like Rebel Moon you could be forgiven for thinking this is yet another sci-fi spin-off from a galaxy far, far away, and you wouldn't be far wrong.
As he told Empire magazine earlier this year, Snyder pitched the story to Lucasfilm about a decade ago, just as the Disney Star Wars era was beginning.
But Disney baulked at Snyder's pitch for a more adult Star Wars film, featuring all new characters, so the director took his ideas elsewhere.
Sofia Boutella stars as Kora, a former Imperium warrior hiding out on a rural world. (Supplied: Netflix)
He told the Screenrant entertainment website he pitched the story to Warner Bros and to video game companies before finally settling at Netflix.
Rebel Moon is an increasingly rare beast — a big-budget sci-fi film not based on a previously existing intellectual property.
Snyder has described it as "The Seven Samurai in space", referencing Akira Kurosawa's legendary 1954 film about a group of desperate farmers who hired the titular warriors to protect their harvest from bandits.
Rebel Moon trailer
Rebel Moon's hero is Kora (Sofia Boutella) — a former member of the evil Imperium, hiding out on the quiet agrarian moon of Veldt, and spurred into action when the Imperium turns up threatening to take the next harvest.
Kora heads off-world to assemble a team of warriors to defeat the Imperium, and picks up a cast of uniquely talented individuals, played by Charlie Hunnam, Djimon Hounsou, Michiel Huisman, Staz Nair, Doona Bae, Ray Fisher and Cleopatra Coleman.
Oh, and there's a robot knight voiced by Sir Anthony Hopkins.
Sir Anthony Hopkins voices a robot knight in the film. (Supplied: Netflix)
Prior to kickstarting the DC Comics equivalent of the Marvel Cinematic Universe with Man Of Steel and Batman Vs Superman, Snyder made his name directing hyper-stylised action movies that people either loved or hated.
His breakthrough second film, 300, was followed by a live-action version of the acclaimed graphic novel, Watchmen, and the cult favourite box-office bomb, Sucker Punch.
Oh, and he directed that underrated computer generated (CG) owl movie, Legend of the Guardians: The Owls of Ga'Hoole, which everyone seems to have forgotten about.
In 2017, while he was in the midst of post-production for the DC superhero film, Justice League, Snyder's daughter, Autumn, died by suicide.
The Flash, Superman, Cyborg, Wonder Woman, Batman and Aquaman in Snyder's, Justice League. (Facebook: Zack Snyder's Justice League)
Snyder dropped out of the film, handing the reins over to Joss Whedon, and spent time with his family.
Aside from a couple of producer credits on DC films, Snyder stayed quiet until 2021 when he got to re-edit and release his version of Justice League, following a huge campaign from fans upset with what Whedon had done with the film.
That same year, Snyder directed Army of the Dead, which he described as a "spiritual successor" to his debut film,  Dawn of the Dead — a remake itself of the 1978 George Romero zombie classic.
Where have you been hiding?
Martin Scorsese, Alfonso Cuaron, the Coen brothers, Jane Campion, David Fincher, Adam McKay and Aaron Sorkin have all delivered films straight to Netflix in the past four years, picking up a few Oscar nominations and wins along the way.
Zack Snyder has directed and co-written Rebel Moon for Netflix, and hopes it will be the first in a series. (Wiki Commons: Gage Skidmore)
Snyder's Army of the Dead was released straight to Netflix and had a budget of about $90 million, but he has coaxed even more money out of the streaming giant for Rebel Moon.
The film, which is subtitled Part One: A Child Of Fire, is part of a two-film deal worth about $170m.
A sequel entitled, Part Two: The Scargiver, was shot back-to-back with Part One and is due out in April 2024.
But that's not all. Snyder is already talking about another two films to follow Part Two, as well as comics, podcasts, animated short films, and other add-ons to tell the story of his Rebel Moon universe.
He's also talking about an "R-rated cut", which will give fans a choice regarding how much violence they prefer in their sci-fi adventures.
Actors include Charlie Hunnam, Michiel Huisman, Sofia Boutella, Staz Nair, and Djimon Hounsou. (Supplied: Netflix)
Only for a week in four cities — Los Angeles, New York, Toronto and London — from December 15.
While the screenings are an opportunity to see the film on a big screen in 70 millimetre, they also mean the film can qualify for the Oscars.
Despite living in the stream-centric age we're in, the Academy Awards still demand movies appear in cinemas for at least a week in at least one of six United States cities — New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Atlanta, San Francisco or Miami — in order to qualify for a nomination.
Rebel Moon streams on Netflix from December 21.

title: Months of work for a few seconds of film: Animator Andy on bringing Chicken Run characters to life
content:
Andy Bailey can still remember watching the first Chicken Run film in the cinema.
"I was just so excited by the whole thing, the animation and all the miniatures," he says.
"It was before I was really in film school, but as the credits rolled by I was like, 'Someday I want to be working on a movie like that'."
Twenty three years later, Andy has had the "mind-blowing" opportunity to work with the stop-motion powerhouse Aardman on Chicken Run: Dawn of the Nugget, achieving something he "had dreamed of being able to do".
The Vancouver-based dad of three boys (and surely the winner of bring-your-dad-to-school-day) is also known for his viral YouTube account Andymation, where he hones in on the art of the flipbook, and his work on Laika studio hits including ParaNorman and The Boxtrolls.
We asked Andy the question he always gets asked — how do you find the patience? — along with a bunch of our other stop-motion wonderings. These are his words.
When I saw claymation and stop motion for the first time I think it grabbed me because as a young kid, it felt like something that I could maybe do. I kind of understood the principle of how it was made, and that I didn't have to be a great artist like the level of Disney movies.
Chicken Run: Dawn of the Nugget | Official Trailer | Netflix
I wasn't able to do a lot because we didn't own a camcorder, but my parents did have an old Super 8 film camera, which had a feature where it could shoot one frame at a time.
That was amazing for me, because I could go outside and set it up on the sidewalk and make some figures move around and play with it that way.
I had these worm-shaped clay figures that I used to make, and I had this one who would kind of ride a skateboard.
It wasn't really a plot, but I feel like as a child it's easier to have that kind of mindset, where you don't overthink it.
It was also interesting shooting that way because there was no instant feedback to what you were doing. There was no preview.
I would shoot on film, send it off to get developed, and I wouldn't see what it actually looked like for a couple of weeks.
There was all this excitement around actually getting the roll of film back and putting it on the projector and seeing it up on the screen for the first time.
It was really exciting getting that call [from Aardman] to come and work on the new Chicken Run.
My whole family and I moved over to the UK for six months. It was four months on the movie, and then we got to travel and see a bit of Europe also.
Animating just a few seconds a day is normal for stop motion. (YouTube: Andymation)
In those months, I worked on a handful of shots. It wasn't like I got to do an entire scene or anything like that, because doing something like a couple of seconds of the film in a day would be kind of normal.
The dialogue is already there, pre-recorded, so that you know what to animate to. You first meet with the director, who will brief you on what shot they're putting you on.
Then you go into your unit and you do rehearsal, where you'll roughly do the shot once just to hit your key poses. Then you'll talk over any changes and get launched on the actual shot.
Andy blended different elements together by hand on Chicken Run. (YouTube: Andymation)
3D printing is definitely being incorporated a lot more — in Laika [films], the faces, the brows and the mouths are 3D printed — whereas on Chicken Run, the heads are still clay.
There's a whole team of assistant animators who press the heads by hand and make all the clay mouths over and over. They have moulds that they use, but it is a lot of handiwork still.
There's metal armature inside the bodies with joints, [covered in] like a silicone rubber. Then from the neck up, it's clay.
We have a whole mouth kit. It's a box full of all the different mouth shapes — there's an E shape and an S shape and a TH and an L and an O.
The mouth kit from Chicken Run: Dawn of the Nugget. (YouTube: Andymation)
Depending on what sound the character's making, you'll pop the mouth off and put on a different shape. And because it's clay, while you've got those prebuilt expressions, you can still modify and tweak them a little bit as you're easing in and out of a shape.
Every time you put a mouth on or off, you'll have to blend it in a little bit, because there's usually some sort of a seam. I usually use my fingers or baby wipes, just to smooth over that edge.
Usually when people find out what I do they say, "You must be very patient".
But I'm not really. There's this kind of artistic focus that happens, where you get into the zone.
Behind the Scenes - Animating 1 Frame in Real Time
Some shots take so much focus and attention that I just need the quiet, but other times it's a little bit easier, and I can have a TV show or some music or something in the background.
Getting to play with these miniature things and having them perform and make them look like they're alive, or having emotions, it's really satisfying.
Animation is interesting because you're trying to convey the magic of those performances, and that acting. You spend years doing what in live action would just happen right away.
I always struggled with being painfully shy as a kid, and I wonder if that was something that drew me to stop-motion animation too.
Because in a sense, it feels like I'm the actor in the movie, but I'm invisible. It means I get to perform, but it's like wearing a mask.
I feel like there's a timelessness with stop motion. It's not always the smoothest animation — you get some chattering and stuff like fur jitters around. But somehow it's part of the charm, and it never looks dated to me.
Chicken Run: Dawn of the Nugget is on Netflix now.

title: The Dude abides: Big Lebowski gear, ET's animatronic head set to go under the hammer
content:
If sipping White Russians while you go bowling with your oddball friends is your thing, you might like to bid on the bathrobe Jeff Bridges wore in The Big Lebowski. But you know, that's just, like, my opinion, man.
The brown flannel robe is one of several items from the Coen brothers' slacker-noir film going under the hammer in California this weekend.
"These are the items that … bring the story to life," said Martin Nolan, chief executive of Julien's Auction.
"When [Bridges] shows up in this outfit … wearing his shorts, his T-shirt, the robe — just incredible."
The 1998 movie stars Bridges as The Dude, a wastrel who criminals mistake for a millionaire in a caper that also showcases the comedic talents of John Goodman and Steve Buscemi.
The film became a cult classic and spawned several memorable lines that fans often trot out, including: "That rug really tied the room together."
Jeff Bridges played perennial slack Jeffrey "The Dude" Lebowski in The Big Lebowski. (Supplied: Working Title Films)
In addition to the robe, which is expected to fetch up to $US50,000 ($A75,000), fans can also bid on The Dude's sunglasses and bowling pin props used in the movie and signed by Bridges.
The lot is part of "Hollywood Legends", a four-day event that will see thousands of items of memorabilia put up for sale.
They include an animatronic model of the head of E.T. The Extraterrestrial, which could go for as much as $US1 million, Mr Nolan said.
The special effects head of E.T. is displayed ahead of the auction. (AFP: Valerie Macon)
"These items are now considered an asset class … not just memorabilia items or a storyline from a time in our lives," he said.
"Something like this is much more fun than stocks or bonds, or a lot of the other items you have in your investment portfolio, and a great conversation piece."
Also up for sale this weekend will be the blouse that Princess Diana wore in her engagement photo in 1981, which auctioneers expect could fetch up to $US100,000.
In this February 24, 1981 file photo Britain's Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer pose following the announcement of their engagement.  (AP)
Designed by Elizabeth Emanuel and David Emanuel, who also designed her wedding dress, the pink chiffon blouse has a bow at the neck.
Other items on offer include a jacket worn by Audrey Hepburn in the 1963 film Charade and the computer used by Carrie Bradshaw, Sarah Jessica Parker's character in Sex and the City.

title: Beyoncé and Lizzo bowed to this Aussie princess and now she's taking on Disney
content:
Hannah Diviney's got some serious runs on the board when it comes to true representation in media.
Armed with nothing more than a phone and a decent social media following, she has taken on Beyoncé and Lizzo, successfully convincing them to remove ableist slurs from their music.
And now the writer and actor has an even bigger target in sight.
The magical world of Disney.
"Trying to get the House of Mouse to do anything is quite tricky," Diviney said with a smile.
The thing she wants is for the Walt Disney Corporation to create a Disney princess with a disability.
Diviney has cerebral palsy, a physical disability that affects her fine and gross motor skills.
As a result, she navigates the world with the assistance of a wheelchair.
"Representation is the most important thing in the world," she told ABC Victorian Mornings.
Diviney believes "ableism is often the forgotten prejudice." (ABC Life: Luke Tribe)
It's been three years since she first started her petition to Disney for better on-screen representation.
More than 65,000 people have joined the cause, something Diviney said made her feel like a rock star.
"I've chosen one of the biggest companies in the world to target," Diviney said.
"It's going slower than I'd hoped; I think that's definitely a slow burn."
Hannah Diviney says she has created her own space in the entertainment industry, through acting and writing. (Supplied: SBS)
Associate Professor Lauren Rosewarne, from The University of Melbourne's School of Social and Political Sciences, has spent years researching representation in media.
Dr Rosewarne said "we're a while away from" the likelihood of Disney acceding to Diviney's request.
"Hollywood is risk-averse and they do not spend big bucks on a film with an unknown talent at the helm … therefore risky projects tend not to be made," she said.
Lauren Rosewarne is an associate professor at The University of Melbourne. (Supplied)
Dr Rosewarne said that fear of fiscal failure was partly why Hollywood was seemingly obsessed with reboots.
She said it would likely be up to TV series and production companies like Netflix to pave the way for larger corporations to have truly representative characters in cinema.
Hannah Diviney is pushing for Disney to develop a disabled princess character.
"You have to prime an audience to demonstrate that they're willing to watch this stuff, that then starts the process of desensitising them to different content, and I suspect that's more likely to happen through streaming services," she said.
Meaning a Disney princess with a disability probably remains a pipedream.
The Walt Disney Company did not respond to questions by the ABC.
Instead, it pointed to a previous statement released to Australian Women's Weekly where a spokesperson said the company was listening.
"We love Hannah's passion and hear her important voice on why inclusive and representative storytelling matters," the Disney spokesperson said in 2022.
The Walt Disney Company did not respond to questions posed by the ABC. (Reuters: Brendan McDermid)
"As storytellers at Disney, we're committed to reflecting the incredibly rich diversity of the human experience in ways that inspire, open minds and hearts, and bring people closer together in a world where we all belong."
However, the company has yet to confirm whether that will include the creation of a character that uses a wheelchair.
Hannah Diviney will not be deterred.
"It's no accident that I want to increase representation for children because that's where I struggled the most," she said
"I've chosen one of the biggest companies in the world to target in doing that.
Hannah Diviney wants to increase representation for children who live with disability. (ABC Everyday: Luke Tribe)
"I'm really lucky to have kind of created my own space in this industry, through acting and writing.
"So even if Disney doesn't necessarily get behind it, I think something will hopefully be coming [soon] for children so they can feel that representation."

title: 'Work harder than everyone else': Mao's Last Dancer gives his parting words of wisdom on eve of retirement
content:
Before he became the legendary Mao's Last Dancer, Li Cunxin was a peasant boy in communist China with nothing to his name but a burning desire to work harder than everyone else.
The retiring ballet dancer gave his parting words of wisdom on Monday at the University of Queensland graduation, where he was awarded an honorary doctorate.
His speech came on the eve of his finale send-off with the Queensland Ballet on Tuesday and Wednesday, when his legacy will be celebrated.
In June, Dr Li announced he would retire as Queensland Ballet's artistic director after 11 years, citing serious heart problems.
Under his directorship Queensland Ballet has ballooned in size and scope, with its staff quadrupling and its budget growing fivefold.
Li Cunxin, the man known as Mao's Last Dancer, says his most valuable lessons have come from mistakes.
Dr Li's life story reached international audiences through his wildly popular memoir, Mao's Last Dancer, which was later made into a film.
Looking back on his life, Dr Li said there were times it had been harsh, uncompromising, and filled with abject poverty.
However, he said it was also characterised by passion, ambition and a determination to make a meaningful mark on the world.
Mao's Last Dancer Li Cunxin to retire from Queensland ballet
He told the graduating class of 2023 that life had no dress rehearsals, and that it should be lived with full intensity.
"If you're the person who could have the final big smile on your face before you leave this earth, knowing that you have done all you can and you're satisfied with your report card, then you would have lived a full and remarkable life with no regrets."
Li Cunxin's vision for the Thomas Dixon Centre was to train the next generation of Brisbane ballet dancers. (Supplied: Queensland Ballet/David Kelly)
Dr Li said he'd been determined to outwork his peers at the Beijing Dance Academy, practising for hours by candlelight when everyone else was asleep.
He would then wake up before the others to hop one-legged up the stairs with sandbags strapped to his ankles in order to improve his leaps.
Without learning the importance of work ethic as a boy, Dr Li said his life would not have turned out the way it did.
Li Cunxin has been Queensland Ballet's artistic director since 2012. (Supplied: Christian Tiger)
He encouraged the assembled graduates to not settle for average, but to pursue their ambitions with all the effort they could muster.
"I hope you will live a life with hunger in your belly, thirst for knowledge, dare yourself to achieve the impossible, and not be afraid to fail," he said.

Sigourney Weaver is in the running for best lead actress in a drama for The Lost Flowers of Alice Hart, which received 12 nominations including best miniseries.
Meanwhile, late comedian Cal Wilson has been recognised at the awards with a nomination.
The performer, who passed away after a short battle with a rare and aggressive form of cancer in October, has been nominated in the Best Comedy Performer award for her work on The Great Australian Bake Off.
Cal Wilson has been nominated in the new AACTA category Best Comedy Performer. (Supplied: Jim Lee)
The awards will be presented across two ceremonies — the industry awards on February 8, and the main ceremony on February 10 at the Gold Coast.
Previously held towards the end of each year, the new date is designed to bring the ceremony in line with the international awards schedule.

title: Forget Hallmark happy endings, this Aussie black comedy celebrates those who find Christmas hard
content:
I usually love Christmas films. But when you've had a hard year, as so many of us have, their garish gleam can feel like too much.
So, what's a Christmas-loving sadgirl to do? That's where new Australian film Christmess comes in.
Written and directed by Heath Davis (Book Week), this unassuming film follows a trio of recovering addicts living together in western Sydney, trying not to relapse when the festive juggernaut beats them over the head with their own loneliness.
In short, this is a film for people who find Christmas hard.
Even with my Grinch spirit growing, when I found out there was going to be a Christmas movie starring Hannah Joy — the lead singer of Sydney alt-rock band Middle Kids — I knew I would have to see it.
I thought it would be cute, fun and have some nice songs in it. It was all of those things — and much more.
The film follows Chris (played with an expert rough vulnerability by Steve Le Marquand): a former Silver Logie-winning actor fresh out of rehab who has lost his career, friends and money to drug and alcohol abuse.
In the weeks leading up to Christmas, Chris moves into a "halfway house" in the heart of Campbelltown with his festively obsessed sponsor Nick (the always wonderful Darren Gilshenan, here a mash-up of cheerful, hardass and tortured) and his charming, oddball musician housemate Joy (this is where Hannah comes in).
"But I'm a Silver Logie winner!" Christ objects when he has to take a job as a shopping centre Santa. (Supplied: Bonsai Films/Sie Kitts Photography)
Washed up and broke, Chris starts taking the slow, aching steps towards getting his life together — including a job as a shopping centre Christmas Santa. It's here where he bumps into his long-estranged daughter Noelle, and her young son, prompting him to have a bit of a breakdown before extending the proverbial festive olive branch.
And yes, all the characters have Christmas-themed names — one of a few little things that had me worried this was going to be lame. The detail stands out because everything else in this film feels so real.
You can feel the baking heat as Chris lugs an empty BBQ gas bottle to the servo to be filled on a 40-degree day. Same for Chris' catatonic frustration, as he sits in the shopping centre surrounded by hordes of screaming children. Or his panic and despair as he stands in front of a line of liquor bottles, wearing his scrappy Santa suit, contemplating breaking his sobriety.
You'll also laugh out loud when Nick calls the liquor store and tells the bewildered attendant he must stop Santa from drinking.
"Do you want to ruin Christmas, Tom?" he asks in a cheery voice. "Then don't let him leave. If you do, I'll fuck you up."
Christmess' laconic script surprised me, often much funnier than I expected it to be.
"Most Santas aren't NIDA graduates," Chris objects to his new manager at the shopping centre — a middle-aged woman dressed as an elf. She looks at him.
"You'd be surprised."
As excited as I was to get to hear Hannah sing during a Christmas film, I was a bit concerned the songs would be shoe-horned in. As Chris says when it's suggested she sings for them: "No offence, but normally when the guitar comes out at a party, it's a bit of a punish."
But as Nick says in response, "Don't worry, she doesn't suck".
She really doesn't, and it all somehow feels natural.
"I was bored and semi-depressed in COVID, and I thought, 'This could be good for my creativity and it’ll be a challenge – let’s do it'," Hannah Joy told triple j about taking on the role of Joy. (Supplied: Bonsai Films/Sie Kitts Photography)
Playing the guitar upside down (Hannah is a leftie IRL, and prefers playing that way) she closes her eyes and sings a snippet of one of the original songs she wrote for the film — her own version of a Christmas song called Empty Chair:
"So come on home/I can't believe that you're gone/Come on Home/It's the end of the year and I'm alone…"
It's funny and also punches you in the guts, sending Chris into a panic attack, which annoys Joy because he's too busy freaking out to tell her whether he liked the song.
She also sings a song called Deadbeat Dad ("People say I have your smile but I wouldn't know"), a tune about Boxing Day, and the best cover of O Holy Night on the electric guitar I've ever heard.
The deep, resounding wail in her voice turns these simple songs into odes for everyone who has ever fucked up.
Now, it seems obvious that the voice behind Middle Kids' emotional anthems would be perfect for this gig. The band's new single Bend, released the day Christmess came out (coincidence?), easily could have soundtracked the film.
Middle Kids youtube: Bend
Hannah was approached directly about the role by Heath, who is a big fan.
"All I knew of her was the music," he told triple j. "Hannah is a natural performer and something inside me gave me the confidence to think she would connect to the material on an emotional and cerebral level and I'm thankful she did."
Hannah says she was drawn in by the story that "really captures the beautiful Australian spirit of the battler that's trying to give it a go".
On a touring hiatus due to COVID, Hannah had time to enrol in an acting course at NIDA.
At times her acting is still a little stilted, but her singing elevates things to a deeper emotional plane. And, above all, it's impossible to deny the very real chemistry she has with Nick and Chris.
Steve Le Marquand does not have the singing chops that Hannah Joy has, but he gives it a red-hot go. (Supplied: Bonsai Films/Sie Kitts Photography)
Their tender, flawed friendship is the standout of this film, making you clutch at your heart throughout.
There may be beautiful tunes, droll Aussie humour and even someone saying "Ho, ho, ho, MOFO", but this is still a movie about serious topics.
Even with some glimpses of Christmas cheer, it tackles addiction head on: the horrible things addiction can make people do; the destruction it can wreak on people's lives and loved ones; and the razor-sharp, sometimes defeating pain that comes around for many during the festive season.
There is no Hallmark ending here, and thank goodness for that. Instead, Christmess is a real, moving story about the long slog of recovery, the slow crawl of forgiveness and the glimmers of connection that keep people going — especially at this time of year.
Christmess is in cinemas and on Binge now.

title: Paper Moon and Love Story actor Ryan O'Neal dies 'peacefully' aged 82
content:
Love Story actor Ryan O'Neal, who starred in some of the most memorable movies of the 1970s including What's Up, Doc and Love Story, has died aged 82.
His son Patrick O'Neal shared the news of his death on social media on Friday afternoon.
"So this is the toughest thing I've ever had to say but here we go," O'Neal wrote in an Instagram post.
"My dad passed away peacefully today, with his loving team by his side supporting him and loving him as he would us."
While it's unclear how O'Neal died, he had been diagnosed with chronic leukemia in 2001 and prostate cancer in 2012.
O'Neal made his way as an actor by starring in various US television shows in the 1960s such as NBC's Empire and later the prime time serial drama Peyton Place.
He catapulted to fame in 1970 upon starring opposite Ali MacGraw in Love Story, which grossed $106 million in the US and Canada.
The film nabbed him Golden Globe and Oscar nominations.
On the heels of his cinematic debut, O'Neal starred alongside Barbra Streisand in What's Up, Doc, and partnered with his nine-year-old daughter in Peter Bogdanovich's Paper Moon in 1973.
He starred in a number of other films including The Main Event, A Bridge Too Far, and Barry Lyndon, among others.
In another post shared by son Patrick, the actor was lauded as a "hero" who was "always bigger than life".
"1970's, a decade he absolutely crushed by starring in movies like What's Up, Doc?, Paper Moon, Barry Lyndon, A Bridge Too Far, The Main Event, and The Driver," O'Neal wrote.
"He is a Hollywood legend. Full stop."
O'Neal is survived by his four children and five grandchildren. (Reuters: Mike Blake)
Actress Mia Farrow, who starred alongside O'Neal in Peyton Place, took to X (formerly Twitter) to express her condolences.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
Barbra Streisand remembered him as a "funny and charming man".
In his personal life, O'Neal was the father to four children: Tatum O'Neal and Griffin O'Neal with his first wife Joanna Moore, Patrick O'Neal with his second wife Leigh Taylor-Young, and Redmond James Fawcett O'Neal with his long time partner Farrah Fawcett of Charlie's Angels.
The pair had a decade-long on-and-off relationship from 1979 to 1997 and then from 2001 until her death at age 62 in 2009.
