title: There's a psychological reason why you find comfort in mediocre Christmas movies
content:
There's something about a Christmas movie that just feels like a warm cup of cocoa on a cold winter's night.
Every year in December, countless new festive films flood streaming services — and let's be honest, they're not always quality.
Whether it's the Freaky Friday spin-off starring Jennifer Garner and Ed Helms, Brooke Shields's Scottish love story, or a movie staring Vanessa Hudgens as three separate, but identical, characters, "bad" Christmas movies have gained a cult following.
Vanessa Hudgens, Vanessa Hudgens and Vanessa Hudgens in The Princess Switch: Switched Again. (Netflix)
Sometimes referred to as "Hallmark movies" — a nod to the US network that produces many, but not all, of the made-for-TV holiday rom-coms — they tend to follow a similar trope.
Two people meet, in the most unlikely of circumstances, usually in a small town.
They butt heads at first, but end up falling in love — just in time for Christmas.
ABC News Breakfast's resident film critic Zak Hepburn describes the genre as "cinematic wrapping paper".
Feel-good Christmas rom-coms dominate streaming services at this time of year. (Netflix)
"As soon as you tear it off and dispose of it, you're immediately on to the next one," he says.
So if they are so easy to forget, what is it about these movies that keeps us going back for more?
Consultant psychologist and former film director Gregory Nicolau says the success of cheesy holiday films could have a lot to do with escapism.
"People like to just escape a little bit from the world around them," he says.
"When you're feeling a bit challenged emotionally, psychologically, you might look for opportunities to distract yourself from those things and often these sorts of movies do that.
"You can take yourself away from those challenges, you don't need to use your mind to think about things and you can sort of live in a slightly fantasy world of the romance."
Gregory Nicolau is a former film director. (ABC News: David Hudspeth)
Christmas is marketed as a happy, joyful time, but Mr Nicolau says for many people the holidays can be stressful.
"Very often, it's people coming together who spend most of the year not coming together, not wanting to interact for whatever reasons, and they feel obliged to do it [at Christmas]," he says.
"Often all those unresolved issues that may have occurred throughout the year sort of coalesce around this time."
Cary Elwes and Brooke Shields, two actually famous actors, starred in the 2021 holiday romantic comedy A Castle for Christmas. (IMDb)
Looking at someone else's success, in the form of movies, can help us to temporarily remove ourselves from these real life issues and experience relief, even if it is just momentarily.
There is also research suggesting the brain secretes a hormone called oxytocin, also known as the love hormone, when we watch compelling stories.
"[Oxytocin] is the attraction hormone that is stimulated when people make connections," Mr Nicolau says.
"When people watch these movies, maybe oxytocin starts to secrete, depending on where people's brains are going when they're watching these films."
There's also comfort in knowing the outcome of these movies ahead of time, Mr Nicolau says, with most Christmas movies including a happy ending.
Hepburn says traditional Hollywood Christmas movies like It's a Wonderful Life or White Christmas have their place in cinema history.
"They're almost like fables in a way, you can go back to them and the sort of storyline, I think, is very pure in many regards," he says.
It's A Wonderful Life is a family classic. (National Telefilm Associates)
He says in order for Christmas movies to leave their mark, there needs to be some sort of underlying narrative which sits on the periphery of the Christmas aesthetic.
"I think this goes back to the discourse of Die Hard and Home Alone or The Nightmare Before Christmas," he says.
"They take the kind of concept of a traditional Christmas film, and slightly twist it.
"So you have the Christmas aesthetic, and you have the Christmas atmosphere, but you've also got a narrative within that film, which doesn't actually rely on the holiday to work."
Die Hard is a Christmas movie. (Supplied: 20th Century Fox)
It's these sorts of Christmas movies that will endure the test of time, according to Hepburn.
But as long as the audience continues to find comfort in the trashy rom-coms that grace our screens annually, we'll continue to see them plastered across streaming services during the festive season.
Hepburn says he's curious to see when that will stop given some big changes in people's viewing trends.
"They're getting tired of superhero films, getting tired of all this other stuff that people were very, very engaged in before, so we'll see if Christmas films can endure. It will be very interesting for sure," he says.
The Grinch, a legitimate cinematic masterpiece. (Supplied: Universal Pictures)

title: A tip-off alerted this Indian double agent he was about to be caught. Somehow, he managed to disappear
content:
From a hidden bunker on a quiet street in New Delhi, a secret agent watches a man ascend the steps of his three-storey home with a nondescript briefcase in tow.
Inside is a trove of top-secret documents taken from India's external intelligence agency.
The man is a mole, believed to have been leaking sensitive information to a powerful ally, as part of a high-stakes political plot to topple a foreign enemy.
It's a scene seemingly ripped from 2023's headlines — as the mission unfolds, the spy is drawn into a complicated web of betrayal and danger, culminating in a daring escape escape across borders.
But the real story behind this Netflix thriller came almost two decades before alleged international assassination plots put India's intelligence agencies under the spotlight.
After Justin Trudeau suggested Indian agents were behind an assassination in Canada, New York prosecutors say a similar "crime out of a movie" was being planned in the US.
Rabinder Singh was working at India's Research and Analysis Wing (R&AW) in 2004 when he became the spy that vanished into thin air.
It is a story so bizarre that it has been rehashed in several dramatic accounts.
Khufiya (House of Spies), released last month, is the Netflix adaptation of a 2012 novel called Escape To Nowhere, written by former spy chief Amar Bhushan.
While it has been promoted as a work of fiction loosely inspired by true events, it bears some striking similarities — and some key differences — with the account offered in another book authored by a former intelligence officer.
RK Yadav's book, Mission R&AW, was released as a tell-all memoir in 2014, detailing "the first eye-opening account ... of the achievements and failures of Indian intelligence".
Piecing together the records of what unfolded reveals a desperate race to catch a double agent and understand how and why the CIA convinced an Indian citizen to turn on his own government.
Singh first joined the R&AW in the late 80s, after a brief military career.
Media reports describe him as a clean-shaven man from an affluent family in Amritsar, the son of a retired lieutenant in the Indian Army.
Having joined the Gorkha Regiments in 1970 and worked his way up to become major, Singh was reportedly overlooked for further promotion due to his "mediocre calibre" as a soldier.
He did take part in Operation Blue Star, a sting in 1984 targeting a group of separatists known as the Khalistan movement who had taken over the Golden Temple, the most sacred site in Sikhism.
According to Yadav's book, which he told the ABC was entirely factual and based on his own career as well as interviews with internal sources, Singh was appointed to the agency by an old family friend who had worked with his father.
Amar Bhushan's novel Escape to Nowhere was published in 2012, and RK Yadav's memoir Mission R&AW was published in 2014. (Konark Publishers/Adhyyan Books)
Stationed in Amritsar, Singh gained a reputation for his close relationships with local police, allegedly getting involved in an embezzlement scheme involving secret service funds meant for clandestine operations in Pakistan.
Singh was eventually posted to the Indian embassy in Damascus, where he once let slip to an American diplomat about a secret Indian Air Force visit to an air strip on the outskirts of the city.
It has been suggested that it was around this time that Singh was first recruited by the CIA.
According to multiple reports in Indian media, Singh's daughter was seriously injured in 1992 or 1993, and he requested a transfer to Washington DC.
"Singh said he needed a lot of money to pay for his daughter's treatment, and that the Washington posting would help," RL Bhatia, the minister involved in external state affairs at the time, told Frontline in 2004.
The request was declined. Instead, after Damascus, Singh was stationed as a counsellor at The Hague.
Colleagues noted his expensive tastes and penchant for throwing lavish dinner parties at five-star hotels where he mingled with senior officers and foreign diplomats.
"Everybody in R&AW knew that he had acquired disproportionate assets to his known sources of income, but no-one dared to take any action against him due to his allegiance with a coterie of senior officers," Yadav wrote.
By the early 2000s Singh had returned to New Delhi, and was working as a joint secretary at R&AW headquarters focused on its South-East Asia operations.
But the man described by his peers as a "fairly ordinary" agent was hiding a secret.
Some time in late 2003, Singh's colleagues began to notice he had become particularly inquisitive, striking up conversations about topics outside his department's purview and spending an unusual amount of time at the photocopier.
One officer approached Bhushan, who at the time was the senior secretary in charge of the Counter Intelligence and Security division that monitored internal threats at R&AW.
Bhushan began preliminary inquiries, and by the new year, Singh was under surveillance.
A scene from Netflix drama Khufiya (House of Spies) depicts the mole photocopying stacks of documents at his office in the Research and Analysis Wing.  (Supplied: Netflix)
Agents installed hidden cameras inside his home and office, tapped his phones and opened a mini control room down the street to monitor the video and audio recordings of Singh's conversations with guests as they came and went.
At one point, Yadav wrote, there were more than 20 agents tracking Singh's every move.
The wire taps seemed to suggest Singh had been collecting intelligence from inside the R&AW and passing it on to an unknown handler believed to be working for the CIA.
The surveillance team were working on the assumption that Singh had somehow been transferring documents through a courier.
But before they could gather enough evidence or catch Singh in the act, he received a tip-off that he was being watched.
"Surveillance is only effective as long as the suspect doesn't know they're being watched. But then once he knows he is being watched, he has power," Bhushan explained in a documentary last year.
Singh applied for leave from work, ostensibly to attend his daughter's engagement ceremony in the United States. The request was turned down, confirming his fears.
According to Yadav's book, tapes from the bugs installed at R&AW headquarters showed Singh desperately ransacking his office in search of hidden cameras — a scene re-created in the film adaptation based on Bhushan's novel.
One morning in April, the counter intelligence team watched as Singh stacked piles of papers into bundles, ready to be squirrelled out of the building. They pounced.
Bhushan directed his officers to frisk every R&AW employee as they left the building.
"Hundreds of classified documents were seized from senior and middle level officers of R&AW being taken out of headquarters," Yadav wrote, including pen drives, CDs and DVDs, and a large volume of pornographic materials.
But still there was not enough to pin down their main target.
Singh, now suspicious that counter intelligence agents were tailing him, needed to hatch an escape plan.
Meanwhile, operatives installed a trick photocopier in his office that recorded digital copies of every page he scanned.
Over 16 days, Singh took copies of more than 210 reports, including classified documents that contained sensitive information about R&AW's assessment of activities in Afghanistan, Pakistan, and several of its neighbours, according to Yadav.
The investigation appeared to be gathering steam, but senior agents were frustrated that there was still no conclusive evidence that would allow them to question Singh or identify who he was working with.
They were under pressure to arrest their target, or drop it entirely.
The trailer for Khufiya (House of Spies)
Singh took his chance. On May 1, 2004, he and his wife Parminder Kaur made their escape.
They borrowed a car and drove to the border with Nepal, crossing over at Nepalganj, where they were met by Singh's CIA contact, David Vacala.
The three of them stayed the night at a hotel before booking a domestic flight to Kathmandu, where they stayed at the American embassy.
There, Singh and his wife were issued US passports under new names: Ram Prasad Sharma and Deepa Jumar Sharma.
On May 7, the Sharmas boarded an Austrian Airlines flight bound for Washington DC.
After Singh had failed to turn up to work for several days, counter intelligence officers checked city hospitals and interrogated family members about his whereabouts.
A team was dispatched south to Chennai, but found no trace of their man.
They contacted international airports, but hadn't enough evidence to block Singh's passport.
"We came fairly close to understanding that there could be a security implication. But we simply did not have conclusive evidence at that point," a senior source told Outlook India in 2004.
A search of Singh's home finally delivered the smoking gun they'd been looking for: a laptop that Singh had been using to send electronic copies of his pilfered documents.
The counter intelligence wing soon figured out his whereabouts, but by the time they contacted the Indian embassy in Kathmandu to try to intercept him, it was too late.
Singh was formally dismissed as a R&AW officer in 2005, under an article of India's constitution that allows the president to do so without holding a formal departmental inquiry if it is not considered to be in the national interest.
A senior official at the agency reportedly completed an internal inquiry, but its findings were never made public.
The Indian media was whipped into a frenzy over the "spy who disappeared", and the secrets he may have sold to one of the country's strongest allies.
So what happens to a double agent once they are forced to flee their home base and are cut off from a network of informants?
In Singh's case, it would seem, they become far less valuable.
According to one account, just a few months after he landed state-side, he was dropped by the CIA.
"They stopped paying him, scuppered his attempt at gaining employment with a think tank, and declined to support his request for naturalisation," wrote Shaunak Agarkhedkar, an Indian spy novelist.
In November 2004, a person calling themselves Surender Jeet Singh petitioned the US Court of Appeals to review a decision by the Board of Immigration denying him asylum.
Court documents include interesting detail about the petitioner named Surender Jeet Singh. (Supplied: US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit)
In court documents, he explained that he had been recruited by a CIA-like department in India called the Research and Analysis Wing, to report on individuals believed to have been pushing for a separate state known as Khalistan.
He claimed to have quit the R&AW when "he was ordered to aid in the assassination of a very religious person he had investigated".
Singh told the court that after hiding with friends for a year, he had used his own passport to come to the US, and testified that he would be killed if he returned to India.
The immigration judge denied Singh's asylum request, finding him not credible. In a subsequent appeal, the decision was upheld on the basis that he presented "no corroborative evidence whatsoever" that the R&AW even existed.
The Ninth Circuit Court, however, decided otherwise.
"We can notice that the government of India exists. We can notice that the office of the Prime Minister of India exists. We can notice that a part of the Prime Minister of India's office is the RAW," the judge wrote, referring the matter back to the board of immigration appeals.
While there is no official record of Singh's final asylum application, it appears he was allowed to stay in the country.
India's Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) — another Indian intelligence agency that runs separately to the R&WA and oversees domestic crimes — had asked Interpol to issue a global arrest warrant for Singh in 2007, but Interpol declined on the grounds that the charges were political.
That same year, the Indian embassy in Washington confirmed to the New York Times that Singh and his wife were wanted by the Indian government for violating India's Official Secrets Act.
Media reports have suggested Singh spent several years living as a recluse in New York, Maryland and Virginia, near his extended family, before dying in a road accident in 2016.
At the centre of these recountings of the Singh case are a few key questions: why would the US need to spy on India, and how did this agent manage to escape?
Several theories have been floated about what exactly the CIA was hoping to gain from Singh's leaks, ranging from intelligence on terrorist activity among India's closest neighbours, particularly Pakistan and Afghanistan, to evidence of Iraq possessing weapons of mass destruction.
Yadav and others have suggested that the top priority would have been information about India's own nuclear capabilities, after recent failures by US intelligence to anticipate a series of nuclear tests known as the Pokhran-II tests.
In any case, Bhushan says the documents that Singh did manage to pass on were mostly minor in terms of sensitivity.
Amar Bhushan was the secretary in charge of counter intelligence at the Research and Analysis Wing when the Rabinder Singh case unfolded. (Facebook: Amar Bhushan)
While the R&AW never made its internal inquiry public, it did confirm in the wake of the Singh episode that eight of its key operatives had gone missing since the agency was formed in 1968.
The revelation prompted considerable backlash in the community, and questions about the integrity of R&AW's officers and its decisions.
In Yadav's book, as well as granular detail about the Singh case that he says was gathered from internal sources, he made the case that R&AW was in urgent need of reform to address unprofessional behaviour and corruption.
The exact details of what went on inside the R&AW in the months leading up to and directly following Singh's escape are difficult to verify. But Yadav offered the following account.
He believes that many officials were quite happy for Singh to vanish, if he took with him the potential consequences of any further investigation that could point to them as conspirators.
"There is a strong Indian myth that a crow never bites a crow," he wrote.
Yadav wrote that 57 officers of the R&AW were found to have been involved in Singh's deception in some way, according to the suppressed internal inquiry.
He listed the names of 19 employees who he argued were conspirators, having either assisted or allowed Singh to flee the country, or provided information that Singh passed on to the CIA.
RK Yadav is a former officer who worked at India's Research and Analysis Wing for several decades. (Twitter: RK Yadav)
Yadav filed a complaint to the CBI asking them to look into the matter.
The complaint landed in Delhi's High Court, which in 2009 declined to press CBI any further, on the grounds that Yadav had not provided sufficient evidence.
"Your complete petition is nothing but hearsay. You have no authenticity and without any evidence you are asking us to initiate action against the officers," Chief Justice A P Shah said.
In his book, Yadav explains the lengths he went to in order to compel an official body to take further action against the people he says helped Singh to escape justice. He maintains to this day that he has only ever sought to expose the truth.
"He was chased away. Had [Rabinder Singh] been arrested here, then those officers who shared information with him would have faced court under the official secrets act. Therefore, they made him escape," he told the ABC.
A review of Yadav's book published by the CIA noted that it was "difficult to analyse as it has no footnotes, no end notes, and no bibliography, which means there are no citations from secondary sources, archives, or documents to support the claims".
"The book is strongest when Yadav discusses what he witnessed and experienced, but the sections that contain historical narrative lack independent sources necessary to document the events," the reviewer wrote.
According to Bhushan's version of events, there was corruption at the centre of the Singh case — but only of one man.
"We have perfect institutions. We have laws, we have rules, we have procedures. What's lacking is people who work within this and implement it," he told the EPIC Channel documentary.
Few former agents have gone on record about what went on at the R&AW.
Retired intelligence officers are now required to seek prior permission from the head of their organisation before publishing any details about the inner workings of government agencies.
One former R&AW officer is currently being sued by the CBI for allegedly publishing classified information in his 2007 book titled India's External Intelligence - Secrets of Research and Analysis Wing.
For now, those with lingering questions about what really happened to Singh will perhaps turn to the accounts penned by his former colleagues — one that calls itself fact, and the other fiction.

title: Hollywood sign has attracted renewal during its 100 years … and vandals
content:
The Hollywood sign has turned 100, with its birthday set at around about December 8.
In the century it has been around, it has experienced quite a bit of change, says film historian and professor of cinema at UCLA Jonathan Kuntz.
"The sign is outdoors on a mountain, basically, 24 hours a day," Professor Kuntz said.
"So it's taken quite a beating."
Most recently, the sign was refreshed with more than 1,800 litres of paint after each letter was pressure-washed and primed last year.
Jonathan Kuntz is a film historian and expert on the Hollywood studio system and American motion pictures. (Supplied: Jonathan Kuntz)
Professor Kuntz says that is only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the sign being spruced up over the years.
"The original sign of 1923, which was wood with electric light bulbs — that decayed over the years and became a mess," Professor Kuntz said.
"Some just wanted to remove it, but eventually it was in the late 1940s replaced with a more metal structure that is not illuminated."
But that would not last either. Thirty years later, it had decayed again.
"In the late 1970s, money was raised by various people contributing quite a bit ... Hugh Hefner, several others and Gene Autry, the western star, and it was rebuilt again."
Gene Autry is said to have contributed money to renovate the Hollywood sign in the 1970s. (Reuters: file photo)
Professor Kuntz says that 45 years on from that rebuild, despite better waterproofing technology, changes in temperature mean the Hollywood sign remains an ongoing project.
"There's also debates about it, of course, it's a controversial site," he said.
"Because, first off, for everybody that lives in that neighbourhood, the tourism that it brings – sometimes people will just be standing in the street taking pictures of the Hollywood sign, or walking across people's [yards] to get closer to the Hollywood sign and that has created a neighbourhood problem up in Beachwood Canyon underneath the Hollywood sign."
While there have been numerous fully sanctioned refurbishments over the years, the Hollywood sign has also inadvertently taken a number of different forms.
"It was an advertising sign originally," Professor Kuntz said.
"Now, of course, it just advertises Hollywood itself, not a real estate development.
"Hollywoodland was the name of a real estate development in Hollywood.
"And so by the late 40s, when the sign was no longer being maintained by the people that had originally built it and it was becoming an eyesore, as they would say, the city and Chamber of Commerce of Hollywood took control of it and said, 'look, we'll pay to have this thing rebuilt in a more weatherproof fashion.
"'But it's not gonna say Hollywoodland anymore. We're taking off the land. Oh, it's just gonna say Hollywood.'
"Several of the letters had caved in already anyway.
"But it's been customised on several occasions in its history to read other things to promote various movies and TV shows and events."
Professor Kuntz says that is not the only thing the sign has been used to promote.
The famous Hollywood sign reads "Hollyweed" after it was vandalised in 2017. (AFP: Gene Blevins)
"There's been attempts, you know, kind of you might say vandalism, where people have gone up there and furtively altered what it says, often to make political statements.
"It hangs right over Los Angeles, you might say, right over the city.
"Millions of people can see it every day, basically, and so in some ways, it's perfectly positioned if you want to get a message across to people.
"And so there have been folks who have taken it over … most famously in, I guess it was in the 1970s they changed Hollywood to Hollyweed – some folks who liked to advocate for the legalisation of marijuana."
While a trespasser got away with altering the sign to again read Hollyweed in 2017, Professor Kuntz says it would be hard for someone to get away with that today.
"You're doing all kinds of things. You're trespassing. You're vandalising. So, they can throw the book at you, I suppose. It may not be hard time, but there'll be trouble."

title: The Boy and the Heron showcases the magical mind of anime master Miyazaki
content:
The world has missed Hayao Miyazaki.
It's been a decade since the Studio Ghibli guru announced his supposed retirement on the back of his elegiac and deeply personal The Wind Rises, and his reputation has only grown in his absence.
There were memes. There were controversies. And of course, there are the movies — arguably the greatest run of any filmmaker, working in live action or animation, across the last 40 years — that continued to win new generations of fans.
Now, at the tender age of 82, Miyazaki is back — and as soulful as ever — with the coming-of-age fantasy The Boy and the Heron.
The Boy and the Heron follows the story of Mahito and is partly based on Hayao Miyazaki's childhood memories. (Supplied: Studio Ghibli)
Though it marks a return to the director's more fantastical style, The Boy and the Heron is something of a spiritual sequel to The Wind Rises, drawing loosely upon Miyazaki's infant memories of his father — a Japanese aircraft designer — and their flight from the war-torn Tokyo of World War II.
It's 1944, and the nation is in the grip of the Pacific War. A year after losing his mother in a hospital fire, 12-year-old Mahito (voiced by Soma Santoki, and Luca Padovan in the English dub) and his father Shoichi (Takuya Kimura/Christian Bale) evacuate Tokyo for the countryside, where they take up residence in a quaint old mansion that seems to be unmoored in time.
The old women love having Mahito in their world. (Supplied: Studio Ghibli)
Shoichi has remarried his late wife's younger sister, the newly pregnant Natsuko (Yoshino Kimura/Gemma Chan), who lives on the estate with a coterie of garrulous old maids who comically fuss and fawn over Mahito like he's a prize new pet.
The kid's already feeling out of sorts when he encounters a majestic and sinister Grey Heron, who swoops upon the house and starts rapping on the bedroom window. Its beak is bursting with leering, unnervingly human chompers, its voice crackling with invitations to the netherworld.
"I shall guide you to your mother," the Heron taunts Mahito, backed by a minion chorus of chanting frogs and fish.
It's been ten years since Miyazaki has made a film with Studio Ghibli. (Supplied: Studio Ghibli)
The Heron is voiced with prickly charm by Japanese actor Masaki Suda, and in the English dub by Robert Pattinson, who lets his freak mode flourish with a mischievous performance that swings between comic bluster and wounded pride.
(It's testament to Miyazaki's pull that the English version is full of big names putting in solid vocal work, though it goes without saying that you should see the Japanese language original if you can.)
Mark Hamill joins actors including Robert Pattison, Christian Bale, Florence Pugh and Willem Dafoe in the English dub of The Boy and the Heron. (Supplied: Studio Ghibli)
Both white rabbit and shapeshifting trickster — the reveal of his true form is too funny to give away here — the Heron soon leads Mahito through a portal into a parallel world, where Natsuko has been kidnapped by an army of anthropomorphic parakeets engaged in a power struggle with a mad wizard (Shōhei Hino/Mark Hamill).
From his earlier feature work, like Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind and My Neighbour Totoro, through to later masterpieces Princess Mononoke, Spirited Away and Howl's Moving Castle, Miyazaki's films contain some of the most indelible fantasy images in cinema.
At the same time, they've always been anchored by a rich emotional thread that reflects their creator's humanist worldview and, in this respect, The Boy and the Heron is no different.
Will The Boy and the Heron be one of Studio Ghibli's best?  (Supplied: Studio Ghibli)
Miyazaki, who was born in 1941, has spoken of the war as one of his earliest childhood memories. The director's affection for his late mother, meanwhile, fuels Mahito's yearning, his petulance, his sense of disconnection from the world.
True to Miyazaki's style, Mahito's journey feels both everyday and dreamlike, where lost mothers become fire-wielding spirits, elderly cleaning ladies transform into seafaring adventurers, and harmless domestic birds take on the puffed-up shape of man-eating warriors.
Cinematographer Atsushi Okui told Deadline he was excited to work on the film alongside Hayao Miyazaki. (Supplied: Studio Ghibli)
The parakeets — led by a grave, stentorian king (Jun Kunimura/Dave Bautista) — are one of those signature Miyazaki creations that mix the threatening with the goofy. They're both unnerving and wildly comical, something a child would conjure in a daydream.
It's classic terrain for a filmmaker who has never dealt in the reductive binary of good and evil, whose worlds are populated by morally complex creatures deserving of empathy.
These unborn souls will delight Studio Ghibli fans. (Supplied: Studio Ghibli)
Just as the film features cutesy little egg-shaped babies whose plush likeness is bound for the Ghibli gift shop, it also contains disquieting scenes of pelicans cruising in through the darkness, like a squadron of fighter bombers, to snap them up and devour them. No mere villains, the pelicans get their own complicated story, relayed — in one of the movie's bleakest and most moving moments — by an injured bird (Kaoru Kobayashi/Willem Dafoe) with the gravitas of a fallen Shakespearian king.
Moments like this reveal the precarity of an ecosystem and an environment in crisis, but also the weight of legacy as new generations inherit the mistakes of the past.
Like Miyazaki's best work, The Boy and the Heron isn't merely nostalgic for its creator's childhood. It's a challenge to that next generation to rethink the way the world works. That's what keeps him vital, seven decades into his career.
The Boy and the Heron in cinemas now.

title: Joel Edgerton's new Hollywood film has divided critics — which he says is what its director wanted
content:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Joel Edgerton received an unexpected phone call.
On the line was Paul Schrader, the veteran screenwriter and director whose credits include Taxi Driver (1976), Raging Bull (1980) and American Gigolo (1990).
Schrader wanted Edgerton to play the lead role in his new film, Master Gardener.
The Australian actor — the star of Loving (2016), The Great Gatsby (2013) and the Star Wars franchise — was equal parts flattered, curious and confused at the surprise offer.
Edgerton, pictured with co-star Sigourney Weaver, says Schrader is interested in "the collision of opposites". (Supplied: Transmission Films)
At drama school in the 90s, Edgerton and his peers had dreamt of playing "complicated characters" like Taxi Driver's anti-hero protagonist Travis Bickle, or Jake LaMotta, the boxing champion from Raging Bull (both played by Robert De Niro).
"Years later, to have a guy that was really in the epicentre of all that to ask me to come and be one of those characters in his film was a real thrill," Edgerton tells ABC RN's The Screen Show.
Master Gardener is the final instalment of a trilogy that includes First Reformed (2017) — an exploration of faith and despair starring Ethan Hawke as a Protestant minister — and The Card Counter (2021) — a revenge thriller starring Oscar Isaac as a professional gambler.
Edgerton was intrigued by the premise of First Reformed, and he saw it at the cinema on the first day it was released.
"I was so impressed by that film," he says.
The Screen Show brings you reviews and in-depth conversations with leading film and TV directors, actors and screenwriters from Australia and around the world.
Schrader originally planned to shoot Master Gardener in Melbourne, however COVID made travel to Australia impossible and the location moved to Louisiana.
In Master Gardener, Edgerton plays Narvel Roth, a former white nationalist who is now a horticulturist managing the lavish gardens of an estate owned by Norma Haverhill (Sigourney Weaver). Roth forms a relationship with Haverhill's niece, Maya (Quintessa Swindell), a young woman of colour.
Early in the filmmaking process, Schrader and Edgerton engaged in "deep conversations" about what qualities the veteran director sought in his leading characters.
"For all the bells and whistles and tricks that you might have in your bag as an actor, he wanted the central character in his films to occupy a certain stillness, an unwavering position, and allow all the characters around to be the swirling turbulence," Edgerton says.
In Schrader's vision, the leading man showed little emotion, an "immovable pillar … [like] a rock in an ocean that was swirling around them with … crashing waves," Edgerton explains.
Swindell (pictured left) is a non-binary actor who has also appeared in Netflix teen drama Trinkets and 2022 superhero film Black Adam. (Supplied: Transmission Films)
This was a creative challenge for Edgerton.
"I can often fidget and move around on screen a lot," he says.
Schrader, now 77, has fine-tuned his filmmaking process over a long career that has included at least one bad experience: the making of Dying of the Light (2014), a thriller starring Nicolas Cage as a CIA agent.
"The studio took the edit off him and recut the film," Edgerton says. "It killed him."
As a result, creative control is paramount for Schrader, who reportedly considered quitting filmmaking after the release of Dying of the Light.
"His methodology is to make a film for less money and [on] a tighter schedule so that he has full autonomy," Edgerton says.
Operating with a budget of $US4 to 5 million, Schrader is free to make films that fulfil his artistic vision.
"The sincerity of Schrader's filmmaking and his insistence on the possibility of redemption for the irredeemable is deeply affecting," wrote the New York Times. (Supplied: Transmission Films)
"We shot Master Gardener in 18 days," Edgerton says.
"I shot The Gift, my own film, in 20 days, and I felt like I was being chased down the street by a bear. It feels frantic.
Dr Karl knows the best app for free podcasts, radio, music, news and audiobooks … and you don't need to be a scientist to find it!
Edgerton says filming on such a tight schedule is a testament to Schrader's meticulous planning and his decisiveness and economy as a director.
In contrast to the trend in modern filmmaking to "overshoot" and edit later, Schrader always has a clear picture of how a scene will work ahead of shooting.
"There was creative freedom within the margins of the way he saw a scene — but he knew where the close-up was going to come, and he knew how he was going to start a scene," Edgerton says.
With its complex depiction of sexual and racial politics, this film is divisive by design, Edgerton says.
It's a view Edgerton echoes.
"I would hope stories I'm involved in, behind or in front of the camera, become things to think on and ruminate and discuss and debate, rather than just be out-and-out easy entertainment."

title: These classic Christmas songs have one thing in common — they were all written by Jewish composers
content:
When Arthur Levine was growing up just outside New York City in the 1960s, there was no time as lonely as Christmas.
"I was one of a small number of Jews in an Italian-Irish Catholic town.
"And everywhere was Christmas decorations and Christmas specials and Christmas music," he says.
It all felt "very exclusionary".
Arthur Levine felt Hanukkah lacked the joyful mythology of Christmas. (Supplied: Candlewick Press)
Christmas appeared to have its own specific magic of trees, tinsel and a larger-than-life jolly man in red.
The Jewish festival of Hanukkah, also celebrated in December, seemed to pale in comparison.
To Levine, Hanukkah seemed to have "no mythology … no storytelling".
"There was the [biblical] story of Hanukkah … but we didn't have any holiday legends, no Santa Claus, no Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, no Frosty the Snowman."
"I really felt that we Jews deserved to have a legendary figure, the equal of Rudolph or Santa Claus," he says.
So, he invented one.
Levine is a children's author and book publisher, who has edited beloved children's titles like Harry Potter and The Golden Compass.
In 2020, he wrote and published The Hanukkah Magic of Nate Gadol.
Nate is a "great big spirit", whose special power is that he can make anything last as long as it is needed.
Nate's name comes from the Hebrew letters on the dreidel, a traditional spinning top used at Hanukkah. (Supplied: Candlewick Press)
It's a nod to the original Hanukkah story, which centres on a holy miracle that made an oil lamp last for eight days, sustaining the Jewish people through a 2nd century BC rebellion against persecution under Greek rule.
Levine's story, which is set in 19th century America, sees Nate watch over a Jewish family of European immigrants and their Irish-Catholic neighbours, and attempt to help both through poverty and hardship.
One night, Nate runs into Santa Claus, whose sleigh has run out of magic. He helps Santa on his merry way in exchange for presents to give to the Jewish family, thus establishing a new tradition of gift-giving at Hanukkah.
After Levine's story was published, it raised eyebrows among some in the Jewish community, who bristled at what they saw as the "Christmas-ification" of the Jewish holiday.
But experts say Levine's story taps into a long, rich history in which Jewish culture and Christmas traditions were inextricably entwined.
Hanukkah, which takes place over eight days in late November or early December, is actually a relatively minor holiday, compared to other High Holy Days like Passover and Jewish New Year.
The holiday was established by rabbis rather than holy scripture. The story behind it dates back to the 2nd century BC, when Judea was conquered by Alexander the Great. Military leader Antiochus IV Epiphanes became the ruler of the Jewish people.
"[Antiochus] tried to suppress the Torah [Jewish scripture] and the observance of Jewish law and custom, and instead impose Greek religion, including setting up a statue of Zeus in the temple in Jerusalem," explains Rabbi Dr Benjamin Elton, the chief minister of the Great Synagogue in Sydney.
"This was too much for many members of the local Jewish community and … they rose up in rebellion."
A painting by Peter Paul Rubens depicts the battle and triumph of Judas Maccabee. (Public Domain)
As the conventional story goes — though some contest it — the Jews, led by five brothers called the Maccabees, reconquered the temple and rededicated it to Judaism. However, according to Jewish scripture, when they went to light the temple's menorah, a seven-branched candelabra lit with olive oil, there was only enough oil for one day.
But a miracle meant the oil lasted for eight days.
During Hanukkah — a Hebrew word meaning "dedication" — Jews traditionally sing songs of praise, read from the Torah and retell the story of the oil lamp.
Other traditions include spinning the dreidel, giving out chocolate coins, and cooking oily foods like doughnuts and latkes, a type of potato fritter.
Hanukkah was practised quietly for millennia until relatively recently when it made its way into mainstream pop culture.
It became more well known with mass Jewish migration in the 19th century, says David Slucki, an associate professor and director of the Australian Centre for Jewish Civilisation at Monash University.
As record numbers of Jews left Eastern Europe, they gradually gained civic and political rights in the countries they moved to, despite persistent anti-Semitic prejudice and violence.

"There was this kind of bargain that Jews who were emancipated had to accept, which was in order to be fully considered part of the surrounding society, they had to adopt the cultural mores of that place: language, dress, and to some extent, the way they practised [religion]," Professor Slucki says.
America was considered "the golden land, the land of opportunity", and between 1881 and 1924, around two million Jews emigrated there from the Russian Empire, "fleeing poverty, pogroms, and seeking better opportunities in the US," Professor Slucki says.
This coincided with the emergence of the motion picture and mass-produced popular music in the US.
At the time, Hollywood was not the desirable industry it is today. But for Jewish migrants, it was vastly preferable to working in factories and sweatshops.
And it provided a perfect opportunity to blend in.
Irving Berlin, whose original name was Israel Beilin, composed beloved holiday classic, White Christmas. (Getty: Bettmann)
"Jewishness became a private affair, and publicly they became American," Professor Slucki says.
Many of the most famous and well-loved Christmas songs of the first half of the 20th century were written by Jewish composers.
That includes Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, A Holly Jolly Christmas, Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree, Winter Wonderland, It's the Most Wonderful Time of the Year, Let It Snow! Let It Snow! Let It Snow! and White Christmas, written by Irving Berlin.
In the second half of the 20th century, Jewish communities felt embedded enough in American society to confidently express their own religious and cultural heritage.
In 50s TV show The Goldbergs, Molly Goldberg's character is heavily informed by Jewish culture. (Public Domain)
Celebrating Hanukkah was the perfect way to do it.
"Hanukkah has nothing to do with Christmas. There's nothing adjacent about the stories; they take place hundreds of years apart. But it's an opportunity to elevate [Jewish] religious and cultural practices alongside the mainstream," Professor Slucki says.
References to Jewish life and holidays soon began appearing in TV and movies.
Popular TV series The Goldbergs, which ran from 1949 to 1956 and followed a Jewish American family living in the Bronx, was one of the earliest examples of Jewish culture in mainstream media.
By the 80s and 90s, Hanukkah had become a common plot point in American TV and filmmaking.
Take the episode of Friends when Ross is anxious to teach his child about Jewish culture but is left with few options at the costume shop. He dresses up as "the holiday armadillo" to give his son a lesson on Hanukkah.
Ross dresses up as "the holiday armadillo" in Friends
The Jewish holiday has been featured in everything from Rugrats to The Nanny, Saturday Night Live to South Park.
"Maybe the most famous was [2003 TV show] The O.C., with its storyline around "Chrismukkah" and a mixed-faith family who create these traditions that combine Christmas and Hanukkah," Professor Slucki says.
He says the episode spoke to a new generation of Jews who were grappling with "multi-layered identities".
"Chrismukkah was a way to acknowledge those complexities and to try and blend those things."
The writers on the O.C. coined the term "Chrismukkah" to mean a day that celebrates both holidays.  (Supplied)
Professor Slucki says it's important to acknowledge that this mainstream representation of Jewish culture speaks to a very specific Jewish community.
"A lot of Sephardi Jews and Mizrahi Jews, who trace their roots to the Middle East and North Africa, wouldn't necessarily recognise themselves in the depictions of Jews in pop culture," he says.
For Arthur Levine, bringing Hanukkah and Christmas together in his children's book was a reflection of the world he saw around him.
"If you're a contemporary Jew, you are bombarded by Christmas, [so] why not deal with it?" he says.
His protagonist Nate is not "a Jewish Santa" but "a spirit in his own right".
The ABC's Religion & Ethics portal is home to reporting on religion, ethical discussion and inspiring stories of faith and belief.
Levine's son was 17 when the book was published, far "beyond the age of lap-sitting", but they read it together all the same.
"I still enjoyed reading it to him and hearing him say that he would have loved it as a small child," Levine says.
"That is what has been the motivation of my whole life, to give kids, particularly kids from marginalised communities, the chance to see themselves and to enjoy stories that include them.
"We are always writing the books we would love to have read."

title: Jonathan Majors's former girlfriend says Marvel star has violent temper that led to alleged assault
content:
The former girlfriend of Marvel star Jonathan Majors has testified that the actor is prone to fits of explosive rage, something she says ultimately led to him assaulting her in the back seat of a car and his career-halting arrest earlier this year.
During hours of tearful testimony in a New York courtroom, Grace Jabbari traced the downfall of her relationship with Mr Majors, who she described as a "kind and loving" partner increasingly unable to control his "violent temper".
She said he hurled household objects at walls and often threatened to take his own life, at times referring to himself as a "monster".
"It felt like I was walking around on eggshells," Ms Jabbari, a 30-year-old professional dancer from the United Kingdom told the court.
"I had to be perfect."
The troubled romance came to a head on the evening of March 25, as the couple were riding back to Manhattan from a dinner already marred by a heated argument over Mr Majors's recent outbursts, she told the jury.
During the drive, Ms Jabbari was leaning on his shoulder when he received a "romantic" text message sent by a woman named Cleopatra.
Grace Jabbari (centre) leaves the court after testifying. (AP: Bebeto Matthews)
After she snatched the phone out of his hands, she said Mr Majors twisted her arm behind her back in a position that left her in "excruciating" pain.
"Next I felt a really hard blow across my head," she said, pantomiming the motion of an open hand making contact with the back of her skull.
"He's very strong. I couldn't move," Ms Jabbari continued.
"It feels very loud when you're hit in the head, and just shocking."
Mr Majors eventually pried the phone from her hands and took off through the streets of Lower Manhattan as Ms Jabbari chased after him, according to a video compilation taken from various surveillance cameras that was shown to jurors.
The testimony came on the second day of the trial against Mr Majors, a rising Hollywood film actor whose portrayal of the comic book supervillain Kang the Conqueror was set to anchor the next phase of the Marvel cinematic universe.
Paul Rudd as Ant-Man (left) and Jonathan Majors as Kang the Conqueror in the movie Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania. (Supplied: Marvel Studios)
The fate of those films and others starring the 34-year-old remains uncertain since his arrest in March for allegedly assaulting Ms Jabbari in the back of the car.
An attorney for Mr Majors has maintained that she was the instigator of the confrontation and suggested that race – Mr Majors is black; Ms Jabbari is white – may have factored into his arrest and prosecution.
Mr Majors is charged with misdemeanours that include assault and he could be sentenced to up to a year in jail if convicted.
The actor avoided eye contact with his former girlfriend for much of the day's testimony on Tuesday, scribbling notes to his lawyer or thumbing through his gold-leafed Bible as she recounted how he quickly toggled from emotionally sensitive to abusive.
In the US summer of 2022, while struggling with a gruelling diet and exercise regimen for his role as a bodybuilder in the film Magazine Dreams, Mr Majors became "full of rage and aggression" without explanation, Ms Jabbari said.
He lashed out at her, she recalled, throwing objects during one argument that left dents in the walls and sent her ducking for cover in their West Hollywood home.
Jonathan Majors starred as Damian Anderson in Creed III. (Supplied: Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Inc.)
A few months later, while filming in England, Mr Majors allegedly blew up at Ms Jabbari again after she came home from a bar "tipsy" with a friend.
In a recording played for the court, Mr Majors can be heard berating his girlfriend for not living up to the standards set by other spouses of famous men, like Coretta Scott King and Michelle Obama.
"I'm a great man. A great man!" Mr Majors declared.
"There needs to be a great woman who makes sacrifices."
On Tuesday, Ms Jabbari also addressed a series of videos that showed her partying in a Manhattan nightclub hours after the alleged assault.
Speaking to jurors, Ms Jabbari said she had met a group of "generous" strangers on a corner after chasing Mr Majors out of the vehicle following the attack.
"The worst thing in my head would've been to go back to the empty apartment we shared in that moment," Ms Jabbari said.
Acknowledging that she can be seen on videos smiling, dancing, and taking shots with the new friends, she added: "I was having the nicest time I could've had within the situation."
Ms Jabbari is expected to return to the stand on Wednesday local time.

title: 'It's OK to show messy humanity on screen': Striking the right note with mental health in film
content:
It's likely you've seen at least one, if not all, of the following: A Beautiful Mind. Sybil. The Joker. Psycho. Fatal Attraction. The Shining. Suicide Squad.
If so, you've seen how not to depict mental illness on the silver screen, according to experts.
Macquarie University history professor Michelle Arrow says there are many movies and TV shows that offer broad-brush, negative depictions of mental ill health.
"They reproduce the stereotype that people with mental illness are inherently violent, that people who have experienced trauma are most likely to develop some kind of significant serious mental illness," Professor Arrow said.
"If your two options are to be depicted as a sort of violent, mad person or a genius who is deeply troubled, neither of those are particularly helpful for anybody who's trying to see themselves in culture.
"I think we have a very long way to go in terms of how we depict mental illness in cinema.
"It doesn't have to always be a uniformly positive representation, but I think it could be something a little closer to reality as most people experience it."
Michelle Arrow says broad-brush depictions of mental ill health reproduce harmful stereotypes.  (Macquarie University)
Sometimes, it's not that clear-cut. Take Girl, Interrupted for example.
"I think Angelina Jolie sort of embodied almost like a stock character in that film. You know, she's mentally ill, but she's sexy and bad and a bit dangerous," Professor Arrow said.
"And I think that kind of idea of the mentally ill young woman who is sort of using her sexuality — it sort of feels like a trope in popular culture that we've long relied on, I suppose, someone's like a hot mess.
"But it also, I think, was important because it was almost like a female re-reading of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. It was like a retelling of that story for young women.
"And so, I think that film was probably quite important in that respect."
Moviegoers watch One Flew Over The Cuckoo's Nest — just one film famous for its depiction of a mental health institution.  (Reuters: Chris Helgren )
Professor Arrow says mental health conditions such as bipolar and schizophrenia are often misunderstood, and the way in which they are depicted in popular culture plays a part in these misconceptions.
It can be damaging when Hollywood doesn't get it right.
Clinical psychologist and global director of research at Movember, Zac Seidler, said the TV series 13 Reasons Why led to an increase in calls to Lifeline and Headspace, as well as increased suicide rates among those who watched the series.
"The way that they depicted suicide, the way that they depicted distress … any expert worth their salt would have immediately said, 'You cannot put this on television,'" Dr Seidler said.
"You cannot show somebody taking their own life.
"More importantly, she was getting back at an ex, which is a very uncommon reason for taking your own life and really is extremely shame-inducing for many people."
13 Reasons Why was commercially acclaimed but Zac Seidler says any expert worth their salt would have issues with its depiction of suicide.  (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)
There is a lot of power in pop culture and the stakes are high.
So, how do filmmakers do it better?
When it comes to the script, Dr Seidler says intentions are important.
"You need to give a shit," he said.
"You need to really care about doing this well, and that means understanding that there are multiple points of view here.
"You can't only talk to a mental health expert or clinician; you need to also include lived experience.
"There may well be, you know, I'm a clinician with lived experience. So, I tick a couple of boxes, that's important.
"But we need to make sure that we see the different angles here. When it comes to grief, for instance, there are the people who are experiencing it [and] there's the ripple effect. There are people on the outer ring."
Zac Seidler says intention is important in the writing of a script. (Supplied)
He said this was not about making filmmaking an impossible endeavour, but rather presenting a more nuanced portrayal.
"The way that dialogue might work, the way that certain imagery might work, I think it's important that when we're writing those scripts, we're ready to stomach things not looking as neat and tidy and perfect as we'd like and that the characters might have some inconsistencies, which are common — and that's just the human experience," he said.
Dr Seidler worked closely with the cast and crew on the ABC TV series In Limbo.
"The fact that I got to speak with the cast and crew and ask and answer questions and really get to the bottom of some of their own biases and assumptions [was important]," he said.
"It's that stuff. It's the expectation setting that we need to break down, which is, what do you think that this is? What do you think it should look like? And how does it manifest in the real world, because that's what they're trying to reflect.
"It's OK to show messy humanity on-screen."
It's not often I'll review an ABC show, but rest assured, if I thought it was trash, I would say so. In Limbo is exquisite, writes Mawunyo Gbogbo.
Dr Seidler says newer shows are doing it better and he has encouraged people to check out shows such as Ted Lasso, Sex Education, BoJack Horseman and Normal People.
The Newsreader is also interesting because it hints at the fact Helen Norville (Anna Torv) has had mental health struggles, but these struggles don't define her. They're just part of the character.
Professor Arrow also enjoys the depiction of mental ill health in Please Like Me.
"What I think about that story that was really powerful was that it was a young man who's kind of venturing out into the world and having his first relationships and forming share houses and all of that.
"And on the other hand, he's also dealing with his mum who attempts suicide.
"And the undercurrent throughout the entire series is how is he managing and helping his mum.
"And how does he deal with that situation of being a child/carer of someone with a mental illness, and I think also depicting the mother's mental health challenges in a way that was really honest really appealed to me because I think it showed you how caring for someone with a mental illness can be frustrating, challenging, difficult, it reverses the relationship between the parent and the child.
"There's all those kinds of complexities around the relationship. And I think that, to me, seems like a more useful and a more honest depiction of that issue."

title: Domestic assault trial begins for Marvel star Jonathan Majors
content:
A domestic violence trial against Marvel actor Jonathan Majors has begun in New York with the court hearing competing accounts of a violent confrontation that derailed the actor's Hollywood ascent.
Mr Majors is accused of grabbing his former girlfriend's hand so hard he fractured her middle finger, then twisting her arm behind her back and striking her on the side of the head
Mr Majors's attorney argued her client was the true victim, claiming he was left bloodied by the attack
Mr Majors could be sentenced to up to a year in jail if convicted
Mr Majors is accused of assaulting his former girlfriend, Grace Jabbari, in a car after she read a text message sent to his phone by another woman in March this year.
Prosecutors allege Mr Majors grabbed the woman's hand so hard he fractured her middle finger, then twisted her arm behind her back and struck her on the side of the head.
Mr Majors's attorney argued her client was the true victim, claiming he was left bloodied by the attack, while Ms Jabbari spent the rest of the night clubbing.
Throughout the opening statements, Mr Majors listened silently, head cocked and eyes down.
His attorney, Priya Chaudhry, painted Ms Jabbari as a wilted lover who sought to derail her partner's career as revenge.
Actor Jonathan Majors (left) arrives with actress and current girlfriend Meagan Good (right) at court for a trial on his domestic violence case.  (AP: Yuki Iwamura)
She also suggested Mr Majors's race was a potential reason that he was arrested the following day.
Since a breakout role in The Last Black Man in San Francisco, Mr Majors became a major Hollywood player through roles in Creed III and his emergence as a key supervillain in the Marvel multiverse.
However, the allegations have seen the 34-year-old's work pulled or postponed, including the release of Sundance award-winning film Magazine Dreams.
Jonathan Majors stars as Damian Anderson in Creed III. (Supplied: Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Inc.)
Assistant district attorney Michael Perez told jurors the alleged assault was the culmination of a "cruel and manipulative pattern of psychological and physical abuse" Mr Majors directed at his partner of two years.
He said the trial would show Mr Majors "demanded total compliance" from his girlfriend, at one point telling her she needed to maintain the same standards as Michelle Obama.
In addition to the struggle, both the prosecution and defence offered differing narratives about the aftermath of the alleged assault.
Once the driver pulled over, Mr Majors fled the scene with his phone as Ms Jabbari chased him "on foot, through traffic, like in a movie", according to Ms Chaudhry.
Unable to find Mr Majors, she met three strangers and followed them to a Manhattan nightclub where she spent the next few hours drinking and dancing, the defence attorney said.
Actor Jonathan Majors will allege Ms Jabbari sought to derail his career as revenge. (AP: Yuki Iwamura)
Mr Perez said Mr Majors picked Ms Jabbari up and threw her inside the car on multiple occasions after the driver pulled over.
He said she accepted the invitation of bystanders in hopes of "temporarily blocking out" the abuse committed by Mr Majors.
She returned home after a few hours, took two sleeping pills and fell asleep on the floor of her bathroom, he said.
Ms Jabbari awoke the next morning to Mr Majors standing over her with police officers, initially reluctant to report the abuse "because of how he's manipulated her in the past and trained her to stay silent", Mr Perez said.
Paul Rudd as Scott Lang/Ant-Man and Jonathan Majors as Kang the Conqueror in Marvel Studios' Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania. (Supplied: Marvel Studios)
She was hospitalised with minor injuries.
Six months later, she was arrested by police after Mr Majors brought a counter-claim against her for assaulting him in the vehicle.
Those charges were dismissed by the Manhattan district attorney the following day.
Mr Perez referenced the arrest on Monday, telling jurors that Mr Majors's "attempts to control and intimidate Ms Jabbari extended well after he assaulted her."
Ms Jabbari is expected to testify against her former partner in the coming days, and Mr Majors could be sentenced to up to a year in jail if convicted.

title: 'I'm so proud of you': Home Alone stars Macaulay Culkin and Catherine O'Hara reunite at Walk of Fame ceremony
content:
Macaulay Culkin has wiped away tears as his one-time on-screen mum Catherine O'Hara honoured the actor while accepting his star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.
The two performers played mother and son Kate and Kevin McAlister in the 1990 film Home Alone.
The film was a box office smash hit, grossing $US476 million ($713 million) and spawning a six-film franchise.
Culkin and O'Hara reprised their roles just once for the 1992 sequel Home Alone 2: Lost In New York.
In her speech, O'Hara touched on the immense pressure Culkin experienced as a child who was launched into super-stardom.
Culkin wiped away tears as O'Hara spoke about their three decade-long friendship. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)
"This beautiful little 10-year-old boy was called a superstar, a money maker, one of the hottest leading young men by the world over. How does anyone survive that?" O'Hara asked.
"I believe you would have to posses a certain quality, a gift … your sense of humour, it's a sign of intelligence in a child and a key to surviving life at any age.
Culkin and O'Hara met while filming Home Alone. (Supplied: IMDB/Photo 12/Alamy Stock Photo)
"Thank you for including me, your fake mum who left you alone, not once but twice to share in this happy occasion. I'm so proud of you," she said.
Friend and fellow actor Natasha Lyonne also spoke at the ceremony. The two co-starred in the 2003 film Party Monster together.
Lyonne also started acting professionally in her childhood.
Natasha Lyonne praised Culkin's sense of humour while speaking at his Walk of Fame ceremony. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)
"Mac, I'm so proud of you … there's a very rare and unspoken language that happens between child actors that make it out alive," she joked.
"Nothing makes me happier than seeing you exist so concretely on your own terms … I love you, you're a king, congratulations."
Culkin for his part, used his speaking time to thank his partner Brenda Song.
Culkin with his wife Brenda Song and his eldest son. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)
Song, who is most recognisable as London Tipton in Disney series The Suite Life of Zack and Cody, co-starred with Culkin in the 2018 film Changeland.
The couple's first son was born in 2021, with their second son born in 2022.
"You are absolutely everything. You're my champion … you're the best person I've ever known. You've given me all my purpose. You've given me family," Culkin said, holding back tears.
Culkin was joined at the ceremony by his goddaughter Paris Jackson, siblings Rory and Quinn Culkin and actor Seth Green, among others.
To round off his speech, Culkin tipped to the holiday season and the film that made him a star by reciting his famous Home Alone line, "Merry Christmas, ya filthy animals."
Quinn Culkin, Seth Green, Rory Culkin, Macaulay Culkin, Brenda Song and Paris Jackson at the Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)

title: Despite blockbuster successes, regional cinemas are still waiting for their COVID comeback
content:
Independent cinema owners in regional South Australia are struggling to get audiences back through the doors after COVID, with concerns that US movie industry strikes will cause further pain in years to come.
Mount Gambier's Oatmill Cinema has one screen out of action because of a faulty projector that has needed replacing for 18 months.
Owner and manager Shane Fulwood said it is the second time faulty equipment has affected screenings, with the previous fault happening just six days before the opening of the year's highest-grossing movie, Barbie.
He said he had hoped to have replaced the projector, but has been unable to due to a lack of revenue.
"Our bounce back is well below what I expected," he said.
"I thought there might be a gradual grind back towards our pre-COVID levels … that hasn't happened.
"We haven't had the revenue there to be able to [replace the project] easily, which is why we're patching up with bandaids rather than replacing entirely."
Cinema Augusta and Kadina Cinemas manager Michelle Coles is considering the future of the businesses. (ABC News)
Mr Fulwood is not the only regional cinema operator impacted by a slow post-COVID recovery.
Michelle Coles runs cinemas in Port Augusta and Kadina, but said the latter is on the brink of closure due to a lack of demand.
Two years after taking over the lease at Kadina Cinema, Ms Coles said low audience numbers and concessions sales are unsustainable.
"The age group from 18 to 35 are the ones we've lost," she said.
Independent Cinemas Australia CEO Brett Rosengarten said cinemas are still feeling the impact of fewer films being made due to COVID, and that had only been worsened by writers' and actors' strikes in the US.
"It's been a conflation of so many things happening all at once that's just been borderline disastrous in slowing down production," he said.
"There are terrific signs that we will get back to normal at some stage ... but we need regular volume and supply."
Mr Rosengarten said he expects operators will face a tough six to 12 months, and that the association is working on strategies to assist members with cost reductions during that time.
"Christmas looks like it's going to be fine, but from February through to May is looking a little bit lean," he said.
Shane Fulwood has been unable to replace a digital projector due to revenue shortages. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)
Mr Fulwood, who also runs Naracoorte's Landmark Cinema, said it is an "extremely challenging environment".
"People are really interested in a pop culture event [but] everything else that's not that has underperformed," he said.
Mr Rosengarten said in such situations, independent regional cinemas are always going to be worse off than than major exhibitors.
"They [the major cinema chains] are reinvesting in premium offerings to encourage people to come back to the cinemas," he said.
"I think a lot of the independents would love to be able to do that too, but when you're a single screen or twin and you haven't had the volume of product for the best part of three or four years, you just don't have the cash reserves."
Mount Gambier's Oatmill Cinema has been open for 26 years. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)
Ms Coles said the loss of local cinemas would have a major impact on regional communities.
As Mr Rosengarten notes, regional cinemas also bring customers to other businesses in town.
"They're big drivers of not just the economy of these country towns, but they're cultural hubs," he said.

title: The first trailer for Mad Max prequel Furiosa — starring Chris Hemsworth and Anya Taylor-Joy — has dropped
content:
Australian director George Miller has returned to the wasteland, giving fans a first look at the much-anticipated next film in the Mad Max series.
While the original Mad Max came out in 1979, the series attracted a new legion of fans with Miller's 2015 instalment Mad Max: Fury Road.
It grossed about $US375 million ($486 million) at the box office.
After the success of Fury Road, Miller is back with his fifth film in the franchise.
The trailer for Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga attracted more than 250,000 views in the first hour it dropped, which speaks to its popularity.
So, here's what we know about the film.
According to a press release from Warner Bros, the film is a "standalone action adventure that will reveal the origins of Furiosa", originally played by Charlize Theron in 2015.
Here's how Warner Bros describes it:
"As the world fell, young Furiosa is snatched from the Green Place of Many Mothers and falls into the hands of a great Biker Horde led by the Warlord Dementus.
"Sweeping through the Wasteland they come across the Citadel presided over by The Immortan Joe.
"While the two Tyrants war for dominance, Furiosa must survive many trials as she puts together the means to find her way home."
Furiosa stars actress Anya Taylor-Joy in the title role.
You may recognise her from the Netflix series The Queen's Gambit.
Continuing Mad Max's tradition of using Australian actors, Chris Hemsworth stars in the film as Warlord Dementus.
He is virtually unrecognisable in the trailer, with long hair, a beard, and what appear to be facial prosthetics.
Chris Hemsworth looking pretty wild in his role as Dementus. (YouTube: Warner Bros)
English actor Tom Burke also stars in the film.
Returning to the franchise for the fifth film is director and Mad Max creator George Miller.
Miller co-wrote Furiosa with Nick Lathouris, who has been involved with Mad Max since the first movie in 1979. He also co-wrote Fury Road.
In NSW.
Back in 2021, it was announced the film would be shot in the state with NSW and federal government incentives.
Miller said the movie would be filmed "all over NSW", including parts of Broken Hill.
Parts of Fury Road — the previous film — were supposed to be filmed around Broken Hill, but unusual rainfall meant the landscape was too green and the film had to be relocated to Namibia in Africa.
Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga is set for release on May 24, 2024.
So for those of you eager to watch the film, you'll have to wait a little longer.
But for now, here's the official trailer.

title: TV Show the Artful Dodger is a twist on a Charles Dickens classic
content:
British actor David Thewlis didn't learn how to pickpocket in his latest role as Fagin, a master pickpocket from Charles Dickens's novel Oliver Twist, but he did get away with stealing a few glass eyeballs from the film set in Australia.
"I was encouraged to by the director," Thewlis said in an interview with ABC News.
"Because I'm trying to be a method actor, and the director Jeffrey Walker absolutely encouraged me to steal things, so I did."
Asked if anyone noticed him stealing anything, he responded, "not until now."
Thewlis stars in the new show the Artful Dodger, a spin-off that reinvents characters from Charles Dickens's novel Oliver Twist, planting them in Australia during the 1850s.
Shot over five months in Sydney, the show follows Jack Dawkins (Thomas Brodie-Sangster), also known as the Artful Dodger, who now works as a surgeon in Australia after escaping his life as a pickpocketing youth in London. Those plans are thrown into disarray with the appearance of Norbert Fagin (David Thewlis), his criminal mentor and a surrogate father figure.
Thewlis's career has spanned decades — he's appeared in films including Naked, the Boy in Striped Pyjamas, and the Harry Potter series as Professor Remus Lupin. Those unfamiliar with Dickens' work will still find the series accessible, Thewlis said.
"It's not a Dickens adaptation. We've just taken to the main characters of the book and we're reinventing them. The spirit of it is very, quite joyous, very gritty, the surgery, the medical elements dealt with are kind of quite visceral, and sometimes a little hard to watch, but beautifully done.
"There's a gorgeous romance story in there and there's some just absolute ridiculous goofiness and silly silly humour as well, which I love about it. But it's a real mixture of all these things."
While the lead actors are British, the show is rounded out by a supporting cast of Australians including Maia Mitchell, Damon Herriman and Miranda Tapsell.
The show also spotlights the character of Lady Belle, played by Australian Mitchell, who has aspirations to become the country's first female surgeon.
Lady Belle (Maia Mitchell) in the Artful Dodger. (Supplied)
"Lady Belle is the heart and soul of the whole story. It's a real, very, very beautiful, strong character, and she's fighting the patriarchy. And it's sort of a very strong feminist message, I think, for her, and I think Maia Mitchell gives an incredible performance.
"I think it's going to make her a bigger star than she already is. I think my favourite part of the whole show is her story. Her narrative becomes stronger and stronger and stronger. And it's really her you very, very much care about by the end."
Thewlis lived in Bondi during the shoot and spent his free time doing coastal walks and travelling to the Blue Mountains.
"I realise when I'm here, for some reason I never feel down when here, and I think it's something to do with the water. I was raised by the sea in England. I think the city completely surrounded by water does something rather positive for me," he said.
In the show, Thewlis plays Fagin, a pickpocket thief and a father figure to Jack, played by Brodie-Sangster, who shot to fame as Liam Neeson's love-sick son in Love Actually.
"He [Fagin] wants to be redeemed and he wants to show his deep love for him [Jack]. That's something that I just kept, as a little secret for myself that isn't necessarily there in the intention of the directors or writers — but every day I would sort of have this little secret — it's all about my love for him."
The Artful Dodger is currently streaming on Disney+.

title: Sex and the City actor and broadway star Frances Sternhagen dies aged 93
content:
Tony Award-winning actor Francis Sternhagen, best known for her Broadway success and recurring Sex and the City appearances, has died aged 93.
The stage and screen star died at her New York home on Monday night, according to a statement from her son, John Carlin.
"Frannie. Mom. Frances Sternhagen. On Monday night, Nov 27, she died peacefully at her home, a month and a half shy of her 94th birthday," he said.
"I'm very lucky I was able to call her my mum, my friend, my song and dance partner. We were together last week, and we spoke Monday afternoon, said how much we loved and missed one another."
Sternhagen’s publicist confirmed she was in New Rochelle, New York, at the time of her death.
Sternhagen won a Tony for best featured actress in a play in 1974 for her role in Neil Simon's The Good Doctor, and a second one in 1995 for a revival of The Heiress. Her last turn on Broadway was in Seascape in 2005.
She gathered four other Tony nominations over her illustrious stage career for starring or featured roles in The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window, Equus, Angel and Morning's at Seven.
TV viewers knew her for playing the rich grandmother of Dr John Carter (Noah Wyle) in the long-running ER. On Cheers she was the know-it-all mother of postman Cliff Clavin (John Ratzenberger) — the role brought her two Emmy nominations.
More recently, she had a recurring role in Sex and the City as Bunny MacDougal, the strong-minded mother-in-law of Charlotte (Kristin Davis), which earned her a third Emmy nomination.
Between her more recognisable feature television roles, Sternhagen lent cameos to shows ranging from 90s horror anthology Tales from the Crypt to a 2002 episode of The Simpsons where she voiced wealthy recluse Mrs Bellamy.
Playwright Paul Rudnick called her "a wonderful actress, capable of the highest comedy and deeply moving drama". She was, he wrote on X, formerly Twitter, "an indelible presence".
The Walking Dead actor Jay Huguley also took to social media to remember Sternhagen's impact on theatre lovers.
"I was fortunate enough to see this great actor in so many plays. Often sitting in between my parents," he said.
"It had such a deep impression on me as a young actor to see this woman always be great in so many different parts."
Sternhagen was born in 1930 in Washington, DC, where her father was a tax court judge. As a child, she loved to perform — she recalled herself as "a shameful show-off" — but she never considered an acting career. She entered Vassar College as a history major, but a friendly teacher suggested another direction: acting.
After graduation she taught drama, modern dance and singing outside Boston, earning $2,000 for the year before deciding to pursue work in the theatre.
She met her husband, actor Thomas A Carlin, while appearing in a production in Maryland. He died of heart failure in 1991.
She did not let her pregnancies interfere much with her work schedule, explaining that as an only child, "I always longed for a big family".
Frances Sternhagen and actor Tom Aldredge celebrate the opening of their play On Golden Pond in New York in 1979. ( AP: Paul Burnett)
She and Carlin had four sons — Paul, Tony, Peter and John — and two daughters, Amanda and Sarah. She also is survived by nine grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.
"A celebration of her remarkable career and life is planned for mid-January, near her 94th birthday," said a statement from her family. "We continue to be inspired by her love and life."
