title: Nazi Germany's influence on the new Hunger Games film
content:
The dystopian Hunger Games franchise is all about the power, control and oppression of a society living under an apartheid-like dictatorship.
So, it's fitting that the production designer of its prequel, Uli Hanisch, grew up in post-war Germany.
"For me, as a German, I take the whole question of 'what if' more seriously," he says.
Production Designer Uli Hanisch says post-war Germany was a key influence on The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. (Supplied: Roadshow)
"For me, it's a very real thing … the whole question of how would I have behaved, if I was born in that time, is a very present one … so I think it influenced me quite strongly."
When tackling The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds of Snakes, Uli and his fellow filmmakers approached the story — which is set 64 years before the original Katniss Everdeen films — like a period piece.
"We had the idea to compare the fictional history of Panem with our real history. If you count back 60-something years … then you have Berlin in the 60s, in a very comparable situation."
The prequel follows a young President Snow – who goes on to become the tyrannical dictator of Panem in the original films – living in a country recovering from war.
Grand architecture used throughout the film was inspired by the aesthetics of various restrictive political systems. (Supplied: Roadshow)
In a rare move for a major franchise, most of Songbirds and Snakes was filmed on location across Germany and Poland, including in and around the grandeur architecture constructed by Nazis.
It sets an imposing scene for the first Hunger Games film in eight years, which has already topped the box office in Australia and abroad.
Slight spoilers ahead.
The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes is set in the early days of the Hunger Games.
In their 10th year, they are held in a simplistic, Roman-style fighting ring, where tributes are penned in and provided with weapons to fight to the death. While the event is televised, almost no-one watches.
It's a far cry from the interactive landscapes that define the games in Katniss's story but, as the film progresses, we start to see the beginnings of the high-tech spectacle that is to come.
In the novel, this early-days amphitheatre is described as open-air, like the Colosseum or the other fighting arenas of the gladiators.
Uli and the team deviated for the film, choosing a closed-in arena to add a "prison-like" feeling to the set.
The exteriors of the arena were shot at Berlin's Olympic stadium, built by the Nazis for the 1936 Games. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Its exteriors take shape at Berlin's Olympic stadium, which was built by the Nazis and unveiled at the 1936 Berlin Olympic Games.
It's where a famous real-life misfit made a name for himself – African American athlete Jesse Owens won four gold medals at a Games that was hoping to prove the "superiority" of the Aryan race.
Metaphors aside, the stadium was a fitting piece of grand, fascist architecture.
"The first thing we did was research the aesthetics and architecture of restrictive systems [like] the Soviet Union, fascist Germany, Italy and Spain," Uli says.
The arena's interiors were filmed in Poland's Centennial Hall. (Supplied: Roadshow)
The arena's interiors took shape at Poland's Centennial Hall, a UNESCO World Heritage site with a 23-metre-high dome of steel and glass.
When a rebel bombing rocks the barren arena, the games are forever changed.
"This boring, empty, dusty place becomes like a real battlefield," Uli says.
Rather than a quick-fighting, ring-style showdown, slabs of concrete now give tributes somewhere to hide, as do underground tunnels that have been blasted open.
Uli says the film's director Francis Lawrence "came up with the idea of this huge piece falling from the ceiling and becoming this centre rubble piece, which almost looks like the cornucopia" from the original films.
Rubble in the bombed arena resembles the cornucopia centrepiece of the original films. (Supplied: Roadshow)
In the original Hunger Games films, Katniss's home of District 12 is a poor and struggling mining town. But in the period piece that is Songbirds and Snakes, it's thriving.
"The coal mining part of District 12 is more important for Panem than it was 65 years later," Uli explains.
District 12 is thriving in The Hunger Games prequel. (Supplied: Roadshow)
"It's like in our real world, where our coal mines and steel factories used to be more important than they are now."
Scenes here were shot in Landschaftspark in Germany, where former industrial buildings have been transformed into a public park – and make the perfect setting for District 12.
Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord 🇩🇪 Drone Aerial 4K | Germany Deutschland Duitsland
Watching the film, there's plenty of small details for fans to pick up and analyse. Weatherman (and amateur magician) Lucky Flickerman casually brings up a map of Panem while making his forecast, which has long been an integral part of the franchise's fan-lore .
Uli also challenges you to spot "this little red pulsating light … on every TV, every radio, even cars – everything which is a machine or device".
Look out for small red pulsating lights throughout the film. (Supplied: Roadshow)
"We were connecting to 2001 [A Space Odyssey] where you have the computer HAL … this controlling computer that had this big red light, almost like a face.
"[We] never really explain what it is, [you just] have a feeling that it's connected to whoever might control everything."
The film closes on Panem in full swing, with an imposing centrepiece.
"[There's] this big statue, which we call the Panema," Uli says.
Lady Liberty is subverted in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. (Supplied: Roadshow)
"It looks like Lady Liberty, but instead of having a torch and a text, welcoming everybody, it has two swords [crossed together] that says really clearly: Fuck off."
For Uli, this comes down to the message of the film, and the "morale aspect within the story".
He says while you may be "sitting very comfortably in the cinema watching the movie, there are moments where you get an idea of how it really could happen". And you start to wonder who you might be, and what you might do in that alternate reality.

Paul Lynch has won the 50,000-pound (AUD$96,000) Booker Prize for his novel Prophet Song, a dystopian novel set in Ireland in the near future.
This book describes a world of increasing political repression and social disintegration from the perspective of Eilish Stack, a mother of four living in Dublin.
The Garda National Services, Ireland's newly formed secret police, come looking for her trade unionist husband Larry, who soon goes missing. As the terror and violence ratchets up, Eilish carries on with her everyday life: caring for her children, going to the shops and helping her father.
"She's just an ordinary person living her life and trying to get back to what we all consider now to be normality," Lynch told ABC RN's The Book Show.
Judge Esi Edugyan described the winning novel as "a triumph of emotional storytelling" and praised Lynch for his visceral use of language.
"In these troubled times, we sought a novel with a guiding vision, a book to remind us that we are more than ourselves, to remind us of all that is worth saving," she said.
— Nicola Heath

We don't want to spoil things too much, but maybe this recent quote from star Jacob Elordi about a masturbation scene with his co-star will provide a little context: "I was very proud. I was very proud to have Barry Keoghan guzzling it like that." Let's leave it at that.
— Jared Richards
Lead stars Melissa Barrera and Jenna Ortega won't feature in Scream 7, with Barerra fired as a result of pro-Palestinian sentiment on her social media.
Barerra, who played lead Sam Carpenter in both the annoyingly titled 2022 reboot Scream (actually Scream 5), and 2023's Scream VI, was let go by production company Spyglass due to posts interpreted as anti-Semetic — specifically, one in which she criticised "Western media" for showing only "the [Israeli] side".
After the news broke via Variety, director Christopher Landon posted and deleted a tweet in reaction to criticism, writing, "Everything sucks. Stop yelling. This was not my decision to make."
According to Spyglass, Ortega left the upcoming Scream 7 prior to this, due to a scheduling conflict with Wednesday's second season. The two played sisters in the series – now, without them, the film's writers are having to retool their script and find new leads.
— Jared Richards
Everyone's favourite surreal, murder-driven black comedy is back!
Following a slight departure for season four, starring Chris Rock and Jason Schwartzmann in a sprawling 1950s gangland epic, the series returns to its roots, set in the snowy present-day(ish) climes of 2019 Minnesota and North Dakota, with a focus on class, gender and lethal foul play (naturally).
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
With a reputation for all-star casts, this time around we get Jon Hamm (in his first major TV role since Mad Men) playing a shady local lawman investigating typical housewife Dot, played by Juno Temple (Keeley in Ted Lasso), after a very bad parent-teacher night involving a misfired taser. But then Dot is kidnapped, which may or may not involve her wealthy, acerbic mother-in-law, played by Jennifer Jason Leigh. Cue the intrigue.
There's only three episodes so far (streaming via SBS On Demand), but the set-up signals another gripping ride with unexpected twists and turns, including the trademark blend of arch dialogue, stylised direction and a ripping soundtrack selection, featuring surprising uses of prog rock titans Yes and The Prodigy's Smack My Bitch Up.
Oh, and Spoiler Alert: Jon Hamm gives us nipple-rings and some full-screen derriere action. How's that for a drawcard?
— Al Newstead
While the Gen Zs are having possibly their first experience of fully comprehending the interminable march of time, parents are having flashbacks to their toddlers screaming "AGAIN!" at them as they weep on the floor.
It's seriously been ten years? (Supplied: Parent Circle Facebook page)
Although you will later be quietly cursing me, Disney and the whole Arendelle royal family when you realise you have Let it Go stuck on loop in your head, I think it's also fair to share the love for a story with women fighting their own battles, heartwarming sisterly bonds, songs you can truly belt along to and an animate snowman. The wider world also got to realise the witchy power of Idina Menzel, and is better for it.
Also, we got a full decade of creative covers like this one.

title: 'Remarkably tender': Why Adam Sandler as Leo the lizard is more emotional than expected
content:
Adam Sandler has played some slimy types in his career — his performance as a slippery New York jewel dealer in Uncut Gems is an all-timer — but never one with literal scales.
In Netflix's animated musical comedy Leo, the Sandman stars as a talking tuatara dispensing wisdom to a bunch of fifth graders — his croaky voice a cross between an old rabbi and some hoary Catskills comic.
The ancient Kiwi reptile (tuatara is derived from Māori, meaning 'peaks on the back') is a pretty loopy choice for the hero of a film set in the pastel-pop suburbs of Florida, but it's exactly the kind of off-kilter non sequitur that Sandler relishes.
Turns out this prehistoric pet is the perfect pivot for a charming kids' movie that combines life lessons with grade-school existential crises, a musical lament for a depressed drone and a scene with an upturned turtle peeing on itself.
Adam Sandler stars as Leo, in the animated Netflix film of the same name, about an ageing lizard. (Supplied: Netflix)
The stories this reptile could tell. Confined to a terrarium in a fifth-grade classroom for the better part of his 74 years, Leo (Sandler) has seen generations of kids come and go from behind the glass. Little wonder he's learned a thing or two, even if his knowledge is limited to the daily dilemmas of the pre-teen set.
He's also stuck with a grouchy cellmate in Squirtle (comedian Bill Burr), a turtle with whom he trades comic routines that are, after decades in captivity, getting a little long in the tooth.
When Squirtle informs him that tuataras only live to age 75, Leo freaks out — a life wasted! — and decides it's time to make a break for the fabled Everglades, where myth tells that creatures are free to run wild.
The little green guy gets his chance when the class's tyrannical new substitute teacher, Ms. Malkin (Cecily Strong), orders the kids to take one of the pets home for the weekend and look after them to learn some responsibility.
But something odd happens: in the midst of a failed escape attempt, Leo strikes up a conversation with his caretaker, Summer (voiced by Sandler's daughter, Sunny), an awkward over-sharer to whom he gives some offhand — and, as it turns out, life-changing — musical advice.
Soon all the kids are clamouring to take this scaly sage home for a transformative weekend — from a kid who enlists Leo to help him "break up" with his needy drone (in a musical sequence that is truly inspired) to a pre-pubescent mean girl whose popularity is a mask for her unhappiness.
The catch? They all think they're confiding in Leo exclusively.
Leo tells the story of a tuatura confined to a terrarium in a fifth-grade classroom for the better part of his 74 years. (Supplied: Netflix)
"So, you got this E.T. scam going," cracks Squirtle, anticipating the inevitable moment of betrayal. "Got every kid thinking he's Elliott."
This is the second movie this year from Sandler's Happy Madison Productions that's tailored specifically to a younger audience, and both have been family affairs. Sandler's teenage daughters Sunny and Sadie led the high school comedy You Are So Not Invited To My Bat Mitzvah, and they return to voice characters here.
Both films are remarkable for the tender treatment of their characters, displaying an empathy that might suggest being a dad to teenage girls has had a lovely influence on Sandler's work.
As a kids' film, Leo hasn't so much softened the comedian's more abrasive edges — there's still plenty of his trademark persona here — than it has allowed his warmer, more inclusive side to flourish.
Adam Sandler co-wrote the screenplay as well as starring as the lead voice. His teenage daughters Sunny and Sadie also voice characters in the film. (Supplied: Netflix)
The star's childlike naïveté is well suited to this pre-teen world, where the tone meets kids on their own terms — and the life lessons are delivered with a refreshing lack of sentimentality.
"Don't cry, crying's for weaklings," Leo sings to a kid in one scene, hardly a role model for child psychology. "Dry those tears, they make you look ugly."
(Concerned parents can rest easy: there's a scientifically approved rebuttal that assures us that yes, it is okay to shed a tear.)
These songs, penned by Sandler's co-screenwriter Robert Smigel — who also co-directed with animated comedy vets Robert Marianetti and David Wachtenheim — are musical theatre pastiches that never take themselves seriously, frequently veering into nonsensical asides and crass jokes.
It's an effect that can be surprisingly moving. In one moment, a chorus of weary 11-year-olds reflect on their life as though they were performing a reverie of the ancients, a song that's made all the more poignant for its ridiculous lines and straight-faced delivery.
And why wouldn't they be dramatic? After all, these are kids on the cusp of high school: it's a very tumultuous time, especially for those of us who didn't have a talking tuatara to confide in.
Leo is out now on Netflix.
Leo | Official Teaser | Netflix

title: Baz Luhrmann's new TV series Faraway Downs returns Jackman, Kidman and 'Bowenwood' to the screen
content:
He may be one of the most famous filmmakers in the world but when Baz Lurhmann was spotted by Merle Jochheim outside her north Queensland pie shop, she assumed he was just another sightseer with a camera.
"I sat with him thinking he was a tourist … and we talked for nearly an hour," she said of the chance encounter in 2007.
"I was selling Bowen as a tourist destination."
Within days, the headline "Pie lady's script seals movie deal" was splashed across southern newspapers.
Merle Jochheim was credited by media for bringing the Australia film to Bowen. (ABC North Qld: Baz Ruddick)
Luhrmann had travelled to the small town of Bowen to scout for locations to film his 2008 epic Australia, starring Hugh Jackman and Nicole Kidman.
The coastal community clearly fitted the bill, and soon a cast and crew of hundreds moved in to make movie magic.
Sixteen years on, Australia is being reimagined and recut for a new audience as a six-part miniseries called Faraway Downs, premiering this weekend.
Ms Jochheim had a chance encounter with director Luhrmann outside her Bowen pie shop. (ABC North Qld: Lily Nothling)
The big-budget production of Australia transformed Bowen's sleepy waterfront into 1940s Darwin.
Set designers constructed a two-storey pub, police station, theatre, Chinatown and a brothel.
"To walk around the little village they had built, the roads [covered] with red dirt, and coming down on a Sunday afternoon and watching 100 head of longhorn cows being trained how to run around the town down your main street, it was just unbelievable," former mayor Mike Brunker said.
The two-storey Territory Hotel was the centrepiece of the Australia set in Bowen. (Supplied)
Locals were cast as cowboys, soldiers, drivers, drunks and policemen.
The film's star-power attracted the eyes of the world and paparazzi swarmed to the the area.
The town embraced the moniker Bowenwood, replicating the famous Hollywood sign on the side of a local water tower.
"We milked it for everything we could," Cr Brunker said.
"We had 23,000 visitors sign the visitors' book.
Mike Brunker says watching the transformation of Bowen into wartime Darwin was unbelievable. (ABC News: ABC North Qld: Lily Nothling)
Other parts of the production were filmed in Sydney, Darwin and Kununurra.
Ben De Luca, the longtime owner of Bowen's Summergarden Cinemas, got closer to the action than most.
He was responsible for showing the "rushes", or raw footage, to the cast and crew on the big screen – giving him a sneak peek of how the film's narrative would unfold.
"It was quite thrilling to be with such a mob," Mr De Luca said.
"They'd say, 'Oh, how did you get up at four o'clock every day and put [the rushes] on?'
Locals were swept up by the movie magic.  (ABC North Qld: Lily Nothling)
Mr De Luca recalls having to smuggle Nicole Kidman into the cinema's side office, away from the prying lenses of the paparazzi.
He also proudly boasts having Hugh Jackman's mobile number.
"Every girl in the town and every other town wants to steal my phone," he laughed.
The cast and crew of Australia reviewed the day's "rushes" at Ben De Luca's cinema.  (ABC North Qld: Baz Ruddick)
His small cinema later rolled out the red carpet for one of the film's official world premiere events in 2008.
While Australia was a hit among Bowen locals, the 165-minute epic received mixed reviews.
Luhrmann's decision to create an extended edit of the story – including footage that did not make the original cut – came during the pandemic after production on his Elvis biopic was shut down.
Cr Brunker said he hoped the new Faraway Downs TV series would help the story reach a new audience.
Luhrmann's Australia has been a tourist drawcard for Bowen. (ABC North Qld: Lily Nothling)
"Out of the three-hour movie, we probably haven't seen a lot of what was left … on the [cutting room] floor, so I'm looking forward to seeing the miniseries," he said.
Merle Jochheim's treasured memories of the time Hollywood came to Bowen will never fade.
She has photo albums filled with newspaper clippings from the time and snaps with the stars.
Hugh Jackman became a regular at Ms Jochheim's Bowen pie shop. (ABC North Qld: Lily Nothling)
"[Hugh Jackman] used to just park up the back of the shop, sit under our clothesline and have a coffee with [then wife] Deb, and the kids played in the backyard," Ms Jochheim said.
"I went to the premiere in Sydney, and all the stars and even the people that were just horsemen came up and made us feel so welcome.
"They became just like family."

title: 'No kissing, no touching': Iranian filmmakers can get censored by strict Islamic laws but they are finding ways around it
content:
Protests across Iran sparked by the death-in-custody of Mahsa Jina Amini in September 2022 ushered in a new kind of challenge for Iranian filmmakers.
For decades Iran's artistic community have carefully navigated the country's strict censorship rules that ban certain portrayals of women and Islam.
Its filmmakers have earned worldwide acclaim for subtly revealing the struggles and contradictions of life under a theocracy.
But since Amini's death more than one year ago, which triggered widespread protests across Iran and around the world — and gave birth to the global #womenlifefreedom movement — prominent members of the Iranian film industry have been arrested, put on trial and/or banned from making movies.
Protests in Iran, which started with the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini after being detained on the grounds that she did not comply with the headscarf rules, continue at the Iranian consulate in Istanbul Türkiye in October 2022. (Getty Images)
In June, the Islamic Republic of Iran's film watchdog warned producers that their movies could be banned if they hire actresses who remove their hijab (compulsory headscarf) in public in support of anti-government protests.
"Since the events in September 2022, basically, many filmmakers said they're not going to work — that the government didn't give permission for many of the films to be made," says Iranian Film Festival director Armin Miladi.
He says this year's film festival, which is currently screening around Australian capital cities, almost never happened.
"It's been such a difficult year for us — until even three, four months ago, I didn't know if we could have a festival in terms of finding good films," Miladi says.
Armin Miladi says Iranian filmmakers are facing challenges both inside and outside of Iran.
Miladi says only a handful of independent films get off the ground, and when they do, they sometimes get rejected by film festivals internationally.
Despite Iranian filmmakers having to work hard and get creative to get past Iran's censors, Miladi says if they get the Iranian government's tick of approval to screen inside Iran, that can be misconstrued by some in the diaspora as filmmakers not being defiant enough of the regime.
"Not everyone is happy to go to jail or … to leave Iran to make a film," Miladi says, adding that he fears over time there may be fewer social issue movies filmed in Iran.
"There are real people living in society that …. need to be able to work. Already, they are facing so many limitations from the censorship in Iran, but now they are being censored outside Iran as well."
Despite many Iranian filmmakers moving underground, making movies in Iran has become more challenging since the protests erupted and amid an associated government crackdown that's seen hundreds killed and thousands arrested, according to estimates from the Human Rights Activists News Agency.
A woman, wearing the chador, a head-to-toe garment, walks on a sidewalk in front of a mural showing the late Iranian revolutionary founder Ayatollah Khomeini, right. (AP: Vahid Salemi)
After the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Iranian cinema came under pressure, viewed by its leaders as a symbol of cultural corruption.
As Iran's authoritarian regime becomes more brutal, its citizens have become more defiant — in Tehran's streets and in cyberspace.
Films made in Iran must first get a production permit from Iran's Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance, and after a film is produced it is reviewed again for a screening permit.
What's not allowed to be shown on screen reflects the rules that govern life under the Islamic Republic.
Negative depictions of religious figures and overt criticism of the government or Islam are forbidden.
Women must appear in the hijab and are barred from singing or dancing on screen. Sexual contact, or even romantic gestures of love — kissing or embracing in any form – is banned.
Consumption of alcoholic beverages and people shown intoxicated is also not allowed.
An Iranian woman walks past a mural with a picture of the Iranian flag on a street in Tehran, Iran, October 6, 2023.  (Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS)
Iranian filmmakers have challenged the restrictions they face, sometimes meaning their movies don't screen in Iran despite earning praise in the West.
In fact, Iranian cinema has long been the darling of the international film festival circuit, earning awards at prestigious events such as Cannes, Berlin, Venice and San Sebastian.
The 2000 Iranian drama The Circle (Dayereh), produced and directed by Jafar Panahi, criticised the treatment of Iranian women and was banned in Iran but won several awards, including the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival.
Blacklisted Iranian film director Jafar Panahi starring in his film Taxi, which premiered in Berlin. (Supplied)
Similarly, Crimson Gold (Talaye Sorkh), a 2003 Iranian film directed by Jafar Panahi, and written by the late Abbas Kiarostami, was never distributed in Iranian theatres but won the Cannes Film Festival, Un Certain Regard Jury Award.
And while Iran's filmmakers have navigated the restrictions imposed by the regime, they have in some cases had the government's approval to proceed with making films that make it to the world stage.
Most notably, Iranian film director Asghar Farhadi's A Separation (2011) and The Salesman (2016) snapped up awards for Best Foreign Language Film at the Oscars.
Asghar Farhadi, director of Iranian film "A Separation", poses with his award for Best Foreign Language film during the 84th Academy Awards in Hollywood, California February 26, 2012.  (REUTERS/Mike Blake )
Despite that, it's not an all-rosy relationship between the regime and filmmakers. Some have been personally targeted.
For instance in 2010, Jafar Panahi was convicted by Iran's regime of "making propaganda against the system" and sentenced to six year's prison.
He was also given a 20-year ban on directing any movies, writing screenplays, giving interviews or leaving the country.
But Panahi has continued making films documenting the absurdities of life under the Islamic Republic that earn acclaim — after his arrest and sentencing, Panahi's 2015 film Taxi, won the Golden Bear at the Berlin film festival.
Iranian film director Jafar Panahi after his release from Evin prison is seen in his home in Tehran, Iran February 3, 2023.
He was arrested again last year when heading to a prosecutor's office to follow up on the case of another arrested filmmaker.
In February Panahi was released on bail after a hunger strike.
Despite these threats, Iranian filmmakers continue to make movies that test the boundaries.
It's unclear who inside Iran would lead a new government if the regime is toppled, but Iranians are no longer willing to support the idea that the Islamic Republic can be reformed.
While not overtly political, they bring to international audiences the realities of life under the Islamic Republic.
It's also telling that many of the latest films screening at this year's Iranian Film Festival are made by Iranian filmmakers who live abroad but who travel to their homeland to make films that resonate with global audiences.
Hassan Nazer was born and raised in Iran but is now based in the UK, and his latest film, Winners, received the 2023 BAFTA feature film award.
Set in a small provincial Iranian town where Nazer says he grew up, the plot follows two children who discover the lost Academy Award statuette of Asghar Farhadi.
Filmmaker Hassan Nazer's 'Winners' faced many restrictions from Iran's censors during filming.   (Supplied.)
Nazer says it pays tribute to the great achievements of renowned Iranian filmmakers, including the late Abbas Kiarostami, as well as Asghar Farhadi, Majid Maijdi and Jafar Panahi.
During the making of the movie Panahi was imprisoned and Nazer's certificate to make the film was revoked.
"I told them, 'you already give it [the certificate] to me'," he says.
Hassan Nazer (left) says says during the making of the movie Jafar Panahi was imprisoned and his certificate to make the film Winners was revoked.  (Supplied.)
Another restriction Nazer faced in making the movie was that he wasn't allowed to show Panahi's face or anyone resembling the great filmmaker.
Nazer says the way he dealt with it was to show Panahi from behind, which in some ways made his presence more prominent.
"This is a big challenge for directors in Iran, you know, going through censorship," Nazer explains.
"You want to bring something into the world, you want to create something, and having this limitation is stopping you. So, we have to be so much more creative."
Hassan Nazer says Iranian film censors can revoke the permission to film at any time. (Supplied.)
German based Iranian filmmaker Behrooz Karamizade speaks of similar struggles with Iran's censors.
He is the director of Empty Nets, which was awarded the 2023 Adelaide Film Festival Feature Fiction Prize for its portrayal of the dire socio-economic reality for Iran's youth.
Karamizade says he uses symbolism and metaphors to convey messages, and thereby, "it's not a political film, it's a social issue film".
Behrooz Karamizade says he uses symbolism and metaphors to convey messages about life in Iran. (Supplied.)
He says by shedding light on the economic hardships faced by Iran's poor — the lack of employment opportunities and low wages — and focusing on the environmental harm caused by waste and illicit fishing in the Caspian Sea, his movie brings to light these daily problems.
"It's about the struggle of the young people in Iran — it shows a very dark situation for them," he says.
But he adds that it was tough to get the permission to shoot the film: "You have to first give the script to [Iran's censors] and they have to check it," he explains.
Beating Iran's censors means getting more creative says Behrooz Karamizade. (Supplied.)
"And if there are elements, which are not representing something good in their opinion — I still don't really know what that is exactly — that has to be taken care of.
"But we try our best to keep our main idea and not to change our stories completely. For example, you cannot show kisses, hugging and touching, it's the law. So we have to find different ways to show it. We decided to show love through poetry and images of the sea."
Foreign film festivals still feature the underground work of Iranian filmmakers, ones that often defy mandatory hijab.
And like Nazer and Karamizade's films they continue to shine a spotlight on pressing social and economic issues.
An Iranian woman walks on a street in Tehran, Iran August 13, 2023. Iran's unemployment and inflation rates remain high.  (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency via REUTERS.)
But as Iran's unemployment and inflation rates continue to soar, it's become far harder to attract investment to make independent movies.
Iran has conducted the first known execution in relation to the anti-government protests, hanging a man for "waging war against God". Now there are fears many more could face execution under these "sham trials".
Miladi, who lives in Iran, says there are currently two types of movies that are profitable in Iran – ones that are backed by the government or low-budget comedies.
"But the rest — if they're arthouse films or social issue subjects … not many people [in Iran] go to see these films," he explains.
"They're already seeing a lot of real stuff happening in their society, so it's not much of interest for them to go to the cinema and watch that. And many of the relevant social issue films don't get permission to be made anyway."
He says just because a movie is made within the Islamic Republic's censorship guidelines, "doesn't mean the government is backing them".
"That's just how the rules are in Iran," he says.
But for Iranian filmmakers working abroad, the rules can be bent, at least if the censors don't know about it.
Los Angeles-based award-winning Iranian filmmaker Elika Rezaee says her recent short film, Fereshteh, which depicts a day in the life of an ageing Iranian mother and has scenes of her partially nude, will never see the light of day in Iran.
The film "Fereshteh" depicts a day in the life of an ageing Iranian mother. (Supplied.)
But for Razaee that's the price she was willing to pay.
She used her own mother to tell the story and filmed the entire movie inside a Tehran apartment to avoid ever having to deal with Iran's censors.
"I always wanted to have the 100 per cent freedom [to make films]," says Rezaee, who earned her editing and directing skills under the most significant filmmakers in Iran but was later educated in the West.
She partially attributes her success as an editor and filmmaker to her Iranian upbringing. But she also notes that it's because she lives abroad, that she can make films like Fereshteh, and the Australian movie, Shayda, which she was the editor of.
"I can go against the censorship that is happening in Iran, which in the past couple of years, has been getting worse and worse," she says.
But because she's avoided Iran's censors with a film that they may take offence to, Razaee says she is worried about returning to her country of birth.
"I do fear going back," she says. "But at some point, I might have to."

title: 'Gonna have to be OK with male attention': Australian drinking culture through the eyes of two outsiders
content:
Midway through the Australian gothic classic Wake in Fright, the leading man peels off from one of many manic, beer-fuelled brodowns in order to seek out the company of the woman of the house.
It's a move regarded with suspicion by his drinking companions in the fictional town of Bundanyabba ('the Yabba'): "Whattsa matter with him? He'd rather talk to a woman than drink?" inquires one.
In The Royal Hotel, Kitty Green's thriller-adjacent follow-up to The Assistant, and the director's first production on home soil, these are two things that inevitably go together — men want to get soused AND chat to women. Sometimes this makes for a merry exchange, sometimes menacing; the tenor is liable to shift without warning.
South By South West's opening film The Royal Hotel re-examines the classic outback thriller through a female lens, and asks: When is it OK to say no?
Like Wake in Fright, Green's film probes the darker side of masculinity as magnified by a remote outback setting and alcohol consumption on a liver-defying scale — and evokes the spectre of horror without ever actually letting it loose — but it does so from an emphatically feminine perspective.
Julia Garner, who carried Green's elegantly pointed fiction debut — which remains the most compelling of the #MeToo movies — returns for another uneasy shift at a workplace where the gendered power imbalance can easily tip into sexual exploitation or outright violence.
THE ROYAL HOTEL - Official Trailer
Garner's Hanna and her bestie Liv (Jessica Henwick, Glass Onion) are introduced as carefree backpackers, revelling in the beauty of Australia as experienced on a thumping Sydney Harbour daytime cruise.
When the money runs out however, the gals have little choice but to take the first gig that comes their way: The Royal Hotel, a faded, far-flung outpost that caters to a sparse mining community, beckons.
"You're gonna have to be OK with a little male attention," advises the woman at the job agency, with an ease with euphemism that seems straight out of the film production office in The Assistant.
The line is more or less lifted straight out of real life, however.
As the story of the two outsider backpackers unfolds, each of the girls' interactions with The Royal's regulars has the potential to turn sour. (Supplied: See Saw Films)
Together with co-writer Oscar Redding, Green modelled her fiction on Pete Gleeson's 2016 documentary Hotel Coolgardie, which vividly captures the precarious relations between two young Finnish women hired to sling beers at the eponymous WA pub and their solicitous rough-hewn regulars.
"They grow a leg when there's new girls in town," chuckles the real-life pub's proprietor.
At the Hotel Coolgardie, the euphemisms that get thrown around are far less oblique than those used in the corporate space, and so perhaps register as less sinister.
The industry seems to have evolved, with skimpies and pub customers saying respect is at the forefront.
Both kinds of double-speak, however, point to the same troubling assumption that, when a woman is behind the bar, the price of a pint buys something more than beer.
In their take, Green and Redding sideline Hotel Coolgardie's leering but gentle old codgers, who come bearing odd gifts (plastic bracelets, cheap banana liqueur), opting instead to foreground younger men, whose overtures towards Hanna and Liv are weighted with greater intent — and danger.
Both Toby Wallace (Babyteeth), as the flirty, affable larrikin who just might turn pushy, and Daniel Henshall (Snowtown), as the simmering, short-fused loner, are perfectly cast, although followers of Australian cinema will have seen them do variations on these acts before.
In so narrowing the focus, Green ratchets up the tension (even as Hugo Weaving's farcically drunken publican stumbles in every now and again, shaking up the tone).
As seen mostly through the eyes of Hanna, being the more cautious of the two friends, each of the girls' interactions with The Royal's regulars has the potential to turn sour.
And yet, to betray any such fear might in itself be a catalyst for violence, insofar as it seems an insult; a pre-emptive condemnation of whatever man is seated on the other side of the bar, or lingering outside the bedroom door.
Hugo Weaving appears in The Royal Hotel as the farcicly drunken publican. (Supplied: See Saw Films)
Hanna's increasing reticence to soothe fragile male egos (even as Liv errs on the side of going with the liquored-up flow) is a kind of rejoinder to the passivity of the demure assistant Garner played in Green's previous chamber piece.
It makes sense, then, that that film concludes without offering any kind of resolution, whereas The Royal Hotel culminates in a big, impulsive act of defiance — embodying the fury of these women scorned. Unfortunately, this finale feels rather tacked on; a flashy quick fix for a narrative at a murky impasse.
In The Royal Hotel, the story of two female outsiders plonked into the Australian desert takes on the feel of a parable.  (Supplied: See Saw Films )
It seems a little paradoxical to posit that The Royal Hotel is both less cartoonish and less complex than the documentary that inspired it — and yet, in the transition from documentary to fiction, the story of two female outsiders plonked into the Australian desert has taken on the feel of a parable.
It seems designed to illustrate a point, rather than the particulars of a group of people. Green acquits herself here with intelligence, style, and precision, but doesn't achieve the hair-raising looseness of a night at the Hotel Coolgardie, nor in the Yabba.
The Royal Hotel is in cinemas now.

title: We all know about Napoleon, but we've never seen it played quite like Joaquin Phoenix
content:
Joaquin Phoenix plies his trademark eccentricity in Ridley Scott's engrossing, if somewhat broad-brushed, portrait of Napoleon.
The actor's fidgety, low-key erratic performance is so pivotal to this two-and-a-half-hour saga of tortured romance, rolling wars and political power plays, after a certain point you begin to wonder if it's more his film than Scott's.
The truth is it's a bit of both. If you've seen Phoenix's movies of the last decade at least, the neurosis and flashes of volatility will be familiar. But you'll also recognise Scott's bizarro streak, an under-utilised sensibility that made his 2013 thriller The Counsellor such a kinky outlier.
But let's remind ourselves first of this story.
Napoleon is a Corsican artillery officer who rises to power in the comedown of the French Revolution to become, for a time, the world's most brilliant and ruthless military strategist. He wages bloody wars across Europe, Russia and Egypt that kill hundreds of thousands, crowns himself Emperor of France but then is forcibly exiled — twice.
He also falls hard for a widowed mother of two, Josephine, born outside the French establishment like him, on an island (Martinique).
The film was shot in just 62 days. (Pictured: Scott and Phoenix on set) (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
By any measure, the story is unwieldy, and it famously eluded the late Stanley Kubrick, one of Scott's heroes, who was said to have been obsessed.
Truth be told, there's an echo here of a film Kubrick did make: Barry Lyndon, a 1975 period drama with a similar rise-and-fall plot and themes of doomed romance.
The difference is that Kubrick cast Ryan O'Neal, an actor whose almost vacuous handsomeness made him harder to read and resulted in a more enigmatic, understated film.
The Screen Show brings you reviews and in-depth conversations with leading film and TV directors, actors and screenwriters.
Scott aims for something more operatic with Phoenix; a depiction of psychological torment that's on the surface of his performance, fluctuating amid extremes. The result is a Napoleon who is at once impatient and detached, contemplative and ruffled.
The hardened military officers and political veterans interpret this volatility and social awkwardness as a charismatic aloofness. It also charms the battle-weary men of the French army, who follow him through Egyptian deserts and Russian winters.
We, the audience, recognise the erraticism as the anxiety of a man who fears he will never be good enough, but the only character on screen who understands this is Josephine (a superb Vanessa Kirby, delicate and formidable).
In establishing her agency in this peculiar relationship, Scott sets up the couple's first date in a formal, wood-panelled sitting room, then has her open her legs wide, beckoning him to look up her dress.
"[Napoleon] was, without question, a dictator … and yet he was vulnerable on one side of his life to a woman," Scott told GamesRadar. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
This crude sexual gesture — which comes from nowhere to disrupt the scene's starched formality — is a moment in the film where you realise Scott is pushing all his chips into the centre of the table.
It's a gesture so bold, you have to admire him for trying and, in hindsight, it lands pretty well as a harbinger of the couple's fraught dynamic.
It certainly works much better than Cillian Murphy reading from the Bhagavad Gita during sex with Florence Pugh in Oppenheimer — this year's other studio movie about a wartime genius whose actions also resulted in the suffering of millions.
Scott's depiction of Napoleon and Josephine — their tender confidences and fierce arguments — is ultimately very moving, and it's remarkable how well he flicks between this intimate register and the grander tapestry of Napoleon's military dramas.
"If you don’t think there was mass killing, you’re naive," Scott told Deadline. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
The battle scenes are among the film's highlights.
Scott frames them with restraint, often staying wide like a landscape painter, but the action unfolds with coarse violence and shocking randomness.
A cannonball rips through the flesh of a charging horse, an army falls through the ice of a frozen lake.
There's undoubtedly a lot of digital manipulation in these sequences, but there's also a sense of grit, conveyed in small details like flecks of mud or raindrops on the camera lens.
This grit extends to Phoenix's ruddy and scarred features, which are in stark contrast to the porcelain-skinned portraits of Napoleon bequeathed to us by French painters like Ingres or David.
"[Joaquin Phoenix] is the best player of damaged goods," Ridley Scott told Empire. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
Scott's Napoleon is flesh and blood.
He's also a walking signifier of self-belief, and the film eventually succeeds in transmitting that power.
For a time, at least, this is Napoleon's world, and we're all just living in it — but it could very well double as a late-career self-portrait from one of Hollywood's most enduring directors.
Napoleon is in cinemas now.

title: 'It's taking the piss': Victorian youth justice staff frustrated by film crew in Malmsbury
content:
Workers at the Malmsbury Youth Justice Precinct are questioning why a film crew has been allowed to shoot a movie at the centre before it closes next month.
The Department of Justice and Community Safety has confirmed Charles Williams Films is producing a film at the precinct, despite there being a small group of young people still held at the site.
"The safety and security of Malmsbury is of paramount importance," the department said in a statement.
It did not address why filming was taking place before all young people had transitioned out of the centre.
Staff, who spoke to the ABC on the condition of anonymity due to fears over their employment, said there were still security concerns that had yet to be addressed after a "riot" on October 3, which saw three young people taken to hospital.
"To put it really bluntly, it's taking the piss," a staff member said.
"You've got young people and staff that have been traumatised by the incident.
"It's rubbing salt in a wound."
Film production trucks parked outside the Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre. (
               ABC News: Kristofor Lawson
            )
The ABC understands seven workers at the youth justice centre were held hostage during the "riot", and one young person was so severely injured that they were "unidentifiable".
Shadow Youth Justice Minister Brad Battin said the government "had its priorities wrong".
The ABC understands the film in progress stars English-born Australian actor Guy Pearce, and centres on a young person transferred from a juvenile detention centre to an adult jail.
Comment has been sought from Charles Williams Films and the film's producer.
The Department of Justice and Community Safety has confirmed Charles Williams Films is producing a film at the centre. (ABC News: Kristofor Lawson)
All young people will be transitioned out of the Malmsbury Youth Justice Precinct by the end of the year, the department said.
The transition process has been underway for months, and the ABC understands there are fewer than 20 young people left at the site.
The department said there would be no contact between the film crew and young people, and filming would not take place in occupied units.
"There will be no impact on the secure operation of Malmsbury and young people's movements around the precinct won't be affected," its statement said.
Film crews entering the Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre via a side entrance. (
               ABC News: Kristofor Lawson
            )
However, workers told the ABC that young people were being moved around to accommodate filming and would be unable to access parts of the site for several days.
"It's impacting the young people that are still there," a staff member said.
Another staffer said they first learnt about plans to film in the youth justice centre from young people at the centre, who had noticed crew members walking around the site.
"It's just mind-boggling," the worker said.
The youth justice precinct is closing next month. (ABC News: Kristofor Lawson)
Staff told the ABC security issues that were raised after the October 3 "riot" had yet to be addressed.
"WorkSafe continues to monitor the site to ensure occupational health and safety obligations are being met," a spokesperson for the state's workplace safety watchdog said.
Asked whether it would be paid for the use of the space for filming, the department said it would be "cost neutral," but that it would receive compensation for any extra expenses.

title: Australian teen snags big role in Hunger Games prequel after losing part of arm in painful childhood accident
content:
When Knox Gibson was three, his right arm was accidentally severed by a ride-on lawnmower being driven by his grandfather in central western New South Wales.
"I was behind the lawnmower, and he didn't see me, and he reversed back over the top of me, and the blade cut essentially through my arm and down to the bone twice on my leg," Knox said.
"My arm had to be amputated, and I had a broken leg."
His life was saved because the lawnmower blades were so hot they cauterised the wound and temporarily stopped the bleeding.
"[My grandfather] was pretty devastated after it happened, but we never blamed him for it because something like that is a freak accident."
Knox Gibson spent more than a month in hospital after his part of his arm was severed by a mower. (Supplied: Knox Gibson)
Knox spent more than a month in hospital recovering from the accident.
"I ended up getting a prosthetic for my birthday ... so that was a cool birthday present," he said.
Now 16, Knox made his first foray into television by appearing in a washing detergent advertisement.
"It was a really good ad actually for inclusion, and that was just kind of the gateway into everything," he said.
"From there, I just kind of did more modelling things and runways and then more commercials — and then eventually the short film that I did for Netflix."
The cast of the new Hunger Games movie including Knox Gibson (third from left). (Supplied: Knox Gibson )
Knox's next stop was Hollywood and the fictional world of Panem, for the latest Hunger Games movie, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.
The movie is a prequel to the previous three films.
"It was pretty nerve-wracking; we didn't get told when we were auditioning that it was the Hunger Games, but we had worked it out because Mum had recognised the name of my character [I was auditioning for]," he said.
"About a week and a half later, they told me I'd got the role.
Knox plays Bobbin, a tribute from District 8 and the first victim of Coriolanus Snow, who later becomes the dictator of Panem.
Knox Gibson as Bobbin on the set of the new Hunger Games movie. (Supplied: Knox Gibson)
"He's tough, but he's a little bit overlooked by essentially everyone, and he really wants to prove that he's got a chance at winning the games," the teenager said.
Knox spent six months filming in Germany and Poland and said he was awed by the Hollywood actors he worked with.
"Filming with some of those actors who are so experienced, like Peter Dinklage and Viola Davis, they're all so talented, and to be able to watch them and learn from them, it was amazing," he said.
Knox is one of several actors in the movie with a disability.
Why Francis Lawrence cast Rachel Zegler and Tom Blyth in the new Hunger Games prequel.
"It's incidental. It's not really spoken about that the characters have any sort of disability, which I think is a really, really good thing," he said.
"It's just a representation of the real world really — if we had a Hunger Games now, there'd be people with disabilities in it.
"I think [the director's] goal was to show that even if you had a disability, there wouldn't be any mercy on you, and it was to show the cruelness of the games and the origin of how they came to be in the later films."
Knox said his grandfather was proud of everything he had achieved in the past 13 years.
"To see me kind of start getting into swimming and be successful in that and then coming to this [movie] now, I think he's really happy."

title: Nat Bass comes out, The Crown tackles Diana's last days and Blak artist makes Paris debut
content:
There's a pretty good chance you don't need me to tell you that The Crown's final season is upon us, with the first four episodes dropping last week. How did the Royal Family drama handle Princess Diana's final days?
Well, it depends on who you ask. Reviewers, across the board, didn't love it — you can find our review wrap-up here, but The Guardian was the most brutal. Their reviewer broke out the rare one-star review and called the season "the very definition of bad writing", especially the scenes where 'Ghost Diana' returns. Ouch.
Social media is much more positive, as people take the show for what it's become — a soapy, scandalous take on history — and enjoy the recreations of iconic moments, including of Diana's amazing wardrobe. And one thing everyone can agree on? Melbourne's own Elizabeth Debicki excels in Diana's final moments.
But if you're all Royal-ed out, we've got you covered: from rap legends becoming flautists to your TikTok crush taking centre-stage, find the week's entertainment news below.
Best known as one half of hugely influential Atlanta duo Outkast, André 3000 is regarded as one of the greatest rappers of his generation. But you won't hear any of his showstopping rhymes on New Blue Sun — the 48-year-old's new solo album and first full project in 17 years.
Instead, he's delivered a meditative set of jazz-leaning instrumentals orbiting around his woodwind and flute playing, boasting lengthy song titles like 'I swear, I Really Wanted To Make A "Rap" Album But This Is Literally The Way The Wind Blew Me This Time'. (And that's the least bizarre example.)
YouTube 3000 I Swear, I Really Wanted To Make A 'Rap' Album  But This Is Literally The Way The Wind Blew
It's one of 2023's most surprising releases, but also one of its most soothing. Who'd a thunk the brains behind 'Hey Ya!' was capable of such cosmic ambiance?
— Al Newstead
Former Neighbours star, Rogue Traders frontwoman and Alive singer Natalie Bassingthwaighte has opened up about her new relationship.
In an interview with Stellar magazine and their podcast Something To Talk About, the performer spoke for the first time about her recent split from her Rogue Traders bandmate and husband of 12 years, Cameron McGlinchey.
While she continues to co-parent her two children with her ex, the 48-year-old also revealed she's in a new relationship with a woman.
While Nat says she was "terrified" about sharing her "beautiful" same-sex relationship with the world, and hasn't yet publicly identified her partner, she's found someone "who makes my heart smile and makes me happy".
Sounds like she's seeing 'One Thousand Stars'! Perhaps she's even breathing one thousand breaths, hearing one thousand voices singing and feeling one thousand heartbeats, too?
— Rachel Rasker
Even if you don't know Matt Rife's name, you'll likely recognise his cheekbones … and abs. The 28-year-old American stand-up has made a name for himself by posting videos of his crowd work to TikTok, racking up more than 17 million followers for his quick wit. And yes, lets be honest, his good looks have a lot to do with it, too.
YouTube trailer for Matt Rife: Natural Selection.
Now, we can see him outside of short videos, as his first Netflix special, Natural Selection, dropped this Friday — perfect for those who missed tickets to his sold-out Australian tour this January.
His hour-long set has no audience interaction at all. Instead, he sticks to written material, covering everything risqué from new-age healing, social media trolls, cancel culture and plenty of dick jokes.
While some critics aren't sold — Vulture called it "uninspiring and entirely underwhelming" — it's immediately jumped up Netflix's trending charts, second only to The Crown. Sure, some of the viewers are probably just staring at his biceps, but a stream's a stream.
— Jared Richards
Acclaimed UK author AS Byatt has died in London at 87.
Byatt won the Booker Prize in 1990 for her fifth novel, Possession: A Romance, described by the New York Times as a "literary blockbuster". Gwyneth Paltrow and Aaron Eckhart starred in the 2002 screen adaptation of the novel.
Byatt was born Antonia Susan Drabble in Sheffield in 1936. She published 11 novels and six short story collections in her writing career. She was also known for her literary criticism — particularly of the work of her idol, mentor and friend, Iris Murdoch.
Byatt — appointed CBE in 1990 and made a dame in 1999 — was renowned for her intellect and erudition.
Appearing on ABC RN's The Book Show in 2009 to discuss her novel The Children's Book, she said: "The more research you do, the more at ease you are in the world you're writing about. It doesn't encumber you; it makes you free."
— Nicola Heath
Dylan Mooney is a legally blind Mackay-born artist is known for his vivid comic-book-inspired digital illustrations, depicting queer and First Nations identities and experiences of love.
His first-ever retrospective, featuring more than 25 of his signature illustrative portraits, has just opened in Paris, with support from the National Gallery of Victoria (NGV).
Each portrait in Mooney's new collection has been painted with ochre taken from Yuwi Country. (Pictured: Stuck on You, 2020) (Supplied: N. Smith Gallery)
A Yuwi, Torres Strait and South Sea Islander man, Mooney won this year's Brisbane Portrait Prize, worth $50,000, for his portrait Still Thriving, which combines digital illustration with Yuwi ochre and ink. If you're in Sydney, you may have seen the Olympic pool-sized mural of the same work painted on the Top of the Town building, which was unveiled as part of World Pride.
The director of the NGV Tony Ellwood, described Mooney as "one of the most compelling emerging voices in Australian contemporary art".
Blak Rainbow: The Art of Dylan Mooney is at the Australian Embassy Gallery, Paris until May 24, 2024.
— Anna Freeland
The Tillies make us proud on the pitch, but it's the love and friendship that surround the team that have inspired me to pick up soccer again, and feel more comfortable in my own skin.
After making an entire nation obsessed with them at the Women's World Cup, our beloved Tillies have taken out the coveted Word of the Year, too.
The Australian National Dictionary Centre has picked the word "Matilda" as the Word of the Year for 2023, so I can only assume their team has a TikTok fyp full of unhinged edits, just like me.
The Strawberry-Kisses loving superstars have taken over from 2022's word of the year, "teal", (think: election; teal wave).
I can only assume they celebrated with Australia's unofficial national anthem (Nikki Webster version).
— Rachel Rasker
Rebecca Gibney and Richard Roxburgh make one powerful husband-and-wife duo in the trailer for Prosper: a new Stan drama about a fictional Australian evangelical church called U Star.
In the series, the actors play Cal and Abi Quinn, leaders of the Sydney megachurch, as it looks to expand into the US.
YouTube trailer for Stan original series Prosper.
The drama follows the family's internal power struggles — promising tears, fires and conniving Christian pop stars. Consider us intrigued.
The series arrives on January 18.
— Jared Richards

title: 'Guileless charmer or calculated schemer': Academy Award winner Emerald Fennell puts her spin on class envy in Saltburn
content:
Emerald Fennell's films could be masterpieces of deceit and degeneracy, pop and provocation — if only she could stick the landing.
In 2020, the English actor-turned-director cannonballed into view with her film Promising Young Woman: an astounding sugar rush of a debut, with a plot that sliced and diced its way through a stadium's worth of lecherous men.
Hollywood took notice: from the film's candied stylings (including a hall-of-fame needle drop courtesy of Paris Hilton); to its wounded, vengeful protagonist (Carey Mulligan); to its timely rebuke against the rot of patriarchy.
It's a shame that Promising Young Woman concluded with a final-act curveball so convoluted it blurred the laser focus of its preceding 90 minutes.
The same could be said for Fennell's latest film Saltburn, a lightly farcical joy-ride through the trials and trivialities of the upper crust.
Oliver's story is tragic, a dead father and an absent mother. (Supplied: MGM and Amazon Studios)
It's 2006, and it's move-in day at Oxford University — that rarefied Petri dish of wealth, frippery and weaponised intellect.
Oliver (Barry Keoghan, from The Banshees of Inisherin) is a wide-eyed freshman who gazes at the campus with religious awe. Softly spoken and painfully overdressed, he is a bespectacled oddity amid a sea of nattering classmates who have already gathered into cliques.
All except Oliver possess a fluency with the elite – though you get the sense he's wilier than he lets on, fuelled by a hunger to blend in with his blue-blooded peers. The film might as well be called Promising Young Man.
He meets his foil in Felix (Australian actor Jacob Elordi, from Euphoria), the gravitational centre of campus life, whose eyebrow piercing and rakish allure belie his aristocratic roots.
Felix is the stuff of Abercrombie and Fitch mood boards: impossibly hunky, armed with a smile as sharp as a blade and permanently haloed in sunbeams. Oliver eyes him off with equal parts suspicion and desire.
Director Emerald Fennell has said that Australian actor Jacob Elordi did an exceptional audition for the role of Felix. (Supplied: MGM and Amazon Studios)
A chance run-in between the pair leads to a fast friendship forged over sloshing pints, though an uneasy question always threatens to puncture their bliss: Is Oliver merely a charity case?
Any existential dilemmas, however, quickly take a back seat to the arrival of summer break when Oliver is spirited away to Felix's family manor – an Edenic estate that gives the film its title.
It's larger than a postcode, replete with chandeliers dangling from every gilded surface and managed by a small army of butlers. "Wow," Oliver gawps. "Just wow."
He wields the tragic story of a dead father and an absent mother as his entry ticket into these hallowed halls, where the residents coo and fuss over his misfortunes.
Among them are Felix's immediate kin, as well as his American cousin Farleigh (Archie Madekwe), slippery and disdainful, and the troubled family friend Pamela (played by Carey Mulligan with an increasingly crazed glower).
Saltburn has not-so-subtle references to Brideshead Revisited, The Talented Mr Ripley, Call Me By Your Name and and Marie Antoinette.   (Supplied: MGM and Amazon Studios)
Saltburn, with its winding corridors and labyrinth of hidden passageways, is ripe for intrigue. It's here that Oliver indulges in the frivolities of wealth, frolicking naked through grassy meadows and popping champagne with his new playmates over rounds of tennis.
Soon enough, he has ingratiated himself with the clan.
Keoghan walks a razor-thin line between guileless charmer and calculated schemer. Is Oliver a buffoon who's lucked his way to the top, or has he successfully exploited the vulnerabilities of each family member in a series of sinister machinations?
The film works best when it tunnels into these ambiguities, a streak of catty, psychosexual suspense thrumming beneath an endless stream of formal dinners and society soirees.
Fennell's cinematic references here aren't particularly subtle. The most glaring is Brideshead Revisited, another parable of an interloper amidst English aristocracy.
It doesn't take long for Oliver to embrace the champagne lifestyle of those gathered at the Saltburn manor. (Supplied: MGM and Amazon Studios)
In Oliver and Felix's homoeroticism – the kind of friendship that could devolve into smut at any given second – there's more than a whiff of Luca Guadagnino's Call Me By Your Name and Anthony Minghella's The Talented Mr. Ripley.
Sofia Coppola's Marie Antoinette, too, looms large above Saltburn's rococo reverie and anachronistic soundtrack.
Fennell's take is just stylish enough to transcend mere mimicry. But the thrills can only last so long.
In its denouement, Saltburn relinquishes the voyeuristic pleasures in favour of a plot twist that bludgeons any underlying tensions to a pulp.
It is overly neat, overly long and overly explanatory, dulling the acuteness of Fennell's class satire.
In all its excess, the film mirrors its titular estate: a grandiose statement with a hollow core. You might wish it ended 30 minutes earlier.
Saltburn is in cinemas now.

title: Historian traces steps of Aussie outback cult classic film ahead of high-definition makeover
content:
A film and television historian is retracing the steps of a cult classic Australian movie ahead of it being given a high-definition makeover.
The upcoming Blu-ray re-release of 1971 film Wake In Fright, which starred Broken Hill-born actor Chips Rafferty, prompted Andrew Mercado to start making a documentary to go with it.
He said that while the bottom had fallen out of the DVD market due to streaming, something else was working well.
"One thing that is still working is collector's editions," Mr Mercado said.
"Because Wake In Fright is such a well-regarded Australian film and because it has so many fans, we were determined to make a new featurette documentary for this next release that would really kind of be an ultimate documentary on the making of the film."
The movie, which was filmed in and around Broken Hill, tells the story of John Grant, a teacher dissatisfied with his job in the fictional outback town of Tiboonda.
It also starred Gary Bond and Jack Thompson.
Andrew Mercado is making the documentary in far west NSW. (Supplied: Andrew Mercado)
Mr Mercado and his crew set out to Broken Hill to find the original locations that were in the film.
While they were determined to find every location, there was one in particular they wanted.
The cloudless sky and desert landscape in far-west New South Wales have enticed filmmakers for decades but there is hope that a locally driven initiative will do even more to attract the industry.
"Back then when they filmed in 1970, the region was in drought so it's this incredible shot where the camera revolves 360 degrees and all you can see is flat red scorched desert earth in all directions."
The film crew from the original movie had transported the set pieces they used for the school and the pub to the site, but Mr Mercado wasn't sure what they may find.
"We knew that this schoolhouse and pub had not been kept there and that all we might find would be a few remnants, a couple of bricks or something like that to give us a clue of where it was," he said.
Luckily, Terry Smith from Scarsdale Station had heard an interview Mr Mercado had done on radio and got in contact.
"Would you believe it, the very grazier who owned the property and had been told where the location was, he was listening to that radio broadcast," Mr Mercado said.
"We met Terry as soon as we arrived at the airport, and he was able to drive us to this exact location which we never would have found without his local knowledge."
June Marie Bennett was in the audience on opening night of the Wake in Fright.  (Supplied: Andrew Mercado)
Wake In Fright wasn't received well when it opened in cinemas as the content of the film shocked people.
"[Thompson] turned around and said, 'Sit down, it bloody well is'."
June Marie Bennett, who was at the cinema on opening night, was interviewed for the documentary about her experience.
"I can remember we were excited because this was something new for Broken Hill," she said.
"We embraced the idea that the film crew came here, so the night I attended it was packed and there was all this buzz and excitement."
Donald Pleasence, Gary Bond, Peter Whittle and Jack Thompson star in 1971's Wake in Fright. (Supplied: Madman Entertainment )
However, she said things took a bit of a turn during the screening.
"As the movie progressed, there's a hush coming over," Ms Bennett said.
"And then it's hitting us, this is too much for our senses and they started walking out."
Ms Bennett said the movie did nothing for the city.
"It was just like a person alcoholic state the whole movie," she said.
Wake In Fright is set to be re-released on Blu-ray in early 2024 by Umbrella Entertainment.

title: David Holmes was flying high as a Harry Potter stunt double – until he was paralysed on-set
content:
In the wizarding world, Harry Potter was known as "the boy who lived" — but it's a stunt double for the blockbuster franchise who knows he's lucky to be alive.
In a new HBO documentary, David Holmes: The Boy Who Lived, we meet Holmes, who played Daniel Radcliffe's stunt double in the Harry Potter films before he was paralysed in an on-set accident.
With Holmes teaming up with Radcliffe to share his story, here are some of the key moments from the 90-minute documentary.
From the Philosopher's Stone to the Half Blood Prince, Holmes performed countless manoeuvres, from "flying" through the air playing Quidditch to swimming underwater during the Triwizard tournament.
But it was during rehearsals in 2009 for Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part 1 where everything changed.
In the film, Harry and Hermione visit the cemetery where Harry's parents are buried before following a witch into her home in their search for Voldemort's remaining horcruxes.
Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows was split into two films. (IMDb)
It's then the old woman turns into Voldemort's snake Nagini and launches at Harry, sending him slamming through a wall of the house.
In the documentary, Powell explains how the stunt performer would be jerked backwards on a wire, with the force increasing in rehearsals until the landing was perfected.
Fellow stunt performer Marc Mailley describes how Holmes rehearsed the scene the day before, and turned down Mailley's offer to step in to give himself a break.
"And the last thing I said to Dave before he went, I was like 'after yesterday Dave, this one should be a lot easier'," Mailley says.
He describes what happened as "a blur".
David Holmes: The Boy Who Lived trailer.
"As soon as I left the floor, as soon as the load hit me, I thought 'nope, that's too big,'" Holmes says.
"[David] literally said straight away 'I've broken my neck'," Mailley recalls.
David was immediately rushed to hospital where his father, Andy, says he was "presented with the fact that it was a pretty serious injury".
"He needed to have an operation because at that stage, potentially at any time he could have been fatal."
Holmes was paralysed from the chest down and spent weeks in hospital.
Things were complicated further when he developed a cyst in his spinal cord after surgery, resulting in continued deterioration.
David's mother, Sue Holmes, recalls how she was "very angry and bitter" following the accident and sought someone to blame —  but her son disagreed.
David Holmes worked on the Harry Potter films for years and said the crew became a second family. (Supplied: HBO)
"He said 'why Mum? My life's ruined. Why would I want to ruin anyone else's life?'"
David says: "Straight away I was like, do I go for the specifics of the blame, the individuals that are in charge?"
"And I just went, what is people getting sacked really going to change? You’re paralysed. You’re not gonna get fixed.
"It’s just a catalogue of errors that led to my paralysis and I had to focus on being positive and I still do."
Filming began shortly after David's accident, and he was also adamant about having his friend and colleague Marc Mailley take his place as Harry Potter's stuntman.
Stunt performers risk life and limb to create our favourites films. Before actors in the US went on strike, many say they were cashing in on Queensland's booming film industry, thanks to new interest from Hollywood.
"Dave made it very clear to Marc early on that he wanted only him to do it and didn't want anyone else to do it," Radcliffe says.
But for Marc, it was the last thing he wanted to do.
"I didn't want to do the job my mate's broken his neck on, not because I'm scared but because that's his job," Marc says.
"You know, I've nicked his job off the back of him having an unfortunate event.
"Every time I got ready, I'd sit there and think I shouldn't be sitting here, getting hair and makeup done, looking like Harry. This isn't right, this isn't the plan.
"It's a lot to work out in your head."
The Harry Potter series took years to film and threw Daniel Radcliffe into the global spotlight at just 11 years old.
Daniel Radcliffe admits his career had no structure once he finished filming all eight Harry Potter installments. (Reuters: Toby Melville)
As the phenomenon came to an end, he told the documentary he "didn't know what was important" and he went into "freefall."
"It was something that I talked to Dave about and he was, as he always had been, a really good guiding star in all that," Radcliffe says.
"He was like, I'm not going to let you throw the opportunity you've got away.
"There was something about seeing somebody have their career taken from them involuntarily where I realised you can't get complacent and think you'll be in this industry forever.
Growing up in Essex, England, Holmes spent hours getting skilled at gymnastics with the dream of one day becoming a stunt performer.
After small roles on productions such as Lost in Space, Holmes was hand-picked by stunt coordinator Greg Powell to become Daniel Radcliffe's main stunt double.
David Holmes also doubled for other Harry Potter characters including Draco Malfoy, played by Tom Felton. (Instagram: @davidholmes83)
Powell reveals that he continues to blame himself for what went wrong that day on the set of the Deathly Hallows.
"I hate seeing him like that," Powell admits.
"In the nicest way, I want to say I wish I never met him, when I see him like that. Because it wouldn't be like that if he never met me.
"I was the last one to touch him when he could actually walk and I was the first one to touch him when he couldn't walk. And that's an awful feeling. I'm getting choked up now.
"I still blame meself because I was there."
David says that for all the hardships that have come from his accident, "a lot of positives have come from the negative".
In the following years, his mates and colleagues have worked to make stunts safer on set.
"After Dave's accident, our focus was on trying to make stunt rigging, or the wire work, the flying you see in films, as safe as possible," Mailley says.
"That's been the main achievement since Dave had his accident.
Since 2020, David has hosted his own podcast series devoted to stunt performers and coordinators, and he's keen to create a stunt training facility for young performers.
In the documentary, Holmes and Radcliffe visit a warehouse where Harry Potter costumes and props are stored. (Supplied: HBO)
He's also raised more than 100,000 British pounds ($192,000) for hospitals and other spinal charities through the David Holmes Cricket Cup.
Since 2009, his friends, family and former Harry Potter colleagues have come together each year to play cricket and raise money for the Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital.
"I was in love with my job. Still am, in a weird way," Holmes says in the documentary.
"It was the biggest love of my life. One of my only loves, really.
David Holmes: The Boy Who Lives is available on Binge.

title: Sex, style and spoiled rich boys: Promising Young Woman director returns with a fever dream thriller
content:
When Oscar-winning director Emerald Fennell set out to cast her second film, Saltburn, she knew who she wanted for one of the lead roles: Australia's Jacob Elordi.
He plays Felix, a privileged Oxford student from an aristocratic family, who draws fellow student Oliver (Barry Keoghan) into his opulent world.
The film is a thriller-slash-black-comedy-drama, and is a sharp, unhinged satire that pushes boundaries.
"Jacob, he just came in and did the most exceptional audition," Fennell told ABC News.
"He did such a genius, genius bit of observational comedy. He really really understood that for all of [Felix's] beauty and charisma, he's just sort of a spoiled little boy. He came in and just absolutely blew us all away."
Director Emerald Fennell is also an actor, most recently as Barbie's pregnant best friend, Midge. (Warner)
In her second film (her first, Promising Young Woman, won the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay), Fennell focuses on excess and the obsession with things we can't have, setting it against the backdrop of one formative summer at an English manor in the mid-2000s.
"I drew from my own experience of being a human person, who has felt that thing we all feel at that time in our life which is that absolute insane grip of obsessive love," she said.
"But obviously I didn't quite go to the lengths that some of the people [in the film] do."
The film features intense sequences, and Fennell said part of shooting was having ongoing conversations about the scenes. The film also had an intimacy coordinator: a person on set who works with the director, actors and crew to plan out the more intimate scenes.
"For the most part, it's in the script. People kind of know ahead of time, so we have lots of time to speak to each other," Fennell said.
"Both cast and crew in this film is looking to really get into stuff that's complicated and sticky and difficult.
Costumes and fashion from the 2000s (glittery jackets, rugby tops, click-clacky jewellery) are used as a storytelling tool; Fennell wanted the inner lives of the characters to be shown through what they wore.
"Even if it's just somebody wearing boxers, you know — are they boxers that they've washed today? Do they have a hole in the back? You know, what's the colour? — We're really, really drilling down."
A lot of thought went into the clothes, even if they were quickly discarded. Barry Keoghan in Saltburn. (Supplied: Warner Bros. Pictures)
The film culminates in a Midsummer's Night Dream party held for Oliver, where each character attends in fancy dress specific to their character.
"The concept of midsummer is sort of upending the kind of norms and it's about characters role playing and changing identities," Fennell said.
For instance, one character — someone Fennell said is never really going to be loved in the way he wants to be — dresses up as a court jester.
Fennell, who is also an actor, is known for creating complex characters. She said Hollywood is changing when it comes to representation, but it could change faster.
"A huge part of that, I think, is also the people at the studios, the things that are commissioned right from the get-go, the people who are able to actually get things made, to greenlight things — I think that's where it starts," Fennell said.
"Because by the time your kind of making the film, you really want that diversity to start much, much sooner in the process. I think that'll help enormously."
Saltburn made its Australian premiere at SXSW Sydney and opened the British Film Festival in October. It's in cinemas November 16.
