title: Writer of musical hit Hamilton shares the advice that powered 'three years of writing'
content:
Lin-Manuel Miranda first crossed paths with Stephen Sondheim during the revival of one of the biggest musicals in history.
Miranda had been brought in to do Spanish translations of Sondheim's West Side Story lyrics.
"He said, 'What else are you working on?' He was more interested in that than West Side Story," Miranda recalls.
At that point, Miranda was in the process of writing what would become his record-breaking show Hamilton.
"I'll never forget, he threw back his head, he went, 'That is fantastic. No one will expect that from you. That's great. That's exactly what you should be doing," Miranda told Take 5 with Zan Rowe.
Those three years also cemented a friendship between the pair, with Miranda taking Sondheim at his word and sending him songs for feedback as he went.
It led to a single word of advice from Sondheim that Miranda still keeps front of mind.
"He would always write back, 'Variety. Variety,'" Miranda said.
"Surprise is the one thing; every eight bars change up what's happening underneath the music. Change it.
"That was the biggest lesson he taught me."
Icons in music and screen join Double J host Zan Rowe to delve deep into intimate moments in their lives as they share five songs they love.
Miranda said he knew he wasn't the only artist to have benefited from Sondheim's guidance and shared how hard his death had been in 2021.
"He leaves us two enormous legacies — he leaves us the eclecticness and mastery of his work, all these musicals, every single one, a completely different work unto itself," Miranda said.
"I'm one of thousands of artists he encouraged personally. His encouragement is [also] ... a legacy as the work itself."
When it comes to the legacy Miranda plans to leave, his goal is to be "well remembered by the people I love and who loved me and who I knew".
Lin-Manuel Miranda says he was one of many artists mentored by Sondheim. (ABC: Take 5 with Zan Rowe)
After working by himself to craft the songs and story for Hamilton, Miranda's preference now is to seek out and tap into the expertise of others.
He said it had been "staggering" and "really humbling" to collaborate with composer Alan Menken, who wrote the music for a wide array of Disney's animated classics.
They worked together on the live-action remake of Disney's The Little Mermaid — a movie whose music had felt revolutionary when he was a kid watching on in the 1990s.
"Time has taken away how weirdly contemporary that song felt. That was a pop song.
"I just remember the thrill of that, so when I'm writing those moments for Encanto or Moana, I'm chasing that. I want kids to feel the way I felt in 1989 under the water."
Miranda says he wants to write songs that thrill kids as much as hearing Under The Sea thrilled him.
It's safe to say Miranda has successfully recreated those feelings, with children and adults enthralled by the songs he has created for the screen — including the ones even he didn't expect to land.
"I was the most surprised by anybody that We Don't Talk About Bruno was the biggest hit to come out of the Encanto soundtrack," Miranda said.
"It is the most specific song in that score. Yet, I think that that's why it resonated with people.
"I think we all have those stories in our families that are like … 'We can't talk about that in front of Mum', or 'We can't talk about that in front of your brother.'"
Miranda also shared he didn't find out the song was gaining momentum through any of the usual channels.
"Really, my son was the town crier," Miranda recalled.
"He's the one who told me, 'Daddy, everyone in school is singing it. It's crazy.'
"He went from being freaked out … to being really proud pretty quickly."
Watch Lin-Manuel Miranda on Take 5 tonight at 8pm on ABC TV or on ABC iview, and hear the extended conversation on the Take 5 podcast on the ABC listen app.

title: The Marvels has had the MCU's worst opening weekend at the box office. What went wrong?
content:
Marvel Cinematic Universe's (MCU) latest instalment, The Marvels, has had a disappointing opening weekend at the box office, recording $US47 million ($73 million) in sales in the United States — the lowest amount the comic book franchise has recorded to date.
The Marvels sees Captain Marvel/Carol Dancers (Brie Larson), Ms Marvel/Kamala Khan (Iman Vellani) and Captain Monica Rambeau (Teyonah Parris) get their powers entangled due to some unintended consequences of quantum chaos.
The all-female led film reportedly had a budget of $US220 million, yet the 33rd film from the MCU has failed to draw in crowds.
So what went wrong? Film critics Luke Goodsell and Matthew Neal break it down.
During the 118-day Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists strike, actors were not allowed to promote any movie or show from the major studios and streamers.
Negotiations came to an end on November 9, the day before The Marvels' US release.
Neal said this definitely played a role in the low audience attendance.
"The inability for the star cast to promote the film has probably hurt it somewhat," he said.
"I think there just wasn't as much anticipation around this film."
Goodsell agreed that not being able to promote the film would have had an impact, but both said it was not the sole reason.
Goodsell and Neal both said there would have been a small portion of Marvel fans who did not want to see the film because of the women in the lead.
The all-female reboot of Ghostbusters (2016) received massive backlash upon its announcement, and the female adaption of the Oceans series, Oceans 8 also was harshly criticised.
However Neal said MCU past female leads had performed well at the box office.
The Marvels lead Brie Larson copped criticism from the film's prequel Captain Marvel.  (Supplied: Disney)
"Captain Marvel did over $1 billion so I'm reluctant to say whether misogyny is a factor in this," he said.
But even in Captain Marvel, Larson copped criticism from some MCU fans, with some leaving negative reviews on Rotten Tomatoes prior to the films 2019 release.
Goodsell said even prior to The Marvels release there was a lot of buzz within fan groups saying of course certain types of men were going to reject the film.
However the film managed to draw in a 61 per cent male audience according to early estimates.
The Marvels is a sequel to Captain Marvel (2019) and the Ms Marvel six-episode series on Disney+.
But to get a full grasp of the leading characters backgrounds, you would need to have seen the nine WandaVision episodes and Avengers: Endgame. The four combined would take almost 16 hours.
Goodsell said having lesser known characters who require so much background knowledge has deterred viewers from giving The Marvels a chance.
"Audiences are genuinely feeling a bit over it," Goodsell said.
"Marvel have probably overestimated how much their hardcore fan base drives box office performance."
He noted The Avengers: End Game grossed more than $US2 billion due to the general audience showing up rather than just the hardcore fans.
"The regular punters are finding it hard to keep up," he said.
However the other 2023 MCU releases — Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 and Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania — have both had far more successful opening weekends, earning $US118 million and $US106 million respectively.
"In 2021 we had four MCU films, maybe there is some fatigue setting in there, but people have been saying that for the past three or four years," Neal said.
Depends who you ask. Goodsell was not a fan, but Neal was.
Market research company CinemaScore had an exit interview rating of a B.
Rotten Tomatoes rated the film 64 per cent, while the audience score is 85 per cent.
Neal said he believed word-of-mouth from audiences who did enjoy the film should help bolster its earnings.
"In itself it is a really fun and entertaining film, and if you're into superhero films I think it does a great job."
Teyonah Parris's character Monica Rambeau also featured in Captain Marvel and WandaVision.  (Supplied: Disney)
Goodsell said Marvel had been coming off a year of decreasing quality in the eyes of the audience. And with big hits outside the superhero genre released this year including Barbie and Oppenheimer, he said Marvel movies had become less of a "must see".
The Marvels is directed by Nia Dacosta (Candyman, Little Woods) who Goodsell said was not able to work to her full potential.
"The movie for all its good intent is kind of forced to snap into that very generic Marvel template at a certain point, and that's what the audiences are sick of," he said.
"If you're going to bring in a talented film maker like Nia Dacosta or Chloe Zhao for The Eternals, you need to let them do something genuinely creative with their skills."

title: Wonka star Timothée Chalamet tries his newest role: Impersonating Aussie pop icon Troye Sivan on SNL
content:
With the actors strike finally over in the US, we can now return to normalcy: witnessing famous people participate in increasingly unhinged activities to promote their movies.
We've had mass behind-the-scenes photo dumps from film and TV that has long since been released, as well as films going straight back into production (Sydney Sweeney in Bondi!), and an American/Frenchie superstar attempting to imitate an Aussie on SNL (more on that later).
In case you missed the BTS shots and other entertainment goss from the last few days, we've got you covered.
2000s pop princess Ricki-Lee's new single cover, Ghost. (Supplied)
Think back to the simpler time of 2007. You still bought CDs from Sanity or Borders. You'd watch The Simpsons at 6pm on Channel Ten every night. And one of Australia's greatest songs ever was released: Can't Touch This by Ricki-Lee Coulter.
Once you've stopped crying at the nostalgia, dry your tears with the blessed news that the former Young Diva will release her first new studio album in a decade, and has celebrated the announcement with a new single.
But if you're after tunes that feel a little more modern, look no further than The Kid Laroi's debut album, released on Friday.
The Kid LAROI - I THOUGHT THAT I NEEDED YOU (Official Audio)
The 20-year-old is one of the biggest Australian musicians in the world right now, and his record THE FIRST TIME is full of collabs with stars like Jung Kook and Central Cee.
triple j described it as an album of "back to back hits that sees the proud Kamilaroi star navigate growing up, fame, love and everything in between".
And if that's somehow not enough new music for you, Dula Peep — sorry, Dua Lipa — is back with another earworm with her latest release Houdini, a co-production with Danny L Harle and Tame Impala's Kevin Parker.
— Rachel Rasker
Water. Earth. Fire. Air.
Long ago, the four nations lived together in harmony. Then in 2010, everything changed when then live action remake attacked.
Only the master of all four elements could attempt to recreate the beloved animated series, and in 2024, Netflix thinks it has what it takes.
Avatar: The Last Airbender | Official Teaser | Netflix
Avatar: The Last Airbender fans were burnt by M. Night Shyamalan's attempt at a live action film more than a decade ago, which was widely panned as "terrible," or "the worst film ever made".
But they're cautiously optimistic at the upcoming series, with the top comment on the trailer's YouTube post carefully declaring that "the redemption arc hopefully begins".
— Rachel Rasker
The Grammy nominations are here, leading everyone to join into the annual exercise of googling the difference between Song of the year and Record of the Year.
Minogue and Sivan are both up for the same award, in the Best Pop Dance Recording category.
These awards have been criticised heavily over the years for their apparent exclusivity, and a dearth of gender and racial diversity among the winners.
That being said, this year saw women absolutely dominating, with rapper/singer/songwriter SZA (pronounced "Sizza" for those trying to impress their friends) leading the pack with a whopping nine nominations.
Album of the year was almost exclusively women (the likes of Miley Cyrus and Olivia Rodrigo, plus queer icons Janelle Monáe and boygenius), and song of the year saw much of the same crowd, plus two Barbie movie tracks (What Was I Made For and Dance the Night).
And, because it's our year of the lord 2023 and you simply cannot do anything without mentioning Taylor Swift, Anti-Hero being nominated for Song of the Year makes her the first songwriter to get seven noms in that category, overtaking the six held by both Sir Paul McCartney and Lionel Richie.
— Katherine Smyrk
While rumours of Beyoncé's Renaissance tour coming down under haven't yet crystallised into an announcement just yet, Australian members of the Beyhive can flock to cinemas December 1 for the next-best-thing: Renaissance: A Film By Beyoncé.
And, to get us hyped, the superstar dropped a trailer for the concert film on Friday.
RENAISSANCE: A FILM BY BEYONCÉ | Worldwide Trailer
Like Bey's 2019 concert film Homecoming, Renaissance is a blend of on-stage footage and behind-the-scenes moments. The film also marks our first official visuals of the Renaissance era, with Bey not-yet dropping a single music video for the acclaimed album.
In the meantime, there's a few weeks left to practice the "everybody's on mute" challenge — maybe it'll prove easier in the cinema?
— Jared Richards
Rob Harvilla has a lot to say about songs from the 90s. His popular podcast, 60 songs that explain the 90s, has already ballooned to 120 songs (without a name change) and, from tomorrow, it'll also available in book form.
Heartbreak High actor and disability rights advocate Chloé Hayden has taken a step back from Instagram, due to abuse affecting her mental and physical health.
If you're unfamiliar, 60 songs covers every genre of significance from the 90s — from Mariah to Metallica, and even one-hit-wonders like Vanilla Ice and the Macarena. He shares insights, secret histories and personal anecdotes. If you were around in the 90s or just have an awareness of the 90s, there's bound to be something there for you.
Now for the audiobook version… oh wait…
— Christian Harimanow
The National Theatre of Parramatta is making Australian theatre history today as it announces a program for 2024 that is entirely led by Black, Indigenous and People of Colour (BIPOC) theatre-makers.
"We are putting the nation on stage," says the company's executive producer Joanne Kee.
"Our stories reflect and resonate with the people you see in our streets and we go that extra mile to make sure they are on our stages, behind the scenes and in our audiences."
Leading the NTofP 2024 program is Things Hidden Since the Foundation of the World, which centres on the unsolved murder of 70s Iranian pop star Fereydoun Farrokhzad. (National Theatre of Parramatta)
The announcement marks the first time a non-Indigenous theatre company has programmed an all-BIPOC-led season. (Credit where credit is due: companies like Ilbijerri Theatre Co and Moogahlin Performing Arts have a strong history of programming First Nations-led work.)
For anyone wanting to see more theatre that reflects contemporary Australia, watch this space.
— Anna Freeland
Speaking of Australian pop idols going big internationally, former YouTube personality and viral Rush singer Troye Sivan has had a bumper year — and it's just gotten more surreal.
The 28-year-old from Perth was impersonated on Saturday Night Live by none other than "American actor who can't do an Australian accent", Timothée Chalamet.
The Wonka superstar attempted to mimic the dance style from Troye's recent videos, on the verge of breaking the entire time.
Troye's responded to the skit as like something out of a "weird f--king dream" and, reflecting on Troye's rise, I can't help but agree. Incredible content though.

title: 'We went for the throat': Matrix producer brings horror show to Tiktok in one-minute episodes
content:
Most people are used to getting their TV fix from the couch, staring at a plasma.
But for people under 25, most content is now being watched on the small vertical screen of a phone.
Filmmakers are trying to keep pace with younger audiences, increasingly turning to platforms like TikTok and Instagram to tell their stories.
An upcoming horror-drama series – Greystanes — will be released exclusively on TikTok in one-minute episodes.
Matt Ferro and Ryan Cauchi directors of Greystanes say TikTok is a way to keep track with a younger audience (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)
"You have to hook an audience early online and not allow that slow burn and traditional build-up for horror that would then deliver a scare," Greystanes writer and producer Matt Ferro said.
"We went for the throat right from the beginning to show people a taste of what they have in store in future episodes."
Ferro was a producer on blockbusters like The Matrix (1999) and Happy Feet (2006) and said filmmaking for TikTok had brought a whole new set of challenges.
"That excludes the desirability of certain wide shots that would be traditionally used to show a landscape or a panorama."
Greystanes is set in the 1990s in the Western Sydney suburb of the same name.
Two children visit their grandmother's house where they uncover a host of dark family secrets rooted in terrifying stories from Maltese folklore.
Australia has the largest Maltese diaspora in the world – about 200,000 people, according to the 2021 Census.
But their their culture had rarely been reflected in films and on TV.
Malta is known for its Mediterranean landscape and pastizzis but it also has a side of dark folklore, like the child-hunting demon. (Supplied)
"Being a Maltese-Australian, I had never seen a Maltese person in a scripted series before," Greystanes writer and director Ryan Cauchi said.
"I've also never seen any of the unique monsters or superstitions from Maltese folklore depicted on screen."
For Cauchi, Malta is represented by idyllic Mediterranean beaches and delicious pastizzi.
The culture, he said, has a darker side — with popular tales about child-hunting demons and tunnel-dwelling beasts.
"One of the key images of Maltese mythology is the idea of another world — of alternate timelines and multiple dimensions," Cauchi said.
"Each of these cavernous realms have their own race of nightmarish monsters and beasties.
"Through portals and holes, these creatures are able to traverse through these realms."
AACTA-nominated actor, Frances Duca, is hoping the series she appears in will help share her culture with wider audiences.
"It's exciting to be able to be in a series on a platform that will deliver that."
Frances Duca appears in the horror-drama film called Greystanes, shot specifically for TikTok. (Supplied)
Greystanes was co-funded by Screen Australia, TikTok and NZ On Air, through their Every Voice initiative.
Head of online at Screen Australia, Lee Naimo said vertical videos on TikTok, and Instagram will be a significant part of the film industry's future.
"Traditionally, we've seen short film as a real pathway into feature filmmaking. The reality is that that opportunity and that pathway has narrowed," Mr Naimo said.
Screen Australia funded 15 TikTok series over the past two years through its Every Voice project.
Rather than taking over the industry, Mr Naimo said vertical video projects are likely to exist alongside traditional film and TV.
"Audiences still want to see projects on the big screen," he said.
Head of online at Screen Australia Lee Naimo says it's hard to monetize content on TikTok. (ABC News: Helena Burke)
"They want to see great content on their TV screens, on devices, and on mobile phones. I think it's just about that ecosystem of supporting Australian creators at every level."
Screen Australia said monetising content on TikTok is difficult.
Filmmakers like Ferro and Cauchi are optimistic that the platform and the industry will adapt.
"We asked the same question about musicians and streaming services," Ferro said.
"Although it might not be clear how to monetise everything yet, as TikTok develops and more and more people rely on it for more substantive content besides just funny videos … that monetisation will find itself."
Greystanes will be released on TikTok in early 2024.

title: Hollywood's strike has ended, but Australian actors are still fighting for the same protections
content:
Hollywood's longest-ever writers and actors' strike has ended, but an Australian union says it is still fighting for the same wage increases and protections.
Film productions are set to return to Queensland in the coming months after Hollywood struck a tentative deal for actors on Thursday.
Tens of thousands of actors had walked off the job in July, alongside writers, over pay demands and fears they could be replaced by artificial intelligence (AI) copies in what became Hollywood's longest actors' strike in history.
The deal, which puts an end to the six-month-long stand-off between actors' unions and studios, offers wage compensation for actors and protection against AI.
Michelle Rae from the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance said AI was a "concern" affecting Australia's film industry too.
"Artificial intelligence is absolutely booming and it's something we can embrace and use in real life," she told ABC Radio Brisbane.
Australian film contracts will include clauses to allow studios to capture the voice and images of an actor.
But Ms Rae says studios are increasingly including clauses that will allow them to sell actors' voices and image recordings to third parties.
She says third-party technology companies can then use the captured images and voices to make AI-generated virtual avatars that look and sound like the actor — and even replace the actor.
The stand-off between writer-actors and major Hollywood studios began in July. (AP: Chris Pizzello)
"[Actors are concerned that] 'I mightn't even get my next job, because my AI-interpretive one might get it'," Ms Rae said.
AI also caused a stir last month after a video using a fake, AI-generated version of Hollywood actor Tom Hanks circulated online.
"We're seeing in crew agreements the same thing — clauses to capture them behind-the-scenes, and their voices, and wanting to sell it to a third party," Ms Rae said.
"And these are people who aren't even paid for their image."
The Hollywood actors-studio deal is reportedly worth more than $1 million and includes compensation increases, protections for actors' likeness, and a new "streaming participation bonus".
But the deal does not cover actors or crew employed by Australian studios.
As the US actors' and writers' strike continues on with no end in sight, workers here say our industry is facing similar, if not worse, issues.
"Australian industrial action isn't set up for industry strikes. You have to be negotiating directly with your employer to gain the protections to get an industry strike.
"[Australian performers] can't do what the Americans have just done because we don't have that ability."
Ms Rae said local Australian performers had been negotiating for a dollar-based increase to live performance wages over the past ten months.
She said 70 per cent of Australian performers earnt less than $29,000 a year and, in some cases, have had wages cut compared to 2018 and 2019 rates.
"In Australia, because we're negotiating an industry agreement [not an employee agreement], the only option available to actors is to talk to the community about what their struggles look like," Ms Rae said.
"Next week in Sydney, performers are going to take their stories to the audience, because they're not feeling heard."
Julia Roberts and George Clooney on the set of Ticket to Paradise. (Supplied: Universal Pictures)
Screen Queensland chief executive Jacqui Feeney said cameras were set to roll across the state, with some local productions already underway.
Queensland actors say they're more likely to get hired when they pretend to be from another state.
Apples Never Fall and Mortal Kombat 2 are among some of the big-budget Hollywood productions expected to resume in Queensland now that strikes have ended.
Ms Feeney said the Queensland industry was now managing a "pipeline of productions" from local and international studios, including some embargoed projects that were yet to be revealed.
"We're hopeful of some work coming back quickly in the next few weeks, or couple of weeks even," she said.
"But there is a lot of work sitting there that we're aware of that will get up and running next year."

title: Streaming costs are rising, and there are more platforms than ever to choose between. Some people are going back to piracy
content:
Australians on average are spending $5 less a month compared to last year on streaming services as price hikes and a growing numbers of services drive them away, new data reveals.
For people like James* it has drawn them back to digital piracy.
Digital piracy is the act of illegally copying or distributing copyrighted material, such as music, TV shows or movies, via the internet.
Data released in the the Deloitte Media and Entertainment Consumer Insights annual report, which contains self-reported data from more than 2,000 Australians, shows households are spending $57 a month on streaming, down from $62 in 2022.
For some the shift away from streaming means sourcing entertainment by unlawful means.
Associate Professor at the RMIT University School of Media and Communication Ramon Lobato said piracy levels were related to a number of different factors, including disposable income, willingness to pay, users' digital skills, and the availability and convenience of both legal and pirate services.
"All of these factors work together to shape people's decisions about how to access content," he said.
For James, the increasing number of streaming platforms has driven him away from paid for services.
Pricey entertainment subscription services are getting the chop from more Aussie households as consumers turn to free or cheaper ad-based content for entertainment, a new report reveals.
"There's a proliferation of platforms. So you're looking at multiple subscriptions to get the same results," he said.
"Content also seems to shift a lot across platforms depending on which rights holders have done a deal."
He said it was easier to use a pirating website to find all the content he wants in high quality without any ads or cost.
The Deloitte report shows 48 per cent find it hard to know what content is available and where, 70 per cent wish they could manage multiple subscriptions in one place, and 73 per cent wish they could search and discover content across all their subscriptions in one place.
Dr Lobato said fragmentation meant users often struggle to know where to go to stream a particular show.
Aggregation is clearly in demand from Australian households. But fragmentation not the only driver away from streaming.
Availability also plays a role. For James two shows come to mind, The Mandalorian and Star Trek Picard.
"(Star Trek Picard) was available in America, I think more than 12 hours before it was here and I skipped the queue and went straight to the torrent to get it," he said.
Data from TorrentFreak, which tracks BitTorrent news and trends, reveals the 10 most torrented films week on week throughout 2023.
It is important to note data on piracy cannot be drawn as entirely conclusive as it relies on self-reporting and information availability is limited due to its criminal nature.
Out of the 110 films on the list, 39 of them were not available on Australian streaming services at the time of publication.
Avatar: The Way of Water makes the top 10 list for 30 weeks. The film was released in Australian cinemas on December 15, 2022, became available for purchase or rent on March 28, 2023 and was released for streaming on Disney+ on June 7 —  174 days after theatrical release.
Dr Lobato said delayed releasing of movies and TV shows has historically been a driver of piracy in Australia, but the studios and distributors have worked hard to reduce this in recent years.
The cost of almost everything is going up and streaming services are no exception. In the past 12 months multiple streaming services in Australia have increased their price.
In 2023 to stream all the most torrented films would cost $97.95 a month for standard ad-free services — and that still would not get you access to all of the films.
Where streaming is unavailable, one off purchases and rentals are mostly available, but this can add up. Rental prices tend to vary between $2.99 to upward of $24.99, while purchase prices can range from $7.99 to upward of $34.99 depending on the film.
The Deloitte report showed 70 per cent of respondents unsubscribed from their streaming service due to price.
While some people will opt for a cheaper ad-based service, a small percentage — like James — will unsubscribe from all their services.
Piracy is not exclusive to film and TV, and how people unlawfully consume content can differ depending on what that content is.
The Attorney-General 2022 Consumer Survey on Online Copyright Infringement, which has the latest official Australian data, showed an increase in piracy across the music, movies, TV programs, video games and live sport compared to the year prior.
The survey found 39 per cent of the 2,400 people who responded had consumed content online in at least one category in ways that were likely unlawful.
The most popular form of unlawful consumption was paying a small fee to access one or many subscription services through a shared or unknown account with 16 per cent of respondents using this method.
The survey also found the majority of infringers were male, aged between 25 and 34, and earning more than $80,000 a year — a demographic James falls perfectly into.
Dr Lobato said the dynamics of piracy varied across media.
"TV and sport all have their own licensing and availability structures, and piracy looks quite different in each of those markets," he said.
"As legal streaming services have evolved, so has piracy.
"There are now many options including torrents, streaming apps, live streams, websites, and cloud-based services."
James said he used a number of different methods for different forms of entertainment, including stream ripping music — turning streamed content into a downloadable file — and code cracking — using an unauthorised code to access subscription software or games.
He said he turned to these forms of piracy when content he wanted, such as music or older video games, were not easily available.
The Deloitte report highlighted that there is still a willingness to pay for entertainment, especially above other spend items such as alcohol and tobacco or dining out.
Piracy is a crime. Under the Australian Copyright Act it is an offence to:
Individuals risk fines of up to $117,000 and up to five years imprisonment.
And even James says he's willing to pay if he sees value in the service.
"I have paid for Netflix and I did pay for it for many years, probably up to about 2021," he said.
"I would probably be willing to pay upwards of $39- $49 if (a platform) had everything available."
In terms of harm to the film and TV industry, anti-piracy group Creative Content Australia report piracy undermines confidence to finance movies in the first place, meaning investors are less likely to invest in other films when piracy impacts their returns.
However, James said he did not believe it came down to the individual.
Many streaming services in Australia are recording profits. Netflix, for example, is understood to have made about $1 billion in Australia in 2022, up from $30.7 million the previous year after cracking down on password sharing.
"These massive conglomerates can afford to pay the content creators," James said.
"I think the individual doesn't matter, but if it was super widespread... then I could see it having major impacts on the content."
*James's name has been changed.

title: Robert De Niro's former assistant awarded $1.88 million in gender discrimination lawsuit
content:
A jury has awarded more than $US1.2 million ($1.88 million) to Robert De Niro's former personal assistant, finding that a company he formed to look after his personal needs was liable for gender discrimination and retaliation after the former assistant accused the actor of subjecting her to a toxic work environment.
While the jury found De Niro was not personally liable for the abuse, they said his company, Canal Productions, should make two payments of $US632,142 to his longtime personal assistant, Graham Chase Robinson.
Mr De Niro, who spent three days at the two-week trial — including two on the witness stand — has been ensnared in duelling lawsuits with Ms Robinson since she quit in April 2019.
He was not in the courtroom when the verdict was read aloud on Thursday afternoon.
Ms Robinson, 41, testified that Mr De Niro, 80, and his girlfriend, Tiffany Chen, teamed up against her to turn a job she once loved into a nightmare.
She smiled and hugged all her lawyers after the jury exited the room. She also smiled as the verdict was being delivered.
Mr De Niro's attorney, Richard Schoenstein, said outside court that lawyers would try to reduce the size of the award with post-trial motions.
Mr De Niro and Ms Chen each testified that Ms Robinson became the problem when her aspirations to move beyond Canal Productions, the De Niro company that employed her, led her to make escalating demands to remain on the job.
In two days on the witness stand, the actor told jurors that he boosted Ms Robinson's salary from less than $US100,000 annually to $US300,000 and elevated her title to vice-president of production and finance at her request, even though her responsibilities remained largely the same.
When she quit, Mr De Niro said, Ms Robinson stole about $US85,000 in airline miles from him, betrayed his trust and violated his unwritten rules to use common sense and always do the right thing.
In this courtroom sketch, Robert De Niro, seated background right, is questioned by his attorney Laurent Drogin. (AP: Elizabeth Williams)
At times, Mr De Niro acknowledged from the witness stand many of the claims Ms Robinson made to support her $US12 million gender discrimination and retaliation lawsuit, including that he may have told her that his personal trainer was paid more than her in part because he had a family to support.
He agreed he had asked her to scratch his back on at least two occasions, dismissing a question about it with: "OK, twice? You got me!"
He admitted that he had berated her, though he disputed ever aiming a profanity her way, saying: "I was never abusive, ever."
He also denied ever yelling at her, saying every little thing she was trying to catch him with was nonsense and that, at most, he had raised his voice in her presence but never with disrespect.
Then, he looked at her sitting between her lawyers in the well of the courtroom and shouted: "Shame on you, Chase Robinson!"
Mr De Niro said Ms Robinson was wrong to take 5 million airline miles from his company's accounts, but he acknowledged that he had told her she could take 2 million miles and that there were no strict rules.
Ms Robinson testified that Mr De Niro and his girlfriend Tiffany Chen teamed up against her. (AP: Evan Agostini/Invision)
Ms Robinson testified that she quit her job during an "emotional and mental breakdown" that left her overwhelmed and feeling like she'd "hit rock bottom".
She said she has suffered from anxiety and depression since quitting and hasn't worked in four years despite applying for 638 jobs.
"I don't have a social life," she said.
Mr De Niro's lawyers sued Ms Robinson for breach of loyalty and fiduciary duty even before her lawsuit was filed against him in 2019.
They sought $US6 million in damages, including a return of the 5 million airline miles. The jury flatly rejected the claims.
In a closing argument on Wednesday, Mr Schoenstein said the miles that were taken were worth about $US85,000. He said jurors could order Ms Robinson to return some of her salary, but, he added: "We're not looking for you to punish her."
In his closing, Ms Robinson's attorney Brent Hannafan called the two weeks of court proceedings a civil rights trial and urged jurors to return a verdict "not just for Ms Robinson, but for all civil rights litigants".
Mr De Niro — who has starred in films such as Raging Bull and The Deer Hunter — has won two Oscars over the past five decades.

title: Is this the end of Marvel's dominance at the cinema?
content:
Are we finally (blissfully, some might argue) witnessing the long-rumoured end of Marvel's multiplex dominance?
This year's three biggest global hits are a pastel feminist vision of a 64-year-old plastic doll, a candy-coloured retro gaming adventure, and a three-hour talkfest about the father of the nuclear bomb — all signs, however anecdotal, that audiences may be wearying of a certain brand of superhero fare.
The Marvels — a sequel to Captain Marvel (2019) and the TV miniseries Ms. Marvel (2022) — arrives in cinemas this week with considerably subdued buzz, and reports of mounting crises within the MCU content factory.
The lack of expectations does the movie favours.
Iman Vellani (pictured right) is a comic book writer and was a huge fan of Ms. Marvel before landing the role. (Supplied: Disney)
As The Marvels opens, it's like being thrown into the middle of some Saturday morning kids' TV show, with a refreshing sense of disorientation.
There's angular spacecraft zipping through cosmic portals, a team of villains excavating some ancient artifact on a faraway moon, and a mutant teenage girl in Jersey City (Iman Vellani, reprising her role as Kamala Khan from Ms. Marvel) dreaming of being a superhero like her idol, Carol Danvers, aka Captain Marvel (Brie Larson).
Danvers, meanwhile, is hanging out on her ship with her orange tabby cat Goose (whose mouthful of tentacles make him look like Alien's Jonesy genetically spliced with a xenomorph), and Nick Fury (Samuel L. Jackson) is leading a deep space operation with electromagnetically powered astronaut Monica Rambeau (Teyonah Parris).
Hell-bent on finding a magic bangle that will afford her untold power, the film's ostensible villain, hammer-wielding Kree warrior Dar-Benn (Zawe Ashton), is busy tearing wormholes in the time-space fabric of the universe.
Ashton (pictured) recounted to EW advice she received from actor Tom Hiddleston: "Make sure you have enough zippers to go to the bathroom in your costume." (Supplied: Disney)
The resulting quantum chaos causes Captain Marvel, Kamala and Monica to randomly switch places mid-combat as their powers become entangled.
Once you get past the usual perplexing mythology (at least for those who haven't sat through the last 400 hours of Marvel's Disney+ shows), it's a fun-enough premise, full of wacky wormholes, body swapping and space cats who swallow villains only to vomit them out without warning.
There are sketchbook animations, seemingly inspired by the Spider-verse films, irreverent needle drops (M.I.A., Missy Elliott, Beastie Boys) and moments of pulpy space fantasy that might have taken their cues from Guardians of the Galaxy — not to mention a Cats gag set to Barbra Streisand's rendition of Memory.
Executive producer Mary Livanos told ABC News there are opportunities for more female villains in the MCU's future  (Supplied: Disney)
The Marvels motors along in a ramshackle fashion, relishing the chaotic entanglement of its central trio and leaning into its goofy visual effects, which are actually more effective, in a cartoonish way, the shoddier and more abstract they become.
There's a mid-movie sequence set on an all-singing planet — featuring South Korean star Park Seo-joon (Parasite) as a dreamy prince — which feels like a straight-up Disney musical moment, making for a nice change of pace and a shot of personality.
Still, there's no escaping the fact that most of this is better intended than executed.
To suggest that The Marvels is an affable romp for kids and pre-teens does a disservice to the intelligence of those audiences, who really deserve better.
"Brie and Teyonah and Iman care so deeply for their characters and know what they mean to so many women and so many people," executive producer Mary Livanos told ABC News. (Supplied: Disney)
The spirited leading trio do what they can with the material, but they run up against the screenwriters' usual witless attempts at comic banter, while Indian actors Zenobia Shroff and Mohan Kapur, playing Kamala's parents, get saddled with tired sitcom family schtick.
Director Nia DaCosta — who made a promising debut with 2018's Little Woods and a mess of the 2021 Candyman remake — gets few chances to show off much personality here, her skills in service to the standard dull CGI fights and explosions.
It's a shame that talented filmmakers and performers of colour are saddled with underwhelming material, taking the hit for a creatively flailing conglomerate.
In its better moments, The Marvels is a silly, throwaway adventure that suggests the true calling of its studio's future output: content streaming exclusively on Disney+, freeing up the multiplex for new modes of blockbuster imagination.
The Marvels is in cinemas now.

title: Sydney cop sentenced for pointing gun towards colleague over spoilers for Tom Cruise movie
content:
A Sydney police officer who pointed his gun towards a colleague after warning him not to reveal spoilers about the movie Top Gun: Maverick has been handed a two-year good behaviour bond and a conviction.
Constable Dominic Francis Gaynor was working behind the counter at Day Street Police Station, in the CBD, in May.
According to court documents the complainant, 26-year-old Probationary Constable Morgan Royston, saw the Tom Cruise blockbuster the previous night and told Gaynor: "I'll spoil it for you."
The agreed facts state Gaynor, 30, then laughed as a different colleague left the room and said: "Don't spoil the movie, c***".
Gaynor is also quoted as saying: "I'll shoot you."
The agreed facts say Gaynor then took his Glock out of its holster.
"He pointed his firearm at the vicinity of the complainant and held it stationary for five seconds," the documents say.
"The offender's finger was on the receiver and not the trigger. The offender was laughing throughout this incident."
Top Gun: Maverick starred Tom Cruise. (Supplied: Paramount)
Gaynor pleaded guilty to carrying a firearm with disregard for the complainant's safety.
On Thursday, Mr Royston, who has since left the force, became emotional in Downing Centre Local Court as he described falling into depression following the incident.
He recalled wanting to become a police officer and being aware of serious dangers and many challenges the job could entail.
Mr Royston said it was common for juniors to "share jokes and tease each other", but he would never forget the "overwhelming shock and fear" he felt.
The court heard he previously regarded the station as a "home base" away from danger, but that was replaced with anxiety and hyper vigilance.
"I have completely lost the trust I had and my admiration for the NSW Police Force," he said, reading from a victim impact statement.
"When I see a police officer now, I feel compelled to watch them and check their hand is not on their firearm."
Gaynor's counsel, Chris Micali, said his client made an awful mistake and acknowledged the misuse of the weapon could have had serious consequences.
But he said there was no malicious intent to scare or intimidate.
"This is a case where the skylarking and tomfoolery in an employment context has gone awry," Mr Micali told the court.
A conviction would "definitely see him removed from the police force", Mr Micali said, and his client was remorseful.
"This is going to cost him dearly."
Alison Graylin, for the Director of Public Prosecutions, submitted the court would take a "very dim view" of the so-called skylarking.
The community placed a great deal of trust in armed police officers, she said.
"The victim was as entitled to that trust as any lay person in the community."
In sentencing, Magistrate Michael Maher noted the "power imbalance" between the defendant and his more junior colleague.
He had regard to several character references which painted Gaynor positively, suggesting there had been "an unfortunate lapse of judgement" which was "not representative of his true character".
Magistrate Maher said a police officer was entitled to carry a firearm but doing so was "a great responsibility".
He placed Gaynor on a Community Corrections Order for two years, handed him 100 hours of community service, and recorded a conviction.
Earlier this week, NSW Police said Gaynor remained suspended without pay.

title: Mean Girls returns in musical form, but you wouldn't know it from the trailer
content:
Nearly 20 years after Mean Girls hit theatres and launched an endless amount of quotes into our cultural lexicon, the franchise is returning with a musical twist.
Not that you really get that from the trailer, though.
The first look at a hotly anticipated adaption of the Broadway musical is here, and it's got some fans scratching their heads.
Australian actor Angourie Rice plays Cady Heron. (Paramount Pictures)
In case you missed it, comedian Tina Fey (who wrote the original Mean Girls film in 2004, based on Rosalind Wiseman's 2002 book Queen Bees and Wannabes) adapted the story into a Broadway production in 2017.
It starred actress and singer Reneé Rapp as Regina George, whose solo World Burn has become one of the highlights of the production.
Reneé Rapp peforms World Burn.
Mean Girls: The Musical ran for three years, eventually wrapping up in March 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
Now, Fey returns with a film adaption of the Broadway musical.
I repeat, this is not a live recording of the Broadway production, or a Gen-Z reboot of the original film.
But to muddle that distinction, there's not one original song featured in the new trailer, which is instead set to get him back! by Olivia Rodrigo.
It's a questionable choice to those expecting to get a sneak peek of Cady, Regina and the rest of The Plastics belting out a number.
There are subtle hints to musical elements, such as the line "a new twist from Tina Fey", some flashes of dance sequences and the addition of a musical note in the pink logo.
But the line "not your mother's Mean Girls" is not flying with millennials.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
With Reneé Rapp embodying Regina George in the Broadway production, she's back reprising the role of queen bee for the film adaption.
Reneé Rapp continues to play the role of Regina George. (Paramount Pictures: Jojo Whilden)
Ashley Park (Emily in Paris, Only Murders in the Building) also starred in the Broadway production as Gretchen Wieners, but this time she's playing French teacher Madam Park.
Tina Fey is back playing Ms Norbury, with Tim Meadows also returning as Principal Duvall.
Australian actress Angourie Rice is playing the iconic role of Cady Heron, originally played by Lindsay Lohan, with Busy Philipps replacing Amy Poehler as Regina's regular cool mum.
Busy Philipps joins the Mean Girls universe by playing Regina's mother. (Paramount Pictures)
Jon Hamm (Mad Men, Good Omens) has also joined the cast, playing the small but crucial role of Coach Carr.
The film adaption of the Mean Girls musical is heading to cinemas on January 12, 2024.
If you're keen for a taste of what to expect, the original Broadway soundtrack is available on streaming.
And if you're looking to revisit the original film, the 2004 Mean Girls is available to watch on Netflix and Binge.

title: Actors' union announces tentative deal to end strike that shut down Hollywood
content:
The union for striking Hollywood actors says it has reached a tentative agreement with studios to put down pickets after a 118-day shutdown of the entertainment industry.
The union was asking for an increase in minimum salaries, a share of streaming service revenue and protection from being replaced by artificial intelligence
Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) members walked off the job in mid-July.
They were asking for an increase in minimum salaries, a share of streaming service revenue and protection from being replaced by artificial intelligence.
The union says negotiators reached a preliminary deal on a new contract with the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP), which represents Walt Disney, Netflix and others.
Actors will be able to put down their pickets just after midnight Thursday, the union said in a statement.
SAG-AFTRA members have been on strike for 118 days.  (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)
The breakthrough means Hollywood can ramp up to full production for the first time since May, once union members vote to ratify the deal.
SAG-AFTRA's national board will consider the agreement Friday, and the union says it will release further details after that meeting.
Representatives say they secured a contract of "extraordinary scope" including a streaming participation bonus for the first time.
"We have arrived at a contract that will enable SAG-AFTRA members from every category to build sustainable careers," their statement said.
The 65,000 striking film and television actors joined screenwriters belonging to the Writers Guild of America (WGA) in walking out following failed studio negotiations.
Actors had similar concerns to writers, who argued compensation for working-class cast members had dwindled in a streaming world.
Streaming TV series currently do not offer the same residual payments actors enjoyed during the heyday of broadcast TV.
George Clooney and other A-list stars voiced solidarity with lower-level actors, urging union leadership to reach a resolution.
"I'm relieved," actor Fanny Grande said.
"It's been really difficult for most people in the industry, especially people of colour.
"As it is, we don't have as many opportunities. We aren't big celebrities that have money in the bank for months.
Major Hollywood studios have given their last offer to striking actors, according to the union. But will it bring an end to the strike?
WGA members agreed to form a deal with studios and returned to writing scripts in late September, but the ongoing SAG-AFTRA strike left many productions in the dark.
The disruptions cost California more than $US6 billion ($9 billion) in lost output, according to an estimate by the Milken Institute.
Hollywood's work stoppages led movie studios to delay big releases such as Dune: Part 2 because striking actors could not promote them.
Other major films, including the latest instalment of the Mission: Impossible franchise and Disney's live-action remake of Snow White, were postponed until 2025.

title: The Marvels showcases power of teamwork as female leads break new ground
content:
The Marvels, the latest film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), is the first in the studio's history to feature three female leads — Brie Larson as Captain Marvel, Teyonah Parris as Monica Rambeau and Iman Vellani as Ms Marvel.
"These are characters that we grew up with, who we love. Brie and Teyonah and Iman care so deeply for their characters and know what they mean to so many women and so many people," said executive producer Mary Livanos.
"Getting to see them all team up is wonderful, especially because part of what we're saying — a theme of this film — is that together, we're even more than the sum of our parts."
In the Marvels, the characters' powers become entangled due to a mysterious wormhole; each time one of them uses their powers, they chaotically switch places with each other.
"Ms Marvel — her DNA in the comics is as Captain Marvel's biggest fan and it's a wish fulfilment for her that she gets to meet Captain Marvel in this film," Livanos said.
"It's through her lens that we're able to examine the idea of Captain Marvel, the idea of heroism, talk about it, and get to know Carol Danvers for the person she is behind that moniker."
The film also introduces new characters, including South Korean actor Park Seo-joon, who plays Captain Marvel's husband Prince Yan, and Zawe Ashton as the baddie Dar-Benn, who has been gender-swapped from the comics.
Zawe Ashton as Dar-Benn and Daniel Ings as Ty-Rone in The Marvels. (Supplied: Marvel Studios)
Livanos said there were opportunities for more female villains in the MCU's future — her next project is centred on Agatha Harkness, the witch antagonist who made her debut in the Disney+ show Wandavision.
Captain Marvel was a milestone for the MCU, becoming the first female-led Marvel film when it premiered.
Despite alleged review bombing — where users post negative reviews en masse to drive down a film's rating on sites like IMDB and Rotten Tomatoes — Captain Marvel was a box office hit, making over US$1.1 billion, while also receiving favourable reviews from critics.
"I've been super privileged to be able to work on projects that feature incredible women. Of course, women have an incredible history in Marvel Comics — Monica Rambeau at one point even led the Avengers," Livanos explained.
"To be able to further the trend of fair and equal representation has been awesome and I really look forward to continuing to do that over the course of my career and at Marvel."
The film is a sequel to 2019's Captain Marvel and continues storylines from TV shows Ms Marvel and Secret Invasion. Its run-time clocks in at 105 minutes, which makes it the shortest film in the MCU.
The Marvels enters Australian cinemas on November 9.

title: Tiger King star 'Doc' Antle pleads guilty to wildlife trafficking and money laundering
content:
An exotic wildlife preserve owner who gained notoriety on the popular Netflix series Tiger King, has plead guilty to animal trafficking and money laundering.
Bhagavan "Doc" Antle oversaw the sale or purchase of cheetah cubs, lion cubs, tigers and a juvenile chimpanzee that were all protected as endangered species, according to a United States Department of Justice release.
Officials said the 63-year-old man, who featured in a documentary miniseries about the tiger trade, tried to hide animal payments as "donations" to his nonprofit organisation.
"The defendant held himself out as a conservationist, yet repeatedly violated laws protecting endangered animals and then tried to cover up those violations," Assistant Attorney-General Todd Kim of the department's Environment and Natural Resources Division said in a statement.
Antle faces a maximum of five years' imprisonment, fines up to $US250,000 ($385,000) and three years of supervised release for each count.
Bhagavan Antle plead guilty on Monday in a South Carolina court.  (Supplied: Horry County Sheriff's Office)
Antle operates Myrtle Beach Safari in South Carolina and is the founder of a nonprofit registered in the state called the Rare Species Fund.
Investigators found evidence that Antle and a co-conspirator had also used cash acquired through the transportation and harbouring of immigrants who illegally entered the country.
In June a jury acquitted Antle of five counts of animal cruelty.
Joe Exotic, the US "Tiger King" who was involved in a murder-for-hire plot, will be presentenced.
The judge in that case dismissed four more animal cruelty charges facing Antle and all charges against his two adult daughters.
It is the latest fallout for the subjects of Tiger King: Murder, Mayhem and Madness.
Joe Exotic, the show's star, is serving a 21-year prison sentence for trying to hire two different men to kill animal welfare activist Carol Baskin.
The ongoing feud between Exotic — whose real name is Joseph Maldonado-Passage — and Baskin featured prominently in the show.
Maldonado-Passage had one year shaved off his penalty last year as he began treatment for early-stage cancer.

title: Hollywood studios present 'last, best and final offer', striking actors say
content:
Striking Hollywood actors claim they have received what negotiating studios called the  "last, best, and final offer" in their attempt to end the 115-day standstill of the entertainment industry.
The latest round of negotiations comes as frustrations grow for both studios and actors and box office numbers continue to plummet.
Here's what you need to know about this latest development.
The Screen Actors Guild and the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) said they have received what the studio association, Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP),  "characterised as their Last, Best, and Final Offer" on Sunday local time.
SAG-AFTRA members have been striking for over 115 days, looking for protections in a streaming world.  (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)
"We are reviewing it and considering our response within the context of the critical issues addressed in our proposals," the union said in a statement.
They did not disclose what the newest offer contained.
However, according to the New York Times, the talks included a wage increase that "could be the highest in four decades", according to a person familiar with the offer.
A new way of determining streaming residuals based on performance metrics, AI protections, and increases to pension and health funds were also offered, according to the same report.
Residuals refer to the amount paid to actors in the case of re-runs, syndication or DVD releases.
In the streaming world, there is no clear cut method to calculate residuals and actors are typically paid a flat fee regardless of a project's performance.
The latest offer came after a video conference that reportedly included top executives from NBCUniversal, Netflix, Disney and Warner Bros.
Walt Disney chief executive Bob Iger has been sitting in on the latest round of negotiations with SAG-AFTRA.  (Reuters: Aly Song)
Executives from Paramount Pictures, Amazon Studios, Sony Pictures and Apple Studios have also regularly participated in the latest round of negotiations.
An AMPTP representative did not immediately respond to Reuters's request for comment.
There are reports that Hollywood's biggest stars are also willing to take dramatic steps in an effort to end the strike.
A proposal supported by stars including George Clooney, Emma Stone and Ben Affleck could see Hollywood's big earners cover the cost to AMPTP signatories and eliminate the cap on union membership dues, according to Deadline.
George Clooney was involved in a proposal that would see Hollywood's top earners pay more to the unions to cover insurance and pension funds.  (Reuters: Henry Nicholls)
The plan also floated giving pay cheques first to the lowest names on the call sheet who most need the money.
Clooney confirmed the proposal.
"A lot of the top earners want to be part of the solution," he told Deadline.
"We've offered to remove the cap on dues, which would bring over $US50 million ($76 million) to the union annually.
"We think it's fair for us to pay more into the union."
SAG-AFTRA president and The Nanny star Fran Drescher (right) with WGA president Meredith Stiehm.  (AP: Chris Pizzello)
It is another sign of growing desperation by both the studios and struggling actors after negotiations were suspended by AMPTP in October.
"It is clear that the gap between the AMPTP and SAG-AFTRA is too great, and conversations are no longer moving us in a productive direction," the alliance said at the time.
We'll have to wait and see.
Already, some SAG-AFTRA negotiating committee heads have called upon Hollywood superstars to make studios accept the union's asks — indicating this might not be the end of the strike just yet.
"The time has come for you to put pressure on the CEOs. Call the studio heads. Shout at them on social media. Tell them to accept our deal," SAG-AFTRA strike captain Chelsea Schwartz said on social media, shortly after the latest talks.
She tagged celebrities including Oprah Winfrey, Taylor Swift and Jennifer Aniston.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
Another strike captain, Marlo Su, posted on social media, saying "SAG WILL DECIDE" in response to the claims it was the best AMPTP could offer.
Union members will also have to agree to any deal before shooting can resume.
HBO is the latest studio to announce a rescheduling of highly anticipated shows.
Programming chief Casey Bloys told IndieWire that he has had to "adjust across the board" due to both the SAG-AFTRA and WGA strikes.
Viewers of smash hit The Last of Us will have to wait until 2025 for season two.  (HBO)
The White Lotus season three won't come back until 2025 and The Last of Us season two will now shoot in early 2024 for an Autumn 2025 release, he told the publication.
After 146 days of Hollywood shutdowns and strikes, screenwriters have struck a tentative deal with studios. But here's why there will be no return to TV and film as we know it.
It prequel Welcome to Derry, which was expected to hit our screens in time for Halloween next year, is now slated for 2025.
The new Mission Impossible film and Disney's live-action Snow White have also been pushed back to 2025.
Actors have been striking to address growing concerns in a streaming world.
In July, 65,000 striking film and television actors joined screenwriters belonging to the Writers Guild of America (WGA)  in walking out following failed negotiations with major studios.
The SAG-AFTRA union shared concerns over issues of pay, streaming residuals and the looming threat of AI.
Actors joined the striking Writers Guild of America (WGA) members on the picket line in July 2023. (Reuters: Shannon Stapleton)
The result was an almost complete shutdown of Hollywood, and marked the first joint writers and actors strike in over 60 years.
In late September, writers struck a deal with studios, ending their strike, but actors are yet to reach a deal.

title: ICYMI: Kylie is well and truly in her villain era, but Disney seems to have forgotten how to write one
content:
It might be hard to believe, but things did happen in the arts and entertainment world over the weekend that had nothing to do with Taylor Swift.
Swifties went into full flight over 1989 (Taylor's Version), the re-recording of the 2014 album that arguably transformed her into the Pop Diva to Watch.
Billboard reports 1989's past week was the biggest for any album by units earned since Adele's 25 in 2015 (although Jung-Kook's album Golden won their fan poll).
Somehow managing to score the single-largest sales week for any of her albums with a record everyone had already heard, Taylor proved once again what we already knew: she is an outstanding businesswoman who knows her way around a catchy hook.
Not everyone (nobody?) has quite the cut-through she does, so we thought we'd spotlight some other stuff. And this way, you can stay up-to-date without ever having to pause your 20th repeat of Blank Space today.
The original Pop Diva to Watch is, obviously, Kylie Minogue.
This was made very clear over the weekend, as she performed her first ever Las Vegas residency, in a show creatively titled More Than A Residency.
As per the online reaction, it was a high-energy performance, with Kylie herself saying she felt the "VEGAS HIGH" on her social media.
It's the latest in a recent spate of wins for Kylie, with her new album Tension debuting at number one on Billboard's Dance/Electronic Albums chart, and reportedly delivering her largest US sales week for an album in almost two decades.
Our girl is at the Venetian Resort in Las Vegas for three months, giving lucky audiences plenty of time to padam padam.
— Allison Jess
The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame has been criticised roundly (and often rightly) for many reasons over the years.
They've been on a long redemption tour, one that came to a head when founder Jann Wenner was ousted from its board of directors after comments he made about Black and female artists. The 2023 induction over the weekend also shows some encouraging progress when it comes to equality in the Hall.
Kate Bush, Sheryl Crow and Missy Elliott were all inducted as performers, while Chaka Khan received one of the musical excellence awards.
ncs youtube: St. Vincent - Running Up That Hill (Kate Bush Tribute)
Elsewhere, George Michael, Willie Nelson, Rage Against the Machine and The Spinners were also inducted as performers, session musician and producer Al Kooper, and Elton John's songwriting partner Bernie Taupin were also given Musical Excellence awards, hip hop progenitor DJ Kool Herc and guitar icon Link Wray took out Musical Influence Awards, and Soul Train host Don Cornelius took the Ahmet Ertegun that goes to non-performing industry professionals.
"I'm honoured to be in the class of 2023, alongside such a group of profoundly articulate women and outstanding articulate black artists," Taupin said in his speech, referencing Wenner's comments earlier in the year.
Other highlights include Carrie Underwood performing George Michael's 'One More Try', St. Vincent covering Kate Bush's 'Running up That Hill' (Bush did not attend, but sent a note of thanks), and a tribute to The Band's Robbie Robertson from Elton John, Chris Stapleton, Sheryl Crow and Brittany Howard.
— Dan Condon
The Real Housewives franchise has never shied away from heavy topics and, perhaps because of that, the series can dip into murky moral territory — with breakdowns turned into memeable moments.
Criticisms against the franchise and its network Bravo have increased recently, as a series of former housewives and Bravo stars have filed lawsuits, alleged mistreatment and campaigned for the creation of a reality TV union.
Last week, fuel was added to the fire with an 8,000 word exposé by Vanity Fair writer Anna Peele, featuring interviews with previous housewives Leah McSweeney, Eboni K. Williams, Bethenny Frankel and more.
They say the TV empire does little to care for its stars' mental health, with McSweeney stating she broke nearly a decade of sobriety out of pressure to be good TV.
It's also alleged that ex-New York cast member Ramona Singer used racial epithets in conversation and expressed that Williams — the first Black New York housewife, cast for its 13th season — shouldn't be on the cast, as her presence "ruins the show".
Neither Bravo or parent company NBC have publicly commented, though Singer was removed from the line-up of Bravo Con, a three-day convention held over the weekend in Las Vegas. During it, Bravo released a trailer for the upcoming season of Ultimate Girls Trip, featuring Singer.
— Jared Richards
The week after British actress Ruby Barker wrapped filming for her character Marina Thompson in Bridgerton, she was admitted to hospital for mental health reasons.
"I was deteriorating, and then the minute we wrapped…" the 26-year-old told the LOAF Podcast in an episode released last week.
A year later, in the run-up to when the show was to be released, she returned to hospital for similar reasons.
Barker said "not a single person from Netflix, [and] not a single person from SHONDALAND" contacted her to check on her welfare or to offer support in the wake of either stay.
"I was just then coming out of hospital [for the second time] … my Instagram following was going up, I had all these engagements to do. My life was changing drastically overnight and yet there was still no support and there still hasn't been any support."
Unsurprisingly, the content mill had a field day over this news. Barker has been described as "slamming" Netflix and Shondaland by numerous publications.
Barker is having none of that. In a video to her Instagram followers, she said: "I literally stated fact very calmly."
"I said what I said because the crux of the point I was making is about a duty of care…
"I think that as people we can do better."
And in the comments, she continued: "I never deep dived or exposed any of the nuanced behind the scenes experiences I had as a 21 year old, working class woman of colour, descending into psychosis on that job. And I likely never will due to the very real climate of fear and repercussion for those that use their voice to catalyse change in this world."
— Yasmin Jeffery
The release date for Disney's hotly anticipated new musical Wish is drawing closer, and TikTok is already set on hating it.
Villain song 'This Is The Thanks I Get?!' by Chris Pine has TikTokkers like @reuben declaring "Disney is truly in its flop era — it's giving AI generated, it's giving writer's strike".
"I don't know who decided that every song has to sound like a Lin Manuel Miranda rip off but we need to end it."
Walt Disney Animation Studios youtube: Disney's Wish | "This Is The Thanks I Get?!"
The video's at almost 3 million views and compares the Wish track to villain songs from years gone by, wondering why "Disney thinks that the audience can't understand nuance anymore", pointing to hits like Hellfire, Poor Unfortunate Souls and Mother Knows Best.
While it's a little early to tell just how good (or bad) this film's going to turn out, recent division around yet another "adorkable" protagonist and the merging of 2D and 3D animation styles don't have fans particularly hopeful.
— Rachel Rasker
What is DanceRites, you may ask? It's kind of like So You Think You Can Dance but First Nations, and without all the speccy smoke and mirrors.
In its biggest program to date, the annual festival will bring together 350 performers from some 30 different nations and clans, for an incredible exchange of culture and storytelling in the form of a dance-off at the Sydney Opera House.
Ian Kaddy, Douglas Kaigey and young dancer Zarius Wosomo of Meuram Murray Island Dance Group at DanceRites 2018. (ABC Arts: Teresa Tan)
It'll be held on the forecourt of the Opera House at Tubowgule (Bennelong Point), a traditional meeting place for the Gadigal people. Dancers will battle it out for the top prize in front of a panel of five judges, performing song and dance in two categories: "Cultural Dance and Song Cycle" and "Wildcard".
This is the first time the competition is happening in person since 2019 — it was held virtually in 2020 because of COVID and has been on hiatus since.
Oh, and did we mention it's free?
— Anna Freeland
Things got a bit weird on Drew Barrymore's show over the weekend.
Drew's longtime friend and former babysitter (???) Pauly Shore proposed to her on stage, after saying it was hard for him to let love in. He then interrupted her final spiel to promote his one-man show.
The Drew Barrymore Show youtube: Pauly Shore Proposes to Drew Barrymore | The Drew Barrymore Show
It is unclear whether this was a publicity stunt or just a man being weird and intense again, but it has raised a lot of questions, like: Why did her producers let this man on the stage? Is that fear or excitement in her eyes? Who is Pauly Shore?
Even though we're a bit iffy on Drew for her previous strike-violating behaviour, I don't think anyone should EVER be totally blindsided with a rando proposal. At least he didn't do a flash mob.
— Katherine Smyrk

title: You can stop flicking aimlessly through streamers. Here are five new shows we think you’ll love
content:
Welcome to What to Watch!
I'm so into this month's new-to-streaming releases that I wish I could watch them again for the first time.
In lieu of a time machine, I guess I'll have to settle for knowing the experience lies in wait for you.
The Buccaneers — Official Trailer | Apple TV+
Nan St George (Kristine Froseth), is one of those thin, white, conventionally attractive, brunette young women whose entire personality revolves around the fact they're always the side character.
She's *kooky*, she's *different*, she takes issue with women being paraded about like "cattle" – and her life goals definitely do not involve marriage.
Unfortunately, this story takes place in 1870s America, where none of these traits are socially acceptable.
We meet Nan as her beautiful and vivacious best friend Conchita (played by Alisha Boe — yes, this is another colourblind cast period drama) gets married in New York City to an ultimately uptight English lord.
Out of fear of the way his new, extremely American (read: raucous) bride will be received in restrained England after the wedding, Lord Richard Marable invites each of her bridesmaids to London to keep Conchita company and debut in high society.
Our protagonist, Nan St George, is a walking trope factory but her story is still an irresistible one.  (Supplied: Apple TV+ )
They're barely off the boat before Nan steals the show from her extremely jealous and marriage-hungry sister. She then has a series of *'I'm just so clumsy but also surprisingly educated for a woman of my time'* mishaps, garnering the attention of two very different men she's extremely attracted to in the process.
The Buccaneers may be inspired by the unfinished novel by Edith Wharton, but the vibe of this show is: very silly period drama with a modern twist.
Each of The Buccaneers speak with tone and inflection that feels more like they're California Valley girls, with dialogue occasionally to match. There's a pink poodle. The soundtrack includes the likes of Olivia Rodrigo.
It's very Bridgerton-esque, but better. (Admittedly, all The Buccaneers needed to do to improve on the Bridgerton formula was not include a "the Duke is a 'broken' asshole because he doesn't want kids" storyline or have the same premise as Gossip Girl.)
Yes, there are a few eye-roll moments in The Buccaneers, but that doesn't mean the swoon-worthy moments don't land. As you proceed, finding out what happens to our dear "I'm not like other girls" Nan feels like a must.
Will she end up with the mysterious Duke, the "greatest match in England"? Or the unnamed softboy she met at Conchita's wedding in New York and ran into again in London? And is he really a softboy?
Near the end of the first episode, the chemistry between our protagonist and one of said suitors — I won't reveal which — gave me goosebumps.
For fans of: Christina Hendricks (who plays Nan's mum!), Bridgerton, Little Women, Emma, The Great, The Empress, Gold Diggers.
Last Stop Larrimah: Murder Down Under | Official Trailer | HBO
Welcome to Larrimah, population approximately 11. At least, it used to be.
On December 16, 2017, Paddy Moriarty and his dog disappeared from the remote Northern Territory town.
Everyone in Larrimah became a suspect, and the search for answers continues to this day.
Was Paddy fed to the resident crocodile? Was he cooked into some pies? What did the ongoing feud he had with his nearest neighbours have to do with his disappearance?
Last Stop Larrimah may be available to stream on Netflix in Australia, but this is a HBO original documentary — which is to say the production value is incredibly high.
Still, it's hard not to marvel at the way a US television network took such a bizarrely Australian story and did it such cinematic justice.
This is a sensational true crime story, yes, but it's also an achingly beautiful depiction of some uniquely Australian characters, who are frankly mesmerising to watch.
For fans of: Tiger King, Gunther's Millions
Erotic Stories | Premieres Thursday 26 October on SBS and SBS On Demand
Please don't sleep on this show. It's Australian TV excellence.
Erotic Stories is being marketed as a "steamy" series that explores sex and intimacy through eight standalone stories, but don't let your eyes glaze over at the short story-ness and Australian-drama-ness of it all.
This is the real deal. It has a cast of household names (Frances O'Connor, Kate Box, Catherine McClements and many more) who embody their characters so well you forget they're even famous.
Many of the episodes are written in such a way that it's beautifully challenging to work out what's coming next. I cannot recall a single line across the series that was delivered in a way that felt stilted, fake or predictable.
It's provocative, but not exhaustingly so.
Instead, it's titillating. It's taboo. It's torrid. And it's honest, delicate and healing. Yes, I ran out of words beginning with T. Just, watch it.
For fans of: 1985, Four Walls, A Beginner's Guide to Grief
Twin Love — Official Trailer | Prime Video
I haven't had the privilege of watching Twin Love yet because it's still under embargo, but I genuinely believe I don't need to watch this before recommending it.
You don't need me to tell you to watch this show for XYZ reason. You can tell from the title alone that this is just pure reality dating-show mess — with an exciting identical twin twist.
But OK, some premise. Hosted, of course, by identical twins Nikki and Brie Garcia (who were professional wrestling tag team The Bella Twins), Twin Love takes 10 sets of twins and separates the siblings across two houses, creating two "identical" casts.
While they're separated, they can't communicate with their twin. The aim is to find out if they end up going for the same twin set, or whether their choices in partners differ vastly. There are challenges and eliminations along the way, and new twin sets get added to the houses.
TL;DR this would be the perfect reality show *if only* Jedward were among the cast. I mean, come on.
For fans of: Love Island (Twin Love was created by the same people behind ur fav UK reality show), Love Is Blind, Queer Ultimatum, The Ultimatum, Love Trip Paris

Yasmin Jeffery goes deep into the ABC iview catalogue to curate a list of shows and films to consider when you feel like you've seen everything old everywhere else, and nothing new looks good.
I don't think any of us had a musical version of six defining Australian news stories down on our list of television shows that simply must be made.
So, the conclusion I have come to after watching Australian Epic is that ABC iview knows what we need before we do.
Written by The Chaser's Chris Taylor and Andrew Hansen and performed by an ensemble cast, this series gives stories like Steven Bradbury's bizarre 2002 Olympic gold-medal speed-skating win and the Schapelle Corby story a part-documentary, part-musical treatment.
The songs are a little grating at times — though this is arguably true of any musical production — but ultimately funny.
The episodes are short and sweet at just under the 30-minute mark, and the talking heads trotted out to speak to the documentary side of things are engaging, so much so that you don't even notice you're learning, because you're also laughing, groaning, oohing and aahing.
