title: Quiz Lady, the romping new sister comedy starring Sandra Oh, Awkwafina and Will Ferrell
content:
We truly are living in a golden age of Asian-American film.
The newest addition to the genre comes in the form of Quiz Lady, which had its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival in September, and is now coming to streaming.
The film centres on a couple of down-on-their-luck sisters who turn to a television game show to pay their mother's gambling debts and, in turn, save a pet pug called Mr Linguini.
And those sisters are played by the beloved Sandra Oh (Killing Eve) and Awkwafina (Crazy Rich Asians; The Farewell).
Competing on a gameshow to win money to pay off a blackmailer is sure to make someone sweat. (Supplied: Disney+)
The buddy comedy-style film is directed by Oscar-winning Chinese-American director Jessica Yu, who told the ABC's Stop Everything that it was the cast that drew her to the project. We don't blame her.
"I first read the script, I could imagine Awkwafina and Sandra Oh in it and I was just like, in love," Yu said.
Benjamin Law and Beverley Wang host your end-of-week blitz on what everyone's watching and listening to right now.
The film has the leading ladies playing against type — Jenny (Sandra Oh) is in her hot mess era who is there for the hustle; Anne (Awkwafina) takes on the role of the shy, nerdy one who is really good at game shows.
And, like most of us with siblings, both characters find themselves regressing around each other.
"When you're with your sibling, all of a sudden, you're back in grade school," Yu says.
Awkwafina plays Anne, a brilliant but tightly wound, gameshow-obsessed young woman. (Supplied: Disney+)
"We had so much opportunity to talk about the script and talk about our own experiences as siblings … you know, talk about our families, talking about our Asian American experience.
"So, I think that a lot of that chemistry came out of those conversations; came out of them just becoming friends."
Director Jessica Yu says there was a lot of on-set banter and chemistry among the film's comedic stars. (AP )
Unsurprisingly, the shoot for Quiz Lady was a lot of fun — not only because of time hanging out and laughing with Oh and Awkwafina.
The film also features the comedic stylings of Jason Schwartzman (as the gameshow's obnoxious champ) and Will Ferrell.
"There was so much funny banter," Yu said.
"Sometimes I'm working on a shot or something and I hear them laughing. I'm just having FOMO because I know there's something hilarious happening across the room."
Will Ferrell bringing his comedy and charm as gameshow host Terry McTeer. (Supplied: Disney+)
Ferrell is a producer-actor double threat here, playing quiz host Terry — who is written as a calming and warm presence.
"When you have somebody like Will Ferrell, there's just this natural humour that bubbles up," Yu said.
"So, there's not a lot of like, punchline moments that you have to write for him, just the way that he delivers lines where you just laugh, because it's Will. It's just that timing and comedic charisma."
Yu also told ABC that Hollywood has hit a tipping point for Asian casts.
She referenced a line in the film where Jenny (Sandra Oh) — remember, she's the hot mess — complains about how hard it is to be an Asian woman in the US. The twist? Instead of it representing a genuine moment, she is manipulating the situation to be about her.
Sandra Oh plays Jenny, a "trainwreck" who is determined to help her sister, and Mr Linguini. (Supplied: Disney+)
"I think that we are at a place where we're beyond the Asian character either being kind of a punchline or being there to explain their experience to the general audience," she said.
"I think it is a signal that we are expanding the kinds of characters that we see in the way that they're Asian American. This can be the fabric of their character, but is not the reason for the story."
Quiz Lady is available on Disney+ from November 3.

title: Meg Ryan is back with her first romantic comedy in over a decade: We look back at her impact on the genre
content:
It's been eight years since Meg Ryan last starred in a movie, and even longer since she starred in a romantic comedy (rom-com).
The genre has become synonymous with Ryan's career, even though — as she stated in an interview with the Associated Press recently — she's done "roughly 40 movies and only seven of them were rom-coms".
What Happens Later is Ryan's long-awaited cinematic return to the genre that made her a movie star.
It's also dedicated to her long-time rom-com collaborator, writer and filmmaker Nora Ephron, who died in 2012 at the age of 71.
Movie Trailer for What Happens Later (2023)
And Ryan's not just the lead, alongside David Duchovny, but also the director, and one of the screenwriters of the film that opens in United States (US) theatres this week.
Originally meant for worldwide release in October, the film was rescheduled due to the release of Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour movie.
Nora Ephron wrote and directed Meg Ryan in several successful romantic comedies in the late 80s and 90s.  (Lateline)
The plot reads like your typical rom-com set-up. Two ex-lovers, Willa (played by Ryan) and Bill (played by Duchovny) run into each other in an airport during the holiday season (cue romantic snow).
Both their flights get delayed, and they're forced to revisit their relationship and explore what went wrong.
In the film's trailer, they bicker, laugh, dance, and seemingly poke fun at the rom-com cliches that many would associate with Ryan's career in particular.
The trailer looks like it has all the essential ingredients, a recipe that film and television writer Cameron Williams said comes easily to Ryan.
He adds that her stereotype in the cinema landscape has, for a long time, been that of the "romantic comedy darling".
"That stereotype was very much established in the 1980s during her collaboration with Nora Ephron in When Harry Met Sally … in that film, she arrived on the scene after playing many supporting roles in her career and established herself as just a really talented, comedic actress."
So what has been Meg Ryan's impact on the rom-com genre? Let's look back.
"A lot of romantic comedies during that time were very conquest driven … and a lot of the time it was mainly from the male's point of view," Williams said.
According to him, by all accounts, the romantic comedies in the 1980s looked very different to the wave of cosy rom-coms we witnessed in the late 80s/early 90s.
That was mostly due to Nora Ephron's hit film, When Harry Met Sally, starring Ryan and Billy Crystal.
Released in 1989, it was the start of a film partnership between Ephron and Ryan that would cement Ryan as a rom-com movie star.
For the rom-com genre, it was a turning point.
When Harry Met Sally was a career-defining moment for Meg Ryan.
"It was very much part of a wave of romantic comedies that we're like, 'We're going to show both sides of the relationship and we're going to understand both the female character and the male character … so you can understand what makes their relationship dynamite," Williams added.
The film is well-known for its New York setting, Autumn fashion, and a fake orgasm scene in a deli that goes down in movie history for this quote;
It was the start of a trio of movies: When Harry Met Sally, Sleepless in Seattle, and You've Got Mail, which would make Ephron and Ryan a powerful force in the rom-com genre.
It was 1993, and Ephron united with Ryan once again for the romantic comedy film Sleepless in Seattle — joined by Tom Hanks, who would go on to cement his own role in the rom-com genre with Ryan by his side.
The film, written and directed by Ephron, had Ryan playing Annie Reed — a loveable reporter who is engaged but feels like there is something missing in her life.
Meg Ryan and Tom Hanks's movie Sleepless in Seattle proved to be another commercial success for Nora Ephron.  (Website: IMDB )
After she watches the film An Affair to Remember she responds to a radio segment with a young child who is hoping to find his widowed father (Hanks) a new wife.
Hanks and Ryan don't get within hand-holding distance of each other until the final scene of the film (sorry, spoilers) and, in fact, they don't even kiss which is a rare feat in rom-com land.
The film was a commercial success for Ryan, Ephron, and Hanks — which doesn't surprise Williams.
You've Got Mail is known as one of the 90s most popular rom-com films.  (Photo: Shutterstock)
In a name perfect for the rom-com genre, Ryan played Kathleen Kelly in the 1998 hit film You've Got Mail — which reunited her with Ephron and her Sleepless in Seattle co-star, Hanks.
The film included email and chat rooms as the landscape for a serendipitous meet-cute — a reflection of the late 90s adjusting to life with the internet.
Hanks and Ryan's characters, Joe Fox and Kathleen Kelly, are rival bookstore owners who don't realise they're also each other's online chat partner — both falling in love (of course).
The film was another commercial success for Ryan and Ephron, and would be their last romantic comedy together.
But it was not their last film together — that was the comedy-drama Hanging Up in 2000.
As Ryan returns to the rom-com genre with What Happens Later opening in US theatres this week, Williams is adamant that the golden era of rom-coms is tightly connected to Ryan's presence on screen.
For many rom-com devotees, the Ephron-Ryan partnership was the genre's peak.
Since then, the romantic comedy has, according to many, taken a side step.
Big films like Barbie and Oppenheimer now dominate the landscape, and many wonder if the rom-com era will ever be as good as it was during the Ephron-Ryan years.
Carrie Fisher and Meg Ryan in When Harry Met Sally. (Supplied)
Williams said that big-budget films, like the ones we see from the Marvel universe, mean rom-coms are being made cheaper than ever.
"The romantic comedy became a comfort space for streaming services, especially Netflix, who churned out a lot of OK rom-coms, like To All The Boys I've Loved Before …  I think once those films fell into the algorithm it has just seemed to become a content churn," he said.
So, will Meg Ryan's What Happens Later bring back the rom-com magic? Only time — and audiences — will tell.
author: Megan Macdonald

title: 'It's where the most viewers are': Australian content reaching tens of millions around the world
content:
Australian creators are reaching tens of millions of people around the world by creating content that appeals to under represented audiences and using non-traditional media to distribute it.
Screen Australia has released its 2022-23 Drama Report which shows $2.34 billion was spent in Australia across 213 productions last financial year.
While there are plenty of successful homegrown shows on streaming platforms and on mainstream media channels, scroll roughly a third of the way down the 100-page report, and you'll get a glimpse of what's happening in the online space and why this is an ecosystem worth keeping an eye on.
Viewing numbers on platforms such as YouTube, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok are eye-watering and as the CEO of Screen Australia Graeme Mason points out – it's a sector that's continuing to grow.
"It's where the most content is.
"A lot of it is obviously self-generated and self-funded and even self-uploaded. But we do a lot in that space and have done for many years … because I think it's vital, culturally, it's vital creatively and it's where a lot of our new real content and content creators are."
Mr Mason said creators can experience enormous success on social media platforms.
He cites the RackaRacka brothers as an example.
He says twin brothers Danny and Michael Philippou have been funded by Screen Australia since 2015, creating content on their YouTube channel, which has amassed more than 1.1 billion views.
Viral YouTube creators RackaRacka made a horror movie, and it’s cursed in all the right ways.
Mr Mason said one of the benefits of posting content to social platforms is the immediate reactions from viewers and the RackaRacka twins are good at capitalising on that.
"They put so much stuff up and they get feedback from their peers and the audience really fast," Mr Mason said.
"So, they hear and see what's working, what isn't working, and that really informs their stylistic and creative choices.
"That's much more efficient than you spend millions of dollars and two years of your life making a TV show or five years of your life making a film and it doesn't land."
Making it big on social media can, lead to opportunities and recognition in other formats and the RackaRacka brothers are a good example of that too with the success of their 2023 feature film Talk to Me.
"You look at that film, it's extraordinary," Mr Mason said.
"And it's become one of the most talked about films of the year with huge directors like Jordan Peele and Peter Jackson saying it's the best thing they've seen."
The Head of Online and Games at Screen Australia Lee Naimo says part of the reason online creators reach so many people is that their content travels internationally.
"That content obviously isn't Geo blocked," Mr Naimo said.
"So, it's accessible by anyone, anywhere in the world with a device and with an internet connection.
"And that often results in some really big numbers."
He offered a number of examples. The sketch comedy creators behind the Superwog YouTube channel have run up more than 460 million views.
Meanwhile, the series Black As Rebooted, which went out on Facebook, is sitting at around 195 million views.
Glitch Productions released a pilot episode of The Amazing Digital Circus two weeks ago and it's already racked up 55 million views with a single episode of their Meta Runner series garnering almost 30 million views.
Actor Chloe Bayliss has turned a bunch of "horrendous" dating stories into an exciting new series called Next which is rolling out on TikTok. It's another example of creatives choosing social media as the platform to launch their work.
"In terms of online, Screen Australia recognises that as a real pathway for emerging creators to not only get their first taste of working on bigger budget projects, but also access huge audiences locally and globally," Mr Naimo said.
"It's kind of become a real pathway for that talent to prove themselves, to create really unique and distinctive and often quite niche and specific work that speaks to audiences that are really under served on broadcast and on mainstream TV and feature film."
Expenditure on online drama and other content that has first been released on social media or emerging online services has increased by 74 per cent since 2021-22 and the number of titles that entered production in 2022-23 was double the previous year.
With budgets typically much lower than a feature film or TV series, more and more creators are turning to premium web series, as well as audiences.
There's lots more in the 2022-23 Screen Australia Drama Report which you can access here.

title: Saoirse Ronan and Paul Mescal star in this R-rated sci-fi romance filmed in regional Victoria
content:
"I don't want a robot living with my wife," protests Paul Mescal's beleaguered grunt in Foe, banging his fist on a table with all the conviction of a sketch comedy performer trying to keep from cracking up in front of a live studio audience.
It might sound like high farce, but Australian filmmaker Garth Davis's ambitious, sometimes mysterious sci-fi romance is deadly earnest in its delivery.
It's a film that is bravely, and admirably, committed to the kind of big emotional swing that unfortunately proves to be its undoing.
The film was shot over three months in outback Victoria and South Australia. (Supplied: Transmission)
Based on the 2018 novel by Canadian writer Iain Reid, who also co-wrote the screenplay with Davis (Lion; Mary Magdalene), Foe poses that age-old question: What if your partner was replaced with a replicant?
Mescal and fellow compatriot Saoirse Ronan play an unlikely Mid-Western American couple in 2065, where — as a title card all but copied-and-pasted from Blade Runner informs us — climate change has rendered the planet uninhabitable, the population is moving to off-world space stations, and "simulants" have been created as substitutes to humans.
Factory worker Junior (Mescal) and diner waitress Hen (Ronan) are among the few holdouts on Earth, stubbornly clinging to their rustic farmhouse in a magic-hour America that looks suspiciously like regional Victoria. (The film was shot there, and in parts of South Australia, early last year, with Mescal also delighting Melbourne celebrity spotters by seamlessly blending in with the mullets of the inner north.)
“Even though the book was written through Junior’s point of view, we felt it was Hen’s story,” Davis told Inverse. (Supplied: Transmission)
Late one night, they're visited by an enigmatic, vaguely threatening stranger, Terrance (Aaron Pierre), a consultant from an off-world government initiative who informs them that Junior has been selected to travel to a space station for two years, leaving Henrietta alone.
To observe the couple ahead of their separation, Terrance moves into the farmhouse's guest room, complicating an already fraying marriage.
It all seems both a little off, and a little familiar. Does Hen know Terrance? Why is Junior acting so out of character?
There are hopes the cinema release of Foe will increase the profile of Victoria's Winton Wetlands.
Foe arrives as the latest in a mini zeitgeist of movies tangling with the hot topic of artificial intelligence, following the camp antics of M3GAN; and the action epic The Creator, also set in 2065. (Mark your calendars for the robot invasion, I guess.)
But Davis is less interested in asking existential questions about technology than he is in using science fiction as a jumping-off point to explore a human relationship in flux.
For a while, at least, the film holds the audience in a captive trance, simmering with a sense of intrigue and menace. We're never quite sure which version of Hen and Junior we're about to encounter, a slipperiness that Ronan and Mescal play in a state of sultry, sweaty dissonance.
“I guess what really drew me to it was the central relationship.," Davis told The Hollywood Reporter. (Supplied: Transmission)
With its uncanny setting and strange accents, Foe can often seem abstract and otherworldly, with Hungarian cinematographer Mátyás Erdély (Son of Saul) shooting the Australian outback — all surreal red salt flats, wild horses and burning barns — to resemble a dream unfolding out of time.
Once Terrance reveals the overarching plan, however — that the off-world corporation will replace Junior with his synthetic clone to keep Hen company while he's away — the movie takes a dramatic turn for the accidentally comedic, lapsing into increasingly cornball dialogue and trite visual motifs. (Not to mention the billionth use of Skeeter Davis's all-purpose apocalyptic anthem, The End of the World.)
Oscar nominees Ronan and Mescal are both charismatic, gripping performers, and they give Hen and Junior a rich sense of lived-in love and loathing. But despite the stars' best, hot-and-bothered exertion, Davis and Reid's screenplay eventually hangs them out to dry.
“The work in this film was finding out what it’s like to be in a tired relationship. That’s not a sensation I’m familiar with," Mescal told Harper's Bazaar. (Supplied: Transmission)
The film's overheated dramatic climax is — albeit unintentionally — one for the ages, a perfect storm of great ideas run aground on terrible execution: gruesomely sincere performances, laugh-out-loud lines and a maudlin violin score wailing away at every turn.
Still, Foe is, in many ways, too odd and too precious an object to deserve the critical scorn it's going to attract.
As someone who's generally a sucker for this kind of bravely earnest sci-fi, I almost feel the need to be protective of Davis's film, or at least hope that it finds its defenders.
Foe is in cinemas now.

title: 'It's about choice': Cinema CEO blasts studios over no interval for Killers of the Flower Moon
content:
In order to run a film with an intermission, cinemas must get permission from the studios behind the movie.
That hasn't stopped a small number of movie theatres from showing Martin Scorsese's 206-minute film Killers of the Flower Moon without that permission.
US media outlets are reporting a handful of independent theatres in North America, the UK, Europe and South America began screening the movie with breaks ranging from six to 15 minutes.
The studios behind the film have reportedly informed those venues it violates their licensing agreements.
ABC News has contacted the film's producer, Apple Original Films, and distributor Paramount but has received no further comment.
The news has reignited debate about the length of some movies and whether intervals should be introduced for lengthy features.
Palace Cinemas, which runs 24 movie theatres across Australia, approached Paramount to ask if they could insert an intermission into Killers of the Flower Moon but the answer was no, says Chief Executive Benjamin Zeccola.
"They checked with their head office in California, LA, and the response came back that that would not be permitted," Mr Zeccola said.
"They've got this concept of how the director intended the film to be seen.
"And I find that somewhat awkward because, obviously, when these films are shown at home, on streaming on Apple TV, or any other platform, or DVD, there's a pause button, which people frequently use.
"It feels like cinemas are being discriminated against.
"It's unfair."
Benjamin Zeccola says customers should be given a choice. (Supplied)
Mr Zeccola says the needs of the customer should be considered over and above any stylistic considerations.
"I think that it's absolutely imperative that the people that are contemplating this put the customer at the centre of the decision-making process," he said.
"It's not about the director, it's about the viewer.
"It's our duty, it's our obligation to put the viewer at the centre of the universe and make decisions that suit the viewer. Not the director, not the studio, not the exhibitor.
"Let's put the emphasis back on the customer."
Mr Zeccola said people usually want a break after 2 hours, and Palace has received complaints about the length of some movies.
"During Oppenheimer was when we noticed customers requesting that we put a break into the films and then, knowing Killers of the Flower Moon was coming down the line with a long running time, that's what prompted the requests to Paramount."
Martin Scorsese returns with a devastating yet beautifully rendered film exposing America's shameful history of genocidal violence.
He said any break does not need to be too long.
"A 10-minute break would be ideal," Mr Zeccola said.
"It's really a comfort stop that you can get up, stretch your legs and go to the bathroom if you need to.
"If you want to grab more refreshments, great.
"However, really, it's about that comfort factor."
He said at cinemas where the clientele tends to be older, the break could run up to 15 minutes.
"And then we can advertise which sessions have the break and which sessions don't and customers can make their choice.
"And I think that's the most important thing, is that people want choice these days.
"It's about choice."
From the 1950s and into the 1970s, intermissions during movies were commonplace.
"Part of it was technical," Mr Zeccola said.
"The film prints were running through projectors, and you'd get to the halfway mark and you had to change the reels of film being projected through the projector.
"So, there was a break there for the projectionists to get the next spool up. And customers loved it as well."
Zeccola said it is not the first time Palace Cinemas has requested an intermission and in 2015, they were successful.
"There was an intermission in Quentin Tarantino's The Hateful Eight some years ago, which was very well received."
He believes in some cases there are directors who let their movies go on for too long and he would personally prefer if movies ran between 90 – 120 minutes.
"Beyond that, it's probably a bit over-bloated."
He said the incentive for studios to run shorter films is long gone.
"This comes down to the fact that when film was printed on film, when it was actually printed on celluloid, each print of the film cost a lot of money — thousands and thousands of dollars and you paid per foot.
"So, the longer the film, the more expensive the print, so the studios used to have a reason to ensure that the films didn't run too long. They had a financial motivator there.
"And since digital, the cost of a digital file for a film is the same regardless of its length.
"So, there's no longer any sort of restriction from the studio or producer point of view. So, they're getting a bit long and a little bit self-indulgent."
Some popular movies have been known to run over 3 hours. Here are a few.
Mr Zeccola said it could be hard on an exhibitor because it forces them to show fewer movies, which can affect a movie theatre's business model.
But it is not all bad news.
"We kind of love it as well because it really is the most incredible art form," he said.
"The way it combines the art of music, the mise en scène, the cinematography, acting and storytelling into one art form is just incredible.
"We're madly in love with it, as you can tell.
"So, when a film is truly spectacular, I don't think you feel the time dragging.
"It's only if they're padding out a story or if it's not quite efficient or economical enough that it's a problem."

title: 'He totally helped me get sober': How Matthew Perry's honesty about his addiction changed lives
content:
"Hi, my name is Matthew, although you may know me by another name … My friends call me Matty. And I should be dead."
This is the opening line of Friends, Lovers and the Big Terrible Thing, the unflinching 2022 memoir from actor and comedian Matthew Perry, cataloguing his lifelong battle with addiction.
He died on Saturday, aged 54, a few days shy of the one-year anniversary of the book's release.
Perry knew he'd be remembered primarily for his role as the sarcastic and lovable Chandler on Friends — could he BE any more iconic? — but he hoped he would also be celebrated after his death for the things he did to try and help other people. Specifically, other people grappling with addiction like he did.
"I've had a lot of ups and downs in my life. I'm still working through it personally, but the best thing about me is that if an alcoholic or drug addict comes up to me and says, 'Will you help me?', I will always say, 'Yes, I know how to do that for you'," he wrote.
Matthew Perry was cast as Chandler Bing when he was 24 years old; the youngest of the cast. (Supplied: WarnerMedia)
And while the news is full of big-hearted recaps of Chandler's best moments and how much the show meant to so many, it's clear his candid discussions and revelations about addiction and mental health have also had a huge impact.
Megan Lee, a senior teaching fellow in psychology at Bond University, says what he described is known as peer mentoring or peer support in the context of addiction recovery, which includes programs such as Alcoholics Anonymous.
This involves people with similar conditions or circumstances giving non-professional assistance to those struggling with addiction or other drug-related problems.
"Peer support and outreach in addiction recovery can be highly impactful and are considered an essential component of many recovery programs," Dr Lee said.
"While there is no one-size-fits-all answer to how important or impactful it is, the evidence and research generally support the idea that peer support in addiction recovery can have significant benefits."
Perry's frank accounts of his own life are moving, and will hopefully continue to help people long after his death.
"There is a hell," Perry wrote in his memoir.
"Don't let anyone tell you different. I've been there; it exists; end of discussion."
Perry said he had his first drink at 14 and was immediately hooked. He details how he followed the path of his father, actor John Bennett Perry, into alcoholism. He said the "best part of his day" would be drinking six vodka tonics every night.
Putting the stories of his addiction into print wasn't easy for Matthew Perry, but he wanted to help people. (Supplied: Macmillian)
Then, while filming Fools Rush In with Salma Hayek in 1997, he had a jet ski accident. He was given Vicodin for the pain.
Within 18 months of that moment, he said he was taking 55 pills a day, inventing elaborate schemes to get the drugs he needed.
The entire time, he was working on one of the biggest shows in the world.
"You can track the trajectory for my addiction if you gauge my weight from season to season," he wrote.
Perry said the pressure of the show and fame only made things worse.
"I had a secret and no one could know," he said.
"I felt like I was gonna die if the live audience didn't laugh, and that's not healthy for sure. But I could sometimes say a line and the audience wouldn't laugh and I would sweat and sometimes go into convulsions."
Arguably one of the biggest episodes of Friends was the season seven finale, The One with Monica and Chandler's Wedding, which aired in May 2001.
It was an amazing moment in the life of Chandler Bing, but not as amazing for the man who played him.
Perry revealed in his memoir that he was living in rehab at the time of filming.
Jennifer Aniston almost broke Instagram when she posted this photo, showing that the Friends cast were together once more. (Instagram: Jennifer Aniston)
"I married Monica and got driven back to the treatment centre — at the height of my highest point in Friends, the highest point in my career, the iconic moment on the iconic show — in a pick-up truck helmed by a sober technician."
He had previously been confronted by Jennifer Aniston about smelling like alcohol, and said one table read had be cancelled after drugs and alcohol made him incomprehensible. That pushed him to get help.
"In nature, when a penguin is injured, the other penguins group around it and prop it up until it's better," he wrote.
"This is what my co-stars on Friends did for me."
In July 2019, Perry woke up from a two-week coma. His opiate abuse over the years had caused his colon to explode. His family were told he had a "two per cent" chance of living. He was in hospital for five months and had to use a colostomy bag for nine months.
"My therapist said, 'The next time you think about taking Oxycontin, just think about having a colostomy bag for the rest of your life'," Perry wrote.
"And a little window opened and I crawled through it and I no longer want Oxycontin anymore."
Perry had faced a lifetime of health impacts from what his body had been through.
He was hospitalised with pancreatitis at the age of 30. Some of his teeth fell out when he bit into an apple.
A few years after the colon explosion, his heart stopped beating for five minutes, after opioids he had secretly taken interfered with surgery anaesthesia.
In January 2023, he had his 14th surgery pertaining to his opiate abuse.
"No one knew — not my family, my friends, no one. I was impossibly sick all the time," Perry wrote in his memoir. (Reuters: Fred Prouser)
"The best thing about me, bar none, is that … I can help a desperate man get sober."
Matthew Perry was committed to using his experiences to help others.
He turned his former home in Malibu into a sober living residence for men. He wrote the play The End of Longing, saying it was a "personal message to the world" and that he had "something important to say to people like me, and to people who love people like me".
And it wasn't an easy thing, to put some of his worst moments in cold hard print. But he knew it could actually make an impact.
"Whenever I bumped into something that I didn't really want to share, I would think of the people that I would be helping, and it would keep me going," he told the New York Times.
In the hours after his death, people had already started saying how much he helped them with their own addictions, including Hank Azaria, who said Perry took him to his first AA meeting.
"As a sober person, he was caring and giving and wise and he totally helped me get sober," Azaria said.
Perry said repeatedly he had countless conversations with people that were struggling.
Dr Lee says while peer support is not a replacement for professional treatment, it can still be invaluable for people's recovery.
And, for people like Perry, helping other people can be an important and meaningful part of recovery themselves.
"It serves as a positive distraction, builds self-esteem, reinforces commitment to recovery, strengthens accountability, altruism and empathy, and fosters community and connection," Dr Lee said.
For Perry, this is arguably his true legacy.
"When I die, I know people will talk about Friends, Friends, Friends. And I'm glad of that, happy I've done some solid work as an actor," he wrote.
"But when I die, as far as my so-called accomplishments go, it would be nice if Friends were listed far behind the things I did to try to help other people."

title: Celebrating Halloween in Australia 'about having a bit of fun'
content:
Brenda O'Connor knows some Australians don't like Halloween, but she doesn't mind.
She is among the people in Warrnambool getting into the spooky spirit and dressing up ahead of Tuesday.
"The main negative argument I constantly hear is that it's an American thing. It's really not," she said.
"We've got to move on from that conversation it's an American thing, that myth is busted.
"It's an acknowledgement of a Celtic ritual and the change of seasons.
"In Australia, we're coming out of winter and into spring. We're marking a that change and we're getting out and about, we're having fun."
Brenda O'Connor loves dressing up for Halloween. (Supplied: Brenda O'Connor)
Ms O'Connor said there were different events happening in her regional Victorian town to celebrate the day.
They included flash mob dances to Michael Jackson's iconic song, Thriller, and a sustainable scarecrow trail highlighting the importance of recycling and repurposing materials.
Ms O'Connor said she relished the opportunity to plan a scary costume for Halloween.
"I am a fan of people getting out and roaming the streets, getting dressed up, and having fun," she said.
"It's great when you forget that you're wearing [a costume] and you have drop to into the supermarket on the way home."
About 80 people dressed as various creatures of the undead. (
               ABC News: Jean Bell
            )
Ms O'Connor said the celebration of Halloween had picked up momentum in recent years, with more Warrnambool residents getting involved.
"That growth can only continue when you get more interest and participation," she said.
People as young as four got dressed up for the event. (
               ABC News: Jean Bell
            )
Another Warrnambool event launched from the growing popularity of Halloween was the zombie parade.
About 80 people of all ages dressed up as the undead staggered down Liebig Street to gather in the Civic Green in front of the Warrambool Art Gallery on Sunday.
Face paint and fake blood helped people perfect their undead look for the event, organised by local community agency Brophy Family and Youth Services.
One of the organisers, Kerri Ryder, said the gathering was intended to spark joy and connection between people of all ages.
Kerri Ryder says the event was about being silly. (
               ABC News: Jean Bell
            )
Linda Said and Maria Russell show off their scariest selves. (
               ABC News: Jean Bell
            )
"Zombies are the great equaliser," she said.

title: Matthew Perry's five iconic moments as Chandler Bing on Friends
content:
Matthew Perry's 10 seasons on Friends made him one of Hollywood's most recognisable actors, playing the sarcastic, yet insecure and neurotic, Chandler Bing.
The Emmy-nominated actor was found dead at his Los Angeles home on Saturday at the age of 54.
Starring opposite Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Matt LeBlanc, Lisa Kudrow and David Schwimmer, Chandler quickly became a beloved character on Friends with his quirky demeanour and displays of underdog desperation.
Here are some of the highlights and evolution of Chandler Bing over the course of the Friends television show.
Opening the very first episode of Friends, Chandler and the rest of the characters are seen sitting together in the show's iconic hangout location — Central Perk.
Chandler then starts telling the others about his dream where he is naked, and he gets an unusual call from his mother.
Opening Scene: Friends, Season 1: Episode 1, The Pilot.
A recurring support character throughout the show's run is Chandler's on-again, off-again girlfriend Janice, who he struggles to break up with on more than one occasion.
Perhaps the funniest attempt is his very first.
In Season 1, Episode 5 we cut back to Chandler throughout the episode, as he drinks more and more coffee — and gets more and more hysterical and jittery — trying to lay out his reasons for cutting Janice loose.
Thankfully Phoebe is there to save him.
Chandler breaks up with Janice: Friends, Season 1: Episode 5, The One with the East German Laundry Detergent.
Chandler and Joey's antics throughout the series are among the most memorable moments on Friends.
As close as the two roommates are, they definitely get on each other's nerves, as Joey's relaxed, chilled demeanour doesn't always gel with Chandler's high-strung peculiarities.
In Season 3, Episode 2 things come to head as the pair fight over a chair in Monica and Rachel's apartment while they are supposed to be leaving for a function at Ross's museum.
The fight spills out over the chair to each other's wardrobes, to hilarious results.
The Chair Fight: Friends, Season 3: Episode 2, The One Where No One's Ready.
Ross and Rachel enlist the help of Chandler in order to get a new couch up to their apartment.
In a relatable scene for anyone who has helped friends move furniture up a stairwell, Chandler is crushed by the couch.
As they approach a turn in the stairs, Ross loudly commands the other to "pivot!".
With the couch eventually stuck in the turn, Chandler jokingly responds: "What did you mean when you said pivot?"
Ross's New Couch Pivot: Friends, Season 5: Episode 16, The One with the Cop.
By Season 6 the commitment-phobic Chandler has turned a corner himself, as romance blossoms between him and Monica.
In one of the show's most heartwarming scenes, Monica sets up a surprise marriage proposal with the help of Joey.
But when the moment gets a too emotional for her, Chandler steps up to the plate.
Chandler and Monica's proposal: Friends Season 6, Episode 25, The One with the Proposal.

title: Garth Davis needed a 'distressed environment' for his next film. A camping trip invite would provide the answer
content:
An ecologist hopes the cinema release of Foe, starring Academy Award nominees Saoirse Ronan and Paul Mescal, will increase the profile of Victoria's Winton Wetlands.
Director, co-writer and producer Garth Davis, known for the Oscar-nominated film Lion, needed a "distressed environment" to tell the sci-fi drama, set for cinema release this week.
Paul Mescal and Saoirse Ronan star in Foe. (Supplied: Transmission Films)
Adapted from Iain Reid's novel, the plot centres around a couple Hen (Ronan) and Junior (Mescal) who live on an isolated farm in America's Midwest that has been damaged by climate change.
A stranger from a government organisation — played by Aaron Pierre — arrives and explains that Junior has been pre-selected for a program in space, which means leaving the farm and a biological replacement will be created to keep Hen company.
While scouting for possible shooting locations with Reid in Canada, Davis came across properties that were "too idyllic".
He said he didn't know Winton Wetlands in Victoria's north-east existed before joining neighbours, who wanted to use their new telescope, on a camping trip.
"As we're setting up the tents, I saw a car driving through the trees at dusk," Davis said, "and it reminded me of the opening of the movie".
The site was flooded in 1969 to create artificial Lake Mokoan for water storage, drowning thousands of river red gums before it was decommissioned in 2009.
The uppermost branches of river red gums protrude from Lake Mokoan. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Anna Chisholm)
In the years since, work has been underway to restore the wetlands to its former ecological glory.
Davis said the drowned river red gums helped tell the story.
The generational farm is the centrepiece of Hen and Junior's life, he said, and the landscape of skeletal gums invites the audience to imagine a time when they were living and healthy – and perhaps the farm was thriving.
In the film, Hen and Junior live on a secluded farm that's been in Junior's family for generations. (Supplied: Transmission Films)
"Sometimes you can feel haunted by it, and sometimes you can feel welcomed by it," Davis said of the landscape.
"It's a pretty powerful place."
In early October, the area that had served as the Foe set was underwater. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Anna Chisholm)
The natural changeability of the wetland did throw up some challenges.
"I did move the set quite a few times before we started building. I had it a lot further in the middle and I had to move it much further to the edges," he said.
Then there was the wildlife, the snakes and "cockatoos made themselves known".
A snake wrangler was employed to sweep the set before filming.
"There's a lot of spirit in that place."
Restoration manager Lisa Farnsworth hopes Foe, released by Amazon Studios, will help attract visitors and raise the wetlands' profile.
Dr Farnsworth said the Winton Wetlands Restoration Project had worked to repair the environment and reintroduce wetland fish species and the growling grass frog.
Lisa Farnsworth says she's glad the filmmakers loved the wetlands in its dry state. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Anna Chisholm)
"The 40 years of Lake Mokoan … drowned somewhere in the vicinity of 150,000 if not a little bit more red gums," Dr Farnsworth said.
"That's what you see in the landscape today."
It's an expansive space, circled by ranges and dotted with river red gum skeletons.
Dr Farnsworth said the area has a longer history serving as a meeting place for Yorta Yorta and other communities in the area.
Dr Farnsworth says the creation of Lake Mokan flooded about 150,000 river red gums. (Supplied: Rene Martens)
The wetlands naturally go through phases of dry and wet, Dr Farnsworth said.
"I love it at both ends of the spectrum and I'm glad that the filmmakers loved it at the dry end as well," she said.
She's waiting to see the film.
"I'm going to be really interested to see what remains, what they've edited out, and how they've edited different things out," she said.
Winton Wetlands education officer Rowan Barrow grew up nearby and remembers kids from school sailing on Lake Mokoan.
Rowan Barrow says the area has transformed since her childhood. (Supplied: Rowan Barrow)
The Yacht Club is now an education centre.
Ms Barrow said people could see the effects of the restoration efforts.
"As a teacher, it's just magical because you can step out from [the] Education Centre, and you can see it all happening in front of your eyes".

title: Redditors made billions on the US stock market during the pandemic. Now they've made a movie about it
content:
In the opening months of 2021, when the world was still in the throws of the COVID-19 pandemic, a group of amateur investors on a social media platform made billions on the US stock market, nearly bankrupting huge investment firms in the process.
Two years later, Hollywood has got their hands on the David v Goliath story and turned it into a feature film called Dumb Money.
Based on the non-fiction book The Antisocial Network by Ben Mezrich and starring Paul Dano as the unofficial leader of the movement, Dumb Money will attempt to dramatise the already dramatic events of the 2021 GameStop short squeeze.
Here's what you need to know before you see the film.
Dumb Money will centre around the events of the 2021 GameStop short squeeze.
GameStop is a chain of bricks-and-mortar video game stores in the US.
GameStop is the parent company of the Australian equivalent, EB Games.
Like EB Games, GameStop is mostly seen in suburban shopping centres across the US.
Before mid-July 2020, GameStop stocks weren't really anything to write home about. They were trading at about $US4.
But then something strange happened. GameStop stock began to rise.
By October 2020, it was at $US12 and by December, it was $US18.
By the end of January 2021, GameStop stock had risen to $US347.51 — a monthly surge of 1,915 per cent.
At first, Wall Street was baffled at why a usually unattractive stock like GameStop would soar so high.
It quickly became clear that the surge in demand for GameStop stock had been driven by an enthusiastic bunch of individual investors, many of whom hung out on the subreddit r/WallStreetBets.
WallStreetBets is a place where users post their stock holdings and talk about their trades.
At the start of 2020, a WallStreetBets member going by the name of DeepF**kingValue — who we now know is US financial analyst Keith Gill —  posted on the subreddit that he had invested $US50,000 into GameStop stock.
Undeterred by those saying he was foolish, Gill stuck to his guns and his investment grew.
By the end of January 2021, his $US50,000 investment was worth $US47 million.
Gill led the way for a legion of WallStreetBet users to buy GameStop stock.
What is Gamestop and how did Reddit send its share price "to the Moon"?
The online resistance led by Gill didn't just cause a near-defunct stock to resurrect, it also caused a lot of rich people to lose a lot of money.
It's got to do with something called short selling.
When you buy shares in a company, you're usually betting that it will become more profitable over time. So you're going "long" on the stock.
But if you believe that a company's shares will tank — like the shares of a video game retailer — you can borrow shares at their current price and sell them to others, even though you don't own them.
If your bet was right and the share price falls, you buy them back from the market for less than you sold them for.
Then you return the shares to the original owner and pocket the profit.
But if your "shorted" shares increase in price, then short sellers have to scramble to buy the shares back in order to be able to return the shares to their original owner.
This can lead to increased demand for the stock, lower supply, and its price to soar.
This is called a short squeeze.
This is what happened with GameStop.
Redditors found out that some big Wall Street hedge funds were making a quick buck off failing GameStop shares, so they banded together and bought a bunch of stock to drive up value — and teach the hedge fund traders a lesson.
Shorting shares in GameStop cost hedge funds a total of $US12.5 billion over January 2021, according to financial analytics firm Ortex.
It's hard to say for sure, but many of the characters in Dumb Money are based on their real-life counterparts.
Keith Gill, aka DeepF***ingValue, aka the man credited with igniting Redditors against Wall Street, will be played by Paul Dano.
Pete Davidson will play Kevin Gill, Keith's real-life brother, and Shailene Woodley plays Caroline Gill, Keith's wife.
The film also features a number of real-life Wall Street personalities who lost huge amounts of money.
Seth Rogan will play Gabe Plotkin, whose Melvin Capital lost billions during the GameStop short squeeze.
Nick Offerman (left) as Kenneth Griffin and Seth Rogan as Gabe Plotkin in Dumb Money. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Once one of Wall Street's most successful hedge funds, Melvin Capital never fully bounced back from 2021's losses and shuttered operations in May of 2022.
Vincent D'Onofrio plays billionaire investor Steve Cohen.
Cohen's Point 72 hedge fund injected millions into Melvin Capital to help it survive the GameStop short squeeze. When Redditors found out, they targeted Cohen to the point he deleted his X (formally Twitter) account.
Nick Offerman will play Kenneth Griffin, whose hedge fund, Citadel LLC, along with Point 72, invested $US2.75 billion into Melvin Capital in January 2021.
In August of 2021, Griffin announced plans to redeem $US500 million of that investment from Melvin Capital.
Sebastian Stan and Rushi Kota play Vlad Tenev and Baiju Bhatt, the current CEO and former co-CEO of investment and trading app Robinhood.
Sebastian Stan as Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev in Dumb Money. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Many Reddit traders used the platform to buy and sell GameStop stock, with the company accused of shutting down GameStop stock buying to tank the inflated stock price.

title: 'Pinch-myself moment': Meet the Aussies who made the Darth Vader suit and your favourite monsters
content:
Adam Johansen makes monsters for a living.
After growing up on a healthy diet of Alien, Star Wars, Gremlins and The Thing, in 2002 Adam and his co-Director Damian Martin founded Odd Studio, and got to work with their heroes.
"I was obsessed with Star Wars and obsessed with Darth Vader," Adam says.
"And I was one of the five people that worked on the Darth Vader suit for George Lucas for Revenge of the Sith. It was crazy — my little self was just going nuts.
"Working with Ridley Scott on an Alien film … was a pinch-myself [moment too]."
Adam Johansen sculpting and designing an early version of the Adult Neomorph for Alien: Covenant. (Instagram: odd_studio)
Tucked away in a workshop in Marrickville, many locals might be surprised to learn this Australian team are also behind hits including Mad Max: Fury Road, Where The Wild Things Are, Aquaman, Thor: Love & Thunder, multiple films in the Matrix franchise and loads more.
In their decades in the industry, Adam and Damian have created some of the most iconic moments in film; from prosthetic make-up to animatronic characters and practical effects.
Their latest challenge? Creating a pregnant werewolf for Isla Fisher's character in the new season of TV show Wolf Like Me.
After doing work experience for a puppet company, one of Adam's early jobs involved building animatronic puppets for theme parks like Warner Brother's Movie World on the Gold Coast.
As a kid, he "would never have dreamt" he'd end up working on blockbusters at home.
But before long he had his first film under his belt; Babe: Pig in the City was followed by "a whole flurry of things coming through from the US", aligning with the opening of Fox Studios at Moore Park in Sydney.
A young Adam works behind the scenes on Farscape in 1998. (Instagram: @odd_studio)
Adam and his business partner Damian met on the Channel Nine sci-fi show Farscape, "which was awesome — we were just building aliens and monsters every week".
Since founding Odd Studio over two decades ago, the pair have had their pick of local and international productions.
Comedy-drama Wolf Like Me starts with your classic boy meets girl: single dad Gary (Josh Gad) meets Mary (Isla Fisher), whose baggage is a little deadlier than most — she's a werewolf.
Odd Studio created the auburn-haired wolf for the show's initial season. They have a range of versions, including a soft wolf puppet head for close-up attacks, a human-length wolf suit for stalking prey and an animatronic wolf that can sniff, snarl and snap at your fingers.
In the recently released season two, Mary is pregnant, which means Andrew Crawford, the creature performer in the wolf suit, "gets put through the wringer".
Squeezing into the wolf, Adam says Andrew's "vision is really impaired, it's really really hot, he's on all fours, walking through a house with arm and leg extensions".
"Season two wolf is heavier than season one wolf because there's obviously this big pregnant belly and boobs."
The wolves are mostly made of silicone and punched hair — a laborious and meticulous process that literally involves punching each individual strand of hair into the prop.
Most props and masks are sculpted on a computer before being 3D printed, with features like detailed skin tones hand-painted on.
With every monster, Damian and Adam will try on suits themselves as they build, to ensure they're as comfortable as possible, but also to make sure they can come on and off "really quick".
Andrew Crawford wears the pregnant wolf suit in Wolf Like Me. (Supplied: Stan)
"There's access panels so that, after a take, we can all run in with fans and get some air moving through," Adam says.
"Some suits, depending on the size, we can have a fan in there, or things like a cool suit, which is a vest with some tubes running through that we pump chilled water through to keep his core temperature cool."
While CGI has developed in recent years, so too have practical effects.
"The standard has gone so high, especially with the [higher] resolution of filmmaking, you can't get away with subpar colouring or skin tones — it has to look real," Adam says.
A recreation of Isla Fisher's head is used to show her werewolf transformation. (ABC: Christian Harimanow)
While CGI was all the rage when it was first introduced, in recent years, Adam says "it's actually swung back the other way".
"It becomes an aesthetic choice for some people," Damian says.
These days, the pair say most projects use a mixture of computer generated and practical effects.
"Like any approach to an effect or an illusion, if you just choose one trick, you're limiting yourself," Damian says.
If they're fine-tuned or even completely replaced in post-production, practical effects give actors something to work with, lighting designers something physical to light off and are, overall, a "really rewarding" reference tool.
The wolf suit from Wolf Like Me is big enough for a creature performer to squeeze into. (ABC: Christian Harimanow)
Adam adds that directors sometimes like to stick with practical effects "to have that limit of what looks real — because it is real".
"Some of the scariest and best films of all time have practical effects, people in suits coming out of the shadows, which is suspense building and great and terrifying.
"If you see this big CG thing running around from the first act it's kind of like: 'Oh, OK' … so sometimes [those] limitations can actually assist in storytelling."
Damian says the Odd team has been fortunate to work on a lot of overseas productions.
"When they come through, they buoy the whole industry — there's a lot of jobs.
"So when something like the writers' or actors' strikes in the US happen, that really affects us here."
Odd Studio Reel 2022
While the local industry has fallen into a bit of a slump, Damian's confident "it will rise again … there's incredible filmmakers here and the talent of local crews is phenomenal".
Adam says it's given the team a chance to work on some new Australian content, adding that we're currently in "a bit of a global pause [that] can't last forever".
From her Kentucky roots to costume designing for The Handmaid's Tale and The Sopranos, Ane Crabtree remains inspired by music, nature and the everyday fashion of strangers on the street.
When it does get busy, pinning down local artists becomes the difficulty. Luckily for them, the next generation is being trained up already.
"My youngest daughter Charlotte has started working with us here, she's sixteen," Adam says.
"I love having her here, and she's shown extreme talent already — and I'm not just saying that as a proud dad."
Damian's seven-year-old isn't quite up to werewolf creation yet, but is starting to think her dad's job among the monsters and aliens is "pretty cool".
"It was scary for her at first, but now she's embracing that."
Wolf Like Me is streaming now on Stan.

title: Dumb Money: The story of how an amateur vlogger took on Wall St bros… and won
content:
It almost feels like another century now, but it wasn't too long ago that America seemed to be losing its collective mind.
After a year of pandemic lockdowns and a US election that descended into a carnivalesque farce, the bubble burst in January 2021 when rioters stormed the capitol and small-time investors took on Wall Street — two freak occurrences that appeared to go hand-in-hand, at least in the news cycle.
With its ripped-from-the-headlines premise, Dumb Money looks to bottle some of the manic energy for a movie audience, repackaging that fraught period as something of a feel-good morality play.
It's the story of the little guys who took on the big corporate sharks and, for a moment anyway, seemed to score a victory for society's underdogs.
"Even though it's a wild and fun ride … I want people to feel activated by it," Australian filmmaker Craig Gillespie told Deadline. (Supplied: Roadshow)
The hero is thirty-something Boston market analyst Keith Gill (the deceptively guileless Paul Dano): a suburban schlub who moonlights as amateur YouTube investment pundit RoaringKitty — issuing stock tips in his signature red headband, he looks like a cross between a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle and an overgrown college kid.
"Wall Street gets it wrong all the time," he tells his followers while buying shares in floundering retailer GameSpot, a 'penny stock' that hedge fund managers regard as a joke, but which has unexpectedly galvanised the denizens of Reddit forum r/wallstreetbets.
In preparing for the role, Dano watched hours of Keith Gill's YouTube videos. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Gill's financial advice attracts amateur investors that serve as the movie's delineators of the debt-ridden working class: An embattled GameStop employee (Anthony Ramos); two University of Texas students (Myha'la Herrold and Talia Ryder) on the verge of turning to OnlyFans to pay their tuition; a struggling nurse and single mother (America Ferrera); and Gill's delivery driving stoner brother (Pete Davidson, playing firmly and satisfyingly to type.)
They're crosscut with billionaire hedge fund managers Gabe Plotkin (Seth Rogen, nicely bucking his cuddly pothead persona), obliviously cocooned in his Miami mansion; Steve Cohen (the great Vincent D'Onofrio), padding around his capacious office while tossing scraps to an actual pig; and the vaguely sinister Kenneth C. Griffin (Nick Offerman), a man so obscenely wealthy that everything seems to be little more than Monopoly money to him.
In an interview for EW, Gillespie described Davidson's approach to acting as "spontaneous and improvisational". (Supplied: Roadshow)
Australian filmmaker Craig Gillespie (I, Tonya; Cruella) lays the smash singles (Cardi B, Megan Thee Stallion, Kendrick Lamar), TikTok clips and memes on thick, his weakness for obvious needle drops and derivative style for once in sync with the subject matter, effectively cultivating a sense of a society out of whack. (The approach isn't without its careless moments, however: At one point "Black Lives Matter" gets slathered indiscriminately across the screen, the movement's significance reduced to the slogan of a car commercial.)
It all sets the stage for the unlikely events that follow, as Gill leads his amateur army to put the short squeeze on Wall Street, driving up the stock price of GameStop to the point of making the big fund managers panic.
The short squeeze was instigated by followers of the subreddit r/wallstreetbets. (Supplied: Roadshow)
If the movement comes off somewhere between collective, anti-establishment action and basement-dwelling trolling — sticking it to the man while revelling in retrograde terms like "retard" — then it's an accurate reflection of the conspiracy-riddled wild west of a nation still reeling under Trump, where it was perfectly easy to mistake reactionary ogres for revolutionaries.
The movie gets it right in its depiction of investment team Robinhood, the disruptors who abetted and then turned on the small-time punters. Played by an amusing Sebastian Stan and Rushi Kota, they're like a combination of fashion models and school shooters.
Lauren Schuker and Rebecca Angelo's screenplay — drawn from Ben Mezrich's sensationalised 2021 novel The Antisocial Network — makes for a brisk, buzzy film. And Gillespie knows how to milk the entertainment, perhaps to a fault, from this David versus Goliath tale of class warfare.
Dumb Money's neat packaging of human triumph can feel disingenuously glib, lacking the moral outrage and political subversiveness — for better and sometimes worse — of Adam McKay's recent work like The Big Short, Vice and Don't Look Up.
A short squeeze is a rapid increase in the price of a stock due to excessive short selling. (Supplied: Roadshow)
An end credit explains that the 'movement' permanently altered the way hedge funds looked at investing, but then shows its underdog heroes with an on-screen summary of their earnings casting their victory — however satisfying in terms of the narrative — as a financial rather than moral one.
A real-life story so potentially game-changing demanded a radical form of cinematic storytelling — not something to be expected from a filmmaker who reverts to rousing montages set to Meatloaf.
Dumb Money is slick, admittedly entertaining stuff but, in reconfiguring whatever fleeting battle was won as a series of fist-pumping financial figures, it merely confirms that the system wins in the long run.
If we're willing to give the movie the benefit of the doubt — and that would be admittedly generous — then maybe that's the point.
Dumb Money is in cinemas now.

title: The Rock says French wax figure needs 'updating' over skin tone
content:
A French museum has said it is working urgently to fix a much-derided waxwork of Dwayne 'The Rock' Johnson after the US actor complained about its pale skin tone.
Johnson, who is of Samoan and Black origin, took to Instagram this weekend to joke about the Grevin Museum's botched wax figure, which appeared to depict him with white skin, and bears only a vague likeness to his features.
"For the record, I'm going to have my team reach out to our friends at Grevin Museum, in Paris, France, so we can work at 'updating' my wax figure here with some important details and improvements -- starting with my skin color," wrote Johnson, best known by his stage name The Rock.
On Monday, the museum told AFP that staff were "reworking" the wax figure, and that an updated version would be reinstalled Tuesday morning.
"They're going to work all night on it so that it's more in line with fans' expectations," Yves Delhommeau, the museum's director, said in a statement.
"Crews will work through the night to ensure the likeness is more in keeping with the expectations of his fans.
The figure of Johnson was unveiled on social media last week by the Grevin Museum, which draws nearly 800,000 visitors a year.
But a photo intended to promote the new statue drew an outcry from Johnson's fans, ranging from bemusement to anger.
Comedian James Andre Jefferson Jr released an online video mocking the statue, prompting Johnson to respond.
Jefferson said in the video that The Rock was being made to look like former England soccer star David Beckham or "part of the Royal family".
"I'm low-key offended," Jefferson said.
In 2018, the museum drew similar mockery for an unflattering figure of French President Emmanuel Macron.
Producing a Grevin sculpture takes six months and costs 50,000 to 60,000 euros ($84-100,000).

title: This international star surprised a Sydney pub and was blown away by local talent
content:
It's been a big few days for celeb spottings.
Sydneysiders lost the plot yesterday when rumours flew around that Queen of Pop Britney Spears would be touring Sydney in a bus this week to promote her book.
Meanwhile on Saturday, rap sensation Chance The Rapper was spotted in a Sydney pub, bopping along to local musicians.
Read on to find out which of these sightings is actually true, plus the other pop culture moments you may have missed.
American superstar Chance The Rapper popped into a Sydney pub on the weekend, and seems to be a fan of one of our own.
The All Night singer-songwriter took to the stage at The Lord Gladstone (aka The Gladdy) to introduce the crowd to local young rap sensation, Inkabee.
The 11-year-old Noongar Wongi musician performed with 3%, a brand new Blak music collective with Nooky, Dallas Woods and Angus Field.
Chance can be seen vibing along to Inkabee's set on the night as part of the OUR PEOPLE SXSW First Nations showcase.
— Rachel Rasker
You want a piece of her? Britney Spears' memoir The Woman in Me is out tomorrow (Australia Time), and a series of leaks posted online over the past week have seen it soar to #1 on Amazon's best seller list.
The memoir is Spears' first tell-all after her conservatorship was terminated in 2021 — a 13-year-long legal guardianship that saw her father (and, later, a court-approved professional) in control of both her personal and financial affairs.
With copies accidentally on sale early across Mexico and the United States, excerpts published by The New York Times, People Magazine and more are packed with never-before-known details about Spears' life. Spoilers: it's been a hard battle, one of postpartum depression, isolation and coercion.
The book covers her rise to fame from child star to teen pop princess in the 90s, her relationship with Justin Timberlake, her mental health struggles and life under the conservatorship — including the lack of control she had over her career, despite releasing four albums during that time. We can't wait to dig in.
But for those wanting to learn more about her recent divorce to Sam Asghari this August, you're out of luck; the book wasn't updated post-split.
Meanwhile, Australia went wild yesterday when Concrete Playground reported the international pop star would be visiting Sydney to hand out copies of her memoir, in a Britney-themed bus. The article has since been corrected to read Britney Spears impersonator, but one can dream, right?
— Jared Richards, Rachel Rasker
If you don't know what I'm talking about, within a few weeks of each other Jada Pinkett Smith and Meryl Streep have both revealed they have actually been separated from their husbands for quite some time.
Bill and Melinda Gates divorced after 27 years together. They're not the only ones.
Earlier this month, Jada revealed she and Will Smith — married in 1997 — have been split for seven years, including during the infamous Oscars slap of 2022.
Over the weekend, Meryl announced after 45 years of marriage that she and Don Gummer have also reached the end of the road — separating more than six years ago.
The celebrities cite their own reasons for continuing to publicly present as a couple and, unlike many of us regular plebs who may be forced to continue living with an ex-spouse, finances doesn't seem to be one of them.
— Kellie Scott
As striking actors in the US prepare for spooky season, SAG-AFTRA, their union, has laid down some rules.
If members wish to celebrate Halloween "while also staying in solidarity" with the strike, the union says they should avoid dressing up as characters from struck series and movies.
That means no costumes from Barbie or The Bear, and if you've been prepping your look based off Netflix's Wednesday, we have some sad news for you.
Instead, The Screen Actors Guild suggested "costumes inspired by generalized characters and figures (ghost, zombie, spider, etc.)".
After receiving some heat, the guidelines were later updated to specify that only adults need comply with these restrictions.
— Rachel Rasker
Director Emerald Fennell's upcoming thriller-slash-black-comedy-drama Saltburn made its Australian premiere at SXSW Sydney on Friday.
Fennell won the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay for 2020's shocking and powerful Promising Young Woman; this time, she casts her lens on Oxford student Oliver (Barry Keoghan), who is drawn into the opulent world of Felix (Jacob Elordi) and his aristocratic family.
The film is a sharp, unhinged satire with caustic one-liners and scenes that deliver equally in laughs and exasperated groans.
It's an unflinching film that pushes boundaries, supported by a stellar cast including Rosamund Pike, Richard E Grant and Archie Madekwe.
Saltburn | Official Trailer
Saltburn is in cinemas November 16, and is the first of two major films out this summer for Australia's Elordi, who will also star as Elvis Presley in Sofia Coppola's upcoming Priscilla.
— Thuy Ong
Now Mario's conquered the box office and broken the video-game adaptation curse, he's returning to his roots with Super Mario Bros. Wonder — the first traditional 2D Mario game since 2012.
Released on Nintendo Switch on Friday, the game has raked in rave reviews for its inventive additions to the four-decade strong series, including from ABC Gamer's Joe Reardon.
"Super Mario Bros. Wonder is just an absolute delight," he reviews.
"It delivers the series staple tight platforming, and smartly overloads the classic formula with the most out-there level design ideas and gameplay freedom Mario has ever seen."
Super Mario Bros. Wonder Review – Delightful, Surprising, Wonderful
The game's secret weapon? The 'Wonder Flower', a new pop-up that transforms each level in weird, unpredictable ways — like warp pipes coming to life or creating a stampede of enemies.
But that's not all that's new: Mario himself sounds a little different, with voice actor Charles Martinet retiring this year, having voiced the plumber (and his brother Luigi) since 1992. Twenty-six-year-old voice actor Kevin Afghani has taken up the role, even offering up a new catch-phrase: "Wowie-Zowie!"
— Jared Richards
Have you always wanted an even longer version of Baz Luhrmann's 2008 film Australia? No? Well you're getting one anyway.
The six-part series premiered its first episode at SXSW over the weekend, ahead of a Disney+ release later in November.
Often described as a "cringe" melodrama, this "re-imagining" and recut of the original includes a new First Nations soundtrack to "deepen" the film's Indigenous perspective.
Faraway Downs | Official Trailer | Disney+
The new trailer also dropped a few days ago, so you can decide for yourself whether it's worth streaming, or if you're better off just rewatching the magic that is Strictly Ballroom instead.
— Rachel Rasker

title: Sydney rappers ONEFOUR have had shows cancelled by police for years. They say change is on the horizon
content:
For a rapper who's now "used to" police raids, ONEFOUR member J Emz wasn't surprised by the presence of uniformed and undercover officers at the group's film premiere in Sydney this week.
ONEFOUR: Against All Odd's debut at cultural festival SXSW on Monday night was complete with metal detectors and riot squad officers monitoring those in attendance.
Mount Druitt raised J Emz — real name Jerome Misa — said the attention of police, including searches of his family home, was a constant in his life.
"You know, having thick skin where we're from … [you find] other ways to, I guess, manoeuvre around and be able to work through it," he told the ABC.
It was a moment of life imitating art for ONEFOUR, with the documentary chronicling its members' struggles with the authorities while trying to build their careers.
SXSW declined to comment on the extra security conditions police requested for the screening, which the ABC understands were paid for by the organisers.
But University of Technology Sydney law professor Thalia Anthony said the requirements were "an overreach of police powers."
"It's clearly diverting police resources to an event that appears to be benign," she said.
"I think the issue is the NSW Police acting in a way that is about protecting their own image but also trying to intimidate those people who it feels may look critically towards the police as a result of the experience of ONEFOUR."
NSW Police said its officers were regularly tasked to major events either as part of major operations or in a user-pays capacity to ensure safety and security for all attendees.
"NSW Police will continue to undertake high-visibility police operations at major events and festivals for everyone's safety."
ONEFOUR performing at the Listen Out festival this year. (Supplied: Jordan Munns/Listen Out)
Director Gabriel Gasparinatos, who followed ONEFOUR over four years for the film, said their journey had been a roller-coaster punctuated by breakthroughs and challenges.
"ONEFOUR's experience over these years is that with every kind of small success that they find, there's some factor that comes in the way and you know, dampens it or it all comes crashing down," he said.
This tension between regular interactions with police while also garnering millions of views and streams, ARIA nominations and global attention for their music is not new.
Three members of ONEFOUR were jailed for their roles in an affray at a pub in Rooty Hill in 2018, during which a man was beaten with a hammer and chair leg.
They were Pio "YP" Misa, Dahcell "Celly" Ramos and Salec "Lekks" Su'a.
All three have since served their sentences, with Su'a deported to New Zealand after being released.
It came just as their music was starting to gain worldwide attention and was racking up millions of streams online.
Receiving a standing ovation at its world premiere at SXSW Sydney, ONEFOUR: Against All Odds provides a look at rising Pasifika excellence, as it does a grim reality for those trying to make it out of the streets.
Over the past four years, several ONEFOUR shows have been cancelled, with police also stopping members from promoting a new song while walking out with boxer Paulo Aokuso in March.
Senior police in NSW have spoken about their belief the group is linked to Sydney's so-called "postcode gangs" — which play out with violence between rival street gangs from neighbouring suburbs.
ONEFOUR has repeatedly denied being involved in gang violence.
Police figures argue, in the documentary, the lyrical content in drill, a sub-genre of rap known for its dark themes and often violent content, posed a serious risk for violence across Sydney.
The risk of violence, police argued, would be exacerbated at live shows in particular, many of ONEFOUR's have been cancelled including a national tour in 2019.
However, in a sign of what may be changing for the group, they were recently allowed to perform at Listen Out music festival.
Missing during that run was Pio Misa, who was arrested in September and is set to be sentenced next month for an assault to which he has pleaded guilty.
He remains in custody.
J Emz says the group's lyrics were a reflection of their upbringing in Western Sydney rather than a call to action for any behaviour.
"When we create music, we talk about our experiences, our life experiences," he said.
"It might not relate to people, it's just what makes our music real. And it's just what's real to us. So that's where we come from when we make music."
Mr Gasparinatos said the police were "fundamentally misunderstanding" the idea that music causes crime or incites violence.
"The debate of whether music could incite violence has been around for as long as music has been around, you know, we've seen this kind of repeat itself over the ages with gangster rap in the 90s," he said.
"I think there's more functional ways in which the police should be engaging with this type of stuff and ways in which they should engage and work with these groups rather than against them."
He said this group's treatment raised a broader question about freedom of expression for artists.
Jerome 'J Emz' Misa says the group is hopeful they can do a headline tour soon. (ABC News)
Against All Odds spans four years of the group's explosion onto the Australian hip-hop scene.
In their wake, several groups with Pasifika heritage across the country began to make similar music including Melbourne-based HP Boyz and Logan group NME.
Beyond the headlines, Mr Gasparinatos felt much of ONEFOUR's story had been missed in media coverage.
"Something we wanted to do with the doco, as well is show this audience, the human side of ONEFOUR show a different side of these guys that you might not see in mainstream media, you might not even really see or, you know, hear in the music," he said.
"This kind of more personable community-oriented side of these guys show what they're really like, as people because I think that that has been missing from a lot of the narrative."
Spencer Magalogo aka 'Spenny', J Emz and YP in 2019. (Instagram: OneFour)
J Emz says the negative attention and criminal proceedings that have dogged the group has "affected everyone" in their inner circles.
But he holds an optimistic view for the future: "You always gotta be hopeful, man."
Hopeful to him means the chance to do a headline tour, something ONEFOUR has never done despite drawing critical acclaim.
"Obviously our first one got cancelled or shut down. I know everyone's waiting for that and we need to make that happen for sure," he said.
"I know the fans have been waiting patiently … There's actually a whole project in the works at the moment [we're] working on an album at the moment. We're hoping to get that out early next year."
