title: Late novelist John le Carré 'could've become really bad guy' during his spy years, new doco shares
content:
In this so-called post-truth era of media disinformation, the late secret service agent turned best-selling author John le Carré looks like a prophet of deception — a 20th-century sage who saw the future coming.
Or maybe it was just that he understood the essential duality at the core of human nature — the fantasies we tell ourselves in order to survive.
In the new documentary The Pigeon Tunnel, drawn, in part, from his 2016 memoir of the same name, le Carré — born David Cornwell — sat down with US filmmaker Errol Morris (The Fog of War; The Thin Blue Line) for what would become his last recorded interview before his death, at age 89, in 2020.
The late John le Carré recounts his childhood and career as a spy and author during the documentary. (Apple TV+: David Appleby)
It's a fascinating, career-ranging conversation, taking in le Carré's childhood, his years spent as an operative in both MI5 and MI6 and his breakout success as the greatest author of spy fiction during the Cold War — a period that yielded such classics as The Spy Who Came in From the Cold (1963), Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy (1974) and A Perfect Spy (1986).
For Morris, a filmmaker who is frequently drawn to complicated subjects who move in morality's liminal spaces, le Carré — and his existential grasp of human deceit — proves to be a perfect foil.
Conducted in 2019, the interview finds le Carré reflectively holding forth in his study, with Morris using split screens and canted camera angles to evoke the hall of mirrors in which le Carré existed, both in reality and his fiction.
Even archival photographs — spliced with re-enactments of his life and clips from the many film and television adaptions of his work — are obscured, clipped or presented at askew angles.
John le Carré (centre) and his sons Stephen Cornwell (left) and Simon Cornwell during the filming of The Pigeon Tunnel. (Apple TV+: David Appleby)
It all begins with his childhood — where else? — in which the young le Carré was quick to experience a sense of life's deception.
His father, Ronnie, was a notorious con man, while his birth mother passed away when le Carré was five, leaving him with a series of surrogate maternal figures.
The Pigeon Tunnel — the final interview with John le Carré — is on Apple TV+ from October 20.
"Reality did not exist in my childhood. Performance did," says le Carré, who would later create his enduring spy George Smiley as an idealised version of a father he never had.
His actual father, an elaborate chancer who even attempted to extort his own son later in life, remained a powerful spectre who hovered over him.
Asked by Morris if he ever really loved his dad, le Carré's reply is chillingly matter-of-fact: "I really don't know what love is."
Much of his perspective seems to circle back to a formative, haunting teenage memory that gives his memoir its title.
At a shooting range in Monaco, his father and a group of men would use shotguns to pick off pigeons that had been trapped for the express purpose of sport, the hapless birds looping back through a shadowy tunnel, unaware they were being duped into death.
Morris and his visual effects team render the incident in gruesome, bloody close-up, with feathers and guts scattered midair to reinforce the impact on le Carré's adult psyche.
Martin Scorsese returns with a devastating yet beautifully rendered film exposing America's shameful history of genocidal violence.
In recounting his post-Oxford years spent in the British secret service, and his early successes as an author, le Carré emerges as a compelling conduit for the anxieties of the Cold War and a clear-eyed analyst of its political and moral vagaries — what he evocatively describes, at one point, as "the self-imposed schizophrenia of the secret agent life".
"I could have become a really bad guy," he says of his espionage experience, "but mercifully I found a home for my larceny".
In one of the film's most gripping passages, there are extended recollections of Kim Philby — the British spy who was later revealed to be working for Soviet intelligence — leading to astute reflections on the nature of power.
History is chaos, le Carré ventures, and those in charge of making policy are usually doing so ad hoc.
What might begin as ideological conviction eventually becomes another form of addiction — to power, but also to the perverse thrill of betrayal.
It speaks to the enduring appeal of his writing and its labyrinthine, if often mundane, imaginary worlds, in which faceless men in suits play drab parlour games with the fate of the world — a universe away from the high-stakes glamour of James Bond's escapism.
John le Carré says he "could have become a really bad guy" during his formative years as a spy. (Apple TV+)
In Morris's reliable hands, The Pigeon Tunnel approaches both a definitive portrait of le Carré and a deft primer on the essential unknowability of human nature – where truth is an abstract concept that proves infinitely elusive, especially for those deep in the corridors of power.
Follow @abc_arts on Instagram, where life and culture collide.
In taking stock of his life, le Carré arrives at the ultimate non-revelation: that what he calls the "inmost room", that supposed repository of life's secrets, is empty.
Devoid of trite life reflection, the moment is refreshing in its clarity, leaving only the soothing calm of the void.
Morris taps into le Carré's essence – which is to say, his absence — where, as the author puts it, there is "no centre to a human being".
To the film's credit, it is content to allow its subject's rich contradictions to speak for themselves, to let his art — that ultimate synthesis of reality and fiction — be the thing that really matters.
The Pigeon Tunnel is streaming on Apple TV+.

title: 'I have peed in the bush': Nicole Kidman on what it takes to be successful in Hollywood
content:
Being a famous actor is one thing.
But Oscar, Emmys and Golden Globes winner Nicole Kidman was on the South By Southwest Sydney (SXSW) stage on Thursday to talk about what it's like to produce film and television as opposed to starring in it.
Kidman said it was the first time she'd spoken in this capacity and was joined on stage by her production company co-founder at Blossom Films Per Saari, with her childhood friend Peter Overton, from the Nine Network, asking the questions.
While they couldn't talk about specific projects due to the actors' strike in Hollywood, Kidman and Saari gave an insight into what it's like to work behind the scenes, with topics ranging from knocking on doors, never giving up and teaming up with people you'd have dinner with, to being unable to find a bathroom on set.
"I have peed in the bush," Kidman told the audience.
"Because there was nothing around and we had very little time when we were losing the light. So, it's like, go behind the tree."
Nicole Kidman has gone to great lengths to get the perfect shot. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)
The audience reacted with laughter, with Kidman continuing.
"Hey, you've got to do what you've got to do to get the shot."
Speaking about finding a great location, only to realise once the cameras were rolling that it was on a flight path, Kidman said embracing the mistakes is often the key to making great content.
SXSW Sydney has a range of panels and activities throughout the week. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)
"I've worked enough to know now, you never fight the situation," she said.
"If that's what it is, then you just stay very, very calm, almost like in a trance. Because if you do fight it, you'll get even worse.
"It will give something to the scene.
"Don't resist it, don't fight it… a lot of the mistakes are the things that actually make it magic."
Kidman and Saari revealed Blossom Films was about to start filming a John Polson-directed project, The Last Anniversary, based on the book by Liane Moriarty, having already adapted her novels Big Little Lies and Nine Perfect Strangers.
"[It's an] Australian project with Australian accents for the world," Kidman said to applause.
Around 2,500 people gathered to witness the SXSW featured session with Nicole Kidman and Per Saari in conversation with Peter Overton. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)
The audience clapped again when Kidman mentioned the late TV pioneer Brian Walsh.
"This is his project," she said.
"He was watching over it.
"He wanted Binge and Foxtel to have it and he fought like crazy to get it and it's devastating that he's not here to … but maybe he is.
"Brian's been a huge part of my life, through my whole career. And to be able to just still continue his legacy is fantastic.
"So, Brian Walsh, we miss you and we love you."
Peter Overton, Nicole Kidman and Per Saari greeted a captivated audience at SXSW Sydney. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)
The panel acknowledged Kidman's mother, who was in the audience, but Kidman pushed back when Overton referred to Saari as her "second husband".
"My other husband," she laughed and later gave a shout-out to Keith Urban when Overton again used the word husband to refer to Saari.
Budgeting was another topic on the agenda, with Kidman saying they "haven't lost money for anyone".
Per Saari says the production company takes investors' funds seriously and is committed to delivering a return. (ABC News:  Brendan Esposito)
Saari said returning money to investors was something they didn't take lightly.
"That's a responsibility that we really take seriously," he said.
"Whether it's a studio or an independent financier or the dentist down the street, they invest in us and what we believed in and we owe that back."
SXSW Sydney will come to a close on Sunday.

title: New Martin Scorsese film exposes America's shameful past of genocidal violence
content:
Martin Scorsese's 27th feature film — an urgent, devastatingly bleak crime drama about colonialism and murder — arrives right in time to rattle the collective Australian psyche in the aftermath of the Voice referendum.
Killers of the Flower Moon is the story of the systematic fraud and killings of members of the Osage Nation, an Indigenous community in Oklahoma whose oil wealth made them one of the world's richest per capita populations in the early 20th century.
But, as the film's shocking string of crimes proves, there isn't a resources boom big enough to safeguard you from genocidal violence.
Lily Gladstone (second from left) made her film debut alongside Benicio del Toro in French film Jimmy P: Psychotherapy of a Plains Indian (2012). (Supplied: Apple+)
Inspired by real events and based on journalist David Grann's non-fiction book of the same name, Killers sees Scorsese once again burrowing into the underbelly of American history with a morality tale of greed and political power.
It is also, perhaps more than usual for Scorsese, an attempt to commemorate the dignity and resilience of the story's innocent victims.
Having consulted extensively with the Osage Nation, the film is spoken in both the English and Osage language, and there are many local First Nations performers on screen.
The Screen Show brings you reviews and in-depth conversations with leading film and TV directors, actors and screenwriters from Australia and around the world.
It begins after World War I, in a drab oil rush town of muddied streets crowded with desperate men seeking their fortune.
The Osage occupy the top of the food chain here, with big houses, luxury cars and white servants.
But their oil money is also tied up in the red tape of administrators, and their life expectancy is shockingly low because of chronic diseases that arrived with colonisation, like diabetes.
Into this microcosm of American frontier life comes Ernest (Leonardo DiCaprio), a freshly demobbed soldier whose Uncle William "King" Hale (an excellent Robert De Niro) is one of the pillars of the local settler elite.
Far from a returning hero, Ernest is an alcoholic, womanising gambler whose only war injury is a hernia picked up working in an army kitchen.
Still, King sees promise in his nephew and gets him a job as a driver for a young Osage woman named Mollie (a magnetic Lily Gladstone).
"Lily is absolutely astonishing in this movie … She carries the entire film and the story," DiCaprio told British Vogue. (Supplied Apple+)
It doesn't take long before you realise King is something of a matchmaker, and the two are in fact soon married — but there's a dark side to their union.
We learn that intermarriages between settlers and First Nations women have become a lucrative racket in the town, because the men who inevitably outlive their Osage spouses wind up with large inheritances.
King and his associates use their influence to take a cut of the spoils, and have begun expediting matters with bullets, bombings and poison.
Much later in the film, when Jesse Plemons arrives in a huge cowboy hat playing a softly spoken and methodical FBI agent, the strands of this criminal conspiracy — which stretch as far into respectable town society as the local doctors and the Masonic lodge — seem almost too far-fetched to be true.
It's little wonder that Scorsese was inspired by the material; so many of his gangster films have been about men conspiring to attain power in the shadows through similar acts of strategic violence.
Martin Scorsese returns with an epic, elegiac film about the decline of mob masculinity and 20th-century America, starring De Niro, Pacino and Pesci.
But in contrast to some of these — notably Casino or Goodfellas — Killers feels, stylistically, more restrained.
Scorsese has been on record recently saying he's less interested in bravura camera moves these days and in Killers, just like in The Irishman, some of the most powerful, tense sequences unfold using the simplest of film grammar.
Sit-down conversations simmer with ominous innuendo, and even explosive violence unfolds with matter-of-fact bluntness, sometimes in just a single take.
In many of these killing scenes, Scorsese places executioner and victim — who usually know each other — in the same frame, to emphasise the betrayal between them.
But the ultimate betrayal of the film is not a sudden, violent murder — it's the slow, cruel betrayal at the heart of Ernest and Mollie's marriage that lasts almost as long as the film's three-and-a half hours.
"Marty just instinctively knew Lily was the one," DiCaprio told British Vogue. (Supplied: Apple+)
Why does this determined, strong woman, who Gladstone plays with such enigmatic calm and wisdom, not see her husband's darker side? Perhaps because Ernest hides it even from himself.
Scorsese revels in the ambiguity of their relationship, and in many scenes captures the tenderness between the couple — at one point showing Ernest lying in bed next to Mollie in the foetal position, like a vulnerable child looking for comfort.
Killers of the Flower Moon is a poignant, terrifying film for these small details.
It's about the perversity of power, and the cruelty of people who can deny their own abuse.
There's a metaphor here of larger injustices, of course, and in the film's coda, in which the director himself appears to say a solemn word or two, we're reminded of the broader significance of this story — especially in a settler state like the USA or Australia.
The real events might be long passed, and the characters long gone, but Scorsese's brilliantly unflinching drama implores us not to forget.

Killers of the Flower Moon debuts in cinemas on 19 October before streaming on Apple TV+ at a later date.

title: How a country doctor's film camera captured Europe's dark Nazi past
content:
A rare collection of images and videos on display in Albury showcases life from a regional perspective at a level of detail never seen before.
Leslie Samuel Woods, known as Sam, was a physician in the Albury area in the 1900s, building a house called Valetta on the exact site where the Albury LibraryMuseum sits today.
Dr Woods bought a Filmo Double Eight film camera while on a study trip to the UK and Europe in 1937.
Traipsing around the continent, Dr Woods recorded plenty of images and events.
Dr Woods loved animals and photographed many on his travels — including this dog wearing a hat. (Supplied: Albury LibraryMuseum)
Another dog, a dachshund no less, photographed by Dr Woods in Germany. (Supplied: Albury LibraryMuseum)
Upon his return, he continued to film and take photographs around Albury between the 1930s and 1950s capturing buildings, people, gardens, and events.
His photos and videos have come full circle, now on display in the LibraryMuseum.
"My great grandfather was one of the original doctors in town, and of his siblings — [there were] nine of them — there were four who were also doctors and they all practised in Albury," said Dr Woods' great-nephew Richard Woods.
The mantel from Dr Woods' beloved home Valetta is on display in the LibraryMuseum. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Sarah Krieg)
While the doctor had a keen interest in photography and film, it took more than half a century for his collection to be found — a discovery that almost came too late.
Dr Woods pictured on his European study tour of 1937. (Supplied: Albury LibraryMuseum)
In the 1950s, Dr Woods popped all his used film in a box and gave them to his secretary for safekeeping.
She would later pass them on to a film enthusiast in Melbourne in the box that was rarely, if ever, opened.
It was not until the collector approached Albury's LibraryMuseum team more than two years ago with the trove that they began to understand its historical importance.
Its significance is difficult to overstate. In the 1930s it was rare for regional residents to have a still camera, let alone a film camera.
Mt Buffalo Chalet photographed by Dr Woods. (Supplied: Albury LibraryMuseum)
Dr Woods' films were taken on acetate — a non-flammable type of film that rose to prominence in the 1920s to ensure pictures could be shown in homes without posing a fire risk.
But with the low fire risk comes the danger of deterioration known as "vinegar syndrome".
When acetate film starts to decompose it begins to smell acidic, like vinegar, and the stronger the smell the more advanced the deterioration.
"They'll get to a point where you can't play them or even record them anymore," said Sandra Endresz, the museum collections officer at AlburyCity Council.
Sandra Endresz says it is lucky the undisturbed film rolls had not fallen victim to decomposition. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Sarah Krieg)
Luckily, the undisturbed film rolls had not fallen victim.
"The donor said that there was a little bit of shrinkage, and they do smell of vinegar, but we were able to digitise them," Ms Endresz said.
Dr Woods kept detailed records of his travels. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Sarah Krieg)
The discovery and digitising of the photos was a special moment for the Woods clan, and the exhibition's launch doubled as an impromptu family reunion to see the exhibition unveiled.
It was an illuminating night for LibraryMuseum staff and the Woods family.
"They shared a few interesting stories and they also identified a couple of people in the images that I had not identified before," Ms Endresz said.
The Woods family heads off on an adventure with the family's dog in tow, of course. (Supplied: Albury LibraryMuseum)
Dr Woods purchased his film camera in the 1930s, with the first dated 1937 when Dr Woods visited a number of European countries.
He saw the coronation of King George VI and filmed Nazis marching through the streets of Germany.
Dr Woods photographed some of Europe's most famous landmarks. (Supplied: Albury LibraryMuseum)
Upon returning to Albury, Dr Woods began using the camera to capture what we now call home videos of his family.
One of Dr Woods' children with their family dog. (Supplied: Albury LibraryMuseum)
Dr Woods' collection also contains some of the earliest known film of the Hume Weir, with water cascading out of the fully-open gates of the just-finished dam.
"The Hume had only been completed a couple of years earlier so that would have been the first time that we saw water filling from all the gates," Ms Endresz said.
He captured one of Albury's first Anzac Day marches in around 1938.
"There's the Anzac troops on Anzac Day marching up to the Albury War Memorial there. All these guys would have been obviously from First World War," Mr Woods said.
It is a snapshot of how everyday life looked on the border between the world wars.
Dr Woods photographed local sights including Albury's St Matthew's Church before it burnt down. (Supplied: Albury LibraryMuseum)
"There's a diggers' golf tournament, which was a golf competition to raise money for families of the returned soldiers from World War I," Ms Endresz said.
"That's, I think, what this whole exhibition has brought together," Mr Woods said.

title: Three-time Oscar nominee and Twin Peaks actress Piper Laurie dies
content:
Piper Laurie, the strong-willed, Oscar-nominated actor who performed in acclaimed roles despite at one point abandoning acting altogether in search of a "more meaningful" life, has died at her home in Los Angeles aged 91.
Laurie died of old age early on Saturday, her manager, Marion Rosenberg, told The Associated Press via email, adding that she was "a superb talent and a wonderful human being".
Laurie arrived in Hollywood in 1949 as Rosetta Jacobs and was quickly given a contract with Universal-International, a new name that she hated and a string of starring roles with Ronald Reagan, Rock Hudson and Tony Curtis, among others.
She went on to receive Academy Award nominations for three distinct films: The 1961 pool room drama The Hustler; the 1976 film version of Stephen King's horror classic Carrie, and the romantic drama Children of a Lesser God, in 1986.
She also appeared in several acclaimed roles on television and the stage, including in David Lynch's Twin Peaks in the 1990s as the villainous Catherine Martell.
Laurie made her debut at 17 in Louisa, playing Reagan's daughter, then appeared opposite Francis the talking mule in Francis Goes to the Races.
Piper Laurie played Catherine Martell on David Lynch's television show Twin Peaks.  (AFP: ABC)
She made several films with Curtis, whom she once dated, including The Prince Who Was a Thief, No Room for the Groom, Son of Ali Baba and Johnny Dark.
Fed up, she walked out on her $US2,000-a-week ($3,176) contract in 1955, vowing she would not work again unless she was offered a decent part.
She moved to New York, where she found the roles she was seeking in theatre and live television drama.
Performances in Days of Wine and Roses, The Deaf Heart and The Road That Led After brought her Emmy nominations and paved the way for her return to films, including in an acclaimed role as Paul Newman's troubled girlfriend in The Hustler.
For many years after, Laurie turned her back on acting.
She married film critic Joseph Morgenstern, welcomed a daughter, Ann Grace, and moved to a farmhouse in Woodstock, New York.
She said later that the civil rights movement and the Vietnam War had influenced her decision to make the change.
"I was disenchanted and looking for an existence more meaningful for me," she recalled, adding that she never regretted the move.
"My life was full," she said in 1990.
"I always liked using my hands, and I always painted."
Tony Curtis and Piper Laurie starred in several films together and also dated.  (AFP)
Laurie also became noted as a baker, with her recipes appearing in The New York Times.
Her only performances during that time came when she joined a dozen musicians and actors on a tour of college campuses to support senator George McGovern's 1972 US presidential bid.
Laurie was finally ready to return to acting when director Brian De Palma called her about playing the deranged mother of Sissy Spacek in Carrie.
At first she felt the script was junk, and then she decided she should play the role for laughs.
Piper Laurie returned to acting in Brian De Palma's film Carrie, with Sissi Spacek. (AFP: Archives du 7eme Art/Photo12)
Not until De Palma chided her for putting a comedic turn on a scene did she realise he meant the film to be a thriller.
Carrie became a box-office smash, launching a craze for movies about teenagers in jeopardy, and Spacek and Laurie were both nominated for Academy Awards.
Her desire to act rekindled, Laurie resumed a busy career that spanned decades.
On television, she appeared in such series as Matlock, Murder, She Wrote and Frasier and played George Clooney's mother on ER.

title: 'Assumption is they're going to die': How The Royal Hotel subverts the Aussie outback thriller
content:
The Royal Hotel is the most common pub name in Australia.
It's also the title of the opening film at the South By South West (SXSW) festival in Sydney.
Coming from Melbourne-born director and writer Kitty Green, it's a fresh take on the outback thriller.
"There's a Royal Hotel in every town, in every city in this country, [so there's this feeling that] it could be anywhere," she says.
Filmed in a tiny town north of Adelaide, the movie follows two American backpackers who take a live-in bar job in a FIFO mining town, under the direction of owner Billy, played by none other than Hugo Weaving.
THE ROYAL HOTEL - Official Trailer
It's a fitting choice to open the first annual Asia-Pacific instalment of SXSW, as the festival leaves Texas for the first time.
"Our remit for South by Southwest … is to profile up-and-coming [voices] from the Asia-Pacific region," says SXSW Sydney's Head of Screen, Ghita Loebenstein.
"[Kitty's] got a unique perspective on that classic Aussie outback genre [with this] feminist, female gaze lens … it was the perfect way to launch the festival and celebrate Kitty as a director to definitely watch."
In part, Green made this film to keep her mum happy.
"My mother was encouraging me to make a movie in Australia, because she missed me," she says.
Making waves in the US with a suite of films including The Assistant — which also stars The Royal Hotel's Julia Garner — Green came across the documentary Hotel Coolgardie, which follows two Finnish backpackers working in an outback town.
"I had seen movies set out there, but I hadn't seen any through that lens, through the eyes of two young women, foreign women who were in this environment, trying to make sense of it," she says.
Hotel Coolgardie | Official Trailer | DocPlay
The cast of The Royal Hotel even look like the doco's colourful characters, with Green inspired by how these real-life women refused to be the victims in their story.
"Here were two women that weren't going to put up with it, who weren't going to accept some of the behaviour that I had grown up learning to just go: 'Ah, he's alright.'"
"I hadn't seen that before … there was something interesting in their ability to defend themselves."
While flicks like Wolf Creek, Wake in Fright and The Nightingale defined the outback thriller genre with horrific scenes of murder, suicide and rape, Loebenstein's description of the Royal Hotel as "fun, irreverent [and] energetic" may come as a surprise.
"You see two women wearing backpacks in the Australian outback and an audience's assumptions are that they're going to die," Green says.
"Our film goes in to sort of challenge your expectations and play around with the genre a little bit, have a bit of fun."
What is it about the Australian outback that has attracted filmmakers for decades?
For Loebenstein, it comes down to internal and external ideas of navigating the great unknown.
"I think a lot of the characters that turn up in in those outback thriller genre films [often] symbolise our collective psychological shadows … how we grapple with the hidden parts of ourselves, and the hidden parts of our culture," she says.
For Green, it's also about the specificity: The Royal Hotel isn't just set in the regions, but in a FIFO mining town, which are often home to little-to-no women — or rules.
Kitty Green is behind The Royal Hotel, which explores toxic masculinity and power dynamics. (Supplied)
In filming, Green's team essentially "took over" a town of 29 people. Yatina in South Australia couldn't house everyone for the two weeks they filmed there, so they all shacked up in various surrounding towns.
Fittingly, the film's two American leads stayed in a room above a pub.
The first SXSW in Sydney is a cultural moment, and while Green doesn't bring The Royal Hotel to Australia "with an agenda", she does hope it sparks discussion.
In its world-first debut outside of Austin, Texas, groundbreaking festival South by Southwest is coming to Sydney. So what is it? And how can punters get involved?
"I really wanted to have a conversation about what we tolerate or put up with, and when we stand up for ourselves in those spaces when we feel uncomfortable," she says.
"When is it OK to say no, to really put your foot down? I think as women, we are often a little afraid to do that for fear of looking uptight."
There's also the question of 'the line'.
If behaviour never actually crosses it, does that make it OK?
"[The film's] about the type of behaviour that is the gateway or entry point to sexual violence," Green says.
With the rest of SXSW also exploring other moral grey areas — from the police presence surrounding Onefour to the privilege and opulence of Emerald Fennell's Saltburn — it's hard to know what else to see.
Loebenstein suggests trying a film you know nothing about, "especially from our Asian neighbours", and prepare to be "pleasantly surprised".
The Royal Hotel premieres at South By South West on Sunday October 15 2023.

title: 'Weird energy' and a singing Hugh Grant: What fans think of the new Wonka trailer
content:
Oompa-Loompa doompa-dee-doo, we've got a new Wonka trailer for you.
After our first look at the world of Wonka divided audiences back in July, a second trailer has dropped for the musical prequel to Roald Dahl's beloved Charlie and The Chocolate Factory. Fancy another serve of sweets?
Warner Bros. Pictures Youtube: Wonka | Trailer #2
The film, out December 14, stars Timothée Chalamet (Dune, Call Me By Your Name) as a young version of the magical chocolatier, before he starts his empire — as the tagline says, it's how "Willy became Wonka".
In the new trailer, the plot is further sketched out: An eccentric inventor, Wonka starts selling his weird and wonderful sweets, while a cabal of chocolatiers try to thwart his plans — and we see a LOT more of the extended cast, with posters dedicated to each character a la Barbie, as one Twitter user points out).
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
Directed by Paddington's Paul King, Wonka is stacked with faces from the PCU (Paddington Cinematic Universe), including Sally Hawkins, Olivia Colman, Rowan Atkinson and Hugh Grant, who plays an Oompa Loompa. The cast also includes Natasha Rothwell (The White Lotus), Keegan-Michael Key, Matt Lucas and newcomer Calah Lane as Wonka's friend and fellow mischief maker.
Where the first trailer just offered a glimpse of Oompa-Hugh, we get a LOT more of him this time — including a song, the first we've heard from the musical! Now that the shock has worn off, he's become a (tentative) fan favourite.
There has, however, been criticism of Grant's casting. Back when the first trailer dropped, George Coppen, a British actor with dwarfism, expressed frustration that the Ooompa Loompa role went to Hugh, considering how few roles are available to people with dwarfism.
When the first trailer dropped, people were super skeptical. They made fun of Timothée's Southern-lilted accent and weird energy, as well as the need for the film to exist in the first place.
After-all, Wonka has the double-pressure of not just one but two iconic films to live up to: the 1971 classic starring Gene Wilder, and the 2005 Tim Burton remake, starring Johnny Depp.
Comparisons were inevitable but, now we've seen more, it's clear that Wonka is more of a cotton-candy take on the character. Timothée's Wonka and the film itself is far lighter, brighter and far less foreboding than what we've seen before. Even so, people are divided over whether he was the right man for the job.
It's also notable that we haven't heard Wonka sing in either trailer. Considering the movie is a musical and Timothée's singing capabilities are largely unknown (his rapping abilities, however, are verified), the absence has some people worried.
We'll find out soon enough, when Wonka arrives in cinemas December 14.

title: Fleabag, Michael Scott and Bluey: The safe worlds that give us comfort when the real one is too much
content:
Rewatching the same favourite TV show can be like receiving a warm cosy hug. If you're burnt out, struggling, or just really tired, sometimes the "safe" option is the best.
This is where "safe shows" come in. Decision fatigue is real, and the cognitive load required to weigh up choices and pick something new to watch can be too much.
Sometimes the sheer volume of content available to stream can be overwhelming. It can be hard to know if you'll like something new, or if it will suit your mood and you'll want to commit. But comfort watches are relatable and dependable.
I am addicted to a reality show called Below Deck, which is so formulaic it's like a broken record, but that also means it's dependable and safe — so even when watching new seasons, I know what to expect!
I have been watching some of my fave safe shows on a loop since childhood and wanted to know if my colleagues did the same. Here is what they said.
My family and I LOVE this show. It's been a real bonding and calming experience for us since my kids discovered the first episode in 2018.
We sit together to watch it (some of us last longer than others in binge sessions) and we laugh-out-loud together or at each other (in a good way of course) — depending on the age appropriateness of the joke.
As a parent, I've learnt a lot from Bluey. But I still have more to ask.
For those who (somehow) don't know, Bluey is an animated show about a young Blue Heeler dog and her family. It's about friendships, family and nature.
For us Bluey has moved beyond the couch. We've also wasted many (good) hours playing Keepy Uppy and Toilet-Tag, and I'm told these Bluey-inspired games are also popular in the school yard.
I love the surprising, but awesome guest cameos that have included Rose Byrne, Natalie Portman, Eva Mendes and Lin-Manuel Miranda.
Yes, it's nice. I just love it.
Allison Jess, ABC Everyday.
Bluey: Toilet Tag
The show I turn to again and again is Phoebe Waller-Bridge's Fleabag. Specifically, season two — there's something deeply relatable and forgivingly human about season two.
The characters are familiar and sensationally flawed. I love the excruciating familial exchanges, the brutal British candour, and shameless passive aggression. Olivia Colman. J'adore.
It's a portrait of an exquisitely dysfunctional family. It's also a love story.
But Fleabag is not your cereal box variety romantic. She falls for the unlikeliest of love interests: A priest. (A cool, sweary priest.)
Like all great love stories, it's completely doomed. And yet it's not melancholic, it's heartfelt and hilarious and full of levity.
"Being a romantic takes a hell of a lot of hope."
Fleabag forgives herself in this season and I think that's what I find most comforting — that it's about accepting the things you can't change.
I've watched season two more than 20 times. It has buoyed me through many existential crises, break-ups and catastrophic hangovers. To me, it's flawless and I will hear no bad words against it.
Anna Freeland, ABC Arts.
Fleabag's monologue in the church confessional perfectly captures what it's like to be in the existential abyss of your late-20s-early-30s, pleading to a higher power to make sense of everything.
There are many reasons why the US version of Ricky Gervais's game-changing sitcom/mockumentary The Office continues to loom large in our lives more than a decade on from its final episode.
In our house, it's down to consistency. The jokes are always funny (even on the 29th watch), the drama is never too dramatic, and it never tries to be either too smart or too inane.
What is perhaps most significant is that these people lead consistent lives. They don't necessarily love their jobs or their coworkers, but they do find a certain joy and comfort in the weird little community of Dunder Mifflin's Scranton branch, and that comfort translates through the screen in charming fashion.
Dan Condon, Double J.
The Office US: First Aid fail
Say what you will about Harry Potter's creator, She Who Must Not Be Named, but the books and movies themselves are endlessly watchable.
There's nothing I like more on a hungover Sunday morning, or when feeling gross and sickly, than sitting down for a bit of over-the-top British shenanigans.
This series is endlessly quotable, and at times very funny, even when it's not intending to be.
From Emma Watson's over-acting to Rupert Grint just being his silly little self, lines such as "in the rest-RICTED section" and "bluddy hell, Harry" become instantly iconic. Honourable mention to Harry screaming "your hand's all sweaty!" while dangling from a flying car.
I think I know these movies shot-by-shot, the audiobooks/novels line-by-line, and every bit of BTS goss by heart at this point. But I'll still waste hours and hours of my life on this magic little orphan, because every binge feels like coming home to Hogwarts.
Rachel Rasker, ABC Everyday.
Ron Weasley's Bloody Hell Count in Harry Potter
Could laughing at awkwardness actually help us release some of our own complicated feelings about it?
The comfort in Peep Show episodes only comes after you watch them a second or third time. The first time watching the show is actually an incredibly uncomfortable and stressful experience.
If you're unfamiliar, Peep Show follows dysfunctional housemates and best friends Mark and Jez, who, right from the start, are both clearly ill-equipped to succeed in life. The show is also mostly viewed from a first-person perspective to further disorient you. This is cringe comedy at its best.
You might never want to have people like Mark and Jez in your actual lives, but you'll be surprised by how often you miss them.
Christian Harimanow, ABC Everyday.
Peep Show: Mark buys Jez a lovely curry
The internet is obsessed with watching shows years after the fact.
As an angsty teen who had been called "precocious" a lot as a child, I spent a large part of my teen years in Stars Hollow. I loved inhabiting the lives of Lorelai Gilmore and her daughter Rory; laughing, crying and mooning over useless boys (I am firmly Team Jess – an obvious choice for a book nerd who disliked authority and later turned out to be queer).
I hadn't revisited the Gilmore Girls for more than a decade when I ended up bed-bound after an injury — grumpy and bored and on painkillers that made using my brain a largely fruitless exercise.
Before long, I was deep into the world of fast-talking, large coffees, family drama and wholesome small-town antics.
The beauty of Gilmore Girls is that it's very low stakes. You can dive right into each episode, safe in the knowledge that it will include a lot of dialogue, a bit of angst and no dying at all.
In the ensuing decade since, I've watched all seven original seasons through many more times (plus the reboot miniseries), immediately soothed by the autumnal colour palette and the "la la la la la lah lah lahs" ringing in my ears.
Katherine Smyrk, Entertainment and Features.
Remember, back in the day of VHS, when you'd tape things off the telly so you could watch them again and again? That was me in the 90s with Absolutely Fabulous. I knew every line off by heart.
When I rewatch now, which of course I still do (via streaming services these days, I've upgraded from VCR), I realise that a good 90 per cent of the jokes probably went way over my head. It was really quite adult humour and I don't think I had a clue what was actually going on, just as I'm sure my classmates didn't either when I forced them to act out scenes from a book of scripts I had.
With wild outfits and physical escapades, you didn't need to understand every joke to find Eddy and Patsy entertaining.  (BBC)
I think I was just drawn to the bright colours, outrageous outfits and the physical spectacle of two grown women with plummy accents acting like giant misbehaving toddlers. And while I now understand more of the jokes, I'm still mostly drawn to those things — because honestly, who doesn't aspire to a life like that? Eddie and Patsy are truly #CoupleGoals.
Genevieve Dwyer, ABC Everyday.

title: Jada Pinkett Smith says she and Will Smith were separated when the Oscars slap happened
content:
Jada Pinkett Smith and her husband Will Smith married in 1997.
Their marriage came under an intense public gaze last year when Smith slapped Chris Rock after he mocked Pinkett Smith's alopecia while presenting at the Oscars.
"Keep my wife's name out of your f***ing mouth," Smith shouted at Rock before he assaulted him on stage, all while people around the world watched the ceremony live.
And Pinkett Smith has decided that now, a week before her tell-all memoir goes on sale, is the time to reveal that she's still technically Smith's wife, but they've been separated for seven years.
And they were separated at the time of that now infamous Oscars ceremony.
As part of the publicity campaign for her memoir, Pinkett Smith sat for an interview with US television journalist Hoda Kotb and a cover story with People Magazine.
Kotb's interview with Pinkett Smith will air on Friday night in the US as a one-off TV special.
But overnight, snippets of the interview were broadcast on American morning show Today, featuring the revelations about the Smiths' marriage.
Here's what Pinkett Smith said.
Pinkett Smith tells Kotb that, since 2016, she and Smith have been living separately.
Kotb says it was a "pretend life" they were living.
"As time went on, there were different stages in my marriage where Will and I decided we were not together where we didn't tell the public," she tells the magazine.
"I was actually thinking about divorcing, separating and there have been several of those [stages] where we've gone and lived our separate lives."
Pinkett Smith tells Kotb she considered a legal divorce, but couldn't go through with it.
"I made a promise that there will never be a reason for us to get a divorce, we will work through whatever," she says.
"And I just haven't been able to break that promise."
The pair also don't plan on getting legally divorced.
"We've been doing some really heavy-duty work together," she tells People.
"We just got deep love for each other and we are going to figure out what that looks like for us."
Back to the Oscars incident, where Smith called Pinkett Smith "my wife".
In an excerpt from her book published by People Magazine, Pinkett Smith writes that they were at the event as a family, not a couple.
She says there was a moment after he said "my wife" when she realised that she was, despite living a separate life from him, his wife.
Chris Rock and Will Smith were the subject many conversations after last year's Oscars ceremony.  (AP)
She tells People she didn't think the confrontation between Smith and Rock was real.
"It didn't look like Will hit Chris, because, number one, I'd seen Will in the boxing ring with pro fighters — Will's a heavy hitter," she says.
"So when Chris moved, it looked like he ducked or he missed the shot."
But it became clear to her that it was no act.
"It wasn't until Will started to walk back to his chair that I even realised it wasn't a skit," she says.
In a separate article on People's website, Pinkett Smith says Rock tried to apologise to her.
"He said, 'I didn't mean you any harm,'" she says.
She says the pair haven't spoken since the incident.
"There's a time in your life where you say, 'Why am I still pretending, let me just say it,'" speculates Kotb.
"So this book, Worthy, is that."
In her interview with Kotb, Pinkett Smith says she and her husband kept their living arrangement secret because they weren't ready to reveal it.
"[We were] still trying to figure out between the two of us how to be in partnership," she says.
"We hadn't figured that out."
She tells People magazine they didn't want people to know the dynamic between them.
"We didn't think that that was anybody else's business," she says.
Of course there will be.
All these snippets are coming out before the special airs this weekend and Pinkett Smith's book goes on sale next week.
"There's a whole chunk of the book that we're going to get into in the Dateline special … of what happened in that moment," Kotb says.
"There's a whole backstory there too."
Nothing on his social media accounts, as yet.
However, he's also got a new podcast, Class of '88, coming out later this month.
It hasn't been promoted as touching on the issue though. It's being sold as a series of interviews with his "old friends" like Queen Latifa and Salt-N-Pepa.
The Oscar-winner has been banned from the Academy Awards for the next 10 years.
Smith apologised to Rock and Oscars viewers later in March before releasing a video apology in July.
In that video, he says he's open to talking with Rock about it when he is ready.
Will Smith apologises to Chris Rock, saying behaviour was "unacceptable".
He's also not said anything on his social media account since these recent Pinkett Smith stories were published, but his social media accounts don't appear to be overly active.
As for the Oscars incident, he told a crowd in Boston that he was "still kind of processing what happened" three days after the ceremony.
Rock reportedly did not want Smith arrested and did not file any legal proceedings against him.
Chris Rock uses his comedy special to speak about being slapped by Will Smith.
He also turned down many interview requests about the incident and mentioned it only briefly on the Sydney leg of his stand-up tour last year.
Instead, he opted to speak about it in a stand-up show called Selective Outrage earlier this year, saving most of his insight until the final few minutes of the show.
Right at the end of the show Rock said: "A lot of people go, 'Chris, how come you didn't do nothing back that night?'
"Because I got parents. Because I was raised. I got parents.
"And you know what my parents taught me? Don't fight in front of white people," he said, before dropping his microphone and ending the show.

title: Flying cars and film stars: The 'Olympics of Festivals' lands in Sydney next week
content:
For the first time in its 36-year history, creative arts festival South by Southwest (SXSW) is debuting outside of its home in Austin, Texas.
This year, the enormous event lands in Sydney, with a program of musical performances, film screenings, gaming competitions, tech showcases and industry talks running from October 15–22.
The city will have visits during this time from Chance the Rapper, Nicole Kidman and Black Mirror creator Charlie Brooker, alongside exhibits of flying cars and robotics demos.
But as an industry-targeted event, the ticket prices for the inaugural Asia-Pacific iteration of this festival are out of reach for most.
So, what actually is SXSW? And how can you get involved without spending big?
"SXSW is the World's Fair for creative content industries," says Colin Daniels, managing director of SXSW Sydney.
Managing director of SXSW Sydney Colin Daniels has attended the event in Austin, Texas, 16 times. (Supplied: SXSW Sydney)
Since its launch in 1987, the event has encompassed a range of creative fields, spanning music, film, gaming, tech and innovation, with a conference filled with big-name keynote speakers at its centrepiece.
"Someone else called it, 'the Olympics of Festivals'," Daniels says.
"It's a festival of festivals — that allows you to experience all of them at once."
This is the festival for big industry moments.
Girls and Handmaid's Tale both premiered at SXSW.
An exiled Edward Snowden gave a keynote talk in 2014 via Skype (the year after he Wiki-Leaked) and Twitter was launched at the festival in 2007.
Many a famous musical career has been launched after early appearances at SXSW, from Amy Winehouse to James Blunt and Kid Cudi to Haim.
Prince, Johnny Cash, Kanye West and Jay-Z have all appeared and, one time, Bill Murray took up spontaneous bartending to keep festival-goers watered.
SXSW Sydney begins the slow reveal of creatives who will take part when the music, gaming, technology and screen festival travels outside North America for the first time in October.
"Why not?" Daniels says.
"Sydney is a diverse city that's full of creativity and innovation. We have a music industry, a film and television industry, a tech and innovation industry and a gaming industry that are all thriving.
"So it makes sense for Sydney to be a conduit between the Asia-Pacific and the rest of the world for seven days a year."
The Sydney event will be a smaller, scaled-down version of the usual Texas fare, with a focus on platforming creators from a different part of the world.
"The focus on the Asia-Pacific region is a major difference," Daniels says.
"Over 40 per cent of our talent is from outside of Australia and we are showcasing the creativity of the Asia-Pacific region."
Filmmaker Baz Luhrmann will debut an extended version of his 2008 film Australia, adapted into a six-part TV series called Faraway Downs, starring Nicole Kidman and Hugh Jackman.
Kidman will also give a talk alongside Per Saari, her partner in production company Blossom Films, to discuss some of their successes, such as HBO's Big Little Lies.
The seven-day conference is the centrepiece of the event, with other headlining talks including Black Mirror's Charlie Brooker, Coachella chief executive Paul Tollett and Chance the Rapper in conversation, celebrating the 50th anniversary of hip hop.
Feature length documentary Hot Potato: The Story of the Wiggles will make its world premiere at the festival.
As will The Royal Hotel, starring Julia Garner and Jessica Henwick as backpackers at a desolate small-town Australian pub in a story inspired by the documentary Hotel Coolgardie and the experiences of women in the outback.
The event's musical line-up includes TikTok stars Flyana Boss, Indonesia's Feby Putri and homegrown artists including Ben Lee and Barkaa.
The inaugural South By Southwest (SXSW) Sydney has revealed the first slate of local artists that will be hitting stages across the city in October.
Yes and no. While it is targeted at the creative industries, tickets are open to the public — but not necessarily at accessible prices. A 'platinum badge', which allows you to attend every event, goes for $1,895. More affordable badges under $500 have been sold to individual streams such as gaming and film, but many have already sold out.
At this stage the most affordable ticket is the $40 Expo day pass, which will get you into the Tech and Innovation Expo at the International Convention Centre. The expo features exhibits from business and creators spanning tech, gaming, entertainment, health and wellness and promises a range of interactive and immersive experiences for attendees.
"What we're showcasing in the tech and innovation expo, whether it be UTS's flying car, or whether it be what CSIRO are up to, or whether it be the new cabin for the Qantas Sunrise project — which is the non-stop flight to London — there's so much new and different," Daniels says.
"There's an AI vending machine that you need to reason with. That's going to be exciting."
Never fear! There are many free events that will be held around the city, with Tumbalong Park being taken over as a key location for the general public with stages, screens, pop-up bars and food trucks.
It will feature talks from UNICEF, Adam Spencer and Dr Karl Kruszelnicki, the Real Housewives of Sydney, meditation workshops, breakdancing sets, live cooking classes, augmented reality and robotics demonstrations, an outdoor cinema screening classic films, an afternoon of esports and gaming presentations.
There will be a live play of the murder-mystery game, Blood on the Clocktower and one evening will play host to a Rock & Roll circus, where artists including Dan Sultan, Hayley Mary, Redhook and "secret acts" cover iconic rock songs — perhaps an opportunity for locals to rub shoulders with famous acts.
Sydneysiders can get involved in free events, talks, gigs, gaming demos and more at Tumbalong Park in Darling Harbour. (SXSW: Jordan Kirk)
Organisers are big on encouraging people to get involved by simply wandering the streets.
With events always spread out around a walkable footprint, festival devotees say the general vibe that takes over downtown Austin every year leads to a high probability of simply stumbling across something interesting.
With surprise pop up gigs and brand activations on street corners and bars, you may just unexpectedly bump into a big star in a humble venue — such as Boygenius's surprise gig at the Austin airport earlier this year.
Events are spread across Sydney's CBD, encompassing Haymarket, Ultimo, Darling Harbour and Chippendale, but designed to be walkable and all within 25 minutes of each other on foot.
Venues include museums, such as the Powerhouse, parks and outdoor venues, such as the Darling Quarter, as well as pubs inlcuding the Lansdowne, which will be taken over by Spotify to showcase a range of artists, including a K-Pop night.
SXSW Sydney will run from from 15–22 October.

title: Penelope made her first film when she was seven, now she's sharing her Indigenous culture on YouTube
content:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised this article uses the name of a person who has died with the permission of his family.
When she was just six years old, Palawa and Wiradjuri girl Penelope Towney made an unplanned appearance in front of a Black Lives Matter rally in Dubbo.
"The crowd was asked if anyone wanted to come up and say anything, and I looked at my mum and I said, 'Mum, I want to go up', and she said, 'I can't go up with you', and I was like, 'OK'," Penelope said.
The now nine-year-old then walked up to the stage and raised her sign.
"I said, 'I just wanted to say that this always was and always will be Aboriginal land'," she said.
For Penelope, that moment was the start of what would become her passion for preserving her culture.
Penelope Towney has so far released two episodes of Towney Time. (ABC Western Plains: Emily Middleton)
Penelope – who grew up in Gilgandra in Western NSW and now lives at Bellambi in the Illawarra – has since become a filmmaker and YouTuber.
Penelope Towney at a recent showing of her YouTube channel in Gilgandra. (ABC Western Plains: Emily Middleton)
Her Towney Time channel has monthly videos that feature Penelope speaking with experts about legends, stories, culture, games and everything in between.
Her big dreams include filming an episode with Dolly Parton.
In the first episode, Penelope speaks to Wiradjuri astrophysicist Kirsten Banks about the constellation of the "Emu in the Sky".
TOWNEY TIME - Episode 1 - The Emu in the sky
Ms Banks and Penelope discuss how the constellation can help people find emu eggs.
"My pop, Doongbung, Graeme Towney, he just passed away recently. He was very clever," Penelope said.
"He showed me the Dinawan emu in the sky, and when it moved throughout the year and how you would know the differences between what it was doing — breeding, nesting."
It wasn't Penelope's first time behind, or in front of the camera.
She became one of Australia's youngest First Nations filmmakers when she was just seven, performing an Acknowledgement of Country for the Yuin and Dharawal Nations in her documentary The Land We're On.
In the short-form documentary, Penelope explained the difference between an Acknowledgement of Country and a Welcome to Country.
Penelope Towney (second from left) with members of her Gilgandra family. (Supplied)
"I rehearsed it and memorised it off by heart for months, basically the whole year, and I got it on my second attempt," she said.
Penelope has recently released a second episode of Towney Time. She hopes her videos continue to inspire and educate her viewers.
Penelope said that without the support of her loved ones, she wouldn't be where she was today.
"All the people that believe in me and all the people that helped me, and all my friends," she said.
YouTuber Penelope Towney says it's important to keep First Nations languages and culture alive. (ABC Western Plains: Emily Middleton)
Being behind and in front of the camera is not Penelope's only skill. Later this month, she will attend the South by Southwest festival in Sydney.
Penelope will be the conference's youngest speaker on the Young, Blak and Proud panel, alongside Barkaa, Soju Gang and ABC foreign correspondent Isabella Higgins.
Towney Time's second episode is filmed at Bellambi Beach, Wollongong. (Supplied: Towney Time)

title: Cool Runnings turns 30: Why people gravitated towards a film about a Jamaican bobsled team
content:
It's been 30 years since the feel-good movie Cool Runnings was released based on the true story of the Jamaican bobsled team at the 1988 Winter Olympics.
If you're yet to see the 1993 film, spoiler alert, the team loses.
But to former Miss Jamaica and former cultural ambassador for Jamaica Johnnel Smith, that takes nothing away from the impact the movie continues to have.
Ms Smith is a PhD candidate and a lecturer in tourism and business at Griffith University.
She's seen Cool Runnings about half a dozen times.
"When I think of Cool Runnings, I think of real good Jamaican vibes," Ms Smith said.
"The movie documented a significant aspect of our history that communicated the resilience of the Jamaican people, the can-do attitude of the Jamaican people.
"It showed that we literally had a country that was never exposed to winter, or cold, because Jamaica is a Caribbean country, very tropical, very warm. And so, there's no snow in Jamaica and we were able to compete internationally in an Olympic sport that required us to go bobsledding down a snowy mountain.
"It spoke to what we are as a country, but more so the Jamaican spirit. It speaks to our resilience, it speaks to our creativity, it speaks to our ingenuity and our innovativeness, and how we can make something out of nothing."
Johnnel Smith has watched Cool Runnings many times and would love to see a sequel to the film. (Supplied)
Ms Smith has lived in Australia for three years, and says whenever she meets someone new, she already knows what's likely to come next.
"Whenever I introduce myself as a Jamaican, [there are] three things people bring up.
"They bring up Bob Marley, Usain Bolt and the Cool Runnings movie.
"That's almost signature."
Johnnel Smith was the 2010 Miss Jamaica festival queen and cultural ambassador for Jamaica in 2005 and 2010. (Supplied)
Ms Smith worked in tourism marketing when she was in Jamaica and said Cool Runnings helped to set Jamaica apart. And Hollywood has continued to come knocking.
"There's been a lot of movies that focused on other cultural outputs that we have lended to the world on an international stage," Ms Smith said.
"So, we do get a lot of interest from film producers all over the world to film in Jamaica.
"So, that's something else I did as a part of my job in Jamaica. So, for instance, the recent James Bond movie No Time to Die that came out in 2021, a portion of it was actually filmed in Jamaica and I had to work to organise that.
"So, the James Bond crew came and they filmed in Port Antonio in Jamaica.
"Also, the movie Cocktail starring Tom Cruise was filmed in Jamaica.
"How Stella Got Her Groove Back. There have been tonnes of movies with a lot of Hollywood heavyweights and superstars.
"I just think this one because of the storyline and how uncanny it was, you know, Jamaicans competing in a winter Olympic sport, that was just so ironical and it was really funny, we've become synonymous as a people with that movie."
Thirty years on, she'd love for filmmakers to revisit the narrative.
"I'd love to see Cool Runnings, part two," Ms Smith said.
"I'd really love to see a sequel to the movie Cool Runnings that features a more modern Jamaica."
There's a reason Cool Runnings did so well at the box office.
It made $243.4 million dollars globally and only cost $23.6 million to make.
Dr Coghlan says Cool Runnings is a story about mateship. (Supplied)
Jo Coghlan, who is an associate professor of sociology and the co-founder of the Popular Culture Research Network at the University of New England, puts it down to the fact that Cool Runnings is "a bit of an outlier".
"There are a whole lot of other films in this genre where they start off as that kind of underdog, [undergoing] adversity, but they ultimately win," Dr Coghlan said providing a list of movies that match this description including Jerry Maguire, I, Tonya, The Blind Side and Any Given Sunday.
She said Cool Runnings is a clear departure from that narrative and is instead a celebration of the human spirit.
"It becomes a story about, what in Australia we might call, mateship," Dr Coghlan said.
"It's very inspirational. It's about overcoming adversity, the lack of technical knowledge, the backgrounds of the coaches, and that kind of backstory in the film.
"The story of the athlete that was injured and he couldn't be a sprinter. So, he's had individual adversity.
"Yet it's done with this good humour and good grace.
"And it's inspiring and it's a lovely uplifting film that does remind us that sport's not about winning.
"And I think for adults, but also for younger audiences that's a really important message and I think that's what people gravitated to.
"Add to that, it's got a great soundtrack. It's got all those great popular culture elements."
Dr Coghlan does think, however, that there aren't many films like it because sport is big business.
"Modern sport is all about performance. It's all about winning," she said.
"And winning is celebrated and winning is rewarded."
Next Goal Wins from writer/director Taika Waititi will hit Australian cinemas in January 2024. (Supplied: Disney)
Among the films that are about more than just winning are the 2016 biographical sports film Eddie the Eagle about Michael David Edwards, the first competitor in 1988 to represent Great Britain in Olympic ski jumping. He finished last in his events.
The upcoming Taika Waititi film Next Goal Wins follows the American Samoa soccer team, infamous for their brutal 31-0 FIFA loss in 2001.
That movie will hit Australian cinemas in January 2024.
And a movie is in the works on Eric Moussambani, nicknamed Eric the Eel by the media – the swimmer from Equatorial Guinea who was selected in a wildcard program to compete at the Sydney 2000 Olympic Games.
Eric Moussambani, or Eric the Eel, had trouble completing the 100 metres but he refused to give up, turning himself into one of the favourites of the Games. (REUTERS/Pool)
Moussambani won his heat after his competitors recorded false starts and were disqualified, but he didn't progress to the next round, because he had recorded the slowest time in Olympic history.
He did, however, finish the race setting a new personal best time and later becoming the national swim team coach in his home country, Equatorial Guinea.
As the world awaits these films, for those wanting a dose of nostalgia, Cool Runnings and Eddie the Eagle are available to stream on Disney+.

title: Why the Irish are so serious about being funny as film festival gets underway
content:
A widow who has given up on life becomes convinced that a stray dog is the reincarnation of her husband.
That's the zany plot of Róise & Frank, which is one of more than a dozen movies on the Irish Film Festival (IFF) schedule from today.
The IFF will screen across Sydney, Brisbane, Canberra, Perth and Melbourne, with selected films made available online.
Róise & Frank is part of the digital program.
Along with Rachael Moriarty, Peter Murphy is a co-writer and co-director of the award-winning Irish-language film.
"I guess what we were always aiming to do was to make a film that dealt with grief, with really significant grief from loss, in a light-hearted, comic way," Murphy told ABC News.
Rachael Moriarty and Peter Murphy are co-writers and co-directors of Róise & Frank. (Supplied)
Grief was a topic Murphy and Moriarty wanted to explore because it's something most people, the creative team included, had experienced.
"I suppose it's just so universal," Murphy said.
"We were fascinated by the idea of what people would view as excessive grief.
"We have a very strong tradition in Ireland, it's probably the same in Australia, but there's a great old tradition of the wake.
"And Irish funerals are a particular type of funeral.
"So, you have a wake, where traditionally people would have come around to your house, the body would have been laid out. A lot of alcohol would have been consumed.
"Stories would have been shared about the person who had died, the following day the person will be buried and then you're kind of expected to move on."
Murphy said other than marking someone's passing a month later with another traditional event, people are essentially expected to get over it.
"So, we were kind of fascinated by the idea that for some people, that's impossible," he said.
"For some people, grief just takes over their life, and they struggle and we wanted to tell a story about that."
Don't be fooled, however. Róise & Frank isn't a dark film.
Murphy said they'd also heard a lot of stories from people about signs from beyond the grave, such as animals that had never appeared before, visiting the bereaved.
Róise & Frank takes that to the extreme in an easy-to-watch heartwarming film.
"We've [had] quite a few people tearing up, people come up to us and say 'oh god, I don't cry at films, and I was crying, but also laughing' and I think people find that a very enjoyable combination.
"Tragedy and comedy are so close. I certainly enjoy when it's close to reality, when it feels relatable, and yet, there's a touch of comedy."
Murphy said most Irish people can find humour in most things, but he's not sure what he'd put it down to.
"We're very quick to say 800 years of oppression … you have to have a sense of humour," Murphy said.
"But I don't know.
"But Irish people are kind of obsessed with being perceived as having the craic (being fun).
"The worst thing you could say about a person is that they have no craic. So, if someone has no craic, it is beyond damning.
"It doesn't get more damning than that about an Irish person. And it means essentially, that they're no fun. So, we're kind of obsessed with it as a nation.
"And I think we know our reputation as people who are supposed to be fun and have good craic. Where it comes from, I don't know."
Irish Film Festival trailer.
The 2023 Irish Film Festival will screen from October 5 to November 5, with selected movies screening online till October 15. For a full list of movies visit the Irish film festival website.

title: Actor sues Harvey Weinstein over alleged sexual assault
content:
Actor Julia Ormond, who starred in films alongside the likes of Brad Pitt and Harrison Ford in the 1990s, has filed a lawsuit accusing disgraced movie producer Harvey Weinstein of sexually assaulting her in 1995 and then hindering her career.
Ormond, who also accuses The Walt Disney Company, Miramax and her former agents of knowing Weinstein was a problem but doing nothing about it, filed the case in state Supreme Court in Manhattan on Wednesday.
The Adult Survivors Act, which was passed last year, allows a temporary window for those who allege sexual assault to file past the state's normal deadlines.
In her suit, Ormond says she was a star on the rise when she met Weinstein in 1994.
She says she kept in touch with him to discuss scripts and projects, and in 1995 entered into a production agreement with Miramax, where he was co-chairman.
She accuses him of committing sexual battery against her in December 1995 after a business meeting, and then retaliating against her and negatively affecting her career after she confronted him weeks later.
Julia Ormond has accused disgraced movie producer Harvey Weinstein of assaulting her in 1995 and then hindering her career. (AP Photo: Rich Fury)
The British actress says she told her US agents at the time, Creative Artists Agency (CAA), but received no support and was advised not to take any legal action or other steps.
She accuses CAA, Disney and Miramax, saying that they knew Weinstein presented a danger to women but did nothing to stop him or to help her.
"None of these prominent companies warned Ormond that Weinstein had a history of assaulting women because he was too important, too powerful, and made them too much money," the filing says.
While former movie producer Harvey Weinstein's court case isn't a barometer for #MeToo as a whole, it does offer some insights into the experiences of victims in the justice system, and it comes at a pivotal time for the movement.
The lawsuit marks the first time Ormond has publicly accused Weinstein of sexual assault.
The Associated Press generally doesn't name the alleged victims of sexual assault, but is in this case because Ormond has spoken publicly about it, including in an interview with Variety.
Weinstein, 71, was convicted of rape and sexual assault in New York in 2020 and is in prison in the state.
Last year, he also was convicted of another rape in Los Angeles. He has appealed both convictions.
Weinstein's attorney Imran Ansari said his client "categorically denies" the allegations made against him by Ormond and he is prepared to "vehemently defend himself".
Emails seeking comment were sent to CAA, Disney and Miramax.
Ormond's films include Legends of the Fall with Pitt; Sabrina with Ford, and First Knight with Sean Connery and Richard Gere.

title: C-3PO's head, Titanic costumes among memorabilia for sale at film auction
content:
From Star Wars droid C-3PO's head to Leonardo DiCaprio's Titanic costume, a trove of costumes and props will be up for auction next month in a sale of film and television memorabilia worth around 12 million British pounds ($23 million).
More than 1,800 items are being sold by entertainment memorabilia auctioneer Propstore at its annual live auction in London in November.
Leading the sale is the light-up head actor Anthony Daniels wore to play C-3PO in Star Wars: A New Hope, with a price of between 500,000 and 1 million pounds.
Daniels is also selling other Star Wars memorabilia.
"We have his complete archive from his time of working on the Star Wars films so that includes some of the props and body components and parts, his head, his hands, his feet," Propstore founder and chief executive Stephen Lane said.
"We have his original scripts with the annotations in there as well."
Source material from the 1977 film Star Wars: A New Hope which is part of Anthony Daniels's personal collection to be auctioned. (Reuters: Suzanne Plunkett)
Costumes for sale include a shirt, waistcoat and trousers DiCaprio wore in Titanic (100,000 — 200,000 pounds), Honey Ryder's bathrobe as worn by Ursula Andress in Dr. No (70,000-140,000 pounds) and Johnny Depp's stunt costume from Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides (50,000-100,000 pounds).
Don Vito Corleone's coat worn by Marlon Brando in The Godfather, Jack Dawson's costume worn by Leonardo DiCaprio in Titanic, and James Bond's tuxedo worn by Daniel Craig in James Bond: No Time to Die. (Reuters: Suzanne Plunkett)
Props include Harrison Ford's bull whip from Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom (100,000-200,000 pounds), Nightmare on Elm Street character Freddy Krueger's hero metal glove armature and hand-drawn schematic (200,000-400,000 pounds) and Tom Hanks's sneakers from Forrest Gump (15,000-30,000 pounds).
Other lots include Stanley Kubrick's hand-annotated shooting script for The Shining (30,000-60,000 pounds) and a coat worn by Marlon Brando in The Godfather (25,000-50,000 pounds).
Lane said the lots came from collectors, curators, archives, film studios and production companies.
"The demand is growing and we're seeing things travel all over the world…and they're bought by passionate fans and lovers of the movies, collectors," he said.
"But some of these items also end up in museums and studio archives as well."

title: In just 39 minutes Wes Anderson brings The Wonderful Story of Henry Sugar to life
content:
Of all the movie adaptations of Roald Dahl's work — from Mel Stuart's endearingly strange Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory to Robert Zemeckis's ill-fated redo of The Witches — perhaps none has gotten closer to the author's spirit than Wes Anderson's Fantastic Mr. Fox, a beguiling stop-motion animation pitched between acerbic comedy and droll whimsy.
The Wonderful Story of Henry Sugar, Anderson's return trip to Dahl's pages, proves that magic wasn't a fluke.
The author's short story, nestled in a 1977 anthology aimed at older teens, tells of a very Anderson-esque character: 41-year-old Henry Sugar, a wealthy Englishman who wears fancy suits, drives a Ferrari and — like many an idle rich guy — is largely concerned with ways to make more money.
Men like Henry were, in Dahl's words, "part of the decoration" who drifted "like seaweed all over the world".
The tale of his existential and moral unravelling is tailor-made for Anderson's deceptively fussy storybook style.
At just 39 minutes, Anderson's mini-feature sticks faithfully to the text, with his actors speaking Dahl's prose verbatim — often delivering descriptions of their dialogue to camera, in keeping with the director's love of theatrical conceit.
"Even doctors … who blindfold me in the most expert fashion, refuse to believe anyone can see without his eyes," says Imdad Khan (Ben Kingsley).  (Supplied: Netflix)
Dahl himself (played by a curmudgeonly Ralph Fiennes) introduces the story, perched on a sofa in the luridly orange 70s interior of his writing cottage in Buckinghamshire.
He takes us into a starchy, late-50s London that seems to be made from decorative wallpaper — a world away from the Looney Tunes pastels of Anderson's recent mid-century jaunt, Asteroid City.
Here, on one of his many listless errands, Henry Sugar (Benedict Cumberbatch) finds a book concerning the exploits of Imdad Khan (an amusingly be-wigged Ben Kingsley), an Indian man who once trained with a yogi and has miraculously acquired the ability to see without using his eyes.
Relaying his life to a pair of Calcutta doctors (played by Richard Ayoade and Dev Patel) who came across him back in the mid-30s, Imdad explains that "there are other ways of sending images to the brain".
Dr Marshall and Dr Chatterjee first hear the story of Imdad and his technique for seeing without using his eyes. (Supplied: Netflix)
Seeing a perfect opportunity to game the blackjack tables at the casino he frequents, Henry decides to train himself in Imdad's technique, dedicating himself to learning the ancient ways of mysticism until he too can envision another dimension.
But the ease of winning loads of money with little challenge soon leads to a spiritual crisis and … well, no need to spoil things for anyone who hasn't read the story.
Like most of Anderson's recent work, The Wonderful Story of Henry Sugar is stylised to within an inch of its pretty life, utilising sliding theatrical backdrops, gorgeously painted physical sets and stop-motion miniatures — including tigers and trains that call back to the filmmaker's soulful, unjustly maligned 2007 adventure, The Darjeeling Limited.
Of course, that artifice also goes hand-in-hand with Anderson's usual rich sense of melancholy, and here — as in the oddly moving Asteroid City — it's sprinkled with a kind of spiritual wonder that embraces a world beyond the physical.
It's yet another sign that Anderson is only getting weirder, and more wondrous, the further he plunges into middle age.
Once he learned Imdad's technique, "Henry was almost certainly capable of making money faster than any other person in the entire world." (Supplied: Netflix)
Though Dahl's short story is rife with the author's familiar contempt for greed, it's also one that — a little less typically — locates the potential good in humanity, however fleeting and unusual it may be.
In staying true to that sensibility, Anderson finds a touching connection within his own career gallery of broken adults and lost souls.
Neither Dahl nor Anderson condemns their Henry to the aesthetic prison he's made for himself, preferring instead to find a path to redemption — and the result is all the more moving for it.
The Wonderful Story of Henry Sugar may seem like something of a trifle in Anderson's filmography, but with the director delivering three more (shorter) Dahl adaptations — The Swan, The Rat Catcher and Poison — for Netflix, there's plenty more of this fruitful creative partnership to enjoy.
The Wonderful Story of Henry Sugar is out now.
