title: 'Nothing to do with it': Tom Hanks warns fans against AI-generated insurance scam
content:
Actor Tom Hanks has issued a warning to fans after an AI-generated video of him promoting a dental plan began circulating online.
The online advertisement used a digital version of the Oscar-winning actor's face and voice to promote dental insurance.
"BEWARE!!" Hanks wrote over a screenshot of the video.
"There's a video out there promoting some dental plan with an AI version of me. I have nothing to do with it."
Hanks has previously been a vocal critic of artificial intelligence and deepfake technology, saying during a podcast interview in May he could be "32 years old from now until kingdom come".
"Anybody can now recreate themselves at any age they are, by way of AI or deep fake technology," he told The Adam Buxton Podcast.
"I could be hit by a bus tomorrow and that's it. But my performances can go on and on and on.
The use of artificial intelligence and celebrity faces has been a key part of negotiations in the ongoing Hollywood strikes.
Concern over use of their own faces and voices has even sparked some actors to take legal action, including Indian actor Anil Kapoor.
Kapoor, who is best known for his role in 2008's Slumdog Millionaire, last month won a landmark court case against unauthorised AI-generated images of himself.
A Delhi court has now prohibited "misusing his personality attributes without his permission in any manner", with a judge in the case saying courts "can't turn a blind eye to such misuse".
Meta unveils new celebrity AI chatbots, smart glasses and a refreshed mixed reality headset.
The 66-year-old actor filed the lawsuit after discovering deepfake content of himself and his characters online.
"It's not only for me," he told Variety after the ruling.
"Today I'm there to protect myself, but when I'm not there, the family should have the right to protect my (personality) and gain from it in future.
"Because of the way technology and the AI technology […] which can completely take advantage of and be misused commercially, as well as where my image, voice, morphing, GIFs and deep fakes are concerned, I can straight away, if that happens, send a court order and injunction and they have to pull it down."
AI creations used to be garbled and incomprehensible, but now it's hard to pick the fake images from the real one.
In April, a German tabloid was threatened with legal action after it used AI to create the "first interview" with former Formula 1 racer Michael Schumacher.
Schumacher suffered a near-fatal brain injury in December 2013. His family has since been fiercely private about his condition.
The magazine did not reveal the quotes had been generated until the end of the article.
A spokesperson for Schumacher's family said it plans to sue the magazine over the incident.
Celebrities have increasingly become the target of cybercriminals using AI to make cryptocurrency scam ads, according to an investigation by UK newspaper Evening Standard.
The ads are paid for by their creators to look like they come from certified influencers and organisations.
Among popular targets are adventurer Bear Grylls, former footballer and TV personality Ian Wright and Tesla boss Elon Musk.
Wright, a former Arsenal player, posted on social media in June warning fans of "scams".
"People think I've been arrested," he said on TikTok. "They're superimposing me with handcuffs.
"This is a scam, people are scamming you."
Fake videos of Musk promoting a "new investment project" or claiming Australians will "receive an income of $5,700 a day" have also been circulated online.

title: Film set for box office hit Tasmania Story still stands, but only just after vandals and neglect take toll
content:
An hour out of Hobart, at the far end of a paddock, is a house built for a Japanese feature film.
Called Tasmania Story, the Japanese-language film became a multi-million-dollar box office hit in Japan when it was released in 1990.
The film follows the travels of a young Japanese boy to Australia as he searches for his estranged father. He eventually tracks him to rural Tasmania, where his father has become obsessed with finding a thylacine.
The cast and crew of Tasmania Story pose in front of a house built for the film. (Supplied: Junichiro Hayashi)
Three decades on, location property owner Stuart Archer says the house will soon be demolished after extensive vandalism and years of disrepair.
For the Japanese and Australian crew involved in filming Tasmania Story, memories beyond what was seen on screen dominate.
Behind the scenes, it was a cross-cultural feat of overcoming language barriers to work and socialise as one team.
There was also romance.
Along a stretch of highway in southern Tasmania it would be easy to miss a gateway leading to the Tasmania Story house.
A faded and peeling sign, written in Japanese and partially obscured by tall grass, welcomes visitors.
A faded and peeling sign welcomes visitors to the Tasmania Story house. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)
After a five-minute bumpy gravel, then off-road drive through a paddock, the Tasmania Story house appears.
At a cursory glance and with imagination, the now-dilapidated house looks like a once-functional residence: wooden floorboards, a kitchen, lounge room and fireplace fill the interior.
But upon closer inspection, the house reveals itself as a convincing ruse.
On the roof, there are sections of brick-patterned plastic; and in the kitchen, the sink has no plumbing.
Farmer Stuart Archer plans to dismantle the Tasmania Story house soon. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)
In July 1990, Tasmania Story opened in more than 200 cinemas in Japan.
Mr Archer saw the potential for a tourism operation taking Japanese visitors to the film set, and hoped for a sequel that would require use of the house.
Visitors came, but not enough to sustain a business.
Three years in, he closed the business and placed a sign on the fence welcoming the odd visitor to stop by the house without his assistance.
The Tasmania Story house as it stands today. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)
Curious people did, but so did vandals. They upturned furniture, stole memorabilia and broke every window. In the lounge room lies a heavy trough, carried from one room to another, in an apparent attempt to steal it.
"They've done a number on it," Mr Archer said.
Mr Archer soon plans to dismantle the house and burn non-salvageable props.
Vandals have destroyed much of the set. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)
Although the task ahead is large, he is not bitter about events.
Finances from accepting the request to build the set on his property propelled a pivot from wool to crop farming during the wool crisis of the early 90s.
A tough year turned around by an unlikely and unexpected saviour, Tasmania Story.
A Japanese language prop in the Tasmania Story house. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)
Tasmanian-born Karyn-lee Miyoshi was 22 years old when she was hired as a bilingual production assistant on the film, and it changed her life.
"It was incredible being back [in Tasmania]," Ms Miyoshi said.
"Sometimes I would get sent on little jobs … we went to Geeveston [to record nature sounds] and we were just down the road from where I had been born."
Visits to nightclubs, the casino and parties in crew members' rooms in North Hobart kept nights busy.
Filming at Hobart's Salamanca Markets. (Supplied: Junichiro Hayashi)
When filming finished Ms Miyoshi packed her bags left for Japan.
With encouragement, an apartment arranged for her and a job offer, all by the Japanese contingent of the Tasmania Story team. Ms Miyoshi went on to work in Japan for the better part of five years.
Film producer Charles Hannah (Supplied: Charles Hannah)
There she met her former husband at a party hosted by a crew member.
"When I got married, a lot of people from Tasmania Story arranged this big party in a wonderful restaurant, and then when it was time for me to leave Japan, they threw a big surprise party for me." Ms Miyoshi said.
"It was a massive part of my life."
Film producer Charles Hannah describes Tasmania Story as "one of the happiest shoots" he's ever been on.
He recalls tales of romance among crew, but friendship also.
On days off the Japanese film crew would play baseball and socialise together. He recalls Australian crew members observing the fun and getting involved in baseball games.
"It was almost like it became communication without language, with action," Mr Hannah said.
"The crews got on so well … we made a sweet little film."
An inkling of the film's projected success was felt in Tasmania, with the purchase of 24 shipping containers of thylacine-branded beer and 850 dozen bottles of wine ahead of release.
Upon screening, plush wombats began to sell out in Japan. Then-premier Michael Field spent 12 days there, investigating opportunities for trade and investment.
An estimated doubling of Japanese tourists to Tasmania was expected the following year.
Starring household name Kunie Tanaka and rising star Hiroko Yakushimaru and with a well-known director, the film was set to succeed.
Alongside the stars, an estimated 10 to 12 million Japanese movie goers saw Tasmania's spectacular forests, native animals and the almost mythologised species, the extinct thylacine.
The Tasmanian government said it brought "unprecedented publicity" to the state, moving it from "relative obscurity", with an increase from 30 per cent to 80 per cent of the Japanese population knowing of Tasmania.
Audiences were wowed by Tasmanian landscapes and native animals. (Supplied: Junichiro Hayashi)
Screenwriter Narito Kaneko can recall impressing students with his connection to the film a decade after its release.
"I told them that I had written "Tasumania Monogatari", to which a female student told me that she saw it when she was in primary school," Mr Kaneko said.
"It had moved her so much that she begged her parents to visit Tasmania, which they duly did apparently."
Screenwriter Narito Kaneko. (Supplied: Nobuyoshi Shinohara)
Knowing nothing of thylacines ahead of writing the film, Mr Kaneko later walked Tasmania's mountains and forests, wondering if a thylacine was hiding somewhere in the bush.
Cinematographer Junichiro Hayashi was similarly captivated by wildlife, one of his strongest memories is of two illuminated wallabies, running in front of his car at night.
"I was fascinated by the majestic nature that is not found in Japan," Mr Hayashi said.
"The [challenge] was whether I could capture the great nature of Tasmania as I felt it.
"Majestic nature and animals!"

title: Netflix shutters the remnants of the largest publicly accessible film library in history
content:
In 1997 – a decade before the first movie was streamed on Netflix – Marc Randolph enclosed a disk in an envelope and dropped it off at his local post office in Santa Cruz, California.
The Netflix co-founder was testing a theory: could a DVD rental service even work?
If it wasn't for a stroke of blind luck, he might've abandoned the idea for Netflix that same day.
25 years – and 5.2 billion red envelopes – on, the final batch of the company's DVDs are winding their way through the US postal system.
Friday marked the final day of its rental service, and the milestone has had Randolph reflecting on the role of fortune in the company's early days.
Marc Randolph is nostalgic for the early days of Netflix. (Wikipedia: Gage Skidmore)
In the intervening years, Netflix has inspired and then crushed Australia's Quickflix, assembled the largest film catalogue ever, taken down a corporate giant and ushered in the era of streaming.
Not bad for an almost failed experiment.
If the idea of posting DVDs feels anachronistic in 2023, it's a testament to the disruptions Netflix has engineered in the last two and half decades – and the luck they've enjoyed along the way.
When Randolph and his co-founder Reed Hastings hatched their revolutionary idea, neither of them had even seen a DVD before.
He'd heard there was a "thin light disc that might actually fit into a first class mailing envelope".
Even though few Americans even owned a DVD player at that point, it was enough to convince the pair to explore the idea.
This is what triggered Randolph to make that trip to the Santa Cruz post office in 1997 – he wanted to test whether a disk would survive a trip through the US postal system.
Marc Randolph stands outside the Santa Cruz post office where he mailed a Patsy Cline CD in 1997. (AP Photo: Michael Liedtke)
It did, and the rest is history. At least that's what he believed for a while.
On revisiting the same Santa Cruz post office months later, he found out that it was only the proximity of the delivery address that saved the disk from being mangled.
If they had tried posting it further away, a post office employee explained, the disk would've likely been crushed by a sorting machine – along with their nascent business idea.
"We dodged a bullet there," says Randolph.
And this was only the first in a series of near misses that defined Netflix's ascent to becoming the second-largest media company in the world.
In a famous incident in 2000, Blockbuster declined an offer to acquire the fledgling startup for a reported $US50 million ($77 million).
The dotcom bubble had just popped, and, desperate for funding, Netflix made their pitch to Blockbuster CEO John Antioco at the video store franchise's Dallas headquarters.
According to Randolph, Antioco was so unimpressed he had to stop himself laughing in the meeting (Antioco disputes this characterisation of events).
Regardless of how the interaction played out, the short-sightedness of Blockbuster's decision became clear in a matter of years.
Soon, Netflix was lending over a million DVDs a week, and bringing in over $US1 billion a year in revenue.
Marc Randolph and Reed Hastings celebrating the Netflix IPO in 2002.  (Supplied: Marc Randolph)
At its peak, Netflix was the US Postal Service's fifth-largest corporate customer, operating 58 shipping facilities and 128 shuttle locations across the country, according to a Netflix spokesperson.
Blockbuster's fortunes couldn't have been more different.
Less than a decade on from the opening of their 9,000th store, the company collapsed into bankruptcy after failing to adapt to the changing market.
Miraculously, a lone Blockbuster store in Perth's suburbs managed to survive until 2019, before it too closed down.
Dickson Blockbuster DVD store closing down. (ABC News: Greg Nelson)
"You can't underestimate how challenging it is to change an incumbent business," says Amanda Lotz, a professor of Digital Media and Communication at QUT.
"It was in Blockbuster's interest to try and not have the world change. Blockbuster had a business that was working really well."
It's a familiar story to Stephen Langsford, who founded Australian DVD rental company Quickflix in 2004.
"There were some 3,500 video stalls on the corner streets around Australia [when Quickflix launched]," he told ABC News.
Stephen Langsford founded Quickflix in 2004. (Supplied: Stephen Langsford)
"By the time we finished, there were almost none."
Because Netflix never brought their DVD rental service to Australia, there were "three fairly organised, funded competitors, including ourselves having a shot in this nascent market," recalls Langsford.
Less than a decade after launching, Quickflix had acquired one of those competitors and boasted more than 41,000 Australian subscribers.
"We had millions and millions and millions of DVDs swirling around the country," he says.
Langsford attributes Quickflix's success partly to customer dissatisfaction with brick-and-mortar stores, specifically around late fees, and limited range.
"We saw an opportunity [to] provide a greater range, credit, convenience, late fees, and change the game."
He recalls visiting a Netflix warehouse in Los Angeles with Netflix's then-CEO Hastings.
"I saw their largest distribution centre and the automation that they had put in place and robotics that were involved in unpacking the DVD and repackaging.
"That was a bit more sophisticated than where Quickflix was at."
But dominating the DVD rental market was never Netflix's ultimate goal.
From the start, Randolph had always had one eye on what he saw as the holy grail – streaming.
"I don't think either of us really thought [DVD rentals were] going to last more than five or six years," he said.
Sure enough, in 2007, almost a decade after sending its first DVD in the mail, Netflix launched its streaming service.
Through the early years of streaming, it was the DVD service that paid the bills.
"We were the cash cow that was propping up streaming," a former Netflix DVD director of engineering told The Verge.
"Every dollar we could save was a dollar that would go to pay [for] House of Cards."
Only five years later, streaming was generating double as much revenue as the DVDs were.
By 2015, the DVD service was accounting for less than 1 per cent of the company's total revenue.
This decline meant meant its days were numbered, explained Lotz.
"We remain in this space, especially in the US, where if there isn't potential for growth, it's not going to be something Wall Street values," she said.
With Netflix's streaming business booming, Quickflix once again followed its lead.
This time round, though, the proposition was different. Without geographic and physical constraints, Netflix could take its service global without dramatic increases in its distribution costs.
Boasting the reach of a global empire, a stable of original content and a huge technological head start, Netflix was a formidable competitor.
"When Netflix arrived, it was nuclear warfare," says Langsford.
Netflix entered the Australian market in 2015, a year in which it generated annual revenue of $US6.7 billion compared to $US11 million for Quickflix.
Netflix began producing original content in 2011. (Supplied: Netflix)
Quickflix closed down the next year, having failed to capture a significant segment of Australia's streaming market.
"Maybe we should have stuck to online DVD rental," laughs Langsford.
"It's very, very difficult for an Australian player with a population of 26 million or so to be able to compete."
A confluence of factors largely outside its control led to Quickflix's demise – a reminder of the importance of luck and good timing.
"I'm a huge believer that luck plays a tremendous role in success," says Randolph.
"We bet on DVD at a time when there were less than a quarter [of a] million DVD players sold in the entire United States."
Netflix began life as a DVD rental service. (Supplied: Netflix)
Against all odds, this bet came off.
"They did something that is largely impossible, which is, enter an existing industry with very high barriers to entry and change the way that industry operates," notes Lotz.
While few will mourn having to pick up DVDs from Blockbuster – or the mailbox – the switch to streaming has resulted in the breaking up of the largest film catalogue in history.
With over 100,00 titles once available to rent through Netflix, US customers had access to an unprecedented range of options.
Quickflix's catalogue was half as big at its peak, but that's still many times more than any of today's streaming platforms.
"It's not a small thing, the loss of diversity of content and range of content," says Lotz.
"If we want to have those libraries I don't think we can expect them to come from for-profit entities.
Amanda Lotz says there are opportunities for public libraries to fill the gap left by fragmenting digital media offerings. (Supplied: Katherine Griffiths for City of Sydney)
"I think these come back to the questions of who is responsible for these things and what is the role of public libraries in an environment of digital assets.
"We spend quite a bit on supporting Australian production, but it's also recognising that we now have opportunities to create access for Australians to digital libraries."
As for the now-defunct library, a Netflix spokesperson told ABC News it will be recycling the majority of its DVDs, with a portion of them being donated to organisations focused on film and media.
It's a reflective moment for Randolph, who admits he hasn't watched a DVD in a couple of years.
But that doesn't mean there's nothing to mourn.
"Maybe we are saying goodbye to the world's largest content library that will ever exist," he says.

title: Michael Gambon achieved an incredible amount before he put his stamp on Harry Potter
content:
Harry Potter fans around the world are putting their wands up in memory of veteran actor Michael Gambon, who died on Thursday age 82.
Those born during the Harry Potter craze of the early 2000s would better recognise Gambon as Professor Albus Dumbledore, with flowing wizard robes and long, white beard.
And while his tenure as Harry Potter's father figure opened his stardom to a whole new generation of fans, Gambon's career reaches back far further.
After becoming a fully qualified engineering technician at age 21, Ireland-born Gambon set his sights on the stage.
His early performances caught the eye of Shaksperian great and first artistic director of the UK's Royal National Theatre Laurence Olivier.
In 1963, Gambon was recruited as the first ensemble of National Theatre actors alongside soon-to-be British acting greats, including future Harry Potter co-star Maggie Smith.
Gambon worked under the guidance of Olivier for four years, performing in numerous stage shows in the 60s and 70s.
He received wide acclaim and cemented his influence on high school drama classes for years to come in 1980 by taking the leading role in Bertolt Brecht's The Life of Galileo.
It would be six years later, in 1986, that Gambon would win his first Olivier award, named after his former artistic director.
Gambon would go on to win two more Oliviers — in 1988 and 1990.
Gambon took the leap from stage to screen in the mid-60s, racking up a filmography as varied as it is long.
It's so wide-spanning that you could recognise Gambon as a stoic dramatic actor or a silly comedian, depending on which decade you were born in.
Michael Gambon with Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G at the 2002 London premiere of Ali G Indahouse. (Getty Images: Gareth Davis)
His pre-turn of the century highlights a breakout into TV with the lead role in 1986's The Singing Detective, in which he played a writer suffering from a debilitating skin condition whose imagination provided the only escape from his pain.
The performance won him one of his four BAFTAs.
Gambon's film work of the time encapsulates crime dramas like 1989's The Cook, The Thief, His Wife & Her Lover and the 1999 Tim Burton-led horror Sleepy Hollow.
It was post 2000 that Gambon let his comedic chops shine through his screen work.
In 2002, when Sacha Baron Cohen's satirical Ali G character was taking the UK by storm, Gambon stepped into the straight man roll as the prime minister in Ali G Indahouse.
A couple years later he struck up a working relationship with quirky auteur Wes Anderson, featuring alongside a star studded cast in 2004's The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou.
Gambon would return to the Wes Anderson Cinematic Universe in 2009 to voice fierce farmer Frank Bean in 2009's Fantastic Mr Fox.
His stately vocals would once again be put to good use as Paddington Bear's Uncle Pastuzo in the 2014 film and 2017 sequel.
Most recently he featured in 2019's Judy, the biopic of screen legend Judy Garland.
Of course, if you missed him in everything else, Harry Potter fans recognise Gambon as Professor Albus Percival Wulfric Brian Dumbledore.
Gambon did not originate the character, with fellow veteran actor Richard Harris playing the wise wizard in the first two films — Harry Potter and the Philosophers' Stone and Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets.
When Harris passed away from cancer before filming of the third movie, Gambon stepped up to fill his shoes.
Michael Gambon as Dumbeldore in Harry Potter (Supplied: Imdb, Warner Bros)
He would stay with the franchise until its completion, portraying Dumbledore for a total of six films.
He once said he had not read any of J. K. Rowling’s books, arguing that it was better to follow the script than be influenced by the books.
And this acting approach was never more evident to fans than in 2005's Harry Potter and The Goblet of Fire.
The same line is said in both the book and the film when Dumbledore is attempting to access how Harry's name had been placed in the Goblet of Fire, granting him entry into the very dangerous Triwizard Tournament.
"Did you put your name into the Goblet of Fire, Harry?" he asked calmly — is how the question is described in the original novel.
However, Gambon decided to put his own dramatic flare on the line in the film, yelling the question while barrelling towards and shaking Harry Potter actor Daniel Radcliffe.
The performance was quickly seized upon by Harry Potter fanatics and since become a popular meme within the community, lovingly known as "Dumbledore Asked Calmly".

title: Five of Sir Michael Gambon's most memorable scenes as Professor Dumbledore
content:
In his death, actor Sir Michael Gambon will be remembered as an actor who could do anything from Shakespeare to comedy but for younger fans, he is best known for bringing Professor Albus Dumbledore to life in the Harry Potter films.
Gambon, who died on Thursday aged 82 after a bout of pneumonia, took over the role after the death of Richard Harris in 2004.
He once said he had not read any of J. K. Rowling’s books, arguing that it was better to follow the script than be influenced by the books.
However, it didn't prevent him from embodying the spirit of Professor Dumbledore, the powerful wizard who fought against evil to protect his students.
With five films in the role, each Harry Potter fan will have their favourite Dumbledore scenes. Let's take a look at some of his most memorable scenes.
Dumbledore dies in Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince.
This scene needs no introduction.
In Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, Draco Malfoy has his wand pointed towards Professor Dumbledore at the top of the Astronomy Tower.
Dumbledore: Draco, years ago, I knew a boy who made all the wrong choices. Please let me help you.
Malfoy: I don't want your help! Don't you understand? I have to do this! I have to kill you! Or he's going to kill me …
Then Professor Severus Snape steps up.
"Severus, please," Dumbledore says.
"Avada Kedavra," Snape says as Dumbledore falls to his death.
Dumbledore and Voldemort duel at the Ministry of Magic.
In the halls of the Ministry of Magic, Dumbledore comes face-to-face with Voldemort, who he knows as Tom Riddle.
In the Order of the Phoenix, the two face off while Harry Potter watches on.
"It was foolish of you to come here tonight, Tom. The Aurors are on their way," Dumbledore warns.
Fawkes the phoenix helps Professor Dumbledore escape.
In the Order of the Phoenix, Minister of Magic Cornelius Fudge orders that Professor Dumbledore be escorted to Azkaban prison to await trial for conspiracy and sedition.
But he has other plans.
"I thought we might hit this little snag," he says.
"You seem to be labouring under the delusion that I am going to, what was the phrase, come quietly?
"Well I can tell you this, I have no intention of going to Azkaban."
His phoenix Fawkes then swoops down and Dumbledore disappears in flames.
"You may not like him, minister, but you can't deny, Dumbledore's got style," Auror Kingsley Shacklebott says.
Professor Dumbledore speaks to Harry after Voldemort's curse.
After Voldemort's killing curse in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, Harry Potter speaks with Dumbledore in a place that appears to be London's Kings Cross station.
In his conversation with Harry, Dumbledore tells him: "Help will always be given at Hogwarts Harry, to those who ask for it.
"I've always prized myself on my ability to turn a phrase.
"Words are, in my not so humble opinion, our most inexhaustible source of magic, capable of both inflicting injury and remedying it.
"But I would in this case amend my original statement to this:
"Help will always be given at Hogwarts to those who deserve it."
He goes on to tell Harry not to pity the dead but rather to "pity the living and above all, all those who live without love".
Harry: Professor, is this all real or is it happening inside my head?
Dumbledore: Of course it is all happening in your head, Harry, why should that mean that it's not real?
Professor Dumbledore addresses Hogwarts students at the Great Hall.
As Professor Dumbledore said himself, he has a way with words.
With dementors surrounding Hogwarts at the start of the school year in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, Professor Dumbledore relied on his words in his opening address at the Great Hall.
"Happiness can be found even in the darkest of times, if one only remembers to turn on the light."
This quote has been embraced by fans of the franchise, to become one of the most well-known lines spoken by Professor Dumbledore.

title: Team Human or Team Robot? New film The Creator takes a surprising side
content:
In this era of widespread scepticism over artificial intelligence, there's something refreshingly optimistic — if perhaps a little naive — about a film that dares to pitch its sympathies in with the robots.
So it is with The Creator, the new film from Rogue One director Gareth Edwards, a sci-fi action epic that's both topical and strangely progressive — but whose execution can be as creaky and old-fashioned as humanity itself.
The year is 2065, and humanity — having created AI to do its dirty work — finds itself at global war with the upstart technology, which has nuked Los Angeles (or so we're led to believe) in order to show they mean evolutionary business.
It's a battle that's created bitter division between East and West: A vast region known as "New Asia" is sympathetic to AI, while the US-led western territories want to terminate the bots with extreme prejudice.
Australian Greig Fraser, known for his work on Dune, was one of the cinematographers on The Creator. (Supplied: Disney+)
On a remote island in New Asia, western special forces operative Joshua (John David Washington, Tenet; BlacKkKlansman) has been sent undercover to infiltrate the AI, but he's fallen for local sympathiser Maya (Gemma Chan, Eternals; Crazy Rich Asians) and the two are expecting a child.
Their blissful idyll is interrupted when the anti-AI warship Nomad — which hangs in the sky like some futuristic Van Halen logo, raining down a wall of laser fire — razes their home, leaving Maya missing and presumed dead.
Five years later, Joshua is enlisted into an operation to wipe out the AI by locating its creator, a mysterious entity known as Nimrata.
On a gung-ho military mission deep into AI terrain, he discovers Alphie (newcomer Madeleine Yuna Voyles): a biotech child who holds the key to ending the machine-human conflict.
With humans as the rapacious oppressors and the AI hiding out in a jungle that looks distinctly like Vietnam (Edwards has said one of the film's touchstones was Apocalypse Now), the visual analogies are classic Hollywood mix-and-match — audacious and striking, if borderline politically incoherent.
Could Alfie (played by newcomer Madeleine Yuna Voyles) help put an end to the war? (Supplied: Disney+)
The Creator is — to its unfashionable credit — aggressively pro-technology, regarding its artificial life with humanity and correctly assuming that AI is only as evil as the people who created it.
It helps that these AI aren't the faceless, insidious kind of the current moment, but old-school humanoids inhabited by the likes of the great Ken Watanabe (Edwards' Godzilla; Tampopo). Their cybernetic faces have something recognisably human and damaged to them, not unlike the Mecha of Spielberg's A.I. Artificial Intelligence.
The ruthless military operation, meanwhile, lends an unflattering face to humanity's self-preservation instincts.
At one point their leader (played by an unlikely Allison Janney) straight up admits AI are the superior life forms, and that humans need to kill them off to avoid their own extinction.
That's a provocative idea for a major blockbuster — but also one that might scan as a sinister admission on the part of the studios that have been siding with AI in the dispute with writers and actors.
Allison Janney plays Colonel Howell, who is fighting for the humans. (Supplied: Disney+)
As in Rogue One, Edwards shows off his impressive sense of scale and scope, shooting on location in South-East Asia with cinematographers Oren Soffer and Australian Greig Fraser (Dune), who seamlessly blend the sweeping locales with high-end visual effects.
An exhilarating sequence set to Radiohead's eerie Everything in its Right Place, with insectoid spacecraft menacing the landscape, is just the kind of pop sci-fi filmmaking we don't see enough of these days.
Still, for a film so willing to embrace the possibilities of technology, its sometimes perfunctory execution is all down to human error. Its generic sci-fi action narrative lacks the necessary magic — that old Speilbergian touch — to really induce the empathy for the AI to which it aspires.
Will artificial intelligence turn on humanity?
With so many ideas in the mix, it's a shame The Creator leans on the familiar sci-fi playbook, from Blade Runner to Aliens to Edwards's own Rogue One. The latter's worst aspects — stunning visuals in the service of flat characterisation — tend to get repeated here.
Edwards's sympathies again gravitate toward the hardware, and in one case — maybe the movie's best moment — a monkey armed with a remote control and the inclination to detonate a bomb.
But he's not as effective with the human performers, nor a screenplay, co-written with Chris Weitz (Rogue One; Pinocchio), that unfortunately goes through the motions.
The Creator is a film dedicated to empathising with technology that gets undone by human cliche.
That might be a comfort in this charged AI climate, but doesn't always make for great science fiction, where the thrilling terror of the unpredictable can push the limits of the form.
The Creator is in cinemas now.
The Creator is dedicated to empathising with technology.

title: Blockbuster films and stand-up comedy. What do the new Golden Globe categories mean?
content:
The Golden Globes has added two new categories to its name, in one of the biggest changes in its 80-year history.
The new categories will celebrate box-office smashes and comedians, in addition to 25 existing awards paying tribute to the best of film and TV.
It is the latest in changes for the awards show since the embattled Hollywood Foreign Press Association (HFPA) sold the Golden Globes to private investors earlier this year.
But what does it mean and how did we get here?
The two new categories are bound to shake up the awards show and its nominations.  (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)
The awards show has unveiled  two new categories:  The Golden Globe for Cinematic and Box Office Achievement and Best Performance in Stand-Up Comedy on Television.
The former hopes to showcase box-office breaking achievements while the latter highlights some of the year's best stand-up talent.
But here's what that means exactly:
Meryl Streep, left, at the 2018 Golden Globes ceremony. (AP: Jordan Strauss)
Nominations include works released by broadcast, streaming and pay-per-view cable on recognised media platforms
Margot Robbie attends the 2023 Golden Globe Awards and could be in the running for the new categories with Barbie.  (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)
"The new Cinematic and Box Office Achievement award is more than just rewarding the year's top-earning and most viewed motion pictures," Golden Globes executive vice president Tim Gray said.
"The Golden Globes has a rich history of supporting and celebrating the work of comedians, and we're thrilled to honour their brilliance alongside outstanding motion picture and television performances of the year," Golden Globes president Helen Hoehne said.
Golden Globes president Helen Hoehne says the awards will "honour" the talent of stand-up comedians.  (AP Photo/Chris Pizzello)
It's been a mixed reaction to say the least.
Many say it's an attempt to copy a similar idea floated by the Oscars in 2019.
The Academy Awards try at a "Most Popular Film category", however, was swiftly retracted before the show's broadcast due to backlash.
Variety TV critic Owen Gleiberman said copying the idea could force audiences to put films into boxes.
"Some of us really were not crazy about this idea," he said.
"What bothered me about what was called the 'popular category', introducing that to the Oscars, was not so much the idea of honouring the box office but for me, it created this kind of dichotomy in our thinking — where we have the quality films over here and then we have the blockbusters that the people go to see over here.
Others thought the Golden Globes already favoured popular films over art-house darlings.
But Mr Gleiberman praised the comedy category, saying there has been a history of great comedy performers who have gone unnoticed.
The categories could be a way for the awards show to get back into the good graces of Hollywood after a slew of controversies.
While the Golden Globes has scandals dating back to 1958, they have been rocked in recent years by accusations of soliciting favours from celebrities and studios, racism and sexism.
Opposition reached a fever pitch in 2018 when everyone's favourite mummy hunter Brendan Fraser told GQ former HFPA president Philip Berk had sexually assaulted him in 2003.
In 2021, Berk then sent an email calling the Black Lives Matter initiative a "racist hate movement" and was expelled from the organisation.
Fraser refused to attend the 2022 Golden Globes, despite being nominated for Best Actor for his role in The Whale.
It was also revealed the organisation had no black members in its 87-person cohort of journalists and Hollywood figures, according to a Los Angeles Times expose.
NBC nixed the award show's broadcast in response and Tom Cruise returned his three Golden Globe Awards.
Last year, Fraser boycotted the awards show despite being nominated for Best Actor.
"I have more history with the Hollywood Foreign Press Association than I have respect for the Hollywood Foreign Press Association," he told GQ.
It took just seven weeks for Barbie to hit the box office milestone. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
Well...probably.
If you're a savvy pop culture consumer, it's no surprise Barbie has already been touted as a top contender for the new box office achievement category.
Early in September, the film starring Australian actress Margot Robbie became the highest-grossing film of 2023 with over $US1.38 billion ($2.13 billion) globally.
Mr Gleiberman noted the Greta Gerwig film is also a critic favourite, and could very well take out the Best Picture nomination too.
The Super Mario Bros Movie, Oppenheimer and The Little Mermaid have also been suggested as front runners.
As for 2023's best stand-up performances — John Mulaney's Baby J, Marc Maron's From Bleak to Dark, and Mae Martin's SAP have all been critically acclaimed and could earn themselves the inaugural nod.
Winners will be announced at the 81st Golden Globe Awards on Sunday, January, 2024.
Mae Martin's SAP has been listed as one of the best 2023's stand-up specials.

title: Hollywood writers strike to end after guild leaders approve deal with studios
content:
Leaders of the screenwriters' union say their nearly five-month strike will finish after board members approved a contract agreement with studios, bringing Hollywood partly back from a historic halt in production.
The governing boards of the eastern and western branches of the Writers Guild of America and their joint negotiating committee all voted to accept the deal, and declared that the strike would be over and writers would be free to work starting on Wednesday (local time).
Late-night talk shows — the first to go dark when writers walked out on May 2 — are likely the first shows that will resume.
The writers still have to vote to ratify the contract themselves, but lifting the strike will allow them to work during that process, the Writers Guild told members in an email.
Jimmy Kimmel and Jimmy Fallon could both resume filming their late-night talk shows within days.  (AP/NBC)
After Tuesday's board votes, the contracts were released to the writers, who had not yet been given any details on the deal, which their leaders called "exceptional".
The members will vote between October 2-9.
Hollywood actors remain on strike with no talks on the horizon, but a new spirit of optimism animated those who were picketing on Tuesday for the first time since writers reached their tentative deal.
"For a hot second, I really thought that this was going to go on until next year," said Marissa Cuevas, an actor who has appeared on the TV series Kung Fu and The Big Bang Theory.
"Knowing that at least one of us has gotten a good deal gives a lot of hope that we will also get a good deal."
Writers' picket lines had been suspended, but they were encouraged to walk in solidarity with actors, and many were on the lines on Tuesday including Mad Men creator Matthew Weiner.
"We would never have had the leverage we had if SAG (Screen Actors Guild) had not gone out," Weiner said.
The alliance of studios, streaming services and producers has chosen to negotiate only with the writers so far, and has made no overtures yet toward restarting talks with SAG-AFTRA (Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Radio and Television Artists).
SAG-AFTRA leaders have said they will look closely at the writers' agreement, which includes many of the same issues, but it would not affect their demands.
Striking actors also voted to authorise their leadership to potentially expand their walkout to include the lucrative video game market, a step that could put new pressure on Hollywood studios to make a deal with the performers who provide voices and stunts for games.
SAG-AFTRA announced the move late on Monday, saying that 98 per cent of its members voted to go on strike against video game companies if ongoing negotiations are not successful.
Acting in video games can include a variety of roles, from voice performances to motion capture work as well as stunts.
Video game actors went on strike in 2016 in a work stoppage that lasted nearly a year.
Some of the same issues are at play in the video game negotiations as in the broader actors strike that has shut down Hollywood for months, including wages, safety measures and protections on the use of artificial intelligence.
The companies involved include gaming giants Activision, Electronic Arts, Epic Games, Take 2 Productions as well as video game divisions at Disney and Warner Bros.
"It's time for the video game companies to stop playing games and get serious about reaching an agreement on this contract," SAG-AFTRA president Fran Drescher said in a statement.
Audrey Cooling, a spokesperson for video game producers, said they are "continuing to negotiate in good faith" and have reached tentative agreements on more than half of the proposals on the table.

title: Hollywood screenwriters have put down their pickets so what happens next?
content:
After 146 days of picketing and shutdowns across film and TV, Hollywood writers have struck a tentative deal with studios.
However, with actors still striking and a walkout looming for the gaming industry, a new hurdle now faces the entertainment world.
When will Hollywood get back its A-listers, and what happens next exactly?
Here's everything we know:
In case you've not been keeping up-to-date with the biggest hit to Hollywood since 1960, writers and actors have been striking to address growing concerns in a streaming world.
On May 2, screenwriters belonging to the Writers Guild of America (WGA) walked out following failed negotiations with major studios over issues of pay, the size of writing staffs on shows and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the creation of scripts.
More than two months into the strike, writers got a dose of solidarity and star power when they were joined by 65,000 striking film and television actors.
The Screen Actors Guild — American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) union shared concerns over streaming residuals and the looming threat of AI.
The result was an almost complete shutdown of Hollywood, and marked the first joint writer and actor strike in over 60 years.
After five months of strikes, screenwriters may soon be able to put down their placards.  (AP: Chris Pizzello)
There's still a lot we don't know about the writers' deal announced on Monday.
Details of the three-year agreement haven't been made public or even shared with writers themselves because the contract language is still being finalised.
But the WGA said in an email to its 11,500 members the deal was "exceptional – with meaningful gains and protections for writers in every sector of the membership."
It is understood writers were able to reach an agreement on all deal points, including previous stalemates over AI and writing room staffing.
From there, governing boards for the two WGA branches are likely to vote on the contract on Tuesday local time.
With their approval, writers will then vote on the deal, and the strike can officially end.
While picketing is suspended, union leaders have told writers not to return to work yet.
The agreement comes five days before the strike would've become the longest in the guild's history, and the longest Hollywood strike in decades.
The between writers and studios deal was reached after Hollywood’s writers were on strike for nearly five months.  (AP: Jae C. Hong)
SAG-AFTRA extended their "heartfelt congratulations" to writers for reaching an agreement, applauding their "dedication, diligence and unwavering solidarity".
But it doesn't look like this will change things for striking actors.
"(We) are proud to stand shoulder to shoulder with you as creative partners in the entertainment industry," the union wrote on X, formerly Twitter, shortly after the news of the deal.
"We look forward to reviewing the terms of the WGA and AMPTP's (Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers) tentative agreement.
"And we remain ready to resume our own negotiations with the AMPTP as soon as they are prepared to engage on our proposals in a meaningful way.
Actors will continue to picket on Tuesday, and many urged writers to picket in solidarity until the WGA deal was cemented.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
AMPTP last talked to the actors' union 74 days ago.
"I think the membership of SAG-AFTRA is going to say we've been out of work for months, we want to go back to work, we don't want to be the ones that are keeping everybody else on the sidelines," entertainment lawyer Bobby Schwartz told The New York Times.
The SAG-AFTRA deal will depend on the terms of the WGA deal.
US actor's union president Fran Drescher accuses streamers and studios of greed.
That could depend.
Once the writers' deal is firmed out, network shows including NBC's The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon and ABC's Jimmy Kimmel Live! could return to the air within days.
And while some writers may want to remain on the picket lines to to support actors, they may be left with limited choice.
The WGA negotiators were unsuccessful in receiving the contractual right to honour other unions' picket lines, according to The New York Times.
Jimmy Kimmel and Jimmy Fallon could both resume filming their late-night talk shows within days.  (AP/NBC)
This means writers could be asked to return to work before SAG-AFTRA has the chance to strike a deal.
Work on uncompleted projects will also need to be finished first, before other projects can get under way, film and television producer Todd Garner says.
Network execs say it could take drama series eight to 10 weeks to be back up and running and six to eight weeks for comedies, according to Deadline.
Now that the WGA strike looks to be at a close, many productions hope to resume filming as soon as possible.  (AP: Chris Pizzello)
It looks likely.
This time, the gaming industry could be faced with a walkout of voice actors and motion capture performers if a new labour contract fails.
SAG-AFTRA has signalled its intention to strike, with 98.32 per cent of those who cast ballots voting in favour of the strike on Monday.
The union is scheduled to begin contract talks with gaming companies on Tuesday local time.
The SAG-AFTRA agreement covering video game performers expired last November and has been extended on a monthly basis as the union negotiated with major video game companies.
Activision Blizzard is one of the companies who would face game actor strikes if a new contract is not negotiated.  (AP: Jae C Hong/File)
These include Activision Blizzard, Electronic Arts, Epic Games, Formosa Interactive and others.
And in case you were looking for a theme — the most pressing issues for video game actors is higher pay and protection against AI, alongside medical treatment and breaks for motion capture performers.
"This is at an inflection point for our industry. In particular with AI, because right now there aren't any protections," Horizon Zero Dawn voice actor Ashly Burch told Reuters.
The estimated economic toll of the joint strikes is expected to total at least $US5 billion ($7.7 billion) in California and the other US production hubs, according to Milken Institute economist Kevin Klowden.
Warner Bros Discovery have warned the company's full-year adjusted core profit would take a hit of up to $US500 million.
Its shares have dropped nearly 14 per cent since the writers' strike started while Paramount, Disney and Netflix have lost between 20-45 per cent in shares.
Walt Disney chief executive Bob Iger had previously called the joint strikes "very disturbing".  (Reuters: Aly Song)
Emmy nominated television writer Zack Bornstein said those downfalls were a direct result of studios refusing to negotiate for months.
"Giving us every single one of our demands from day one would have cost them only two pennies on the dollar off just the profits they make from our work alone," he told ABC NewsRadio's Thomas Oriti.
Rosenblatt analyst Barton Crockett says studios could reduce the number of shows they green light to curb the losses and pay for the wage increase for writers.
The strikes have also wrecked havoc on associated industries such as camera operators, carpenters, production assistants alongside caterers and costume suppliers

title: Bruce Willis's wife says 'it's hard to know' if he is aware of his dementia
content:
The wife of famed actor Bruce Willis has spoken publicly for the first time about her husband's dementia, saying "it's hard to know" if the Hollywood legend is aware of his condition.
Emma Heming Willis appeared on US morning program Today, hosted by broadcaster NBC, speaking about Frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
Willis, 68, was diagnosed with dementia in February, a year after he was diagnosed with aphasia — a disorder leading to speaking, reading and writing issues.
Joining the program on Monday morning (US time), Heming Willis was asked if her husband was aware of his health predicament.
"Hard to know. It's hard to know," she said.
Frontotemporal dementia causes progressive damage to either or both the frontal or temporal lobes of the brain, according to Dementia Australia.
It can have an affect on behaviour, personality, language and movement.
Heming Willis appeared on the Today program as part of World FTD Awareness Week, and said those who care for others with dementia also need to take care of themselves.
She said she called herself a "care partner" instead of a caretaker, as often those in relationships are working through the ripple effects of the condition.
"It's hard on the person diagnosed, it's also hard on the family," she said.
"And that is no different for Bruce, or myself, or our girls. When they say this is a family disease, it really is.
"As a care partner it's so important to be able to ask for help and support.
Willis began his acting in the 1980s, achieving fame with a leading role in the series Moonlighting.
His most famous movie roles were in the Die Hard franchise where he played protagonist John McClane.
Actor Bruce Willis was diagnosed with dementia a year after his retirement.

title: Hollywood writers strike set to end as tentative deal is reached, but actors remain on strike
content:
Union leaders and Hollywood studios reached a tentative agreement on Sunday to end a historic screenwriters strike after nearly five months, though no deal is yet in the works for striking actors.
The Writers Guild of America (WGA) announced the deal with the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP), the group that represents studios, streaming services and producers in negotiations.
"WGA has reached a tentative agreement with the AMPTP," the guild said in an email to members.
"This was made possible by the enduring solidarity of WGA members and extraordinary support of our union siblings who joined us on the picket lines for over 146 days."
The three-year contract agreement — settled on after five marathon days of renewed talks by negotiators WGA and the AMPTP — must be approved by the guild's board and members before the strike officially ends.
The terms of the deal were not immediately announced. The tentative deal to end the last writers strike, in 2008, was approved by more than 90 per cent of members.
The agreement comes five days before the strike would've become the longest in the guild's history, and the longest Hollywood strike in decades.
As a result of the agreement, nightly network shows including NBC's The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon and ABC's Jimmy Kimmel Live! could return to the air within days.
But as writers prepare to potentially crack open their laptops again, it's far from back to business as usual in Hollywood, as talks have not yet resumed between studios and striking actors. Crew members left with no work by the stoppage will remain unemployed for now.
The proposed solution to the writers strike comes after talks resumed on Wednesday for the first time in a month. Chief executives including Bob Iger of Disney, Ted Sarandos of Netflix, David Zaslav of Warner Bros Discovery and Donna Langley of NBCUniversal reportedly took part in the negotiations directly.
About 11,500 members of the WGA walked off the job on May 2 over issues of pay, the size of writing staffs on shows and the use of artificial intelligence in the creation of scripts.
On July 14, more than two months into the strike, the writers got a dose of solidarity and star power — along with a whole lot of new picketing partners — when they were joined by 65,000 striking film and television actors. There have been no discussions about resuming negotiations with the actors union.
Actors joined the writers on strike in July this year.  (AP: Chris Pizzello)
The writers strike immediately sent late-night talk shows and Saturday Night Live into hiatus, and has since sent dozens of scripted shows and other productions into limbo, including forthcoming seasons of Netflix's Stranger Things, HBO's The Last of Us, and ABC's Abbot Elementary, and films including Deadpool 3 and Superman: Legacy. The Emmy Awards were also pushed from September to January.
As the US actors' and writers' strike continues on with no end in sight, workers here say our industry is facing similar, if not worse, issues.
More recently, writers had been targeting talk shows that were working around strike rules to return to air, including The Drew Barrymore Show, Real Time With Bill Maher and The Talk. All reversed course in the face of picketing and pressure, and are likely to quickly return now.
The combined strikes made for a pivotal moment in Hollywood as creative labour faced off against executives in a business transformed and torn by technology, from the seismic shift to streaming in recent years to the potentially paradigm-shifting emergence of AI in the years to come.
Screenwriters had traditionally gone on strike more than any other segment of the industry, but had enjoyed a relatively long stretch of labour peace until spring negotiations for a new contract fell apart. The walkout was their first since 2007 and their longest since 1988.
It was the first time the actors and writers had been on strike together since 1960. In that walkout, the writers strike started first and ended second. This time, studios opted to deal with the writers first.
The AMPTP first reached out to suggest renewing negotiations in August. The meetings were short, infrequent, and not productive, and talks went silent for another month.

title: Russell Brand speaks for first time amid sexual assault claims — and his choice of platform is revealing
content:
Not for the first time this year, Russell Brand is yelling.
In this case, it's about UFOs, and his sermon is almost over.
Eyes fixed on the camera, trademark messy mop tumbling past his shoulders, the 48-year-old exclaims: "But that's just what I think!"
"Let me know what you think in the comments below, share your material with us, it really helps us."
Welcome to Brand's YouTube channel, where clicks equal coin.
The internet already has plenty to offer people chasing conspiracy theories and wellness advice.
But in the years leading up to allegations of sexual assault made against him last weekend, Brand has carved out a space somewhere between the two, and his audience is growing.
When he decided to respond on Saturday to claims of sexual assault and emotional abuse made by four women, he chose to post a three-minute video online.
He described the past week as “extraordinary and distressing" and thanked his followers for "questioning the information you are being presented with".
He also suggested, without evidence, that the UK government, tech companies and mainstream media outlets may be colluding to silence him.
His video was posted on X, formerly known as Twitter, and Rumble, a video site popular among conservative commentators and conspiracy theorists.
Notably, Brand did not post the video to YouTube, which blocked him this week from making money off the videos he posts there.
Brand's metamorphosis from mainstream Hollywood star to online conspiracy theorist has been years in the making.
Russell Brand leaves the Wembley Park Theatre in London last Saturday. (Reuters: Susannah Ireland)
The Hollywood flicks and presenting gigs on which he built his fame are long gone. Now it's about likes, comments, shares and subscriptions.
"He's very sophisticated," says Karen North, a professor of digital social media at the University of Southern California.
"In the request [for you to comment], that's him demonstrating that he understands what's going to get him not only more money, but also what's going to get the algorithm to favour him."
In a video from two months ago questioning why the US government was sending cluster bombs to Ukraine, Brand breaks into his rant after seven minutes to start selling something.
He points out questions like "is AI going to destroy all mankind?" and "are we powerless to choose peace in the face of military industrial complex objectives?" can be exhausting.
"But thanks to Genucel Skincare, you can still look, and feel amazing," Brand says, gesturing to a collection of lotions on the table in front of him.
It's the sort of plug he'll still be paid for, even after YouTube announced this week it had blocked Brand making money from the ads it places in his videos.
Brand has over 6.6 million subscribers on that platform.
Over on TikTok he's got 2.3 million followers. On X (or Twitter) it's 11.3 million. Instagram? 3.8 million.
A video he uploaded to Rumble last Friday on health secrets that changed his life has been viewed 330,000 times.
Another he posted later that day, denying claims of rape and sexual assault about to be made against him, got almost 500,000 views.
Russell Brand performs his Messiah Complex show in London in 2014. (Reuters: Olivia Harris)
Brand's social media accounts fell silent after descriptions of his allegedly predatory behaviour were published in British media.
The accusations date from a period when Brand was known for his stand-up and acting, appearing in mainstream movies, and working as a presenter for the BBC and Channel 4.
"Yeah, we all knew," comedian and political activist Kate Smurthwaite told her YouTube followers this week, in reference to the allegations.
"In fact, if you are somebody who worked in comedy and you didn't know about it, then you're evidently someone people didn't feel very comfortable discussing these kinds of things around."
Smurthwaite, a veteran of two decades on stage, said journalists had "contacted every woman I know in comedy" to ask about men in the industry.
"One thing women in any industry do when they get together is talk about which guys should you avoid, and which guys you have had problems with," she told the ABC this week.
"And, you know, there are various names that come up regularly and his is absolutely one of them."
Kate Smurthwaite says there's a strong community of women in comedy. (Supplied: Jon Cartwright)
The story was years in the making. One of Brand's accusers described his alleged behaviour as "an open secret" in the industry.
In a video uploaded last Friday, Brand said he had been "aware of news media making phone calls, sending letters to people I know for ages and ages".
He questioned whether the "co-ordinated media attacks" meant there was "another agenda at play".
"I'm aware that you guys have been saying in the comments for a while: 'Watch out, Russell, they're coming for you, you're getting too close to the truth …"
By building his brand around distrust in mainstream media and institutional authority, Brand has created a loyal audience that can be reliably expected to question the allegations against him.
Brand has cultivated his following across multiple platforms over years, and now has a seemingly bomb-proof suite of outlets in which to publish.
After YouTube decided to stop Brand making money from its advertising, Dame Caroline Dinenage, chair of the UK's media committee, asked Rumble to do the same.
It said no.
"You don't put all your eggs in one basket in this business," says Dan Jackson, a professor of media and communication at Bournemouth University.
"While YouTube is where I expect he was best able to monetise his content, it's not the only platform he's on.
"If one platform cancels you, then you have other ways for people to reach your content."
They're allegations even the most beloved of Hollywood A-Listers would struggle to explain away, but Russell Brand and his millions of online followers exist in a different dimension, far away from cancel culture.
While Brand had been posting on social media for a long time, his audience skyrocketed when he began broadcasting conspiracy theories in 2021.
A video titled "The Power Of Comedy!" from three years ago has had 42,000 views on YouTube.
Meanwhile, one from 2022 called "Bill Gate's INCREDIBLY AWKWARD Interview — Is He Hiding Something??" has been watched 2.2 million times.
"If you want to stand out on platforms like YouTube, you have to be controversial and it helps to be anti-establishment," Professor Jackson says.
"I think that's where he's at, and it is rewarded in the algorithms. You're not going to stand out if you're just mainstream because you compete with established news brands.
"He's a good example of that ecosystem."
While video views are important, advertisers are increasingly prioritising subscribers — the people who are committed and regular visitors of your content.
"Advertisers don't care if you did something outrageous and millions of people clicked once," Professor North says.
"They want to know who are the people who are going to come back tomorrow."
It's something Brand is trying to do.
"Turn on the notification bell and subscribe right now," he insists at the start of a video from two months ago.
"We need you on this voyage so that you watch our daily content, lest the algorithm direct you elsewhere."
After that, arms flailing and adorned in costume jewellery, he begins another rant.

title: Sophie Turner sues Joe Jonas over refusal to hand over children's passports
content:
Actor Sophie Turner is suing her estranged pop star husband Joe Jonas to force him to turn over the passports of their two young daughters so she can take them to England.
Best known for playing Sansa Stark on HBO's Game of Thrones, Turner said in her petition that the couple had planned to raise their daughters in her native country.
It also said the girls "are both fully involved and integrated in all aspects of daily and cultural life in England".
The couple had a daughter, Willa, in 2020 and last year had another daughter whose name they have not made public.
Amid their high-profile divorce, they are now locked in a legal battle over where the children will live.
Jonas, 34, filed for divorce in a Florida court on September 1 but according to Turner, 27, she only learned about the divorce through the media five days later.
Jonas has disputed this saying he did not surprise Turner with divorce papers but rather filed for divorce after what he said were "multiple conversations with Sophie".
Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner met in 2016 and married in 2019. (Reuters: Danny Moloshok)
Turner said that she and Jonas made a mutual decision to raise their daughters in England and to relocate there in April of this year.
During August and September, while Jonas began a tour with his band the Jonas Brothers in the US, Turner was due to be working long hours filming a television series in England.
So, Turner said, she and Jonas had agreed the children would travel with Jonas and a nanny.
The plan was for Turner to travel to New York after filming wrapped on September 14 to collect the children, but in the meantime "the breakdown of the parties' marriage happened very suddenly," Turner said.
Turner says she and Jonas saw each other on September 17 — and she asked him for the children's passports so she could take them back to England.
But Jonas refused to turn over the girls' passports, who were born in the US, and have dual US-British citizenship.
Turner then filed her petition in federal court in New York under the child abduction clauses of the Hague Convention — an international treaty aimed at compelling the return of a child taken from their country of "habitual residence."
Jonas filed for divorce after four years of marriage to Turner citing: "the marriage between the parties is irretrievably broken."
The pair then issued a joint statement on their Instagram accounts saying:
"After four wonderful years of marriage we have mutually decided to amicably end our marriage.
"There are many speculative narratives as to why but, truly this is a united decision and we sincerely hope that everyone can respect our wishes for privacy for us and our children."
The court filing says the girls are temporarily living with Turner in a Manhattan hotel.
Jonas and Turner had a prenuptial agreement that Jonas expects will be enforced, according to the filing.
Jonas's representative alleged giving the children's passports to Turner would breach a Florida court order restricting both parents from relocating the children.
Jonas said in a statement that he is "seeking shared parenting with the kids so that they are raised by both their mother and father" and that he is "okay with the kids being raised both in the US and the UK".
"This is an unfortunate legal disagreement about a marriage that is sadly ending," he added.
"When language like 'abduction' is used, it is misleading at best, and a serious abuse of the legal system at worst."
AP/Reuters

title: Euphoria actor Angus Cloud died of accidental overdose, coroner says
content:
Actor Angus Cloud died of an accidental overdose from a lethal combination of drugs, a northern California coroner’s office has ruled.
Cloud, who starred in Euphoria, died at his parent's home in Oakland, California, in July. He was aged 25.
His cause of death was "acute intoxication" due to the "combined effects of methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and benzodiazepines", the Alameda county coroner’s bureau said.
At the time of his death, his family said the young actor had been struggling with the grief of losing his father.
"The only comfort we have is knowing Angus is now reunited with his dad, who was his best friend," they said in a statement.
"Angus was open about his battle with mental health and we hope that his passing can be a reminder to others that they are not alone and should not fight this on their own in silence.
"We hope the world remembers him for his humour, laughter and love for everyone."
Angus Cloud died at his family home in Oakland, California. (AP: Evan Agostini/Invision)
Cloud was acclaimed for his role as drug dealer Fezco 'Fez' O'Neill in the award-winning HBO show Euphoria.
He was scouted for the show while walking through Manhattan, in a move he originally suspected was a scam, he told the Wall Street Journal in 2019.
Cloud then met with casting director Jennifer Venditti and series creator Sam Levinson, who eventually made him a co-star in the series alongside Zendaya for its first two seasons.
Cloud often pushed back against the notion he was identical to his Euphoria character.
"It does bother me when people are like, 'It must be so easy! You get to go in and be yourself.' I'm like, 'Why don't you go and do that?' It's not that simple," Cloud told Variety.
He was most recently cast in the horror film Scream 6.
Many of Cloud's Hollywood peers expressed their sadness over his death.
Euphoria co-star Zendaya wrote on Instagram: "I’m so grateful I got the chance to know him in this life, to call him a brother, to see his warm kind eyes and bright smile, or hear his infectious cackle of a laugh."
Euphoria network producer HBO posted on Instagram and X, stating they were "incredibly saddened" to learn the news.
While Drake, who is an executive producer of the series, remembered Cloud as a "good soul".
AP/ABC

title: PAW Patrol vs Teenage Kraken: Which is a more bearable school holidays flick for adults?
content:
You might not get much of a choice when it comes to which movie you watch this school holidays.
If you're taking along a niece, nephew, or child of your own, you may have to be a team player and choose a flick suitable for their age group (snore). Or, they may be so completely obsessed with PAW Patrol that not a single alternate thought can enter their tiny little brains.
But if you do get a vote — or are just going to see a kids movie by yourself (same) — we did the hard work of watching the two big offerings for the September hols to find out which is the best for grown ups.
Age range: Preschool and kindy littlies.
PAW Patrol: The Mighty Movie | Official Trailer (2023 Movie)
Hate to break it to you, but this children's movie is indeed a movie for children.
I went into this film a PAW Patrol virgin, and boy did I leave feeling cultured by the phenomenon that is "Chase on the case".
If you're also new to the franchise, it's summed up pretty early on in the film by a news reporter: "They're cute little puppies who drive around in cars! I know that sounds weird but just go with it."
Except, in this movie, our dogs have powers! It's a kind of Tron meets Avengers, but with a soundtrack that includes Olivia Rodrigo and Charli XCX (slay).
Whatever you do, do NOT call PAW Patrol's Victoria Vance a mad scientist.  (Supplied: Paramount Pictures)
The film includes a villain whose origin story is that everyone calls her a "mad scientist", which she hates, so I like to think that'll become the newest insult in the playground now.
I'm also obsessed with Mr Monopoly/chief corrupt capitalist Mayor Humdinger — a very cheeky guy!
Growing up a Ninja Turtles kid, taking my son to see Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem turned out to be a nerve-racking experience.
Most of this movie's jokes weren't particularly funny, and the plot was too predictable to be exciting.
Even a four-year-old in my cinema loudly proclaimed that the climax would easily be resolved, "because the PAW patrol always saves the day". I guess you could say the same for most Marvel movies though.
As a film, PAW Patrol isn't much fun if you have more brainpower than a toddler.
But the kids in my cinema screamed "again! again! again!" as soon as the credits rolled, and were pretty obsessed throughout. So, if you're trying to impress a cute little mega-fan, this will still be more than worth your time.
Age range: Primary school kiddies (both early to late primary).
RUBY GILLMAN, TEENAGE KRAKEN | Official Trailer
Ruby Gillman, Teenage Kraken is also a little predictable for adults, but makes up for it in every other department.
This DreamWorks Animation follows Ruby: your classic awkward teen who's at war with a mum who just doesn't get her.
Ruby's really good at maths, and is planning to ask her crush to the prom with an advanced quadratic equation, the answer to which will display 'PROM?' on the calculator (instead of the 80085 most of our calculators suffered through in high school).
Oh, and Ruby's also secretly a giant kraken.
Sure, Ruby and her family are blue, but no one's realised they're kraken's yet — they just say they're from Canada.
While she may be blue, Ruby Gillman is definitely a normal teenager, not a kraken in disguise. (Supplied: DreamWorks Animation)
But after an unfortunate mishap over said prom-posal, involving a commercial grade confetti canon, Ruby finds it increasingly difficult to keep her true identity under wraps.
Before long, she gets drawn into the underwater world of her kin, where she learns of her legendary royal lineage, and her family's war with the evil mermaids (a nice subversion of the classic girl-to-mermaid trope).
This movie is at once funny, silly and exciting, and you can't help rooting for Ruby as the suspense builds.
It's refreshingly modern, with jokes that are entertaining for adults too — I enjoyed grandma kraken's mention that she goes to therapy now: "I see a wise hammerhead shark on Wednesdays and I let my rage go." There is also a (subtle) queer character and detailed, imaginative animation.
The Beanie Bubble is the latest in what looks to be an endless line of products-based movies. Are they all just cynical ploys to sell merch?
I do wonder why Ruby's mum, a giant kraken, would choose to live on land as a "real estate warrior" though. But perhaps all real estate agents are secretly deep sea monsters.
I imagine this film would be enjoyable for children too, but who really cares what they think? (I joke, I joke).
If you haven't already caught them yet, you can check out older releases like Disney's Haunted Mansion or the new Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, which both look to be aimed at slightly older kids.
Or put yourself first and drag your kid along to My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3, which is only rated PG. Start 'em on the classics young I say!

title: 'Positive sign': Hollywood writers talk with studios in hopes of ending strike
content:
Hollywood writers and producers have reignited talks, with hope from some sources close to the two parties that an imminent end to the writers strike is possible.
The Writers Guild of America (WGA) met with studios on Wednesday and hoped to finalise a deal as soon as Thursday, CNBC reported, quoting insider sources.
The WGA and the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP), which represents Walt Disney, Netflix and other media companies, held talks for the first time in about a month.
"The WGA and AMPTP met for bargaining today and will meet again tomorrow," the two sides said in a joint statement following the meeting.
The meeting was attended by Disney CEO Bob Iger and Netflix Co-CEO Ted Sarandos, among others, according to a source close to the negotiations.
This is the first time the two parties have released a joint statement in this strike cycle, according to The Hollywood Reporter.
"If they're putting out a joint statement, I'm taking that as a positive sign," a studio source told the news outlet.
"Given what's transpired, this feels different from before."
People in the room described the session as "encouraging," the CNBC source said, and the executives are expected to return to the talks on Thursday.
The writers strike could continue until the end of the year if a deal is not made.  (Supplied: David Koutsouridis)
CNBC noted if a deal is not reached, the strike could last through to the end of 2023.
The WGA went on strike in May after negotiations reached an impasse over issues such as  compensation and the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in Hollywood.
The SAG-AFTRA actors union joined the WGA on strike in July.
No talks are currently scheduled between the actors and the studios.
