title: 'Handsome Italians in chunky knitwear': This award-winning, wistful film oozes rustic chic
content:
There are sad films that are a bit like sad songs. They're distillations of melancholy and grief, where a sense of mournfulness hangs in the air from the beginning.
They're also a joy; like singing in the shower about a broken heart can be a joy. And The Eight Mountains — a sad movie about friendship that won the Jury Prize at Cannes — is a bit like that.
It's a bittersweet drama centring on two men who meet as children in the mountainous wilderness of north-west Italy.
It's about the innocence of youth giving way to the disappointments of adulthood, about the impact of overbearing fathers, about the struggle to find your own place in the world. Their friendship proves to be a refuge they both need.
The film is based on the award-winning 2016 novel by Paolo Cognetti, who also stars in the film. (Supplied: Palace)
I haven't read the book on which this film is based, written by Paolo Cognetti, but the fact it was translated into more than 30 languages speaks to its wide appeal.
It also explains why the screen adaptation isn't, strictly speaking, an Italian film, but an international co-production between France, Italy and Belgium, written and directed by Belgian couple Felix van Groeningen (Beautiful Boy) and Charlotte Vandermeersch, with a wistful country music score by Swedish musician Daniel Norgren.
The main location, however, is still very Italian — a mountain village near the French border, surrounded by densely forested slopes, turquoise lakes and rocky peaks.
Beautiful Boy, adapted from a father and son's memoirs, is less interested in the mysteries of middle class addiction and more interested in the parental nightmare.
In the lead roles, Luca Marinelli (Martin Eden) and Alessandro Borghi (Suburra) bring a deft touch to the material, holding the film back from sliding into egregious self-pity.
Both actors underplay their inner turmoil, and the filmmakers do well to weave moments of levity, grace and joy into the narrative.
The story is told from the perspective of Pietro, with an intermittent, ruminative voice over.
We first meet him as a middle-class city kid in the 1980s, arriving in the fictional village of Grana with his parents for the summer holidays.
He meets Bruno, the son of local labourers, and the two become fast friends.
“Pietro has an urge to communicate, but Bruno has a closedness that pushes away,” van Groeningen told Slant. (Supplied: Palace)
Bruno teaches him words in the local dialect, shows him how to milk cows and takes him roaming around the mountains, while Pietro recounts his life in the city where his father works as an engineer in a large factory.
These joyful encounters are soon over, however, as the film skips forward through Pietro's rebellious teenage years, and a heart-wrenching argument with his father (a superb Filippo Timi) that foreshadows their future estrangement.
Then the film lands in adulthood, after Pietro's father has died.
Pietro (Marinelli) is a struggling writer moonlighting as a cook, while Bruno, who has also become estranged from his father, is trying to live off the land.
Together they begin restoring a dilapidated stone cottage that belonged to Pietro's father, reigniting their friendship in the process.
The Screen Show brings you reviews and in-depth conversations with leading film and TV directors, actors and screenwriters.
You can see how it must have leapt off the page — two handsome Italians in chunky knitwear, a house renovation and a location that oozes rustic chic. Add to this a subplot where Pietro goes trekking for extended periods in Nepal and you have an influencer's Instagram feed.
But the film has a lot more going for it.
Van Groeningen showed skill at staging high drama in dirt-under-the-fingernails locations in his breakout 2012 tragedy about a couple of country music performers who lose a child, The Broken Circle Breakdown.
Here, the telling is not as melodramatic but it's equally powerful.
As the film progresses, a desperation creeps in to the lives of both men, born of a sense of confusion and a lack of confidence.
Cognetti’s novel won the 2017 Premio Strega, Italy′s most prestigious literary award. (Supplied: Palace)
Van Groeningen and Vandermeersch shoot in a squarish Academy ratio frame, and often look downwards into the valleys, using zoom lenses that creep almost imperceptibly forwards, or longer lenses that crush the background and foreground together. The overall effect is as claustrophobic as it is dramatic, apt for a film about two men struggling to find breathing space amidst the suffocating pressures of life.
There's perhaps a broader statement here about masculinity in crisis — in particular the generation of men who grew up in the late 20th century and came of age in the 21st — but the film leaves you to make up your own mind.
The truth is, unlike their fathers, Pietro and Bruno were born into a world where many of the old certainties could no longer guide them.

The film's central location — a village in decline — is integral to this idea.
Bruno's attempt to live like his ancestors belies the fact that most of the other young people have left the village, and the old farmers have died.
It underpins the tragedy at the heart of The Eight Mountains: that the world has changed, and for those who are unable — or unwilling — to adapt, there is a price to pay. It's a simple but profound story told with rare eloquence.

title: Nostalgia, ninja and No Diggity: Taking my son to go see Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles
content:
When I took my young son to see Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem, we turned up early to the already early 10:30am session.
The cinema was smattered with young kids and other parents who also design their weekends around maximising the number of hours in a day.
My son wore a plastic turtle half shell on his back and a blue bandana over his eyes (Leonardo inspiring the leaders of tomorrow). I managed to talk him out of bringing his ninja sword, but he won the argument over the throwing disc.
Will he be won over by the heroes in a half shell? (ABC Everyday: By Christian Harimanow)
We sat down on our oversized comfy seats, popcorn and token healthy snacks at hand. The new Paw Patrol movie trailer came on and he got excited.
This was only his third ever trip to the cinema.
Growing up, there were two TV shows I loved above all others: The Transformers and the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.
I watched the shows, had the toys (not enough of them, I say), collected the trading cards (had the full set) and read the comics (but preferred the cartoons).
In the latter half of the 2000s, Michael Bay took it upon himself to revive both these franchises with big-budget, live-action adaptations — but somehow made them both darker and blander at the same time.
But Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem promised to be a departure. It would bring back the colour and the fun. It would emphasise the "Teenage" in the title. And it would be a cartoon once more.
There is a simple version of this story where I take my son to see the movie and we both love it so much and we have a great time bonding over the Turtles. We'll recall our favourite parts for the next few days and he will become a Turtles fan for life. The end.
But I couldn't completely give myself to this movie-going experience. I wanted to like the film so badly and I really wanted my son to like it, too.
I kept looking to check if he was enjoying himself. And every time I laughed I would question it: was that bit actually funny or was I just laughing loudly to convey to him (and perhaps to myself) that I was really having fun?
Picture a young lanky boy, standing mouth agape in front of a large format poster on a comic book store window.
It depicts New York City at night, with skyscrapers towering over a half-open sewer manhole cover. And peeking from underneath are four green faces, each wearing a different coloured bandana over their face. Orange. Blue. Purple. Red. On the top of the poster are four words, in big capital letters: TEENAGE MUTANT NINJA TURTLES.
My world changed when I saw this.  (New Line Cinema)
These were pre-internet days when we found out about new movies from comic-book-store windows. And the idea that we were getting a live action Ninja Turtles movie was mind-blowing to kid me.
The original Turtles movie was great. Ignore the reviews. It's kinda my favourite movie, and I only say "kinda" for fear of public judgement. I still rewatch it every few years and it never disappoints.
Look, there are some things that haven't aged well.
If you watch it for the first time today, for instance, the first thing you might notice is the lips. The Turtles — played by sweaty people in animatronic rubber costumes — were the creation of the late, great puppeteer, Jim Henson. They look believable for their time, but to a generation used to seeing CGI, their lip movements leave a lot to be desired.
It's also cheesy in the way everyone thought all comic book/cartoon adaptations needed to be cheesy in that era, and there's some casual racism and gender stereotyping.
On the other hand, the fighting choreography is an entertaining mix of martial arts and slapstick comedy popularised by Jackie Chan and Hong Kong cinema of that era.
And for a movie built around puppets, it's got a strong emotional core and the chemistry between the turtles feels more real than many CGI films can manage today.
Then there's the theme song.
Turtle Power by Partners in Kryme (KRYME stands for Keep Rhythm Your Motivating Element, of course) is a supercharged motivational anthem in the tradition of other movie-based motivational anthems, such as Rocky's Eye of the Tiger and 8 Mile's Lose Yourself.
Take a listen for yourself.
Turtle Power song
On the way out of the cinema, another kid points out my son's turtle shell to his dad. He's wearing a Turtles T-shirt. The two kids acknowledge each other and exchange meek waves and hellos. Us dads acknowledge each other, too.
Here we go! (ABC Everyday: By Christian Harimanow)
Overall, it was a good movie, but it did feel a little too deliberate to me — like they designed the film in a lab to please young kids and the people around the age group of their parents who grew up on the original cartoons.
But it was fun, funny, a little gnarly and had real heart: everything I could ask for in a Turtles adventure.
Writer Seth Rogen pays homage to his 90s childhood in a fast and funny animated film packed with pop culture references.
I loved the chemistry between these four turtles who acted like actual kids (for once). And the fight sequence played to No Diggity was a real moment. My son didn't get the significance of that song, so I tried to explain in the cinema how important that Blackstreet song was in the late 90s, but I didn't get anywhere.
My son also enjoyed the movie. He said he liked the bit where the turtles met the bad guys for the first time because it was funny, but he didn't like the scary bit at the end (spoilers). From the three movies he's seen at the cinema, he rates it below Super Mario Bros, but ahead of Disney's Elemental.
He also then said that he's looking forward to seeing the new PAW Patrol movie. Of course he is. PAW Patrol is to him what Ninja Turtles were to me.
You might think I'd be disappointed afterwards, considering how much I hyped up the movie going into it. But we both had a great morning seeing a fun movie. And it just made me want to rewatch the original again.
Right now, my son is a PAW Patrol kid and that's OK, too. Besides, I already got him onto Transformers. You should see how many bots he's got.

title: The US screen industry is facing an existential crisis. Is Australia next?
content:
While the Australian screenwriters of the original Heartbreak High continue to earn money from the beloved 90s series, the writers of the reboot — which was a global hit for Netflix — probably won't see another cent from their work on the first season.
While Netflix made more than $1 billion from Australians in 2022, the Australian Writers Guild (AWG) says its writers are unlikely to ever receive royalties or residuals (the fees paid when episodes of their shows are rebroadcast or made available to watch on other platforms).
Residuals are either fickle or non-existent in the streaming age, when shows are available on-demand globally and streamers keep their viewing numbers close to their chests. Instead, writers and actors earn their wages up-front.
For more pop culture coverage.
The streamers argue that they pay more up-front and take risks on shows that previously had no chance of being commissioned; however, this model means actors and writers aren't profiting when their streaming shows become hits.
For example, Kimiko Glenn, a cast member of Orange Is The New Black — an early success for the nascent Netflix and hailed as a win for representation — made only US$27.30 in royalties last year.
And even though the hit 2021 series Squid Game increased the value of Netflix by US$900 million, the show's South Korean writer and director Hwang Dong-hyuk earns no residuals, having signed over his intellectual property (IP) rights to the streaming giant.
Squid Game was Netflix's most-watched series ever. (Netflix series Squid Game (Noh Juhan/Netflix))
Residuals are one of the reasons US writers have now been on strike for nearly 140 days and actors have been on strike since mid-July.
Production has halted on Abbott Elementary, Euphoria and Emily in Paris, among a slew of other Hollywood shows, and the 2023 Emmy Awards ceremony has been postponed to 2024.
While Australian writers and actors on US productions are taking part in the strike (and US productions in Australia have been cancelled), our local industry is also being shaped and shaken up by international streamers.
Australian screen professionals say that much of what their US counterparts are fighting for are issues here, too.
And, in some cases, our local industry has actually provided a blueprint for the troubled US industry.
Anchuli Felicia King is a Thai Australian playwright (White Pearl; The Poison of Polygamy) and screenwriter. She's worked on screen projects in Australia (The Twelve; Deadloch), Britain (The Baby) and the US (HBO's upcoming adaptation of Viet Thanh Nguyen's The Sympathizer).
Deadloch is an Australian Amazon Prime series. (Supplied: Prime Video)
"The only way that I can cobble together a living is by working back-to-back, sometimes simultaneous, jobs in three different countries," King told ABC RN's Stop Everything!
The strike was called on May 2 by the Writers Guild of America (WGA), which represents 11,500 screenwriters, after it was unable to reach an agreement with the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP). At the time, King was part of a writer's room in New York working on a new series idea; when that was cut short, she returned to Australia.
"There was a sense, even when they internally authorised the strike within the guild, that this one was going to be a long one. The last strike [in 2007-8] lasted 100 days, and we're in a really different landscape now with streamers," King reflects.
"The blanket reason that we're striking is to make sure that writing for screen remains sustainable as a career."
King says: “It's worth noting: It's not just screenwriters, it's our assistants, people who work in the rooms with us who are non-WGA members who don't want to become scabs, they can't work either.” (ABC Arts: Teresa Tan)
Writers' demands include increases to minimum wages and streaming residuals, the introduction of mandatory staffing numbers and minimum duration of employment, and stronger contributions to retirement and health care funds.
"We're not asking for a crazy amount of money: We're asking for 2 per cent of the streamers' global profits," says King.
An Australian actor who works regularly in Hollywood and Australia — and is one of the 160,000 striking members of SAG-AFTRA (Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists) spoke to ABC Arts for this story but asked to remain anonymous, fearing studio "backlash".
"The vast majority of actors are [used to] gigging; they are living pay cheque to pay cheque, they are working second and third jobs to make it through — and not complaining about it, either," they say.
"But streaming is really starting to eat into people's livelihoods."
They say while some actors in the US used to be able to live off royalties during audition periods or between jobs, streaming has put an end to that.
Claire Pullen, the executive director of the AWG, says that the majority of the guild's members have to work other jobs while pursuing screenwriting.
"A lot of the things that the WGA is striking for look like a dream [to Australian screenwriters]. Our industry is much smaller … We have always had a gig economy," she told ABC Arts.
King echoes Pullen: "A lot of the things that the WGA are fighting to protect in the States, we don't even have in the UK and Australia."
Meredith Stiehm (left), president of Writers Guild of America West, and Fran Drescher, president of SAG-AFTRA, take part in a rally by striking writers outside Paramount Pictures studio in Los Angeles on May 8, 2023.  (AP: Chris Pizzello)
Before the age of streaming, US TV series had longer runs (10 or more episodes) and large writers' rooms; now, it's common to have "mini-rooms" with fewer writers who work on shorter seasons of shows.
In Australia's smaller industry, "mini-rooms" have long been the norm. In fact, screenwriter Blake Ayshford (Mystery Road: Origin) says we've already devolved to "micro-rooms" and that we no longer have staff writers who do sustained work on a show, thereby developing their careers (and paying their bills).
King says she's previously been called in to do only three days of work on a show in Australia.
"You're playing this insane game of [broken] telephone after that … where you're redrafting [scripts] over email. It's frenzied. It's chaotic … It's a very frenetic system in Australia and it's something that the WGA is fighting to stop happening in America," says King.
"For a lot of my colleagues, particularly emerging writers of colour who are just entering the industry, it's hard for them to climb the ladder because they end up doing so much unpaid work [just to sell a show to streamers], or they staff on one job and then spend six months of the year not getting staffed on another one.
"Even when they do get staffed, it's hard for them to ascend to the next position."
Previously, writers would stay with the production and gain on-set training, with a view to one day becoming showrunners (the screenwriter who has creative control over a series). But in Australia — and, increasingly, in the US — writers hired for short stints in mini-rooms aren't given that opportunity.
Australia's screen industry is smaller in scale, making it hard for screenwriters and actors to earn a living exclusively through their craft (Mystery Road pictured here). (ABC TV)
Over the last three years, King has worked on five shows for some of the biggest international streamers (including Prime and Max); the first time she saw one of her episodes shot was in Los Angeles this year, on her own dime.
"That's a big problem for training the next generation of showrunners … We [need to] put some protections in place to make sure that the diverse stories that we all want to see on our screens are being told by people with those lived experiences."
Pullen adds: "If the rooms are smaller, and there's fewer of them, the commercial decision is going to be: What is a safe bet? … When there's such focus on what might guarantee a commercial return, it doesn't incentivise creative risk-taking."
While screenwriters in Australia don't need to fight for healthcare and retirement funds like their US counterparts do, the question of residuals is globally relevant.
"Our media landscape is rapidly changing in Australia. At some point there will be a reckoning about how little our work is compensated, versus how much the streamers are profiting off our work," says King.
Pullen says the AWG is invested in what happens with residuals in the US negotiations.
"In Australia, you do not get any chance at royalties and residuals with the streamers. Broadcast TV is better, but they're a shrinking part of the market," she explains.
Pullen is a fan of local content quotas for streaming services, which the government says will come into effect from mid-2024, thanks to their national cultural policy; the next step is ensuring that the profits from that Australian work is shared by Australian writers.
The AWG and the Media Entertainment Alliance Australia (MEAA) are in conversation with the federal government about IP rights, which affect creators' share of any potential profits from their work.
"Our ask is that to meet the quota, to be counted as Australian content, the Intellectual Property belongs to an Australian [rather than the streaming company]," says Pullen.
"A small number of creatives have smash-hit successes that make them wealthy, but the majority of writers working in Australia are not in that category; they are people doing normal [non-writing] jobs, trying to pay mortgages or rent, [and] feed their families."
The anonymous Australian actor says that, typically, local actors haven't been able to make a living off residuals from Australian productions.
"What is happening in America [with streaming residuals] could really positively affect what happens here in Australia, too."
The AWG has advised members against taking up jobs from American producers, which would be seen as crossing the picket line and would result in those writers being barred from joining the WGA in the future. (AP: Marcio Jose Sanchez)
Erin Madely, the chief executive of the MEAA, which represents actors, told ABC Arts: "What the SAG-AFTRA performers and [WGA] writers are fighting for in the US sets a new precedent.
"Any gains that happen there [we'd be hoping to replicate here], and while our performers here have our own agreements, we absolutely stand in support of their pursuit of updating the business model."
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is developing at an unanticipated pace and is a contentious issue in both the actors' and writers' strikes.
Screenwriters are concerned that studios will use AI to generate scripts. King says: "We feel very strongly that this might be our last opportunity to put some of this clear contractual writing in place … [to ensure] that writing remains a human endeavour."
Pullen says: "Every worker in Australia should be concerned about AI … [but] my concern is that studios, producers and the streamers will see it as a cheap way to make fast content."
While she says there are interesting works being made with AI — for example, a recent episode of South Park was co-written by ChatGPT — she is concerned about copyright and consent.
"If you are training a generative AI [such as ChatGPT], [in other words] a large language model, on material that someone else has produced — then you're stealing their copyright."
"[AI] by its nature is derivative. You put someone else's work in and it spits out an amalgam of that work. There is no new idea coming from that. It can't by definition generate new ideas," says Pullen. (Reuters: Aude Guerrucci)
American studios are reportedly proposing that background actors (aka extras) have their likeness digitally captured and then be used in perpetuity, for one day's pay.
"[That behaviour] is a real sign of where they [studios] stand," says the Australian actor, while conceding, "I haven't seen Australian producers arguing for the same things that they have been doing in America [in terms of AI]."
While US productions are on hold here and elsewhere — with knock-on effects for crew members too — Australian productions are unaffected.
But, Madely says, "We'd love for this [strike] to be resolved quickly, because when the US jobs do come here, it's a really important part of our industry [in terms of] employment of our crews [and] the creative development of our people.
"In the meantime, Australian stories should continue to be made, continue to be told, and we hope that our members, during this time, go back to our industry and tell our stories."
Both King and the anonymous Australian actor are determined, and so are their unions.
"We have to make a stand now because we're at a real, historical, existential crisis point for our industry," says the actor.
"Whatever happens now is going to set the tone for decades to come.

Celebrate with us and enjoy all the special arts-focused programming for the week across our stations.
Arts Week is on 18 – 24 September.

title: Australian film star to take lead role in stage production of bestselling novel
content:
Australian film star Tilda Cobham-Hervey is set to end a seven-year break from the stage, confident her role in an adaption of an international bestselling novel will wow audiences.
She was headhunted for the lead role in The Dictionary Of Lost Words, which will premiere in Adelaide, before moving to the Sydney Opera House in late October.
Performing live on stage every night is a challenge that has beaten the best of many actors, but the 29-year-old said she was ready for the challenge.
"I haven't done stage for seven years so I'm quite intrigued myself as to how that's going to go," she said.
With her parents working in the industry, Cobham-Hervey grew up by the stage, before being discovered in the 2013 coming-of-age film 52 Tuesdays.
She performed in the acclaimed movie Hotel Mumbai alongside now real-life partner Dev Patel, and the biopic of feminist icon Helen Reddy in I Am Woman.
Splitting her time between Australia and overseas, she is revelling in returning to the stage in her home town.
"It is so different, I mean at the end of the day you're still just trying to find the truth of the moment and be in it with the other people around you," she said.
"The main big difference is you get to rehearse and it's so amazing."
The Dictionary Of Lost Words was the debut novel for Adelaide Hills-based author Pip Williams.
The Dictionary Of Lost Words was written by Australian author Pip Williams. (ABC News: Che Chorley)
It has now sold more than 500,000 copies, was a New York Times bestseller and was the first from Australia to be selected for actor and producer Reece Witherspoon's popular book club.
The story centres around the creation of the first Oxford Dictionary and the role of a young woman to preserve "women's words" that were neglected by the male lexicographers creating it.
Williams was not initially sure the book would work.
"My greatest fear was writing a novel about that idea and writing it badly which is partly why I didn't tell many people really what I was doing, not even my publisher knew," she admitted.
Now the whole world knows, and the success came despite being launched two days after Australia went into COVID lockdown in 2020.
It was not just book lovers who fell in love, but key figures at South Australia's leading theatre company.
"When [artistic director] Mitchell Butel from the State Theatre rang I was just beside myself," she said.
"He said can we have a chat over a coffee about adapting the book to stage, [and I thought] 'oh sure yeah'."
More than 500,000 copies of The Dictionary Of Lost Words have been sold. (ABC News: Che Chorley)
But finding the right person to play the lead role of Esme would be critical and that is where Tilda Cobham-Hervey came in.
"When I saw Tilda I was struck by just, there's just something about the way she holds her body, the way she moves her head that was familiar to me."
Already the show is nearing a sellout in Adelaide and also proving popular for its Sydney Opera House season.
Rising star Tilda Cobham-Hervey says she'll always be drawn back to Adelaide, as her burgeoning career takes her around the world.
Cobham-Hervey knows there will be plenty of lovers of the book in the audience with high expectations.
But with intense rehearsals nearing an end, both Williams and Cobham-Hervey believe Verity Laughton's adaption will succeed.
"I feel so confident about the adaptation that I don't feel nervous about it and so confident about all of the actors who have been case and Jessica Arthur the director," Williams said.
Cobham-Hervey is revelling in yet again playing a strong female role, after the success of the Helen Reddy movie.
She is confident the entertainment sector has come a long way, as has society, in its treatment of women.
"A lot has changed recently, I think things like the Me Too movement is still doing amazing things and have pushed a whole lot more conversation, even when you see it in just women having all different kinds of jobs," she said.
Tilda Cobham-Hervey says she can't wait to play the strong female role. (ABC News: Che Chorley)
"There's a lot more female directors, you're seeing a lot more female led stories in screen and them getting funded."
The work will continue at a fast pace for Cobham-Hervey after the stage show wraps up.
"It's been really nice that there's been a lot of amazing stuff that's been made in Australia, it is always my goal to work here as much as possible," she said.
As for Pip Williams, months of touring to promote The Dictionary Of Lost Words and her second novel The Bookbinder of Jericho will ease up early next year.
"I have started two projects and so now they're vying for my attention," she said.
"One of them is I suppose in some ways in the same universe as Bookbinder and Dictionary, but the other one is completely separate and much more contemporary and closer to home."
The Dictionary Of Lost Words is at the Dunstan Playhouse from September 22 to October 14, before moving to the Sydney Opera House from October 26 to December 16.

title: 'Laughable and insulting': Russell Brand accuser hits out at his denials in fresh interview
content:
London police say they have received an allegation of a sexual assault dating back 20 years, following media reports about comedian and actor Russell Brand.
The comedian and actor has been accused of rape and sexual assaults between 2006 and 2013 following a joint investigation by UK network Channel 4 and the Times and Sunday Times newspapers.
He has denied all of the allegations and said all of his relationships have been consensual.
Police said that since these were published and broadcast they had received a report of an assault alleged to have taken place in Soho, central London, in 2003.
The Met statement does not identify the accused person, but says the report was made directly to them following the Sunday Times report and Channel 4 documentary about Mr Brand.
"Officers are in contact with the woman and will be providing her with support," the Metropolitan Police statement said.
"We first spoke with The Sunday Times on Saturday, 16 September and have since made further approaches to The Sunday Times and Channel 4 to ensure that anyone who believes they have been the victim of a sexual offence is aware of how to report this to the police."
The allegation came after a woman who accused Mr Brand of sexual and emotional abuse said his denial of the allegations is "insulting".
Alice, which is not her real name, had a three-month relationship with him in 2006, when she was 16 and he was 30.
Mr Brand, who has been censured by YouTube over COVID-19 misinformation, also suggested that the reports were part of a coordinated attack designed to discredit him because of his views.
Speaking to the BBC's Woman's Hour podcast on Monday, Alice said Mr Brand's claims were "laughable".
"I think it is insulting," she said.
"It's laughable that he would even imply that this is some kind of mainstream media conspiracy.
"He's not outside the mainstream — he did a Universal Pictures movie last year, he did Minions, a children's movie.
"He's very much part of the mainstream media."
Mr Brand rose to fame as a stand-up comic in Britain in the early 2000s, which led to starring roles on Channel 4 and later BBC Radio, where he capitalised on a reputation for outrageous behaviour and risque banter.
In recent years, he transformed himself into a political commentator and influencer, posting YouTube videos on subjects such as personal freedom and the COVID-19 pandemic.
Alice said Mr Brand, now 48, groomed her and referred to her as "the child" during their relationship, even sending a BBC-supplied car to pick her up from high school.
"He had a friend who was taking him to do his radio show so he said to me, 'You get in the car and you go wherever you need to go from there', so I took the BBC car that time," she said.
"And on another occasion it picked me up from school… back to his house."
Russell Brand said that all of his relationships have been consensual.  (Reuters: Olivia Harris)
Alice told Women's Hour that the alleged experiences with Mr Brand were her first sexually and that he had instructed her on how to keep their relationship quiet.
"Russell groomed me, he coached me on what to say to my parents ... he told me to save his number in my phone in a different name."
She said she had told Mr Brand that she was 16 before their first date.
"He just replied saying, 'OK, so we're still on for dinner at 7.30?'" she said.
The age of consent in the United Kingdom is 16, meaning it is against the law to have sex with someone under the age of 16.
A spokesman for Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, said the claims were "very serious and concerning," and those making the allegations should be "treated seriously and treated with sensitivity".
Conservative MP Caroline Nokes, who chairs the House of Commons Women and Equalities Committee, urged police in both Britain and the United States to investigate the "incredibly shocking" allegations.
"This merits and needs a criminal investigation, because for too long we have seen men -- and the perpetrators of these sorts of crimes are almost invariably men -- not being held to account for their behaviours and their actions," she told BBC Radio.
London's Metropolitan Police said it had not received any reports in relation to the allegations.
Britain's BBC says it is "urgently looking into the issues" raised by allegations of sexual assault made against the broadcaster's former employee, British comedian and actor Russell Brand, who denies the accusations.
"If anyone believes they have been the victim of a sexual assault, no matter how long ago it happened, we would encourage them to contact the police," the police said in a statement.
The BBC has said it is "urgently looking into the issues" raised by the allegations against Mr Brand.
A BBC spokesperson said in a statement: "The documentary and associated reports contained serious allegations, spanning a number of years. Russell Brand worked on BBC radio programmes between 2006 and 2008 and we are urgently looking into the issues raised."
Mr Brand resigned from the BBC in 2008 following the "Sachsgate" prank calls row, when he made prank calls to actor Andrew Sachs, who played Manuel in the comedy series Fawlty Towers, with offensive comments about the actor's granddaughter.
The 48-year-old had been touring the UK with a stand-up show, but on Monday promoters announced the remaining dates had been postponed.
ABC/Reuters

title: Neighbours actor Joy Chambers-Grundy dies aged 76
content:
Joy Chambers-Grundy has died at the age of 76.
The award-winning actress died peacefully in her sleep, while surrounded by loved ones, her family said in a statement.
Best known for her role as Rosemary Daniels in Neighbours, she also starred in other Australian soaps such as Rita in The Restless Years and Dr Robyn Porter in The Young Doctors.
Her stellar performances have clinched multiple awards including Logies for Best Female Personality in 1969 and 1970.
However, her talents extended beyond the silver screen.
In the statement, her family also wrote:
"Joy will be remembered as a Logie Award-winning actress, a best-selling author, a poet, a philanthropist, and an exceptional businesswoman who worked alongside her husband to build one of the largest independent production companies in the world."
Chambers-Grundy was born in Ipswich, Queensland, in 1946.
She was married to multimillionaire media mogul Reg Grundy from 1971 until his death in 2016, at aged 92.
Joy Chambers was Reg Grundy's second wife. (AAP:Tracey Nearmy)
Together, they dominated the television industry as their production powerhouse peaked in 1985, with roots in over 20 countries across 5 continents.
Their success includes soaps such as The Young Doctors (1976), The Restless Years (1977), Sons and Daughters (1982) and Neighbours (1985).
Before pursuing acting, she worked behind the scenes of Grundy shows as a production assistant and a screenwriter.
Chambers-Grundy's Neighbours' debut was in 1986 when she played Rosemary Daniels, but it was in the 1970s that her television career soared.
In 2010, she made her final appearance on Neighbours, which at its height aired in 76 countries.
Touted as her fifth career, Chambers-Grundy found her niche in writing historical fiction in 1990.
She released her final novel The Soldier's Choice in 2014. Other titles include Mayfield, For Freedom, The Great Deception and Vale Valhalla.
Fellow Neighbours actor Stefan Dennis led tributes, describing her as an "exceptional woman and dear friend".

title: Drew Barrymore postpones return of daytime talk show until after Hollywood strikes
content:
Drew Barrymore says she will wait until labour issues are resolved in Hollywood before resuming her talk show after drawing criticism for taping new episodes during the ongoing writers and actors strikes.
"I have listened to everyone, and I am making the decision to pause the show's premiere until the strike is over," Barrymore posted on Instagram on Sunday.
"I have no words to express my deepest apologies to anyone I have hurt and, of course, to our incredible team who works on the show and has made it what it is today."
Barrymore's initial decision to return to the air Monday — without her three union writers and with picketers outside her studio — was met with pushback on social media.
Her show resumed taping in New York last week and was picketed by striking writers.
"We support Drew's decision to pause the show's return and understand how complex and difficult this process has been for her," CBS Media Ventures spokesperson said.

Other daytime shows have resumed, with The View returning for its 27th season on US-based ABC, and Tamron Hall and Live With Kelly and Ryan — neither of which are governed by writers guild rules — have also been producing fresh episodes.
The Jennifer Hudson Show is set to restart on Monday but The Talk scrapped its restart.
"We will continue to evaluate plans for a new launch date," CBC said in a statement Sunday.
Drew Barrymore apologised in a now-deleted video on social media.
Ariel Dumas, head writer and supervising producer for The Late Show With Stephen Colbert reacted on X, formerly Twitter, said The Drew Barrymore Show "decided to do the right thing. I hope @TheView and others will follow suit".
As long as the hosts and guests do not discuss or promote work covered by television, theatrical or streaming contracts, they are not technically breaking the strike.
Hollywood's been hit with the biggest strikes in decades leaving unions in the US and Australia concerned about the dominance of movie studios and streaming platforms changing the way we watch our favourite shows and movies.
Talk shows are covered under a separate contract — the so-called Network Code — from the one actors and writers are striking.
The Network Code also covers reality TV, sports, morning news shows, soap operas and game shows.
Barrymore's stance prompted the National Book Awards to uninvite her as host in November.
The organisation rescinded her invitation "in light of the announcement that The Drew Barrymore Show will resume production".
The ongoing strike pits Writers Guild of America and the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists against the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers, which represents Disney, Netflix, Amazon and others.

title: 'Not a great move': Drew Barrymore and other talk show hosts to return, despite backlash and Hollywood strike
content:
A number of daytime US talk shows will return this week, despite pushback on social media and picketers continuing to protest as part of the ongoing Hollywood labour strike.
Shows including The Drew Barrymore Show, The Talk and The Jennifer Hudson Show will begin airing fresh episodes from Monday.
The ongoing strike pits the Writers Guild of America (WGA) and the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) against the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers, which represents Disney, Netflix, Amazon and others.
As long as hosts and guests don't discuss or promote work covered by television, theatrical or streaming contracts, they are not technically breaking the strike. That's because talk shows are covered under a separate contract — the so-called Network Code — from the one actors and writers are striking over.
But this hasn't stopped calls for talk show hosts to stand with the workers who some of them have claimed to support.
A lot of off-air controversy will be clinging to The Drew Barrymore Show and its typically bubbly host when the show returns.
Barrymore — a daughter of an acting dynasty — is making new batches of her syndicated talk show despite picketers outside her studio.
The show will be operating without its three union writers, and its decision to return to the air has been met with pushback on social media.
Barrymore's stance was also met with some puzzlement since she walked away as host of the MTV Movie & TV Awards in May, the first big awards show to air during the strike. Back then, she wrote: "I have listened to the writers, and in order to truly respect them, I will pivot from hosting the MTV Movie & TV Awards live in solidarity with the strike."
The actor claimed the return of the show "is bigger than just me" as striking writers plan to picket the return of the show's fourth season.
She has since lost another hosting gig — the National Book Awards in November. The organisation rescinded her invitation "in light of the announcement that The Drew Barrymore Show will resume production".
"I know there is just nothing I can do that will make this okay to those that it is not okay with. I fully accept that," Barrymore said in a video posted on Instagram on Friday, which was later deleted.
Actor and activist Alyssa Milano, whose friendship with Barrymore stretches back years, also criticised the return, calling it "not a great move".
"I love her very much — I grew up with her — but I'm not sure that this was the right move for the strike. I'm sure in her eyes it's the right move for her and the show, but as far as the WGA and SAG and union strong — not a great move."
SAG-AFTRA president Fran Dresche speaks outside Paramount Pictures Studio in Los Angeles on Wednesday, September 13 2023. (AP: Richard Shotwell/Invision)
Michael H. LeRoy, a professor of labour and employment relations at the University of Illinois, warned that TV shows like Barrymore's may think they can get by without using union writers, but may find long-term costs.
"No members of the Writers Guild will ever work with that show again," he said.
"It's a short-term, feel-good moment or get-by moment for Drew Barrymore and maybe the others, but long term they really have, in my view, basically given themselves an early retirement.
"We're four months approximately into this strike and it's not surprising that there are defectors. I couldn't predict that this would happen on daytime TV, but everybody has a breaking point in a labour dispute."
Other daytime shows have already resumed: The View has returned for its 27th season, while Tamron Hall and Live With Kelly and Ryan — neither which are governed by writers guild rules — have also been producing fresh episodes.
Viewers who tune into new episodes will find a changed landscape. Guests aren't always the A-listers with blockbuster TV shows or films to promote. Since the strike began, authors, musicians and comedians are filling the gaps.
Last week, astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson was on Live With Kelly and Ryan talking about the science behind the Hulk, while Cedric The Entertainer was telling Hall about his debut novel. Matthew McConaughey was on The View to promote his new book.
Hollywood workers are striking over issues including pay, conditions, and the use of artificial intelligence. (AP: Richard Shotwell/Invision)
The return of daytime hosts, producers and studio crews will also make for some awkward exchanges, predicted Zayd Ayers Dohrn, a writer and professor at Northwestern University.
Hosts like Barrymore may be caught in a lose-lose situation — contractually obligated to return to work but certain to anger colleagues when they do. Last week she noted, "This is bigger than just me."
On July 14, actors union SAG-AFTRA joined the Writers Guild Of America in strike. Now, Hollywood is seeing the consequences.
Bill Maher, who also announced he would return to his late night talk show, couched his reasoning as wanting to help all his staff, saying writers "are not the only people with issues, problems, and concerns".
Mr Dohrn isn't buying it.
"They talk about wanting to support the people who are just getting by. But Bill Maher and Drew Barrymore and the hosts of The View are not just getting by. They could very easily stand with their fellow workers in the industry and say, 'We're not going to feed the studio pipeline until they make a fair offer,'" he said.
"They're deciding for a whole host of complicated reasons to go back to work and to ultimately try to break the strike."
ABC/AP

title: My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3 may be cheesy, but it captures the joy of second-generation migrants going 'home'
content:
Eight years ago this week, I took my then-fiance, our friends and families to a little Greek island and had a big Greek wedding.
When we first got engaged, there was very little debate about where we would get married. I had three of my grandparents alive and well, and if they couldn't travel to Australia for the wedding, we would take the wedding to them.
It had everything a good Greek wedding should have: spectacular scenery, a grumpy priest, an over-catered dinner, and Greek dancing until dawn (or at least, in our case, dancing until the island had a complete power outage).
Coincidentally, this week also saw the release of My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3.
In this third iteration of the famous franchise, Toula is tasked with reuniting her deceased father's diary with his childhood friends, having to travel to her father's village in Greece to do so (and, predictably, attending a wedding in the process).
I too had a Big Fat Greek Wedding. (Supplied: Gianluca Adovasio)
When the first movie in the My Big Fat Greek Wedding trilogy was released more than 20 years ago, it felt revolutionary.
I was in my early teens and it felt like the first time in my life that I saw someone on screen like me who wasn't a complete caricature of my culture.
Instead of Effie or Con the Fruiterer, here we had an ambitious, intelligent daughter of migrants — a woman struggling to reconcile her family's culture with that of her birthplace.
Like Toula, my life has followed the typical trajectory of a second-generation migrant. I grew up not feeling entirely Greek, but not feeling entirely Australian, either.
I married someone outside of my culture who had to learn and adapt to our customs and traditions. We have half-Greek and half-Australian children, who I am trying to raise to be filled with pride and passion for their Greek culture.
And, like Toula, I, too, have made the pilgrimage back to the family village.
There are three parts to any migrant story: leaving home, starting a new life in a strange land, and, for many, but not all, coming home again.
As children of migrants, we, too, are a part of this story.
From birth, the legend of our "home" country is woven through everything we do. We are raised to miss a place we have never been to before.
Taking your first trip back to your ancestral homeland to trace your roots is a momentous moment in any migrant family's life.
My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3 attempts to capture the heart-wrenching joy felt the first time you land in Athens, when you have your first swim in the Aegean Sea, your first steps through your family's village.
Focus Features: My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3 Official Trailer
While it makes a strong start, the issue with My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3 isn't that it doesn't have enough to say but, like many of my relatives, probably has a little too much to comment on.
For Greeks in Greece, the film attempts to touch on various political and social issues facing the country today.
We see the meeting of traditional agriculture and modern technology perfectly encapsulated by a weathered farmer on a donkey pulling out an iPad to manage his crops.
We see the emptying of our ancestral villages, with the next generation leaving farming behind for bigger and better opportunities, the villages at risk of ruin.
We see the impact of refugees entering Greece to find a new home and how it forces local Greeks to face and examine their internalised xenophobia.
Going back "home" is not always smooth sailing for Toula. (Focus Features)
For Greeks in the diaspora, the film touches on the never-ending pressure to continue our cultural traditions and questions how we can do that after our parents and grandparents, our guiding lights, are no longer with us.
It asks the valuable question: who leads the family when the leader is no longer there?
Two decades on from the original, where My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3 falls down is its continued reliance on stereotypes and cheap jokes that are becoming less and less relevant as we see third- and even fourth-generation migrant children being born.
The idea of what makes someone "Greek", particularly in the diaspora, is evolving.
The next generation of yiayias won't wear black for the rest of their lives once their husband passes. They don't speak in broken English. They're just as comfortable and adept at making a Shepherd's Pie as they are at making dolmades.
I would like to see a more modern and sophisticated representation of Greeks within our storytelling — one that doesn't rely on outdated ideas that to be Greek means behaving or looking a certain way.
It does make me think that I am on the cusp of having a cultural identity crisis. If I start to lack that which is stereotypically Greek, am I still Greek?
There's no place like (your ancestral) home. (Supplied: Gianluca Adovasio)
Maybe that's why, as migrants, a connection to our homeland is so deeply drilled into us.
We forge a love with a country that is both foreign and familiar to ensure we have a place to come back to that reminds us of who we are and where we come from.
Despite its shortcomings, if My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3 does nothing else but convince those Greeks in the diaspora to book their first ticket to Greece and visit their village, it will be a success.
And here's hoping they feel that unbridled joy during their first swim in the Aegean.
Chryssie Swarbrick is a writer and mum of two from Melbourne.
My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3 is out now.

title: Kenneth Branagh teams up with Tina Fey to solve a supernatural mystery in new Poirot 'boo-dunnit'
content:
Agatha Christie's moustachioed meddler is back, and this time he's tangling with a case of the supernatural.
After a pair of underwhelming movies that might pass for someone's favourite in-flight entertainment — 2017's star-studded Murder on the Orient Express and last year's dreadful if unintentionally camp Death on the Nile — Kenneth Branagh's take on super-sleuth Hercule Poirot could do with the presence of some spirits that aren't Gal Gadot's champagne.
In A Haunting in Venice, Branagh's hirsute ham has retired to the Floating City to mind his own peculiar business, even if the ghosts of crime, and the recently ended World War II, seem to follow him around.
A visit from his old friend Ariadne Oliver (Tina Fey) — a mystery novelist who played a part in minting his legend — is about to lure him back to detective duties.
"It's not only a murder mystery … there's also a supernatural element [that] takes it to another level," Fey said in the film's featurette. (Supplied: )
Poirot and Oliver head to the spooky palazzo of opera star Rowena Drake (Kelly Reilly), where a rogues' gallery of soon-to-be suspects has gathered for a seance to contact the singer's late daughter Alicia (Rowan Robinson) — a young woman who plunged to her death in a suicide that carried signs of foul play.
Among those in attendance are Alicia's social-climbing ex Maxime Gerard (Kyle Allen), Rowena's religious housekeeper Olga Seminoff (Camille Cottin), the troubled family doctor Leslie Ferrier (Jamie Dornan) and his precocious kid Leopold (Jude Hill, the latter two reuniting after Branagh's Belfast) — each of whom arrives with the usual ulterior motives.
Presiding over the ghostly ceremony is the renowned medium Joyce Reynolds — played, with a shock of grey hair and some scenery-chewing personality, by recent Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh. Her witchy gyrations leave the sceptical Poirot none too impressed. He's here for a whodunnit, not a boo!-dunnit.
Amidst all the cheesy thunderclaps and dramatically blown light fuses, one of the guests finds themselves unceremoniously impaled on a statue — and Poirot is soon on the hunt for a murderer who may or may not be of this world.
"[Branagh] brought everyone together as an ensemble. He's very collaborative," Yeoh told Entertainment Tonight. (Supplied: Disney)
For Branagh's third crack at Poirot, he and returning screenwriter Michael Green turned to one of Christie's lesser-known works, 1969's Hallowe'en Party, relocating the novel's action from London to Venice and reshaping elements of the plot to fit the film franchise's more familiar contours.
The new movie's smaller, more contained focus allows it to cultivate a richer sense of atmosphere, though Branagh is again torn between playing it straight and fully committing to the strange and the grotesque.
As Poirot attempts to unmask the killer, Branagh and his go-to cinematographer Haris Zambarloukos wheel out wide-angle lenses, canted angles and kooky point-of-view shots to suggest the disorientating presence of the beyond, with little nods to Fellini, Dario Argento (there's an extreme close-up of a bird's eye that would make the horror master grin) and the unnerving Venice of Nicolas Roeg's classic Don't Look Now.
Branagh's second Poirot film, Death on the Nile, was poorly received by critics. (Supplied: Disney)
There's more than a touch of Branagh's own dark thriller, 1991's Dead Again, lurking around the edges of the frame too.
But all their Gothic exertion can't summon the dark magic needed to make the movie truly weird, nor the kind of baroque trashiness that might have sent it enjoyably over the top.
When Branagh resorts to the old phantom-in-the-bathroom-mirror trick for a fright, you start to wonder if he isn't out of ideas entirely — or whether the movie would have been better served in the hands of someone who savours the ridiculous, like Malignant's James Wan.
Branagh himself feels oddly subdued, even morose, while the supporting players do what they can with characters whose eccentricities barely rise to the level of Rian Johnson's murder mysteries, let alone match the nutty oddballs of something like Clue. (As Joyce Reynolds's unnerving assistant Desdemona Holland, British actor Emma Laird manages to find the right note of psychic unease.)
The cast was surprised with unannounced effects during shooting. "[The] actors had no warning about what would happen, what we did with lights, wind, doors opening," says Branagh. (Supplied: Disney)
Poirot's crisis of faith — the possibility that he might be wrong to doubt the supernatural — is a potentially fascinating angle here, but it largely amounts to the filmmaker throwing every destabilising camera move at the wall in the hope that something will stick.
Perhaps the fundamental problem is that the screenplay, with its deference to Christie's logic and reason, refuses to seriously entertain the mysteries of the unknown, keeping the film firmly rooted in the dreariness of the real.
Whatever Branagh's talents, conjuring up a genuine sense of screen sorcery isn't one of them.
A Haunting in Venice is in cinemas now.

title: 'Devastating': Screen industry warns of job losses, reputational damage after NSW funding cuts
content:
The screen industry is warning cuts to funding for film and television production in New South Wales could jeopardise the state's status as a cultural hub and send thousands of jobs interstate.
The NSW government has flagged that next week's budget will include $188 million in cuts to a number of screen and innovation programs such as Made in NSW, a fund which has been used to attract blockbuster films and high-end television productions.
Projects that have been saved from cuts include the upcoming film The Fall Guy starring Ryan Gosling, Amazon's The Lost Flowers of Alice Hart starring Sigourney Weaver, and ABC TV's Mystery Road.
The funding was also used to help secure Taika Waititi's Thor: Love and Thunder in 2020.
In 2021, then-premier Gladys Berejiklian said the Made in NSW fund had helped cement the state as the "cultural capital of Australia", after announcing Mad Max: Furiosa would be filmed in the regional towns of Hay and Silverton, using some of the funding.
Aaron Pedersen's Mystery Road was partially supported by Made in NSW funding. (ABC TV)
At the time, the producers of Mad Max said the film would not have been possible without government incentives.
New projects are on the chopping block, along with a Screen NSW rebate scheme for game developers and visual effects and the Blockbusters Funding Initiative, aimed at bringing major cultural exhibitions from across the globe to Sydney.
The Minns Labor government has argued the cuts were secretly made by the previous government just days before the March election, and that it was unable to reinstate them due to budgetary pressures.
The opposition denies this.
Screen Producers Australia CEO Matthew Deaner said the cuts would affect NSW's standing as a hub for film and TV productions.
"It came completely out of the blue for the sector," Mr Deaner said.
"You would no longer be able to call Sydney a film or TV centre for the nation if this cut goes ahead.
"We are seen as a partner of choice for production, but if we are sending out bad signals to the market and whether or not funding is secured from state governments, that is creating huge chaos.
Screen Producers Australia CEO Matthew Deaner argued the cuts would also have implications for consumers of film and TV. (Supplied: Phil Jackson Photography)
Mr Deaner argued the cuts would also have implications for consumers of film and TV in the state.
"You stop being able to see New South Wales, and Sydney particularly, on-screen, so if we're dealing with an environment where people enjoy watching themselves or their cities captured and for film and television to tell their stories, we are no longer going to see that if this is allowed to happen," he said.
Thor: Love and Thunder was also supported by the Made In NSW fund. (Supplied: Walt Disney Studios)
The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA), the union representing screen industry staff, said the Made in NSW program had helped bring 33 domestic and international productions to the state since 2016, creating more than 14,000 skilled jobs.
MEAA chief executive Erin Madeley said there was "despair" within the industry at the cuts.
"It's a devastating blow to the cultural and creative workforce in New South Wales," Ms Madeley said.
Both the MEAA and Screen Producers Australia held crisis talks with Arts Minister John Graham on Thursday to discuss the cuts.
In a statement, Mr Graham said he was looking at ways to protect the sector and would hold an industry round table later this month to consider a "revised approach" to supporting it.
"We are evaluating current submissions on a case-by-case basis to find a way to support the sector and protect the screen and production sector as best we can."
Arts Minister John Graham says the funding was cut by the previous government.
Mr Graham said the government was developing a new arts and creative industries policy to "give NSW the competitive edge".
Opposition arts spokesman Kevin Anderson denied the Coalition had cut the funding before the last election.
"That's been a well-worn line by the government so far, to say that when they're cutting stuff that they didn't put it in the forward estimates," Mr Anderson said.
"We made sure Made in NSW, Screen NSW was something that we were very proud of and wanted to continue.
"The government needs to reconsider these cuts and instead bolster the screen industry in NSW rather than further deplete it because it will see an industry that has got projects that are already planned and existing now in jeopardy."

title: A Haunting in Venice is a spookier reimagining of Agatha Christie's original novel
content:
The third Kenneth Branagh-directed adaptation of Agatha Christie's beloved murder mystery books, featuring detective Hercule Poirot, makes major changes.
A Haunting in Venice takes the 1969 novel Hallowe'en Party and trades murder at an English country house for one in a Venetian Palazzo instead.
It's a loose adaptation, but one that's more accessible.
In the film, a seance is held during a Halloween party and, when someone is killed, Poirot has to investigate the murder and its possible links to a past death.
"There is nothing more haunted than a Venetian palazzo," said screenwriter Michael Green in the film's production notes.
James Prichard says detective Hercule Poirot is tested by the seemingly supernatural in the film. (Supplied: Walt Disney Studios)
The film is still a double mystery, but it changes a fair chunk of the original tale.
James Prichard, the great grandson of Agatha Christie and a producer on the film, says there was a lot of trust, given the same creative team has been in place across the three films.
"This film takes him [Hercule Poirot] to a completely other place where, to some extent, he's tested by whether or not there's another being, whether there's evidence of the supernatural, whether there's a God, whether there's something above and beyond," Prichard told ABC News.
"At the beginning of the story, Poirot is retired again, and the story is bringing him back and giving him a zest for life, and I think that is quite an important passage of the story."
Movie producer James Prichard is the great grandson of Agatha Christie. (Supplied: Walt Disney Studios)
The film has a Cluedo-ish feel, and the script is deliberately specific with each part of the story unfolding in a different room.
This includes a murder that happens in the music room and a key scene involving Poirot and bobbing apples in the library — a reference to the death in the original book.
"[Branagh] did try and make the fear real. And I think that comes through," Prichard says.
"I mean there is a definite element of fear here, there's almost a horror feel to the film and that was deliberate to change the tone, to surprise our audience and maybe to bring a new audience by that route.
"But it definitely will feel very different to our reasons, but it will also feel like an Agatha Christie — it is still a murder mystery."
Similarly to the mystery board game Cluedo, each part of the film unfolds in a different room. (Supplied: Walt Disney Studios)
The film stars an ensemble cast, including Branagh as the beloved detective, Tina Fey, Michelle Yeoh, Jamie Dornan and Kelly Reilly.
Prichard is also currently the CEO and chairman of the company that manages Christie's literary and media rights.
When receiving pitches, Prichard says there isn't a list of questions they ask, but a gut feeling of whether something mounts up to an "Agatha Christie experience".
"This is a proper test of it [the film] because obviously the story has been changed from the original that my great grandmother wrote, and it was important to us that it still passes that test. And absolutely it does."
James Prichard says the film has a horror feel. (Supplied: Walt Disney Studios)
Prichard says Christie's work has stayed relevant into modern popular culture because she created plots that are credible and challenge the reader.
Christie has sold more than a billion books in English and another billion in over a hundred different languages, according to the film's production notes.
A Haunting in Venice opens in Australian cinemas on September 14.

title: 'I own this choice': Drew Barrymore brings back talk show amid Hollywood strikes
content:
Actor Drew Barrymore has defended bringing back her talk show amid ongoing Hollywood strikes.
Barrymore hosts The Drew Barrymore Show on CBS and announced on Monday the show was returning for its fourth season.
In an Instagram post, Barrymore said the show would return in accordance with the rules of SAG-AFTRA strikes.
"I own this choice," she wrote.
"We are in compliance with not discussing or promoting film and television that is struck of any kind."
But the Writers Guild of America (WGA) said the show itself was "struck", and that it planned to picket tapings of the show, criticising its "violation of WGA strike rules".
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
A struck production means union members are prohibited from performing labour for the show while the strike is ongoing.
Various media outlets confirmed the show will be produced for the first time without literary material, similar to talk shows like The View.
"The Drew Barrymore Show will not be performing any writing work covered by the WGA strike," a CBS Media Ventures spokesperson told The Hollywood Reporter.
In her lengthy post, Barrymore noted how she had previously walked away from hosting the 2023 MTV Movie and TV Awards because she supported strikers.
The talk show host added the third season of the show had wrapped on April 20, and avoided strike action so far.
"I am also making the choice to come back for the first time in this strike for our show, that may have my name on it but this is bigger than just me," Barrymore said.
The show, which was launched in the COVID-19 pandemic, was "built for sensitive times" Barrymore added.
Barrymore said the decision to bring back the talk show was "bigger than just me".  (Reuters: Andrew Kelly)
"We have navigated difficult times since we first came on air," she wrote.
"And so I take a step forward to start season 4 once again with an astute humility."
Following the announcement, actors and writers alike condemned Barrymore for the choice.
The West Wing's Josh Malina posted a picture of Barrymore alongside the word "scab" on social media platform X, previously known as Twitter.
The term is an insult for those who leave or decline to join a union, freeing them to work during a strike.
Crazy Ex-Girlfriend actor Benjamin Siemon said Barrymore was "making a mistake" and questioned who she would interview, given the SAG-AFTRA rules.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
Adam Ruins Everything creator Adam Conover said the news was "incredibly disappointing".
"Drew: This harms your writers and all union workers. Please reconsider," he wrote on X.
Unlike other television shows, daytime TV has avoided strikes interfering with production, because most do not rely on writers who are part of the Writers Guild union.
The two exceptions were Barrymore's show and The Talk, which continues to air re-runs like late-night talk shows.
The program could also face difficulty finding talent as striking actors are unable to promote new works, per the SAG-AFTRA rules.

title: Atomic bomb debate overshadows Power's AFL finals clash with Brisbane
content:
Port Adelaide coach Ken Hinkley has fired back at criticism of his side following an admission it was taking inspiration from the movie Oppenheimer going into this year's AFL finals series.
Earlier this week, star midfielder Ollie Wines was asked whether the Power had identified any motivational themes ahead of Saturday night's qualifying final against Brisbane at the Gabba.
Wines told radio station SEN that the players had been inspired by the blockbuster biopic, and were impressed by its emphasis on teamwork to achieve an outcome.
"It's a little bit about just how much work goes into something, and in the movie Oppenheimer it was to go into the atomic bomb that ended World War II," Wines said.
"So many people have to come together and work hard for a number of years and this finals campaign isn't just something that's just been building this year — it's probably been the last four years.
"The general grasp of it is so many people have to come together and work hard to reach a common goal, which hopefully for us is a premiership."
But those comments quickly triggered backlash on social media,
"They may want to go rewatch the film a few more times, because this is a dreadful take and incredibly insensitive to theme things around," one person wrote on X (formerly Twitter).
Ollie Wines (centre) says Port Adelaide players had been inspired by the movie Oppenheimer. (AAP: David Mariuz)
Others also questioned how appropriate it was to invoke the creator of the atomic bomb in a positive light ahead of a sporting fixture.
"Dunno mate but it sounds a bit dodgy to be taking inspiration from a biopic about the development of a nuclear weapon that killed hundreds of thousands of civilians," one person wrote.
"The Atomic Bomb!! Serious??? Tore apart more than it brought together," another said.
Power coach Ken Hinkley on Friday fronted a media conference at Adelaide Airport ahead of his side flying to Brisbane for the clash with the Lions.
But the encounter became heated when Hinkley was quizzed about his side using J. Robert Oppenheimer as a role model.
The story of the first nuclear weapons is, in some respects, the story of a human chain reaction behind an atomic one.
"Every club has some type of theme that they may or may not use," he said.
"The key part about that, as I think Ollie explained incredibly well, is that it's just a little story around how people had to come together over a long period of time to work really hard on one single thing to get an outcome we're trying to get, and for us we've been at this task for a good period of time — four or five years.
"I haven't seen the movie myself so it's not that big a theme for us."
When pushed about whether the outcome of the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki made the movie an inappropriate reference, Hinkley fired back, saying that was "a silly question to ask" and "really unfair".
"That's a silly question to put in the same conversation," he said.
"It was around a group of people coming together and the need to work together to get an outcome. Let's not go to that dark spot that you're trying to take it.
"I think it's an unfair response to what we're trying to achieve."

title: Arts Week 2023
content:
ABC Arts Week is celebrating its second year of arts and creativity throughout Australia! Kicking off on Monday September 18, we'll be sharing special arts-themed content across ABC platforms.
This year's theme, "Happy Making", encourages and inspires Australians to get creative: take that pottery class, pick up that sketchpad, join that local choir. Research shows the direct benefit to mental health and wellbeing from being engaged in the arts — in whatever creative form that takes. With a suite of content across platforms, Arts Week is a reminder to us of the happiness, relaxation and community spirit that creativity provides.
Arts Week is to inspire people to get involved because art is for everyone!
Join us in celebrating Arts Week with the hashtag #ArtsWeekABC
Wendy Whiteley opens up about the scandal that embroiled an art dealer and conservator who marketed paintings purporting to by her late husband Brett Whiteley. (Supplied: In Films/Georgia Quinn)
The riveting story of the greatest art fraud case in Australian history is captured in this documentary that takes a rarely granted, behind-the-scenes look at the glamorous and high-stakes world of art dealing.
There's something for every maker, mover and tinkerer this week. From eel skin violins to paper flowers, from self-care compositions and healing ceramics to pressure-sensitive floors you can perform on — join us as we meet creatives from across Australia for insights into their making motivations and some how-to inspiration.
A special Arts Week presentation featuring eight incredible artists and creative workers from around Australia. Meet the recipients of the 2023 Creative Australia Awards.
Old wool sorting tables are being transformed from shearing shed relics into highly sought-after dining and board room centrepieces. Country town carpenter Jason Porter has started making replicas from recycled timber to keep up with demand for the sought-after conversation starters.
Some of the best live performances from around Australia featuring titles from the Australian String Quartet, Tasmanian Symphony Orchestra, Musica Viva and Australian Theatre Live.
During Arts Week, head to the ABC listen app or tune into ABC RN for your daily fix of arts content delights from our premier Arts programs: The Art Show, The Stage Show, The Book Show and The Bookshelf, The Screen Show, Blueprint for Living and The Music Show.
Blaque Showgirls is Nakkiah Lui's ninth play. (Supplied: Audible)
Playwright Nakkiah Lui and co-directors Shari Sebbens and Ursula Yovich discuss Blaque Showgirls: the sparkly, smart-arsed spoof of the so-bad-it's-good cinematic masterpiece Showgirls.
Literary fiction is good at the hard stuff  grief, pain and conflict. But what about the books that make you feel good? Authors Joan Silber, Toni Jordan and Andy Weir bring joy to The Book Show, talking about the radical act of writing optimistic fiction. You'll also hear from Richard Ford, Douglas Stuart, Jennifer Down, Anita Heiss, Marlon James and Monica Ali.
The Book Show will be broadcast at 10am on Monday September 18 on ABC RN and ABC listen.
There's a memoir in everyone: Healing by telling your story
They say to write/paint/sing what you know, and what do you know better than your own life? Narrative therapy allows us to tell our own stories in a way that empowers us and improves our mental wellbeing, and art is the perfect medium for those stories. We look at how to get creative with your life story and boost your mental health in the process.
Keeping up with the Coppolas
Sofia Coppola's latest film Priscilla, about the life of Priscilla Presley, premiered earlier this month at the Venice International Film Festival. (Getty Images: Frazer Harrison)
The Coppolas are one of cinema's great family dynasties. The patriarch is Francis Ford Coppola, the Oscar-winning director of The Godfather trilogy, Apocalypse Now, and many others. His children, Sofia and Roman, have charted creative paths in their own right. Roman — an award-winning music video director and regular collaborator of Wes Anderson — was a recent guest of Melbourne's inaugural Now or Never Festival. Roman tells host Keri Elmsly, head of programming at ACMI, why he's on a mission to democratise film funding through blockchain, and why Luna Park was a recent source of inspiration.
Hear the latest stories from stages across the country.
We catch up with a very talented person, the recipient of the Creative Australia Dance Award.
Air kissing and free drinks aside, the competitive art world isn't always "happy making"! So, host Daniel Browning will be meeting some artists who actively practice what they call an "ethics of care" in their work, extending to ideas of environmental sustainability and deep listening.
The Art Show will be broadcast at 10am on Wednesday September 20 on ABC RN and ABC listen.
Daniel Browning is the co-host of ABC RN's The Art Show and former host of Awaye! (Supplied: NITV/Kelly Gardner)
Classic Choir Hour
A special hour of your favourite choral music presented by Vanessa Hughes. Find out about the joys of singing together and how singing in a choir can enrich your life.
Classic Choir
The health benefits of singing in a choir are numerous and for the last three years ABC Classic has commissioned a new song for Australians to sing together as part of the Classic Choir project. This year, the music is written by Australian composer Elena Kats-Chernin with words by Gunai poet Kirli Saunders. The sheet music, practise tracks and backing tracks for this year's Classic Choir are up online and we are encouraging choirs around Australia to sign up and sing from the Classic Choir Songbook.
Classic Playlists
Improve your sleep, exercise and concentration with the best classical music playlists. Find them on the ABC Classic website and ABC listen.
ABC Classic is inviting you to warm up those vocal cords with a new song for Classic Choir.
What are the ingredients that go into making happy and liveable cities for families with children? Is it just a question of creating more open spaces, or something more? Blueprint host Jonathan Green speaks with design critic and mother Alexandra Lange about ways to build better neighbourhoods and cities for little people.
This week's show is art-themed, with the team reviewing The Modern, a debut novel by Kiwi author Anna Kate Blair with guest reviewer, Rosa Ellen, producer of RN's specialist visual arts program, The Art Show. The Modern is set in the heady world of MoMA, and is a brilliant take on art, sexuality and desire, and asks what it is to be a modern person today.
For Arts Week, we ask the question: "How can we create/think/work like an artist?" We'll learn tips and insights about inspiration, innovation and flow states from artists and experts to take and apply to our own jobs.
