title: New Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles movie delivers 'a cinematic pizza-with-the lot'
content:
Four wisecracking, pizza-loving amphibians and the stoner prince of 21st-century comedy? It's a match made in pop culture heaven, or at least a radioactive New York City sewer.
Cruising for an oozing, Seth Rogen (Superbad, Pineapple Express) blazes up a different kind of green as he and screenwriting bestie Evan Goldberg take a crack at the latest iteration of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.
This is a franchise that's managed to endure across multiple generations since the radical reptiles were first conceived, as a kind of punk rock superhero parody, by Peter Laird and Kevin Eastman all the way back in 1984.
Director Jeff Rowe describes Mutant Mayhem's style as lo-fi. "We're like the grunge bands in the 90s," he told Gizmodo. (Supplied: Paramount Pictures)
The series' surprise longevity has resulted in something of an identity crisis in Mutant Mayhem, a fast and funny new animated film that's split between pitching to Gen-Xers and Millennials — those kids raised on the totally tubular 80s cartoons and early live-action films — and the Zoomers who partied on with Nickelodeon's multiple animated series.
The result is a cinematic pizza-with-the lot: a family platter with something for everyone. References to Vanilla Ice sit side-by-side with Beyoncé shout-outs and BTS singalongs; Ratatouille gags meet Shrek trash-talk and battle-cries of "Cowabunga" — a catchphrase whose 50s origins make it practically stone-age by comparison.
Rogen and Goldberg's screenplay — written alongside Dan Hernandez and Benji Samit (Pokémon Detective Pikachu) and director Jeff Rowe (The Mitchells vs the Machines) — is effectively a reboot of the franchise's origin story, so you know the drill: It's slime time for four baby turtles, whose exposure to toxic ooze transforms them into humanoid mutants under the martial arts tutelage of a wise-old radioactive rodent.
An adult in the original series, April O'Neil (pictured left) is a teenage amateur reporter in Mutant Mayhem. (Supplied: Paramount Pictures)
The teenage sewer-side squad — leader Leonardo (voiced by Nicolas Cantu), motormouth Raphael (Brady Noon), tech-geek Donatello (Micah Abbey) and party dude Michelangelo (Shamon Brown Jr) — spend their nights running covert missions to the surface and dreaming of one day becoming heroes, or at least high-school legends like their obsession, Ferris Bueller.
But their ever-watchful master Splinter — voiced by a sensei-tionally goofy Jackie Chan — forbids his charges from engaging with the humans he so distrusts.
All of that changes when the quartet crosses paths with plucky high school reporter and fellow outsider April O'Neil (Ayo Edebiri).
They team up on the trail of Superfly (Ice Cube), a militant mutant with designs on radioactively enhancing the Earth's animals and enslaving humanity. (For an outcast consigned to a life of being hunted through the sewers, it does sound like a pretty reasonable plan.)
Voiced by Cube in all his pissed-off baritone glory, Superfly, as the name suggests, is a creation straight out of the Blaxploitation genre, quoting from gangsta anthems and pulling up in a ride that would make Isaac Hayes proud.
Mutant Mayhem's lead character designer Woodrow White drew on Japanese monster design when creating the villain Superfly. (Supplied: Paramount Pictures)
His gnarly crew of mutants — who include a boombox-toting warthog (Seth Rogen), a melismatic toad (Hannibal Buress) and a skateboarding gecko (Paul Rudd, playing Pauly Shore, playing Poochie) — are like subway graffiti come to life as nightmare toy commercial.
Mutant Mayhem wraps this winning grotesquerie around Rogen and Goldberg's recognisably neurotic banter — landing somewhere between PG-rated teen hangout, irreverent comic strip and the darker, funkier tones of the original, and still unmatched, Jim Henson Workshop film.
It's not quite the dazzling formal reinvention of the Spider-Verse, but the computer animation, rendered to resemble the scrawl of a maladjusted teenager's sketchbook, brims with sassy energy.
There are training montages spliced with online martial arts videos, Shaw Brothers bangers and — it's only correct — Jackie Chan's own movies, while Nine Inch Nails' Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross have the time of their movie-scoring lives dashing off hyper-charged industrial synth flourishes.
Rogen, Goldberg and co have delivered a pretty irresistible love letter to their childhoods, even if their soundtrack of 80s and 90s needle-drops — which includes everything from Grandmaster Flash & Melle Mel and A Tribe Called Quest, to dance punks ESG — sometimes prizes nostalgia over visual synchronicity (a high-octane action montage feels a little enervated set to a loping Blackstreet classic.)
Mutant Mayhem marks the first time teenage actors have voiced the titular characters. (Supplied: Paramount Pictures)
It's all part of the fabric of the franchise, of course, which has long drawn its aesthetic playbook from the hip-hop nation and its broader roots in Black culture.
And if Mutant Mayhem occasionally wanders into terrain it can't quite handle in its characterisation of Superfly — the justifiably aggrieved villain who nearly becomes the movie's uncontainable Killmonger — then the creators get around it by offering a sinister big-tech force against whom the mutants must unite.
By the time Superfly has mutated into a city-stomping Kaiju, the movie has become a rallying call for the outcasts against their oppressors, giving New York back to the weirdos and the sewer dwellers — and, by extension, delivering the multiplex from the clutches of puffed-up superhero tedium.
May the freaks and geeks (and beaks) reign once more.
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem is in cinemas now.

title: Smash Mouth's long-time frontman Steve Harwell dies from liver failure at 56
content:
Steve Harwell, the former lead singer of American rock band Smash Mouth, has died, according to a post on the band's official X account (formerly Twitter).
US media earlier reported that the Smash Mouth frontman had begun receiving hospice care at home, where he was in the final stages of liver failure.
Manager Robert Hayes told breaking tabloid news site TMZ that Mr Harwell was surrounded by family and friends as he received treatment.
Mr Harwell was 56.
Fans of the band — perhaps best remembered for their 1999 hit All Star, which was featured in the 2001 animated movie Shrek — have expressed their condolences online.
In 2019, footage emerged of Mr Harwell appearing disorientated during a live performance in Syracuse, New York, and he announced his retirement in 2021.
Smash Mouth - All Star (Official Music Video)
At the time, it was reported that his declining state was due to health issues and substance abuse.
Smash Mouth was founded in 1994, and the band enjoyed early success with their 1997 hit Walkin' on the Sun.
In the years since, the band, and All Star in particular, have become a potent cultural force online.
Smash Mouth is currently touring in the US with its new frontman Zach Goode.

title: Former Smash Mouth frontman Steve Harwell gravely ill
content:
US media outlets are reporting former frontman of the American rock band Smash Mouth Steve Harwell is gravely ill.
Harwell's manager Robert Hayes has told breaking tabloid news site TMZ that Harwell is in the final stage of liver failure, which he was receiving care for in hospital until recently.
Hayes has told the US Sun that Harwell is surrounded by family and friends.
"Steve is resting at home and being cared for by his fiance and hospice care," Hayes told the publication.
"My only additional comment is that we would hope that people would respect Steve and his family's privacy during this difficult time."
Acute liver failure develops quickly and is a medical emergency that can cause serious complications and requires hospitalisation.
In some cases, it can only be cured via a liver transplant. Chronic liver failure develops at a slower rate.
Without treatment, both can lead to death.
Harwell is 56.
Smash Mouth was twice featured on the 2001 Shrek soundtrack. (Image: Shrek / Dreamworks)
The news comes years after troubling footage emerged of Harwell appearing disorientated during a 2019 live performance in Syracuse, New York.
He announced his retirement in 2021. At the time, it was reported that his declining state was due to health issues and substance abuse.
Smash Mouth is behind the hits Walkin' on the Sun and All Star, the latter featured on the Shrek soundtrack in 2001 along with their cover of I'm a Believer by the Monkees.
On the 20th anniversary of All Star in 2019, Rolling Stone reported that the band went into the studio to prove they weren't a one hit wonder following the success of their 1997 track Walkin' on the Sun.
All Star was released in 1999, with Shrek giving the single a second life.
Smash Mouth is currently touring in the US with its new frontman Zach Goode.

title: Barbie dethrones The Super Mario Bros. Movie to become the year's highest-grossing film
content:
Barbie is still breaking records even after seven weeks in theatres.
This weekend, Greta Gerwig's Barbie, produced by and starring Australian actress Margot Robbie, became the highest-grossing film of 2023 with over $US1.38 billion ($2.13 billion) globally.
The title was previously held by The Super Mario Bros. Movie, which was released in Australia back in April.
It's the latest in a growing list of records set by the film, which became Warner Bros. highest-grossing film of all time just last week.
It toppled Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows Part II, which earned $US1,342,359,942 (not adjusted for inflation).
Just three weeks after its release, Barbie has collected more than $1 billion at the global box office — and it's on track to become the biggest movie of the year.
Back in August, Barbie passed the Barbillion milestone when it reached $US1 billion at the box office, with experts calling its relentless marketing campaign "a masterclass."
The Barbillion milestone saw Barbie become the first billion-dollar film from a solo female director writing Greta Gerwig into the history books.
Its opening weekend also smashed records, earning Barbie the title of the biggest US opening weekend for the year with $US162 million, and the biggest opening weekend of all time for a female director.
Meanwhile, Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer has sailed past $US850 million globally to become the third highest-grossing film of the year.
The consistent box office figures have delivered Nolan his third highest-grossing film of all time, behind 2008′s The Dark Knight and 2012′s The Dark Knight Rises.
Both Barbie and Oppenheimer had a budget of $US100 million. (Supplied: Universal)
The continued success of both Barbie and Oppenheimer comes at a fraught time for Hollywood, with actors seven weeks into a strike for fair contracts with major entertainment companies and movie theatres bracing for a somewhat depleted autumn season as a result.
Despite the strikes, both the Venice and Toronto film festivals are currently underway, though with fewer stars making an appearance.
The last time Hollywood's actors and writers went on strike at the same time, the biggest stars were fighting for residual pay cheques. Decades later, streaming giants and artificial intelligence are at the heart of the debate.
Director David Fincher, promoting his new film The Killer, told the Venice Film Festival he "can understand both sides" of the joint actors and writers' strike.
"I don't know what it says about the industry. I'm very sad, obviously I sit in the middle of both parties," he said, as reported in Variety.
"This movie was made during the pandemic and I never want to make a movie with a visor again.
"But having said that, [we] just got done with three years of having to set our brushes down and walk away — the idea of that continuing on, especially now, is very sad to me.
"I can understand both sides, and I think all we can do is encourage them to talk."

title: For 60 years, X-Men comics have tackled themes of racism, homophobia, anti-Semitism and more
content:
Racism. Homophobia. AIDS. Anti-Semitism. Socialism. Prejudice. Puberty.
These subjects aren't your typical fodder for comic books, but for the past 60 years, these kinds of themes have been at the heart of Marvel's mutant superhero squad, the X-Men.
Partially born out of laziness (yes, really), the X-Men have become an integral part of the Marvel universe, and their comics have been a place where boundaries have been pushed and diversity embraced.
No other heroes have represented the underdogs, misfits and outsiders quite like the X-Men — and it's helped make the mutants one of the most cherished teams in the Marvel stable.
X-Men: First Class, one of the most highly regarded film adaptations of the comics. (Supplied: 20th Century Fox)
In 1963, Stan Lee was on a roll.
Along with artists Jack Kirby and Steve Ditko, the Marvel comic book writer had created an astonishing line-up of superheroes in less than two years, including The Fantastic Four, Ant-Man, The Hulk, Spider-Man, Thor, The Wasp, and Dr Strange.
Stan Lee poses for a photograph taken in the late 1960s. (Twitter: Stan Lee)
But after the hugely popular debut of The Fantastic Four in November 1961, Lee and his Marvel colleagues were pedalling like crazy to keep up with demand and create new superheroes.
Lee in particular was finding it increasingly difficult to come up with character origin stories.
"I was bored with cosmic rays and gamma rays and radioactivity and I was running out of things, and I figured, 'What if they're just mutants?'" he told director and comic book fan Kevin Smith, in an interview.
"It was a cop-out. Look how easy it is — you want somebody who can walk through walls? He was born that way — he's a mutant!
"That was done out of laziness."
But Lee's laziness proved to be an opportunity for a richer level of storytelling not seen in the pages of his other superheroes' comics, such as Iron Man and the Fantastic Four.
The front cover of the first X-Men comic, released in September 1963. (Supplied: Marvel)
"I thought it might be fun to get an analogy with the way some people are picked on by bigots," Lee explained in the DVD extras for the animated anthology, X-Men: Legend of Wolverine.
"Here are characters that are going to look different, who are going to have certain strange powers — what if the human race is afraid of them, hates them perhaps, and [persecutes] them, torments them?
"Suddenly, I became really fascinated by this because I could see there was such a parallel between things that were happening in society and these stories that we were trying to write."
Lee and artist Jack Kirby created the X-Men against the backdrop of the American civil rights movement, with the first issue appearing in September 1963, and it didn't take long for themes of prejudice to seep into the comic.
"When I was young, normal people feared me, distrusted me," X-Men leader Professor X tells new recruit Jean Grey in the very first issue.
In issue #4, villainous mutant Magneto suggests that humans would kill all mutants if they could, purely because they were different, while in issue #5, a mutant athlete is attacked by a crowd at an athletics carnival due to his record-breaking sporting prowess.
Magneto tells Quicksilver humans will "kill us if they could" in a panel from X-Men #4. (Supplied: Marvel)
But the exploits of the original X-Men line-up — Professor X, Cyclops, Beast, Iceman, Angel, and Marvel Girl AKA Jean Grey — never quite took off like The Fantastic Four or Spider-man, and by December 1970, the series was effectively done, with Marvel reprinting old stories instead of spending time and money on new ones.
The title languished until 1975, when British-born writer Chris Claremont helped kick off a new era for the X-Men, with a fresh, more multicultural line-up including a Kenyan-American (Storm) and a native American, as well as mutants from Russia (Colossus), Japan (Sunfire), and Germany (Nightcrawler).
The team also featured a certain indestructible, cigar-chomping, claw-sprouting Canadian named Wolverine, who first appeared in a Hulk comic years earlier, and would ultimately become the most famous mutant of all.
Hugh Jackman as Wolverine in a scene from the movie X-Men Origins: Wolverine, released 2009. (Supplied: IMDB/20th Century Fox)
Suddenly, the X-Men were a melting pot of races, nationalities and religions, and themes that were only hinted at during Lee's initial run began to come to the fore.
Under Claremont's stewardship, X-Men mentor Professor X and chief villain Magneto became two sides of the same coin — the former fighting for mutant acceptance by defending humanity, and the latter lashing out at humans in retribution for their prejudice.
This would lead some commentators to liken them to Martin Luther King and Malcolm X respectively, though, as Claremont told Empire magazine in 2016, that was not his intention.
"[That comparison] is totally valid, but for me, being an immigrant white, to make that analogy felt incredibly presumptuous," he explained.
Chris Claremont wrote X-Men comics for 16 years. (Supplied: Luigi Novi/Wikimedia Commons)
Instead, he was inspired by two months he spent in Israel working on a kibbutz (a communal settlement) in 1970.
For Claremont, Israel's first prime minister David Ben-Gurion was a truer inspiration for Professor X, while terrorist-turned-Nobel Peace Prize-winner Menachem Begin (Israel's sixth PM) was the source for Magneto, who went from villain to anti-hero over Claremont's run.
Claremont's time in Israel also informed his re-writing of Magneto's backstory, turning him from power-hungry supervillain to Holocaust survivor.
"[Working] on a kibbutz … affected me on levels that I hadn't anticipated, working on a daily basis with people who were actual survivors of the Holocaust," Claremont said.
Claremont's writing of women characters was also influenced by the country's compulsory military service for all citizens.
"There is nothing so disconcerting as sitting on a bus and having a young lady walk on with an Uzi flung over her shoulder," he told Empire.
"In 1970, you weren't used to seeing someone you might ask out on a date packing hardware.
"So it's taking that realisation and applying it to the fictional reality of the X-Men and seeing where it leads."
Jennifer Lawrence as Mystique in X-Men: Dark Phoenix. (Supplied: IMDB/20th Century Fox)
The result was a run of strong female characters unlike anything Marvel had seen before — Storm, Kitty Pride, Rogue, Mystique, a reborn Jean Grey, and the villainous Emma Frost.
Through the 70s and 80s, Claremont took those strong characters and gave them weighty themes to match.
Metaphors about racism were drawn, with the creation of a number of mutant-hating groups, including firebrand preacher William Stryker's Purifiers, who also featured in the 1982 graphic novel God Loves, Man Kills, which explored religious extremism.
The much-loved Days of Future Past storyline in 1981 imagined a Holocaust-like future for mutants, who were hunted down and killed or locked in concentration camps.
The X-Men have been one of Marvel's most interesting teams since they began 60 years ago. (Supplied: Marvel)
In the 90s, the Legacy Virus story arc introduced a disease that killed only mutants, leading to reviewers calling it an AIDS allegory.
Then screenwriter/director Joss Whedon's mid-2000s run on X-Men introduced a mutant "cure", which was seen by many as analogous to so-called "gay conversion therapy", and the misguided notion that homosexuality was something that needed to be cured.
Members of the X-Men line-up have often been members of the LGBTQIA+ community.
Northstar, one of the first openly gay superheroes in American comics, debuted in an X-Men comic, while versions of popular characters Iceman, Psylocke, Mystique and Colossus have come out as gay or bisexual over the years.
Arts and culture critic and X-Men enthusiast Cassie Tongue said Marvel's mutants and their real-world analogies were "hugely important" in the world of comics.
"These are the representatives of anyone who doesn't quite align with society's standards or values, and they have a commitment to fighting for the underdog," Tongue said.
Cyclops, Iceman, the Angel and the Beast, led by Professor X, in the X-Men's 1963 comic debut. (Supplied: Marvel)
"Often superheroes are on the right side of popular favour, they tend to be on the right side of the police and the government, and they tend to fit into these structural systems of oppression that exist in the world.
"But when you have a superhero team that fights in opposition to the structural powers that oppress people, what you're starting to see is an example of resistance … and you start to get the sense that just fighting to maintain the status quo is perhaps not the best thing that we can do.
Tongue said X-Men's 60-year history meant writers who grew up reading the comic and feeling seen, or impressed by its themes, had taken them further in recent decades.
Cassie Tongue says the X-Men are "hugely important" for their diversity and representation. (Supplied: Cassie Tongue)
"I think that's what's really interesting about comics being these ongoing, multi-decade storylines is that you end up with these new generations of writers who are influenced, not just by what's on the page, but by how people have received it for decades," she said.
While X-Men comics haven't always been perfect in their attempts to tackle themes typically explored by "serious literature", Tongue said the mutant storylines were often welcomed by those who identified as outsiders.
"Speaking personally, I found the comics when I was really coming to terms with my queer identity," she said.
"So even these things that were just gestured at, or were clumsy, or were potentially actually quite offensive … what they were doing was establishing room … for queerness, or for taking some pride in these other identities."
She said for people looking for something to cling on to, "even if it's not the best or greatest politically … it does mean something to you".
"The difference between the other [Marvel] superhero teams [is that they are] colleagues or they're families — but the X-Men is a community that makes itself a family.
Mutant superhero Northstar (right) married his partner Kyle Jinadu in Astonishing X-Men in 2012. (Supplied: Marvel)
"There's that sense of finding a place in the world … [and] that gives you hope that you will also find your people."
Despite dying a quiet death by unpopularity in the early 70s, X-Men grew to become Marvel's biggest-selling comic by the start of the 80s.
From that point, it splintered off into multiple titles, and a revamp of the series at the peak of its popularity in 1991 led to the release of a new X-Men #1 comic.
It sold in excess of 3 million issues, making it the biggest selling comic book of all time.
The X-juggernaut has spawned more than 12,000 comics written over the past 60 years, selling more than 260 million issues, and making it the second-biggest Marvel property behind Spider-man, and the fourth overall behind DC's Batman and Superman.
Deadpool, who was created in the 90s, has become one of Marvel's best-known mutants. (Supplied: 20th Century Fox)
There have been 13 live-action X-Men movies, which have helped make characters such as Wolverine, Deadpool and Jean Grey household names.
The first X-Men film in 2000 is even credited with kickstarting the current superhero movie craze, earning almost $300m at the box office, and scoring an 82 per cent rating on critic aggregator Rotten Tomatoes.
Today, X-Men fans are eagerly awaiting a new big screen era for the mutants.
A stack of Spider-Man-related movies are set to swing into cinemas, and fans of the web-spinning superhero couldn't be happier.
Disney's purchase of 20th Century Fox in 2019 means the X-Men can finally be integrated into the gargantuan film franchise that is the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU).
There have already been hints in the Doctor Strange in the Multiverse Of Madness film, and the Disney+ TV series Ms Marvel.
But the first real MCU foray for the X-Men will be Deadpool 3, which sees Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman returning as Deadpool and Wolverine respectively.
How exactly Reynolds's irreverent "Merc With The Mouth" will break down the walls between the X-Men universe and the MCU remains to be seen.
But fans are bracing for it to kickstart the next phase of the biggest film franchise in the world, and to give the mutants a new burst of popularity, 60 years on from their "lazy" creation.

title: Sliding doors-style romance explores the past loves and missed connections that can haunt us
content:
Movies, as filmmaker Andrei Tarkovsky famously put it, are capable of sculpting in time, making them the perfect medium to tangle with tales of loss and longing; to approximate the vagaries of memory – both individual and collective – and to reanimate those missed connections that can haunt us.
The big what-if at the heart of South Korean Canadian playwright turned filmmaker Celine Song's debut feature is custom-made for the movies. It's a story of childhood sweethearts separated by decades, distance and domestic partners; a relationship that lingers despite (or because of) its defiance of logic, and one that will be instantly recognisable to anyone who's experienced the cruel passage of time.
Song's buzzy, semi-autobiographical Past Lives pivots on 30-something New York playwright Nora (played with a keen, casual warmth by Russian Doll's Greta Lee), who we first encounter at a late-night cocktail lounge, sat between two men: Hae Sung (Teo Yoo, Decision to Leave) and Arthur (John Magaro, First Cow).
It might be a love triangle, except Nora's enigmatic glance toward the camera tells us there's something deeper, more inscrutable at play.
"It's a very intimate thing when you're working with an actor … [on set] I felt really married to my actors," Song told ABC RN's Stop Everything! (Supplied: A24)
So begins a story of sliding doors and alternate realities that unfolds across 24 years and three moving chapters, a movie possessed with an uncanny sense of time, memory and dream.
As 12-year-olds back in Seoul in the late 90s, Nora – then Na Young (Seung Ah Moon) – and Hae Sung (Seung Min Yim) are overachieving school rivals and inseparable besties, a friendship-turned-puppy love after the pair go on a sweet, parent-chaperoned date that ends with hands entwined and sleepy heads on shoulders.
But Na Young is soon whisked away to live in Toronto with her artist-filmmaker parents, cutting short a childhood romance that seems forever banished, like so many adolescent things, to the mists of time.
Like Nora, Song emigrated from Korea at age 12 to Toronto, Canada, before moving to New York in her 20s. (Supplied: A24)
More than a decade later, Na Young, now going by Nora, is embarking on a writing career in early 2010s New York when she reconnects with Hae Sung over Facebook – as was the style at the time – and the childhood friends strike up an online correspondence, full of disjointed time zone Skype chats and shared observations on life back home.
If their relationship displays a renewed intensity, then it's not for long: Feeling overwhelmed by the long-distance connection, Nora puts her friendship with Hae Yung on indefinite ice, and by chance falls for dreamy, doe-eyed fellow writer Arthur at a pastoral artist retreat in upstate New York.
As they swoon over candlelight, Nora explains to Arthur the Korean concept of "in-yun": providence, or the fate that connects souls from one life to the next. (Nora then jokes to Arthur: "That's just something Koreans say to seduce people.")
"When Nora and Hae Sung connect for the first time … it feels like a miracle," Song told ABC RN's Stop Everything! (Supplied: A24)
The idea ripples like temporal waves across Song's film, both thematically and as a cinematic conceit: Past Lives bears the DNA of a whole history of movies that wrestle with time and memory, from the Celine and Julie Go Boating poster tucked away in Nora's father's office to the explicit invocation, via an on-screen clip, of Michel Gondry's high-concept heartbreaker, Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind.
It's a brave filmmaker that puts their tale of thwarted romance in the same space as that high-water mark of the genre, and there are moments when Song's relatively straightforward screenplay – which can feel schematic to the point of being opaque – seems to want for some of the more ambitious time-scrambling of the movie it so reveres. (The subject matter is certainly something that a more slippery filmmaker – the late genius Alain Resnais, say, or contemporary time-poets Ryusuke Hamaguchi or Hong Sang-soo – might have twisted to different ends.)
"They're not really exes, right? But they're not strangers either," Song told ABC News. (Supplied: A24)
Yet the film's directness, its relative storytelling simplicity, is also its asset. Past Lives unravels at a rhythm that weaves a slow-burning spell, one that allows an audience the space to project their own experience onto the screen. Caressed by Shabier Kirchner's soft-touch cinematography, reminiscent of his work on Steve McQueen's Small Axe series and Crystal Moselle's gauzy Skate Kitchen, the film seems to unfold in the watercolour haze of a half-remembered daydream. Meanwhile, the wispy soundtrack, by Grizzly Bear musicians Christopher Bear and Daniel Rossen, bleeds into diegetic pop songs – think John Cale's indelible You Know More Than I Know – that bubble up and then vanish into the ether.
Things that slip away, forever just out of grasp. Why does Hae Yung remain so obsessed, a less forgiving audience might wonder, in the face of Nora's very obvious, indisputable love for another? It can seem like a slender, maybe farcical – or worse, creepy – peg on which to hang an entire plot, until it clicks: So often we cling to the feelings that can never be acted upon, even when – especially when – they become more distant as time passes.
Though it successfully conjures romance lost, Past Lives is as much a reverie for a culture as it is for any one person; an impression of cultural displacement and the ways in which culture lingers and ruptures across generations of diaspora. Emigration can separate families from culture just as it can enrich and birth new ones, but traces of vanished pasts remain.
Lee was a musical theatre star on Broadway before she moved into film. (Supplied: A24)
Past Lives is, as Song has remarked, a lament for the Korean girl – and culture – she has long lost.
"He's so Korean," Nora says of Hae Sung at one point, teasing out a cultural notion she appears to have sublimated. "I feel so not Korean when I'm with him, and also more Korean."
Time evaporates in a heartbeat in Past Lives, and life – in the words most commonly attributed to John Lennon – is what happens while you're busy making other plans. In Song's film, the passage of time is a phenomenon that brings together the personal and the cultural; a filmmaker's memory and that of her audience.
And that's – to put Tarkovsky's sentiment another way – the magic of the movies, baby.
Past Lives is in cinemas now.

title: Is Netflix in its flop era? Subscribers are down for the first time since 2015
content:
In a first since its launch in Australia, Netflix's subscription numbers have taken a dip.
With a crackdown on password sharing and a more competitive market than ever before — is Netflix's presence in Australia fading?
The streaming giant entered the Australian market in 2015, and since then has been Australia's most popular subscription video service, with an estimated 6.1 million Australian users today.
But for the first time since its launch in Australia, Netflix's subscription numbers have declined, falling 3 per cent as of June 2023, according to research firm Telsyte's annual Australian Subscription Entertainment Study.
Australia's video streaming market is more competitive than ever before.
The study tells a different story for the other streaming offerings like Amazon Prime Video and Disney+, which all experienced an increase in Australian subscribers.
The results aren't surprising to film and television writer Cameron Williams, who says the numbers indicate that Netflix's content offering isn't engaging local audiences like it had previously.
Alongside more competition, Netflix has also been getting stricter with its subscribers.
You may have been confronted recently with a message on your screen when using the streaming service, asking you to confirm that your device is part of your account's household.
The television show Stranger Things has been one of Netflix's biggest international hits.  (Netflix/21 Laps Entertainment)
That's because this year Netflix announced it was cracking down on password sharing across households, often done by users to save money.
Worldwide, Netflix estimated that 100 million people were getting passwords from others to access Netflix content from 232 million paying subscribers.
Combined with an increase in the costs of living and a more competitive streaming market, the study reports that while Netflix remains the streaming leader in Australia, the dip is a first for them.
And just last month Netflix reported its biggest springtime growth in subscribers internationally, following the password-sharing measures and the rollout of cheaper subscription plans that included advertising for the first time.
The study shows that password sharing is rife in Australia, with one in three streaming subscribers sharing their log-ins with friends and family.
Interestingly, the study also showed only 7 per cent of those who had subscribed to Netflix in the previous 12 months ended up canceling due to the new sharing rules.
"Netflix has always been a leader in Australia as a streaming platform because of the headstart they got," Williams said.
Netflix is still Australia's market leader when it comes to streaming, but the study shows us that Australian subscribers are more savvy than ever before.
The study showed that nearly half of the subscribers in Australia claimed they were more likely to switch between different services to save money, and only a small percentage said they found it "difficult to unsubscribe".
Alvin Lee, senior analyst at Telsyte, said the study told us Australian consumers still prioritised streaming services in their budget, but were more likely to move around.
When it was released, Squid Game hit number one on Netflix in 90 countries including Australia. (Reuters: Kim Hong-Ji/Illustration)
"They have to make a conscious choice depending on where the content is that they're interested in … they might be more encouraged to switch between services more as a result, try something different, and then come back again," Lee said.
That behaviour, alongside a change in the ways in which streamers are releasing their content, looks to be contributing to Netflix Australia losing audiences for the first time.
Not quite, but Cameron Williams said the decline in Netflix subscription numbers in Australia showed that binge-watching a show was no longer viewed as superior to a more traditional weekly drop.
"With Netflix, one of the biggest challenges is that in the last few years, audiences have gone from the binge model where they've really enjoyed watching everything all at once," he said.
Succession's final season was aired in Australia via weekly episodes on the streaming platform Binge.  (Supplied: HBO/BINGE)
"But now we're seeing the week-to-week format has slowly crept back in popularity," he said.
The study shows that, despite Netflix's dip, the overall gain in subscriptions across streaming services available in Australia means that audiences prioritise spending money on streaming, and are more likely to give up other costs before they give up their streaming accounts.
The study estimates that the total number of video-on-demand subscriptions could reach over 30 million by June 2027.
"I think what we are witnessing is the market has slowed down a little bit, compared to previously, but subscription services are still in over  70 per cent of Australian households," Alvin Lee said.
"It's still a very significant number … but what we're seeing is that there's increasing competition across services, and consumer interest in new content across multiple services."
As the international streaming industry faces uncertainty ahead, with the writers and acting strikes in the US continuing, Cameron Williams says Netflix can still turn things around in Australia.
"All it will take is a few shows that get people talking and get them back on the platform … People can be pretty fickle sometimes when it comes to the choices that they make," he said.

title: Celine Song explores 'destined connection' in tender directorial debut Past Lives
content:
How different would your life be if you'd been given different choices?
Director Celine Song's debut film, Past Lives, which has received critical acclaim, explores the connections made between people and the yearning for paths not travelled.
Song was born in South Korea before moving to Toronto at a young age, leaving behind a childhood sweetheart.
The film stars Greta Lee, Teo Yoo and John Magaro and is inspired in part by Song's life.
In the film, Nora (Lee) and Hae Sung (Yoo) are childhood best friends, who are separated after Nora's family immigrates to Canada.
Moon Seung-ah plays young Nora alongside Lee Seung-min playing young Hae Sung. (Studio Canal)
They reconnect briefly in their 20s over Skype and, 12 years later, Hae Sung travels to New York to visit Nora, who is now married to Arthur (Magaro) and working as a writer.
"I think the reason why it is connecting with people universally is because I think we all have an experience connecting with the part of ourselves that's left behind in a place, in a person, or in a time in your life," Song told the ABC while in Australia for the Melbourne International Film Festival.
"I think that really is at the heart of what the movie is."
Past Lives trailer YouTube
Past Lives also introduces audiences to the Korean concept of inyun, or "destined connection", where meeting someone means you've met them in a past life. People in love are those who have met repeatedly throughout their past lives.
In other words, inyun is the "feeling of being connected and appreciating the people who enter your life— in this one, or the one before, or the ones to come", according to the film's production notes.
"It really came to the answer to the mystery of the story -- the question of who are these three people to each other? It really came from the need to actually answer that question, because I would say who Hae Sung and Nora are to each other is inyun because there's no other way to really describe them," Song said.
Lee (right) who plays Nora says it's "so unfair" that people only have one life. (Studio Canal)
"They're not really exes, right? But they're not strangers either.
"I think you would say that they're inyun because it's so deep like that. I would also say that Hae Sung and Arthur are inyun.
"Hae Sung and Arthur are inyun, because again, there's no other way to describe who they are.
Childhood friends Nora (Greta Lee) and Hae Sung (Teo Yoo) reconnect in New York in Past Lives. (Studio Canal)
The film is subversive to romance films, in that it doesn't force Nora to choose between both men, but rather contemplates what could have been.
"It's so unfair, the devastating thing about us as people, the fact that we only have one life," said Lee, who plays Nora, in the film's production notes.
John Magaro plays Nora's husband Arthur.
For Song, living life without regret has to do with how you think about your own life and what you're willing to change.
"It has to do with knowing and feeling empowered to make a change if you need to. When you don't feel like you need to make a change, to me, that's really a sign that you're very happy there, right?" Song said.
"Even though maybe, of course any kind of life is going to involve some unhappiness and some happiness, but I think to be properly in a happy moment in your life, I think you really do need to feel empowered, to be in charge of your own life."
The film's opening scene is at a bar, with Nora, sitting in between Hae Sung and Arthur as other people try to guess who they are to each other.
The three share a conversation, with Nora as the translator between both men. It's a scene that mirrors a moment in Song's own life, with her own husband and childhood sweetheart meeting up at a bar in New York several years ago.
South Korean-Canadian director Celine Song's first film is Past Lives. (Supplied: Matthew Dunivan)
Describing that point in time, Song said: "It's the moment that made me feel like the scale of my life, even though I feel like the scale of my life is usually just very small because I'm an ordinary person."
"It felt like the scale was fully expanded, and I felt like I was so much bigger and more epic as a result of that moment.
"I think that's what really made me feel like this was kind of a special thing.
Past Lives releases in Australian cinemas on August 31.

title: Australia drops perjury case against Amber Heard over importation of Pistol and Boo
content:
The Australian government has dropped its case against actor Amber Heard over allegations she lied about the illegal importation of her two dogs, Pistol and Boo, in 2015.
Ms Heard was charged eight years ago with breaching Australia's strict quarantine laws by bringing her two Yorkshire terriers to the country without declaring them.
It caused an international storm after then-agriculture minister Barnaby Joyce threatened the dogs would be destroyed unless Ms Heard and her ex-partner Johnny Depp returned them to California.
Ms Heard paid a fine for the quarantine breach but escaped conviction after pleading guilty and expressing remorse in an awkwardly taped video apology with Mr Depp.
Mr Joyce accepted the apology from the Hollywood actors, though he said it was unlikely to win them an Academy Award.
Depp and Heard posted an apology over the Pistol and Boo incident.
But in 2020, during a libel case against a British newspaper outlet, Mr Depp claimed that Ms Heard had known she was illegally bringing her terriers into the country, and had pressured Mr Depp to lie under oath after she was charged.
Ms Heard's former assistant also backed that allegation in court, saying Ms Heard had ignored advice that taking the dogs to Australia would be problematic.
Following those claims, the Australian government launched an investigation into the claims of perjury.
The Agriculture Department said it had investigated the claims with assistance from Australian and overseas agencies, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation, and prepared a brief for prosecutors.
But in a determination published by the department, it confirmed the Commonwealth director of public prosecutions had decided not to proceed with a case against Ms Heard.
In 2021, Heard named a new puppy "Barnaby", posting photos online of her hiding the dog under her coat, and joking that "some habits die hard".

title: Bradley Cooper has been accused of 'Jewface' over his new movie — here's what that means
content:
Bradley Cooper has faced an onslaught of criticism for wearing a prosthetic nose to play the late conductor and composer Leonard Bernstein, in his latest film Maestro.
The backlash came after Netflix released the first trailer to the romantic biographical drama, which was also directed and co-written by Cooper.
Critics are calling it a classic case of "Jewface" and it's not the first of its kind Hollywood has seen.
Let's unpack why this has blown up all over the Internet.
While there's nothing wrong with actors using prosthetics in order to look more like the person they are portraying, the act of enlarging one's nose to resemble a Jewish person has deep historical ties to antisemitism.
The offence cuts deeper than aesthetic mockery.
It reinforces a negative connotation towards the community that dates all the way back to the 12th century.
Chair of the Anti-Defamation Commission, Australia's leading civil rights organisation fighting antisemitism, Dr Dvir Abramovich expands on this.
Dr Dvir Abramovich is the head of Jewish Studies at the University of Melbourne and chair of the Anti-Defamation Commission. (Supplied: Dvir Abramovich)
"When it comes to this firestorm, I don't think that Bradley Cooper is antisemite — let's get this [straight]," says Dr Abramovich.
"[But] the idea of wearing a prosthetic nose to say this is what Jews look like, has always been problematic.
Nazi propaganda referenced a large, hooked nose as an identifying feature of a Jewish person, which Dr Abramovich says was used to "fan the flames of hatred and distrust towards the Jewish communities".
The matter lies in distinguishing the difference between intent and effect.
Dr Abramovich, who is also the Head of Jewish Studies at the University of Melbourne, says the harm comes from the message it perpetuates and the effect it brings to community.
Believing Cooper's decision to be an oversight, he says, "You could argue that it was an artistic judgement, but I think there also needs to be sensitivity to the fact of what a Jewish nose means."
Media and pop culture expert Lauren Rosewarne from the University of Melbourne breaks down the layers to the issue.
The first relates to casting, she says.
Bernstein was of Jewish background, born to Ukrainian parents who migrated to the United States.
While the film is premised on the romantic relationship Bernstein had with his lifelong wife Felicia, critics took offence to Cooper for not having any religious or ethnic relations to Judaism.
Bradley Cooper plays Leonard Bernstein alongside Carrey Mulligan as his wife in the movie Maestro. (Source: Netflix)
"This was the perfect opportunity to have a Jewish actor in the role that it makes no sense to use a gentile actor," says Dr Rosewarne.
Dr Rosewarne says that Cooper's "distinctively troublesome" use of prosthetics compounds the issue at hand.
"They could have cast an actor who actually looked more like the character being portrayed," she says.
"Instead, they've used prosthetics to make Cooper look more stereotypically Jewish with an oversized nose synonymous with the Jewish caricature."
Bernstein's three children, Jamie, Alexander and Nina, have taken to social platform X to stand in solidarity with Cooper, saying they have been consulted throughout the making of the project.
In a statement posted on Bernstein's official account, they wrote:
"Bradley Cooper included the three of us along every step of his amazing journey as he made his film about our father.
"We were touched to the core to witness the depth of his commitment, his loving embrace of our father's music, and the sheer open-hearted joy he brought to his exploration.
"It breaks our hearts to see any misrepresentations or misunderstandings of his efforts."
They were also fully aware and supportive of Cooper's editorial decision for his character to wear a prosthetic nose and said Bernstein would not have had an issue with it either.
"It happens to be true that Leonard Bernstein had a nice, big nose.
"Bradley chose to use make-up to amplify his resemblance, and we're perfectly fine with that.
"We're also certain that our dad would have been fine with it as well."
Drawing on parallels from Bernstein's life experiences, they see the criticism as an attempt to make a dent on Cooper's career.
The statement ended on a strong note, highlighting the success of the film in showcasing the romance between their parents and how they were happy to be involved.
The film industry has had a long-standing battle with representation and inclusion for decades.
Casting a light-skinned woman to play a brown character in a Disney movie is one version of colourism, but in Hollywood and the Pacific there are more layers of complexity
Cooper's stunt is one of many other cases of "Jewface" on screen.
In 1948, actor Alec Guinness portrayal of Fagin in Oliver Twist involved him wearing a prosthetic nose and it was deemed "incredibly insensitive" and incited a lot of anger from Holocaust survivors.
The film release was withdrawn after the New York Board of rabbis labelled it "a vehicle of blatant antisemitism", said Dr Abramovich.
Associate Professor Ted Nannicelli from UQ's School of Communication and Arts outlines the reasons behind the struggle.
"For a long time in Hollywood, there was an under representation of people of particular races and ethnicities," says the screen studies and ethics expert.
"Then there's the history of under representation of actors of those races and those ethnicities."
Mr Nannicelli says the two are not to be confused with one another where the former happens when non-flattering or substantive roles were given to certain groups of people.
It's easy to think that underrepresentation is due to the lack of talent in the pool but that's not quite the case.
Mr Nannicelli says, "It's a complex mix of local laws, consideration of who the market is and what the perceived moral norms of the target audience are" among other things.
This resulted in people of minority groups — whether that be racial, ethnic, or religious — to be excluded from job opportunities based on those characteristics.
He says, "That was undeniably the case in Hollywood cinema."
"But that problem has been addressed to some extent over the past decades and there has been more progress more recently, within the last decade or so.
Then there's the issue of ethnic cosplay — when actors outside of a particular ethnic group dresses-up as a person from another ethnicity using props or costuming.
Mr Nannicelli says, "Intuitively, it seems like it's much worse to have someone who is white performing "blackface" than it is to have a non-Catholic play a Catholic because there [have] different histories [relating to oppression]."
Not to forget, it's also easy to dismiss the latter when it can't be clearly seen or have not been made known in the role.
But according to Mr Nannicelli, studios do show a clear interest in aligning themselves with the current norms and values of society.
"Or at least if not aligning themselves, most certainly not alienating," he adds.
Maestro is a towering and fearless love story chronicling the lifelong relationship between cultural icon Leonard Bernstein and Felicia Montealegre Cohn Bernstein.
Dr Abramovich argues this is when true authenticity comes in.
"There's quite a lot of angst about this idea of casting non-Jews in roles that are deeply and profoundly Jewish," he says, bringing it back to Cooper's casting decision.
"When you talk about the Jewish lived experience, which is often fundamental and critical to the actual role, you should cast Jewish actors.
It also helps to dispel stereotypes which can be damaging.
Media and pop culture expert Dr Rosewarne says, "Stereotypes work to frame certain groups of people as different, as less human".
"Through such normalised dehumanisation, certain people come to feel justified in not only harbouring bigoted views but acting on them.
"In recent years, spikes in attacks on certain communities have been documented including antisemitic violence."
Dr Abramovich too observes this in Australia and wants Hollywood to do better.
"Anti-Jewish bigotry is becoming part of our daily lives and is creeping into every facet of our society.

title: As Australia's film industry booms, workers are wanted behind the scenes
content:
From Baz Luhrmann's blockbuster biopic Elvis to Russell Crowe's vision for Aussiewood, Australia is gaining popularity as a location for long-form TV drama and film productions.
More "below-the-line" workers are needed to manage large-scale productions both in studio and on location, but how realistic is it to find work behind the scenes and what is the formula for success?
The 2020-21 ABS Film, Television and Digital Games Survey highlights significant employment growth within Australia's screen industry — a jump of 37 per cent since 2015-16.
"The Australian film industry is booming, and we acknowledge that alongside the rise in production has come staffing challenges, leading to increased demand for below-the-line roles," says Graeme Mason, CEO of Screen Australia.
"This demand also creates exciting employment opportunities for our talented workforce, which will ultimately provide career pathways and employment opportunities in the screen industry.
"Screen Australia is committed to supporting the industry in meeting these demands."
Behind the scenes on Frances, a film shot on Sharkies Beach in the Illawarra, by Eye Candy Films director Sharon Lewis. (Supplied: Sharon Lewis)
Louise Hodgson, industry programs manager for Screenworks in Ballina, says it's a "brilliant time" to get into the industry.
Australia is crying out for crew members now, she says, adding that below-the-line workers can be anyone who isn't a director, writer or producer.
"There is a shortage of below-the-line crew across Australia," Hodgson says.
The Kiama workshop was hosted by representatives of Cato Logistics, Screen NSW, 2Kats Productions and Screen Illawarra. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)
Conferences, industry events and workshops facilitate opportunities for writers, producers and directors to meet up and talk shop, but where do you go for support if you are keen to work as a regional screen practitioner?
Both Screen Illawarra and Screenworks in Ballina are examples of how grant funding, specifically from Screen Australia, is helping to boost workshops across NSW.
The workshops aim to address a shortage of location managers on film sets in New South Wales. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)
A recent, well-attended workshop held by Screen Illawarra in Kiama, with funding from Screen NSW, provided an opportunity for experienced location managers Keiran Cato, Lisa Scope and Karen Illesca to talk about the role.
Karen Illesca's job as a location scouting agent involves influencing where shows are filmed. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)
"Screen NSW have recognised a lack of locations people in NSW, particularly in regional areas, which is why they are running workshops," Illesca says.
Illesca was a stay-at-home mum before participating in a short film course and then volunteering at the Australian Film and Television Radio School (AFTRS).
"I did some scouting initially and a short course with Screen NSW where I met people from the film industry," she says.
Keiran Cato delivers traffic management, security, safety and vehicles on location.  (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)
After a decade in the film logistics business, Keiran Cato is enthusiastic about the growth of the Australian screen industry, especially as it spreads into the regions.
"The industry has been growing, especially the last couple of years pre-COVID and then once COVID hit, it has absolutely boomed," he says.
"It comes down to what the location requires so, Poker Face with Russell Crowe, they were looking for undulating road locations.
"I spoke to the team about doing stuff down in Gerringong and Nowra way."
The rolling green hills of Kiama and Gerringong provide a luscious rural backdrop. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)
Over the past few years the Illawarra has supported productions such as Poker Face (2022), the Invisible Man (2020) and the yet-to-be released Planet of the Apes, which was shot in Jamberoo.
The Appleton Ladies' Potato Race (2023) was also filmed in the Southern Highlands.
Cato didn't start at AFTRS, he focused on networking and events to meet people in the industry, starting out as a personal assistant to Toby Maguire in the Great Gatsby and continually networking at events until moving into logistics.
50 years of Australia's Film Television and Radio School
Louise Hodgson agrees that attending AFTRS is not the only way to get a job on set.
She says it's about looking for opportunities beyond education.
"Education is brilliant, and you can get certain skills in certain areas for certain departments, but other departments you can take a school leaver, train them up properly, give them an opportunity and they can be working."
Screenworks, which is in its second year of a regional crew trainee program, is assisting people to find work.
Crew members whose names appear in the credits at the end of the show can use this as currency to get ahead and forge a career in the industry.
"I've got three school leavers on set up on Troppo, shooting on the Gold Coast, and they are amassing credits, which are gold for them," Hodgson says.
Lambs of God (2018) was partly shot in the Illawarra.  (Supplied: Screen NSW)
In July, Screen Australia announced $1.7 million in funding to meet the production needs of the industry.
Programs like Screenworks' Set for Success aim to reduce workforce gaps through mentoring, guidance and training.
Illesca says they are a valuable experience for people who want to get a foot in the door in the industry.
"Networking through industry events and workshops facilitates respect and establishes trust that you will be reliable," she says.
"So it's a really good opportunity to make new relationships, catch up with old friends, learn something new and share knowledge."

title: Does Mozart’s Magic Flute hold the key to our existential crisis? Simon McBurney says yes
content:
In 2014, British actor and theatre-maker Simon McBurney went to the Amazon rainforest. Twenty years earlier, he had been given a copy of Petru Popescu's book Amazon Beaming: an extraordinary account of a National Geographic photojournalist, Loren McIntyre, who in 1971 was stranded in a remote part of the jungle with the Mayoruna people — an Indigenous tribe untouched by modern civilization — and had his 'doors of perception' blown wide open.
Among the many incredible experiences McIntyre recounted to Popescu was what he called "thought transference": non-verbal communication between himself and the tribe's headman. Over the course of his sojourn with the Mayoruna, McIntyre's understanding of himself and the world was turned upside down and inside out.
Decades later, McBurney wanted to turn this story into a theatre show that would similarly blow the minds of his audience. Why? He gives an eloquent, persuasive explanation in his 2015 preface to the reprint of Amazon Beaming:
"It is both salutary and necessary to have our assumptions challenged in the self-centred times we live in. To really consider the idea that we are deeply interconnected, inseparable from one another, just as we are inseparable from nature even when we do not think of ourselves as 'living in nature'. To truly accept that we are part of the ecosystem wherever we are and that we cannot escape it, just as we cannot escape the planet. And also to accept that our ability to hear, to listen to each other, is perhaps essential for our collective survival. These thoughts are urgent because, in order to survive, we need to acknowledge that there is another way of seeing the world and our place in it."
In 2015, McBurney premiered his stage adaptation, The Encounter: A tour de force combination of a solo live performance, on-stage foley art and in-ear sound design — delivered through individual headphones worn by audience members. It's a perfect marriage of form and content: Through the power of the story being told to us by the performer on stage (McBurney), and astoundingly 'immersive' binaural sound design, each audience member — sitting alone in their cone of sound, but together with many others in the theatre — undertakes the very act of collective imagination that the story is grappling with.
McBurney (pictured) co-directed The Encounter with Kirsty Housley, as well as performing in the show. (Getty Images: Walter McBride)
The Encounter went on to tour Europe, North America, Russia and Australia (where it showed in Sydney, Melbourne, Perth and Adelaide), garnering rave reviews and selling out seasons. In 2019, The Guardian ranked it #13 in the 50 best theatre works of the 21st century. In 2020, with the world in COVID lockdown, The Guardian screened a filmed version of the show.
Suffice to say: The Encounter put Simon McBurney on the global map in a way that no other show in his four-decade career has — and consolidated his reputation as theatre-maker of rare inventiveness and vision.
As an actor, McBurney's screen credits include Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and Mission: Impossible — Rogue Nation, Stan series The Loudest Voice, and Apple series Hijacked.  (Getty Images: AFP/Anne-Christine Poujoulat)
This month, McBurney returns to Australia with a very different offer: His interpretation of Mozart's opera The Magic Flute. Filmed by New York's Metropolitan Opera, where it opened in May, it will beam into Australian cinemas from Saturday for a limited run.
The Magic Flute is a world away — quite literally — from McIntyre's mind-blowing adventure in the Amazon, and more than two centuries separate The Magic Flute's genesis in 1791, Vienna, from its contemporary audience.
McBurney closes the gap with his production, which resonates clearly in the present, and carries a message almost as urgent as The Encounter, if more subtly telegraphed: That art literally holds the answer to humankind's existential crises.
McBurney first tackled The Magic Flute in 2012 for the Dutch National Opera, and reworked that production for the Metropolitan Opera's 2023 season. (Supplied: The Metropolitan Opera)
Talking to McBurney, you quickly understand the power of a good story — and realise that he's a master at spinning one.
When I reach him, via Zoom, it's near midnight in Stroud, Gloucestershire, the small market town in the Cotswolds where he lives with his wife, concert pianist Cassie Yukawa, and their three children. He's 90 minutes late to the call because he's been on bedtime duties; but listening to him talk about the valley and community his family lives in, and the birdlife, and the garden where his children grow vegetables, any angst about deadlines fades.
McBurney paints Stroud as an intriguing, left-of-centre community that runs the gamut of "witches covens", hippies and climate activists (it's the birthplace of Extinction Rebellion and the location of Stop Ecocide's international headquarters, he tells me) — with only a "handful of Tories".
"It's slightly different to the rest of the Cotswolds, which are a little bit 'chocolate box' — and full of David Cameron clones, which is unspeakable," he says drily.
McBurney played "the appalling Rupert Murdoch" (as he describes him) in the 2019 mini series The Loudest Voice, opposite Russell Crowe. (Supplied: Stan)
He tries to get back home as much as he can when working internationally, and says that pre-COVID, he had it written into his work contracts that he would return each weekend. Family is at the front of his mind.
McBurney, 65, became a father in 2009, and he tells me having kids has affected his activism around climate change and the work he does — as a solo operator, and with his world-renowned company Complicité, which he co-founded in 1983.
McBurney's current Complicité projects include the series Figures in Extinction, in collaboration with Nederlands Dans Theater; the digital theatre production Can I Live?, in which young British actor Fehinti Balogun shares his journey to climate activism; and an adaptation of Nobel Prize-winning Polish author Olga Tokarczuk's 2019 novel Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead, a droll murder mystery in which nasty men who abuse nature get their comeuppance.
Beyond his work, he's been a vocal, public proponent of both Extinction Rebellion (XR) and Stop Ecocide, attending and Tweeting about rallies. In an impassioned video promoting XR's April 2019 London rally, he said:
"Everything has to change, and that is our challenge, as Naomi Klein puts it: not simply to spend a lot of money [or] change a lot of policies … It's that we need to think differently, or radically differently, for those changes to be possible."
McBurney (with his daughter) at the premiere of Carnival Row, in which he plays plays a street performer - appropriate, given his early days as a student of Jacques Lecoq. (Getty Images: AFP/Anne-Christine Poujoulat)
So what does all this have to do with Mozart's 'chocolate box' opera, about a prince who ventures into a magical kingdom to win the love of a princess, with the aid of a magic flute; an opera whose most popular iteration to date has been Julie Taymor's abridged, English language version for families, featuring colourful animal puppets?
And why is one of the world's most experimental theatre-makers shackling himself to an artform that is inherently constrained by its set score and libretto, but also by the limitations of performers whose main business is singing?
As with most questions posed to Burney, the answer is a cracking story. But it starts with a disclaimer: "I grew up not enjoying opera at all, and I had no real relationship to it."
"But then I was persuaded into it about 14 years ago, to do a new opera. And one of the reasons I did that was that I got to rewrite the libretto so that the dramatic shape of it really worked, and [so] I felt I could make it [the production] work. And it had a dog in it — so that was also a big draw for me. It was based on [Mikhail] Bulgakov's short story Heart of A Dog, which is a fantastic piece."
That opera, titled A Dog's Heart, was commissioned and produced by the Dutch National Opera (where it premiered in 2010) and English National Opera, in collaboration with Complicité, and looked more like avant-garde theatre than a typical, capital-o "Opera".
"It happened to be a huge success — and so on the back of that I was asked to do Mozart. First I was asked to do Don Giovanni, and I said I wouldn't do that. And then I was asked to do The Magic Flute, and I said I wouldn't do that. But then I was persuaded to do it. And the reason I wouldn't do it [initially] is that it's very difficult and the libretto is very complicated. It's a mess, basically. And it's full of oddities and misogyny and weirdness," he explains.
"But the music is sublime."
McBurney's production of Alban Berg's opera Wozzeck, about "the tyranny of the the patriarchal structure of the world", premiered at the Festival d'Aix-en-Provence in July.  (Supplied: Monika Rittershaus)
Die Zauberflöte (The Magic Flute) premiered in 1791, in Vienna, just two months before Mozart's death from illness at the age of 35. The second-last piece he wrote, it represents a composer at the peak of his powers — but it was essentially a "money job".
On the down and out after a couple of dry years, and impoverished, Mozart took up an offer by theatre impresario and performer Emanuel Schikaneder to write the music for an existing libretto — a fairytale "singspiel" (a popular form at the time, mixing spoken dialogue and singing) aimed not at the elite (as most of Mozart's work was) but the lower-class audiences who frequented Schikaneder's theatre.
The libretto, a rehash of an old story, is generally considered a bit of a mess, and involves an outsized, comedic role — a bird-catching buffoon called Papageno — that was written by Schikaneder for himself. The plot revolves around the adventures of a young prince who is asked by the Queen of the Night to rescue her daughter from her rival, the priest Sarastro, who presides over the Temple of Wisdom and rules the kingdom of the Sun. The prince succeeds both with the help of and despite Papageno, and with the aid of a magical flute.
Production still from the Metropolitan Opera's 2023 production of Die Zauberflöte or The Magic Flute. (Supplied: The Metropolitan Opera)
McBurney, an opera neophyte, approached the project as a curious outsider: "I was interested in what people actually heard at the time. What was going on [in the world]? Why did he [Mozart] do it?"
He enlisted his brother: composer and academic Gerard McBurney (who had also had a huge hand in A Dog's Heart, having studied in the USSR and specialised in Russian music).
"He showed me what was going on musically, and I [also] started to piece together historically, what happened," says McBurney.
In 1791, Europe was at the tail end of its so-called Enlightenment, with massive leaps forward in science and technology (including the steam engine, the seed drill and the hot air balloon) transforming every aspect of life and ushering in the Industrial Revolution.
In France, meanwhile, a different kind of revolution was in its bloody infancy — with its tremors felt through Europe.
"And suddenly in Vienna, probably the greatest composer in the world at that point takes on a popular piece of theatre — the equivalent of what we call a pantomime," says McBurney.
Production still from the Metropolitan Opera's 2023 production of Die Zauberflöte or The Magic Flute. (Supplied: The Metropolitan Opera)
The premiere took place against a backdrop of deep unrest in Vienna.
"There's also deep oppression — people are not really allowed to talk about the political situation. There's terror at the idea that there is going to be blood running in the streets of Vienna, because you have a tyrannical monarchy and the middle class desperately want to get rid of it; for people to be able to get on with their lives and to start living a modern existence," McBurney explains.
The theatre-maker threw the weight of his imagination behind Mozart: "Let's imagine that Mozart is relatively smart, and that he's aware [of the political context]: He's been in Paris, he knows what Europe is like; he knows what the world is like. And he knows that if society is to change, people's consciousness has to change," he speculates.
"And here, I'm slowing down [and] my tone is becoming a little bit pompous, as I start to say these things," he says, pausing for effect and smiling mischievously. "But what I mean to say is: As well as something light and pantomimic and funny, there is, I think, something serious underneath [The Magic Flute]; there is a dramatic point.
"The story is about a young man who falls in love with a girl just through a picture, and then fights to liberate her from what he thinks is a tyrant — and then discovers that this is not a tyrant — and goes through a series of trials which test his inner resolve.
"And this woman herself is, as portrayed by Mozart in particular, extraordinary in the arias that she sings, and very strong. She insists on going through the tests with him … She takes the power, if you like. And then the conjunction of the two [lovers] sets off the possibility of a new world, which is what Sarastro is looking for. It's been a world torn apart by the Queen — and the Queen, in a sense, is a little bit like the monarchy in Austria. And Sarastro is perhaps the spiritual centre. But the point is: It's a world on the cusp of disaster, in which something must change in the way that people think.
Production still from the Metropolitan Opera's 2023 production of Die Zauberflöte or The Magic Flute. (Supplied: The Metropolitan Opera)
"My fantasy is that Mozart understood the necessity for a new consciousness in the middle of the Enlightenment — and his belief was that you could change consciousness through music.
"The flute is magic: It makes people behave in a different way. And [Papageno's] bells are magic. They reveal a new world and they make people do different things. For Mozart, there's no question that he believed that music had a transformative effect on people. He had seen it, he had experienced it [himself], [and] he had manipulated people with it. He knew what it could do."
This fantasy is the foundation stone of McBurney's vision — and his reason for hewing close to the context of the original production in creating his (extremely contemporary) version.
The key elements of his staging concept directly honour Schikaneder's populist theatre, the Freihaus-Theater auf der Wieden: The orchestra pit is raised so it's level with the stage and the stalls (these days the orchestra is below stage during an opera), and the visuals and special effects are created much as they would have been in the day — including a foley artist who we see on stage, and an artist whose live-drawn images and visual effects are projected onto the stage.
The sound and visual effects are created live, on stage, in McBurney's production of Die Zauberflöte (or: The Magic Flute). (Supplied: The Metropolitan Opera)
The live creation of theatrical effects is a trademark of Complicité's physical, visual brand of theatre, which is informed by its co-founders' training under influential French 'clowning' maestro Jacques Lecoq, in the early 80s. Other Complicité signatures make their way into McBurney's Magic Flute, such as performers fluttering paper programs to evoke a flock of birds.
Cumulatively, it's as if the audience is peeking behind the veil of mystery shrouding the spectacle — which is, of course, precisely the point.
"One of the interesting things of making theatre still, for me, is that when you're in a space collectively, at a certain moment, you all imagine the same thing at the same time. It gives the lie to the idea of the individual consciousness and the solo imagination," says McBurney.
He cites a scientific survey of theatre audiences: "When they hooked all these people up, they found that everybody's hearts begin to beat in unison [when they're watching the same show]."
"We are collective beings," he says, emphatically. "And I think, you know, if there's any hope for us, then we need to act collectively."
The Magic Flute is showing in limited cinemas from August 19.

title: Depp v Heard: Jurors told to stay away from social media, but social media was its own courtroom
content:
Cast your mind back to June 2022 and the day a jury found that actor Amber Heard had defamed her ex-husband and fellow actor Johnny Depp and the reaction on social media.
Depp had sued Heard over a 2018 op-ed in the Washington Post in which she referred to herself as a public figure representing domestic abuse.
If you need help immediately call emergency services on triple-0
Heard counter-sued with the jury finding that Depp, through one of his lawyers, defamed Heard in one of three counts in her countersuit.
By all accounts, Depp was the victor.
But he had already won in the court of public opinion.
A three-part Netflix series looks at what it calls the world's first trial by TikTok. The series is pieced together without a narrator. Instead, the story is recounted via the live tweets, live streams, and influencers expressing their opinions in videos that were prevalent during the court case.
Both testimonies are shown side-by-side and viewers are given a reminder of the overwhelming attention the case garnered on social media.
Johnny Depp received an overwhelming amount of public support on social media from content creators. (Supplied: Netflix)
While the jurors were sworn off social media, in an interview after the trial, Heard told the Today Show on NBC that social media played a role in the verdict, saying it would have been impossible for even the most well-intentioned juror to avoid the wall-to-wall coverage.
What contributed to the social media frenzy was the fact that cameras were allowed in the courtroom and the case could be streamed around the world.
The series shows Depp meeting with a vlogger after the case wrapped to thank him and others for being his "warriors" saying they lifted him above "the horror show".
For Heard however, there was little shield from the vitriol with the actor reporting abuse and harassment.
"People want to kill me," she told the court.
"People want to put my baby in the microwave. They tell me that."
The Netflix series highlights the intense scrutiny Amber Heard came under on social media. (Supplied: Netflix)
Creators took serious allegations and intimate details about the couple's relationship and turned it into entertainment, with many making money from their content – some for the first time.
Subscriber counts increased exponentially. Videos went viral.
Episode two of the series is the most compelling. There's a recap of the social media reaction to revelations made in court when Depp and Heard visited Australia as a couple in 2015.
Content makers got online to throw in their two cents, accusing the two actors of acting on the stand. Influencers dressed up as Heard, imitating her responses to questions in court.
Live reactions were edited into court footage.
Conspiracy theories abounded.
Depp v. Heard Netflix trailer.
So far, reaction to the series on social media has been mixed, with some calling it a "biased attempt at justice" and others saying it's a much-watch, but triggering.
It does not contain interviews with Depp or Heard.
Director Emma Cooper told Netflix's You Can't Make This Up podcast she found it compelling that people could watch the same court proceedings and have completely difference responses and opinions.
"It's a curious element of the human mind and brain that we observe the same scenarios differently, and have different perspectives," Cooper said.
"I simply wanted to put forward that these two people passionately believed their own truths, but those truths were not interlocking. They were not the same."
Depp v. Heard is streaming now on Netflix
