title: Red White & Royal Blue isn't trying to be good, and that's what makes it worth watching
content:
Enemies to lovers. A royal wedding. Lines like "when we're apart, your body comes back to me in my dreams" delivered unironically.
Red White & Royal Blue isn't worried about being corny.
This straight-to-streaming release tells the heartwarming story of a British prince and the son of the President of the United States who fall for each other, but whose love is tragically forbidden by their opposing geopolitical responsibilities.
The plot doesn't exactly scream award winner, and it'd certainly be out of place at the Melbourne International Film Festival. But that's exactly why I wanted to see it, and I'm not the only one. The trailer has 8 million views on YouTube, and Amazon Prime says it was the app's number one movie globally in its premiere weekend.
Red, White, & Royal Blue - Official Trailer | Prime Video
Red White & Royal Blue is based on the 2019 Casey McQuiston novel of the same name.
It's about gay men, but it's the kind of book that was written for women. Trust me, it's a thing.
The book has amassed a cult following, attracting fan art, fan fiction and handmade merch.
Fangirls were beside themselves with excitement from the release of the trailer, and sexy little edits set to Taylor Swift songs have already infested TikTok.
Red White & Royal Blue follows Alex Claremont-Diaz, an American First Son who falls for the British Prince Henry Fox-Mountchristen-Windsor.
Much of the film hinges on their brash American vs stuck-up Brit dynamics, with the walking stereotypes starting off as nemeses.
After an unfortunate incident involving a nine-tiered cake (I counted!) goes viral, the boys must pretend to be friends, if only for the camera.
Meanwhile, Ms President mum herself (Gen Z audience bby!) is trying to win an election. She's played by none other than Uma Thurman, who blesses us with a very creative "Texan accent".
Our love interests soon fall for each other, after Mr USA sees Mr UK being nice to some sick kids and thinks: "Huh. Maybe this man is kinda handsome."
This film (and also the book, apparently) is really quite raunchy.
There's a joke about being as hard as Stonehenge, and so so many phallic motifs, ranging from Big Ben to the Washington Monument (it is an international love story after all).
We're even blessed with the line "your royal hardness".
There was also quite a tender sex scene (featuring a consent conversation and condoms on the bedside table because, again, 2023), which felt more intimate and thought-out than the norm.
The representation of sex and queer love was appreciated by many in the community who have been misrepresented and sidelined time and time again.
The film was predictable and cheesy, making it the perfect comfort watch.
I did become frustrated by the end though, when I felt the movie started to drag.
There were multiple "motivational" speeches and "heartfelt" scenes, and I ended up cleaning the kitchen rather than sitting through another minute of our loved-up couple playing a very slow song on the piano together. Let's just stick with the dick jokes please.
Most of the time when I'm looking for a movie, finding something that's clever, meaningful and educational doesn't even cross my mind.
My main genres of choice are kids' movies, 2000s rom-coms and repeat-watching comfort films I've seen 5,000 times.
There's something so freeing about a film that isn't really aiming for quality.
There's a reason why Hallmark Christmas films are so popular, why people switch to reality television, and why The Room has a cult following.
Sometimes, we all just want a bit of fun. It's OK to like things that aren't perfect, that aren't saying something about the world.
And this isn't to say rom-coms — or movies aimed at women — are instantly silly or frivolous. But for me, the worse, the better. Action blockbusters fall into the same category.
I recently had the pleasure of diving into Meg 2: The Trench. I didn't come out of that movie with a new lease on life, but boy did I see some Big Sharks chomping people to bits.
MEG 2: THE TRENCH - OFFICIAL TRAILER
Want Jason Statham jumping off a cargo ship and being totally fine? Check. One-dimensional bad guys who say things like "before you start whining about the ecosystem, who cares"? Check. What about Jason Statham shooting a meg while riding a jet ski on a wave? Big. Check.
In the packed cinema, there were zero laughs at the movie's "gags", but a few giggles at various other "serious" scenes and lines of dialogue, which was delightful.
Heartstopper Season 2 is one of the best explorations of the pressure and stress of coming out that I've ever seen.
I still haven't seen Oppenheimer, but I can't think of a weekend more perfect than Red White & Royal Blue followed by Meg 2. His and hers <3
If you want a beautifully written film with artistic shots, powerful acting and an orchestral score, this movie probably isn't for you.
But if you want a sweet, frivolous movie with pop songs and more innuendos than Austin Powers, give Red White & Royal Blue a go.
You might even find it "good". I had a gay friend message me to say he "cried five times" (were we watching the same movie??) and for the legion of fans who stan the book, I hope it was a satisfying adaption.
But if you'd prefer sharks, dinosaurs and bad CGI, try Meg 2.
Red White & Royal Blue is for fans of: Young Royals, Julia Stiles' The Prince & Me, Heartstopper, First Daughter, Love Simon.

title: 'The original came out in 1937, and evidently so': Actress Rachel Zegler's Snow White interview goes viral
content:
Disney's next live-action remake, Snow White, won't be out till March next year — but it's already attracting plenty of attention.
The movie, starring Rachel Zegler as Snow White and Gal Gadot as the Evil Queen, is the next instalment in a path of live-action remakes from Disney including Aladdin, The Lion King and, most recently, The Little Mermaid.
But social media has been running rampant in recent weeks with resurfaced interview clips of Rachel Zegler discussing Disney's new direction for the Snow White story, and what audiences could expect in 2024.
The original Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs film, based on the 1812 German fairytale by the Brothers Grimm, was the first full-length traditionally animated feature.
Zegler warned the public in an interview with ExtraTV in September last year, that the modern version of the story would be a different take.
"There's a big focus on her love story with a guy that literally stalks her ... weird, weird — so we aren't going to do that."
She said Snow White "won't be saved by the prince, and she won't be dreaming about true love ... she's dreaming about being a leader."
"Really what's important is that she finds her own voice."
Those comments have now gone viral on TikTok, with some users on the platform branding Zegler's interview about Snow White as "smug", "pseudo-feminist" and "problematic".
When it was announced that Zegler was cast as Snow White in June 2021, there was initially some racist backlash to the casting choice.
The actress, who is of Colombian descent, said in a 2021 interview with Variety "at the end of the day, I have a job to do".
"I'm really excited ... I get to be a Latina princess."
Following backlash around her casting in Disney's live-action Snow White movie, Rachel Zegler shared a photo of herself as a child on social media.  (Photo: X (formerly Twitter))
In response to the movie's controversies, Lena Nahlous, CEO of Diversity Arts Australia, said the response shows a lack of understanding about how society looks today.
"It's funny to me that people seem to be upset that Snow White isn't 'historically accurate' ... it's a fairytale, it's a myth and it's ripe for a re-imagining," she said.
"We know that historically in film and television there's been, and continues to be, an exclusion of people of colour.
"If this film is going to engage with the diversity of audiences that we have, then it also needs to reflect that diversity."
Just last month, Zegler responded on X (formerly Twitter), after being tagged in online discussions surrounding her casting in the movie.
"Extremely appreciative of the love I feel from those defending me online, but please don’t tag me in the nonsensical discourse about my casting," she said.
Rachel Zegler has experienced backlash about being cast in Disney's upcoming live-action Snow White movie since it was announced in 2021.  (Photo: Instagram)
The online controversy since Zegler was announced as Snow White echoes similar conversations following the casting of Halle Bailey as The Little Mermaid.
That choice was met with viral videos of young children reacting to the movie's trailer, seeing themselves reflected in the film.
"Casting in movies like Snow White and The Little Mermaid is such an inspiration to a broader group of young people ... it's exciting," Ms Nahlous said.

title: Blind Side parents agree to end Michael Oher's conservatorship
content:
A couple accused of falsely representing as the adoptive parents of the former American football player who inspired the movie The Blind Side, have agreed to end a conservatorship he is challenging in court, their lawyer has said.
Lawyer Randall Fishman told reporters that his clients Sean and Leigh Anne Tuohy intend to enter into a consent order to end the conservatorship of Michael Oher.
Mr Oher filed a petition earlier this week in a Tennessee probate court accusing the Tuohys of lying to him by having him sign papers making them his conservators rather than his adoptive parents nearly two decades ago.
The 37-year-old wants a full accounting of assets, considering his life story produced millions of dollars, saying he received nothing from the Oscar-nominated movie The Blind Side.
The Tuohys have called the allegations ridiculous and part of a shakedown attempt.
They said he had threatened before the court filing to plant a negative news story about them unless they paid him $US15 million ($23 million).
Attorney Randall Fishman told reporters the Tuohy's intend to end their conservatorship over Michael Oher. (AP: Adrian Sainz)
Mr Oher accuses the Tuohys of never taking legal action to assume custody of him before he turned 18 in May 2004, with the conservatorship paperwork being filed months after, though he was told to call them "Mom" and "Dad."
He alleges the Tuohys had him sign paperwork almost immediately after he moved in as part of the adoption process but says he was "falsely advised" that it would be called a conservatorship because he was already 18, but that adoption was the intent.
Mr Oher said that he discovered in February 2023 that the conservatorship was not the arrangement he thought it was — and that it provided him no familial relationship to the Tuohys.
Mr Oher, who has never been a fan of the movie about his life, asks that the Tuohys be sanctioned and required to pay damages and what he is due, along with interest.
Michael Oher says he was lied to about being adopted. (AP: Nick Wass/File)
The Tuohys' statement says the idea that they sought to profit off him is ridiculous, adding that they are worth "hundreds of millions of dollars" and would not have sought to withhold money from Mr Oher.
"They have consistently treated him like a son and one of their three children," the statement said.
The Tuohys' statement says agents negotiated a small advance from the movie's production company which included "a tiny percentage of net profits" divided equally among a group that included Mr Oher.
Martin Singer, an attorney for the Tuohys, said that profit participation checks and studio accounting statements support their account.
When Mr Oher refused to cash the checks, the statement says the Tuohys deposited his share into a trust account.
The Tuohys said that they set up the conservatorship to help Mr Oher with health insurance, a driver's license and being admitted to college.

title: Strays will leave you roaring with laughter and gasping in disbelief
content:
There are a few different ways to look at the movie Strays.
As a heartwarming story about friendship, camaraderie and loyalty. As a revenge tale with dogs at its centre. As a commentary on Stockholm Syndrome and its dangers.
Or as the hilarious, no holds barred comedy it is.
The premise is this: sweet, naïve Border Terrier Reggie (Will Ferrell) is abandoned by his owner Doug (Will Forte).
Except, Reggie doesn't realise he's been abandoned. He thinks Doug is playing a game with him.
When Reggie meets the loveable foul-mouthed Boston Terrier named Bug (Oscar winner Jamie Foxx), it dawns on him that Doug actually treats him atrociously, and so he gangs up with his newly found dog buddies to seek revenge.
Bug (Jamie Foxx) and Reggie (Will Ferrell) are stray dogs who become buddies.  (Supplied: Universal Studios)
Australian Shepherd Maggie (Isla Fisher) and Great Dane Hunter (Randall Park) are part of the canine quartet.
While Strays may give you the warm and fuzzies, don't take your young children along thinking it's a few cute dogs on an adventure.
It's R-rated. Strays is strictly for adults — and that's its appeal.
Cleverly scripted by Dan Perrault, Strays beautifully ties up loose ends throughout the film and comes to a highly satisfying conclusion – for everyone except Doug.
Australian Shepherd Maggie is voiced by Isla Fisher. (Supplied: Universal Studios)
Real dogs were used when filming and those that didn't have a permanent home were found new owners once the production wrapped up.
One of the dogs was even adopted by director Josh Greenbaum, who revealed in the production notes that he was told the two adorable puppy Border Terriers that played young Reggie wouldn't have a home to go to after the shoot.
"So, I decided to adopt one of them and asked my kids to name him," Greenbaum said.
"They immediately said we've got to name him Reggie because he played Reggie in the movie.
"I came home after shooting the film, introduced Reggie to the family, and now I have Will Ferrell in my house."
With a random cameo from Dennis Quaid and a scene featuring a hilariously creepy narrator dog, Strays is the deep belly laugh you didn't know you needed till the credits rolled.
Strays opens in cinemas Thursday, August 17

title: From overly detailed spreadsheets to sponging off your friend's free tickets — which type of film festival goer are you?
content:
Do you have a gnawing sense of dread that something very important and very cultural is happening, but you are too disorganised or maybe not quite cool enough to know exactly what it is?
Don't worry, that just means its film festival season!
Film festivals are everywhere (and, let's be honest, there's so many of them that maybe film festival season is just all the time?). They can be small and niche; they can be wide-ranging and eclectic. And, as Melburnians can attest right now, they can take over an entire city.
But, despite the fact that we all like to think we are very unique, film festivals — like most things — make most of us fall into distinct camps. Don't fight it babe, there's a certain comfort in being predictable.
So, which one are you?
(Adobe Stock/ABC Everyday: Luke Tribe)
We all know this person; they are probably a Virgo
They have scoured the program, made a shortlist, created multiple group chats with select different arrangements of friends and then shared a detailed spreadsheet about which movies clash, and the closest restaurants and bars to each film.
Everyone else going to the festival is very grateful for and a little bemused by The Organiser, and they LOVE that.
(Adobe Stock/ABC Everyday: Luke Tribe)
Closely associated with The Organiser, the Tag Alonger is happy to just go to whichever film they are told to, then will tick the job of "go to film festival" off their to-do list and feel smug about it.
They will not do any research and they may require you to book their ticket for them. They are also big fans of comp tickets and have a knack for getting their hands on them.
Very valuable company, however, for people who hate going to movies by themselves.
(Adobe Stock/ABC Everyday: Luke Tribe)
This person booked annual leave in January. They have rented a hotel room in the city. They will cook up hotdogs in said hotel room and take them to screenings in a thermos so they don't have to waste time with pedestrian things like eating whole meals.
They will know a lot about directors, types of film used and whatever an oeuvre is. They will likely say things like "Film festivals are not about fun".
Do not ask The Devotee for recommendations unless you, too, are a Devotee. May require a welfare check and lemons to ward off scurvy at some point.
(Adobe Stock/ABC Everyday: Luke Tribe)
Cute, they booked a 12 pass!
They've told themselves they just have to get along to six films with one friend each time and think that is absolutely achievable despite not having been able to catch up with any of their friends for months.
They have not, however, done research into what films are on and when, and will soon discover many of them clash with work, prior engagements or the important occupation of going home and staring into the abyss.
Check in with The Aspirer in the last throes of the festival for some cheap/free tix.
(Adobe Stock/ABC Everyday: Luke Tribe)
This person will not be attending any films and they would like to tell you why.
It's too expensive. Their lives are too busy and full. The festival isn't what it used to be. They used to be a Devotee but work/babies/the pandemic has made them change their ways. They just want to go see Meg 2: The Trench.
Do not engage for too long with The Shunner or you will never actually make it to that futuristic reimagining of a Buddhist folk tale you booked in for at 10.45pm on a Monday.

title: 'Apple huts' keep scientists warm in Antarctica — they come from a little town called Penguin
content:
In a set of 1970s-era manufacturing sheds in the tiny Tasmanian town of Penguin, military and Hollywood secrets sit side by side.
Each day, roughly 35 employees from Penguin Composites get to work designing, cutting, rolling, painting, and grinding layers of sticky resin and glass, creating unique, fibreglass structures that eventually make their way to places all over the world.
Their bread and butter is more mundane jobs like caravans, boats and buses, but a peek into some of the company’s sprawling collection of sheds reveals an intriguing set of side projects, including a water slide and a portable toilet.
Nathan Hall with parts of an igloo bound for a US movie studio. (ABC Rural: Meg Powell)
"We also make igloos," CEO Nathan Hall said, pointing to set of bright green moulds shaped like giant citrus peel segments.
"They literally look like a dome that is put together … I liken it to an old-fashioned fruitcake where you cut them into wedges."
The design for the Antarctic capsules is now owned by Anthea Wallhead, whose husband was the original designer and manufacturer. (Supplied: Penguin Composites)
Created in the 1970s by fibre glass designer Malcolm Wallhead, the first igloos were made in Tasmania for the Australian Antarctic Division (AAD), which refers to them as "apple huts".
The AAD says they can comfortably hold two people for a short-term stay, but there are berths for three people and they can be used in an emergency by up to 15 people.
The interior of one of the igloos used at the Spanish Camp Byers, in Antarctica, which uses extension panels to increase the living space. (Facebook: Icewall One)
Mr Wallhead's widow, Anthea Wallhead, now owns the design and Penguin Composites handles the manufacturing.
Mr Hall said the igloos were made out of individual fibreglass wedges, which were then flat-packed "like an Ikea package" and shipped all over the world.
"And they don't even get an Allen key," he laughed.
The most common use for the brightly coloured domes is for research accommodation in Antarctica, but they've been sent as far away as the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, Switzerland, Greenland, Germany, France and America.
Workers fit together the base of an igloo destined for a film studio. Each igloo is assembled and checked before being shipped. (ABC Rural: Meg Powell)
Penguin Composites has made coloured igloos for Google's Zurich offices. (Supplied: Penguin Composites)
The igloo taking shape in the workshop now has a different destiny.
"We're actually making this for a company that produces movies," Mr Hall said.
The fibreglass makers have had plenty of experience keeping secrets — they've completed one top-secret military project and recently won a second lucrative army contract.
A vehicle component is hand rolled by a mechanical engineer.  (ABC Rural: Meg Powell)
The Australian government's LAND 400 Phase 3 program is a multi-billion-dollar project to supply 129 infantry fighting vehicles to the Australian Army.
South Korean-linked company Hanwha Defence Australia’s Redback fighting vehicles won the bid over a German-linked competitor in late July.
Penguin Composites, along with Tasmanian companies CGB Systems and Elphinstone will form part of the supply chain.
Mr Hall said the specifics of the work were being kept secret for security reasons, but building the components would involve baking them at a high temperature for a prolonged period to ensure they could withstand the extremities of battle.
Male and female moulds are used to create fibreglass igloos for Antarctica and other countries. (ABC Rural: Meg Powell)
Fibreglass mat is hand cut from a template. (ABC Rural: Meg Powell)
The fibreglass mat will be ready for resign once cut. (ABC Rural: Meg Powell )
A fibreglass spout made for Grange Resources is measured. (ABC Rural: Meg Powell)

title: The man behind the Blind Side movie story sues parents for not really adopting him
content:
A former American football player known for inspiring the movie The Blind Side has sued the people who supposedly adopted him two decades ago, saying they lied to him and became his conservators instead.
Michael Oher filed a petition in a Tennessee probate court accusing Sean and Leigh Anne Tuohy of lying to him by having him sign papers making them his conservators.
The movie, which Mr Oher has never been a fan of, tells the story of how he went from being a homeless teenager to a successful NFL player with the help of his adoptive family.
It was nominated for an Oscar for Best Motion Picture and Sandra Bullock won Best Actress for her portrayal of Leigh Anne Tuohy.
In the petition filed in Shelby County Probate Court, Mr Oher asks for the conservatorship to be terminated and to be paid what he is due from the money earned off the use of his name and story along with interest.
He accuses the Tuohys of enriching themselves at his expense by continuing to "falsely and publicly" represent themselves as his adoptive parents "to the date of the filing of this petition".
"Oher discovered this lie to his chagrin and embarrassment in February of 2023, when he learned that the Conservatorship to which he consented on the basis that doing so would make him a member of the Tuohy family, in fact provided him no familial relationship with the Tuohys," according to the petition.
He asks in the petition that the Tuohys be sanctioned and required to pay both compensatory and punitive damages determined by the court.
Steve Farese, a lawyer for the Tuohys, told the Associated Press they would file an answer to the allegations in court but declined to comment further. He was among three attorneys who served on behalf of the Tuohys on Monday.
Sean and Leigh Anne Tuohy are accused of misleading Mr Oher into signing several documents. (AP: Gerald Herbert/File)
Leigh Anne Tuohy did not immediately respond to an email sent via her personal website.
Sean Tuohy told The Daily Memphian that the conservatorship was done to satisfy the NCAA as Mr Oher considered Mr Tuohy's alma mater Mississippi for college, but said he and his wife would end the conservatorship if that is what Mr Oher wants.
"We're devastated," Mr Tuohy said. "It's upsetting to think we would make money off any of our children. But we're going to love Michael at 37 just like we loved him at 16."
Michael Oher is seeking a full accounting of his assets and the millions made from his life story.  (AP: Chuck Burton/File)
Mr Oher accuses the Tuohys of never taking legal action to assume custody from the Tennessee Department of Human Services before he turned 18, with the conservatorship paperwork being filed months after he turned 18 in May 2004.
He moved in with the couple just before his senior year of high school and says he was told to call them "Mum" and "Dad".
He also alleges they had him sign paperwork almost immediately afterwards as part of the adoption process and also encouraged him to call the attorney who made the filing "Aunt Debbie" Branan.
Mr Oher says he was "falsely advised" that it would be called a conservatorship because he was already 18 but the intent was adoption.
"At no point did the Tuohys inform Michael that they would have ultimate control of all his contracts, and as a result Michael did not understand that if the Conservatorship was granted, he was signing away his right to contract for himself," according to the petition.
Michael Oher, left, is suing Leigh Anne Tuohy, third from the left, and her husband. (AP: The Courier, Eric S. Swist/File)
A book based on Mr Oher's life was released in September 2006 and authored by Michael Lewis, who was described in the petition as a childhood friend of Sean Tuohy's.
The petition alleges the Tuohys began contract negotiations for movie rights and reached a deal for them — as well as children Sean Jr and Collins — to be paid $US225,000 ($385,000) plus 2.5 per cent of future defined net proceeds hinging on Mr Oher's signature.
A contract titled "Life Story Rights Agreement" was "purportedly signed by Michael Oher" and dated April 20, 2007, according to the petition.
The petition says Mr Oher believes the signature is similar to his own but that he "at no time ever willingly or knowingly signed this document and that nobody ever presented this contract to him with any explanation that he was signing such a document."
In the petition, Mr Oher asks for a full accounting of his assets and how they were used, considering his life story produced millions of dollars and he received nothing for the rights to something that would not have existed without him.
Nick Clouse had a wife, a baby and job — but he couldn't buy nappies without asking his parents. He's among more than a million Americans living under strict legal arrangements.
Mr Oher was the 23rd overall pick in the 2009 draft out of Mississippi, and he spent his first five seasons with the Baltimore Ravens.
He wound up playing eight NFL seasons, including 2014 when he started 11 games for the Tennessee Titans.
Mr Oher, who turned 37 in May, finished his career with two years in Carolina, last playing in 2016 and released in 2017.
Spears's high-profile battle put a spotlight on efforts that advocates across the United States have launched raising questions that such strict controls result in more harm than protection.

title: The Barbie you may never have heard of is the hottest new doll in town
content:
Barbie's box office bonanza has sparked a new generation of fans, and what they want and what they'll pay has surprised stalwart collectors like Lynda Wake.
Ms Wake, a member of the Sydney Doll Club, has noticed a rise in demand for the vintage Barbies she collects, with some fans willing to pay top dollar.
"Recently I saw that a Barbie #1 had gone for in excess of US$40,000 [$61,000]," Ms Wake said.
"The Barbie movie has really had a very interesting effect on doll collecting."
Lynda Wake proudly demonstrates her Barbie #3. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)
While she's happy to see others sharing her passion, the new rush of people looking to buy their own vintage Barbie is having a "bit of a downside".
Ms Wake said there had been an increase in online scammers, particularly on Facebook Marketplace.
"People are on fire at the moment about collecting Barbie, so there are a whole lot of fake profiles and fake people that are advertising things that don't exist," she said.
The first Barbie doll was released by Mattel in 1959. Now there are hundreds to choose from.  (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)
Ms Wake said it was disappointing the internet was being used in this way, after it had brought accessibility for collectors in past decades.
"We used to have to wait for a doll fair to see whether we could have a doll and add that doll to our collection," she said.
"Then … [online shopping] came along, you put in Barbie and suddenly you've got 100,000 hits, so it's a very different marketplace."
Margot Robbie stars as Barbie in Greta Gerwig's film. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
Michael Cera as Allan in Barbie. (X: IGN)
Ms Wake said a surprising result of the Barbie movie had been the rise in popularity of the Allan doll.
"Previously, he [Allan] was a doll that was very much overlooked," she said.
"People glanced sideways and said, 'Oh he's more Ken's friend, they might have a bit of a relationship there'.
"With Allan now, he's the doll that everyone wants in their collection."
Doll and bear auctioneer Graham Horne, from Melbourne, is not surprised by the new interest in Barbie dolls.
He said merchandise had often been the bigger money maker when it came to entertainment.
"Shirley Temple made more money out of her dolls than she did out of her movies … it's the merchandise where they make their money," he said.
Mr Horne said collectors were not just looking for Barbie dolls, they wanted all the accessories as well.
He said as a rule of thumb most collectors who wanted certain dolls had them already.
"It's the outfits that they don't have, so they are looking for the outfits and any trinkets, what we call 'vacuum cleaner items' such as handbags and shoes."
Mr Horne said his buyers were people who were teenagers in the 1960s, and the current generation of younger girls.
"Mattel is throwing everything at this and what it does is catch the next generation of collectors who will buy all the stuff from the movie, which makes the earlier stuff more valuable," he said.
An in-the-box 90s doll in mint condition, which used to go for $20, Mr Horne said, was now selling for $100 to $150.
It's all about the outfits with Barbie, and always has been. (Facebook: Abbingdon Auctions)

title: Mad Max director George Miller reveals his views on creativity, faith and living as a 'verb'
content:
George Miller was studying medicine at the University of New South Wales when he popped into a lecture being given by Buckminster Fuller.
The American architect, systems theorist and futurist had amassed a devoted following by that time for his sometimes brilliant, sometimes wacky ideas.
What Miller heard during Mr Fuller's 1969 lecture changed the way he thought about his identity.
"He said, 'I am not a noun. I seem to be a verb, an ongoing evolutionary process, an integral function of the universe'," Miller told a Head Room podcast series where high-profile Australians discuss their beliefs.
"In those words, he basically defined everything for me."
George Miller released Mad Max: Fury Road in 2015, 36 years his first feature film. (Supplied: Warner Bros Pictures)
Miller was studying medicine at the time and realised he "wasn't just a medical student".
Now 78 years old, Miller believes verb thinkers embrace change.
"Because they realise it's inevitable. It's part of the adventure of existence," he says.
Miller's first feature film, Mad Max, which he made with producer Byron Kennedy, was an unexpected hit after its release in 1979.
"I found it to be a really bewildering experience because I never made a film before," he says.
"It was a really hard film to make, very low budget, and all of us were inexperienced, but somehow, after thinking I wasn't cut out to make movies, it was a success all around the world except in the United States."
Different cultures identified with Max, the vengeful Australian policeman played by Mel Gibson.
"In Japan, they saw Max as a Samurai. The French called it a Western on wheels. To the Scandinavians, he was some sort of lone Viking."
Mel Gibson played a vengeful cop in the first Mad Max, released in 1979. (Supplied: MGM Studios)
He wanted to understand what was happening, and Joseph Campbell, an American professor of literature, gave him the answers.
Professor Campbell had spent decades working his way through the world's mythologies and religions and found recurring themes and stories.
"He saw these patterns, which he called the 'monomyth', and, in particular, the hero myth," Miller said.
With that understanding, Miller has made a diverse range of Hollywood hits, from the post-apocalyptic action movies, medical drama Lorenzo's Oil and comedy horror Witches of Eastwick to joyful classics Happy Feet and Babe.
The fifth instalment of the Mad Max franchise, which focuses on the origins of the Furiosa character, is set to be released next year.
Miller was born in Chinchilla in regional Queensland in 1945 and, up until Mr Fuller's speech, his life had followed exactly the same path as his twin brother, John.
Listen to George Miller on the Head Room podcast.
"For the first 20 years of our life, we were in every class together," he says.
Miller notes that while his brother became a "wonderful doctor" while he "drifted into filmmaking", they both shared a love of analysing the day and telling stories.
Their experiences in very different fields have influenced the way Miller thinks about the creative process.
"It's kind of an interplay between the intuition, which is fuelled by the intellect," he says.
"The intuition guides the intellect, and the intellect fuels it. In every great actor I've worked with, every great sportsman, every great athlete, every great scientist, composer, musician, at every level, it's the same process."
Asked if he has a faith, Miller hesitates.
"Faith is a tricky word. Faith can be noun thinking. If it's rigid, then you're in trouble."
Returning to Professor Campbell and his universal myth, Miller talks about religion in terms of a collection of stories to help humans make sense of what they do not understand, like the seasons.
"So you invented gods, often lots of gods. Sometimes it was one god to explain, and they were metaphorical, and they're powerful, and important, because they give you understanding and comfort, and a way to find your way, navigate existence," he says.
"The problem with dogmatic religious belief is that they concretise the metaphor."
But he does believe in a "something else". As Einstein explained, the more you know, the greater the mysteries.
Or another of his favourite quotes is from physicist Paul Davies, who said "science offers a surer way to God than religion".
"I think that makes sense to me," Miller says.

title: Nicolas Cage movie rumours spark teen stardom dreams in renowned Aussie surf spots
content:
Drama teachers, film buffs and young actors in WA's South West are "pumped" about whispers that Hollywood heavyweight Nicolas Cage could soon be shooting in their area.
WA's famous surfing and wine regions of Margaret River and Yallingup, three-and-a-half hours south of Perth, are set to be the backdrop for the film The Surfer starring Cage, with filming expected to start later in the year.
The local rumour mill intensified when a casting agency sent a call out to local high school students to audition for roles in the film — and a chance to act alongside Cage.
The call-out said teenage boys would play young surfers who hung out with a surf gang.
"We are looking for kids who are really confident with a bit of 'attitude' ... we see them riding their BMXs delivering beer and generally causing trouble around town," the call-out said.
Margaret River Senior High School drama teacher Amy Johnstone said her students were thrilled by the opportunity.
"As soon as we found out, we put it out in the school notices, and we had a stack of boys lining up at our office door by recess, these guys are pumped to be in a movie," she said.
The film's production company Arenamedia said it was unable to confirm any details at this stage.
The WA film community says the movie would have big economic and tourism impacts. (ABC South West: Anthony Pancia)
While qualifying that her specific knowledge of the plot and production was based on publicly available entertainment press coverage, CinefestOZ chief executive Cassandra Jordan said any production of this magnitude represented a significant opportunity for the region.
Ms Jordan said the coverage pointed to the film being a psychological thriller.
Actors in Hollywood are going on strike, bringing many shows grinding to a halt and impacting some Australian productions. Here's what you need to know.
"It is beyond exciting to have something of this calibre shooting in our region," she said.
"[The film] follows Nicolas Cage, a man returning to his hometown after many years of leaving the region, and it's all about him up against a local gang of surfers who claim ownership over a secluded beach of his childhood."
She said local businesses and the community could reap a huge benefit with the production coming to town.
"This also has a really big tourism impact on the region," she said.
"Nicolas Cage and Yallz [Yallingup], it's just keeping our incredible region in the spotlight."
Drama teacher Ms Johnstone said she would begin helping boys prepare for their audition.
"We will be holding lunchtime sessions where we can help give them some tips on audition techniques, how to present and maybe little monologues," she said.
"Some of these boys who have put their hand up are not necessarily drama kids. It's really awesome to see the different range of ages and kind of guys that are interested in doing it.
A Margaret River drama teacher says the auditions will give kids a great opportunity. (ABC South West WA: Anthony Pancia)
"This could be a launching pad for some kids or maybe an opportunity to see that they're interested in something they didn't realise they we're in to."
The Margaret River and Yallingup regions have a history of attracting surf movies, with the 2013 film Drift having also been produced in the area.
Other recent high-profile regional productions include the Ewan McGregor crime thriller Son Of A Gun in Kalgoorlie and Tim Winton adaptation Breath, which was shot in Esperance and the Mid West.

title: From Scarlett Johansson to Tom Hanks, Hollywood A-listers star in Wes Anderson comedy Asteroid City
content:
While the world goes bananas for the retro Americana of Barbenheimer – the beauty and the beast currently burning up the box office – leave it to Wes Anderson to quietly deliver his own dizzy diorama of pastels and cotton candy mushroom clouds, an irresistible synthesis of Looney Tunes, Spielberg and Atomic Age paranoia that pays tender tribute to the power of art and the imagination.
In a career that now spans nearly 30 years, Anderson's latest film, Asteroid City – a carousel of astronomers, aliens and singing cowboys; of mid-century madness, deadpan soul and signature melancholy – might just be one of his finest.
Like so much of the filmmaker's recent work, it's both a fable and a kind of parallel reality, a story nested within another that has the contours of a familiar dream. "Asteroid City does not exist," says the film's Rod Serling-esque narrator (Bryan Cranston), introducing the fictional theatre production that serves as the movie's framing device, "the events an apocryphal fabrication."
Anderson wrote the screenplay from a story he co-wrote with Roman Coppola. (Supplied: Universal)
It's 1955, and somewhere on the edge of the desert in the American Southwest, between kitsch postcard and John Ford vista, sits the eponymous town, a sun-bleached wasteland whose lone "point of interest" – not counting a comically unfinished ramp to nowhere – is a crater said to have been formed when a meteorite hit the earth thousands of years ago.
Atomic bomb tests rattle the windows of the local diner, while a roadrunner bird – complete with a droll "meep meep" – scampers across the landscape.
On the eve of Asteroid City's annual Junior Stargazers and Space Cadets convention, an unlikely cross-section of the American populace – played by a sizeable chunk of Hollywood's acting A-List – descends upon the town.
The film features a stop-motion sequence by Andy Gent, who Anderson has dubbed "the Laurence Olivier of animators". (Supplied: Universal)
There's a recently widowed war photographer, Augie Steenbeck (Jason Schwartzman), and his kids, who number one brainiac teenage son (Jake Ryan) and three little girls (cosmically named Andromeda, Cassiopeia and Pandora), who arrive with a tupperware container full of their mum's ashes on its way to Grandpa (a silvery Tom Hanks). There's a celestial body of a different kind in movie star Midge Campbell (Scarlett Johansson), trailing her genius teen daughter (Grace Edwards); a young teacher (Maya Hawke) with a busload of primary school charges; a slew of middle-aged parents (Liev Schreiber, Steve Park, Hope Davis); and a Greek chorus of Johnny Guitar-cowboys (featuring Rupert Friend, Seu Jorge and Jarvis Cocker).
They've all set up at a motel – run by Steve Carrell's officious, visor-clad oddball — whose vending machines variously dispense soda pop, martinis, and barren plots of real estate.
The occasion also brings scientists, including a loopy astronomer played by (who else) Tilda Swinton, and the US military, with Jeffrey Wright's five-star general capturing the heady, turbulent spirit of the Atomic Age.
"If you wanted to live a nice quiet peaceful life," he tells the assembled kids in his opening address, "you picked the wrong time to get born".
"Wes has a very light, positive, excitable attitude on set … He's so invigorated by work, and he just works constantly," Johansson told Collider. (Supplied: Universal)
After a rare lunar eclipse attracts a visitor for another world – a beautifully expressive stop-motion alien who could have stepped from Edward Gorey's pages – the military swiftly puts the town and its residents into quarantine and denies all knowledge, and Asteroid City becomes the centre of a media frenzy (and a neat analogy for the McCarthy era of communist paranoia).
Anderson's meticulous style can sometimes threaten to betray his considerable gift for comedy and pathos, at least for audiences merely paying attention to the surface, but here everything – his signature concerns and his craftsmanship – is in delicious synchronicity. The painted physical sets are wonderful, the miniature work exquisite (the alien's spacecraft, all luminous green lights and silent gravity propulsion, is a highlight), and Robert Yeoman's colour cinematography evokes the distinctive printing techniques of mid-century tourist postcards.
Scenes from the film's fictional theatre production are shot in black and white. (Supplied: Universal)
At times the film is almost a valentine to early Spielberg, and specifically Close Encounters of The Third Kind: The meteorite crater recalls Devils Tower, Alexandre Desplat's score is sprinkled with tubas, and Bob Balaban cameos as a mysterious government aide. (Even more endearing is Anderson's use of Slim Whitman's eerie Indian Love Call, surely a nod to Tim Burton's misunderstood masterpiece – and one of this writer's all-time favourites – Mars Attacks!)
As always with Anderson, all of this playful artifice is in service of tapping a richer vein of emotion, and Asteroid City effectively captures a nation at a pivotal moment, one that – as both Barbie and Oppenheimer demonstrate – would prove influential on decades of pop culture.
Especially poignant is the film's undertow of grief, with Augie's sadness over the loss of his wife (briefly embodied by Margot Robbie) drawing him into the orbit of Midge's melancholic movie star – "two catastrophically wounded people," as the latter explains, in a classic Anderson line, "who don't express the depths of their pain because we don't want to".
"To me, this movie, the subject matter, is about why people do theatre," Anderson told The Independent. (Supplied: Universal)
Johansson, pulling double duty as raven-haired Midge and the Hitchcock-blonde actress playing her, gives the film's most fascinating performance, a sensitive dialogue on movie stardom that, at its best, summons the spirit of Marilyn Monroe.
Asteroid City; a playground for Wes Anderson's creative genius
The film's framing device allows Anderson to give these artists – actors, directors, stagehands – their due; as in The French Dispatch's love letter to writers, Asteroid City is devoted to the outsiders, the performers whose art is so essential (as corny as it sounds) to illuminating the human condition.
By the time the film's real life and stage play converge in a kind of collective hypnosis, the effect is startling. Led by Willem Dafoe's Actors Studio guru, the cast is united by a somnambulant mantra that invokes the power of art – and the imagination – to absorb the delusions of an insane time. I found it very moving.
Asteroid City is in cinemas now.

title: 'Fighting for the working class': How Hollywood's writers' strike is playing out in Australia
content:
Hollywood's been hit with the biggest strikes in decades and the impact is being felt in Australia, with hundreds of cast and crew working on offshore productions affected.
The 160,000-member strong Screen Actors Guild and the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG_AFTRA) last month joined the Writers Guild of America in walking off the job after pay negotiations with the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers broke down.
There are no signs of the stalemate ending anytime soon.
US film and TV veteran actor James Huang might be a world away in Melbourne, but he backs his union's decision to shut down Hollywood and productions across the world.
James Huang says the strike is about the "working class actor". (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)
"I've been a SAG-AFTRA member since the 90s and this strike is entirely about fighting for working-class people," Mr Huang told 7.30.
"And it's entirely to do with studios taking advantage of actors' likeness with the AI, artificial intelligence, technology, and streaming and accountability for what actors live and breathe on, which is residual income.
"And the celebrities that are standing up and supporting the strike may be the face of it, because they are recognisable but it is not about celebrities, it is about the working class actor," he said.
Unions in the US and Australia are concerned about the dominance of movie studios and streaming platforms and the digital disruption that has changed the way we watch our favourite shows and movies.
Actors and writers have previously been able to rely on ongoing residual income from DVD sales and re-runs but they say that’s dried up since streaming platforms have muscled in.
James Huang says he's received cheques for $0 in the mail. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)
James Huang might not be a household name but he's been in more than 100 films and TV shows like NCIS, Law and Order and Will and Grace, Young Rock and more recently La Brea and Fisk.
He said he's gone from getting multiple cheques in dollars to fractions of cents.
"Somewhere maybe five to eight years ago, I started to get literally zero cent cheques, paper cheques sent to me in the mail," Mr Huang said.
"Now there's an online accounting where you can actually view it and you just see rows and rows and rows of your shows that you've started.
"And then in films that you've been in, and it'll say, internet streams and $0.00."
Peter Mattessi, board member of the Australian Writers' Guild, said the disruption of streamers has made making a career as a writer much tougher.
"The American writers are going on strike because of this vast change in the way television has been commissioned and broadcast has changed the way writers are contracted and employed.
Mr Mattessi said streamers are also employing fewer writers to work on shows with much shorter runs resulting in less money and fewer career opportunities.
"Previously the amount of money that you could make writing a TV show would have a long tail, you get small payments that over time add up to a substantial amount of money," Mr Mattessi said.
The last time Hollywood's actors and writers went on strike at the same time, the biggest stars were fighting for residual pay cheques. Decades later, streaming giants and artificial intelligence are at the heart of the debate.
"Now those payments don't exist if your show goes on a streaming service.
"And in some cases, the streamers are buying them out for much less than you would get from them in the long term. But in Australia frequently, they're just not compensating for those at all," he said.
In Australia two offshore productions on the Gold Coast, Mortal Kombat 2 and Apples Never Fall, have been paused because of the US strikes.
About 800 people employed on the two productions have been stood down without pay, according to the Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA).
"Whilst our work might have been paused or ceased because of the strike, we stand in solidarity because we know that fatigue, job security, AI protections are everyone's problem," MEAA organiser Michelle Rae told 7.30.
"So for our crew, they were expecting to be on the jobs for three, six, eight months, that's now money that they don't have, that's bills they can't pay."
The first casualty of the US strikes in Australia was Apple TV's $180 million remake of Fritz Lang's Metropolis.
The production was shut down in June citing the writers' strike, affecting about 700 cast and crew who were to be employed by Metropolis.
Docklands Studios has been left only half booked, and what's been described as the world's largest virtual production studio built with $12.5 million in Victorian government funding is in maintenance.
Supply chain side businesses like prop shop Prop-A-Ganda have also been left in the lurch.
Tristan Macleod says the strike is not only affecting writers and actors. (ABC News: Daniel Fermer)
"A lot of people got work out of it or were waiting to get work out of it and that was going to be a good one to three years of income for somebody and the potential for us to hire," Tristan Macleod, manager of Prop-A-Ganda, told 7.30.
"Because this industry is always feast or famine anyway.
"So it's a bit of a blow because we don't know next when the big money's going to come in to help for us to pay rent or keep going," he said.
The US actors' and writers' strikes have also pushed back the release of The Dry 2 starring SAG-AFTRA member Eric Bana and left other completed productions without stars to promote them.
Federal and state governments have spent billions in tax rebates and cash subsidies to lure big-budget movies and shows to film in Australia over the past 15 years.
Concerns raised by the US strikes come as the Australian government considers tougher laws for those companies including local content quotas.
"If we base our industry around attracting huge international productions, then as soon as the Czech Republic is cheaper, or Mexico is cheaper, or Belgium is cheaper, they'll go there," Mr Mattessi said.
While streamers have had big global hits with Australian shows like Netflix's Heartbreak High reboot, the Australian Writers' Guild has called for local content quotas for streamers of at least 20 per cent.
"They don't have to make any Australian content at all, they make somehow much not that much," Mr Mattessi said.
Peter Mattessi is calling for local content quotas for streamers. (ABC News: Daniel Fermer)
"Which is why it's so important for us to have some sort of local content requirements on those international streamers to keep our industry alive," he said.
"So what we need to do is ensure that we are continuing to produce our own content."
If the issues caused by the digital disruption of streaming platforms aren't addressed, Mr Mattessi fears there'll be more at stake than just the jobs of those in the industry.
"Without getting too romantic about it stories for time immemorial have been told to help people understand the world and understand why we are the way we are," Mr Mattessi said.
"And if we don't have that then we lose connection completely with who we are as Australian people."

title: If Oppenheimer is an hour longer than Barbie, why are tickets to see them the same price?
content:
I've got two questions about blockbuster movies like Barbie and Oppenheimer.
Why aren't the cinemas charging more for them, given they're so popular?
Why are they the same price, given Oppenheimer is an hour longer?
The opening weekend for both films saw an avalanche of Australians returning to the cinema. Extra staff had to be put on (although probably not enough) to manage queues, turn away pink-clad fans who couldn't get in, and clean up mountains of popcorn trampled underfoot.
An obvious solution to such a rush of demand is to push up prices. Airlines do it when they are getting low on seats. When more people want to get a ride share, Uber makes them pay with "surge pricing".
Even books are sold at different prices, depending on the demand, their length, their quality and how long they've been on the shelves.
But not movie tickets, which are nearly always the same price, no matter the movie. Why? And how much has the cost of a trip to the movies risen over the past 20 years?
Oppenheimer is a full hour longer than Barbie, so should we be paying more to see it? (AP: Warner Bros Pictures/Universal Pictures )
In suburban Melbourne, Hoyts is charging $24.50 for the two-hour Barbie — the same as it is charging for the three-hour Oppenheimer, even though it could fit in far fewer showings of Oppenheimer in a day. It's also the same price as it is charging for much less popular movies, such as Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny.
It's also how things are in the United States, where James Surowiecki, author of The Wisdom of Crowds, blames convention and says:
"It costs you as much to see a total dog that's limping its way through its last week of release as it does to see a hugely popular film on opening night."
Australian economists Nicolas de Roos of The University of Sydney and Jordi McKenzie of Macquarie University quote Surowiecki in their 2014 study of whether cinema operators could make more by cutting the price of older and less popular films and raising the price of blockbusters.
By examining what happened to demand on cheap Tuesdays, and developing a model taking into account advertising, reviews and the weather, they discovered Australian cinemas could make a lot more by varying their prices by the movie shown. We turn out to be highly price sensitive. So why don't cinemas do that?
It's the sort of thing that puzzled Gary Becker, an economic detective of sorts who won the Nobel Prize for Economics in the early 1990s. A few years earlier, he turned his attention to restaurants and why one particular seafood restaurant in Palo Alto, California, had long queues every night but didn't raise its prices.
Just three weeks after its release, Barbie has collected more than $1 billion at the global box office — and it's on track to become the biggest movie of the year.
Across the road was a restaurant that charged slightly more, sold food that was about as good, and was mostly empty.
His conclusion, which he used a lot of maths to illustrate, was there are some goods for which a consumer's demand depends on the demand of other consumers.
Queues for restaurants (or in 2023, long queues and sold-out sessions, as crowds were turned away from Barbie) are all signals other consumers want to get in.
This would make queues especially valuable to the providers of such goods, even if the queues meant they didn't get as much as they could from the customers who got in. The "buzz" such queues create produces a supply of future customers persuaded that what was on offer must be worth trying.
Importantly, Becker's maths showed that getting things right was fragile. It was much easier for a restaurant to go from being "in" to "out" than the other way around. Once a queue had created a buzz, it was wise not to mess with it.
There are other reasons for cinemas to charge a standard ticket price, rather than vary it movie by movie.
One is that it is hard to tell ahead of time which movies are going to soar and which are going to bomb, even if you spend a fortune on advertising as the makers of Barbie did. In the words of an insider, "nobody knows anything".
Cinemas rely on high-margin snacks to make money. (Unsplash: Corina Rainer)
Another is the way cinemas make their money. They have to pay the distributor a share of what they get from ticket sales (typically 35-40 per cent). But they don't have to pay a share of what they make from high-margin snacks.
This means it can make sense for some cinemas to charge less than what the market will bear — because they'll sell more snacks — even if it means less money for the distributor.
But cinemas still charge a lot. From 2002 to 2022, Australian cinemas jacked up their average (not their highest) prices from $9.13 to $16.26 — an increase of 78 per cent.
In the same 20 year period, overall prices in Australia, as measured by the consumer price index, climbed 65 per cent — less than the rise in movie ticket prices.
A 2015 study found Australian cinemas charge more than cinemas in the US.
Yet some of the cinemas' costs have gone down. They used to have to employ projectionists to lace up and change reels of film. Digital delivery means much less handling.
A now-dated 1990s report to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission found the two majors — Hoyts and Greater Union/Village — charged near identical prices except where they were faced with competition from a nearby independent, in which case they discounted.
Whether "by design or circumstance", the two cinema chains rarely competed with each other, clustering their multiplexes in different geographical locations.
I think it might be the multiplex that answers my second question: why cinemas don't charge more for movies that are longer (and movies are getting longer).
In the days of single screens, a cinema that showed a long movie might only fit in, say, four showings a day instead of six. So it would lose out unless it charged more.
But these days, multiplexes show many, many films on many screens, some of them simultaneously, meaning long films needn't displace short films.
Although we have fewer cinema seats than we had a decade ago (and at least until the advent of Barbie, we've been going less often) we now have far more screens.
Long movies no longer stop the multiplexes from playing standard ones. And because cinemas like to keep things simple, you pay the same price, no matter which movie you chose.
Peter Martin is visiting fellow at the Crawford School of Public Policy, Australian National University. This article originally appeared on The Conversation.

title: Racing game becomes universally relatable story in Gran Turismo
content:
Imagine dominating at a racing simulator, then being plucked out from behind the virtual steering wheel and placed into the driver's seat of a real racing car to compete against other professional drivers.
That's the story of British professional racing driver Jann Mardenborough, whose story is now the basis for the new film Gran Turismo.
"When Sony offered it to me, I couldn't understand why it makes sense when it's a racing simulator," the film's director, Neill Blomkamp said in a Zoom interview with ABC News.
"And then I found out about Jann's story — I was struck by this kind of positive, aspirational feeling that the film has, right where it's almost bigger than the idea of racing.
"It's just the idea of following a dream and trying to and going after it despite how difficult or how unrealistic it might be."
Gran Turismo Trailer 2023
In the film, Mardenborough is a working-class kid who plays the eponymous racing simulator game, which was originally released in 1997.
The game was critically acclaimed and commercially successful, and players could have a full physical set-up to control their virtual vehicle, including accelerator and brake pedals and a steering wheel.
It consumed and became an obsession for Mardenborough, who would eventually go on to win a place with Nissan's GT Academy race team, a program that allows skilled Gran Turismo players to make the jump into professional racing in real cars.
Actor Archie Madekwe (Midsommar), who plays Mardenborough in the film, said he was moved by the story.
"When I was growing up, these stories — a young person achieving their dreams — were never told about a person whose face looked like mine. So I was unbelievably compelled to tell this story," he said, according to the film's production notes.
Archie Madekwe plays Mardenborough in the film. (Supplied: Sony)
Madekwe had to train extensively, both for the simulator game and behind the wheel of a car. It's a compelling underdog story, and for Blomkamp — who is known for directing District 9 and the Matt Damon-led Elysium — it was a story worth telling.
"I look at it individually like it was Jann's — it was the particular story of him, what he'd gone through, how he'd gotten into racing, and especially coming from this — hyper-unusual at the time — place of simulation racing. It just seemed very, very interesting."
A universally resonant emotional beat the film focuses on is the relationship between Mardenborough and his father, who is absent and, initially, not supportive of his son's aspirations.
David Harbour also stars in the film. (Supplied: Sony)
"We spoke about his [Jann's] parents all the time, like whether they were supportive or not, how it all happened," Blomkamp said.
"It was a huge component of the movie, and also this idea that the arc of his dad and this sort of reconciliation with his father before the end race.
"That was a really big, emotional sort of piece of the puzzle that we had to attempt to get right."
Shooting the film involved real cars and real tracks, including filming at the Dubai Autodrome and Austria's Red Bull Ring.
For the film's climax at the 24 hours of Le Mans, Hungary's Hungaroring track stands in for the iconic French circuit.
Shooting the film involved real cars and real tracks. (Supplied: Sony)
Cars featured in the movie include a Nissan GT-R Nismo GT3, a Lamborghini Huracan GT3 and a Corvette C8.R GT3.
Actor Orlando Bloom, known for his roles in the Lord of the Rings and Pirates of the Caribbean, plays the Nissan executive who comes up with the concept of the GT Academy.
"Orlando crashed one of our GT-Rs. So he crashed on the white training GTRs but he did it because we were going to shoot a post-credit scene with him, and he was just going out with the drivers to get his bearings with it," Blomkamp said.
"The car had been converted to two-wheel drive from a four-wheel drive so he just kind of lost traction. And I need to get the video — he shot iPhone footage of it in the aftermath."
Gran Turismo stars Madekwe, Bloom, David Harbour and Geri Halliwell and will be released in Australian cinemas on August 10.

title: Barbie has reached the 'Barbillion' milestone. Experts say its marketing was a 'masterclass'
content:
Barbie has surpassed $1 billion at the global box office just three weeks after its release – and it's on track to become the biggest movie of the year.
The film, produced by Australia's Margot Robbie who plays the iconic doll having an existential crisis, hit what the internet has dubbed the "Barbillion" milestone this weekend.
Upon its release, the film earned director Greta Gerwig the record for the most successful box office weekend for a female director.
Barbie has smashed box office records. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
Now, Gerwig has become the first female filmmaker to surpass the billion-dollar benchmark as a solo director.
"As distribution chiefs, we're not often rendered speechless by a film's performance, but Barbillion has blown even our most optimistic predictions out of the water," said Jeff Goldstein and Andrew Cripps, who oversee domestic and international distribution for the studio, in a joint statement.
Now, Barbie just needs to topple The Super Mario Bros Movie to become the most successful flick of 2023.
Barbie was already an iconic piece of intellectual property, but experts say those behind the film did not rest on their laurels, and they credit its "masterclass" marketing campaign for its global success.
ABC Arts film reviewer Michael Sun called the Barbie marketing campaign "simultaneously the most tireless and tiresome of any film in recent memory".
Pictures of Airbnb's Barbie Dreamhouse in Malibu went viral when photos were released before the film's premiere. (Reuters: Mike Blake)
There's a Barbie Dreamhouse Airbnb in Malibu. There are Barbie gaming consoles, Barbie rugs, Barbie suitcases, Barbie burgers (complete with a mysterious pink sauce) and even a Barbie collaboration with an insurance company.
"A lot of fashion retailers have jumped on board as well," Graeme Hughes, director of Griffith's Business Lab, said.
"I don't think there are too many shops that you would pass by these days without some sort of either pink or Barbie-branded items."
Plenty of fashion and beauty brands have done official collaborations with the Barbie movie. (David Canales/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Mr Hughes says Barbie's impact on the retail sector has been "significant", adding the scale of Barbie's marketing campaign has been "outside of the box, no pun intended".
"It's really a triumphant marketing campaign," he said.
Warner Bros remains tight-lipped about just how deep the Barbie marketing team's pockets are, but Variety estimates the company has spent roughly $US150 million (about $227 million). And that's on top of the rumoured $US145 million production budget.
"It's way, way out of the ordinary," said Dee Madigan, creative director of Campaign Edge.
"It was almost as creative as the film itself. Having said that, if the film had not lived up to the hype I think there would have been a huge backlash."
Barbie's marketing campaign started more than a year before its release.
Warner Bros president of global marketing Josh Goldstine said the first "electric" moment of the campaign was at CinemaCon last year, when the company released a single image of Margot Robbie, as Barbie, laughing in a pink Corvette.
"It was one of those moments that took on a life of its own," Mr Goldstine told Variety.
The internet lit up when Warner Bros released the first image of Margot Robbie as Barbie. (Supplied: Warner Bros)
Two months later, the company released the first image of Ryan Gosling's Ken.
What quickly followed were leaked images from the set, a situation which was hard to avoid considering the scene involved Robbie and Gosling rollerblading along Venice Beach in full view of the public.
Greta Gerwig's Barbie movie trailer has dropped and it's looking suitably plastic and fantastic.
When a second teaser trailer was released in April, so too were dozens of cast posters, with Robbie's tagline being "Barbie is everything" and Gosling's reading: "He's just Ken."
The company released a filter so fans could get involved, but the memes came thick and fast and became far more viral.
"There's a real risk to some of that organic stuff because if the movie had been a bomb or people hated the marketing, people could use those assets to create bad memes," Ms Madigan says.
"There's a real risk in letting it go because you lose control of the brand a bit."
In an interview with Architectural Digest, production designer Sarah Greenwood revealed the film used so much pink paint to create Barbieland that "the world ran out of pink".
Greta Gerwig told Architectural Digest she wanted Barbieland to be "very bright, and everything to be almost too much". (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
With just as much pink injected into the marketing, Ms Madigan says the absolute commitment to the colour was critical.
"They absolutely banked on the movie being great. Using pink was brave, as well as stretching it out that long. It's very easy with a cynical audience to over hype things as well.
"I think we get to the point that when you're doing it so over the top, it doesn't become over-promoted, it becomes fun again.
"If you're going to do this, just go all out. And that's what they did."
Mattel will be hoping its other slated productions are just as much a hit at the box office as Barbie. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
In a piece titled After Barbie, Mattel Is Raiding Its Entire Toybox, The New Yorker revealed Mattel has another 45 other projects in development.
The Beanie Bubble is the latest in what looks to be an endless line of products-based movies. Are they all just cynical ploys to sell merch?
That's on top of the 13 it has already publicly announced, from a Polly Pocket movie directed by Lena Dunham and starring Lily Collins, to a Hot Wheels film by JJ Abrams.
But experts say Barbie's success doesn't guarantee every film about toys or products will be a box office blockbuster.
"I think that there is a risk for those that follow to be viewed as sort of infomercials," Mr Hughes said.
"Barbie is quite a storied brand and I think they can play with the tongue-in-cheek [humour] of sliding between it being an advertising piece but also an entertainment piece.
"You lose the impact when you're a follower in the space so it would be quite detrimental for other films to go down this pathway.

title: An Australian helped shift Oppenheimer 'from the shadows of theory' to the Manhattan Project
content:
Among the elegies for the inhabitants of Hiroshima, there exists an especially arresting and resonant example authored by an Australian poet.
Reflecting on the impact of the blast on one of its young victims, Bruce Dawe recounted the morning of August 6, 1945, when a "single plane loosed a single bomb" and the city below — but also the very prospect of posterity — "became suddenly phantasmal".
A suspected "human shadow" left by the vaporisation of a person at Hiroshima. (Wikimedia Commons: Matsuhige Yoshito)
When humans first split atoms, they also split history.
"The atomic bomb," wrote its chief developer, the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, "has led us up those last few steps to the mountain pass; and beyond there is a different country".
That different country is the age in which we now live.
Among the chroniclers who described its dawn were some astute enough to notice that fission had produced unforeseen fissures: with the advent of the bomb, human knowledge itself seemed to fracture, with science on one side and conscience on the other.
Oppenheimer was perhaps an exception to this dichotomy, and combined academic interests from both sides of the divide — erudite, sensitive and cultured, he was, in some respects, an unlikely atomic father figure.
Oppenheimer's name is currently on many a movie-goer's lips, thanks to Christopher Nolan's latest effort to render physics a suitable subject for the big screen.
Cillian Murphy stars as the eponymous central character in the Christopher Nolan movie Oppenheimer. (Supplied: Universal)
But one episode absent from the blockbuster is the meeting, with an Australian scientist, that got Oppenheimer involved with the bomb in the first place.
History teems with chance encounters — instances in which human atoms collide with other human atoms, sometimes causing chain reactions.
The meeting between Oppenheimer and Adelaide-born physicist Mark Oliphant in California, in September 1941, was one such moment.
Oliphant pictured during his September 1941 trip to Berkeley, where he met with Oppenheimer and Lawrence. (Donald Cooksey/Public domain)
Fremantle-based historical researcher and geoscientist Darren Holden, who has investigated the encounter in detail, notes that it was the Australian, not the American, who instigated it.
"Oliphant's meeting brought in Oppenheimer who had, up until then, been part of the chorus line of theoretical physicists and had certainly not been involved in any applied bomb research," Dr Holden wrote in a research paper on the subject.
Darren Holden has investigated the meeting between Oliphant and Oppenheimer, and its role in the Manhattan Project. (Supplied)
By 1939, scientists were aware not only of the latent power of the atom, but of the possibility of a bomb: after the discovery of fission by chemists in Germany and physicists in Denmark and Sweden, a letter signed by Einstein was sent to US President Franklin Roosevelt, warning of unprecedented and "extremely powerful" weapons.
The following year, another major breakthrough occurred when two of Oliphant's colleagues at the University of Birmingham — Jewish refugees Otto Frisch and Rudolf Peierls — demonstrated the feasibility of a "super-bomb" using the isotope uranium-235, rather than the more plentiful but far less fissile uranium-238.
"They came up with the uranium-235 critical mass equations, that show that a nuclear bomb with uranium would be able to be constructed and able to be transported by aircraft," Dr Holden said.
Armed with this knowledge, Oliphant left Britain for America in 1941.
Amid concerns that Nazi Germany could develop such a weapon, and worried that nuclear research was languishing in the UK, he took matters into his own hands.
"He decided that he needed to act, and – I believe – without authority, in order to convince the Americans. He needed an ally," Dr Holden said.
That ally was experimental physicist Ernest Lawrence, whom Oliphant met in Berkeley with the intention of involving America — then still a neutral nation — in Allied efforts to produce a bomb.
J. Robert Oppenheimer several years after the Berkeley meeting with Oliphant. (Wikimedia: Ed Westcott/US Government)
It was Lawrence who sought the assistance of Oppenheimer, by asking him to "check the numbers" in the Frisch-Peierls paper.
"It was essentially at that point that Oppenheimer was brought in," Dr Holden said.
The physicists who built the first nuclear weapons became, in the public imagination, demigods who had unlocked a fundamental secret of the universe to end a world war.
"Oppenheimer became a pin-up boy of American science after the war," Dr Holden said.
In books and films, there has been a tendency to depict Oppenheimer as a tortured soul. (Supplied: Universal)
But literary voices – especially those who specialised in the depiction of dystopias — were among the first to articulate the moral magnitude of what had changed.
"The nuclear scientist will prepare the bed on which [humankind] must lie," Aldous Huxley stated in a 1946 foreword to Brave New World.
George Orwell was more mordant. In a post-war essay, the future author of Nineteen Eighty-Four offered words of caution about where science untempered by moral considerations might lead:
A popular theory persists that the physicists who devised and developed the bomb were racked with guilt.
Hedley Marston was, in many respects, an establishment man — but when he began studying nuclear fallout from British bomb tests at Maralinga, he became incensed.
But did they really regret their involvement? Was Oppenheimer, as two of his biographers have called him, an "American Prometheus"? And to what extent is the label "Australia's Oppenheimer" a fitting description of Oliphant?
In Oliphant's case, the evidence points in different directions.
Dr Holden notes that Oliphant and Oppenheimer continued to collaborate after the war, but on a cause very different to the one that had occupied them in 1941.
"[They] worked together to try and convince the governments of the world, and the United Nations, to ban atomic weapons for everybody," he said.
Nevertheless, less than 50 years after Hiroshima, the putatively pacifist Oliphant (by then Sir Mark) remained sufficiently pleased with his work on the bomb to write a letter to The Advertiser newspaper in 1986 in which he championed the British contributions to the Manhattan Project.
In an incisive evaluation of Oliphant's legacy, Dr Holden has argued that the physicist was "naive to assume" that wartime scientific gains "would be utilised in peacetime only for the greater good", and that Oliphant "remained proud rather than remorseful of his time at the Manhattan Project".
"It is overly simple to consider that it was scientists' remorse — of the part they played in creating atomic weaponry — that drove them to enter the postwar atomic science peace movement," Dr Holden has written.
Oliphant, Oppenheimer and the dozens of other physicists and chemists involved in the construction of the bomb thus remain ambiguous figures in the history of scientific research.
Their proximity to what was one of the most intensive, elaborate, formidable and destructive engineering endeavours ever undertaken perhaps denied them the kind of perspective afforded to non-scientists like Bruce Dawe, whose poem (quoted above) on the shadow of a Japanese child "blasted upon" a surface at Hiroshima ends with these words:
"In your blackened absence, this stencilled outline on the wall haunts us all with its unending play."
