title: Luc Longley steps out of Michael Jordan's shadow in new NBA documentary
content:
While Netflix's The Last Dance was an acclaimed insight into Michael Jordan and the dominance of the Chicago Bulls in the 1990s, it barely mentioned Australian Luc Longley.
The 218-centimetre centre was the first Australian to play in the NBA and was a major part of the Bulls' golden era alongside Jordan, Scottie Pippen, Dennis Rodman, and Steve Kerr.
Twenty-five years since the team's second three-peat, the NBA is making sure the West Australian's part in basketball history is being formally recognised.
First they released a merchandise run of Longley's #13 Chicago Bulls jersey.
Now comes a documentary titled Foundations, featuring unseen footage from his team's dominant era.
"I've seen the documentary and it's cool to see some of the old, original The Last Dance footage," Longley said.
Longley smashes a slam dunk against Orlando Magic. (Supplied: Luc Longley)
"Probably the playing footage was what I enjoyed the most, and there's some bits and pieces of family footage.
"I don't know why it went into the archives for a long time, but it was good to see, and it's cool for the NBA to recognise me and my part in that team and history.
"With the documentary and the T-shirts and jerseys, for me that's top-shelf flattery."
Longley says he is honoured the NBA has chosen to recognise him 25 years after the Bulls' three-peat. (Supplied: Sam Tolhurst)
Not long after the release of The Last Dance, the usually low-profile Longley agreed to a two-part ABC Australian Story about his life.
He has also recently become more active in the Australian basketball scene as a special advisor to the Sydney Kings.
Now with the release of the heritage jerseys and the Foundations documentary, Longley said he is becoming more comfortable with the limelight.
Luc Longley says he has become more comfortable sharing his story publicly in recent years. (Supplied: Sam Tolhurst)
"I'm never sure where the line between me avoiding building a profile and not caring about having a profile was," he said.
"I'm not sure what combination of factors it was when I finished playing, but I knew I wanted to be away from the game for a bit.
He has also taken on some public speaking which he said he never thought he would do.
Wollongong filmmaker Sam Tolhurst has known Longley through his work producing videos and photos for the Sydney Kings, and was a videographer on Foundations.
"I've always been conscious of not trying to bug Luc about his time in the NBA and asking questions about MJ [Jordan] because I know a lot of people want to know about his time in Chicago," he said.
Sam Tolhurst says he and Longley bonded over a shared love of the ocean, basketball, and banter. (Supplied: Sam Tolhurst)
"When the opportunity came up to work on this documentary, I was taken aback by the gravity of what it meant.
It turns out, the respect was mutual.
"When I called him [before the shoot] I expected him to say he's stuck with me again, but he said he was proud of me and that we get to work together because we're a package deal now and that meant a lot," Mr Tolhurst said.
"He's shown a genuine interest in me and we share a healthy love of banter, which I can take, but I don't have much choice when the guy is seven foot two."

title: Disney star CoCo Lee farewelled at Hong Kong funeral
content:
Fans of singer and songwriter CoCo Lee, who was best known for being the voice of Disney's animated Mulan in Mandarin, have gathered with flowers to pay their respects to their idol at her funeral in Hong Kong.
Warning: This story contains themes of depression and suicide. If you need help, call Lifeline on 13 11 14.
In a video for Monday's memorial service, actors and singers from Hong Kong, mainland China and Taiwan recalled their memories with Lee and mourned her death.
Action star Jackie Chan said everyone was proud of her when she sang at the Oscars in 2001.
"To friends like us, CoCo was a passionate and kind friend who showed care to us. She was really a good person. That's why we are so reluctant to accept she has left us," he said.
Lee was born in Hong Kong and attended school in San Francisco before releasing her first album in 1994 at age 19.
She began her career as a Mandopop singer but branched out to release albums in Cantonese and English.
CoCo Lee was sometimes compared to Mariah Carey by her fans in Asia. (AP Photo)
She was the first Chinese singer to break into the American market, and her English song Do You Want My Love climbed to number 4 on Billboard's Hot Dance Breakouts chart in December 1999.
In 2001, she sang A Love Before Time from Ang Lee’s movie Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon at the Academy Awards, becoming the first Chinese American to perform at the Oscars.
Lee was the voice of heroine Fa Mulan in the Mandarin version of Disney's animated 1998 Mulan and sang the Mandarin version of the movie's theme song Reflection — which she reprised for the 2020 live-action remake.
Her death in July shocked fans. Her siblings posted on Facebook that she experienced depression for years, and had attempted suicide at home on July 2.
She died a few days later at age 48.
On Monday afternoon, more than 100 fans dressed in black were waiting outside the funeral home.
Lin Jing, a fan from Fujian province in China's south-east, said she admired Lee's smile and appearance, adding: "She was really talented. She always tried to improve and she inspired women to feel independent."
Inside the funeral hall, three pink hearts made of flowers and other floral decorations were displayed below Lee's photo.
Her close friend, Taiwanese singer Elva Hsiao, told the ceremony she remembered watching Lee's performances as a student and thinking of her as a perfect idol.
After they became friends in the entertainment industry, Lee encouraged Hsiao when she was lost and treated her as "a little sister".
Do You Want My Love was a late 1990s hit for CoCo Lee.
"She brightened my life with her happiness and bravery. I will keep preserving her spirit," Hsiao said in a quavering voice.
Award-winning director Ang Lee recalled his exchanges with the late singer before the Oscars and said it was a pity she died so young.
"We miss her very much. CoCo, rest in peace," he said in another pre-recorded video.
CoCo Lee had sounded notes of positivity in social media posts during the months before her death. In March, she posted about recuperating from surgery for an old leg injury.
"Successful surgery. Even though I'm in a lot of pain and I have to re-learn how to walk again, I know I can do it," she wrote in a Facebook post.
"Yes I can and I will!"
Lee was married to Bruce Rockowitz, former CEO of Hong Kong supply chain company Li & Fung. She had two stepdaughters.
Fans line up near the Hong Kong Funeral Home ahead of the service for CoCo Lee. (AP: Annie Cheung)

title: Euphoria actor Angus Cloud dies
content:
Actor Angus Cloud, best known for his role in Euphoria, has died aged 25.
His family released a statement on Tuesday, announcing the shock death.
"It is with the heaviest heart that we had to say goodbye to an incredible human today. As an artist, a friend, a brother and a son, Angus was special to all of us in so many ways," they wrote.
Cloud's father passed away last week, according to the statement.
Cloud was set to appear in the upcoming Scream 6 film.  (AP: Richard Shotwell/Invision)
"The only comfort we have is knowing Angus is now reunited with his dad, who was his best friend.
"Angus was open about his battle with mental health and we hope that his passing can be a reminder to others that they are not alone and should not fight this on their own in silence.
Cloud's publicist, Cait Bailey, said he died on Monday at his family home in Oakland, California.
Cloud was acclaimed for his role as drug dealer Fezco 'Fez' O'Neill in the award-winning HBO show Euphoria.
Angus Cloud died at his family home in Oakland, California. (AP: Evan Agostini/Invision)
The company and tv show posted on Instagram and X, stating they were "incredibly saddened" to learn the news.
Among the first to chime in about Cloud’s death was actor Javon Walton, who played Ashtray, the younger brother of Fezco.
"Rest easy brother,” Walton wrote in his post on Instagram.
Musician and filmmaker Questlove also spoke on Cloud's death.
“Fez was the spiritual centre of Euphoria and definitely my fav character on the show," he wrote in an Instagram post.
"Love to his entire family and to those who knew him. #AngusCloud.”
Kerry Washington also followed suit, posting a tribute on X.

Cloud was scouted for Euphoria while walking through Manhattan, in a move he originally thought was a scam, he told Wall Street Journal in 2019.
He was most recently cast in upcoming horror film Scream 6.
Cloud often pushed back against the notion he was identical to his Euphoria character.
"It does bother me when people are like, 'It must be so easy! You get to go in and be yourself.' I'm like, 'Why don't you go and do that?' It's not that simple," Cloud told Variety.
The third season of Euphoria has not yet begun filming.

title: Actor and comedian Paul Reubens, known for Pee-wee Herman, dies
content:
Actor and comedian Paul Reubens, whose character Pee-wee Herman became a cultural phenomenon, has died aged 70.
Reubens died on Sunday night after a six-year struggle with cancer he did not make public, his publicist said in a statement.
"Please accept my apology for not going public with what I've been facing the last six years," Reubens said in a statement released on Monday with the announcement of his death.
The character, with his too-tight grey suit, white chunky loafers and red bow tie, was best known for the film Pee-wee's Big Adventure and television series Pee-wee's Playhouse.
Actor Paul Reubens dies age 70 after an undisclosed battle with cancer.  (AP: Danny Moloshok )
The Pee-wee character would become a cultural constant for much of the 1980s, though an indecent exposure arrest in 1991 would send him into entertainment exile for years.
Herman created Pee-wee when he was part of the Los Angeles improv group The Groundlings in the late 1970s.
The live Pee-wee Herman Show debuted at a Los Angeles theater in 1981 and was a success with both kids during matinees and adults at a midnight show.
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
The format was similar to the Saturday morning show Pee-wee's Playhouse which would follow years later.
The show's antics featured Herman living in a wild and wacky home with a series of stock-character visitors.
The series ran for five seasons, earned 22 Emmys and attracted not only children but adults to Saturday-morning TV.
"It's for kids," Reubens told The Associated Press in 2010.
Paul Reubens beloved character Pee-wee Herman was known for his too-tight grey suit, white chunky loafers and red bow tie.  (AP: Jack Plunkett/Invision )
"People have tried to get me for years to go, 'It wasn't really for kids, right?' Even the original show was for kids. I always censored myself to have it be kid-friendly."
Reubens took Herman to the big screen in 1985's Pee-wee's Big Adventure.
The movie was a success, grossing $40 million, and continued to spawn a cult following for its oddball whimsy.
Sequels followed with Big Top Pee-wee in 1988 and 2016's Pee-wee's Big Holiday.
But Reubens' career was derailed when he was arrested for indecent exposure in an adult movie theatre in Florida.
He was handed a small fine but the damage to the character was incalculable.
He became the frequent butt of late-night talk show jokes and the perception of Reubens immediately changed.
"The moment that I realised my name was going to be said in the same sentence as children and sex, that's really intense," Reubens told NBC in 2004.
"That's something I knew from that very moment, whatever happens past that point, something's out there in the air that is really bad."
In 2001, Reubens was also arrested and charged with misdemeanour possession of child pornography, but the allegation was reduced to an obscenity charge and he was given three years' probation.
Reubens would also act as non-Pee-wee characters including in Tim Burton's 1992 movie Batman Returns, the Buffy the Vampire Slayer film and guest-starring on TV show Murphy Brown.

title: 'China will punish a company': Is Hollywood playing a risky game with China?
content:
Like many industries, including those here in Australia, Hollywood has become increasingly dependent on Chinese revenue.
Despite ongoing US-China tensions, Hollywood films — the recent Avatar sequel, for example — can still make hundreds of millions of dollars at the Chinese box office.
But getting films into China means securing the tick of approval from the ruling Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and passing the country's strict censors.
And there's concern about the effect that this influence could be having on films.
The relationship between Hollywood and China goes back a century, says Wendy Su, an associate professor in media and cultural studies at the University of California, Riverside.
Rear Vision puts contemporary events in their historical context, answering the question: "How did it come to this?"
"Hollywood started marching into the Chinese market from the 1920s, and by the 1930s and 1940s, Hollywood occupied more than 75 per cent of the Chinese film market," she tells ABC RN's Rear Vision.
But this abruptly changed when the CCP came into power in 1949 and with the outbreak of the Korean War in 1950.
"China issued a ban on American movies because they believed American movies would poison Chinese people's minds," Dr Su says.
During this time, the Chinese film sector had the "purpose of education and advocating [for] state ideology", she says.
From 1978, the reforms of then-Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping liberalised and modernised Chinese industries, including the local film industry. However it struggled throughout the 1980s and early 1990s.
So, China looked overseas for help.
In 1994, China agreed to start importing 10 foreign films a year on a revenue-sharing basis.
Stanley Rosen, a professor of political science at the University of Southern California, says these films were also a way to win back the country's youth, many of whom resented the government after the Tiananmen Square massacre.
Starting with Harrison Ford's blockbuster The Fugitive, these 10 big annual imports brought audiences back to cinemas in droves.
The 1997 film Titanic was a massive hit in China, with the film winning praise from then-President Jiang Zemin and setting a local box office record.
James Cameron's Titanic earned US$44 million ($65 million) in China, putting the country on the map for Hollywood releases. (Getty Images: Andres Hernandez)
The Hollywood-China relationship seemed rock solid.
But it wasn't to last.
Three films released in 1997 severely irked China.
Kundun, directed by Martin Scorsese, and Seven Years in Tibet, starring Brad Pitt, both featured the Dalai Lama, who China considers a separatist.
Then there was Red Corner, a thriller starring Richard Gere, about an American in China who is wrongfully accused of murder.
Tensions between Canberra and Beijing are nothing new.
"[These films] were never intended to be shown in China. But the Chinese picked up on them and actually banned the entire studio [which made each film] from showing any films in China," Professor Rosen says.
"China showed the clout it had by saying to the studios: 'You're only as strong as your weakest link — if you make a film that we don't like, even if you don't plan to show it here, we will ban all your films'."
It was a sign of things to come.
Neither China nor Hollywood could ignore that there was money to be made in this revenue-sharing arrangement.
So when China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, it agreed to double its annual import quota of revenue-sharing films from 10 to 20.
Around this time, the number of screens in China — so the potential for ticket sales — also grew dramatically.
In 2009, James Cameron's Avatar made a record-setting US$200 million ($290 million) at the Chinese box office. And before long, other Hollywood blockbusters started doing the same.
A string of Hollywood superhero films were box office hits in China during the 2010s. (Getty Images: Wang Zhao)
Then in 2012, the quota went up again — to 34 films a year.
It was a "massive economic opportunity" for Hollywood, says Erich Schwartzel, Hollywood reporter for The Wall Street Journal.
"However, that also means that China's political power increases exponentially, because suddenly getting onto those screens and passing censorship … becomes all the more important."
And passing censorship is not always straightforward. There's a long list of things that can get a film vetoed, like too much violence, too much sex, portraying China in a negative way, or anything featuring Tibet, Taiwan or Xinjiang, the home to many Uyghur people.
As China became an important revenue stream for Hollywood in the 2010s, studios started to make films with Chinese audiences in mind.
Chinese actors and Chinese products were included in some films. For example, in 2014's Transformers: Age of Extinction, an actor stops mid-run for some refreshing Shuhua (a Chinese brand of milk).
China has been a source of big profits for Hollywood, but are there strings attached? (Reuters: Aly Song)
But it's also led to some self-censoring, argues Mr Schwartzel.
He says one of the most dramatic examples is the 2012 remake of the film Red Dawn, which was to feature a Chinese invasion of the US.
After the film was shot, China got wind of the project and state media expressed its outrage, despite no plans to ever release it in China.
"So [the studio] MGM did something quite drastic," Mr Schwartzel says.
He explains how the completed film was taken to a post-production facility, where all references to China were removed and substituted with North Korea.
"So the movie that was released — the new Red Dawn — was about a North Korean invasion of the US, not a Chinese invasion," he says.
"That actually was the last time a major studio put a movie into production with China as the villain … and I think it will be the last example for a long time."
Around 2018, President Xi Jinping sought to tighten the CCP's grip over the country's film industry.
Mr Schwartzel says the Chinese film industry, "[which] had been exciting and promising and artistically auspicious, really started to seem more and more like an arm of the state".
But the industry wasn't suffering as a result. In 2020, China first surpassed North America to become the biggest box office in the world.
A Beijing cinema prepares to reopen after COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns. (Reuters: Tingshu Wang)
In recent years, however, there's been a big shift, with homegrown hits in China increasingly accounting for more of the profits.
"After nearly 40 years of embracing Hollywood movies, the audience became bored with repetitive blockbusters," Dr Su says.
She says China has learned a lot from Hollywood about how to make films more commercially appealing, with rising Chinese nationalism meaning audiences are embracing more local content.
And Mr Schwartzel adds that China is also hoping to export more of its films overseas, as part of its "campaign to expand Chinese influence around the world".
The 2021 film The Battle at Lake Changjin was about Chinese soldiers fighting American troops during the Korean War. (Reuters: Aly Song)
But Mr Schwartzel doesn't think Hollywood's love affair with China is over. This is despite one notable blip in the relationship last year, when a Taiwanese flag was removed, then eventually reinserted on Tom Cruise's jacket in Top Gun: Maverick.
"[Hollywood] might not bend over backwards for [China], but they're not going to make any movies that jeopardise that access," Mr Schwartzel says.
"They've seen in the past how China will punish a company or a conglomerate any way it can."

title: Sonia Kruger wins gold and tributes flow for Jock Zonfrillo: The biggest 2023 Logie Awards moments
content:
The 2023 Logies saw the biggest names in Australian television under one roof in Sydney.
It also saw some rather unexpected wins and heartfelt tributes.
These were the biggest moments of the night.
Early highlights from the carpet included host of ABC’s The War on Waste, Craig Reucassel, arriving in a dress made completely out of recycled plastic.
Over the six years since he became the face of the program, Reucassel has learnt a lot about rubbish and recycling.
"I think fashion continues to be one of the areas that shocks me the most," Reucassel told ABC News earlier in July.
"We've gone from fast fashion to now we have ultra-fast fashion."
The ABC program Crazy Fun Park earned the award for most outstanding children's program.
It surprised many who had assumed the worldwide-popular Bluey would take home the award.
The creators of the winning show even acknowledged the surprise, starting their speech with "I'm really sorry everyone".
Crazy Fun Park follows an introverted teen who loses his best friend at an abandoned theme park.  (Supplied: Channel Seven)
The Graham Kennedy Award for Most Popular New Talent went to Amy Shark, who also seemed genuinely surprised.
"I don't have anything prepared because there were so many incredible actors [up for the award]," Shark said on stage.
"I am in utter disbelief right now."
Amy Shark was also one of the performers at this year's event.  (Supplied: Channel Seven)
Shark joined the Australian Idol judging panel alongside Kyle Sandilands and international performers Harry Connick Jr and Meghan Trainor this year.
She has been confirmed for the show's 2024 season.
Armstrong won the Bert Newton Award for Most Popular Presenter.
A Dog's World with Tony Armstrong and ABC News Breakfast are his programs.
He said he "truly didn't think this would happen," while accepting the award on stage.
Tony Armstrong wins the Bert Newton Award at the 2023 Logies.
The win makes it two Logies in two years for Armstrong after taking out the Graham Kennedy Award in 2022.
"Last year after I was lucky enough to be given the Graham Kennedy Award and I said I was going to be renegotiating contracts," Armstrong said.
"This year I told [ABC news director] Justin Stevens, the big boss, if I won this, there would be another round of renegotiations."
Here are some more of the ABC's wins:
MasterChef Australia's latest season, Fans and Favourites, won the most popular reality program award.
The show's executive producer, Marty Benson, addressed the loss of Zonfrillo on stage.
"As I stand here tonight, it's still hard to believe that my mate and our amazing judge Jock is no longer with us," Benson said.
Melissa Leong (second from right) fought back tears as the cast and crew of the show paid tribute to the late chef. (AAP: Steve Markham)
Zonfrillo was one of the show's three hosts.
The 46-year-old was found dead in his Melbourne hotel room by police doing a welfare check.
Celebrity chef Jock Zonfrillo has been remembered on air. (Supplied)
It's a win for Gen Z.
Weatherall took home the award for most outstanding supporting actor for Heartbreak High.
It was his first Logie nomination and win.
This was Weatherall's first Logie nomination and win.  (Supplied: Channel 7)
The award was introduced by the original Heartbreak Kid, Alex Dimitriades, and the star of the Netflix reboot, Ayesha Madon.
Featuring a cast of diverse actors, thoughtful storylines and plenty of Aussie slang, Netflix's modern take on the 90s classic became a hit at home and overseas.
Veteran media executive Brian Walsh received a standing ovation from the audience at The Star when he was inducted into the TV Week Logie Hall of Fame.
Walsh was the driving force behind various Australian television shows including Neighbours, A Place to Call Home, Wentworth and Colin from Accounts.
Brian Walsh has been remembered as a driving force of Australia's television industry. (AAP: Gaye Gerard)
Walsh passed away at 67 earlier this year.
Sonia Kruger won the Gold Logie for Most Popular Personality on Australian Television.
The award was presented by Daryl Somers.
"I cannot believe that. I have to compose myself," Kruger said on stage.
Sonia Kruger accepts the 2023 Gold Logie award.

title: First Barbie, now Beanie Babies: Why are there suddenly so many movies about toys?
content:
If you weren't around for it, you should know the Beanie Babies fad of the late 90s drove seemingly rational adults to some wild behaviour.
People would spend hours of their lives and thousands of dollars collecting $5 animal soft toys with the hopes that it would pay off big time. There was even a murder linked to Beanie Baby trading.
In hindsight, it's easy to see exactly how the Beanie Babies mass hysteria unfolded — a toy company's canny marketing being supercharged by a network of obsessed American mums and the rise of e-commerce.
The phenomenon was so wild, it's surprising it took a Hollywood studio two decades to make the movie.
The Beanie Bubble — starring Elizabeth Banks, Sarah Snook, Geraldine Viswanathan and Zach Galifianakis — charts the story of the Beanie Babies mania from its founding to the beginning of the end.
Youtube from Apple TV+: The Beanie Bubble — Official Trailer
It's a zany and curious film, exposing the behind-the-scenes shenanigans of how a mercurial man with an eye for detail thrust these toys upon the world.
More significantly, the movie restores the contribution of the women in founder Ty Warner's life, and the outsized roles they played in helping Warner become a billionaire, before he was eventually convicted of tax evasion.
The Beanie Bubble isn't just the story of a trend, it's part of one as well. In the repetitive ecosystem of Hollywood output, The Beanie Bubble is the latest in a string of films centred on brands and products.
Like The Beanie Bubble, some of them are origin stories: The Founder (McDonalds); Air (Nike Air Jordans); Tetris; Flamin' Hot (Cheetos). While others are based on characters, like The Lego Movie, Barbie and a slate of upcoming Mattel properties including the just-greenlit Polly Pocket movie, directed by Lena Dunham, starring Lily Collins.
It's produced by Margot Robbie, directed by Greta Gerwig and stars Issa Rae as President Barbie — and it's become a cultural moment before it even opens in cinemas.
Before the end of the year, there will also be the Blackberry movie and a Poptarts film directed by Jerry Seinfeld. Yes, Poptarts. As in, those over-sugared American toaster pastries.
Fuelled by a mix of nostalgia and familiarity, movie studios believe they've cottoned on to a good thing.
Consumer psychologist Adam Ferrier, founder of marketing agency Thinkerbell, argues that the strategy is all about risk mitigation.
"Making a movie out of existing brands means these films almost become the sequel," he says.
"There's an impression in somebody's mind about a certain brand or a certain product because there are lots of latent memory structures there. So, when the movie comes out, you're leveraging off the pre-existing associations of that brand in people's minds.
"It already feels familiar and personal to them, so it's almost a guaranteed success."
The star-studded cast of The Beanie Bubble — including Elizabeth Banks and Zach Galifianakis — help bring the wild story to life. (Supplied: Apple TV+)
The nostalgia factor also works to evoke an audience reaction, according to Ferrier.
"In the 1980s, you had toys and media properties that cut right through culture that everybody participated in," he says.
"Now you can resurrect those feelings and have a mass communal experience again. That's more potent today because we have media fragmentation, and fragmentation of everything."
By building a story around a brand, studios and companies such as Mattel can also expand that positive association in myriad ways through merchandising and marketing.
The Barbie movie has exploded in brand collaborations. You can buy a Barbie-branded product in almost every category, from burgers and bubble teas to electric toothbrushes and nail polish.
"The Barbie brand can now be monetised and sold as experiences, as well as movie tickets and dolls. It's elevating all these available products into genuine, multidimensional brands."
Ferrier warns that to offset the crass commercialism of a brand-inspired movie, you have to inject as much artistic or creative integrity into the story as possible.
"Therefore, you have to get a very well-known, powerful, arthouse, feminist director to make the Barbie movie. And you have to make sure the script plays on sophisticated themes, and you write the hell out of it," he adds.
"It's almost as if the rule is, the more commercialised it is, the more artistic credibility you have to give it to make sure it's a success."
The Beanie Bubble is on Apple TV+ from Friday, July 28 at 5pm AEST. Barbie is in cinemas now.

title: Aussie paragliders achieve world first with 5,200m-high launch from Nepalese mountains
content:
For the months of effort negotiating a permit with government officials to the expense of getting there, Ken Hutt said even one minute of paragliding through the Everest region of Nepal was worth it.
The 63-year-old veteran paraglider and colleague Marcus Loane spent two days hiking to an altitude of 5,200 metres to fly from the Lobuche Peak in Nepal.
"It's something you know won't be achieved by too many people," Mr Hutt told ABC Illawarra Breakfast presenter Melinda James.
"To fly around the mountains looking at the face of Everest — you can't describe it.
"You then land in a little village in the Khumbu Valley, walk in and have a hot cup of tea, look back at what you've done and think, 'That was very special'."
The expedition was part of Mr Hutt's ongoing work filming a movie to promote the eradication of polio.
After failing to paraglide from Mount Everest last year after developing a chest infection on the trip, he said he needed more spectacular footage for the film.
"It gives you a good feeling of accomplishing something not many people have done," he said.
Berry paraglider Ken Hutt said he had to be ready to deal with changing conditions during his flight in Nepal due to the immense height from which he launched. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)
"But it [also] allows us to get the attention for world polio eradication, and by doing something like this it allows us to talk about that."
Mr Hutt acknowledges the sport he loves is dangerous, especially when it sees him hiking to remote parts of the world and at altitudes where the air is thin.
There is also the added pressure of taking advantage of a rare opportunity to paraglide in Nepal and capture quality footage for the film he is working on.
"If the conditions aren't quite perfect at somewhere like Stanwell Tops [near Wollongong] you'd say, 'Let's go home and come another day'," he said.
"The sheer fact of the effort and cost and cause of getting to Nepal means you do push the boundaries of safe flight a little further than you would. So you take that into consideration.
"But I have a promise to my wife I'll come home every time [after a flight] and it's not the be all and end all."
Paragliders Ken Hutt and Marcus Loane say it is unlikely other paragliders will ever be given government approval to fly in the same area of the Everest mountain region. (Supplied: Ken Hutt)
Unlike popular paragliding spots in the Illawarra where Ken Hutt and Marcus Loane are from, flying in Nepal demands extra skills.
The mountains can make it a turbulent flight, and because of the distance travelled it is hard for paragliders to know exactly what conditions they will have during their flight.
"I suppose that's why it's such an accomplishment."
The men spent about a month acclimatising to the conditions in Nepal before hiking to their launch spot. (Supplied: Ken Hutt)
Mr Loane said he was hoping his colleague would take off first and he would film from behind, but he was busy preparing his equipment.
With weather deteriorating, Mr Hutt told him to go.
"Things don't always go as planned and Ken just said to go because maybe we won't be able to fly again," Mr Loane said.
"Ken followed not long behind me and it was a fantastic flight. It was exhilarating."

title: Creepy, gruesome new Australian horror movie destined to become a slumber party classic
content:
In horror movies, a disembodied hand almost always spells trouble. Who could forget Bruce Campbell's Ash duelling his severed appendage in Evil Dead II? Director Oliver Stone made an entire film about a missing meathook on a murder spree. And then there's 90s stoner classic Idle Hands, in which a teenager's possessed paw goes on a high school prom rampage that culminates in the scalping of a cameoing rock star. (It's a masterpiece, critics be damned.)
Another malevolent hand looms at the centre of the new Australian horror movie Talk to Me, in which a house party trick involving momentary demonic possession leads to gruesome consequences for a bunch of teenagers playing chicken with the supernatural.
The film marks the feature directing debut of Adelaide-born, Los Angeles-based twin brothers Danny and Michael Philippou, aka YouTube creators RackaRacka, who broke out with their 2014 viral smash Harry Potter VS Star Wars and have since attracted a massive global following thanks to their ingenious horror-comedy clips.
The film was shot in Adelaide, where it is also set, and premiered at Adelaide Film Festival in 2022. (Supplied: A24)
The siblings' sensibilities are hardwired into Talk to Me, a nervy, go-for-broke horror movie with lashings of off-kilter comedy and grisly imagery. It puts what feels like the last decade of horror into a blender and serves it up with just enough inventiveness to thrill – a creep show that's destined to become a slumber-party classic for the age of Letterboxd.
It begins in a location right out of a horror-movie nightmare: suburban Adelaide, where, captured in a bravura tracking shot by cinematographer Aaron McLisky, a blowout house party of bored, drunk teenagers rages into the night. It's all teen-movie business as usual until an apparently possessed partygoer comes to a nasty end, the victim of a deadly occult game gone too far.
In a clever variation on the viral challenges that sweep through TikTok, teens have become obsessed with mysterious new videos where their peers get off on the temporary high of being possessed by a demonic force.
After screening at Sundance Film Festival earlier this year, the film was picked up by indie distributor A24. (Supplied: A24)
Among the teenagers watching are 17-year-old Mia (Sophie Wilde, from Stan series Eden and the BBC's series You Don't Know Me), brooding over the death of her troubled mother; her bestie Jade (Alexandra Jensen), and Jade's younger brother Riley (Joe Bird), who form a kind of surrogate family unit. They're soon invited to a basement gathering run by mysterious 20-somethings Joss (Chris Alosio) and Hayley (Zoe Terakes), where an embalmed hand inscribed with esoteric carvings – and said to have been severed from the arm of a psychic – becomes the focal point of a terrifying but exhilarating parlour game.
If a player says "talk to me", the hand reveals to them a shadow dimension of ghouls and waylaid souls who exist in the room. Follow that with "I let you in" and they get a mainline hit as one of those anguished entities possesses their body, all while the assembled onlookers capture the transformation for viral posterity.
The catch: the possession needs to be shut down in 90 seconds, or the player might end up with a permanent demonic cohabitant.
You can bet that the 90s version would have been called Talk to the Hand.
The 29-year-old Philippou brothers rose to success with their horror-comedy YouTube channel RackaRacka, which boasts some 6.74 million subscribers. (Supplied: A24)
It's a great premise – Flatliners as teen-party occult trick – with a spin on the old cursed monkey's paw that works as both an obvious analogy for the high of drugs and a riff on our current desperation to film anything and everything for maximum social media impact.
There's a killer montage of teens taking hits from the hand, as it were, that sees the Philippous in full, thrilling flight as filmmakers: disorientating angles, creative camera movements, a rush of sound and vision to evoke the ecstasy and terror of the high.
They've obviously brought their considerable visual effects experience, and sense of the bizarre, to bear, from some impressive practical work (what appears to be an animatronic kangaroo set to become roadkill) to a string of amusingly off-colour moments (if you've ever wanted to see a possessed teenager making out with a horny bulldog, this is the movie for you).
There are some genuinely gnarly scenes of gore and brutality, too, enhanced by the kind of loud, lurid sound design that takes full opportunity to ramp up the chaotic atmosphere.
It's no surprise that taste-making American distributor A24 was quick to snap the film up after its Sundance screening earlier this year; the Philippous have a head full of seemingly every horror movie to hit the zeitgeist in the last decade, whether it's the explicit references, formally and visually, to Jordan Peele's Get Out, the elevated schtick of Ari Aster (Hereditary; Midsommar), or the spring-loaded crowd-pleasers of James Wan (The Conjuring; Malignant).
At its worst, that might sound like a closed loop of inspiration, of filmmakers feeding on nothing but other horror movies, but for a good while – intentionally or otherwise – Talk to Me works in conversation with its cinematic landscape, reflecting so many of the ways the genre has twisted and turned of late.
"In Australian films, we really like to focus on nature and the bush … But it felt really interesting to see something that was more urban and more about the youth culture," Wilde told ABC News. (Supplied: A24)
The movie has audacious style to spare, and the Philippous' energy is infectious as they unleash a decade's worth of dabbling into a debut that rocks and rolls with relish.
If only they'd committed to running all the way with their instincts and not let the movie take a turn for that dreariest of modern horror crutches: an exploration of trauma.
After a wildly entertaining first half, the narrative becomes preoccupied with Mia's reckoning with the loss of her mother, a grief that becomes the primary motivator for the film's action. (Remember when horror movies were primarily devoted to, you know, unnerving and entertaining audiences, and all the 'trauma' was implied and understood?)
Making her feature acting debut, Wilde is fantastic in the lead, delivering a psychologically fraught, physically gruelling performance that would give a seasoned actor a workout – she's going to be a star, for sure – but she's also stretched to the limit by a screenplay (credited to Danny Philippou, Bill Hinzman and Daley Pearson) that doesn't always have a handle on her character's harrowing backstory.
"Creating is just something we've always been drawn to. We've always got to be making something or writing something," Michael Philippou told ABC News. (Supplied: A24)
The dissonance becomes an issue for the movie as the filmmakers struggle to make all their threads cohere. The rules of the game are inconsistent and appear to change according to narrative convenience, and the imagery is rife with the sort of random, scary imagery that – while certainly commensurate with a frayed state of mind – often sits at odds with a more sobering exploration of mourning.
It's a minor enough gripe. The filmmakers, assisted by some genuinely evocative photography from McLisky, arrive armed with enough stylistic brio – and irresistible passion for the genre – that the film comes through with a rousing, loopy finish, one that's both sinister and funny enough to put any misgivings about tonal incoherence aside.
Talk to Me announces a pair of horror filmmakers with great promise. It'll be exciting to see where they go from here.
Talk to Me is in cinemas now.

title: Dual release of blockbusters Barbie and Oppenheimer a shot in the arm for independent cinemas
content:
Independent cinema owners say the recent releases of Barbie and Oppenheimer are reinvigorating the industry after the rise of streaming giants during the COVID-19 pandemic.
At Griffith City Cinemas in southern New South Wales, assistant manager Stephanie Bertoldo said people were queuing out the door for Barbie tickets over the weekend.
The small theatre saw nearly 4,000 people through the doors over the weekend for Barbie alone, compared to an average 1,000 tickets over a typical week for a big movie.
Craig Lucas said his cinema sold thousands of extra tickets over the weekend. (ABC Riverina: Conor Burke)
It was a similar story in nearby Wagga Wagga, where Forum 6 Cinemas cancelled other movie showings to accommodate demand for Barbie.
"Top Gun: Maverick turned out to be our third biggest grossing movie of all time; Barbie is heading into that realm," cinema manager Craig Lucas said.
His cinema sold four times as many tickets as a regular weekend thanks to what has been dubbed Barbenheimer due to the simultaneous release of the two very different blockbuster movies.
Naomi Darby and Jacinta Churchill dressed up to attend the Barbie premiere at Sale's cinema. (ABC News: Kellie Lazzaro)
Barbie took $21.55 million at the Australian box office this weekend, while Oppenhemier took $9.40 million, combining to be the biggest weekend in Australian cinema history, according to the figures from the Motion Picture Distributors Association of Australia.
Barbie has enjoyed the seventh biggest opening weekend of all time in Australia, the biggest movie opening of the year worldwide, and the 24th biggest opening of all time.
Screen Australia figures show annual cinema ticket sales during 2022 were down by about 27 million when compared to before the pandemic.
Mr Lucas said the big weekend was a welcome reprieve after the pandemic changed the way people watched movies.
He said product supply alongside streaming platforms had been an issue, as had shrinking "windows" — the time between when a movie is released in theatres to when it then hits streaming platforms.
Two of the year's most anticipated movies came out this weekend. Early estimates from the US put Barbie ahead in the box office takings.
"The whole landscape has changed really, and what this shows to me in a lot of ways is people will only come out for really big movies," Mr Lucas said.
He added that the current actors and writers' strike in the United States could further disrupt the film industry by making less movies available.
Independent Cinemas Australia vice president, and regional cinema owner, Kieren Dell said having the dual opening was an "amazing one-two punch" for cinemas, which could have lasting effects for regional theatres.
"We're seeing just about everyone in some of our towns come out in that opening weekend."
Cinema veteran Val Hodges hopes it is a trend that sticks after a few tough years.
Ms Hodges and her husband Barry, who is a projectionist, have owned the only cinema in the eastern Victorian town of Sale for the past 30 years.
"We've really been treading water until now," she said.
Val Hodges has owned the Sale Cinema for 30 years. (ABC News: Kellie Lazzaro)
She said Barbie attracted crowds she had not seen since the release of the Harry Potter and Lord of the Rings franchises.
While she was also worried about the fallout from the actors and writers' strike in the United States and the uptake of streaming services, Ms Hodges said the cinema industry had proved its resilience because movies made people feel something.
In the build-up to Thursday's release of Barbie in Australian cinemas, Margot Robbie has been doing a whole bunch of promotional events — and her outfits have not disappointed fans.
"You sit in your seat with a whole lot of people, some friends, some strangers, and if there's something funny on the screen everyone laughs and it creates this fantastic vibe," she said.
"If it is sad, everyone is crying together and it is a special thing you cannot reproduce anywhere else."
Mr Dell saw both films this week and he said it reinforced everything he loved about film.
"We have two movies that, while they are poles apart, they're both very important," he said.
"Oppenhemier is talking about the invention of the atomic bomb and it's a major moment in history and it's so powerful.
"And Barbie … it has quite meaty themes of equality and feminism and [it's] quite a satire and it took me by surprise … and that's the power of cinema and that's what I love about it."

title: Greta Gerwig has made box office history with Barbie. Here's your guide to her previous films
content:
Greta Gerwig is everything.
The American director made history over the weekend with the highly anticipated release of Barbie, starring Australia's Margot Robbie as the iconic doll experiencing an existential crisis.
Not only did Barbie net the highest opening weekend of 2023 so far with $155 million, but Gerwig broke the opening weekend record for a female director, solo or otherwise, in North America.
Ryan Gosling stars as Ken in Greta Gerwig's Barbie. (Supplied: Warner Bros)
That figure easily surpasses the $103 million domestic opening of Patty Jenkins' Wonder Woman, which Gerwig previously credited as a trailblazing project for women in cinema.
But that's just the domestic figures. Thanks to the relentless marketing campaign, embedded nostalgia and runaway Barbenheimer meme, Barbie has so far grossed $337 million worldwide — a figure which is only set to grow.
So who is Gerwig? Which other films has she directed? And why do they resonate with audiences so much?
Margot Robbie and Greta Gerwig at the Los Angeles premiere of Barbie. (AP Photo: Chris Pizzello)
Gerwig is no overnight success, and she's not just a director either.
The 39-year-old has been working in Hollywood for close to two decades and, along with directing, is also an actor and screenwriter.
Like many artists, she got her start working on independent films.
In the 2000s she co-wrote and co-directed multiple "mumblecore" films — a term given to a subgenre of low-budget, coming-of-age independent films that feature naturalistic acting and dialogue, hence the mumbling.
She collaborated with fellow director Joe Swanberg multiple times, with the pair co-directing, producing and starring in Nights and Weekends.
But it was in 2009, when acting in the film Greenberg, that Gerwig met another director who would become her longtime collaborator and partner.
If you've seen Marriage Story or White Noise, then you're already familiar with Noah Baumbach's directing.
Barbie marks Noah Baumbach, 53, and Greta Gerwig's most recent screenwriting collaboration. (AP Photo: Scott Garfitt/Invision)
After meeting Gerwig while directing Greenberg, the pair collaborated again in 2013 on the film Frances Ha.
Gerwig co-wrote the screenplay with Baumbach and starred in the film as the protagonist alongside Adam Driver, whom Baumbach would later work with again in Marriage Story.
France Ha earned the pair multiple awards, including Gerwig's first Golden Globe nomination for Best Actress in a Musical or Comedy.
Frances Ha trailer.
The pair collaborated again in 2015 for Mistress America, with Gerwig starring in the film and also co-writing and co-producing the project alongside Baumbach.
In 2019, the pair welcomed their first child, a baby boy called Harold, which Gerwig kept under wraps while working. They welcomed their second son earlier this year.
Last year Baumbach wrote and directed White Noise, a Netflix film based on Don DeLillo's novel of the same name, which again starred Gerwig and Driver.
And, of course, there's Barbie, with Gerwig directing the film based on the screenplay she wrote with Baumbach.
But Barbie is by no means Gerwig's first attempt at solo directing.
In 2017, Gerwig wrote and directed comedy-drama Lady Bird, marking her solo directorial debut.
Lady Bird trailer.
What's it about? Lady Bird tells the story of a high school senior and her strained relationship with her mother.
Who's in it? Saoirse Ronan, Laurie Metcalf, Timothee Chalamet
What did it make at the global box office? $79 million
How was it received? Lady Bird received a standing ovation when it premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and has a 99 per cent approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes.
What about awards? The film was nominated for five Academy Awards, including Best Picture, Best Director, Best Original Screenplay, Best Actress and Best Supporting Actress but didn't win in any of its categories. However, Gerwig became the fifth woman ever to be nominated for an Oscar for directing.
Where can I watch it? Amazon Prime Video and Binge
Two years later, while pregnant with her first child, Gerwig wrote and directed another film adaption of Louisa May Alcott's classic novel Little Women.
Little Women trailer.
What's it about? The famous story follows the lives of the four March sisters — Jo, Meg, Beth and Amy — charting their passage from childhood to womanhood.
Who's in it? Saoirse Ronan, Florence Pugh, Emma Watson, Eliza Scanlen, Lauren Dern, Timothee Chalamet, Meryl Streep
What did it make at the global box office? $218 million
How was it received? Little Women premiered on Christmas Day, narrowly avoiding COVID-19 disruptions, and is currently enjoying a score of 95 per cent on Rotten Tomatoes.
What about awards? The film earned six Academy Award nominations, including Best Picture, Best Actress, Best Supporting Actress, Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Original Score and won for Best Costume Design. Despite Gerwig being nominated for her screenplay, this was yet another year no women were nominated for Best Director.
Where can I watch it? Binge
One of the most famous scenes from Gerwig's Little Women is an outburst from Jo March, where Saoirse Ronan says: "Women: they have minds and souls, and they have ambition, as well as just beauty."
Without giving much away, Barbie begins to spiral as she grapples with her identity and her place in Barbie Land.
Greta Gerwig on the set of Barbie with Ryan Gosling and Margot Robbie. (Supplied: Warner Bros)
In a recent interview with W Magazine, Gerwig explained the films she's written and directed "are all talking to each other".
"It is almost a mystery to me when I'm in the middle of it. And then when I step back, I think, 'Oh, you continue to be interested in women. This is something you're fascinated by'.
"That ache of contradictions, of never being able to totally bridge that gap between adulthood and childhood, is present in this movie, too.
"It's this overflowing sense of joy, and then it's also, 'I can never get back there.'"
A recent profile in The New Yorker confirmed rumours that had been swirling for months: Gerwig's entering the world of Narnia with Netflix.
Greta Gerwig is set to direct two instalments in The Chronicles of Narnia series for Netflix. (Supplied: Warner Bros)
Gerwig is reportedly down to direct two movies based on classic fantasy novels by C.S. Lewis.
She told the Total Films podcast she "hasn't even started wrapping my arms around it" but is "proper scared of it, which feels like a good place to start".
Her agent, Jeremy Barber, who also represents Baumbach, told The New Yorker that Gerwig has been "very consciously constructing her career".
"Her ambition is to be not the biggest woman director but a big studio director."
Gerwig told W Magazine: "I want to be able to make tiny movies, big movies, and everything in between."
"It just takes so long to make any given one. That's the only thing I feel limited by.

title: 'I went to hell and back': Jamie Foxx tells fans on Instagram he is recovering from an undisclosed illness
content:
Academy Award winning actor, singer and comedian Jamie Foxx has told fans that he is recovering from an undisclosed medical condition.
"I went to hell and back, and my road to recovery has some potholes as well, but I'm coming back," Foxx, appearing thin and wearing a dark pullover shirt, said in the three-minute, 15-second video posted to Instagram.
"I'm able to work."
Foxx, 55, was hospitalised in April with what his daughter, Corinne Fox, described at the time as a "medical complication" and the actor did not disclose the nature of his condition in his first public comments since being hospitalised.
"I just didn't want you to see me like that … I didn't want you to see me with tubes running out of me and trying to figure out if I was going to make it through," Foxx said, thanking his daughter, sister, God and medical professionals for saving his life.
"I went through something that I thought I would never, ever go through.
Castmates of Foxx's recent movie They Cloned Tyrone — David Alan Grier, Teyonah Parris and Tamberla Perry — told The Associated Press at the Los Angeles premiere of the movie on June 28 that they miss the star.
The writer-director — who also often appears in his own films — is making his 10th and final film, called The Movie Critic. So, here are five Tarantino movies to watch ahead of his final release and where to see them.
"Just praying that he gets better and takes whatever time he needs to heal," Perry said.
Foxx, born Eric Marlon Bishop in 1967 in Terrell, Texas, was a stand-up comedian before breaking into television with various roles on Fox TV's musical-comedy In Living Color in 1990.
Foxx won the Academy Award for best actor for his portrayal of Ray Charles in the 2004 biographical film Ray and a Grammy in 2010 for the song Blame It.
His other credit's include The Jamie Foxx Show, Collateral, and Django Unchained.

title: 'This is the way the world ends': Nevil Shute warned us of nuclear annihilation. It's still a hot-button issue
content:
One of the most haunting poems of the 20th century, T.S. Eliot's The Hollow Men (1925), concludes:
This is the way the world endsNot with a bang but a whimper.
In 1958, on his 70th birthday, Eliot was asked whether he would consider writing these lines, probably his most quoted, again. His answer was both noteworthy and categorical.
He admitted he would not. He said that "while the association of the H-bomb is irrelevant to it, it would today come to everyone's mind". (And he was "not sure that the world will end with either".)
Indeed, Nevil Shute's classic novel of nuclear annihilation, On the Beach, published in June 1957, used Eliot's famous lines as an epigraph. And the nuclear threat is still very much at the top of our collective mind.
The Sydney Theatre Company is staging the very first stage adaptation of Shute's novel. And Oppenheimer, one of 2023's two most-hyped films, tells the story of the man referred to as "the father of the atomic bomb".
Sydney Theatre Company is staging the first stage adaptation of On the Beach. (Supplied: Sydney Theatre Company)
Journalist Gideon Haigh calls On the Beach "arguably Australia's most important novel — important in the sense of confronting a mass international audience with the defining issue of the age".
British-born Shute emigrated in 1950 to Australia, where he lived outside Melbourne. As well as writing novels, he worked as an aeronautical engineer.
The title of On the Beach — which started life as a four-part story called The Last Days on Earth — ostensibly referred to a Royal Navy expression for reassignment. (Shute spent time in the Royal Naval Reserve during World War II.) However, as readers of Eliot's poetry will know, the phrase also appears late in The Hollow Men:
In this last of meeting placesWe grope togetherAnd avoid speechGathered on this beach of the tumid river.
As in Eliot's poem, the characters that cluster together in the pages of Shute's novel, set in and around Melbourne between 1962 and 1963, tend on occasion to avoid speech.
This comes to the fore in the following passage, which focuses on a dinner party hosted by Lieutenant Commander Peter Holmes of the Royal Australian Navy. The atmosphere is both claustrophobic and delirious:
For three hours they danced and drank together, sedulously avoiding any serious topic of conversation. In the warm night the room grew hotter and hotter, coats and ties were jettisoned at an early stage, and the gramophone went on working through an enormous pile of records, half of which Peter had borrowed for the evening. In spite of the wide-open windows behind the fly wire, the room grew full of cigarette smoke.
The reason why the guests at Peter's party are so keen to avoid serious talk is both simple and depressing. They are trying very hard to forget that they are all going to be dead from radiation poisoning in a matter of months.
Nevil Shute's book On the Beach continues to exert a pull on the popular cultural imagination. (Public Domain: Australian Women's Weekly)
Shute brings the reader up to speed after the dinner party wraps up. A massive nuclear war has devastated the entire northern hemisphere, wiping out all forms of life there. And the radioactive fallout generated during the conflict is now creeping — slowly but surely — into the southern hemisphere.
Shute makes it clear there is absolutely nothing anyone can do about this. In tonally dispassionate prose, he reveals that vast swathes of Australia have already been rendered uninhabitable due to radiation poisoning. The only thing the characters who remain can do is wait.
As Moira Davidson says to the American submarine captain, Dwight Towers: "It's like waiting to be hung." Hence the desperate need for moments of temporary respite and distraction.
Different characters deal with the situation in different ways. Those who still have jobs go to work. Those who don't, stay at home or go shopping. Some, like Moira, take to drink and rail uselessly against the unfairness of it all:
"I won't take it," she said vehemently. "It's not fair. No one in the Southern Hemisphere ever dropped a bomb, a hydrogen bomb or a cobalt bomb or any other sort of bomb. We had nothing to do with it. Why should we have to die because other countries nine or ten thousand miles away from us wanted to have a war? It's so bloody unfair."
Moira's anger eventually gives way to something approaching resignation. "A tear trickled down beside her nose and she wiped it away irritably; self-pity was a stupid thing, or was it the brandy?" She comes to accept this is "the end of it, the very, very end".
Moments after this, Moira, who is already gravely ill with radiation poisoning, ends her life. She takes a couple of suicide tablets, puts them in her mouth, and washes them down "with a mouthful of brandy, sitting behind the wheel of her big car".
This is the way Shute's novel of nuclear extinction ends: not with a bang but with a whimper. Released at the height of the Cold War, On the Beach struck a chord with millions of concerned readers.
By the September of 1957, Shute's novel — which sold over 100,000 copies within six weeks of initial publication — had been serialised by dozens of American newspapers. A copy had found its way to the desk of John F. Kennedy, the next president of the United States. And Hollywood was about to call.
Directed by Stanley Kramer, the cinematic adaptation of On the Beach — which was filmed on location in Victoria and showcased the talents of Gregory Peck, Ava Gardner and Fred Astaire — hit the big screen in December 1959.
Gregory Peck and Ava Gardner in Stanley Kramer's film, On the Beach. (Supplied: IMDB)
Shute famously detested the movie, which received decidedly mixed reviews. In a sense, Shute's response is surprising, as the novelist clearly wanted to get his message about the perils of nuclear war across to as wide an audience as possible.
Shute's didactic inclinations are evident towards the end of the novel. "Peter," the character Mary asks, "why did this all this happen to us?" Even at this late stage, Mary, whose radiation-racked body is spasming uncontrollably, wants to know whether things might have panned out differently. Her husband's reply is revealing:
"I don't know … Some kinds of silliness you just can't stop," he said. "I mean, if a couple of hundred million people all decide that their national honour requires them to drop cobalt bombs upon their neighbour, well, there's not much that you or I can do about it. The only possible hope would have been to educate them out of their silliness."
Shute makes a similar point in a letter he wrote in 1960. He holds that a popular writer:
"Can often play the part of the in raising for the first time subjects which ought to be discussed in public and which no statesman cares to approach. In this way, an entertainer may serve a useful purpose."
Knowing this, it seems likely Shute would have been delighted to read reviews that praised the book's "emotional wallop" while simultaneously demanding it "be made mandatory reading for all professional diplomats and politicians".
While the science in the novel was somewhat flawed, Shute's cautionary tale undoubtedly spoke to the collective zeitgeist.
On the Beach was released mere months after the creation of the National Committee for a Sane Nuclear Policy in the United States, and just before the founding of the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament in the United Kingdom.
Director Christopher Nolan is renowned for his massive, cinema-filling films and he's taking his obsession to the maximum with Oppenheimer.
Though it seems fair to say Nevil Shute's general literary standing has diminished in recent years, On the Beach continues to exert a pull on the popular cultural imagination.
The influence of Shute's novel, which was remade in 2000 as a film for Australian television, can be observed in various post-apocalyptic works, including George Miller's Mad Max franchise and the late Cormac McCarthy's The Road. (If anything, the ending of On the Beach is even bleaker than in McCarthy's masterpiece.)
Shute's vision of humanity's self-inflicted destruction is eerily resonant in our time of climate emergency. The nuclear threat remains, too, in our perilous historical moment of democratic backsliding and failing nuclear states.
It seems increasingly likely the world as we know it is coming to an end — if it hasn't already. The question remains: will it be with a bang or a whimper?
On The Beach runs at the Sydney Theatre Company July 24 to August 12, 2023, with previews July 18–21.
Alexander Howard is a senior lecturer in English at the University of Sydney. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

title: Ka-boom times: Australian stunt actors making the most of a homegrown explosion in opportunities
content:
Getting hit by a car, thrown from a roof, crash-tackled into a wall, or set on fire is all in a day's work for a stunt actor.
For Jimmy Christiansen, one of the country's leading stunt coordinators, his list of credits — and injuries — is equally impressive.
"A broken foot, broken ribs, a fractured vertebrae, dislocated shoulders, concussions, knocked out cold a few times, winded heaps of times, lost a tooth," he says.
Christiansen during his days as a stuntman on the Australian police drama Cops LAC. (Supplied: Jimmy Christiansen)
Stunt actors risk life and limb behind the scenes to bring our favourite movies to life.
And many say a pandemic-induced boom provided a much-needed boost to the Queensland film industry.
Until last week, when Hollywood actors went on strike, the Queensland film industry was going gangbusters.
Actors and actresses walked off the job demanding better pay and protection of their digital likenesses from generative "deepfake" AI.
The strike has caused uncertainty in Australia with some US productions being filmed here shut down indefinitely.
But when Covid-19 shut down film sets around the world in 2020, Queensland pitched itself to Hollywood as a lockdown-free safe haven where the show could go on.
Filmmakers landed on the Gold Coast to shoot big-budget blockbusters like Godzilla vs Kong, Ticket to Paradise, Thirteen Lives, Mortal Kombat 2 and a host of major television series.
Baz Luhrmann with Queensland Premier Annastacia Palaszczuk on the Gold Coast. (AAP: Darren England)
Award-winning Australian director Baz Luhrman fell in love with the city while filming his Elvis biopic and moved the headquarters of his production company Bazmark to "Goldiewood".
Last financial year, 45 projects were produced in Queensland, creating more than 5,400 jobs and contributing $229.3 million to the local economy, according to Screen Queensland.
Christiansen, a 22-year veteran of the industry, is one of the homegrown professionals cashing in on the boom.
He recently worked alongside George Clooney and Julia Roberts as the Australian stunt coordinator on the romantic comedy Ticket to Paradise.
Julia Roberts and George Clooney on the set of Ticket to Paradise. (Supplied: Universal Pictures)
He also scored a career highlight overseeing an ad campaign for the Australian Formula One Grand Prix, which involved Daniel Ricciardo racing an F1 car through the outback and trying to outrun a low-flying aerobatic pilot on Grand Pacific Drive, NSW.
Christiansen says the amount of work available to Australian crews has "absolutely exploded" and stunt performers no longer have to move to the United States to earn a good living.
"Over here you can be a medium-sized fish in a small pond. If you head to the States you become a tadpole in a vast ocean," he says.
Christiansen says stunt performers can now earn a good living in Australia. (Supplied: Red Bull Racing)
Gold Coast-based stuntwoman Amanda Giblin agrees.
A karate and muay thai black belt, her martial arts background means she's well-equipped for fight scenes, which she describes as the "bread and butter" of stunt performance.
She landed the biggest role of her 15-year career in 2023 as the stunt double for Emily Blunt, who stars alongside Ryan Gosling in The Fall Guy.
Sydney Harbour Bridge shut down for the Ryan Gosling film shoot. (ABC News)
Production of the upcoming action flick shut down the Sydney Harbour Bridge in January.
Giblin says before the pandemic it was "nearly impossible" to secure consistent work as a stuntwoman.
Now, things have completely changed.
"Ninety per cent of stunt performers, especially females, have always had to have a second job," she says.
Amanda Giblin is a Gold Coast-based stunt performer and lead double. (Supplied: Amanda Giblin)
Giblin, who has worked on blockbusters including Mad Max, Thor and Pirates of the Caribbean on the Gold Coast, says traditionally only a couple of major films were made in Australia each year and most TV series were shot in Sydney or Melbourne.
"We are pretty close to being able to have a sustainable career without having to have a side hustle now," she says.
Not everyone is cut out for the world of stunts.
There are only 74 registered professionals in Australia.
Becoming an accredited stunt actor involves passing a rigorous grading assessment carried out by the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA).
Applicants must satisfy a panel of experts that they are highly proficient in five of the six criteria — body control, water, fire, heights, vehicles, and animals.
After a career as a stunt performer in Hollywood, Ky Furneaux was used to danger. But her most extreme experiment came when she was asked to spend 21 days naked in the wilderness.
Christiansen says this all-round proficiency separates Australian performers from their American counterparts and continues to amaze Hollywood producers.
"We don't just do cars, or just do fight scenes — we don't specialise," he says.
The MEAA is also responsible for negotiating employment contracts for stunt performers.
They get a daily rate, plus overtime if they spend more than 10 hours on set.
Their pay is then adjusted based on the "danger, risk or skill level" of their stunts.
"For example, if I'm doing a car knock-down at 30 kilometres per hour, there's quite a bit of danger and skill involved in that," Giblin says.
"If I have to do that take three times, I would get three adjustments to my pay rate."
Miyuki Lotz was a dancer with the Queensland Ballet before making the switch.
She says stunt women often don't get to wear the same amount of protective gear — like knee and elbow pads — as the men do.
Miyuki Lotz says long days on set are physically demanding. (Supplied: Miyuki Lotz)
"The guys get it easier to hide the protection under their costumes and most stuntman will tell you that," she says.
It's dangerous work and some insurance companies prohibit big-name actors from doing their own stunts.
Stunt performers may be used for scenes that aren't necessarily dangerous — like running in high heels — if the studio decides it's not worth the risk of the star rolling their ankle and delaying production.
Giblin says some work is "purely safety-based".
Amanda Giblin trains actresses to do as much of the fight choreography as possible. (Supplied: Amanda Giblin)
"They rehearse with us first for hours and hours while cameras and lighting get everything ready so that [the lead] can do it in one take," she says.
"I always say, 'Actors do all the boring stuff.' We have the best job, we get to do all the fun, cool stuff."

title: Meet Robert Oppenheimer, the destroyer of worlds
content:
Robert Oppenheimer is often placed next to Albert Einstein as the 20th century's most famous physicist.
He will forever be the "father of the atomic bomb" after the first nuclear weapon was successfully tested on July 16, 1945 in the New Mexican desert.
The event brought to his mind words from a Hindu scripture: "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds".
Oppenheimer I am become Death
Born in 1904 in an affluent New York family, Oppenheimer graduated from Harvard majoring in chemistry in 1925.
Two years later, he completed his PhD in physics at one of the world's leading institutions for theoretical physics, the University of Göttingen, Germany. He was 23 and enthusiastic to the point of alienating others.
J Robert Oppenheimer is often placed next to Albert Einstein as the 20th century's most famous physicist. (AP)
Throughout his life, Oppenheimer would be judged either as an aloof prodigy or an anxious narcissist. Whatever his contradictions as an individual, his eccentricities did not limit his scientific achievements.
Before the outbreak of the second world war, Oppenheimer worked at the University of California, Berkeley, and the California Institute of Technology. His research concentrated on theoretical astronomy, nuclear physics and quantum field theory.
Although he confessed to being uninterested in politics, Oppenheimer openly supported socially progressive ideas. He was concerned with the emergence of anti-Semitism and fascism. His partner, Kitty Puening, was a left-leaning radical and their social circle included Communist Party members and activists. Later, these associations will mark him as a communist sympathiser.
As a researcher, Oppenheimer published and supervised a new generation of doctoral students. One of these was Willis Lamb, who in 1955 was awarded the Nobel Prize in physics. The Nobel Prize eluded Oppenheimer three times.
Physicists Albert Einstein and Robert Oppenheimer in 1950. (Wikipedia)
Two years after Germany and Soviet Russia attacked Poland, the United States entered WWII. Oppenheimer was recruited to work on the infamous Manhattan Project. His ideas about chain reaction in an atomic bomb gained recognition among the US defence community. He started his work by assembling a team of experts. Some of them were his students.
Director Christopher Nolan is renowned for his massive, cinema-filling films and he's taking his obsession to the maximum with Oppenheimer.
In 1943, despite his left-wing political views, lack of high-profile career and no experience in managing complex projects, Oppenheimer was appointed director of the Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico. He was enthusiastic. He seemed to have "reserves of uncommitted strength" recalled physicist Isidor Isaac Rabi. His task was to develop atomic weapons.
Los Alamos Laboratory expanded rapidly as the project grew in complexity, with the personnel exceeding 6,000. His ability to master the large-scale workforce and channel their energy towards the needs of the project earned him respect.
He proved to be more than just an administrator by being involved in the interdisciplinary team across theoretical and experimental stages of the weapons development.
On July 16, 1945, the nuclear test — code-named Trinity — took place.
The first atomic bomb was successfully detonated at 5:29am in the Jornada del Muerto desert. As his chief assistant, Thomas Farrell, recounted:
"There came this tremendous burst of light followed shortly thereafter by the deep growling roar of the explosion."
Oppenheimer later recalled that "a few people laughed, a few people cried, most people were silent". What he knew for sure was that the world would not be the same.
It was too late for the atomic bombs to be used against Germany in the war — the Nazis had capitulated on May 8. Instead, US President Harry Truman decided to use the bomb against Germany's ally, Japan.
Shortly after the atomic bombs were dropped on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, Oppenheimer confronted the US secretary of war, Henry Stimson, demanding that nuclear weapons were banned.
The city of Hiroshima was flattened after the US dropped the atomic bomb in 1945. (Supplied: US National Archives)
Similarly, when speaking with Truman, Oppenheimer talked about his feeling of having blood on his hands. Truman rejected Oppenheimer's emotional outburst. The responsibility for the use of the atomic bombs, after all, rested with the commander in chief (himself).
Truman's rebuttal did not prevent Oppenheimer from advocating for the establishment of controls on the nuclear arms race.
In the postwar years, Oppenheimer settled in Princeton, New Jersey, at the Institute for Advanced Study. He read widely. He collected art and furniture. He learned languages. His well-paid position enabled his pursuit of a deeper understanding of humanity though the examination of ancient scriptures. He argued for the unity of purpose between the sciences and humanities.
Oppenheimer's patronage supported and encouraged other scientists in their research. But his chief concern was the unavoidable arms race. He advocated for the establishment of an international body that would control the development of nuclear energy and its usage.
In 1947, a civilian agency called the Atomic Energy Commission began its work. Oppenheimer urged strongly for international arms control.
The Soviet Union's first atomic bomb test in August 1949 took the US by surprise and pushed American researchers to develop a hydrogen bomb. The US government hardened its position. In 1952, Truman refused to reappoint Oppenheimer as the adviser to the Atomic Energy Commission.
After 1952, Oppenheimer's advocacy against the first test of the hydrogen bomb resulted in the suspension of his security clearance. The investigation that followed in 1954 exposed Oppenheimer's past communist ties and culminated in his security clearance being revoked.
Oppenheimer trailer
In the era of Joseph McCarthy's witch-hunts, his fellow scientists considered Oppenheimer as a martyr of the cause of academic freedom. "In England", commented Wernher von Braun, a former Nazi turned American pioneer of rocket technology, "Oppenheimer would have been knighted".
After 1954, Oppenheimer did not cease to advocate for freedom in the pursuit of knowledge. He toured internationally with talks about the role of academic freedom unrestrained by political considerations. He argued that the sciences and the humanities are not separate human endeavours but interlocked and inseparable.
Oppenheimer died at the age of 62 on February 18, 1967.
Darius von Guttner Sporzynski is a historian at Australian Catholic University. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.
