title: Hollywood actors' strike looms after negotiators fail to reach deal by midnight deadline
content:
The union representing American film and television actors says no deal has been reached with studios and streaming services despite the passing of a midnight deadline, and its leadership will vote within the coming hours on whether to join screenwriters by going on strike.
If the actors do go on strike, it will be the first time since 1960 that both actors and writers have picketed film and television productions in the United States.
The Screen Actors Guild — American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) — said early on Thursday morning that companies at the other end of the bargaining table had refused to engage with the union on some topics.
"Until they do negotiate in good faith, we cannot begin to reach a deal," said Fran Drescher, the star of The Nanny who is now the actors' guild president.
The group representing the studios, the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP), said it was disappointed by the failure to reach a deal.
"This is the union's choice, not ours," the AMPTP said in a statement.
"In doing so, it has dismissed our offer of historic pay and residual increases, substantially higher caps on pension and health contributions, audition protections, shortened series option periods, a groundbreaking AI proposal that protects actors' digital likenesses, and more."
It added that instead of continuing to negotiate, "SAG-AFTRA has put us on a course that will deepen the financial hardship for thousands who depend on the industry for their livelihoods."
There's no end in sight to the writers' strike that has ground both US and international productions to a halt. (Matt Cargill)
If SAG-AFTRA's leadership votes to go on strike — guild members have previously authorised it by a margin of nearly 98 per cent — actors will formally join screenwriters on the picket lines outside studios and filming locations.
Australia's Sarah Snook is one of multiple Succession cast members to be nominated for an Emmy, with The White Lotus, The Last of Us, and Ted Lasso taking up the other top noms.
Members of the Writers Guild of America have been on strike since early May, slowing the production of film and television series on both coasts and in production centres like Atlanta in a bid to get better terms from studios and streaming giants like Netflix and Amazon.
Issues at play in the negotiations include the unregulated use of artificial intelligence, and the effects on residual pay brought on by the massive streaming ecosystem that has emerged in recent years.
Some actors have joined writers on the picket lines for weeks in solidarity, but an actors' strike would prevent those performers from working on sets or promoting their projects.
Whether the cast of Christopher Nolan's film Oppenheimer attends Thursday's London premiere now hangs in the balance.
At a photo event on Wednesday, Hollywood star Matt Damon said that while everyone was hoping a strike could be averted, many actors need a fair contract to survive.
Matt Damon poses at the Paris premiere of Oppenheimer on Tuesday. (Reuters: Sarah Meyssonnier)
"We ought to protect the people who are kind of on the margins," Damon told the Associated Press.
"And 26,000 bucks a year is what you have to make to get your health insurance. And there are a lot of people whose residual payments are what carry them across that threshold.
The looming strike has cast a shadow over the upcoming 75th Emmy Awards, the nominations for which were announced just hours before negotiators announced they had failed to strike a deal.
The strike was on the mind of many nominees.
"People are standing up and saying, 'This doesn't really work, and people need to be paid fairly,'" said Jessica Chastain, who was nominated for her first Emmy for playing Tammy Wynette in George & Tammy.
"It is very clear that there are certain streamers that have really kind of changed the way we work and the way that we have worked, and the contracts really haven't caught up to the innovation that's happened."

title: Mission Impossible 7 promised Tom Cruise’s irresistibly deranged Hollywood charm — did it deliver?
content:
Tom Cruise might have "saved Hollywood's ass" with last year's smash Top Gun: Maverick (and a little help from James Cameron), but the battle for blockbuster cinema is far from over.
With superhero movies bombing and legacy franchises on the wane, it's once again falling to the veteran star to lead audiences, like some perma-grinning pied piper, back to the cinema – an agenda he continues to pursue with endearingly deranged zeal.
And what could be a more apt mission for the famously old-school, CGI-averse action hero than to go up against the creative world's current bogeyman, artificial intelligence?
In Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning Part One, the seventh instalment in the nearly 30-year-old series, Cruise's shadowy super-spy Ethan Hunt faces off with a rogue AI known simply (and somewhat hilariously) as The Entity, a sentient algorithm that's threatening the world's intelligence networks and, if it gets its evil computer way, humanity itself.
Cruise is renowned for his DIY stunt work. In 2018, he became the first actor to perform a HALO jump, a high-altitude skydive, on film. (Supplied: Paramount)
The planet's only hope is a bunch of late-middle-aged men armed with their analog wits, daredevil stunt skills, and a suitcase full of rubber masks.
Running, jumping and tumbling as only he can, the 61-year-old leading man throws himself into the mission with the sort of energy that audiences have come to admire, but Dead Reckoning is arguably the first movie in the storied franchise to show signs of fatigue – even tedium – as it laps a premise that's somehow becoming both absurd and just a little enervating.
Racing to wrest control of the AI, Ethan's IMF team, which includes his long-time sidekick operatives Luther Stickell (Ving Rhames) and Benji Dunn (Simon Pegg), set out in pursuit of a pair of keys that look decidedly like inverted crucifixes; when interlocked, they give the holder access to the world-decimating technology. (Perhaps there's a sneaky agenda on the part of the film's star/producer in having a Christian symbol trigger humanity's doom; one can only speculate.)
"Everything that we do in these stories is about character and emotion," McQuarrie told ABC RN's The Screen Show. (Supplied: Paramount)
This globe-hopping mission takes Ethan from Amsterdam to the Arabian desert, and an encounter with ex-MI6 agent Ilsa Faust (the great Rebecca Ferguson), then on to Abu Dhabi airport, where he gives chase to the slippery Grace (a tough, terrific Hayley Atwell), an international thief in way over her head.
Meanwhile, the sadistic, amoral terrorist Gabriel (Esai Morales), a ghost from Ethan's pre-IMF past, has returned to terrorise his old adversary, with a deadly French assassin, Paris, in tow. She's played by Guardians of the Galaxy star Pom Klementieff, in a menacing, almost silent-movie performance that might be the most memorable of the film, all bleached hair and maniacal grin spread wide across her face.
In many ways Dead Reckoning marks a return to the techno-spy terrain of Brian De Palma's stylish 1996 opener – still the best in the series – especially with the reappearance of former IMF director Eugene Kittridge (Henry Czerny) and a splashy, high-speed duel set atop a train that echoes the iconic set-piece from the original.
On watching Cruise perform his motorcycle cliff dive, Klementieff told ABC News: "We saw him do it seven or eight times in a row in front of us, it was insane." (Supplied: Paramount)
Elsewhere, there are moments that engage with the technology of the present in clever, sometimes inspired ways. Luther's hacking into an airport CCTV to replace random travellers with Ethan's face has fun with the mutability of identity in the digital era, not to mention evoking that deepfake Tom Cruise account that had TikTok enraptured for a hot second.
But the film is less interested in tangling with its algorithmic villain than it is in delivering a traditional action movie – one that frequently resembles a 90s hacker thriller.
There are endless longueurs of exposition, the kind that can seem dumber than the equivalent knucklehead exegeses in a Fast and Furious film.
"The Entity is knocking off satellites faster than I can hack into them," says an exasperated Luther at one point.
Across the film's extremely generous 2 hours and 42 minutes, these dead patches often threaten the narrative momentum.
"We have a motto on this movie now, which is, 'That's a terrible idea. When do we start?'" McQuarrie told ABC News. (Supplied: Paramount)
What's missing this time is a sense of Cruise, whose performance of Ethan Hunt as somewhere between an aging spy and eternal superman has long been a source of the series' strange staying power – and its reckoning with late-career action stardom
Dead Reckoning has little of the last-action-hero weirdness of its predecessor, 2018's Fallout, which saw its star engaged in mano a mano duels with upstart alpha males, while the supporting cast, of women and men alike, gathered in bizarre supplication around Cruise's all-inclusive radiance. (There's some chaste flirtation here between Ethan and Vanessa Kirby's returning arms dealer Alanna Mitsopolis, but the star's romantic charisma has ceded to an avuncular, almost asexual vibe.)
Fortunately, Cruise's commitment to delivering breakneck action remains, and on that front, the movie does not disappoint.
Tom Cruise performs what director Christopher McQuarrie describes as his most dangerous stunt yet in the latest Mission: Impossible movie.
Like the previous instalment, Dead Reckoning has a series of reliable set pieces that lay the groundwork for the show-stopper. There's a knockabout chase through Rome, in which Ethan and Grace flee a squad of cop cars and an armoured truck in a comically tiny vintage Fiat; a close-quarters duel in a Venetian alleyway that makes for an intimate counterpoint to the large-scale mayhem; and of course, multiple sequences of our hero running for his life, which Cruise and director Christopher McQuarrie, with their long tracking shots through cities and airports, have now calibrated to a deliciously expressive art.
Still, you have to wonder at what point does Cruise's stunt work simply become a means unto itself, like one of those weird old fitness freaks who want to live forever but aren't really sure why.
The star's much-vaunted motorcycle leap off a Norwegian cliff (doubling for the Austrian Alps) is undoubtedly impressive (at least if you've never seen a jobbing 007 stuntman performing a similar trick decades ago), but the execution here feels closer to behind-the-scenes footage – essentially Cruise's promo schtick dropped into a climactic reel of suspense.
On improvising on set, Atwell (left) told ABC RN's The Screen Show: "For me, it's like live theatre; anything could happen." (Supplied: Paramount)
For all the stunt's showmanship, the most exhilarating sequence in the film is the one that immediately follows it – a combination of visual effects and physical daring – as an imperilled train dangles from a decimated bridge like the trucks in The Lost World: Jurassic Park.
It's a high point that captures the best of what this series, and its star, can do at their performance peak.
So will it save cinema? Cruise's flagship franchise might be an invigorating reminder of the beauty of physical action, but it's also a series that's predicated, like the recent Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny, on throwback tropes, where giving audiences bang for their ticket buck means car chases, train fights and other entertainments that may not mean much for younger generations weaned on digital immersion.
As a series increasingly concerned with aging men, and movie stars, fighting for relevance in a rapidly changing world, it remains a curious one and, it has to be said, still a pretty good time at the movies. But what happens to Cruise's beloved theatrical experience if the blockbuster – short of literally shooting a film in space – isn't refreshed with new ideas?
Mission: Impossible — Dead Reckoning Part One is in cinemas now.

title: 'He was up to no good': Prosecutors wrap up sexual assault case against Kevin Spacey
content:
Prosecutors have concluded their sexual assault case against Kevin Spacey in his ongoing trial in London.
Four men testified in the past two weeks that the Oscar winner preyed upon them in allegations that date from 2001 to 2013 when Spacey was working at the Old Vic Theatre.
The Usual Suspects star, 63, has pleaded not guilty to 12 charges that include sexual and indecent assault counts and one count of causing a person to engage in penetrative sexual activity without consent.
The court heard statements Spacey gave investigators denying he aggressively grabbed three men by the crotch and performed a non consensual sex act on a fourth.
The defence is scheduled to begin presenting its case on Thursday in Southwark Crown Court.
The stakes are high, with Spacey facing a possible prison term if convicted.
None of the alleged victims knew each other but each testified that they went to police after Spacey was accused of sexual misconduct in the United States in 2017.
He was fired from the show House of Cards after the allegations arose.
Three of the men said Spacey had a reputation of being drawn to good-looking young men and one said he had been warned to avoid him.
"It was well known he was up to no good," the man testified.
One man said Spacey made racially offensive remarks to him and then "like a cobra coming out and getting hold," grabbed his penis when they were alone at a charity event.
An aspiring actor who reached out to Spacey for advice said he regretted meeting up with him for a late-night drink.
He said he ended up at Spacey's flat — after falling asleep or passing out — woke up with the star performing oral sex on him.
A fourth man said the actor gave him an awkward hug and kissed his neck before grabbing his crotch after drinks.
Spacey denied doing anything non-consensual and said he didn't remember meeting two of the men.
Spacey told police last year that the fourth man who came forward had "reimagined" their time together and concocted false allegations.
Defence lawyer Patrick Gibbs suggested the men were motivated by money.
Several of them have filed lawsuits against the star and one testified an American lawyer had said he could win him $US10 million ($14 million).
Spacey is free on unconditional bail.

title: 'Robbing Crocodile Dundee to pay for Forrest Gump': Bryan Brown calls for reinvestment obligation for streamers
content:
Australian actor and producer Bryan Brown AM has used his National Press Club address to call for an Australian content quota at streaming services that run their businesses locally.
The federal government announced in January that major streaming services such as Netflix, Disney and Amazon Prime would be required to invest revenue in the production of local content from mid-2024.
Brown said other countries such as Canada and France had already legislated that revenue that streaming companies got from their countries must funnelled into local production.
He said the same should be done in Australia, and the stories needed to be specifically Australian.
"I mean Australian stories, not stories filmed in Australia with American accents," Brown told the press club.
"That is a cultural death."
Brown has backed the 20 per cent figure the industry has been pushing for and that the government intends to put into law.
Catch up with our live blog of Australian actor Bryan Brown's speech to the National Press Club, as it unfolded.
"A 20 per cent reinvestment obligation, complemented by strong and sound IP arrangements, would help secure the future of our industry and keep it vibrant," Brown said.
"The streaming companies will fight hard to not legislate. They are a business.
"And we must fight just as hard because this is for our culture."
Brown posed a rhetorical question about why Australians knew so much about other countries, pointing out that countries such as the United States exported their art around the world, strengthening their national identity.
"If our ability to present ourselves on film is taken away, we will become unsure of ourselves, in awe of others and less as a people," Brown said.
"A thriving film and television industry presents who we are to the world."
He said there was a time when it was more about moving money around than making good films.
Bryan Brown says Hollywood studios' allegiance is offshore. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)
"We lost our way somewhat, but we kept producing," Brown said.
"Now we have an offset, a tax offset for Australian film, a 40 per cent tax rebate on the budget of the film.
"We nearly lost that in 2021. There was a move to reduce that to 30 per cent. The government announced additional support for offshore production."
He said the idea was to bring the Australian offset in line with the US one at 30 per cent, encouraging Hollywood movies to be filmed in Australia.
"And our film industry, the Australian film industry, the industry that told Australian [stories] was to pay for that increase in offshore production, robbing Crocodile Dundee to pay for Forrest Gump."
He said economically it made sense to film overseas movies in Australia because it created work opportunities locally, but he was relieved the government of the time listened to reason.
Brown said governments of both persuasions had been receptive to the arts.
"Every five years we have to come down here, knock on the door of a prime minister and go, 'Hey, it is the arts,'" he said.
"It is about our culture, it is about who we are, what we aim for as people, and they get it. They know that … do I blame the American streamers for doing American stuff? Not at all. They want their culture up there, but we're saying, fellas, you are getting our money, we want to tell our stories."
Brown started his speech by cataloguing his 40-year career, which has seen him amass more than 90 film and television credits including Breaker Morant, Two Hands, Sweet Country, Cactus, Australia and Red Dog to name a few.
He painted a picture of an unlikely rise to celluloid fame.
"I'm a Westie," he said.
"Born and raised in the western suburbs of Sydney by my mother in a housing commission house".
Brown said he left Australia for England in 1972 to become an actor because he noticed Australian actors were mostly doing English and American plays with English and American accents.
"It seemed pretty silly to do that in Australia, so I went to England to do it first-hand," he quipped.

Actor Bryan Brown has called for Australia to impose a 20 per cent reinvestment obligation on streaming services making content in Australia in his address at the National Press Club in Canberra.
Look back on our live coverage as he recounts stories from his 40-year career and what Australia's film and television industry needs to thrive in the era of streaming.
By Claudia Williams
That is all from Bryan Brown and the National Press Club today.
It was great to hear about how Brown's passion began at a drama club at work to a career spanning more than 40 years that saw him reach Hollywood and the White House.
There is no doubt about his passion for Australian film and TV after his address.
He is calling for Australia to mandate 20 per cent reinvestment obligation for streaming giants, like they have in Canada and France.
"I mean Australian stories, not stories filmed in Australia with American accents," he said.
"That is a cultural death."
Thank you for tuning in to our live coverage today.
By Claudia Williams
Brown has been asked his thoughts on the referendum later this year.
"I will be voting yes," he says.
"If Marcia Langton says it is the right thing to do, then I will do it.
"Simple as that."
By Claudia Williams

"Let's do everything we can to support each other in our endeavours to produce good Australian stories," he says.
Brown has now finished his speech and will be answering questions.

Brown says as Australian audiences tune into streaming it is important that they continue to see Australian stories.

"That is a cultural death."
He says Canada and France have legislated that revenue taken from their countries must go into local production
"A 20 per cent reinvestment obligation, complemented by strong and sound IP arrangements would help secure the future of our industry and keep it vibrant," he says.
"The streaming companies will fight hard to not legislate.
"They are a business, and we must fight just as hard because this is for our culture."
By Claudia Williams
Brown has had the chance to visit the White House to meet US senators and journalists.
He says the experience made him realise the power of film and TV.
He says it was also clear that people wanted to learn more about Australia and its spirit.
He says this was clear when Crocodile Dundee hit the states.
"I believe what film and television and literature do is introduce people to the spirit of a people."
By Claudia Williams
Brown says Australia must remain committed, vigilant, disciplined and persistent to its film and TV industry.
"If our ability to present ourselves on film is taken away, we will become unsure of ourselves, in awe of others and less as a people," he says.
"A thriving film and television inustry presents who we are to the world."
By Claudia Williams
He says after the depression, the resurgance of the industry came in the late 1960s.
And then during the 70s and 80s, a number of the finest films ever made were sent out to the world
"As an actor lucky enough to be part of that time, it was hugely exciting," he says.
By Claudia Williams
The first Australian production was filmed in 1886 and the  first full-length feature film was produced in Australia.
"Australia went on to become the major source of film production, in the world" he says.
From 1906 to 1928, Australia produced a total of 150 films.
By Claudia Williams
Brown was offered a year contract with the National Theatre of Great Britian in 1974.
He says he noticed a change in theatre when he returned to Australia to visit his mother at the end of the year.
"There was no point in returning to England," he says.
"We now had a voice and it was exciting... and I wanted to be part of it."
By Claudia Williams
He resigned from his job in sales and bought a ticket to England to become an actor.
He left Australia in 1972 because he noticed most Australian actors were doing English and American plays and doing English and American accents.
"It seemed pretty silly to do that in Australia so I went to England to do it first hand," he said.
By Claudia Williams
Brown has introduced himself as a "Westie" born and raised in "the Western suburbs of Sydney by my mother in a housing commission house".
He says his interest in acting began when he decided to audition for an end of year revue at AMP.
"That half hour or so audition process led me on a journey that has taken me to some 40 countries," he says.
By Claudia Williams
Brown's speech will be broadcast live on ABC TV.
You can watch it on iview from 12:30pm.
By Claudia Williams
It's a road map that establishes the federal government's priorities for arts and culture.
Arts minister Tony Burke unveiled the new policy in January after a six-month consultation process.
The five pillars of the policy are:
The policy is called Revive and will see $286 million invested in the industry over four years.
Watch the video below to learn more about it.
Labor unveils first national cultural policy in nearly a decade
By Claudia Williams
Brown is no stranger to calling for change and his advocacy has not been limited to the arts industry.
In 2014 he led a group of prominent Australians calling on the government to stop holding asylum seeker children in detention centres.
The group, which included Ita Buttrose, Ian Chappell and Claudia Kraven, released a song called We're Better Than This.
In November 2022, Brown visited parliament to call on the government to implement quotas for Australian made content on streaming platforms.
The government announced it would introduce quotas for streaming platforms from 2024 as part of its National Cultural Policy.
You can read more about it below.
By Claudia Williams
Across four decades Brown has more than 90 film and TV credits to his name.
He made his debut in Scobie Malone in 1975 and went on to enjoy success in the US with A Town Like Alice and Give My Regards to Broad Street.
It'd be impossible to list all of his performances, but some of his most notable achievements include being nominated for a Golden Globe and Emmy for his role in The Thorn Birds in 1983.
And of course I have to mention his performance opposite Tom Cruise in Cocktail.
He played a major supporting role in the 2004 film Along Came Polly and joined Hugh Jackman and Nicole Kidman in Baz Luhrman's Australia in 2007.
In 2018 Brown received the Australian Academy of Cinema and Television Arts' Longford Lyell award for his contribution to the industry.
"We are full of admiration for Bryan's commitment to his craft, his role as a mentor to so many performers over the years and as an ambassador for the Australian screen industry," AACTA CEO Damian Trewhella said at the time.
By Claudia Williams
Australian actor Bryan Brown will be speaking at the National Press Club in Canberra.
As well as telling stories from his 40-year career on screen Brown is expected to discuss hot topics within the arts industry.
This includes the need for support and interventions in Australia’s screen sector.
His address comes as the federal government works to implement its National Cultural Policy.
My name is Claudia and I will be getting you up to speed on the details of the policy and bringing you his speech live when it starts at 12:30pm AEST.

title: 'Some people have a lot of problems with Barbie': Margot Robbie on how Barbie became a feminist film
content:
When Hollywood actor and producer Margot Robbie began toying with the idea of a Barbie movie, it was the doll's polarising success that attracted her to it.
"People feel really strongly about Barbie. Some people love Barbie. Some people have a lot of problems with Barbie. But everyone has an associated memory with Barbie," Robbie told ABC 7.30.
"It just felt like we could ignite something with it […] it seems like over the last 64 years, it hasn't taken much for Barbie to ignite conversation or sometimes, you know, revolutions or protests."
The challenge, Robbie explained, was to find a writer who could embrace the subject in its complexity.
Robbie turned to Greta Gerwig who had just finished filming her acclaimed movie Little Women.
"She's very intelligent," Robbie said.
"You can feel that in how her scripts and stories and characters are constructed and how they kind of come at you and it still feels really … it doesn't feel heady.
"But you can tell there's a lot of thought behind it. And there's a lot of heart most importantly. And the humour is there."
Greta Gerwig and Margot Robbie reveal how they brought Barbie to life. (Sarah Ferguson)
Robbie said Gerwig had the ability to capture the cultural moment.
"You can speak to her for five minutes and know that she just has her finger on the pulse of where society is at today," she said.
"And that's exactly what we needed for Barbie, someone who would be able to honour the legacy and also have a culturally relevant conversation with where we are today."
To Gerwig, the challenge was also terrifying — a potential career killer.
"Number one that there wasn't a story," she said.
"And all of that feeling that Margot was talking about of people like loving it, hating it […] there's a lot of places you could put a foot wrong, and then you'd be off on a terrible tangent."
Gerwig wrote the script with her partner Noah Baumbach. She quickly realised she didn't want anyone else to direct it.
Greta Gerwig described Barbie as a "humanist" film. (Supplied: Warner Bros)
Together with Robbie, they persuaded toy company Mattel to trust them to take risks with their iconic valuable product.
"We have to be up-front and let you know that we're not going to shy away from the problematic parts of this," Robbie said.
"Otherwise, it's not a movie we're interested in making. But it will come from a place of love, it will come from a place of respect, because I absolutely have respect for anyone that can make a toy [with] sustained popularity for 60-something years."
Ahead of the film's opening in Australia, the women were reluctant to share the specific points of contention they had with Mattel.
"Well, luckily, we made a crazy enough script that it was literally the whole thing," Gerwig said.
Mattel decided to trust the pair, but not to the point of accepting a description of the movie as a feminist film. Gerwig has no doubt.
"It most certainly is a feminist film," she said.
"It's that diving into the complexity of it and not running away from it.
"Looking at all the thorniness and stepping into what is the negotiation of what women need to be, and how to give them something other than a tightrope to walk on, is how it feels feminist to me."
Barbie explores themes of teenage insecurity and female solidarity. (Supplied: Warner Bros)
In the movie, Barbie's perfect pink world of high fashion and endless parties is disrupted when she suddenly finds herself having dark thoughts about death. She finds cellulite on her perfect legs and her famous feet suddenly become flat.
With the encouragement of the wise "Weird Barbie" played by Kate McKinnon, Barbie embarks on a journey of self-discovery in the real world, with Ken inviting himself along for the ride.
The idea of female insecurity becomes part of Barbie's story, with Robbie and Gerwig exploring the moment when a teenage girl begins to question her sense of self and worth.
"It's like, there's this age where suddenly you become self-conscious," Robbie explained. "And you kind of like hide yourself instead."
Gerwig says Barbie finds comfort in the words of a young character called Gloria, played by America Ferrera.
"I think for me, I've seen this movie, obviously more than anyone else on planet Earth, and I'm still touched by that ability for a woman to look at another woman and say, 'You're good enough'."
Barbie opens in cinemas across the country on July 20.

title: From The Rock to Nicole Kidman, this Australian designer has kept Hollywood's finest warm
content:
Gold Coast business owner Mark Wemyss has lost count of the number of actors from Australia to Hollywood who have worn one of his suits — wetsuits that is.
"We can potentially do six suits for one scene," Mr Wemyss said.
"Because if the scene starts dry, and then they get wet, obviously, like, the director [yells] cut, do it again they have to have wetsuits on hand to keep the talent warm."
Mr Wemyss, who has been manufacturing wetsuits for three decades for "pretty much all water sports", has expanded his repertoire to include flesh-coloured suits for the film and TV industry.
The suits are worn by actors when in water or under rain machines. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)
Some of his notable clients include Dwayne 'The Rock' Johnson for the blockbuster San Andreas, Johnny Depp for the Pirates of the Caribbean series and Australian actress Nicole Kidman.
Baz Luhrmann's feature film, Elvis, was the first major Hollywood film to be produced from start to finish on the Gold Coast.
The suits are usually worn as undergarments by actors and production crew to keep them warm when filming scenes in water or under rain machines.
But he said one of the biggest projects he had been involved with required wetsuits that were seen on screen.
In 2021 he was commissioned to make costumes for the biopic, Thirteen Lives, a film based on the true story of the Thai cave rescue in 2018.
It was also shot on the Gold Coast.
Mr Wemyss was tasked with creating replicas of the wetsuits worn by the British and Australian divers who rescued 12 boys and their soccer coach from Thailand's Tham Luang cave.
Mr Wemyss made replicas of the wetsuits worn by divers. (Supplied: Amazon Prime)
"Some of these suits were from companies that were since gone so we had to reproduce logos and we had to [make] a lot of wetsuits in a short period of time," he said.
Award-winning special effects makeup artist, Jason Baird, said he had used Mr Wemyss' suits for his prosthetics and costumes.
He enlisted Mr Wemyss and his team to construct the inner lining for his mermaid tails for the Australian television series, Mako Mermaids and H2O: Just Add Water..
"Mark was heavily involved in all the mermaid costumes we built because he made all the under structures for the for the tails," Mr Baird said.
Jason BaIrd's costumes are lined with neoprene material. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)
The Gold Coast is positioning itself as the destination of choice for filmmakers, offering everything from film studios to post-production, makeup and costumes.
City of Gold Coast Mayor Tom Tate revealed in February he was keen to attract more major studios.
He said he wanted to approve construction for post-production facilities and an additional 40 film studios in cane fields to the city's north by the end of the year.
Mr Wemyss welcomed the growing industry but said securing the supply of material up to two years in advance was a challenge.
Mr Wemyss says keeping up with demand can be a challenge. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)
"We've got to forecast where we're going to be in not just six months, but 12 and 18 months down the track, so we've got to have fabric that's ready to go for a certain production," he said.
"With the flesh-coloured fabric, we've got to have it in 1mm, 2mm, 3mm, 5mm, and we've got to have enough supply because sometimes you can have one production in Sydney, one in Melbourne, two on the Gold Coast, a couple in Hollywood and they all want that one thickness at the one time, so we've really got to be in front of having raw material on file like here ready to go."

title: 'Like a muffled scream': Rob Collins on making outback noir film Limbo
content:
In the new film Limbo, actor Rob Collins plays a man haunted by the disappearance of his sister from an outback town 20 years earlier.
His character Charlie believes police bungled the investigation, and when a world-weary cop (played by Simon Baker) turns up to review the case, Charlie doesn't trust him.
Collins says the character of Charlie was familiar to him.
"Very familiar," Collins says.
"Not so much my own experiences, but my family. I'm a Tiwi Islander and I don't think there's a single First Nations person that would look at the characters in Limbo and not have some sort of life experience of what the characters are going through."
Simon Baker plays policeman Travis and Natasha Wanganeen plays Emma, whose sister has disappeared. (Supplied: Dark Matter Distribution/Bonsai Films)
Collins says Charlie and his family are "on the wrong side of the justice system".
"They've largely been forgotten, there's no justice for the family. There are wounds there that haven't healed over and have just kind of festered," he says.
"They're all familiar things with the Aboriginal experience, particularly when you're talking about its intersection with law and in Australia. I mean, it's an ugly truth, but that's the truth of that film and the truth of Charlie's experience.
Collins says Baker was "exceptional" to work with. (Supplied: Bunya Productions)
"It was something that I instinctively felt that I knew."
It was a challenging role to play, Collins says, "mining those little pockets of hurt and angst, and regret and anxiety, and feelings of loneliness and isolation".
As the film progresses, Baker's policeman Travis offers Charlie a glimmer of hope for some sort of closure.
"And unfortunately for a lot of our mob, it's a closure they don't get to have," Collins says.
Ivan Sen, Rob Collins, Natasha Wanganeen and Simon Baker at the 2023 Berlin International Film Festival. (Picture: Reuters/Nadja Wohlleben)
Limbo is directed by Ivan Sen, best known for the films Mystery Road, Goldstone and Beneath Clouds. It also stars Natasha Wanganeen as Emma, Charlie's surviving sister, and Nicholas Hope as Joseph, the brother of a key murder suspect.
The film was shot in the South Australian opal mining town of Coober Pedy, which stands in for the fictional town of Limbo.
Sen's decision to film in black and white accentuates Coober Pedy's otherworldliness, making the pockmarked desert look like a moonscape.
Collins says he can't imagine filming the story anywhere else.
"The whole place feels like a muffled scream, which worked a lot for Charlie," he says.
Collins says he can't imagine filming Limbo anywhere other than Coober Pedy. (Supplied: Bunya Productions)
"I love Coober Pedy but it has that sense of impermanence. It kind of reminded me when I got too comfortable that I actually shouldn't be there.
"It's so sparse and flat and alien."
Collins says Sen helped set the tone for his restrained performance in Limbo by telling him, "you're in a western".
"That was a penny drop moment for me," Collins says.
"Just by saying that one phrase, it kind of made clear to me how to respond, how to act, when to show emotion, when to conceal it. That was a big turning point for me."
Filming in black and white accentuated Coober Pedy's otherworldliness. (Supplied: Bunya Productions)
He says knowing the film was being made in black and white helped. "Somehow the idea that it was black and white lent itself to that sense of restraint."
Collins shares almost all of his scenes with Baker, who he says was "exceptional" to work with.
"I found him warm and generous, as a person and as an actor.
"I learned so much from being with him and then watching him work."
Collins says he's excited to be part of projects this year that look at the Indigenous experience in Australia. (Picture: Reuters/Nadja Wohlleben)
Collins would have to be one of Australia's busiest actors.
Apart from starring in Limbo, which airs this weekend on the ABC, he's currently appearing opposite Catherine Tate in the comedy series Queen of Oz, as a vampire hunter in Firebite (also filmed in Coober Pedy), and in the British production Ten Pound Poms.
He's just finished filming the new season of medical drama RFDS, and is currently making the third and final season of Total Control, the ABC drama about an Indigenous politician.
He says he's going to miss working on Total Control when it finishes.
"I don't think I have seen the kind of show that we're making on TV in Australia," he says.
The creator of Mystery Road returns with an outback noir about a detective on the trail of a cold case — a film he says is a "Trojan horse" for an urgent issue: the alarmingly high rate at which Indigenous women are murdered.
"There's some scenes that are like, I would be open-mouthed going, 'Oh my god, I'm so excited that we're saying this on television.'
"It's said a lot of important, timely things, and not in a polite way."
He says there are similar moments in season two of RFDS. "There are some scenes in that, and themes and topics, about the Indigenous experience in Australia that I certainly haven't seen before on TV, and told in such an unapologetic way.
"Both projects pull no punches in terms of that stuff. And I think the fact that they're coming out this year of all years as well is really exciting to me."
Collins says he's not just referring to the upcoming referendum on the Voice to Parliament.
"I feel like this year there's a groundswell, it feels like something is happening. I can't quite articulate it. Yes, there's the referendum coming up. But it just feels like our focus as a nation has shifted a bit," he says.
"It feels like we're approaching another moment in our country's history where we have to look at our past again, and have to imagine what's the future going to hold.
"And these shows, RFDS, Total Control … all play into this shift of focus this year about Aboriginal relations in Australia."

title: Barbie was banned over a 'child-like crayon drawing'. Here's why Vietnam is taking it so seriously
content:
First Barbie, now Blackpink.
The communist government of Vietnam has caught the sugary pink Hollywood film and the popular K-pop girl band in the crosshairs of a geopolitical stoush in the South China Sea.
Barbie has been barred from release for including an "offending image of the nine-dash line", while authorities are starting to "look into an incident" in connection to Blackpink and the controversial map.
It's not the first time Vietnam's Ministry of Culture has cancelled movies in the country for depicting the nine-dash line — a U-shaped demarcation China uses to make its territorial claims.
China's line — sometimes called the "cow tongue" in Vietnam — includes the Paracel Islands, claimed by Vietnam, and the Spratly Islands, which the Philippines claims.
China's claims in the South China Sea cut through the majority of its neighbours' claims. (ABC News: Jarrod Fankhauser)
China's territorial claims are also disputed by Indonesia, Malaysia, Taiwan and Brunei.
Dr Huong Le Thu, adjunct fellow at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said the Vietnamese government was showing consistency in banning cultural texts that popularise the nine-dash line and normalise China's illegal claims.
Dr Huong Le Thu says geopolitics seeps into popular culture. (Supplied)
"The question should be: why does pop culture, Hollywood and — even more so — K-pop, venture to these geopolitical areas? Is that because they want to please a certain large audience and market?"
The pop culture spat has made global headlines, but how is it being perceived in Vietnam? And what tensions have been simmering in the South China Sea to bring us to this point?
Warner Bros has now said its Barbie film, starring Australian Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, shows a harmless and "child-like" drawing of a world map.
"The map in Barbie Land is a whimsical, child-like crayon drawing," the studio said in a statement.
"The doodles depict Barbie's make-believe journey from Barbie Land to the real world. It was not intended to make any type of statement."
The Barbie film has been banned from release in Vietnam due to a "child-like" map that has stoked geopolitical tensions. (Warner Brothers)
A still from the trailer showing the map in question drew some sardonic critiques, but Vietnam experts say even seemingly innocuous depictions of the nine-dash line are highly sensitive in the South-East Asian nation.
The Philippines is also deliberating about whether to screen Barbie, while Senator Risa Hontiveros said cinemas should include an "explicit disclaimer", according to local media GMA Network.
In the case of Blackpink, it was a map on the website of entertainment company iME, the Beijing-based organiser of their concerts, that drew Vietnam's ire.
Blackpink is set to play two shows in capital Hanoi, but Vietnamese social media users threatened to boycott the concerts — even members of the Blackpink Vietnam Fan Club Facebook group.
China's foreign ministry spokesperson, when asked about the Barbie ban, said: "China's position on the South China Sea issue is clear and consistent."
"[The] relevant country should not link the South China Sea issue with normal cultural exchange," Mao Ning said.
China's Mao Ning says Vietnam should not link the South China Sea issue to "normal cultural exchange". (Chinese Foreign Ministry)
That said, China is no stranger to banning and censoring films, from Seven Years in Tibet to Christopher Robin — the latter perceived as being due to online memes comparing President Xi Jinping to Winnie the Pooh.
Beijing has also banned films due to homosexual themes, including Call Me By Your Name, and scenes were cut from the Freddie Mercury biopic Bohemian Rhapsody.
Dr Khac Giang Nguyen, a visiting fellow with the Vietnamese Studies Program at the ISEAS Yusof Ishak Institute of Singapore, said Vietnamese authorities sought to censor the nine-dash line in books, movies, and even seemingly innocent things like children's toys.
In 2016, Vietnamese authorities even refused to stamp new Chinese passports that depicted the line.
"If anything comes out, the Ministry of Culture will have a look at that and evaluate the seriousness of the situation and decide whether they should take any action," he said.
"From the outsider's perspective, or from the Chinese perspective, I think this looks like an overreaction.
"But if you closely follow the way that China has tried to shape the public opinion in their favour, it's kind of understandable for smaller countries like Vietnam to take drastic actions."
Khac Giang Nguyen says Vietnam is demonstrating a strong stance on the South China Sea to domestic audiences. (Supplied)
Dr Hai Hong Nguyen, senior lecturer of policy and politics at the Queensland University of Technology's school of justice, said Vietnam's actions were about protesting the creeping normalisation of the nine-dash line.
"It's not about merely culture, or it's not merely about commerce, it's about sovereignty."
As highly-anticipated as the Barbie flick is, and as popular as Blackpink is, both Dr Nguyens doubted the moves would backfire locally.
K-pop band Blackpink is due to perform in Hanoi, but a map used by their concert organiser is causing tension. (AFP: Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for Coachella)
"In Vietnam, the anti-China sentiment is quite high and they are hypersensitive about anything related to the nine-dash line," Dr Khac Giang Nguyen said.
Vietnamese authorities had a two-pronged approach, he said: They want to communicate to a domestic audience that they are "trying to protect Vietnamese sovereignty in any way possible, whether it is fictional, whether it's sending vessels out to the South China Sea".
At the same time, they are trying to bring global attention to the issue in a bid to counter the narrative put forward by Beijing.
Bec Strating, director of La Trobe Asia at La Trobe University, agreed Vietnam has sought to "internationalise" the issue as part of their soft power statecraft.
She said while it wasn't clear if the dotted line in the Barbie movie was meant to depict China's nine-dash line, even using dashed lines on ocean maps could be controversial.
The idea of using dashed lines to depict maritime borders was very specific to what China was doing in the South China Sea, she said.
It could be potentially interpreted as "legitimising the use of dashed lines to depict maritime boundaries".
Several countries have claims in the strategic waters of the South China Sea but one is aggressively muscling for the rights to everything above and below the water.
"We don't have other … maritime boundaries across the world that tend to be depicted using dashed lines like that," she said.
Richard Heydarian, a political analyst and senior lecturer in Asian affairs at the University of the Philippines, told Time that Vietnam's hyper vigilance on the popular culture front might be perceived as "petty over sensitivity".
But at the same time, he said getting attention was the point.
"Vietnam is reminding the world that Chinese state propaganda should have no place in supposedly innocuous productions like Barbie movies. It just doesn't make sense," he told Time.
China and Vietnam have a long history of animosity — stretching back more than 2,000 years to when China colonised Vietnam.
Questions of sovereignty over islands in the South China Sea are more recent.
In 1947, Beijing published its almost all-encompassing "nine-dash line" and has relied on this ever since to stake its maritime claims.
In 2016, an international court in The Hague ruled that China had no historic title over the waters of the South China Sea, a ruling in favour of the Philippines. But China refused to accept the finding.
China has been dredging and fortifying land in the disputed Spratly Islands. (Reuters/US Navy)
The islands, as well as reefs and atolls, are resource-rich and of strategic importance in a climate where tensions are rising.
Both China and Vietnam have been dredging and building artificial islands in the South China Sea, which is becoming increasingly militarised.
Last year, the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative described Vietnam's dredging and landfill activities as "substantial", adding they "signal an intent to significantly fortify its occupied features in the Spratlys".
But China's efforts are of a far greater magnitude and have been described as "relentless" in its building and military operations.
Earlier this year, experts anticipated heightened tension and competition in the South China Sea.
Dr Strating said there had been increased interaction between military and non-military vessels, as well as aircraft over maritime areas, "which is quite concerning".
She said Beijing had increasingly militarised coast guard and fishing vessels, engaging in "grey zone" tactics.
"This is an ongoing and significant security challenge," Dr Strating said.
The Philippines intentionally grounded a navy ship near the Spratly Islands in 1999. (Pool via AP: Ritchie B. Tongo)
Dr Khac Giang Nguyen said Vietnamese authorities in the past three months have been concerned about Chinese activities inside Vietnam's exclusive economic zone.
He added that China too had a two-pronged strategy in the South China Sea: first by trying to enforce their claims through power, economic coercion and militarisation, and secondly through culture.
"For the Vietnamese and Philippines, whenever possible, they try to counter that narrative and to delegitimise the Chinese claim on the cultural front."

title: Owners of small cinemas deciding 'to close or not to close' call for more flexibility from film distributors
content:
Ben Curran was born the same year his father, Ron, opened the Glenbrook Cinema in the lower Blue Mountains in 1968.
"I've grown up with the cinema," Mr Curran says.
"I was a projectionist at the age of 13, working in the candy bar as a young kid, so it's part of the family and it's a passion that we've had my entire life."
It's only since taking over the family business three years ago with his wife, Fiona, that he began to see the ugly side of running a single-screen cinema.
Ben Curran wants to be able to show more films at times better suited to his customers. (ABC Radio Sydney: Rosemary Bolger)
Facing the very real prospect of closing, Mr Curran has decided to be up-front with the community about the strict film distribution deals pushing them to the brink.
In a newsletter entitled, To close or not to close?, Mr Curran explained that booking films was not as easy as predicting which films his audiences wanted to see.
Film distributors place conditions on their films, including a minimum amount of screenings per day or week. The bigger the movie, the higher the requirements.
For cinemas with only one screen, that can severely limit the choices of movies available to their community.
"When you're stuck with a major film and you've got to show two or three sessions a day, that blocks your single screen," Mr Curran says.
"And you could get the same number of people for that movie in one session a day, but instead you're splitting them over three."
If they wait to start showing the film two or three weeks after its release date, when fewer conditions are attached, film-goers know they will not have to wait long before they can watch it at home on a streaming service.
Further up the mountain, Mount Vic Flicks owners Kirsten Mulholland and Adam Cousins share the same frustrations.
Adam Cousins and Kirsten Mulholland rarely get a chance to watch the films they show. (ABC Radio Sydney: Rosemary Bolger)
"Every single film with big distributors is a long drawn-out fight," Mr Cousins says.
Longer films are also adding to single-screen cinemas' scheduling headaches, says Peter Cotter from Huskisson Pictures.
"We had a film here a little while ago, and it was one of those long films and we had to show it three times a day and were only getting two or three to it," Mr Cotter says.
Huskisson Pictures' Jan and Peter Cotter have just put up ticket prices by $1 to $11 — still a bargain. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)
Smaller cinemas are urging film distributors to be more flexible and allow them to put on movies at times when they know people want to come.
Independent Cinemas Association Brett Rosengarten, a former Roadshow Films sales director, acknowledges the challenges for smaller cinemas, but says film distributors have cost pressures too, including staffing and millions of dollars in advertising and marketing.
It's easy to mistake the council-owned Glenbrook building as sport clubrooms until you smell popcorn. (ABC Radio Sydney: Rosemary Bolger)
While cinemas want to maximise their returns by showing a greater range of films, he says distributors see other films as competition so it is in their interests to claim as many screening slots as possible.
Some distributors are coming to the table, but change may not come fast enough to save Glenbrook Cinema.
"Even with some of the most difficult distributors, we are seeing a change in the industry, but it's not fast enough for the current conditions of the cinema industry," Mr Curran says.
"We need changes now."
There are fewer than 20 single-screen theatres left in regional New South Wales. Some are run by volunteers, or screen just a handful of films on weekends.
Others like Mount Vic Flicks survive by doing it all themselves, from buying bread and making soup to cleaning up after the last film showing.
"I'm usually out the door by nine o'clock in the morning [and] back home, hopefully, before midnight," Mr Cousins says.
"It amazes me. We still do really love it 10 years in," Ms Mulholland says.
Adam Cousins and Kirsten Mulholland say customers feel like they're visiting a friend's house. (ABC Radio Sydney: Rosemary Bolger)
Mr Rosengarten says small cinemas are often the "heartbeat of a town" but he warns "not every business will survive".
"We definitely think there is a market … particularly in regional areas, for single screens to survive, but it's not easy," he says.
He says the key is to get admission numbers back to pre-COVID-19 levels.
ABC Radio program Overnights examines how independent cinemas are faring post-COVID.
That will be helped by strong films that are coming soon, such as Barbie, Oppenheimer, and the Australian film, Force of Nature.
Glenbrook Cinema's Mr Curran is giving it one more year before making a final decision about the cinema's future.
Since issuing the newsletter about its predicament, the cinema has been as busy as ever, while the Blue Mountains Council that owns the building is investigating how it can assist.
"It's the customers who keep us going," Mr Curran says.
It's the same for Mount Vic Flicks and Huskisson Pictures operators.
"It's kind of like they're visiting their friend's house," Mr Cousins says.
"They come in, they chat with us, they get given some soup and snacks … they like the personal service and the heart that you don't get in the cold multiplexers."
"We're not in it to make our fortune and so forth," Mr Cotter adds.
"We just say we're here to serve our community."

title: Picasso and Polanski committed horrific acts. What do we do with their art?
content:
When the MeToo movement took off across the globe in 2017, it changed how we think about artists and their art.
As victims of sexual harassment and assault spoke out, the public became more aware of the behaviour of well-known people, including successful artists. Audiences immediately began to view these artists' work through the lens of their actions.
As a result, many of our favourite books, songs and art works became irrevocably tainted by the transgressions of their creators.
Admiring the work of Pablo Picasso — the cubist artist who burned his partner Françoise Gilot's face with a cigarette (and painted it) — or Alfred Hitchcock — the film director who tried to destroy actress Tippi Hedren's career when she rebuffed his advances — became a less straightforward proposition.
RN Breakfast provides the most comprehensive coverage and analysis of national and international events on Australian radio.
"In the aftermath [of MeToo], people were left wondering what to do about their heroes," US critic Claire Dederer writes in her new book, Monsters: A Fan's Dilemma.
Many of these fallen heroes were labelled monsters. These included film producer Harvey Weinstein, who was accused of sexual harassment and assault by more than 80 women and later convicted of rape; actor and comedian Bill Cosby, who was accused of drugging and assaulting women as early as 1965; and comedian Louis CK, who frequently masturbated in front of women in his office.
These horrific revelations leave audiences with one question: Can we enjoy good art by bad people?
The answer: It's complicated.
"Nostalgia, personal experience – these things become meaningful in terms of calculating the badness of the act against the greatness of the work," Dederer writes. (Supplied: Hachette)
Dederer came to define a "monster" as someone whose behaviour disrupts the way we view their art. "The work we're looking at is altered by our knowledge of their biography," she tells ABC's RN Breakfast.
For Dederer, an avid film buff, Polish director Roman Polanski offers a defining example of a monster and the problem such a person poses to the audience.
In 1977, Polanski was charged with sexually assaulting 13-year-old Samantha Gailey. The following year, he fled the US after he was convicted of the downgraded charge of unlawful sex with a minor.
At the time, Polanski was one of the world's most respected directors, with many critically acclaimed films to his name, including Rosemary's Baby (1968) and Chinatown (1974).
Polanksi continued directing in Europe after he left the US. He worked with Hollywood A-listers such as Meryl Streep and Kate Winslet and won the Academy Award for Best Director for his 2002 film The Pianist (for which he received a standing ovation).
In 2020, Parisian protesters demonstrated against the nomination of Polanksi's film An Officer and a Spy at the 45th Cesar Film Awards ceremony. (Getty Images: Michel Stoupak/NurPhoto )
"[Polanski's] work is undeniably great. Many people think his film Chinatown is among – if not the – best film ever made," Dederer says.
"At the same time, he raped a young girl, and he was convicted of it."
For Dederer, the contradiction of Polanski's monstrosity and his genius remains irreconcilable.
"As an abuse survivor myself, I was particularly horrified by his crime, and at the same time … I deeply loved the work. It's not just that it was great; it's that it was important to me," she says.
Some say we should view a work of art in isolation from its creator.
But Dederer argues that's sometimes impossible.
In Monsters, memoirist and critic Claire Dederer confronts one of our most topical questions: What do we do with the art of monstrous men?
She uses Woody Allen's critically acclaimed film Manhattan as an example. In the 1979 film, Allen plays a man in his forties who is in a relationship with a 17-year-old girl, played by Mariel Hemingway.
It was a case of life imitating art when it was revealed in 1992 that Allen was in a real-life relationship with a woman 35 years his junior: Soon-Yi Previn, his ex-partner Mia Farrow's 21-year-old adopted daughter.
The revelation of Allen and Previn's age difference, as well as their family connection, earned the filmmaker widespread opprobrium and cast his film Manhattan, with its similar relationship, in a sinister light.
"[Manhattan] really prefigures, and also disturbingly echoes, Allen's later relationship with … Soon-Yi Previn," says Dederer. "[It] makes the film really disturbing to watch."
Allen and Previn (pictured here at a film premiere in 2014) married in Venice in 1997 and have two adopted daughters. (Reuters: Lucas Jackson )
When Dederer discussed the film with her male film critic pals, they counselled her to "separate the artist from the art – [implying] that these two things could be severed in an almost surgical way".
But Dederer found she couldn't detach her feelings about Manhattan from what she now knew about its director.
"I can want to do that, but it's not something I can necessarily make happen," she says. "The idea that I can control that seems incorrect to me."
Whether we should boycott an artist's work or overlook their transgressions is ultimately up to the individual, argues Ashleigh Wilson, a journalist whose 2019 essay On Artists considers artistic legacy in the MeToo era.
"It's what we bring to the debate ourselves," he says. "Acknowledging our own preferences, prejudices, likes and dislikes guides where we are and where we end up."
The 2019 film Leaving Neverland detailed allegations of sexual abuse against Michael Jackson, who died from a drug overdose in 2009. (Reuters: Leonhard Foeger)
The viewer's perspective matters. "If you were a Michael Jackson fan from when you were a kid, you might be uncomfortable [with his alleged child abuse] but less inclined to entirely banish his music from your life," Wilson says.
The quality of the work is another factor. Jackson's reputation is undeniably tarnished, but he is still considered the King of Pop – and his music still gets played on the radio.
However, the revelation of entertainer Rolf Harris's crimes saw his work swiftly expunged from the cultural record with little resistance.
"I think that's probably because of the nature of the work he did … People were more willing to cast aside Tie Me Kangaroo Down Sport and the wobble board because it wasn't so great in the first place," Wilson says.
"[But] Michael Jackson is so immersed in the popular culture of this generation that it's more difficult to imagine a world without his music."
Monsters aren't always male, of course.
While Dederer explores the anti-Semitism of Virginia Woolf and J.K. Rowlings' divisive views on transgender issues, female artists are more commonly considered monsters for being a bad mother.
In her book, Dederer examines women who put their art before motherhood, such as musician Joni Mitchell, who at 21 gave up her baby for adoption.
In a 1992 interview with Rolling Stone, Mitchell described her affinity with other artists who put their art above all else:
"Most of my heroes are monsters, unfortunately, and they are men. If you separate their personalities from their art, Miles Davis and Pablo Picasso have always been my major heroes because we have this one thing in common: They were restless."
Then there's Doris Lessing, who left two of her children with their father to pursue a writing life.
Lessing, a Nobel laureate who died in 2013 at age 94, spoke frankly about her ambivalence towards motherhood:
"For a long time, I felt I had done a very brave thing. There is nothing more boring for an intelligent woman than to spend endless amounts of time with small children. I felt I wasn't the best person to bring them up. I would have ended up an alcoholic or a frustrated intellectual like my mother."
Dederer concludes: "While men's most terrible crime … is rape, of course, for women, I'm exploring the idea that the most terrible crime as perceived by society is the failure to take care of our children."

title: Barbie's world map makes no sense, but even it can cause an international incident
content:
The new Barbie film starring Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling is set for imminent release. But according to Vietnam's state-run Tuoi Tre newspaper, the film's release has been barred.
The head of the Department of Cinema, a government body in charge of licensing and censoring foreign films, said:
We do not grant licence for the American movie Barbie to release in Vietnam because it contains the offending image of the nine-dash line.
Vietnam's response to the Barbie movie's depiction of the South China Sea shows how sensitive these matters are in South-East Asia — and especially in Vietnam.
The South China Sea has a long history of being contested.
China and Vietnam engaged in military clashes over the Paracel and Spratly islands in the South China Sea in 1974 and 1988.
Those disputes were over land, but more recently the focus has turned to claims over the continental shelf (the area of seabed that extends beyond the coast to at least 200 nautical miles), and the economic zones (the area at least 200 nautical miles from the coast).
Since the late 1940s, China has promoted the so-called nine-dash line in the South China Sea. The line, also known as the "U-shaped line" or "cow's tongue", comprises nine dashes.
As depicted in various official and unofficial Chinese maps, the line extends off the coast of China's Hainan Island, and runs close to the coast of Vietnam, deep into the South China Sea, enclosing the Spratly Islands.
North of Borneo, near the coasts of Malaysia and Brunei, the line turns and runs to the west of the Philippines and ends just to the south of Taiwan.
The line has long been the subject of speculation as to what exactly it purports to encompass. Is it a Chinese territorial claim? Is it a Chinese claim to a maritime space? Does it extend to sovereignty over the whole area or just to resources?
China has never been very explicit as to precisely what the claim includes but it has been persistent in seeking to advance the claim.
This has especially been the case since Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam have begun to advance their own claims to parts of the South China Sea, which overlap the nine-dash line.
YouTube Barbie official trailer
A 2009 joint Malaysia/Vietnam submission to the United Nations Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf highlighted competing claims over the continental shelf in the South China Sea, which is what sparked the current controversy.
China made a formal diplomatic response to the UN claiming:
"China has indisputable sovereignty over the islands in the South China Sea and the adjacent waters, and enjoys indisputable sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the relevant waters as well as the seabed and subsoil thereof (see attached map)."
China attached a copy of the nine-dash line map to its formal diplomatic protest to the Malaysia/Vietnam submission and added:
"The above position is consistently held by the Chinese Government, and is widely known by the international community."
It turned out, however, that this was not a widely known or shared view by the international community. Since then, the commission has become something of a de facto legal battleground for various views regarding the status of the nine-dash line.
In addition to China continuously advancing its position regarding the legitimacy of the nine-dash line, countries including Australia, France, Indonesia, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, United Kingdom, and Vietnam have rebutted China's assertions.
But the commission is not a court and is comprised of scientists who assess continental shelf claims.
It was up to the Philippines, as the other nation with possible claims on the region, to separately challenge the legality of China's nine-dash line claim under the law of the sea. In 2016, a United Nations Law of the Sea Convention Tribunal ruled unanimously that China's claim had no basis in international law.
That ruling was clear-cut and conclusive, and immediately rejected by China. While the Philippines conclusively won the legal argument that the nine-dash line had no basis in modern international law or the law of the sea, China refused to respect the outcome of that case and continues to assert its South China Sea entitlements.
China does this in multiple ways. It has built artificial islands in the South China Sea, harassed foreign naval and military aircraft passing through the region, intimidated Vietnamese and other foreign fishermen, asserted rights to explore and exploit maritime oil and gas reserves, and continued to publish maps depicting the nine-dash line claim.
This is why any legitimacy given to the nine-dash line, even in Hollywood movies, is so sensitive.
Maps are reflective of a critical national attribute: territory.
They define the outer limits of territorial claims. Children are familiarised with their home country by maps. Maps have historically been depicted on postage stamps, buildings, and more recently government websites.
Maps now depict a country digitally and this has become contested, as highlighted by the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
University students challenge their professors when maps are shown that depict disputed lands.
Maps have meaning and touch national sensitivities.
Vietnam's response to Hollywood's depiction of China's nine-dash line is understandable. It demonstrates a fierce resistance to any legitimacy that China's ongoing South China Sea nine-dash line claims may generate, even in Barbie's fictional world.
Donald Rothwell is a Professor of International Law at the Australian National University. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

title: 'Incredible opportunity': Cate Blanchett and Warwick Thornton on the Voice referendum
content:
Hollywood star Cate Blanchett says this year's referendum on constitutional recognition and a Voice to Parliament represents "an incredible opportunity" for Australia to embrace its history.
"It's an extraordinary time for an extraordinary country," she told 7.30.
"We have this incredible opportunity to embrace our unique history, shared history, you know, with all of its missteps and all of its successes, to actually evolve into a really modern democracy, like New Zealand, like Canada."
The celebrated Australian actor made the comments alongside director Warwick Thornton, in Australia promoting their film The New Boy.
The film, according to Blanchett, has a fable-like quality. It centres on an Indigenous boy, played by first-time actor 11-year-old Aswan Reid, who is captured by trackers and taken to a remote monastery in South Australia.
A film still from The New Boy featuring Cate Blanchett and Aswan Reid. (Supplied: Roadshow/Ben King Photography)
It was inspired by Thornton's own experience of attending a Catholic boarding school in New Norcia, Western Australia.
"As a child, I had never been into a church. And I was a bit of a ratbag on the streets of Alice Springs, and my mother went, 'Right, up to boarding school you go,'" he told 7.30.
Thornton, whose film successes include Sweet Country and Samson and Delilah, says his movies give a "voice to the voiceless".
"Most films I do, it's about giving people, who are my people, my grandparents, my ancestors, and my grandchildren a voice that they've never had. And that's incredibly important for me," he said.
Director Warwick Thornton on set with young actors from his film The New Boy. (Supplied: Roadshow/Ben King Photography)
Thornton says the Voice to Parliament feels to him like a progression from making those films.
"It's a strange time," he said.
"I feel that we're in a country that feels like a spoilt single child who'd only learned the word 'no' and one day needs to learn the word 'yes'."
Blanchett says the campaign against the referendum has been characterised by fear. She sees parallels with the challenges women faced when they fought for the right to vote.
According to Blanchett, that debate 120 years ago also focused on the negatives.
"Change felt terrible. And the debate was all about, 'The society is going to collapse,'" she said.
"Now, can we imagine a world in Australia where women didn't have the right to vote? Where their voices weren't heard? No, we can't.
"It's time we evolved to include all Australians … The more inclusive cultures are, the more vibrant they are."
"I'm hoping, in another 120 years' time, we'll look back at this moment and say, 'Can you believe we almost missed that opportunity?'"
Cate Blanchett and Warwick Thornton speak about their latest film, The New Boy. (Sarah Ferguson)

title: Robert De Niro's grandson, Leandro De Niro Rodriguez, dies at 19
content:
Leandro De Niro Rodriguez, the grandson of actor Robert De Niro, has died aged 19.
Leandro's mother and eldest daughter of Robert, Drena, announced the news in an Instagram post on Monday.
“I don’t know how to live without you but I’ll try to go on and spread the love and light that you so made me feel in getting to be your mama,” she wrote.
“You were so deeply loved and appreciated and I wish that love alone could have saved you."
Leandro only recently turned 19, news outlets report. (Supplied: Instagram)
Robert De Niro said he was “deeply distressed by the passing of my beloved grandson Leo," in a statement on Monday.
"We’re greatly appreciative of the condolences from everyone," he wrote.
"We ask that we please be given privacy to grieve our loss of Leo."
Later on Monday, De Niro’s publicist shared another statement from Drena De Niro.
“It is with immeasurable shock and sadness that we say goodbye to our beloved son Leo," she said in the statement.
"We thank you for the outpouring of love and support and ask that we are given privacy at this time to process this inconsolable grief."
The family has not released any details about the cause of death.
In response to a request to confirm a TMZ report that Leandro was found in a New York apartment, New York City police wrote that “an 18-year-old male was found unconscious, unresponsive and was pronounced deceased by EMS on scene” at a Wall Street address that houses the Cipriani Club Residences.
Leandro’s father, Carlos Mare, had not made any comment by Monday afternoon, although he posted an image of a black square on Instagram, without adding any words.
The medical examiner’s office will determine the cause of death.
Leandro only recently turned 19, news outlets report.
Drena De Niro, 51, is the oldest of Robert De Niro's now seven children, after the 79-year-old welcomed a baby earlier this year.
Robert adopted Drena when he married her mother, Diahnne Abbott, his first wife.
Also an actor, Drena De Niro has had roles in Joy, The Intern and Mozart in the Jungle and more.
Leandro also had acting credits to his name, with roles in 2005’s The Collection, and 2018’s Cabaret Maxime, also alongside his mother.

title: Vietnam bans Barbie movie over scene featuring South China Sea map
content:
Vietnam has banned Warner Bros' highly-anticipated film Barbie from domestic distribution over a scene featuring a map that shows China's unilaterally claimed territory in the South China Sea, state media reports.
The U-shaped nine-dash line is used on Chinese maps to illustrate its claims over vast areas of the South China Sea, including swathes of what Vietnam considers its continental shelf, where it has awarded oil concessions.
Barbie is the latest movie to be banned in Vietnam for depicting China's controversial nine-dash line, which was repudiated in an international arbitration ruling by a court in The Hague in 2016.
China refuses to recognise the ruling.
Barbie, starring Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, was originally slated to open in Vietnam on July 21, the same date as in the United States, according to state-run Tuoi Tre newspaper.
"We do not grant license for the American movie Barbie to release in Vietnam because it contains the offending image of the nine-dash line," the paper reported, citing Vi Kien Thanh, head of the Department of Cinema, which is the government body in charge of licensing and censoring foreign films.
Several countries have claims in the strategic waters of the South China Sea but one is aggressively muscling for the rights to everything above and below the water.
Warner Bros did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In 2019 the Vietnamese government pulled DreamWorks' animated film Abominable and last year it banned Sony's action movie Unchartered for the same reason.
Netflix also removed Australian spy drama Pine Gap in 2021.
Vietnam and China have long had overlapping territorial claims to a potentially energy-rich stretch in the South China Sea.
The South-East Asian country has repeatedly accused Chinese vessels of violating its sovereignty.
