title: Two-time Oscar winner Glenda Jackson, who mixed acting with politics, dies at 87
content:
Glenda Jackson, a two-time Academy Award-winning performer who had a second career in politics as a British MP, has died at 87.
Jackson's agent Lionel Larner said she died on Thursday at her home in London after a short illness.
"She recently completed filming The Great Escaper in which she co-starred with Michael Caine," he said.
One of four daughters of a bricklayer and a cleaning lady in north-west England, Jackson never forgot her roots even as she made her name as one of the greatest women actors of her generation.
Raw-boned, pallid and angular, with striking, sharp eyes, she had starred on stage, television and film before quitting to take up politics, declaring: "An actor's life is not interesting."
Growing up in Birkenhead, Cheshire, Jackson left school at the age of 15 and found work in a shop before winning a place at the prestigious Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London.
She won her first Academy Award in 1971 as lead actress for her role as a headstrong artist in director Ken Russell's film of DH Lawrence's novel Women in Love.
Glenda Jackson won her first Academy Award for Best Actress in 1970's Women in Love. (AP: Bob Dear)
Her second Oscar came three years later for A Touch of Class, a romantic comedy directed by Melvin Frank in which Jackson played a harried fashion designer caught up in a catastrophic love affair with an American businessman in London.
Jackson also won two Emmy awards for her portrayal of England's Queen Elizabeth I in the BBC's 1971 television series Elizabeth R.
After more than three decades on stage and film, Jackson quit acting and took her no-nonsense, straight-talking style into politics.
She had been angered by the damage she believed was inflicted on the working classes by Margaret Thatcher, Britain's Conservative prime minister from 1979 until 1990.
In 1992, at the age of 55, Jackson won a seat in parliament representing the left-of-centre Labour Party in a constituency in north London.
"We must work for the poor, the homeless, the unemployed, the frail, the sick," she told supporters.
She returned to acting after leaving parliament and had some of her most acclaimed roles, including the title character in productions of Shakespeare's King Lear in London and on Broadway.
She won a Tony Award in 2018 for her role in Three Tall Women.
Jackson was married from 1958 to 1976 to stage director Roy Hodges. She is survived by their son, Daniel Hodges, who was born in 1969.

title: Ben Affleck's Batman and Gal Gadot's Wonder Woman look less than thrilled with their latest outing
content:
We're now at the point in the superhero movie cycle where the villains are being upstaged by the franchises' existential crises – those ongoing brand management dilemmas that invariably play out on screen via some iteration of the multiverse.
It's a potentially fascinating playground in the right creative hands, but DC's The Flash, directed by Andy Muschietti (It; It: Chapter Two) and headlined by troubled star Ezra Miller, struggles to stir up the inventiveness and charm required of the task.
The long-delayed project also has the misfortune of arriving right on the heels of Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, a movie that took on similar ideas with the kind of artistry that makes Muschietti's film look like a relic of another, best-forgotten era.
The Flash marks an ending of sorts for DC's Extended Universe, a decade-long run of films – from 2013's Man of Steel through the ill-fated likes of 2022's Black Adam – that never quite found their popular groove next to the competition at Marvel.
"We did a lot of improvising that led to the scenes being longer than expected," Muschietti told Collider. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
Muschietti's film supposedly serves as a soft reboot to usher in DC's new regime – led by James Gunn and Peter Safran, who've announced an end to the previous films' extended universe – but it carries the unmistakable feel of its predecessors' muddled, creative failures.
After a string of glorified cameos in the Zack Snyder DC films, dating back to 2016's Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice, The Flash's belated standalone adventure comes across as a thankless endeavour hitched to a franchise marked for extinction.
Among the cohort of superheroes in DC's Metropolis, The Flash, aka junior forensics investigator Barry Allen (Miller), remains the team's unsung member ("the janitor of the Justice League," he quips), rescuing horrifically animated CGI babies from exploding hospitals and playing backup to Wonder Woman (Gal Gadot) and Batman (Ben Affleck), neither of whom look enthusiastic to be there. (Batman's rather sad and shabby-looking costume could definitely do with a dry clean and press, for starters.)
But The Flash is about to become a key player: After inadvertently opening up a rip in space-time thanks to his lightspeed power, he decides to travel back in time to save his mother (Maribel Verdú), who was murdered in a crime later pinned on Barry's now-incarcerated dad (Ron Livingston).
The Flash character debuted in the first issue of DC Comics' Flash Comics, in January 1940. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
This, as anyone who's ever seen a time travel film knows, is not the best idea, and Barry's attempt to return to the present instead lands him in the same world as his motor-mouthed 18-year-old self – also played, in an ambitious and sporadically amusing double act, by Miller.
It's a world where, in the inevitable nod to Back to the Future, Eric Stoltz ended up playing Marty McFly, Michael J. Fox starred in Footloose, Kevin Bacon headlined Top Gun – and where the villainous Kryptonian General Zod (a barely engaged Michael Shannon) has returned to menace the planet.
There's also, as The Flash quickly discovers, no Justice League, save for a lone Caped Crusader – though it's not the one Barry expects.
As heavily featured in the movie's marketing, this universe's Batman is none other than Michael Keaton, who the two Barrys find kicking around Wayne Manor in sweatpants, knit cardigans and a desert island castaway beard.
Keaton is the movie's blessing but also its curse: His presence instantly injects the film with personality and gravitas, but he's also an unflattering reminder – along with the bursts of Danny Elfman's iconic Batman score – of the Tim Burton era, when superhero movies were allowed to be rich and authentically strange, and were inhabited by stars with larger-than-life charisma.
Gunn and Safran have spoken candidly about the disarray both on and off screen for the DC franchise. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
It doesn't take long for the delight of Keaton's return to wear off once he's folded into proceedings, as his Batman and the Barrys travel to Siberia chasing a lead: Apparently Superman has crashed to Earth and is being held in a Russian containment facility. Instead, they find Supe's cousin Kara Zor-El (Sasha Calle) – and a makeshift, alternate-world Justice League is born.
Within all the theoretical possibilities of its alternate timelines, The Flash should be a blast, but it's torn between building a narrative for its hero and servicing the wider universe, much of which already feels redundant.
Like so much of the superhero multiverse (Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness; Spider-Man: No Way Home), it's less interested in pushing genuinely imaginative stories than it is in providing fan service, which here – as is the unfortunate whim of recent Warner Bros. offerings – starts to resemble nothing so much as the algorithmic cynicism of Space Jam: A New Legacy.
Miller identifies as transgender non-binary and uses gender-neutral pronouns. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
The film's sweet if generic emotional centre, about not changing the past and recognising the things that make us who we are, is appealing – particularly in maternal moments between Miller and Verdú – but it's buried beneath a mechanical and tonally inconsistent execution.
Miller, who in The Perks of Being a Wallflower showed they can be a livewire, charismatic presence, is mostly left stranded by Christina Hodson's (Birds of Prey) oddly subpar screenplay, which doesn't take itself too seriously but isn't consistently funny enough to justify that approach.
If Miller's Barrys don't have much chemistry with each other, then their mismatched buddy routine does make for curious meta-tension on screen, given the actor's notorious real-life history; the running argument between older, wiser Barry and his younger, more impulsive incarnation might be read as a split-personality crisis for the performer. "I'm not very good with people," adult Barry says to his teenage self at one point, "even myself."
“[The Barrys] have these differences, which makes them a couple at odds,” Muschietti told Deadline. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)
Still, the idea is more interesting to contemplate than it is to watch play out.
There's a whiff of desperation to it all, especially when – in what amounts to a stark admission of creative bankruptcy – DC goes back to the original movie Batman to jazz its flagging fortunes.
The Flash is done no favours by being one of the worst-looking superhero films in recent memory, with the kind of sped-up and slowed-down action sequences that might as well be parodies of the genre (to liken them to video games would be an insult to video games). It's made all the worse by the absence of stakes, which happens when you have time-travelling characters capable of reversing anyone's death.
When the inevitable multiverse cameos arrive – even those canonical embarrassments now reclaimed as easter eggs for fans – it's difficult to engage beyond a level of fleeting, nostalgic amusement. And even then, the joke's on this film: Those supposedly bad DC films of the 80s and 90s – no spoilers, but you can guess which ones – had more personality than anything Muschietti and his team have put on screen here.
A post-credits scene – the funniest in the film – at least proves there's one DCU character with movie star charisma; as for the rest of it, well, Gunn's scorched-earth reshaping of the franchise can't arrive soon enough.
The Flash is in cinemas now.

title: Prosecutors accuse Rust weapons expert in Alec Baldwin case of drinking, smoking marijuana
content:
The weapons supervisor on the film set where Alec Baldwin shot and killed a cinematographer has been accused of drinking and smoking marijuana by prosecutors, accusing her of being likely hungover when she loaded a live bullet into the revolver that the actor used.
They levelled the accusations on Friday in response to a motion filed last month by Hannah Gutierrez-Reed's attorneys that seeks to dismiss her involuntary manslaughter charge.
The prosecutors accused her of having a history of reckless conduct and argued it would be in the public interest for her to "finally be held accountable."
Jason Bowles, Ms Gutierrez-Reed's attorney, said on Tuesday the prosecution has mishandled the case.
"The case is so weak that they now have chosen to resort to character assassination claims about Hannah," Mr Bowles told The Associated Press.
"The prosecution has abandoned the idea of doing justice and getting to the actual truth, apparently."
A preliminary hearing for Ms Gutierrez-Reed is scheduled in August. A judge is expected to decide then if there's probable cause for her charge to move forward.
In the response, the prosecutors also noted they expected to decide within the next 60 days whether to recharge Mr Baldwin, depending on the results of an analysis of the gun and its broken sear.
The items were sent to the state's independent expert for further testing.
Actor Alec Baldwin had his charges dismissed, however, he may be recharged.  (Reuters: David 'Dee' Delgado )
The involuntary manslaughter charge faced by Mr Baldwin, who also was a producer on the film, was dismissed in April, with prosecutors citing new evidence and the need for more time to investigate.
Mr Baldwin was pointing a gun at cinematographer Halyna Hutchins during a rehearsal on the New Mexico film set in October 2021 when it went off, killing her and wounding the film's director, Joel Souza.
Ms Gutierrez-Reed's attorneys had argued in their motion that the prosecution was "tainted by improper political motives" and that Santa Fe District Attorney Mary Carmack-Altwies and the initial special prosecutor she appointed, Andrea Reeb, "both used the tragic film set accident that resulted in the death of Halyna Hutchins as an opportunity to advance their personal interests."
The prop supplier for Rust says the movie's armourer told him she bought the same type of ammunition as the live round that killed the cinematographer.
The defence lawyers contend the permanent damage done to the gun by FBI testing before the defence could examine it amounted to destruction of evidence and a violation of the court's rules of discovery.
They also argued the "selective prosecution" of Ms Gutierrez-Reed was a violation of the equal protection clause of the US Constitution.
New special prosecutors who were appointed after Ms Reeb stepped down disputed those claims in their response, saying "nothing about this prosecution has or will be selective."
The prosecutors also acknowledged the unanswered question of where the live rounds found on set came from, saying the investigation was ongoing.
They also suggested there was evidence to support the theory Ms Gutierrez-Reed herself may responsible and if so, more charges may follow.
They offered no specifics in the filing as to what that evidence might be.

title: Veep's Julia Louis-Dreyfus stars in painfully relatable comedy about our daily little white lies
content:
"No one ever says the truth," gripes the teenage Abby in Nicole Holofcener's 2010 film Please Give. She has taken no comfort in her mother's reassurances that the fresh pimple on her nose is barely noticeable, and the reaction at a dinner party confirms what the self-conscious girl already knows: "It's horrible," coos a tipsy, uninhibited guest.
But Abby understands this expression of disgust to stem from compassion – solidarity, even. "I'd rather someone admit it. At least then I don't feel crazy," she says, looking pointedly at her mother.
The politics of interpersonal truth-telling animate the latest sharply drawn dramedy from Holofcener, a writer-director who has long tangled with the ethical knots particular to the urban upper-middle class, a milieu that is both self-aware and sheltered; entitled and insecure.
Holofcener wrote the screenplay over several years but the film was shot in just 22 days. (Supplied: Roadshow)
In You Hurt My Feelings, the writer-director asks – amongst other knotty questions – where is the line between honesty and cruelty? Between reassurance and hot air? And how does one determine which tack is best suited to any given occasion?
Don't expect any definitive answers, however; that's not Holofcener's prerogative. She approaches social dynamics as a sort of archaeologist: More tender than Curb Your Enthusiasm's Larry David but still ruthless in her excavation, she digs without any pretence of being able to rearrange the pieces into a more favourable configuration. Her characters – often based on herself, her family members and her friends – are far from dead and buried, but their proclivities are almost as hard-wired as their bones.
This film's premise is a rich one: Beth (Julia Louis-Dreyfus, playing a Holofcener analog for the second time, after 2013's Enough Said) is a writer and teacher with a moderately successful memoir to her name, now looking to venture into fiction. Her husband, Don (Tobias Menzies, The Crown), has been a font of encouragement, providing nothing but positive feedback on each and every draft. Their largely contented, mutually supportive equilibrium is upset when she overhears him – in the undignified setting of a sporting goods store, no less – admitting that he doesn't actually like her novel at all.
Holofcener told Vogue the characters are drawn from her life: "You don’t really need to drum up a lot of fake stuff to make relationships fascinating." (Supplied: Roadshow)
"He loves you, even if he doesn't like your book," soothes Beth's sister, Sarah (Michaela Watkins, The Dropout). For anyone who's ever poured themselves into a creative pursuit – Beth and Holofcener included – this statement likely sounds near paradoxical.
Less so to Sarah. As an upscale interior designer, she is used to catering to the tastes of others. She tells Beth that she herself praises her husband's work as an actor, even when she deems it not so praise-worthy. (Incidentally, every member of the film's ensemble gives an entirely worthy performance – including Arian Moayed, as Sarah's husband – much cuddlier here than as Succession's Stewy; and Jeannie Berlin, as Beth and Sarah's distinctly un-cuddly mother.)
Little white lies pepper everyone's days in You Hurt My Feelings, traded as social currency. Beth, for instance, feigns appreciation for the ill-formed ideas her creative writing students pitch; her writing students in turn feign interest in her memoir, which none of them have read.
“Nicole [Holofcener] is collaborative. So if we have thoughts about tweaking something … she's all ears,” Louis-Dreyfus told Collider. (Supplied: Roadshow)
Of course, it's easy enough to defend the idea of bending the truth of one's feelings in the name of social niceties, or for the sake of fostering openness and positivity in the classroom. The calculation gets trickier when the people on the receiving end are closer to home.
As in Please Give, the central couple's offspring proves most sensitive to the way in which familial cheerleading – undoubtedly a vital impulse, and one revealed to have been sorely lacking in Beth's own youth – can register as a form of gaslighting. Beth and Don's son, Elliott (Owen Teague), manages a downtown weed dispensary while harbouring aspirations of becoming a playwright. He resists Beth's exhortations to share his writing with her, having been troubled in his schooldays by the gap between her effusive praise and his sometimes mediocre performance.
And yet, for a film with characters so invested in their work, You Hurt My Feelings seems to proffer quite a generous view of mediocrity. Everything the viewer learns about Beth's work, from the title of her memoir (I Had to Tell It, which gets played for a bit of Who's on First?-esque comedy) to the content (if her father had been more than just verbally abusive, Beth half-jokes, perhaps the book would have sold better) suggests that it's no under-sung work of genius.
Holofcener’s screenplays have been nominated for a number of awards, including a BAFTA and an Oscar for Can You Ever Forgive Me? (Supplied: Roadshow)
The desire for external validation is related to, but not the same thing as, the desire to be good at something – and so it's notable that, although Beth desires approval from her husband and from the literary world, she doesn't seem all that invested in her craft. When she learns of Don's doubts about her new manuscript, she is distraught but doesn't consider revision; when the publisher of her first book passes, she pitches it to a notably slicker, shallower publisher.
This mixture of anxiety and complacency is mirrored in Don's narrative arc: He too has been having doubts about his competence at work – rightfully so, with the sequences set in his therapy practice showing him to be distracted and indecisive. His failure to intervene in a couple's back-and-forth bickering prompts one of them (David Cross, who slots perfectly into Holofcener's New York) to quip, "We can do this at home." When the dissatisfied couple eventually sends Don a letter demanding their money back – totalling a whopping $US33,000 – he bins it, apparently not that perturbed by his unhelpfulness after all.
“I like a more subtle story and a smaller arc for characters,” Holofcener told The Atlantic. (Supplied: Roadshow)
There's something refreshing about Holofcener's commitment to unexceptional characters. They do not prove themselves to be smarter, or kinder, or more moral than anyone else; whatever trials they may pass through, they tend not to change their behaviour dramatically or indeed at all – that's not a prerequisite for occupying centre frame in her films, nor does it prevent them from winning viewers over. We should all be grateful to be met with such a lack of judgement.
This commitment to slice-of-life realism – albeit with zingier dialogue – can also be frustrating, however. In this latest film, the lack of closure beyond a 'that's life' shrug results in a total that feels like a little less than the sum of its brilliantly observed parts.
You Hurt My Feelings is in cinemas from June 15.

title: Australian TV writers risk lifetime bans from Writers' Guild of America if they work for Hollywood during strike
content:
Australian television writers are having their projects put on hold because of the Hollywood writers' strike, as the local union advises them against crossing the picket line.
They are facing pressure to hold off on opportunities or risk bans that could jeopardise their careers.
Queensland-born writer Yolanda Ramke has multiple projects paused due to the strike.
Ms Ramke created the television series Troppo, based on the best-selling novel Crimson Lake.
Set in Far North Queensland, the series aired on ABC TV last year.
She's now working on two Writers' Guild of America (WGA) projects with writing partner Ben Howling.
She said the WGA has strong guidelines in place for non-members hoping to pick up some Hollywood work while the strike is ongoing.
"If an Australian writer who is not a yet a member of the WGA was to explore a writing opportunity with one of the struck companies right now, they would be handed down a lifetime ban from future WGA membership," she said.
"That is a risk that I can't imagine Australian writers would ever want to take."
Ms Ramke is a member of the Australian Writers' Guild (AWG), but isn't part of the WGA yet.
"Even though I'm not WGA, I have two projects tied to the guild that are now in a holding pattern, one of which we had hoped to shoot later this year, which will no longer be possible," she said.
Ms Ramke thought the strike was going to be a challenge for writers around the world, but is in favour of what she considers "long overdue" strike action.
"I'm also in the privileged position that, as I wait for the WGA-tied projects I'm involved with to eventually be able to move forward again, I can still earn a living as a writer on home soil on Australian projects," she said.
Writer Yolanda Ramke giving notes on the Troppo set to American actor Thomas Jane.
The AWG released a statement of solidarity with its US counterpart last month.
"With strike action now in force, the AWG advises members not to work on active projects within the jurisdiction of the WGA," it read.
It also advised against pitching new projects to Hollywood studios and crossing any real or virtual picket lines during the strike.
To show their support, AWG members will erect their own picket line outside the Universal Pictures office in Sydney today.
The Australian union was contacted for this story.
In November 2007, the last time US writers went on strike, Ian Simmons was suddenly offered the opportunity to revive a show that'd been dead for years.
Good News Week had previously aired on the ABC and Network Ten between 1996 and 2000.
Network Ten ordered new episodes of the panel show to fill the gap as US late night talk shows went off the air.
"I don't think it was seen as a long-term proposition at that point," Mr Simmons reflected back on the show's second coming.
"It was more like, come back and put it together quickly, we'll do some shows and hopefully we can keep the wolf from the door."
Mr Simmons didn't have much sympathy for the US writers on strike at the time.
"I think my feelings were probably selfish and mercenary," he said.
"I was heading into 2008 without a job and suddenly out of the blue came this chance to be employed."
International films and television shows being produced in Queensland are yet to be impacted, according to information from Screen Queensland.
This month, limited series Apples Never Fall, starring Sam Neill and Annette Benning, and science fiction series La Brea's third season are both expected to be filmed in the Sunshine State.
Cameras are also set to role on action movie Mortal Kombat 2, which will be filmed on the Gold Coast.
Ausfilm, the body responsible for connecting international studios with Australia, declined to comment on how the production slate of international projects made in Australia would be impacted by the strike.
Writers have walked off the job, partly because they fear something fundamental will be lost if Hollywood allows itself to become a wasteland of AI-generated stories.
Mr Simmons is optimistic about the changing landscape for writers in Australia.
He said when Good News Week was revived it was limited to just broadcasters.
"A show I might've only been able to pitch on the ABC 15 years ago, I can now speak to so many different people and pitch that idea to a lot of different places," he said, referring to the emergence of streaming services.
When the last strike was resolved after 100 days in 2008, Mr Simmons said the writing opportunities dried up quickly, as broadcasters were once again picking up US shows.
"We were lucky," he said.
"We got about four years more out of Good News Week, which we didn't expect, and it certainly wasn't planned for."

title: No scripts and a win for inclusivity — Tony Awards make history amidst Hollywood's writer's strike
content:
This year's Tony Awards were almost cancelled because of the Writers Guild of America (WGA) strike blazing through Hollywood.
But the guild granted a waiver earlier in May allowing Broadway's big show to go on — and so it did, with plenty of song, dance, high spirit and history.
It all took place on Sunday night at the United Palace Theatre in the Washington Heights neighbourhood of Manhattan — a new venue for the ceremony.
These were the most memorable moments (and looks) from the event.
Tony and Academy Award-winner Ariana DeBose hosted this year's event.
Ariana DeBose hosted the 2023 Tony Awards with no script.  (AP Photo: Charles Sykes/Invision)
Hosting for the second time in a row, DeBose's task looked drastically different to her first: she had no teleprompters, no carefully-prepared zingers.
This year's Tony Awards threw away all scripts in honour of the thousands of film and television writers striking in Hollywood.
The only words on the teleprompter would say “please wrap up", she said.
“To anyone who may have thought that last year was a bit unhinged, to them, I say, ‘Darlings, buckle up".
Later in the evening, virtually out of breath after her wordless opening performance, she thanked the union organisers for allowing a compromise.
DeBose and others spoke with their dance moves, doing a brassy number. (AP Photo: Charles Sykes/Invision)
History was made by Alex Newell and J. Harrison Ghee, who became the first non-binary people to win Tony Awards for acting.
Ghee won the award for Best Performance by an Actor in a Leading Role in a Musical, while Newell won Best Performance by an Actor in a Featured Role in a Musical.
Newell, who plays Lulu — an independent, don’t-need-no-man whiskey distiller in “Shucked” — has been blowing audiences away with their signature number, “Independently Owned.”
Alex Newell accepts the award for best performance by an actor in a featured role in a musical for "Shucked". (AP Photo: Charles Sykes/Invision)
“Thank you for seeing me, Broadway. I should not be up here as a queer, non-binary, fat, Black little baby from Massachusetts," Newell said to an ovation.
"And to anyone that thinks that they can’t do it, I’m going to look you dead in your face that you can do anything you put your mind to."
Ghee had a starring role in Some Like It Hot, based on the classic 1959 film.
J. Harrison Ghee accepts the award for best performance by an actor in a leading role in a musical for "Some Like It Hot". (AP Photo: Charles Sykes/Invision)
They play a male musician on the run who disguises as a woman in what becomes a voyage of discovery about gender (the movie role involved disguise, but no discovery).
Accepting the award, Ghee said they had been raised to use their gifts not for themselves, but to help others.
Last year, composer and writer Toby Marlow of Six became the first non-binary Tony winner, taking home the trophy for Best Original Score.
One of the night's biggest awards — Best Play — went to British writer Sir Tom Stoppard for his play Leopoldstadt.
The sweeping play tells the story of a Jewish family in Vienna,.
Stoppard thanked the celebrated playwright “for writing a play about Jewish identity and anti-Semitism and the false promise of assimilation."
He also noted his ancestors, “many of whom did not make it out of Poland".
Tom Stoppard, center, and members of the company of Leopoldstadt accept the award for best play. (AP Photo: Charles Sykes/Invision)
Patrick Marber, who won best director of a play for Leopoldstadt, was among several winners who used their acceptance speeches to express support for the strike.
Marber said the evening was going well without writers because "actors are great improvisers".
Miriam Silverman, who won the Tony for best featured actress in a play for The Sign in Sidney Brustein’s Window, ended her speech with: “My parents raised me to believe in the power of labor and workers being compensated and treated fairly."
"We stand with the WGA in solidarity!” she said.
This was no standard black-tie affair.
The looks that grace each Tony Awards red carpet never fail to perfectly match theatre with couture.
Leading the night was Lupita Nyong’o, who subverted a black suit when she paired it with a silver breastplate by Pakistani designer Misha Japanwala, moulded to her body.
Lupita Nyong'o wears a silver breastplate molded to her body. (AP Photo: Evan Agostini)

title: It's hard to get hired as a Queensland actor. But a postcode can change everything
content:
Queensland actors and crew are turning to making their own films after "decades" of being overlooked for productions in their own state.
Whether on the small screen, big screen or the theatre stage, local actors have told ABC Radio Brisbane they struggle to get hired, auditioned or even considered for work in Queensland.
Instead, actors say they are more likely to get work in the state when they relocate or pretend to be from a different state.
That's despite an abundance of highly trained talent in Queensland, and a $230 million film boom that created 5,400 jobs in the state last year.
The issue has prompted the Media, Entertainment & Arts Alliance (MEAA) to launch a survey campaign — called Local Hires Are Hot — aimed at putting local talent back on employers' radars.
Brisbane actor Mike Goldman said it had become a "State of Origin-style" fight, pushing local creatives to move to Victoria or New South Wales just to be considered for Queensland jobs.
He said it was a problem that had "bugged him" for two decades.
Mike Goldman says many local companies are favouring interstate actors. (Supplied: Mike Goldman)
"I literally had to change my name and be with a Sydney agency to get Brisbane work."
Goldman said his agent would tell employers he was Sydney or Melbourne-based, because talent from those cities were perceived to be of higher quality.
"[Film] teachers even say, 'Ah no, sorry, you've got move to Sydney or Melbourne now,' but then the people in Sydney and Melbourne think they have to move to LA to be taken seriously," he said.
He said other actors would pack their bags and relocate permanently because it was considered difficult to be cast as a Queenslander.
"And now we've all come back to Brisbane and we're fighting to create this incredible Brisbane market for movies and talent to make incredible art," Goldman said.
Queensland-based actor Bianca Zouppas has just finished shooting a lead role in a local "arthouse" independent film after having trouble securing a lead role in a more mainstream production.
"A girlfriend of mine, Candice [Hill], we're definitely in the realm of supporting sisters; she has been desperate to start directing," Zouppas said.
Candice Hill (left) and Bianca Zouppas decided to make their own independent local film. (Supplied: Bianca Zouppas, Fox Hole Films)
The chance came when an industry mate offered to lend the women some of his production equipment and encouraged them to make their own film with it.
From mid-2024, the federal government will require major streaming platforms to put some of their revenue back into Australian content.
"We picked some dates, picked the opportunity, secured the equipment, came up with a basic story, and decided to do something quite arthouse: a semi-improvised, feature film," Zouppas said.
"We ended up shooting in four days, which is basically unheard of."
Zouppas had previously moved from Brisbane to Sydney and Sydney to the United States, before returning to Brisbane after realising "you just have to make it yourself".
"It's put a fire in our bellies — we can do anything," she said.
"It's achievable, if you have the right team and right mindset, you don't have to wait around for work. You can get out there and make it yourself.
"And from that more work usually comes."
Zouppas said one of the big challenges of filmmaking was finding a team of actors and crew while also being short on funds.
"That was the magic thing that happened with this project. We knew who we wanted to work with, but whether they'd say yes or no was the question," she said.
"But when we reached out to people, we said we just wanted to make something — some art, it was new, experimental."
Bianca Zouppas says making your own film helps build a network of local talent. (Supplied: Bianca Zouppas, Fox Hole Films)
The Brisbane actor was shocked and grateful when those they reached out to agreed to take part.
"She [Candice Hill] pulled the whole thing together — the whole camera team, lighting team — it was like a proper set," Zouppas said.
Zouppas said grassroots film projects brought local talent together, building a network of creatives within a community for future projects, and giving crews a sense of purpose.
"It's like a spider web of love and support," she said.
"You're supporting other local artists and filmmakers; there's so many people who came on it who were so grateful, and we were obviously so grateful for them."
For Zouppas, making her own film led to her landing a new acting opportunity with a different director who happened to be on set picking up lights.
"He saw me working, and was like 'I'm already shooting a film, would you be available next Saturday to shoot a role?'" she said.
"And I said yes, I would be!"
Several actors have stressed that some Queensland-based companies, including Cutting Edge, 3P Studio and Jaggi Entertainment, do use mostly local talent for their productions.
These local studios generally make around five feature films each year for international streaming services.
But MEAA's Queensland organising director Michelle Rae questioned why Queensland actors and crew seemed to be "disadvantaged" in the first place.
Michelle Rae says Queensland employers may not realise there is skilled local talent. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)
"People are talking about this — you go into a foyer, you go where arts workers are, and they're talking about lack of opportunity," she said.
"So we want to understand what that looks like."
Ms Rae said there could be a perception that Sydney and Melbourne actors were more skilled, or Queensland employers might not realise that highly trained talent exist locally.
"When we think arts, we think Sydney and Melbourne, so people look there, [but also] I think sometimes it's about not realising that you've got it right here," she said.
Local and international filmmakers are choosing to make more films in North Queensland, so could Cairns be the next industry hotspot?
She said the MEAA's Local Hires are Hot survey aimed not to point fingers, but to find lasting solutions to ensure local talent were being valued and considered.
"[Actors and crew] are saying, we live here, we contribute to this economy, and what we want is the opportunity to have a career, work and pathway that is here.
"We know that the moving away from home and working away from home, it takes a toll on workers and their mental health and fatigue.
"It makes sense to value what we've already got."
The MEAA survey will be open until the end of June, and interim responses are expected to be released as early as mid-July.

title: Spider-Man animator gives that one tip that might make all the difference to budding animators
content:
Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse is a big hit with audiences and critics, with an Australian animator instrumental in bringing to life one of the film's most talked about characters.
Miguel O'Hara, aka Spider-Man 2099 voiced by Oscar Isaac, was a much-loved character in the movie.
Australian Daniel Pozo worked on the film and was the character lead for Miguel at key moments throughout the movie.
"I was fortunate enough to have incredibly talented animators that I could delegate work to and then figure out how he moves, how he performs, how restrained we should keep him and how working off the designs that were provided to us, how much his face emotes and so on," Pozo told ABC News.
Daniel Pozo is delighted with the reaction to Miguel O'Hara aka Spider-Man 2099. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
"And that ranged from watching nearly all of Oscar Isaac's movies to looking at any other actor or person who had Indigenous features.
"He definitely has all these very specific landmarks on his face that we tried to look for in other actors, like Simon McLaren came to mind, who has very prominent cheekbones and a jawline and watching a tonne of stuff just to see how everything moves."
Latest Spider-Man movie is a dazzling, inventive and often hilarious challenge to the status quo.
Pozo, supervising animator for Sony Pictures Imageworks, said Miguel was a great character to help develop from his angular face to his much-discussed body.
"We did a lot of research into how we could make him look intimidating, but also have a soft side to him.
"But also, he's this really large guy. So, we looked at a lot of references about large, bodybuilder-types."
It's not just Miguel's chiselled jawline that has everyone talking. It's also his faultless physique. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
Pozo worked on Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse for almost two years. It's the follow-up to the Academy award-winning Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse.
"It's probably the longest production I've ever been on as a supervisor lead," Pozo said.
"Normally it's a year, the most I've been on [before this] was almost a year and a half. It's just a very big story to tell. And then they wanted to spend the time that was needed to get it right.
Born and raised in Sydney, to parents from Chile, and now based in Vancouver, Canada, Pozo's journey to working on major Hollywood productions began when he was still in Australia.
Daniel Pozo was a supervising animator on Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
"Out of high school, I knew I wanted to be in this industry, the animation industry or the film industry, but I didn't know specifically that I wanted to be an animator until I went to TAFE – Enmore design college at the time – and studied the software that every company at the time was using and it was there that I fell in love specifically with the animation side of things."
According to Pozo, being a great animator doesn't necessarily equate with knowing how to draw.
Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse features Shameik Moore as Spider-Man and Hailee Steinfeld as Spider-Gwen. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
"I don't think I draw very well," he said.
"I don't think it's a prerequisite [but] it definitely helps to learn body form and for design elements, there's a lot of things about appeal that is hard to just instinctively know.
"It's good to study it so that you can draw from that inspiration, and those kind of references that you need for certain things to obtain an appealing pose or with the face knowing design rules, but it's not really a prerequisite.
"That being said, I know so many amazing animators who can draw so well, so I'm sure it helps."
Following the success of 2018's Into the Spider-Verse, Sony Pictures started thinking about the sequel as soon as the first film was completed.
Sometimes it's good to know the rules so you can break them.
"Everybody who gets into this learns the fundamentals.
"There's all these principles that were established by the old Disney guys a long time ago, and every single principle applies to everything.
"And there's a lot of stuff that needs to be grounded in reality, especially on a movie like this where the performances need to be grounded … but the great part about animation is that you can take those rules and just break it and see what comes up."
For anyone wanting to be an animator, Pozo said apart from taking up formal training, one of the key things budding animators should do is watch movies.
Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse is currently in cinemas. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)
"I think if you really want to become an animator it would be just watching film, watching animated films, but not limited to animation.
"I have such a love for movies and film in general and I was always interested in and kind of obsessed with the inner workings of how a film was made.
"Before we had YouTube and stuff it was hard to find the behind-the-scenes stuff or buying DVDs just to watch the audio commentary about the directors talking about it or how they made the movie, like anything, I would just love to watch and learn about that."

title: Léa Seydoux is a single mum caught between a steamy affair and her ailing father in new drama
content:
Despite its auspicious sounding title, Mia Hansen-Løve's new film is not all clear skies and fresh beginnings.
Sex and death are its driving forces, running through even the most uneventful scenes of everyday life like subterranean rivers of grief and desire.
It opens on what might very well be the fine morning of the title, with fortyish Sandra (Léa Seydoux, sporting an unfussy pageboy haircut that suggests she's all about making sensible choices) walking down a narrow Parisian street on the way to visit her ailing dad, Georg.
She's a widow who juggles parenting a tween daughter with work as an interpreter. On top of that, her father's recent diagnosis with a rare neurodegenerative disease, which has nearly destroyed his sight and has forced him out of his job as a philosophy professor, means that she's regularly over at his house, helping out with meals and housework.
Hansen-Løve weaves autobiographical elements into her tale of familial and romantic connections. (Supplied: Palace Films)
But not long into the film, another of life's curveballs further complicates things. While taking her daughter to the park, she runs into one of her husband's old friends, Clément (a smooth, self assured Melvil Poupaud), and soon after, acting with rare impulsiveness, she plunges headlong into an affair.
The catch is that he's married and has a young son.
Hansen-Løve has an instinct for finding the friction points in the lives of her characters. More often than not, these stem from life's most vertigo-inducing challenges — a death, an illness, a break up, a sudden career change.
You might not recognise yourself in the milieu of her middle-class French characters, with their unpretentious but somehow chic comfort clothes, but you will recognise yourself in the chaos and contradictions of their lives.
One Fine Morning turns out to be one of the writer-director's more frenetic films, radiating a life force that's urgent and vivid.
Part of it stems from the erotic charge of the couple's hurried trysts, when Clément steals away from work to come up to Sandra's tiny flat.
Brisk pacing gives the unfolding romance between Sandra and Clément a sense of urgency, and reflects the excitement of falling in love. (Supplied: Palace Films)
But there's also an energy transmitted in the pace and staging of the film. Hansen-Løve shoots her characters moving – particularly when they're walking – with fluid tracking shots down streets, into bars, up stairs (it reminded me of her depiction of stressed-out film producer Grégoire pounding the pavement in 2009's Father of My Children).
Her editing style, meanwhile, has a spring-loaded force – scenes often begin after the action has started, and cut before they've come to rest.
The resulting sense of propulsion reflects the excitement of falling in love, but also the precipitous decline in Sandra's father's health.
Léa Seydoux shines as a single mother trying to balance the needs of her parents, her child and herself. (Supplied: Palace Films)
Shot on 35mm by veteran cinematographer and long-time Hansen-Løve collaborator Denis Lenoir, the film's approach to colour often adds a layer of nuance, and counterpoint, to the emotion. Georg's flat, for example, is bathed in golden sunlight, evoking the tender memories it holds for Sandra.
But a melancholy mood drains the colour from what should be one of the film's most vibrant images, a shot of Sandra in a red dress walking in front of Monet's floor-to-ceiling painting Water Lilies while on a date with Clément. In the subtly sombre colour grade, her outfit seems closer to a shade of purple, as if tarnished by worries she can't escape.
As the film unfolds, we meet an assortment of family members who gather to nut out care options for Georg – including Sandra's mother (Georg's ex) Françoise (Nicole Garcia), a boho boomer with a new lease on life after a recent conversion to direct action ecoactivism (a somewhat comical development given her former support of the centrist Macron).
The family eventually decide on aged care, but it's a struggle to find a place, and there's the question of how to convince Georg to leave his cosy garret, and his precious collection of books lining the walls.
Actor Pascal Greggory is known for La Vie En Rose (2007) and Joan of Arc (1999). (Supplied: Palace Films)
It's not the first time Hansen-Løve has made a film inspired by her philosophy teacher parents (the other was 2016's Things to Come with Isabelle Huppert). Here, veteran actor Pascal Greggory turns out to be a particularly haunting father figure.
What strikes you is that he is not particularly old – his square shoulders and chiselled good looks make him seem like a man near his prime, but his unsteady gait, erratic conversations and childlike stare suggest otherwise.
The irony is not lost on Sandra that a man who once valued mental lucidity over all else is now losing his mind.
It only gets worse, exponentially in fact, and Sandra is particularly shaken.
Sedoux's performance of shellshock is remarkable. She's like someone whose emotional switches can flick at any time, and we witness this early in the film in a chance encounter with one of Georg's ex-students, where she pivots from small talk to tears in an instant.
Léa Seydoux gained international attention for her role as Bond girl Madeleine Swann in Spectre (2015), and No Time to Die (2021). (Supplied: Palace Films)
The other side of the coin to her despair is the irrepressible desire she has for Clément.
Not long after the family moves Georg out of his house, and into a series of grey/ beige facilities that paint a disturbing portrait of a crowded aged care sector in crisis, Sandra and Clément's relationship levels up, and he starts sleeping over.
Given she professes early in the film to having left her love life behind her, the romance unlocks a newfound sense of wellbeing.
But it's also extremely volatile, and morally fraught (something both characters, eventually, come to face).
We’ve dug into the program so you don’t have to – here are nine brilliant films selected by our critics.
Whether it has a future is of secondary importance to the change it ushers into Sandra's life — a rebirth that arrives just at the point she is experiencing the profound, unsettling loss of her parent.
Hansen-Løve performs a miraculous balancing act between the forces of grief and desire in the film.
The life ahead for Sandra, it goes without saying, will have fine mornings and stormy ones. But it will continue, with its contradictions and tragedies, breakthroughs and routines.
This penetrating, lyrical portrait is a kind of cinematic carousel – a whirl of scenes that at times almost blur together.
Its characters may very well want it to stop, but to get off would mean forgoing so much. Life can be difficult, the film suggests, but what's important is that you keep moving.
One Fine Morning is in cinemas now.

title: 'The whole system is about to fall apart': Aussie writer in LA raises alarm as strike continues
content:
When Australian writer David Koutsouridis relocated to the United States this year, he planned to start working on a feature film and television series he was attached to.
But months after the award-winning comedy writer landed Stateside, the Writers Guild of America (WGA) went on strike, meaning his plans were put on ice.
Eleven-thousand Hollywood writers walked off the job in May for the first time in 15 years after a breakdown in negotiations between the WGA and the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP), which bargains on behalf of studios and streaming services.
Koutsouridis, who has written for Ten's The Project and ABC TV's Hard Quiz, said he could not even get work as a barista because his visa is restrictive, meaning he's got no way of earning money to support himself.
Speaking to ABC News from the picket lines in Los Angeles, Koutsouridis said he hoped the strike would have an effect beyond Hollywood.
"When I started to talk to writers, and I read up about it, and I informed myself, I realised how pivotal this fight is, not just for America, but the global entertainment industry and particularly in Australia," Koutsouridis said.
With Australians among the audience for Hollywood content, Koutsouridis said the issue went directly to the quality of the shows available to Australians.
"The reason American content is consumed globally is because it's so high quality," Koutsouridis said.
"And the reason it is so revered is because of that quality. And that quality has been able to be nurtured over decades and decades because America has had a healthy industry.
"So, writers have been afforded the opportunity to make a career for themselves, hone their craft, and pass on that knowledge to the next generation of writers and the next generation of writers. And writers' rooms are a great training ground.
Writers say they're fighting for their livelihoods and for the future of the industry. (Supplied: David Koutsouridis)
Koutsouridis said he would love to work in Australia again but said the industry was already on a lifeline and would slump further if the country did not get ahead of these issues now.
"The reality is, with these corporations now getting a foothold in the country, you've got Netflix, Amazon, Disney+, Paramount now owns Network 10, and Australia has no protections. So, basically, now we're relying on these companies and their goodwill to comply with the recommendations of the Writers Guild, and it's been proven in America right now they're not willing to comply.
"The American writers have one of the strongest trade unions in the country and the streamers are still standing their ground on these issues and trying to suffocate writers."
Koutsouridis said one of the key issues was that writers wanted regulation around Artificial Intelligence, but streaming services wanted AI to remain on the table.
Hollywood writers walked off the job this week, partly because they fear something fundamental will be lost if Hollywood allows itself to become a wasteland of AI-generated stories.
"The studios will probably want AI to punch out a first draft, because that first draft is what is the most expensive for a studio. So, the writer will make the most amount of money from the first draft of a screenplay, for example," Koutsouridis said.
"And then they'll pay a human writer a reduced rewrite fee, because the rewrites always cost less for them, even though that human writer would probably end up having to start all over again because I assume the first draft would be barely comprehensible because the technology is just not there."
Koutsouridis said there were other issues with AI.
"I write queer stories," he said.
The Directors Guild of America has reached a tentative agreement with Hollywood studios, while the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) begins bargaining on June 7 (US time).
SAG-AFTRA has authorised a strike, meaning actors could join writers on the picket line if favourable conditions aren't agreed to for its members.
Ashley Gable is a member of the board of directors of the Writers Guild of America West and is on the negotiating committee.
Gable joined the Guild in 1996 and has worked as a writer mainly in network television for the past 27 years and on shows including The Mentalist, starring Australian actor Simon Baker.
"We're basically fighting for the middle-class writer," Gable told ABC News from the picket lines.
"Los Angeles is a very expensive town. And people are struggling just to make a living to live the American dream and buy a house and raise children here.
"And TV has sort of been systematically devalued and kind of decimated by changes that have occurred."
Gable said the number of episodes per season for most shows had dropped dramatically and the length of episodes were often shorter these days too.
"It started with premium cable, places like HBO, they started to have shorter, shorter seasons.
"The Sopranos, as you may recall, was about 13 episodes per season.
"And so, since writers get paid typically by the episode, that has resulted in less income.
"And that was kind of accelerated when streaming shows began to occur, because now you might have, I think Chernobyl was six episodes [and] you have even shorter episodes, and with streaming, the companies have started hiring people just for a number of weeks, instead of through to the end of production [despite the fact] writing actually happens at all stages of production."
Ashley Gable and Jim Adler have taken up the fight for "middle-class writers". (Supplied)
Gable said often the work writers did was the most important work of the series, but when you separate writing from production, wages dropped dramatically.
"People coming up, I don't know how they're going to make a career out of this. Because as a staff writer, I know staff writers who've had to find jobs waiting tables, because they're not making enough money as a staff writer.
"And this is the next generation of showrunners.
"This is the next generation of people creating things like Succession and The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel and Barry.
"We generate billions and billions of dollars in profit for the studios.
"I think last year, they had $US28 billion dollars [$42 billion] in profit from entertainment products which we create.
"And so, I think writers should be paid what they're worth.
WGA says numerous programs had halted production or writing, or were set to begin writing soon for an upcoming season.
Source: WGA
Jim Adler has worked as a writer and co-executive producer for shows such as The Good Doctor and MacGyver.
He agrees that it makes little sense for streaming services to separate writing from production.
"In American television production, writing and producing is inextricably intertwined," Adler said.
"When it comes to making television shows those two things do not exist independent of each other."
The writers' strike could go on for some time if workers' demands are not met. (Supplied: David Koutsouridis)
Also speaking to ABC News from the picket lines, Adler said the way things had been going for the past few years could not continue.
"There needs to be a very dramatic change in the way that writers are compensated for the work that we do," he said.
Adler had only been in the Writers Guild for about two weeks when the 2007 writers' strike was called.
He said some important wins came out of that strike, which meant companies that didn't exist in their current forms back then (Hulu, Netflix, Amazon, Apple) had to employ writers from the guild.
And now those writers were fighting for their livelihoods.
"We have a lot of new members who have come into the guild in the last five years.
"And not everyone is independently wealthy. And to be able to pursue this career, they need to be able to pay their bills and learn the craft.
"And the only way that they're going to be able to do that is if the companies as a whole pay them a sustainable wage."

title: Anna Shay, breakout star of reality series Bling Empire, dead at 62
content:
Anna Shay, an heiress, philanthropist and breakout star of the Netflix reality series Bling Empire, has died at 62.
Shay died from a stroke, according to a family statement
Her time of death was not immediately clear
Shay amassed a fortune after she and her brother sold their father's company after his death
Shay died from a stroke, according to a family statement provided to The Associated Press on Monday.
It was not immediately clear when she died.
"It saddens our hearts to announce that Anna Shay, a loving mother, grandmother, charismatic star, and our own brightest ray of sunshine, has passed away," the family said in the statement.
"Anna taught us many life lessons on how not to take life too seriously and to enjoy the finer things. Her impact on our lives will be forever missed but never forgotten."
Shay amassed a fortune after she and her brother sold their father's company, Pacific Architects and Engineers, after his death.
In a 2021 interview for OprahMag.com, Shay said she had no idea what she was getting into when she joined the cast of Bling Empire, which chronicled the lives of ultra-wealthy Angelenos of Asian descent.
Originally, Shay thought her friend and executive producer on the series, Jeff Jenkins, wanted her to work behind the scenes.
The series premiered in 2021 and drew comparisons to the blockbuster film Crazy Rich Asians.
After three seasons, Netflix revealed in April that Bling Empire would be cancelled.
Shay, a fan favourite on the show, was a fixture in Los Angeles high society.
She was the only daughter of Edward Shay, the American billionaire founder of the defence and government services contractor, and Ai-San, his half-Japanese, half-Russian wife.
Shay said in the Oprah interview that her mother once told her, “You were born in a crystal ball with a silver spoon.’”
The reality star was born and raised in Japan.
Her only son, Kenny Kemp, earned himself a bit of the spotlight as well, briefly appearing on the series and amassing a huge collection of pricey bongs, according to BuzzFeed News.

title: HBO's The Idol finally dropped and it's being described as a 'toxic man's fantasy'
content:
A troubled young pop star manipulated and taken advantage of by a sinister impresario.
We've seen it before — and some say we've seen it done much better.
This is the premise of HBO's scandal-ridden series The Idol, which debuted after months of criticism around its sexually graphic content and production process.
Here's why The Idol is one of HBO's most controversial and lowest-rated series.
At the centre of the six-episode show is Lily-Rose Depp, daughter of Johnny Depp, who plays a pop star named Jocelyn. After her mum died of cancer, Jocelyn suffered a nervous breakdown which caused her last tour to be cancelled.
But now, Jocelyn's working on her career comeback with a new album on the horizon.
If you weren't already thinking it — yes, the Britney Spears parallel is evident.
"What Britney and Jocelyn have been through is unique … but universal,” decides Jocelyn's publicist Benjamin (Dan Levy).
Jocelyn is introduced as her army of spin doctors and social media handlers fuss over and about her, reacting to a public-relations crisis created when a very private photo of her leaks online.
24-year-old Lily-Rose Depp plays up-and-coming pop star Jocelyn. (Supplied: HBO)
Halfway into the first episode, Depp's character has a night out at a club, where she meets Abel Tesfaye’s Tedros.
He's a nightclub owner with a signature look that's regularly referenced throughout the episode: a rat-tail.
Although her assistant (Rachel Sennott) is convinced Tedros is shady, Jocelyn invites him over and lets him listen to her yet-to-be-released new single.
It creates an opening for his Svengali act.
He tells Jocelyn she needs to open up sexually in order to become a convincing singer, initiating the beginning of their questionable relationship.
Depp's character Jocelyn finds herself deeply under the influence of Tesfaye's Tedros. (Supplied: HBO)
The Idol has tapped a roster of rising actors and musicians for the series.
One of the most anticipated is Jennie Kim, member of the K-pop group Blackpink, who plays one of Jocelyn's backup dancers.
Australian singer Troye Sivan also joins as a series regular, playing Jocelyn's creative director.
Other casting announcements include veteran actor Jane Adams, Schitt's Creek's Dan Levy and more.
Alongside Depp, Jennie Kim, Troye Sivan and Rachel Sennott feature in The Idol. (Supplied: HBO)
There are two main criticisms about the show — the "disturbing" storyline and reported issues with production.
The main source of this comes from a bombshell exposé published by Rolling Stone in March.
It featured anonymous interviews with 13 sources close to the show's production.
Let's break down what the interviews revealed.
The Idol had been in development since June 2021 — two years ago — with Amy Seimetz as the show's original showrunner.
Seimetz was given "half-finished scripts" and a tight schedule, according to an unnamed source quoted by Rolling Stone.
The anonymous source claimed Seimetz was pushed out because Tesfaye was concerned the show was leaning too much into a "female perspective".
The entire series was then reshot with Sam Levinson — the creator behind the gritty high school drama Euphoria — as showrunner.
In the Rolling Stone reports, some crew members claimed the production then descended into "chaos".
The Idol was initially billed as a look into the seedy underbelly of Hollywood and the music industry.
“Instead of subtly skewering the misogynistic and predatory nature of the business, The Idol became a forbidden love story — the stuff of a toxic man’s fantasy," says The Hollywood Reporter’s Lovia Gyarkye.
Levinson allegedly took the show in a more sexually "disturbing" direction, including more explicit content and nudity.
Some sources were concerned about the clothes Depp wore to portray Jocelyn. (Supplied: HBO)
The network addressed the criticism in a statement to Variety.
“The creative team has been committed to creating a safe, collaborative, and mutually respectful working environment, and last year, the team made creative changes they felt were in the best interest of both the production and the cast and crew.”
Let's just say it went a few different ways.
Tesfaye publicly responded on social media with a clip of a scene from the show in which his character calls Rolling Stone "a little irrelevant".
He also captioned the clip, "Rolling Stone did we upset you?"
This article contains external content that failed to load. It may have been removed or is no longer available.
In his June cover story for Vanity Fair, Tesfaye elaborated on his tweet.
"I thought the article was ridiculous," he told Vanity Fair.
"I wanted to give a ridiculous response to it."
As for Depp, she said it was "a little sad and disheartening to see mean, false things said about somebody you care about" at a press conference after the show's Cannes Film Festival premiere.
In a statement provided to Vanity Fair in March, Depp said:
"Never have I felt more supported or respected in a creative space, my input and opinions more valued.
"Working with Sam is a true collaboration in every way — it matters to him, more than anything, not only what his actors think about the work, but how we feel performing it. He hires people whose work he esteems and has always created an environment in which I felt seen, heard, and appreciated."
Jane Adams said critics were "missing a wonderful opportunity to praise an incredible woman". (Supplied: HBO)
Jane Adams, who plays music executive Nikki in the show, argued that by focusing so much on Jocelyn's sexuality, critics have been "missing a wonderful opportunity to praise an incredible woman that I had an incredible time working with".
"Everything becomes about politics and it's boring," she told The Guardian earlier this month.
At the post-Cannes press conference, Levinson said, "We know we're making a show that's provocative".
When he first read the Rolling Stone article, he said he told his wife: "We're about to have the biggest show of the summer."
"In terms of the specifics of what was in the article, it just felt completely foreign to me," Levinson added.
Depp pictured with creators of The Idol, Sam Levinson and Abel Tesfaye. (Stephane Cardinale )
Whether a show is good or not is entirely subjective, but the overwhelming opinion appears to be quite negative.
Less than 24 hours after it was released, users panned the series on review aggregation site Rotten Tomatoes.
Currently, it's got a score of 27 per cent.
Compare that to other HBO shows such as The White Lotus with 90 per cent, or Euphoria with 80 per cent.
The Idol is being hailed as one of HBO's lowest-rated shows to date. (Supplied: HBO)
With the controversy surrounding its explicit content, The Idol has received some rather dismal ratings.
And the majority of critics weren't kind.
"The ultimate try-hard TV," Rebecca Nicholson from The Guardian described it in her review.
"It plays like a sordid male fantasy," said Peter Debruge from Variety.
Throughout the 80s to the mid-2000s, "you could forgive anything if it was at least interesting," says Dr Maura Edmond from Monash University.
Dr Edmond's research addresses changes in contemporary media and arts, with a focus on policy and gender.
"Over the last decade, there has been a huge paradigm shift and now, I think the primary question we ask ourselves about art and culture, is 'is it careful?'," she says.
"Is it careful with what it says and how it represents the people involved? Does it tread carefully with the lives and labour of those involved in making it  — the writers, caterers and make-up artists?"
After watching the first episode, Dr Edmond says The Idol is harking back to this era of "is it interesting?" by being intentionally sleazy and risque.
"Older characters in the show encourage sleaziness, while the younger characters appear worried more about "the price of safety," she says.
Jane Adams and Dan Levy in The Idol.  (Supplied: HBO)
Dr Edmond spent years talking to audiences about cancel culture and the ethics of media consumption.
Dr Edmond says very rarely is it solely a matter of representation, or a problematic male gaze.
"I don't imagine depictions of kink and sleaze on its own is enough to deter people from a show like The Idol," she says.
"What's more interesting to me is the conversation about the production itself, how the cast and crew felt they were treated.
"Based on my research, that's actually what might result in viewers turning off."

title: How director Peter Sohn reflected his immigrant experience in new Pixar film Elemental
content:
Pixar director Peter Sohn's latest film, Elemental reflects his own experiences navigating life as the child of immigrants.
"My grandmother's dying words were like, "Marry Korean!," Sohn told ABC News during a Zoom interview.
"My brothers married Korean, everyone in my family has married Korean except me. I didn't do that purposefully, but it was a big no-no in my family. There were years where I couldn't talk about it. There were years where I was trying to figure out how to merge these cultures and a lot of it was hard, but a lot of it was hilarious."
Those experiences fuel Pixar's latest film, Elemental, which is set in the fictional city called Element City, where residents belonging to the four elements of air, earth, fire and water live together. A fire resident, Ember and a water resident, Wade become unlikely friends after a chance encounter, and the film explores the dynamics of opposites attract as their relationship develops.
Peter Sohn is known for directing 2015's The Good Dinosaur, and he also voiced Emile in Ratatouille and the cat Sox in Lightyear.  (Supplied: Walt Disney Studios)
Sohn says he wanted to explore what the culture clash could be like outside of physical elements, but within community culture as well. One scene depicts characters going to a fire-element matchmaker who can smell true love, a scene that was inspired by Sohn's friend.
"We had a friend that was also going to a matchmaker — she was Indian, marrying a German — and the Indian mother forced them to go to this astrologist, 'to make sure that you guys are a match'," Sohn said.
"The story that she told was so fun and moving to us, that the mother character started to shift more into that."
Sohn is known for directing 2015's The Good Dinosaur, and he also voiced Emile in Ratatouille and the cat Sox in Lightyear. Elemental's voice cast includes Leah Lewis, Mamoudou Athie, and Ronnie del Carmen.
Elemental is another Pixar film that deals with an immigrant family. Turning Red, which was released on Disney's streaming platform DisneyPlus in 2022, also dealt with themes of girlhood through the lens of the Asian diaspora.
Sohn's parents are immigrants, having moved from Korea to New York City in the early 1970s, where he was born. To make the film and story more authentic, the filmmakers spoke to over one hundred first and second generation immigrants about what it was like to pack up and start over completely in another country.
"The experience of hearing people's stories — I think we both found it incredibly inspirational and emotional and just the realization of how many people in the studio have this experience was really striking to me," the film's producer Denise Ream said, adding she hopes viewers find connection to the stories shown in the film.
Elemental is set in the fictional city called Element City, where residents belonging to the four elements of air, earth, fire and water live together.  (Supplied: Walt Disney)
The filmmakers also discussed what kind of things each elemental district would sell that's unique to them. For fire, that includes items like matchbooks, fire sparklers and ceramics. They also wanted to portray what it's like to have traces of history left behind by different families moving to and from particular neighborhoods.
Sohn says working on the film was therapeutic for him, and that story discussions at Pixar sounded like therapy sessions.
"We're just talking about moments and then you start talking about your life. And then people are like, "Oh my god, I'm so sorry that happened to you", "like, no, no, it's okay." But then like, "oh, that happened to me too." And then all of a sudden, it becomes something real, and then you're starting to flow into the story."
Elemental is part of Sydney Film Festival and will play on June 12 at the State Theatre. It will be released in cinemas June 15.
